units.tr: MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND MOST NOBLE LORDS.

units.la: NUllum est in cultu Dei nocentius malum quàm superstitio. Cùm enim Deus Dominus noster Majestatem suam quam maximè apud Mortales in libertate imperii gliscere velit, hanc gloriam piaculari scelere ad se rapit Superstitio. Sedet in throno Dei, suo nutu temperat timorem Numinis, leges rogat sine suffragio, & earum repagulis non se duntaxat coërcet, sed vitio etiam contactus corrumpit, quos afflat. Accedit ad vaecordiam ignorantia, quæ impietate finitur. Nam ut plurimum cùm à recto veri itinere disceditur, superstitio nascitur, ac superstitionem velut paludem fugiendo, in præcipitium, impietatem itur. Quin sibi ipsa acerbissimum est supplicium. Nunquam enim qui anilibus persuasiunculis imbutus est animus, quietus esse potest. Quò impensiùs enitendum, ne tam pudenda labe Christiani nominis cultores contaminentur. Servari enim in cultu externo oportet, quæ legibus jussa, non quæ Deo grata esse putes. De vetero optimus animus pulcherrimus Dei cultus est. Hæc verissima & saluberrima persuasio cùm alibi locum habere debet, tum in præsenti nostro, quod volvimus, negotio, amplissimum sortitur; quando abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato religiosa superstitionis morbo haud leviter pallet. Equidem non attingere, non attrectare, non gustare nemo sapiens crimini deputet. Sed vana religione imbuere homines, legem cæco consilio contexere, cujus jussa reverenter capessant humiles animi, in eam rem voluntatis divinæ tabulas male concinnatas obvertere, denique judicare fratrem, qui meliora edoctus rectè facti conscientiam habet, insanus error est & intolerabile malum. Quamobrem committendum minimè duximus, ut suo sensu abundent zelotæ illi, quibus consilium est in mundo Ἰουδαΐζειν juxta carnalem sensum Mosaicæ legis, quæstui habere captas prava persuasione mentes, & dubitationum fluctibus concutere. Quò vel sic bonas horas in utili ac fructuoso labore consumere nobis liceret. Neque verò sinistra metuimus hominum de instituto nostro judicia. Quorum alii, bono equidem animo, pro hac re, quæ turbat & commovet, in aciem dimicationémque veniendum fuisse negant; alii viles has curas & infra dignitatem subsidere pronuntiant; alii denique in me vires & lacertos ad certamen isthoc cum veterano gladiatore feliciter cœnendum desiderant. Contra quos ita me æquitate bonorum consolor, ut interim quo occurram, ita satis mihi paratum esse putem. Nam quod sapienter olim nonnemo dictitavit, maledictum inferentis, non referentis esse, id causam etiam meam non mediocriter adjuvat. Non respondentis & recta vindicantis delictum est, sed imprudentia quærentis, objicientis, condemnantis. Deinde cùm per has lineas pauci hactenus serram reciprocârint, pro parte minùs tractata par erat majore studio laborari. Quòd si in Divinis luxuria ingeniis concedenda esset, brevi Sacra nostra mirum in modum conspurcata cerneres. Neque res levis adeò momenti est, ab errore liberari. Nihil profecto vile du-co, co, quod ad rem Theologicam pertinet. Plerumque enim minutula contagione nocent, deteriora se agglutinant, & sequitur, quod ajunt, vara vibiam. Compertum etiam est, ubi τὸ μικρὸν negleximus, majora in discrimen venisse. Adversarii non ignoro quo loco emineat doctrina & judicium. Sed est persæpe, ubi lassus dormitet Homerus. Causa cum causa, ratio cum ratione conspligat. Nec nomina, sed argumenta decernant. Rerum novandarum qui laborant noxio pruritu, perverso amoris vel odii studio subacti scribere solent, quæ vel mediocriter exercitati assequi judicio, & redigere in ordinem valeant. Sed nunc ad Vos, ILLUSTRISSIMI & GENEROSISSIMI DOMINI, properat oratio, ad quos non veniunt duntaxat hæ nostræ primitiæ, sed quibus se totas tradunt dicántque. In universum qui lucubrationes suas aliis consecrârunt, sæpius ut consequerentur beneficia, quàm quia consecuti essent, fecisse compério. Quorum ego rationes ad examen non voco, quando cuique conscientiæ suæ calculo vel damnari vel absolvi sufficit. Sed istud profiteri lubet, me beneficiis hactenus vestris cumulatum eum nexum inivisse, ut summæ imprudentiæ esset, non ad Vos omnia mea derivare, quia tot & tam magna consecutus sim. Non solùm enim me clementer ad publicam huc Spartham evocastis, sed etiam evocatum & muneri meo pro virili incubantem hactenus fovere, studia & conatus meos approbare, denique beneficentiæ vestræ imbre irrigare pergitis. Ut post innumera alia documenta vel hac etiam testificatione manifestum faciatis, Vos in complexu & deliciis habere Athenæum, quod Clarissimæ famæ Heros, & immortali prædicatione dignissimus ARNOLDUS, incredibili erga veritatem doctrinæ cœlestis & literarum studia ardore, nec hostium magnopere reveritus invidiam, nec impensarum gravissimo Mortalibus onere ab instituto in obliquum abreptus, hoc loco velut pharum splendere jussit. Vobis ILLUSTRISSIMI MOECENATES, cum cætera omnia summa habeatis, tum manet
units.tr: Nothing is more harmful in the worship of God than superstition. For while our Lord God wishes his majesty to shine forth among mortals as widely as possible, in the freedom of his realm, superstition seizes this glory for itself through a sinful crime. It sits on the throne of God, governs the fear of the Deity by its nod, and proposes laws without any vote. Nor does it merely confine people within its bars; it also infects and corrupts those it breathes upon. Ignorance joins in this madness, and it ends in impiety. For most often, when people depart from the right path of truth, superstition is born, and in fleeing superstition as if it were a swamp, they go headlong into impiety. Indeed, superstition is itself a most bitter punishment. For a mind steeped in old wives' trifles can never be at rest. All the more must we strive that the worshippers of the Christian name not be stained by so shameful a blemish. For in external worship one must observe what has been commanded by law, not what you suppose to be pleasing to God. The best disposition of mind is the finest worship of God. This most true and most wholesome conviction ought to hold its place everywhere, but in our present undertaking, which we are turning over, it has a very wide field, since abstinence from blood and from what is strangled is quite plainly tainted with the disease of religious superstition. Indeed, no wise person would count it a crime not to touch, not to handle, not to taste. But to imbue people with a vain religion, to weave a law from blind counsel whose commands humble minds obey with reverence, to turn badly put-together tablets of the divine will to this purpose, and finally to judge a brother who, being better taught, has a clear conscience of acting rightly, is a madness and an intolerable evil. For this reason we have thought it by no means right to allow those zealots, who intend in this world to Judaize [Ἰουδαΐζειν] according to the carnal sense of the Mosaic law, to abound in their own opinion, to make a profit by ensnaring minds with a perverse persuasion, and to shake them with the waves of doubt. Thus, at least, we may spend some good hours in useful and fruitful labour. Nor do we fear the unfavourable judgements of men about our undertaking. Some of them, meaning well, deny that one should have gone into battle over this matter, which disturbs and stirs people; others declare these cares trivial and beneath one's dignity; others finally wish for strength and muscle in me to fight this contest happily with a veteran gladiator. Against these I console myself with the fairness of good men, so that I think I have enough to meet them as they arise. For what a certain man once wisely said, that it is the mark of one who hurls an insult, not of one who returns it, helps my cause not a little. It is not a fault to answer and to defend what is right, but a lack of prudence to seek out, object and condemn. Moreover, since so far only a few have drawn the saw through these lines, the part that has been less treated ought to be worked on with greater zeal. For if in divine matters we were to yield to the wantonness of wits, you would soon see our sacred things shamefully defiled. Nor is it a slight matter, of such little weight, to be freed from error. I certainly consider nothing trivial that pertains to theological matters. For very often they do harm by a tiny contagion, worse things stick to them, and it follows, as they say, vara vibiam. It is also known that when we neglect the small thing [τὸ μικρὸν], greater ones have come into danger. I am not unaware of the places where learning and judgement stand out among my opponents. But it is very often the case that Homer nods when he is tired. Cause is joined to cause, reason to reason. Let not names but arguments decide. Those who labour under the harmful itch of novelty, driven by a perverse zeal of love or hatred, are wont to write things which even moderately practised judgement can grasp and bring into order. But now my speech hastens to you, most illustrious and most noble Lords, to whom these first fruits of mine come not only, but to whom they devote themselves entirely and declare themselves. In general I have found that those who have consecrated their labours to others have done so more often in order to obtain benefits than because they had already obtained them. I do not bring their reasons to examination, since it is enough for each person to be condemned or acquitted by the reckoning of his own conscience. But I wish to profess this: having been loaded with your benefits so far, I have entered into such a bond that it would be the height of imprudence not to refer all that I am to you, since I have obtained so many and such great things. For you have not only kindly called me to this public Sparta, but you also continue to cherish me, now called and devoting myself to my office as far as I can, to approve my studies and efforts, and finally to water me with the shower of your generosity. So that, after countless other proofs, you may make it plain by this testimony too that you hold in your embrace and favour the Athenaeum, which the Hero of most distinguished fame and most worthy of immortal praise, ARNOLDUS, with incredible ardour for the truth of heavenly doctrine and for learning, neither greatly fearing the envy of enemies nor being turned aside from his purpose by the heavy burden of expense that weighs on mortals, ordered to shine in this place like a lighthouse. To you, most illustrious Patrons, since you hold all other things in the highest regard, there remains

units.la: QUas Autor de Suffocato, & Sanguine chartas Scripsit, nunc iterum plenior aura videt. Primorum quòd sunt scripta haec monumenta laborum, Provida cura fuit, consiliùmque Dei. Enthea vis, sanguisque calens, ardórque sciendi Maturè juveni coepit adesse viro. Seu pia Sacratae (mihi crede) volumina Legis, Seu Sophiae studium volverit intrepidè, Nonnisi divinum semper quaesivit honorem, Summo semper erat gloria summa Deo. Ausonios Satanas ipsi hinc conflaverat hostes, Invidiae stimulis undique cinctus erat, Sanguinis aetherei qui suffocare calorem Tentárunt livida térque quatérque manu, At Pater Omnipotens tantò mage sanguinis aestum Aetherei tanto jussit adesse viro. Egregios hinc vitales jam misit in auras Libros, queis lectis doctior Orbis erit. Queis & mulcentur docti, miratur & Orbis, Queis famam serò posteritásque dabit. Divulget porro tales longo ordine libros, Librorum ut faciant nomina poene librum, Donec sera dies coelo ipsum reddat & astris, Unde illi aethereus Spiritus ipse datur!
units.tr: What the author has written on Things Strangled and Blood now comes before us again, in a fuller light. That these monuments of his labours were written first was the work of a provident care and the counsel of God. A divine power, a warm blood and a burning desire to know came early to the young man and grew into the man. Whether he turned the pious volumes of the sacred Law or devoted himself boldly to wisdom, he always sought nothing but the divine honour, for the highest glory was always to the highest God. Satan had therefore stirred up Ausonian enemies against him, and he was hemmed in on every side by the goads of envy. They tried, with livid hand, three and four times over, to smother the heat of his ethereal blood. But the Almighty Father ordered an ethereal ardour of blood all the more to be present in the man, the more it was attacked. From this he has now sent forth into the vital air distinguished books, by reading which the world will become more learned, books with which the learned are delighted and the world admires, and which will win him fame and posterity late in time. May he further publish such books in a long succession, so that the titles of his books almost make up a book, until the late day gives him back to heaven and the stars, whence the ethereal Spirit himself was given to him!

units.la: Est ita omnino in natura comparatum, ut iis in negotiis, quæ θεωρητὰ nuncupantur, & liberalem habent ac utilem cognitionem, non tantum periculi vel dubitanti immineat, vel definitivam suspendenti; quantum ei, qui ἐν τοῖς πρακτοῖς, iis, quæ actionibus subsunt, fluctuat, & opinionibus subinde pendet, neutram in partem firmiter constitutis. Ac prius sane in mortalitate nostra appetendum etiam ultro esset, omnibus insito vitio ex parte cognoscentibus, & ex parte prophetantibus; etiam iis, quorum ingenium utili exercitatione provectum, & jam corroboratum videri potest. Inde autem isthoc operæ pretium homines tollerent, ne in iis, quorum parum erat ignoratio obfuturà, intempestivè & præposterè decretis judicatisque, prudentibus ludibrium, ac supplicium Deo, qui veritas est, & Filium, qui veritas sit, progenuit, deberent.
units.tr: It is altogether so ordained by nature that in those matters which are called θεωρητά [theoretical], and which have a liberal and useful knowledge, there is not merely a danger for one who doubts or suspends judgement, but for one who wavers in practical matters [ἐν τοῖς πρακτοῖς], which concern actions, and who sometimes depends on opinions not firmly fixed in either direction. Indeed, in our mortal state, it would be desirable above all else, since every man is flawed in his knowing and in his prophesying, even those whose talent, advanced by useful practice, may seem already strong. Hence men would undertake this labour that they might not, in matters where ignorance would do little harm, be made a mockery to the wise and a sacrifice to God, who is truth, and who begat the Son, who is truth, by decisions and judgements made untimely and out of order.

units.la: II. Verùm diversa esse ratio eorum, quæ ad praxin aliquando deduci conveniat, intelligitur facilè. Nam si cujus est rei actio suscipienda, nec an suscipi debeat, ambigi diu, nec quomodo, nescire debet. Omnino enim contingeret, dum in dubitationum lubrico extrahitur tempus, salubrium ut opportunitatum momenta transmitterentur, elongarentur à nobis viæ Domini, & negligerentur partes à Deo rectâ ratione nobis imperati officii. Sed & dictat rectè instituta ratio, pro vero Philosophum asseruisse: eas actiones, quæ à virtute fluunt, non habere τὸ εὖ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς: sed tum fieri demum ἐξ τὰς ἀρετὰς, quando, qui agit, est πέωτον μὲν εἰδὼς, ἔπειτα προαιρούμενος, καὶ προαιρούμενος δι' αὐτὰ, καὶ τὸ τρίτον, ἐὰν βεβαίως, καὶ ἀμετακινήτως ἔχων πάθη. Primùm quidem sciens, deinde eligens, & eligens propter ipsa: tertiò, si firmiter & constanter affectus agat: Ethic. Nicomach. II. 3. Quæ igitur ex virtutis agi debent præscripto, immutabile, certúmque judicium requirunt, altam illam & firmam persuasionem, quam βέβαιον scitè Stoicorum secta appellavit, ne inter omissa appetitáque alternis voluntas fluctuet. Bona & mala, honesta & turpia, pia & impia, virtutes denique usúsque virtutum, æstimatorem omnia desiderant, quanti quidque in censum sit deferendum. Quod ipsum faciendum esse haud obscurè Apostolus docuit, cùm per habitum exercitatos sensus requisivit ad discretionem boni & mali, Hebr. V. 14. Et abundare nos idem voluit ἐν γνώσει, καὶ αἰσθήσει εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν τὰ διαφέροντα, ut ad diem usque Christi maneamus εἰλικρινεῖς καὶ ἀπρόσκοποι, Philip. I. 10. coll. cum Rom. II. 18.
units.tr: II. But it is easily understood that the situation is different for those matters which it is right at some point to bring into practice. For if there is an action to be undertaken, one must not long be in doubt whether it ought to be undertaken, nor be ignorant of how. For it would certainly happen, while time is dragged out in the slipperiness of doubts, that the moments of favourable opportunity would pass by, the ways of the Lord would be kept far from us, and the parts of the duty commanded us by God through right reason would be neglected. Moreover, sound reason rightly dictates, as the Philosopher truly maintained, that those actions which flow from virtue do not have τὸ εὖ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς [the good in themselves]; but they then become virtuous only when the agent first knows, then chooses, and chooses them for their own sake, and thirdly, if he acts from a firm and constant disposition [ἐξ τὰς ἀρετὰς]. First indeed knowing, then choosing, and choosing for their own sake; thirdly, if he acts from a firm and steadfast disposition. Nicomachean Ethics II. 3. Therefore those things which ought to be done according to the prescription of virtue require an unchangeable and certain judgement, that deep and firm persuasion which the sect of the Stoics aptly called βέβαιον [firm], so that the will does not waver back and forth between things omitted and things desired. Good and evil, honourable and shameful, pious and impious, and finally the virtues and the use of the virtues, all require an assessor who judges how much each thing should be counted for. The Apostle plainly taught that this must be done, when he required that our senses be exercised by habit for the discernment of good and evil, Heb. 5:14. And he wished us to abound in this same thing, ἐν γνώσει, καὶ αἰσθήσει εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν τὰ διαφέροντα [in knowledge and all discernment, to approve the things that are excellent], so that we may remain εἰλικρινεῖς καὶ ἀπρόσκοποι [sincere and without offence] until the day of Christ, Phil. 1:10, compared with Rom. 2:18.

units.la: III. Quando igitur etiam nos rectà æstimatione pensare decrevimus: An, quod Veteris Testamenti Ecclesiæ Postdiluvianæ sanctione Divina, & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, cùm suis adhuc in incunabulis esset, latum est de non comedendo sanguine & suffocato præceptum, idem hodiéque Ecclesiam obliget? confidimus procul nos fore sive temerè sive inutiliter incepti laboris suspicione. Est etenim ea de re disceptatio, quæ quotidianum subusum cadit. Inter dubitationum sæpe scopulos conscientiæ mortalium navigant. Judicium pœne præumbratur fastigio ac claritudine eorum, alia omnia qui sentiunt. Interdictum Divinum & Apostolicum videvideri possit haud nullo terrore munitum. Conciliorum authoritas magni est ad consensum momenti. Ipsa naturæ verecundia ferè temeritatem arguit humanæ licentiæ. Neque desunt Viri Magni, qui hæc ipsa vel adstringere authoritate sua, vel rationum pondere satagant.
units.tr: III. Therefore, since we too have resolved to weigh this matter by right judgement: whether the precept, which was given concerning not eating blood and what is strangled, by the divine sanction of the Old Testament Church after the Flood, and by the Apostolic Church of the New Testament while it was still in its cradle, binds the Church today as well. We trust that we shall be far from any suspicion of having undertaken a labour either rashly or uselessly. For this is a dispute that falls under daily use. Consciences of mortals sail amid the rocks of doubt. The judgement is almost overshadowed by the eminence and clarity of those who think otherwise. The divine and apostolic prohibition may seem to be fortified by no small terror. The authority of councils carries great weight for consensus. The very modesty of nature almost argues against the rashness of human licence. Nor are there lacking great men who strive either to bind these very matters by their authority or to press them by the weight of their arguments.

units.la: IV. Nos, ut lucem quæstioni fœneremur, prius quàm ad Stephani Curcellaei, Remonstrantium choragi, argumenta, quibus nuperrimè Christianorum libertatem, & conscientias imprudenter oneravit, judicium nostrum stringamus, & quæstionis terminos ab ambiguitate liberare, & ipsum quæstionis statum formare, & si quæ præliminariter edisseri debent, prælibare destinavimus. Ne, quod vulgò evenire animadvertimus, ex ejusmodi involucris obscuritas, & ex obscuritate error vel levissimus nos circumsidere valeat.
units.tr: IV. In order to shed light on the question, we have decided, before we examine our judgement of the arguments of Stephen Curcellaeus, the leader of the Remonstrants, by which he recently and imprudently burdened the freedom and consciences of Christians, to free the limits of the question from ambiguity, to define the very state of the question, and to set forth beforehand whatever must be explained in advance. This is so that obscurity from such wrappings, and from obscurity some error, however slight, may not be able to beset us, as we see commonly happens.

units.la: V. De sanguine ergo & suffocato instituta quæstio est. Sanguinis autem nomine non quemvis intelligi volumus. Certè non humanum. Sive enim quotidiano ex usu, sive in sacramentum fœderis libavere suum homin:es sanguinem, pro ea, ac meruerunt, crudelitatis & belluinæ feritatis arguere infamia. Notati Sexto Rufo cap. IX. Breviarii, Scordisci, Thraciæ populus, quem haud raro molestum sibi gravémque Romanus exercitus habuit. Hi soliti humanum sanguinem in capitum captivorum ossibus potare: quod crimini ipsis à Rufo versum. Sed & Solinus cap. XXV. commemoravit, eam Scytharum atque Medorum disciplinam usitatam, mutui sanguinis haustu uti fœdera sancirent. Quod & Luciano in Dialogo de amicitia traditum. De Brutis, Aquiliis & Vitelliis Plutarchus in Poplicola cap. VI. Omnibus visum esse hominis jugulati sanguine libato, & visceribus tactis, magnum & dirum jusjurandum concipere. Assiratum veteres hunc designavere infamem potum: Perspicuè etiam Festus affirmavit, priscos Latinos sanguinem Assir vocâsse. Et glossa habet: Assir, aquæ. Catoni de re Rustica eadem usurpata vox est cap. XXXIII. Daps, inquit, Jovi Assir à pecu in urna viri caste profanato sine contagione. Meritò, quibus adhuc humanitas placuit, semper feralem hunc judicavêre ritum, & humanitati probrosum. Ipsi Gentiles, siquando libido incesseret Christianos detestabiles omnibus reddere, ausi ipsis potum humani sanguinis objicere. Quamobrem horribilem calumniam amoliti sunt magna contentione. Dictum Minutio Felici in Octavio: Tantum nos humano ab sanguine cavemus, ut nec in cibis noverimus sanguinem. Cui placet, inspiciat, quæ eam in rem
units.tr: V. The question, then, has been raised concerning blood and what is strangled. By blood, however, we do not wish every kind to be understood. Certainly not human blood. For whether by daily custom or in a sacrament of covenant, men who have tasted their own human blood deserve to be charged with the infamy of cruelty and beastly savagery. Noted by Sextus Rufus, chapter 9 of his Breviarium: the Scordisci, a people of Thrace, whom the Roman army often found troublesome and burdensome. They were accustomed to drink human blood from the skulls of captured enemies, which Rufus charged against them as a crime. Solinus also, chapter 25, recorded that it was the customary discipline of the Scythians and Medes to ratify covenants by drinking each other's blood. This is also reported by Lucian in his Dialogue on Friendship. Plutarch, in Poplicola chapter 6, on the Brutii, Aquilii and Vitellii: It seemed to all that, having tasted the blood of a slaughtered man and touched his entrails, they were pledging a great and dreadful oath. The ancients designated this drink as infamous, calling it assiratum. Festus also plainly asserted that the early Latins called blood assir, and a gloss reads: Assir, water. The word is also used by Cato in his De re rustica, chapter 33: The feast, he says, for Jupiter is assir, from the herd, profaned in the urn of a chaste man, without contagion. Rightly, those who still favoured humanity have always judged this rite to be deadly and a disgrace to humanity. The Gentiles themselves, whenever the desire came upon them to make Christians detestable to all, dared to object to them the drinking of human blood. Therefore they repelled this horrible calumny with great effort. Minucius Felix says in the Octavius: We keep so far from human blood that we do not know blood even in our food. Whoever wishes may consult what Tertullian says on this in his Apology.

units.la: Tertullianus in apologetico habet. Crudelitatem & ferociam in hac consuetudine notavit etiam Florus. Sic enim in Catilinaria conjuratione additum pignus dicitur conjurationis, Sanguis humanus, quem circumlatum pateris bibere: Semmum, inquit, nefas, nisi amplius esset, propter quod biberunt, IV. 1. Et tanta sceleris magnitudo Sallustio visa, ut ficta potius haec existimaret ab iis, qui Ciceronis invidiam, quae postea orta est, leniri credebant atrocitate scelieris eorum, qui poenas dederant, in Bello Catilin. cap. XXII. Neutiquam igitur circa hoc contendemus: An humanum sanguinem bibere fas sit? Inde tamen obiter advertimus, abluisse a genuino interdicti V. T. sensu Tertullianum, Cyprianum & Theophylactum, qui de humano sanguine interpretari illud videntur. Parum solide. Quod enim quodammodo ipsa humanitas horruit, supra fidem est, exerto tali mandato prohibere Deum voluisse.
units.tr: Florus also noted cruelty and ferocity in this custom. For in the account of the Catilinarian conspiracy, a pledge of the conspiracy is described as human blood, which they passed around in cups and drank: Nothing would be a greater crime, unless there were something greater, for which they drank, IV. 1. And Sallust thought the magnitude of this crime so great that he considered these things rather fabricated by those who believed that the odium of Cicero, which arose afterwards, could be softened by the atrocity of the crime of those who had paid the penalty, in The Catilinarian War, chapter 22. We will therefore by no means contend about this: whether it is lawful to drink human blood. Nevertheless, we note in passing that Tertullian, Cyprian and Theophylact, who seem to interpret the Old Testament prohibition as concerning human blood, have wandered from its genuine sense. This is not sound. For what human nature itself in some measure shudders at is beyond belief: that God should have wished to forbid by such a command what is unheard of.

units.la: VI. Restat ut de Brutorum sanguine explicetur quaestio, eoque vel effuso, vel inter viscera animalium venasque contento: quo posteriori modo quaeri de suffocatis mox videbimus. Nec referre hic arbitramur, separatus sanguis, an esculentis permixtus, ad delicias gulae faciendas, intelligatur. Quamobrem frustra etiam olim latebras quaesivisse Christianos illos censemus, qui cum sanguinem esculentis permiscuissent, jam se a sanguine dictitabant abstinere. De quibus intelligenda censura videtur Synodi Constantinopolitanae Sextae, in Trullo habitae, cujus canon 67. referente Caranza, ita habet: Sacra Scriptura nobis praecipit, ut abstineamus a sanguine & suffocato & fornicatione. Merito igitur damnamus eos, qui cujuscunque animalis sanguinem arte aliqua condiunt, & sic comedunt. Qui hoc fecerit, clericus deponatur: laicus excommunicetur. Jam olim apud Gentes sanguis est in cibis usurpari solitus, & ad esum praeparatus, variis omnino modis. Hinc Lucanicae, farciminis genus, intestina vel carnes, cum primis suillae cum sanguine, polenta & adipe. Sic dictae, quod milites a Lucanis didicerint, si fides Varroni est lib. IV. de L. L. & Isidoro XX. 2. Meminit etiam Apicius de re Coquin. IV. 2. cerebellorum elixorum, & Lucanicarum. Graecis est ἀλλᾶς, contractum ex ἀλλαντς, monente Eustathio. Suidas tamen ἀλλὰς habet, & exponit ἐΘ ἐντέρων κατα-σκευαζόμενη, genus intestini praeparati. Ἀλλαντοπώλας etiam Graeci vocant, qui τὰ ἔντερα καὶ τὰς ἀλλαντας τῷ αἵματι καὶ πολέλης ἢ ἀλφίτων ἐμφύουσι, qui intestina & Lucanicas commiscent & macerant sanguine at polenta. Sed & μιμοῤῥαγῶν veteribus ventriculus fuit, vel intestina cum sanguine parata, κοιλίαι κολέντερα μετὰ αἵματος τοιλαοσμένα. Hinc & botulus, propter connexionem à bolis sic dictus, si Festo fides est: quia per bolos farciebantur, Scaligero annotante. Sed à Κολὸς alimonia, vel Κοτὸν pecus, quia ab his farcimina fiunt, qui deriv anc, citius assensum impetrant. A. Gellius tamen XVI. 7. eam vocem inter Laberianas ponit, licentius fictas, & de quibus quæri, an Latinæ sint, soleat. Jus etiam nigrum Laconum ex sanguine paratum. Unde αἵματις & αἱματία dicebatur, ut est apud Pollucem & Moschopulum.
units.tr: VI. It remains that the question be explained concerning the blood of brutes, whether it is poured out or contained among the viscera and veins of animals. We shall soon see that the question about what is strangled arises in the latter way. Nor do we think it matters here whether blood is understood as separated, or mixed into food to make the delights of gluttony. Therefore we judge that those Christians who, when they had mixed blood into their food, already claimed to abstain from blood, sought hiding places in vain. The censure of the Sixth Council of Constantinople, held in the Trullo, seems to be understood in this sense; its canon 67, as Caranza reports, reads: Holy Scripture teaches us to abstain from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. We therefore rightly condemn those who season the blood of any animal with some art and so eat it. Whoever does this, let a cleric be deposed; let a layman be excommunicated. Long ago, among the Gentiles, blood was customarily used in foods and prepared for eating in various ways. Hence Lucanicae, a kind of sausage made of guts or flesh, especially of pork, with blood, groats and fat. They are so called because soldiers learned them from the Lucanians, if Varro in book IV of On the Latin Language and Isidore, XX. 2, may be trusted. Apicius also mentions, in On Cookery, IV. 2, boiled brains and Lucanicae. In Greek it is ἀλᾶς [alas], contracted from ἀλλαντς [allants], as Eustathius notes. Suidas, however, has ἀλλὰς [allas], and explains it as ἐΘ ἐντέρων κατασκευαζόμενη [made from intestines], a kind of prepared gut. The Greeks also call them ἀλλαντοπώλας [allantopolas], those who mix and macerate the intestines and the sausages with blood and groats or barley meal. But for the ancients the μιμοῤῥαγῶν [mimorrhagon] was also a stomach, or intestines prepared with blood, κοιλίαι κολέντερα μετὰ αἵματος τοιλαοσμένα [bellies and intestines prepared with blood]. Hence botulus too, so called, if Festus may be trusted, from its connection with boli: because they were stuffed through the boli, as Scaliger notes. But some derive it from κολὸς [kolos], nourishment, or κοτὸν [koton], livestock, because sausages are made from these; such derivations win assent more quickly. Aulus Gellius, however, XVI. 7, places this word among the Laberian words, freely invented, about which it is customary to ask whether they are Latin at all. Also the black broth of the Spartans, prepared from blood. Whence it was called αἵματις [haimatis] and αἱματία [haimatia], as is found in Pollux and Moschopulus.

units.la: VII. Jam & suffocatum, quid sit, facile cognoscitur.
units.tr: VII. Now it is also easily recognised what strangled meat is.

units.la: Est enim omne animal privatum vita sine emissione sanguinis. Multa animalia ita occidi ad esum constat, tam volatilia, quam terrestria. A bestiis etiam multa capiuntur, canibus, accipitribus, falconibus, aliis, quæ θηριόλωτα Græci vocant. Gangrense Concilium, Gangræ in Paphlagonia habitum, & in Sexto Oecumenico Constantinopolitano approbatum, canone secundo vocat θηριόπνικτον. Justinus Martyr κρέας ἐν αἵματι, ὅπερ ἐστὶ νεκρὸν μαῖον. Et θηριόπνικτα apud Aristophanem Avibus Scholiastes interpretatur νεκρόμαια. Tertullianus in Apologet. cap. IV. de sanguine locutus subjicit: Propterea suffocato & morticino quoque abstinemus. Quæ duo ut paria, ponere Hebræum librum, dictum Chulin, adfirmat Grotius. Inde quod morticinium Latinis est, Hebræi vocant נְבֵלָה quod cadaver significat bestiæ non naturaliter mortuæ, sive vitam exhalantis, sine legitimo ritu mittendi sanguinis. Quæ ratio est cur LXX. Interpretes θηριόπνικτον vertant: & in Apostolica Synodo πνικτὸν, quod simpliciter suffocatum est. Apud Athenæum in Dipnosophistis occurrit: πνίγειν τε παχέων ἀρνίων συνθύνια: quod doctissimus Casaubonus II.24. interpretatus est, parare certo modo, veteribus usitato, cùm in proprio succo coquuntur carnes intra ollam aut patinam conclusæ, sic ut nullis exhalationibus pateat meatus. Unde πνικτὰ κρέα, carnes, quæ ita sunt coctæ. Quod paraturæ genus suffocationem simpliciter vocant.
units.tr: For every animal deprived of life without the letting of its blood is dead. It is well established that many animals are slaughtered for food in this way, both birds and land animals. Many are also caught by beasts, by dogs, hawks, falcons and others, which the Greeks call θηριόλωτα [theriolōta]. The Council of Gangra, held in Paphlagonia and approved in the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, calls such flesh in its second canon θηριόπνικτον [theriopnikton], strangled by beasts. Justin Martyr calls it κρέας ἐν αἵματι [kreas en haimati], flesh with the blood in it, which is νεκρὸν μαῖον [nekron maion], dead meat. The Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds explains θηριόπνικτα [theriopnikta] as νεκρόμαια [nekromaia]. Tertullian, speaking of blood in his Apology, chapter 4, adds: For this reason we also abstain from what is suffocated and from carrion. Grotius affirms that a Hebrew book called Chulin places these two side by side as a pair. What the Latins call carrion (morticinium), the Hebrews call נְבֵלָה [nevelah], which means the corpse of a beast that has not died naturally, or that has breathed out its life without the lawful rite of letting out its blood. This is the reason why the Septuagint translate θηριόπνικτον [theriopnikton], and in the Apostolic Synod πνικτὸν [pniktón], which simply means suffocated. In Athenaeus' Deipnosophists there occurs the phrase πνίγειν τε παχέων ἀρνίων συνθύνια [pnigein te pachéōn arnión synthynia], which the most learned Casaubonus, at II.24, translates as a certain way of preparing, used by the ancients, when meats are cooked in their own juice, shut up within a pot or pan, so that no passage is open for vapours. Hence πνικτὰ κρέα [pnikta kreia], meats that have been cooked in this way. This method of preparation they simply call suffocation.

units.la: VIII. Non pertinet autem ad nostræ quæstionis statum:
units.tr: VIII. But the following does not belong to the state of our question:

units.la: An eius sanguinis & suffocati sive repugnet, sive noceat natura, in physica notione accepta? Quomodo naturæ repugnare intelligitur, quod cum κρόσι corporis & temperamento parum convenit, & impedimundæ est valetudini. Non est enim planè hæc nostri subsellii judicatio, sed ad Medicorum scamna pertinet. Equidem naturæ instinctus quodlibet animal incitat ad prosequendum ea, quae credit profutura, & ad aversandum, quae sunt quocunque modo nocitura. Tenemur enim corporis, quod nobis sociavit Deus, ἐυεξίᾳ qualibet arte parare, appetitione simplicis & naturae conducibilis victus, moderatione nimii motus, & eorum, quae in corpore flagitium faciunt, sollerti aversatione. Nemo tamen facturum contra jus naturae concludet eum, qui in certo genere cibi, quem parum salubrem prudentes judicant, modum non custodiat. Hoc autem infinitis modis contingere sane potest.
units.tr: Whether the nature of blood or of strangled meat, taken in the physical sense, is either contrary to nature or harmful? It is understood how something may be contrary to nature if it does not agree with the constitution and temperament of the body and impairs health. Yet this is not really the judgement of our bench; it belongs to the benches of the physicians. Indeed, the instinct of nature urges every animal to pursue what it believes will be beneficial and to shun whatever will harm it in any way. For we are bound to keep the body, which God has joined to us, in good condition by every skill: by seeking simple food that is suited to nature, by moderating excessive exertion, and by carefully avoiding whatever causes harm to the body. No one, however, will conclude that someone who does not restrain himself in a certain kind of food, which prudent people judge to be not very wholesome, is acting against the law of nature. Certainly this can happen in countless ways.

units.la: IX. Largimur ergo hoc experientiae, cujus etiam scutum ἱεὴιας aliquando obtendunt, multorum naturam a sanguine abhorrere, affectuum quodam ac passionum impulsu, quin & naturali antipathia motorum. Compertum est, multos, quibus velocius sanguis, animi deliquium passos. Gravis est ac terrestris brutorum sanguis: causa multarum aegritudinum si comedatur, teste Pererio Lib. XIV. in Genes. IX. Taurorum sanguinem celerrime coire, atque durescere, proinde pestiferum esse nos docuit Plinius XI. 38. Daniel Sennertus Institut. Lib. II. p. 2. sect. 2. cap. 4. Magnam vim inesse docet, ad corporis & morum mutationem: praecipue arteriosi. Is enim, inquit, sanguis talens & spiritibus plenus, potest mirae mutationes inducere, aut vel generatim saltem bestiarum feritatem exprimere, vel speciatim alicujus bestiae mores imitetur. Cum enim sanguis naturam sui animalis habeat, & omnes animalis actiones potissimum spirituum & caloris nativi beneficio perficiantur, illo abhomine assumto, credibile est in spiritibus ejus & calore, ac consequenter in humoribus & solidis partibus fieri mutationem. Apud S. Aurelium Victorem de viris Illustribus cap. LXVI. M. Livius Drusius hausto caprino sanguine semianimis deportatus domum dicitur. Addo, quod Caelius Rhodiginus ex Plutarcho & Strabone meminit, Midam, antiquissimum Phrygiae Regem, tauri sanguine copiosius hausto, ex humanis concessisse Lib. XIV. cap. XII. Quamobrem haec per nos Physica ratio esto, per quam a sanguine abstineant se, quibus est studium, in valetudinem suam mitius consulere.
units.tr: IX. We therefore grant to experience, whose shield the ... sometimes also hold up, that the nature of many people shrinks from blood, through a kind of impulse of the emotions and passions, and even through a natural antipathy. It is well known that many who have eaten blood quickly have fainted. The blood of brute beasts is heavy and earthy, and if it is eaten it is a cause of many illnesses, as Pererius teaches in his Commentary on Genesis Book XIV, on Genesis 9. Pliny (XI.38) has taught us that the blood of bulls clots and hardens very quickly, and is therefore poisonous. Daniel Sennert, in his Institutes, Book II, part 2, section 2, chapter 4, says: It has great power to change the body and the character, especially arterial blood. For such blood, being thick and full of spirits, can produce remarkable changes, either expressing the savagery of beasts in general, or imitating the habits of some particular beast. For since blood has the nature of its own animal, and all the actions of the animal are carried out chiefly by the aid of the spirits and the native heat, when that blood is taken in, it is credible that a change takes place in its spirits and heat, and consequently in the humours and solid parts. In Aurelius Victor's On Illustrious Men, chapter 66, it is said that Marcus Livius Drusus, after drinking goat's blood, was carried home half dead. I add what Caelius Rhodiginus recalls from Plutarch and Strabo, that Midas, the most ancient king of Phrygia, after drinking bull's blood too greedily, passed from human form (Book XIV, chapter 12). Therefore let this be the physical reason through which those who wish to do so may abstain from blood and take more gentle care of their health.

units.la: X. De religiosa igitur a sanguine & suffocato abstinentia quaestio tota est. Porro religionis praecepta duas videntur differentias recipere. Quaedam enim ita sunt religioni essentialia, nullam ut mutationem patiantur unquam: quae sunt, quae moralem sanctitatem perficiunt, & in Mosaica lege sive formalibus sive virtualibus bus terminis imperantur. Quaedam hactenus religioni sunt accessoria, quatenus constant externis quibusdam officiis, & actibus sua natura neque bonitatem neque malitiam involventibus, adeoque utramque in partem liberis, quum ab initio parum referat, ita an aliter se habeant, referat autem plurimum, ubi voluntate Dei revelata, imperio legis ita ac non aliter habere debent. Talis lex est symbolica illa, qua, resalva & integra adhuc, primi hominis cupiditas circa esum fructus amoeni terrore legis coercita fuit: Lex de sacrificiis, cultu ceremoniali populi Israelitici, & si quid aliud. Quae sunt posterioris generis, ea obligationem directam inducunt in eos duntaxat homines, quibus speciali revelatione tale quid praecipitur custodiendum. Ejusmodi autem praecepta plurima in veteri Testamento lata, quibus Deo cordi fuit, & factae promissionis & implendae certitudinem manifestare; efficere, ut populus sentiret, nullum alium sub Coelo populum suae societatis orbe ambiendum, cum non sacris magis quam moribus cum quoquam esset society cohaerere; denique compellere, ut gens pervicax, & rationis paene impatiens onerioso hoc cultu occupatus, desineret novos cultus detestabili temeritate fingere. Quae autem huiusmodi sunt, orbem suum implevisse, Christo nobis repraesentato, id vero omnes confitentur Christiani. Usque adeo id verum, ut dicantur θεὸν ... Act. XV. vers. 10. Et perspicuè Paulus contra Pseudapostolos, qui perniciosa sua de legis Ceremonialis, moralis ac fidei temperamento doctrina, Galatas εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον transferre laborabant, disputat. Si ex lege sit justitia, frustra igitur Christum mortuum esse. Gal. I. 6. & II.21. Et nihil profuturum Christum, si circumcidantur Galata, docet idem vers. 2. 3. 4. Hoc pridem divino afflatus Spiritu Esaias inter laudes venturi Messiae collocavit, his verbis: Jugum oneris, virgam humerorum, ac exactoris baculum confregisti, Cap. IX. 3. Quamobrem jubemur stare in ἐλευθερίᾳ, in quam nos Christus asseruit, ne postliminio servitutis jugo implicemur, Gal. V. 1.
units.tr: X. The whole question, then, concerns the religious abstinence from blood and from strangled meat. Now the precepts of religion seem to admit of two kinds of distinction. Some are so essential to religion that they never undergo any change: these are the precepts that perfect moral holiness, and which are commanded in the Mosaic law either in formal or in virtual terms. Others are, so far, accessory to religion, insofar as they consist of certain external duties and acts which by their nature involve neither goodness nor wickedness, and are therefore free in either direction. Initially it matters little whether they are done this way or that; but once the will of God has been revealed, and by the command of the law they must be done in this way and not otherwise, then it matters greatly. Such is that symbolic law by which, while still whole and intact, the desire of the first man concerning the eating of the fruit of the pleasant tree was restrained by the threat of the law. Such too are the law concerning sacrifices and the ceremonial worship of the Israelite people, and whatever else is of this kind. Precepts of the latter kind create a direct obligation only for those people to whom such a thing is commanded to be observed by special revelation. Now, of such precepts there are very many in the Old Testament, by which God was pleased to make manifest the certainty of the promise made and to be fulfilled; to bring it about that the people should feel that no other people under heaven was to be embraced within the circle of their fellowship, since they could not cohere with anyone in sacred things any more than in customs; and finally to compel a stubborn nation, almost impatient of reason, occupied with this burdensome worship, to cease inventing new forms of worship with detestable rashness. That precepts of this kind have fulfilled their circle, with Christ set before us, all Christians indeed confess. So true is this that they are called a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear (Acts 15:10). And Paul, plainly disputing against the false apostles, who were labouring to turn the Galatians to another gospel [εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον], by their pernicious doctrine that a mixture of the ceremonial law, the moral law and faith was necessary: If justification is by the law, then Christ died in vain. (Gal. 1:6 and 2:21.) The same writer teaches in verses 2 to 4 that Christ will profit them nothing if the Galatians are circumcised. Isaiah, long before, moved by the divine Spirit, placed this among the praises of the coming Messiah, in these words: You have broken the yoke of his burden, the staff on his shoulders, and the rod of his taskmaster (Isa. 9:3). Therefore we are commanded to stand in liberty [ἐλευθερίᾳ], into which Christ has set us free, so that we are not again entangled by the yoke of servitude by a return of rights (Gal. 5:1).

units.la: XI. Cum igitur prioris generis praecepta necessariam habeant semper & ubique observantiam, quippe à jure naturali, divinam sanctitatem repraesentantes, dictata, & à Mose in Decalogo συλλεγόμενα comprehensa; posteriora autem, ac in specie ceremonialia adventu Christi antiquata, atque adeo nullam post καιρὸν διορθώσεως in nos sive directam sive indirectam obligationem inducentia, quaeri jam coeptum, quo in ordine collocari mereatur illud de esu sanguinis & suffocati interdictum? Ad legemne moralem, quae semper & ubique obligat, an ad ceremonialem pertineat, quae aliquando obligare desiit? Genuinus igitur hic controversiae status est: An interdictum de non edendo sanguine & suffocato sit a jure naturali, a primordio mundi natura humana insculpto, vel alio quocunque modo constituto, ita ut hodieque vim obligandi habeat omnes: an vero a positivo ceremoniali, quod quia aliquando abrogatum, homines obligare ad sui observantiam religiosam cessavit? Prius defendendum suscepit Stephanus Curcellaeus, vir caeterum doctissimus, ac ingentem ubique suae eruditionis ac facundiae plausum habiturus, si orthodoxiae candidius litare, quam novis opinionibus, a fidei Christi & Apostolicae tramite haud leviter resultantibus, cupidius subactum ingenium intendere maluisset. Posterius fatente ipso Curcellaeo, in praefatione Diatribae, maxima Europaeorum hodiernorum pars tam sententia quam observatione tuetur. Quorum ego sensum, pro gratiae Divinae modulo, vindicare a laqueis conscientiis infirmiorum inter Christianos tensis ita constitui, ut Evangelii libertatem nobis sanguine Christi partam in medio sim positurus, insatiabiliter omnibus & appetendam & consectandam.
units.tr: XI. Since, then, the precepts of the first kind have always and everywhere a necessary observance, being derived from the natural law, representing divine holiness, and set down by Moses in the Decalogue as summarised [συλλεγόμενα]; but the later precepts, and especially the ceremonial ones, have been abolished by the coming of Christ, and therefore, since the time of reformation [καιρὸν διορθώσεως] has come, induce no obligation upon us, whether direct or indirect; the question has now begun to be asked in what order the prohibition of eating blood and strangled meat deserves to be placed. Does it belong to the moral law, which binds always and everywhere, or to the ceremonial law, which has ceased at some point to bind? The genuine state of the controversy is therefore this: Is the prohibition against eating blood and strangled meat from the natural law, implanted in human nature from the beginning of the world, or established in some other way, so that it still has binding force on all today; or is it rather from the positive ceremonial law, which, since it has been abrogated, has ceased to bind men to religious observance of it? Stephen Curcellaeus, a man otherwise most learned, who would have won immense applause everywhere for his learning and eloquence, undertook to defend the former view, if he had preferred to exercise his ingenuity, which is too eager for novelties, rather than to offer more fairly to orthodoxy, novelties which do not spring lightly from the path of the faith of Christ and the Apostles. As Curcellaeus himself admits in the preface to his Diatribe, the greatest part of the Europeans of today defends it as much by opinion as by practice. I have resolved, according to the measure of divine grace, to vindicate their view from the snares stretched among Christians against the consciences of the weaker, so that I may place before us, in the midst, the liberty of the Gospel won for us by the blood of Christ, to be both desired and pursued by all without satiety.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Non equidem me fugit, ante Curcellaeum multis aliis Curcellaei sententiam placuisse. Judaeos tamen & Muhammedanos Christianis discordes parum hic curo, quia aliis illi, aliis Christiani sive hypothesibus utuntur, sive telis pugnant. De illorum duntaxat sententia nonnihil editsseremus. Judaeos quidem, quod attinet, eos & experiundo constat a sanguine abstinere, & testatus idem Celeberrimus Buxtorfius in Synagoga Judaica, pag. 403. Animadvertimus autem, alios a sanguine abstinere ideo, quia censeant interdictum illud pertinere ad legem ceremonialem, quam constat satis illos abrogatam esse negare. Alios, quia arbitrentur interdictum hoc comprehensum esse inter מצות בני נח praecepta Noachidarum, seu jus filiorum & posterorum Noachi, quo nomine genus humanum a Noacho secundo, quemadmodum ferme ab Adamo primo propagarum innuunt. Inter ea praecepta postremum est אבר מן החי do membro animalis viventis: sub quo praecepto concludi interdictum de sanguine quidem contendunt. Ita enim legitur in Gemara Babylonica ad Tit. Sanhedrim, cap. VII. אבר מן החי ר' תנינא בן גמליאל אומר אם אליde membro animalis viventis: Etiam ex sententia Rabbi Chanina, Ben Gamaliel, de sanguine. Idem ferè totidem verbis dicitur in Berefchit Rabbah, parascha 34. Et Maimonides in Halach Melakim cap. IX. ראה שעל אלו נאטורה הוסיק לנח אבר מן חי שנא אך בשר בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו: Liquet, propter hac Noacho mandatum traditum esse de membro animalis viventis, juxta illud: Carnem in anima sua, sanguine suo non comedetis. Ita planè etiam Moses Mikotzi Præcept. Affirmat. 132. & Negat. 137. Hi igitur, quia Noachicum præceptum de sanguine accipiunt, statuere debent, non tam interdictum esum sanguinis ceremonialis, quàm naturali lege. Satis enim constat, Judæos Noachidarum præcepta pro jure naturali, æqualiter omnibus cognito, habere. Hinc Abem-Ybbon in Ruach Hachen cap. VI. vocat המצוות שנתפרסמו בכל אומות præcepta, quæ manifestata omnibus gentibus. Sunt tamen, qui אבר מן החי explicent de interdicto non sanguinis, sed membri ab animali vivo decerpti. Atque membrorum hujuscemodi esum Noachidis interdictum בכל שהוא quantulumcunque fuerit. Interdicti sic intellecti rationem affert ex Orientalibus Maimonides, שכן היו עושים מלכי הגוים ונם לעבודת זרה היו שנים כן רוצה לומר שהיו חותנין מן הבהמה אבר ידוע ואוכלים quoniam ita ex seculo facere solebant Reges Gentiles, etiam idololatriæ causa ita facere solebant. Scilicet animali abscindebant membrum aliquod, atque illud comedebant. Respicere videtur Maimonides ad immania illa Bacchanalia, quibus nomen Omophagiis est, in quibus furore commoto, ut scribit adversus gentes Arnobius lib. V. & sequestrata pectoris saniate circumplicans se anguibus, atque, ut se plenos Dei Numine ac Majestate desaneant caprorum ceterarumque viscera cruentatis oribus dissipant. Quam in rem non nulla etiam habent Firmicus Maternus, de errore profanarum Religionum: Augustinus de C. D. VII. 22. Sextus Empiricus in Hypothesibus Pyrrhonii III. 25.
units.tr: I am not unaware that before Curcellaeus many others approved of Curcellaeus's opinion. Here, however, I care little about the Jews and Muhammadans, who disagree with Christians, since they use different hypotheses or fight with different weapons. I will set out only something of their view on this point. As for the Jews, it is established by experience that they abstain from blood, as the most famous Buxtorf also attests in his Synagoga Judaica, p. 403. We observe, however, that some abstain from blood because they think the prohibition belongs to the ceremonial law, which they deny has been fully abrogated. Others do so because they think this prohibition is included among the mitzvot bnei Noach [מצות בני נח], the precepts of the sons of Noah, that is, the law of the sons and descendants of Noah, by which name they mean the human race propagated from Noah the second, just as almost from Adam the first. The last of these precepts is evar min ha-chai [אבר מן החי], "a limb from a living animal," and under this precept they contend that the prohibition on blood is included. Thus it is read in the Babylonian Gemara on tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 7: "Evar min ha-chai. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel says: if..." (de membro animalis viventis: also according to the opinion of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamaliel, concerning blood). Almost the same words are found in Bereshit Rabbah, parashah 34. And Maimonides in Hilkhot Melakhim, chapter 9, says: "Know that because of this, the commandment about a limb from a living animal was given to Noah, as it is said: 'Only flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat'" [אך בשר בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו]. It is clear that the command about a limb of a living animal was given to Noah on account of this, according to that text: "You shall not eat flesh in its life, with its blood." Moses Mikotzi likewise states this plainly in his positive precept 132 and negative precept 137. Those who take the Noachide precept about blood in this way must therefore hold that the prohibition of eating blood is not so much ceremonial as belonging to the natural law. For it is well established that the Jews regard the precepts of the Noachides as natural law, known equally to all. Hence Abem-Ybbon in Ruach Chen, chapter 6, calls them hamitzvot shenitpar'su bekhol umot, "the precepts made known to all nations." There are, however, some who explain evar min ha-chai as a prohibition not of blood but of a limb torn from a living animal. And the Noachides are forbidden to eat such limbs bekhol sheho [בכל שהוא], however small the amount may be. Maimonides gives a reason for this prohibition, understood in this way, drawn from the Orientals: "For the kings of the nations used to do this from of old, and also did so for the sake of idolatry; that is, they used to cut a certain limb from a live beast and eat it." For thus the kings of the Gentiles were accustomed to act from ancient times, and they did so also for the sake of idolatry: namely, they cut off some limb from the animal and ate it. Maimonides seems to refer to those monstrous Bacchanalia called Omophagia, in which, as Arnobius writes against the Gentiles in book 5, with frenzy aroused, and with the gore of the breast poured out, they wrap themselves in snakes, and, so that they may be filled with the power and majesty of God, they tear apart the entrails of goats and other beasts with bloody mouths. Firmicus Maternus, in On the Error of Profane Religions, Augustine in De Civitate Dei VII.22, and Sextus Empiricus in Pyrrhoniae Hypotyposes III.25 also have several things on this matter.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Judæos æmulatus Muhammedes, ineruditissimus Judaicorum rituum, interdixit suos sanguinis esu Surata II. versu mihi 164. ישראל אלהים אמנו בלא מן טהארת מא רוקנאכם O vos, qui creditis, inquit, comedite de bonis, quæ in alimentum vobis bis Deus concessit, Debeque gratias agere, si ipsum tolerit. Ab interdicis vos morti-no, sanguine & carne porci, quódque consecratum est alii quàm Deo. Qui ta-men necessitate adactus fuerit, haud expetens, neque transgredi cupiens, haudquidem crimen illi fuerit. Quippe Deus clemens est & misericors. Confer Su-ratas quintam & sextam, ubi sic concepit impostor interdictum: אלמנבקרה ואלמוקורה ואלמתרדية ומאלכל אלסבע: Suffocati, verberibus occisi, item occisi casu, seu torne, & ejus, cujus
units.tr: Imitating the Jews, Muhammad, the most unlearned man in Jewish rites, forbade his followers to eat blood in Sura 2, verse 164. "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum" [ישראל אלהים אמנו בלא מן טהארת מא רוקנאכם], that is, "O you who believe," he says, "eat of the good things which God has granted you for nourishment, and you ought to give thanks to him if you serve him. He has forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and whatever is consecrated to anyone other than God. Yet whoever is compelled by necessity, not desiring it nor wishing to transgress, will not be guilty of sin; for God is merciful and compassionate." Compare Suras 5 and 6, where the impostor framed the prohibition thus: "wa al-munkhaniqa wa al-mawquda wa al-mutaraddiya wa ma akala al-sabu'" [ואלמנבקרה ואלמוקורה ואלמתרדית ומאלכל אלסבע], that is, the strangled, the beaten to death, the killed by a fall or goring, and that of which

units.la: partem aliquam devoraverunt fera. Eundem in sensum habetur apud Kessæum: ואמרהם אן יתנבוא אלמיתה ואלדם ואלחם ואלכנזיר ומא אהל לגיר אללה ולא יקתלוא אלנפש אלתי תרם
units.tr: the wild beast has devoured some part. To the same effect it is found in Kessaeus: "wa amarahum an yatanabbi'a al-maytata wa al-dama wa al-lahma wa al-khinzira wa ma uhilla li-ghayri Allah wa la yaqtulu al-nafsa allati harrama Allah" [ואמרהם אן יתנבוא אלמיתה ואלדם ואלחם ואלכנזיר ומא אהל לגיר אללה ולא יקתלוא אלנפש אלתי תרם

units.la: אללה ולא באלתך: Es edixit illis, ne morticino, sanguine, carne porcina vescantur, & si quid aliud Deo consecratum. Quem locum Kessæanum debeo indici Celeberrimo Doctori Hottingero, Præceptori meo venerando. Elmacinus in Histor. Sarac. lib. I. cap. I. docet credere jussisse Muhammedem Islamismum amplexuros: אן יוקל אלדם non esse commedendum sanguinem & morticina. Testatur idem Jacobus Bleda de Muhammedanis, qui olim in Hispania: Morischi, inquit, hujus Regni, nimirum Valentia & reliqui Hispania non comedunt sanguinem, carnes suffocatas, morticinas, nec morsas ab aliquo animali, putantes id peccatum esse ob reverentiam sue secte pessime, que id vetat in Alcorano, & vocant eas carnes ואלחם maledictas & prohibitas. Defens. Fidei in causa Morischorum cap. VIII. Mirum tamen videri posset, Avicennam, Muhammedi-ecstatae juratum mancipium, passim inspergere de sanguinis esu & potu, ad morbos aliquos curandos. Sanguinem ad medicamenta usurpandum docet sumi debere ab animali sano, in quo non appareat humoris color, qui minimè corruptus sit aut putridus: Lepo-rinum sanguinem humores cito maturare, ut & hircinum: usurpari autem, postquam concrevit. Sanguinem columbae, palumbi majoris & turturis calentem vulneribus capitis & meningum instillaris commixtum oleo rosaceo tepido inflammationes arcere et tali oriri solitas. Alia huc pertinentia multa tradidit Canon Medic. lib. II. tract. II. pag. 108. 109. editionis nuperae, quam versione accuratâ Plantini commodiorem pro Republica Medicorum reddidit. Ex quibus prona est suspicio, saltem in Medicina Muhammedanos sanguinis usum tolerare.
units.tr: אללה ולא באלתך], "and he commanded them not to eat carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, or whatever is consecrated to anyone other than God, and not to kill the soul which God has forbidden, except in justice." I owe this passage of Kessaeus to the most learned Doctor Hottinger, my venerable teacher. Elmacinus in Historia Saracenica, book 1, chapter 1, teaches that Muhammad ordered those embracing Islam to believe that blood and carrion must not be eaten. The same James Bleda testifies about the Muhammadans who once lived in Spain: "The Moriscos of this kingdom, namely Valencia and the rest of Spain, do not eat blood, strangled or carrion meat, or meat torn by any animal, thinking it a sin out of reverence for their very wicked sect, which forbids it in the Alcoran; and they call such meats al-kham [ואלחם], accursed and forbidden." Defensio Fidei, in the case of the Moriscos, chapter 8. It might seem strange, however, that Avicenna, a servant sworn to Muhammad's ecstasy, everywhere recommends the eating and drinking of blood for curing certain diseases. He teaches that blood for medicines ought to be taken from a healthy animal, in which the colour of the humour does not appear, and which is not at all corrupt or putrid. Hare's blood ripens humours quickly, and so does goat's blood; but it is used only after it has clotted. The blood of a dove, of the larger wood-pigeon, and of a turtle-dove, warm and instilled into head wounds and membranes, mixed with warm rose oil, keeps off inflammations and those that usually arise from them. Canon of Medicine, book 2, tractate 2, pp. 108–109 of the recent edition, which he rendered more conveniently for the Republic of Physicians than the exact translation of Plantin, offers many other things pertaining to this. From these facts there is a ready suspicion that the Muhammadans at least, in medicine, tolerate the use of blood.

units.la: XIV. Ex Philone Pythagoreo de Essenis, quorum instituta Mona-
units.tr: XIV. From Philo the Pythagorean, concerning the Essenes, whose institutions Mona-

units.la: Monachatui Ægyptiaco comparavit Sozomenus, repetiit idem, illos qui ὅσα πεπώκασι καὶ ἐσθίουσι μὴ ἀπέχεσθαι οἴνου ... abstinere & vino, & carnibus sanguinem habentibus, lib. I. Histor. Eccles. cap. XII. Dixerat autem Philo: Essenis ἡ ... ἀναίμων. Sed & Græcanicæ Ecclesiæ caput suæ ab Occidentalibus dissensionis constituere voluerunt illud de non edendo sanguine & suffocato. Nota res ex Synodo Quini sexta, sub Justiniano Juniore Rinotmeto habita in Trullo An. DC. XCII. contra Callinico Patriarcha. Ibi nomine sextæ Synodi ante decennium celebratæ, Canones quamplurimi editi sunt de disciplina Ecclesiastica. Canon LXVII. ita habet: Divina nobis Scriptura mandavit, à sanguine, suffocato & fornicatione abstinere. Eos ergo, qui propter lautum & delicatum ventrem cujuscunque animalis sanguinem ante aliqua esculentum condimus ac instruunt, super est; increpamus ac punimus. Si quis ergo deinceps animalis sanguinem quovis modo comedere aggrediatur: si sit quidem clericus, deponatur; si laicus, segregetur. Et cum inter Canones Apostolicos Canon LXIII. vetaret comedere carnem in sanguine animæ ipsorum, ἡ ... ἀποπνικτόν, ἡ ... θηριοπλήκτον, ad notavit Balsamon, more suo in Latinos invehens, inquit Baronius, non minus tamen pro suo erga Balsamonem amore quam licentiori stylo nunquam non confodit, Casaubono in Exercitationibus suis animad vertente: Nota ergo Canonem propter Latinos, qui suffocata indiscriminatim comedunt. Extat apud Baronium Epistola Michaelis Cerularii, Episcopi Constantinopolitani, & Leonis Acridani, Archiepiscopi Bulgarorum, scripta ad Johannem Tranensem in Apulia Episcopum, adversus Romanam Catholicam sedem, inquit Baronius, imo contra omnem Occidentalem Ecclesiam, tom. XI. ad annum Christi M. D. LIII. In ea cum Episcopi attrociter perstrinxissent usum azymorum in Ecclesia Occidentali, Sabbathi custodiam, propter quam nec Judæi nec Christiani sint, sed similes Leopardo, cujus capilli nec nigri sunt, nec omnino albi; subjiciunt: Quomodo autem & suffocata hi tales comedunt, in quibus sanguis tenetur? An nescitis, quod omnis animalis sanguis sit anima ipsius: & qui comedit sanguinem, animam comedit? Et idcirco secundum hoc nec gentiles ex toto sunt. Illi autem occidunt, aut plagant, comedunt.
units.tr: Sozomen compared them with Egyptian monasticism, and he repeated that they abstain from wine and from flesh having blood, Ecclesiastical History, book I, chapter XII: those who [ὅσα πεπώκασι καὶ ἐσθίουσι μὴ ἀπέχεσθαι οἴνου ...] abstain from wine, and from flesh having blood. Philo had said that the Essenes were [ἀναίμων] bloodless. But the Greek Church also wished to make this point a ground of dissension from the Westerners: the prohibition of eating blood and what has been strangled. The matter is well known from the Quinisext Synod, held at Trullo in the year 692 under Justinian II, called Rhinotmetus, against the Patriarch Callinicus. There, in the name of the Sixth Synod, celebrated a decade earlier, very many canons on church discipline were issued. Canon LXVII reads: Divine Scripture has commanded us to abstain from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. We therefore rebuke and punish those who, for the sake of a dainty and delicate belly, season and prepare the blood of any animal as food. If anyone henceforth undertakes to eat the blood of an animal in any way, let him be deposed if he is a cleric, and excommunicated if he is a layman. And since Canon LXIII among the Apostolic Canons forbids eating flesh with its life-blood, [ἀποπνικτόν] strangled, [θηριοπλήκτον] killed by beasts, Balsamon noted it, attacking the Latins in his usual way, says Baronius; yet Baronius, out of his love for Balsamon no less than with a freer style, never ceases to stab, while Casaubon, in his Exercitations, remarks: Note, then, that the canon is aimed at the Latins, who eat strangled things without distinction. In Baronius there is a letter of Michael Cerularius, Bishop of Constantinople, and Leo of Achrida, Archbishop of the Bulgarians, written to John, Bishop of Trani in Apulia, against the Roman Catholic see, says Baronius, indeed against the whole Western Church, volume XI, at the year of Christ 1053. In it, after the bishops had savagely attacked the use of unleavened bread in the Western Church and the keeping of the Sabbath, on account of which they are neither Jews nor Christians but like a leopard whose hairs are neither black nor wholly white, they add: But how do such people eat strangled things, in which the blood is retained? Do you not know that the blood of every animal is its soul, and that whoever eats blood eats the soul? And therefore in this respect they are not wholly Gentiles. But those others kill or wound, and then eat.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Sed & hodie quoque Græcos plerosque religiosissime isthoc interdictum custodire, liquido constat ex Jeremiæ Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani responsio primo ad Tubingenses. Hinc, inquit, neque quod suffocatum est, apud nos in cibum sumitur in hodiernum usque diem: sed sed aversamur, Patribus & Apostolis constanter obedientes. Quae Graecorum obstinatio etiam Moscovitarum, Armenorum & Habessenorum aemulationi alas videtur dedisse, de quibus videndi Sigismundus Baro ab Heberstein, in rerum Moscoviticarum Commentario; & Damianus à Goes, Eques Lusitanus de Moribus Æthiopum.
units.tr: That the Greeks even today very scrupulously keep this prohibition is clear from the first reply of Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, to the Tübingen theologians. Hence, he says, neither is what is strangled taken as food among us to this very day, but we turn away from it, constantly obeying the Fathers and the Apostles. This obstinacy of the Greeks seems also to have lent wings to the emulation of the Muscovites, the Armenians and the Abyssinians. On these peoples one may consult Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein, in his Commentary on Muscovite Affairs, and Damião de Góis, Portuguese knight, On the Customs of the Ethiopians.

units.la: XVI. Neque desunt inter Orthodoxos Celeberrimi Viri, qui solutum & liberum esse negant Sanguinis usum. Trigam hoc nomino Virorum doctissimorum, Angelocratem, Hassum, Christianum Becmannum, Professorem Theologum, & Superintendentem Servestanum, Exercitatione vicesima sexta, denique Illustrem Salmasium, libro de foenore Trapezitico, p. 438. ubi pertendit, praeceptum illud Apostolicum de non comedendo Sanguine, non propter mysteriorum Judaeorum, ne hi à Gentilibus promiscue sanguine & suffocatis vescentibus nimium offenderentur: sed tanquam rem omnino necessariam positam, ut caput legis ceremonialis, quod imposterum semper, aequè ut illud de non fornicando, observandum esset. Sed haec in antecessum leviter decursa sunto. Animus est nunc arcem rei invadere, & ad limam revocare, quae in hoc argumento Curcellaeus deproperavit.
units.tr: XVI. Nor are there lacking among the Orthodox very celebrated men who deny that the use of blood is free and permitted. I name three of the most learned men: Angelocrates, Hassus, and Christian Becmann, professor of theology and superintendent at Zerbst, in his twenty-sixth Exercise; and finally the illustrious Salmasius, in his book on trapezitic usury, p. 438, where he contends that the Apostolic precept about not eating blood was laid down not on account of the Jewish mysteries, lest these be too offended by the Gentiles eating blood and strangled things indiscriminately, but as a thing wholly necessary, like the head of the ceremonial law, which from then on must always be observed, just as the precept about not committing fornication. But let these matters be run through lightly by way of preface. My intention now is to attack the citadel of the question and to revise, with the file, what Curcellaeus rushed through on this subject.

units.la: CAPUT II. In Statu integritatis carnis & sanguinis esum non fuisse illicitum, probatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. That eating flesh and blood was not unlawful in the state of integrity is proved.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Curcellaei superyacanea industria. 1. In statu integritatis et restitutionis jus habuerunt ad sanguinis esum. 2. Etiam ad carnes. 3. Argumentum primum ac dominio universali. Quaeque se illud extendat? Cornelius à Lapide, & Serrhius refutantur. 4. Probatur, se extendere ad mactationem. Exercitium eius forsasse suspensum. Causa. 5. 6. 7. Arbor vitae an vim physicam habuerit producendi immortalitatem: Augustini sententia probatur. 8. De spatio temporis, quo Protoplasti in Paradiso commorati. Kabbalistarum sententia. Irenaeus, Cyrillus, Epiphanius, Patricides, Ibn-Sera notati. Curcellaeus non omnino probatur. batur. Adamum non peccasse die sexto. Fortasse etiam non se-ptimo. 9. Objectio prima Curcellei refellitur. 10. Mactationem non fuisse Paradiso indignam. 11. 12. Ovidio & Dicæarcho oppositi Plutarchus & Empedocles. 13. Bruta ante lapsum non carnivora. Quomodo facta carnivora? Quo cibo in arca Noachi pasta? 14.
units.tr: Curcellaeus's superfluous industry. 1. In the state of integrity and of restoration they had the right to eat blood. 2. Also flesh. 3. The first argument, from universal dominion. How far does that dominion extend? Cornelius à Lapide and Serrarius are refuted. 4. It is proved that it extends to slaughtering. Its exercise perhaps suspended. The cause. 5, 6, 7. Whether the tree of life had a physical power of producing immortality: Augustine's opinion is proved. 8. On the length of time the first parents spent in Paradise. The opinion of the Kabbalists. Irenaeus, Cyril, Epiphanius, Patrizi, Ibn Sina noted. Curcellaeus not wholly approved. That Adam did not sin on the sixth day. Perhaps not even on the seventh. 9. Curcellaeus's first objection is refuted. 10. Slaughter was not unworthy of Paradise. 11, 12. Plutarch and Empedocles set against Ovid and Dicaearchus. 13. Brute animals were not carnivorous before the fall. How did they become carnivorous? On what food were they fed in Noah's ark? 14.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: CUrcellæus per mundi ætates spatiatur, ut probet, qualibet tempestate interdictum fuisse sanguinis esum. Quinq; potissimum intervalla numerat, status innocentia: temporis antediluviani post lapsum: postdiluviani usq; ad legem Mosis: legis Mosaicæ usq; ad Christum: denique Ecclesiæ Christianæ usq; ad consummationem mundi. Ratio instituti minime improbanda, si præstare, quod suscepit, potuisset. Hoc autem demonstrasse conveniebat, singulis illis ætatibus ita prohibitum sanguinis esum, ut prohibitio non jure positivo voluntario, & mutabili ac mutato, sed naturali ac necessario, omnes & semper ad observantiam obligante niteretur. Jam largiamur, in statu innocentiæ interdictum sanguinis esum, unde constare potest, à jure naturali & necessario magis, quàm à positivo, per liberam Dei voluntatem commutabili, fluxisse interdictum? Nunquid non ibi Deus præcipere aliquid poterat, quod paulò post mutationi obnoxium esset, quale quid fuit illa de non comedendo fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali lex sacramentalis? Largiamur iis temporibus, quæ diluvium anteverterunt, interdictum antediluvianis hunc esum. Qua probabili ratione liquere potest, ideò juris perpetui esse? Nam & hoc constat, sacrificasse Adamum & Abelem. Quod si nec indultum iis duntaxat, uti existimatum quibusdam Patribus, nominatim Origeni, Theodoreto & Hieronymo: nec ideo profectum à jure naturali, & instinctu divinitus ingenito, uti visum Gregorio de Valentia de Missæ sacrificio lib. I. cap. IV. & Bellarmino de Missa lib. I. cap. XX. utrique ut idololatricum Missæ sacrificium tueretur, & Sacrificulis Missaticis asseret ementitum ordinem Sacerdotii: restabit plane, aliquid in eo intervallo præcipi potuisse, cujus non esset perpetim necessaria observantia. Post diluvium & Mosaicam vsq; ultro fatemur, prohibitionem intercessisse. Sed illam perpetui juris, inviolabilis necessitatis, & ad omnes pertinentis non fuisse, facile à nobis suo loco probabitur. Hoc unum igitur si liquido dare veritati Curcellæus potuisset: Synodi Apostolicæ interdictum de abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato inviolabilis fuisse rigoris, & nullo plane tempore dispensabilis, cæteris omnibus, quæ tam operosè tractat, omissis, manus sponte daturi, & illud Sophos acclamaturi fuéramus. Nunc, sive postremum hoc probet, sive probando deficiat, quod facere ipsum apparebit, patet sanè, priora ista parùm ad apodixin instituti negotii proficere, neque à Curcellæo minùs præteriri potuisse, quàm à nobis levi saltu transvolari citra causæ periculum omnino possent.
units.tr: CURCELLAEUS strolls through the ages of the world, to prove that at every period the eating of blood was forbidden. He counts five principal intervals: the state of innocence; the time before the flood, after the fall; the time after the flood until the law of Moses; the Mosaic law until Christ; and finally the Christian Church until the consummation of the world. The plan is by no means to be condemned, if he could have accomplished what he undertook. But it was fitting to demonstrate that in each of those ages the eating of blood was forbidden in such a way that the prohibition rested not on positive, voluntary and changeable law, changed and open to change, but on natural and necessary law, binding everyone and always to observance. Now let us grant that in the state of innocence the eating of blood was forbidden. From what can it be established that the prohibition flowed from natural and necessary law rather than from positive law, which is changeable by God's free will? Could God not there have commanded something that would be liable to change shortly afterwards, such as that sacramental law about not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? Let us grant that in the times before the flood this eating was forbidden to the antediluvians. By what probable reasoning can it be shown that this was of perpetual right? For it is also established that Adam and Abel offered sacrifices. But if it was not granted to them alone, as some Fathers, namely Origen, Theodoret and Jerome, thought; nor for that reason proceeded from natural law and an instinct implanted by God, as seemed to Gregory of Valentia (On the Sacrifice of the Mass, bk. 1, ch. 4) and Bellarmine (On the Mass, bk. 1, ch. 20), both of whom, to defend the idolatrous sacrifice of the Mass, asserted for the mass-sacrificing priests a fictitious order of priesthood: then it will plainly remain that something could have been commanded in that interval, of which observance was not perpetually necessary. After the flood and under the Mosaic law we readily concede that the prohibition intervened. But that it was of perpetual right, of inviolable necessity, and binding on all, will easily be proved by us in its proper place. So if Curcellaeus could have given this one thing clearly to the truth, namely that the Apostolic synod's prohibition of abstaining from blood and from what is strangled was of inviolable rigour and at no time dispensable, leaving aside all the other matters which he handles so laboriously, we would of our own accord have given up our hands and cried out Sophos. Now, whether he proves this last point or fails in proving it, which will appear from what he does, it is clear that those earlier points contribute little to the demonstration of the matter at hand; and that Curcellaeus could no less have passed them over than we could skip them with a light leap without any danger to the cause.

units.la: II. Quia tamen presso pede ipsum sequi decrevimus, in eo statim erimus, implicatam ut animi notionem revolvamus. Judicamus igitur nec in statu innocentiæ, nec temporibus diluvio antiquioribus interdictum religionis ergo sanguinis esum. Non ausimus quidem adfirmare, iis temporibus antediluvianos promiscuè, insuper etiam habitis simplicioribus cibis, esitasse sanguinem. Nam hoc fortasse alienius à simplicitate & moderatione illorum hominum fuisse existimabimus. Cæterùm quin iis & jus & fas ad sanguinem fuerit, dubitamus nulli. Post diluvium ad Christi usque tempora circumscriptus fuit lege, sed ceremoniali & positivo, & cum ritibus Judaicis aliquando sepelienda. Ab Apostolis demum repetita, sed ulterius non duratura, quàm cessaret legis ratio, quæ fuit metus offensæ Judæorum, quorum de cultu religioso ceremoniali, & ejus duratione scientia parùm erat roborata.
units.tr: II. Since, however, we have resolved to follow him closely, we shall at once come to the point and unravel the tangled notion of his mind. We judge, therefore, that eating blood was forbidden on account of religion neither in the state of innocence nor in the times older than the flood. We do not indeed dare to affirm that the antediluvians ate blood indiscriminately, moreover along with simpler foods; for we think this would be rather foreign to the simplicity and moderation of those men. But that they had both right and permission to blood, we doubt no one. After the flood, down to the times of Christ, it was bound by law, but a ceremonial and positive law, and at some point was to be buried together with the Jewish rites. Finally it was taken up again by the Apostles, but it was not to last any longer than the reason for the law lasted, which was fear of offending the Jews, whose knowledge of religious ceremonial worship and of its duration was little strengthened.

units.la: III. Fatetur, exertum interdictum nullum in statu innocentiæ occurrere. Inde tamen illud manifeste colligi contendit, quod tunc animalium carne, in qua est sanguis, nemini vesci licuerit. Quæ probatio non est nisi dialectica, & insuper litem lite resolvit. Si ejusmodi est aliqua connexio inter esum carnis & sanguinis constituta, quis me prohibebit, quò minùs pari lege consequentiâ concludam, post diluvium non licuisse vesci carne, quia non sanguine. Id quod vix Curcellæus indulgebit. Nimis enim vero distat. Porro ille carnis esum in statu innocentiæ illicitum fuisse, aliquot argumentis adstruere conatur. Quæ priusquam dissolvamus, probabimus, non illicitum fuisse in statu innocentiæ carnium usum.
units.tr: III. He admits that no express prohibition occurs in the state of innocence.
