Yet he strongly argues that it is plainly inferred from this that in those days no one was permitted to eat the flesh of animals, in which there is blood. This proof is nothing but dialectic, and moreover resolves one dispute by another. If some such connection has been established between eating flesh and eating blood, who will prevent me from concluding by the same law of consequence that after the flood it was not permitted to eat flesh, because it was not permitted to eat blood? Curcellaeus will scarcely grant this, for it is too far-fetched. Further, he tries to establish by several arguments that eating flesh was unlawful in the state of innocence. Before we dissolve these, we shall prove that the use of flesh was not unlawful in the state of innocence.

units.la: IV. Atque illud quidem extra controversiæ aleam ponere videtur universale illud dominium in pisces maris, volucres Cœli, pecupecudes, & universam terram, divino indultu in protoplastos olim competens. Et dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem secundum imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram, qui dominetur in pisces maris, & in volucres Coeli, & in omnes bestias reptantes super terram, Genes. I. 26. Hic mihi se segniter approbant, qui usque adeò dominium illud coarctant, ut statuant, ad nihil aliud fuisse utilia animalia homini, nisi ad experimentalem quandam notitiam de naturis eorum habendam, & in varietate creaturarum laudandam & celebrandam Sapientiam Dei multiformem. Qui ita sentiunt, non norunt, disparata esse dominium, & quemlibet unum. Sane hunc usum homini integro praestiterunt universa animantia, ut perficerent experimentalem scientiam hominis, atque eveherent ejus ardorem ad venerationem Numinis, quod tantam habuit pollentiam, ut & creare posset tam praestabilia, & ad usum hominis dirigere & gubernare verbo. Id quod magnifice Jobus, & Regius Propheta extulerunt. Sed quis non videt, ab hoc usu distinctum jus dominii fuisse? Etiam Coelum & sidera hanc nobis utilitatem praestant, ut ea contemplantibus admirationem Numinis summam commoveant. Neque tamen illis ita jussi sumus uspiam dominari, quemadmodum in animantia tributum videmus homini jus dominationis. Neque satisfacit Cornelius à Lapide, qui in eo collocare dominium voluit, quod bruta animantia descenderent ad obsequium hominis, vel per scientiam & prudentiam naturalem hominis, qua sciebat quomodo singula essent domanda, cicuranda & tractanda: Vel per providentiam Dei singularem, qui per Angelos animalium omnium phantasiam & corpus flexisset ad nutum; voluntatem & imperium hominis, sicuti eadem per Angelos ad Adamum adduxit: Comment. ad h. l. Quo etiam R. Solomon Jarchi, notante Mercero, inclinat, qui in voce [Hebrew] utrumque inclusum putat, & dominandi & descendendi sensum, pro varietate punctorum: [Hebrew] per Tzere: descendunt, nempe ad obsequium etiam vi coercitionis, si repugnet: [Hebrew] per chirek, dominentur. Quaestratio colligendi est [Hebrew] more allegorico instituta. Nam in eo statu, cum nondum essent animantia bruta [Greek] obnoxia, ne quidem casus fingi potest, quo dominaretur iis homo, cicurando, & ad obsequium inflectendo. Vox autem dominii videtur omnino jus dare ad positivum aliquem actum. Non est enim magnifica vox; res ipsa inanis. Quid ergo si equus vecturus erat tergo, camelus sarcinas gestaturus, & si quid ejusmodi aliud? Ne sic quidem illa dominandi potestas tam excellens absolvi videtur. Quid enim facerent piscibus, quid aliis animantibus?
units.tr: IV. And indeed he seems to place beyond the dispute of chance that universal dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, and the whole earth, which was once held by our first parents by divine grant. "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, who shall have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over all beasts that creep upon the earth" (Gen. 1.26). Here they approve me sluggishly, who so restrict that dominion as to maintain that useful animals were for man for nothing else than to gain a certain experiential knowledge of their natures, and to praise and celebrate in the variety of creatures the many-formed wisdom of God. Those who think so do not know that dominion and any one are different things. Certainly all living creatures rendered this use to the unfallen man, so that they might complete man's experiential knowledge and raise his ardour towards the veneration of the Deity, who had such power that he could both create such excellent things and direct and govern them for man's use by a word. This Job and the royal Prophet magnificently extolled. But who does not see that the right of dominion was distinct from this use? Even heaven and the stars furnish us this usefulness, that they may stir the highest admiration of the Deity in those who contemplate them. Yet we have not been ordered to rule over them anywhere in the way we see the right of dominion granted to man over the animals. Nor does Cornelius à Lapide satisfy, who wished to place dominion in this, that the brute animals would come down to the service of man, either through the natural science and prudence of man, by which he knew how each was to be tamed, domesticated and handled; or through God's singular providence, who through the angels bent the imagination and body of all animals at a nod, so that they yielded the will and command of man, just as he brought them to Adam through the angels (Commentary on this passage). To this R. Solomon Jarchi also inclines, as Mercerus notes, who thinks that both senses, to rule and to descend, are included in the word [radah], according to the variation of the vowel points: with tzere, [yeredu], they descend, namely to service, even by force of coercion if they resist; with hireq, [yiredu], they rule. This gathering of meanings is instituted in an allegorical manner. For in that state, since the brute animals were not yet subject, no case can even be imagined in which man would rule over them by taming and bending them to service. But the word dominion seems to give a right altogether to some positive act. For it is not a grand word; the thing itself is empty. What then if the horse was to be ridden on the back, the camel to carry burdens, and anything else of that sort? Not even so does that power of ruling appear so excellent as it is made out to be. For what would they do with the fish, and what with the other animals?

units.la: V. Restat, ut firmissime approbem, ad dominium illud pertinere jus animantium mactandi & ad esum praeparandi. Jus nomino, non exercitium, de quo non est ut contendam. Nolim autem hoc movere, verbum רדה absolutissimum videri dominium designare. Quod & ipsis interpretibus Orientalibus existimatum, Samaritano, Chaldaico, Syriaco, Arabico. Hi enim omnes verbo רדו usi. Tanquam designatus esset homo, qui more Sultani alicujus praeesset. Hoc validius, quod non aliud dominium homini integro concessum, quam quod a diluvio repetitum; saltem non angustius. Alias Deum offendendo, meliorem conditionem suam reddidissent, quam ante lapsum fuerit. Id quod ipsi Crucellaeo absurdum satis visum pag. 17.
units.tr: V. It remains for me to argue as firmly as I can that this dominion includes the right to kill animals and prepare them for food. I say right, not exercise, and I have no wish to dispute the latter. I would not, however, press the point that the word רדה [radah] seems to designate absolute dominion, though the Eastern interpreters themselves also took it so: the Samaritan, the Chaldee, the Syriac, and the Arabic. For all of them used the word רדו [redu], as if a man were appointed to preside over the animals in the manner of some sultan. This is the stronger because no other dominion was granted to man in his integrity than that which was renewed after the Flood, or at least none narrower. Otherwise, by offending God, men would have made their condition better than it was before the fall. Curcellaeus himself thought this absurd enough, p. 17.

units.la: Repetitum autem jus Dominii ita habet, Genes. IX. 2.3.4. Timor vestri terrorque infesto omnibus bestiis terra: omnibus volucribus caeli: tum omnia quae calcant humum: tum omnes pisces maris in manum vestram traditi sunt. Omne reptile, quod vivum est, ad comedendum vobis esto: ut viridem herbam illis, sic omnia dedi vobis. Hic vide. Repetitur dominium olim etiam protoplastis concessum: & paulo quidem explicatius. Illius autem dominii pars manifeste collocatur in esu concesso reptilium & omnis carnis. Ergo etiam in statu innocentiae ea pars concessi dominii fuit, ut, si adlubesceret, carnibus vescerentur. Quid ultra contendimus? Nam quod Curcellaeus in hac parte novum jus Noachidis promi, cum quibusdam, ac nominatim Lyrano, Carthusiano, Tostato, addo etiam, Tertulliano jam Montanizante existimat, illud & absurdum, ipso judice Curcellaeo, qui existimavit, hac ratione homines Deum offendendo conditionem suam meliorem reddidisse, quam ante lapsum fuerit ; & nulla ratione suffultum, ut infra patebit. Evidenti argumento accedit, quod absque isto jure animantium mactandorum intelligi nequeat, quemadmodum constare potuerit dominium in pisces maris, aves caeli, & universam terram, quam nec in contemplationis dulcedine, nec in labore cicurandorum animantium, quae efferata nulla fuerunt; nec in usu vehentium, & similes operas ministrantium, cum plurima praestare eas non possent, fas sit illud reponere. Nisi forte dici potest piscibus dominari, quem vel delphinus ergo vehit: vel cui echinus praedicat imminere tempestatem: vel qui, ad portum stans agminibus piscium contemplandis oblectatur uti.
units.tr: The renewed right of dominion is stated thus in Genesis 9:2-4: The fear and terror of you shall be on every beast of the earth, and on every bird of the heaven, and on all that creep upon the ground, and on all the fishes of the sea; into your hand are they delivered. Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green herb I have given you all things. Note this. The dominion is repeated, which was earlier granted also to the first parents, and somewhat more fully. Part of that dominion is clearly placed in the permitted eating of reptiles and all flesh. Therefore in the state of innocence too this part of the granted dominion existed, so that, if they had wished, they might feed on flesh. Why should we argue further? For Curcellaeus holds, with certain others, and especially Lyranus, the Carthusian, and Tostatus, and I add, Tertullian already become a Montanist, that in this part a new right was promulgated for the sons of Noah. This is absurd by Curcellaeus's own judgment, since he thought that by this means men, by offending God, made their condition better than it was before the fall. Nor is it supported by any reasoning, as will appear below. A clear argument is added: without this right of killing animals it cannot be understood how dominion could be established over the fishes of the sea, the birds of the heaven, and the whole earth. Animals were not wild, so dominion could not rest either on the delight of contemplation, or on the labour of taming them, or on their use for carrying and performing similar services, since they could not supply most of these things, and it is not right to set that aside. Unless perhaps it can be said that a man rules over fishes when a dolphin carries him, or when a sea urchin warns him of an approaching storm, or when he stands at the harbour and enjoys watching shoals of fish.

units.la: Non sic loquuntur. uti commendebat ille apud Erasmum in Ichthyophagia insulsus salsa-mentarius. Suboluisse videtur etiam ipsi Aristoteli, quod nos volu-mus. Is enim Politic. I. cap. V. editionis Conringianae, ait, πολεμικὴ φύσει κτητικὴ πως ἐστιν. Τῶν δὲ θηρικῶν μέρος αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ χρῆσθαι ταῖς θηρίαις. Artem bellicam esse naturā factam aliquo modo ad rem quaerendam: Studium autem venatorium partem ejus esse, quo deceat uti adversum feras. Perspicuè à jure naturae illud arcessit, quòd feræ capiuntur, & ad quotidianum esum ac usum subiguntur. Sed & Cicero in Tuscul. I. quadruplicem agnoscit usum bestiarum, ob quem primitus à Deo creatæ: nempe ad vescendum, ad cultus agrorum, ad vehendum, denique ad corpora vestiendum.
units.tr: They do not speak so, as that foolish salter of meat once argued in Erasmus's Ichthyophagia. Even Aristotle seems to have sensed what we maintain. In the first book of the Politics, chapter 5, of the Conring edition, he says: The art of war is by nature in some sense an art of acquisition. Part of it is the art of hunting, which is to be used against wild beasts. [πολεμικὴ φύσει κτητικὴ πως ἐστιν. Τῶν δὲ θηρικῶν μέρος αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ χρῆσθαι ταῖς θηρίαις.] He clearly derives this from natural law, because wild animals are caught and brought under control for daily food and use. Cicero too, in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations, recognises the fourfold use of beasts for which they were first created by God: namely for food, for working the fields, for carrying, and finally for clothing bodies.

units.la: VI. Duo hic excipere videtur Curcellaeus.
units.tr: VI. Curcellaeus seems to make two exceptions here.

units.la: 1. Dominium Adami & Evæ in animantia non fuisse illimitatum, sed iis circumscriptum limitibus, quos Deus ipse posuerat: proinde sine gravi peccato violari non potuisse. Posuisse autem, apparere ex eo, quòd tibi genus præscripserat, quo debebant vesci. p. 13. Respondeo, non esse vel à Curcellaeo, vel à quoquam nostrum limites figendos dominio Protoplastorum, quos non prior Deus fixerit. Nequit autem probari, ullos Deum fixisse. Nam quòd certum genus cibi præscripsit, non ideirco putandus est jus dominii in cætera limitâsse. Sed ad extremum exercitium dominii limitavit, sapienter indicando, quem cibum cæteris salubriorem humana conditio requireret: non quem permittere iis vellet.
units.tr: 1. The dominion of Adam and Eve over animals was not unlimited, but was bounded by limits which God himself had set; therefore it could not be violated without grave sin. That God did set them appears from the fact that he prescribed to them the kind of food on which they were to live. p. 13. I reply that neither Curcellaeus nor any of us ought to fix limits to the dominion of the first parents which God had not fixed beforehand. But it cannot be proved that God fixed any. For because he prescribed a certain kind of food, we should not think that he thereby limited the right of dominion over the rest. He limited only the exercise of dominion, wisely indicating which food the human condition would require as more wholesome than the others, not which he wished to permit them.

units.la: 2. Dominium in bruta posse consistere, quia nis non comedantur, quia multa eorum sint species, à quibus sponte abstineamus: ibid. Resp. 1. Non ferit nostram sententiam exceptio, quia ne quidem asserimus, brutorum carnes à Protoplastis comestas esse: sed hoc duntaxat tuemur, jus illos comedendorum habuisse. Quod ita satis ad scopum nostrum facit, qui defendamus, non interdictum Protoplastis carnium esum. Hodieque jus habemus ad θυσίαν animalium ἀναμφισβήτητος. Et tamen à plurimis homines consultò abstinent. 2. Si ideò consistere dominium in animantia integrum potuisset, exclusso jure vescendarum carnium, quia sua sponte homines à quibusdam abstinent; tum pari ego jure concludam, potuisse hominem animantibus Cœli, Terræ & Maris dominari, quamvis neque præberent contemplationis materiem, nec servirent ad vestuam, neque ad alia ejus generis famulitia se applicarent: potuisse hominem plantis terræ dominari, quamvis iis non vesceretur. Quis enim ignorat, multa animantia vel non satis ad ejusmodi famulitium cium idonea: vel minùs necessaria? Quis ignorat, quasdam plantas ipse vescendas non præbere: Persis Persicam malum lethalem: cicutam, hyoscyamum, napellum, alias hominibus mortiferas esse?
units.tr: 2. Dominion over brute beasts can exist even if they are not eaten, since there are many species from which we voluntarily abstain. ibid. Reply, first: the objection does not strike our view, because we do not even assert that the flesh of brutes was eaten by the first parents; we only maintain that they had the right of eating them. This suits our purpose well, since we defend that the eating of flesh was not forbidden to the first parents. Even today we have an undisputed right to the sacrifice [θυσίαν] of animals, and yet many men deliberately abstain. Second: if dominion over animals could exist whole even with the right to eat flesh excluded, because some men abstain from certain kinds of their own accord, then by the same right I shall conclude that man could have ruled over the animals of heaven, earth and sea, even though they did not provide material for contemplation, nor serve for clothing, nor apply themselves to any other service of that kind; that man could have ruled over the plants of the earth, even though he did not feed on them. For who does not know that many animals are either not fit enough for such service or less necessary? Who does not know that some plants do not themselves supply anything fit to eat: the Persian apple is deadly, and hemlock, henbane, monkshood, and others are fatal to men?

units.la: VII. Sed & hinc probari validè posset, non fuisse interdictum in statu innocentiæ carnium usum, quia omnia præcepta Dei in statu illo vel moralia fuerunt, in quibus versabatur interna sanctitas & vera religio: vel positiva. Morale præceptum fuisse de non comedendis carnibus, non putem quenquam temerè asserturum. Nam ex hypothesi mutatum fuit postdiluvianis temporibus. Mutatio autem morali mandato non potest accidere. Deinde in sanctitate illa morali, cui litare protoplastos conveniebat, sita fuit imago Dei, Ephes. IV. 24. Atque adeò per illam sanctitatem redditi fuissemus Deo quàm simillimi. Non reddimur autem per abstinentiam à carnibus Deo similes. Posset etiam aliàs dici, Deum indulgendo usum carnium, aliquid indulsisse, quo impeditur vera sanctitas & religio: quod vel cogitare absurdum. Neque aliam ob rationem legem, quæ ad sanctitatem protoplastos obstringebat, Spiritualis dicitur Apostolo Rom. VII. 14. quàm quia requirit λογικὴ λατρεία, cordis sanctimoniam & internam puritatem. Sed & in cibis nihil apparere, quod Deo nos gratiores, atque sanctiores adeò, religiosioresque reddat, tam clarè in Evangelio docetur, ferè ut clarius nihil. Positivis verò Dei mandatis accensendum illud de non vescendis carnibus, probare poterit nemo. Unicum enim tale mandatum in Paradiso constitutum fuit, de non edendo fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali. De cætero ad regiam eam legem se conformare Protoplasti debuerunt, quæ fuit ipsorum cordibus insculpta.
units.tr: VII. But from this it could also be strongly proved that the eating of flesh was not forbidden in the state of innocence, because all the precepts of God in that state were either moral, in which internal holiness and true religion consisted, or positive. No one, I think, will rashly assert that the precept about not eating flesh was moral. For by hypothesis it was changed in the times after the Flood, and a moral command cannot be changed. Next, in that moral holiness, to which the first parents were bound to conform, the image of God consisted (Ephesians 4:24), and so through that holiness we would have been rendered most like God. But we are not made like God by abstinence from flesh. It could also be said otherwise: that by permitting the use of flesh God granted something which hinders true holiness and religion, which is absurd even to think. Nor for any other reason does the Apostle call the law that bound the first parents to holiness "spiritual" (Romans 7:14), than because it requires a reasonable service [λογικὴ λατρεία], purity of heart and inward cleanness. Moreover, the Gospel teaches so clearly that nothing in foods makes us more pleasing to God, or holier and more religious, that nothing could be clearer. But no one can prove that the prohibition of eating flesh belongs among God's positive commands. For only one such command was laid down in Paradise, not to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Otherwise the first parents ought to have conformed themselves to that royal law which was engraved on their hearts.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Vellet quosdam Curcellæus ita facere argumentantes: Jus habuisse primos humani generis parentes in statu integritatis vescendi carne, si voluissent: si non usurpaverint, id tribuendum brevitati temporis, quod lapsum antecessit: aut, quòd tanta optimorum fructuum terræque copia abundarent, ut de alio cibi genere cogitare opus non esset: pag. 12. Utramque rationem refutat. Ego, qui ita arguant, penitus ignoro. Nisi Doctissimum Rivetum Curcellæus tangit. Is enim tale quid subinnuere videtur. Confiteor, jus Protoplastos habuisse. De exercitio nihil mihi compertum est. Si suspensum est, quod probabile omnino, causæ fuerit isthoc, quòd abundarent copia ciborum simplicium, qui salubriores & conducibiliores sanitati. Neque obstat Curcellæi contraria traria ratio, hoc ostendere, Deum vescendi facultatem non indulsisse: praesertim cum minime deceret homines integros vitam, quam ex arbore vitae consequi poterant, in aliorum interitu quaerere. pag. 16. Resp. 1. Non ideo Deus non indulsit, quia plurimos inter indultos salubriores appetierunt. Hodieque prudentiae est, in multitudine ciborum saluberrimos seligere. Quis vero caeteros inde, qui relinquuntur, non indultos, sed interdictos colligeret? 2. Ex arbore vitae primos homines vitam consecuturos ratione quadam physica, qua illa ad alendum caeteris praestaret, incertum videtur. Non ignoro, ita multos sentire. Sed rationem probabilem desidero. Certe parum veritati consentientia dicunt, qui arborem vitae immortalitatem censent fuisse allaturam: quod visum Bellarmino de Gratia primi hominis, cap. XVIII. & fortassis Chrysostomo etiam, Theodoreto, Irenaeo, Ruperto, quos citat Abulensis. Quibus Scotus, Cajetanus, Durandus & Pererius hoc opponunt merito, quod qualiscunque illa vis fructus fuerit naturalis & finita, ac proinde continua actione caloris naturalis in homine consumenda; fuerit etiam corruptibilis, ac proinde incorruptibilem vitam minime productura. Nobis pro vero Augustinus dixisse videtur: Erat homini in lignis aliis alimentum: in hoc sacramentum. Symbolum fuit & Sacramentum immortalis vitae, si non peccaret. Causam fuisse physicam extrahendae in longius vitae, caeteris praestantiorem, non constat. Neque hoc prae se ferunt verba Genes. III. 22. quippe quae consilium potius hominis peccatoris, quam eventum rei respiciunt. Non igitur magis curandum protoplastis fuit, ut, liberalius decerpto hujus arboris fructu, caedibus animantium parcerent, quam quibuscunque aliis herbis ad esum praeparatis.
units.tr: Curcellaeus would wish certain people to argue thus: The first parents of the human race had the right, in the state of integrity, to eat flesh if they had wished. If they did not make use of it, this must be attributed either to the brevity of the time that preceded the fall, or to their abundance of the finest fruits and of the earth's produce, so that there was no need to think of any other kind of food. p. 12. He refutes both reasons. I do not know who argues like this, except that Curcellaeus touches on the most learned Rivetus, for he seems to hint at something of the kind. I grant that the first parents had the right. Of its exercise nothing is known to me. If it was suspended, which is wholly probable, the cause was this: they had an abundance of simple foods, more wholesome and better suited to health. Nor does Curcellaeus's contrary argument stand in the way: this shows that God did not grant the faculty of eating, especially since it would hardly befit whole men to seek in the death of others the life they could obtain from the tree of life. p. 16. Reply 1: God did not withhold the grant because most of the things granted were the more wholesome ones they chose. Even today it is wise to choose the most wholesome foods from a great variety. But who would conclude from this that the rest, which are left over, were not granted but forbidden? 2: That the first men would obtain life from the tree of life by some physical reason, by which it surpassed the others in nourishing, seems uncertain. I am not unaware that many think so, but I want a probable reason. Certainly those who hold that the tree of life would have brought immortality say things little in accord with the truth. This seemed so to Bellarmine, in On the Grace of the First Man, ch. XVIII, and perhaps also to Chrysostom, Theodoret, Irenaeus and Rupert, whom Abulensis cites. Against them Scotus, Cajetan, Durandus and Pererius rightly object that whatever power the fruit had was natural and finite, and so would be consumed by the continual action of natural heat in man; and that it was also corruptible, and so would by no means produce incorruptible life. For our part Augustine seems to have spoken truly: Man had food in other trees; in this one, a sacrament. It was a symbol and sacrament of immortal life, if he did not sin. That it had a physical power to prolong life further, superior to the others, is not established. Nor do the words of Genesis 3:22 imply this, since they regard the counsel of sinful man rather than the outcome of the matter. Therefore the protoplasts had no more reason to take care, by plucking the fruit of this tree more freely, to spare the slaughter of animals than with any other herbs prepared for food.

units.la: IX. De spatio temporis in statu innocentiae exacto curiosior quam utilior & verior est contemplatio: cum non mactatorum animantium non alia ratio probabiliter fuerit, quam ea, quam modo attigimus.
units.tr: IX. Contemplation of the length of time spent in the state of innocence is more a matter of curiosity than of use, and no more reliable, since for the non-slaughter of animals there was probably no other reason than the one we have just touched on.

units.la: Sive igitur longior, sive brevior mora fuerit, ad summam rei nihil refert. Caeterum, quia ita placuit Curcellaeo, obiter de ea quaestione pauca interspergemus. In universum de tempore in eo statu consumpto nihil a nobis viatoribus definiri potest, quia revelatio deficit. Hinc natae plurimae in ea quaestione & discrepantes sententiae; & conjecturis meris res acta. Kabbalistarum quidem sententia nemini sano accepta, viginti annis in eo statu Adamum mansisse, quia nemo capax sit damnationis, quin totidem annorum sit: id quod per Gematriam ridicule colligunt ex verbo הוה versus 12. Sed & omni ratione carent, quòd alii triginta & tribus annis mansionem definiunt, quia totidem annos Christus vixerit: alii quadraginta diebus, quia totidem Christus in eremo jejunârit. Quis nos docuit in ejusmodi circumstantiis Adamum cum Christo comparare? Irenæus, Cyrillus & Epiphanius, ac hos secuti plurimi arbitrantur, non ultra sex horas in statu innocentiæ Adamum fuisse. Eodem enim die, nempe sexto, horâ creatum tertiâ: lapsum horâ sextâ: expulsum horâ nonâ. Quod similiter ex analogia cum Christo confirmant. Sicut Christus in exordio diei sextæ passionis ante tribunal raptus, sputis sordidissimus fœdatus est, ita de luto formatum Adamum. Sicut horâ tertiâ Christus accepta mortis sententia Hierosolymis ad supplicium ductus est: sic Adamum eadem in Paradisum. Sicus inter sextam & nonam Christus suas manus in cruce extendit: sic hora sexta Adamum & Evam manum ad decerpendum extendisse fructum. Sicut denique horâ nonâ Christus in cruce expiravit, & latro Paradisum ingressus est, ita eâdem horâ Adamum fuisse ex Paradiso ejectum. Idem fere sentit Patricides Arabs: Expulsos eos horâ nonâ diei Veneris in montem quendam India. Sed & Ibn-Sora Jacobita in scripto Apologetico, quod Patricidi opposuit, similia habet, tradente celeberrimo Doctore Hottingero nostro, Smegmat. Oriental. lib. I. pag. 209. Haud immeritò suspecta hæc sententia Curcellæo. Sed ipsius rationes omnes, quas affert pag. 14. 15. probè militare, non dixerim. Certè non tam longum temporis tractum sibi expetiissent ea, quæ exaggerat. Mulierem, inquit, aliquo post intervallo creavit. Sed non longo. Continuus enim fuit creandi actus. Quod innuunt satis verba cap.I. vers. 27. Creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam: marem & fœminam creavit eos. Neque obstat, quod secundo demum capite Evæ creatio delineata: quo etiam argumento vellet Menasse Ben-Israël, aliique Rabbini monstra sua androgynorum persuadere. Sed oportebat & Curcellæum & Rabbinos meminisse Josephi, verè dicentis: Mosen naturam interpretari cœpisse post septimam diem, Antiq. Jud. lib. I. cap. II. Adamo adducta, inquit, animalia, ut pro arbitrio eis nomina imponeret. Non dicam hic cum Cajetano, adducta ad Adamum animalia per visionem intellectualem. Hoc duntaxat dicam, probari non posse; singula potiùs animalia ad Adamum adducta, quàm species eorum. Quod posterius brevi tempore expediviset maxima vi intelintelligentiae praeditus Adamus. Creatis, inquit, legem tulit. Hoc citra moram fieri potuit. Diabolus non statim adfuit, ut eos tentaret, cum recens adhuc esset interdicti memoria: sed per otium eorum speculatus felicitatem, demum invidiam concepit. Mihi vero probabilius, Diabolum, quo est infido ingenio, obliquis statim oculis limatam hominis fortunam insidiis suis appetiisse. Non indiguit otio ad speculandum, cui sudes fuit ante oculos. Exspectavit ad opportunitatem, qua Evam solam non comitatam viro deprehenderet. Atqui haec opportunitas se statim fortasse praebuit. Haec attuli, non quod omnes illas rationes penitus improbem, sed ut liqueret, proxime a conjecturis abesse. Mihi vero haec una ratio vulgari sententiae incidere nervos videtur, quod Moses non obscure indicat, cap. II. vers. 3. Deum septimo die quievisse, & illum sanctificasse, homine adhuc in Paradiso existente. Sanctificatio enim illa quid fuit nisi praeceptum homini datum de eo sanctificando? Ergo homo septimo die nondum peccaverat; saltem tum, cum fieret sanctificatio, quae facta haud dubie mane ejus diei, quia totus dies est sanctificatus. Non igitur die sexto peccavit homo: fortassis ne septimo quidem. Sed de caeteris certi nihil habeo dicere. Redeamus nunc e diverticulo in viam: & rationes lustremus, quibus probat adversarius, in statu Innocentiae carnes non fuisse licitas edi.
units.tr: Whether the stay was longer or shorter makes no difference to the sum of the matter. Still, since it pleased Curcellaeus, we will insert a few words on that question in passing. In general, nothing about the time spent in that state can be determined by us wayfarers, because revelation is lacking. Hence arose many and differing opinions on the question, and the matter has been carried on by mere conjecture. The opinion of the Kabbalists, accepted by no sane person, is that Adam remained in that state for twenty years, because no one is capable of damnation who is not that many years old. They ridiculously gather this by gematria from the word [הוה] in verse 12. But these also lack all reason, since others fix the stay at thirty-three years, because Christ lived that many years, and others at forty days, because Christ fasted that many days in the wilderness. Who taught us to compare Adam with Christ in such circumstances? Irenaeus, Cyril and Epiphanius, and many who followed them, think Adam was in the state of innocence no more than six hours. For on the same day, the sixth, he was created at the third hour, fell at the sixth, and was expelled at the ninth. They confirm this similarly from analogy with Christ. Just as Christ, at the beginning of the sixth day of his passion, was snatched before the tribunal and most foully defiled with spittle, so Adam was formed of clay. Just as at the third hour Christ, having received the sentence of death, was led out of Jerusalem to execution, so at the same hour Adam was led into Paradise. As between the sixth and ninth hours Christ stretched out his hands on the cross, so at the sixth hour Adam and Eve stretched out their hands to pluck the fruit. Finally, just as at the ninth hour Christ expired on the cross and the thief entered Paradise, so at the same hour Adam was cast out of Paradise. The Arab Patricides holds nearly the same view: They were expelled at the ninth hour of Friday to a certain mountain of India. But also Ibn-Sora the Jacobite, in an apologetic writing he set against Patricides, has similar things, as our most celebrated teacher Hottinger reports in Smegmat. Oriental. book I, p. 209. This opinion is rightly suspect to Curcellaeus. But I would not say that all the arguments he brings forward on pp. 14 and 15 fight well for his side. Certainly they would not have sought for themselves so long a stretch of time as the things he exaggerates. He created the woman, he says, after some interval. But not a long one. For the act of creating was continuous. The words of ch. 1 v. 27 sufficiently suggest this: God created man in his own image; male and female he created them. Nor does it stand in the way that the creation of Eve is only outlined in the second chapter. By this argument Menasseh ben Israel and other rabbis wanted to persuade people of their monsters, the androgynes. But Curcellaeus and the rabbis ought to have remembered Josephus, who truly said that Moses began to explain nature after the seventh day, Antiq. Jud. book I, ch. II. The animals, he says, were brought to Adam so that he might impose names on them at his pleasure. I will not say here with Cajetan that the animals were brought to Adam by intellectual vision. I will only say that it cannot be proved that the individual animals were brought to Adam rather than their species. Adam, endowed with the greatest power of understanding, could have dispatched the latter in a short time. Having created them, he says, he gave the law. This could be done without delay. The devil was not at once present to tempt them, since the memory of the prohibition was still recent; but having watched their happiness at leisure, he at last conceived envy. But it seems to me more probable that the devil, who is of a faithless nature, at once desired the man's good fortune with sidelong eyes and filed it for his snares. He had no need of leisure to observe, since the prize was before his eyes. He waited for an opportunity to catch Eve alone, not accompanied by her husband. Yet this opportunity perhaps presented itself at once. I have brought these things forward not because I wholly reject all those reasons, but so that it might be clear they come very close to conjecture. To me this one reason seems to cut the sinews of the common opinion, which Moses indicates not obscurely in ch. II v. 3: that God rested on the seventh day and sanctified it while man was still in Paradise. For what was that sanctification but a precept given to man about sanctifying it? Therefore man had not yet sinned on the seventh day, at least at the time when the sanctification was made, which was undoubtedly done in the morning of that day, since the whole day was sanctified. Therefore man did not sin on the sixth day, and perhaps not even on the seventh. But about the rest I have nothing certain to say. Let us now return from this byway to the main road, and examine the arguments by which the adversary proves that in the state of innocence the flesh of animals was not lawful to eat.

units.la: X. Objicit 1. locum Genes. I. 29. 30.
units.tr: X. He objects first to the passage Gen. 1:29-30.

units.la: Ecce dedi vobis omnem herbam afferentem semen super terram, & universa ligna, quae habent in semet ipsis sementem generis sui, ut sint vobis in escam, & cunctis animalibus terrae, omnibusque volucribus caeli, & universis, quae moventur in terra, & in quibus est anima vivens, ut habeant ad vescendum. Hic nulla, inquit, fit mentio carnis animalium, sive reptilium, sive piscium, sive volucrium, sive quadrupedum, ut facturus erat, si eam hominibus in alimentum concedere intendisset. Jam fateor, hoc telo & Judaeos pugnare, & plerosque Patres, quibus opponit Pererius Cajetanum, Victoria, D. Soto. Parum solide, quantum mihi videtur. Nam evidenter probatum superius, sub universali dominio Protoplastis concessio, mactationem etiam brutorum contineri. Quod semel Deus concessit, illud ne quidem verisimile est, stricto ejusmodi mandato interdicere voluisse. 2. Carnibus vesci sua natura neque bonum neque malum est, sed in genere illorum, quae adiaphora vocamus. In his autem testimonium negativum S. Scripturae, nullam habet vim persuasionis. Atqui hoc testimonium mere est negativum: Non expressit Deus hoc verbo, ut vescendarum carnium: Ergo interdixit. Si haec justa argumentandi ratio, tum fas mihi fuerit inde concludere: in statu innocentiae ne quidem vini, aliusve potûs usum fuisse. Nam hac concessione Deus saltem cibum Protoplastis locavit. Quod si absurdum est, quid juvat in carnium vescendarum non expressa concessione tricari? Ne quidem Deus expressit apud Protoplastos, quis esset usus concessus brutorum. Ideircone verum est, nullum fuisse eorum planè usum? 3. Sed & divinare licet, quamobrem in hac concessione nulla facta carnium mentio. Protoplasti soli in Paradiso agitabant. Plantarum autem proculdubio tanta & varietas, & ex suavitate delectatio, & salubritas, & praeparandarum facilitas, prae his ut carnes foetere deberent. Medicum hic, ut ita loquar, se Deus Protoplastis gessit consulentem, quid potissimum tanta in copia affluente ciborum, quae vae etiam oculis faceret, sanitati conduceret. Non quid vel permitteret, vel interdiceret, explicavit, sed quid potissimum conduceret. Sed & hanc liceat mihi conjecturam promere. Plantarum ingens erat multitudo, ex fecunda terra matre satarum. Bruta autem animantia vix probabile est creata nisi par in qualibet specie. Haec igitur nondum multiplicata sub exordium mundi mactanda praebere Deus noluit, cum esset abundè ciborum & copia & satietas. Placere hoc video etiam Justino Martyri in Resp. ad quaest. 49. Orthodox. Inde autem religiosum aliquod interdictum frustra quisquam conficere satagat.
units.tr: Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and all trees which have in themselves the seed of their own kind, that they may be food for you, and for all the beasts of the earth, and all the birds of the air, and all that move upon the earth, and in which there is a living soul, that they may have them to eat. Here, he says, there is no mention of the flesh of animals, whether of reptiles, fish, birds or quadrupeds, as God would have made, had he intended to grant it to men for food. I admit that the Jews and most of the Fathers fight with this weapon, against whom Pererius sets Cajetan, Victoria and D. Soto. But it is weak, as far as I can see. For it was proved above that the grant of universal dominion to the first-formed man also includes the slaughter of brute animals. What God once granted, it is not even likely he wished to forbid by such a bare command. 2. To eat flesh is by its nature neither good nor evil, but belongs to the class of things we call indifferent. In such matters a negative testimony of Holy Scripture has no force of persuasion. Yet this testimony is purely negative: God did not express by this word that flesh was to be eaten; therefore he forbade it. If this is a sound mode of argument, then I may conclude from it that in the state of innocence there was not even any use of wine or any other drink. For by this grant God at least assigned food to the first humans. But if this is absurd, what is the point of fussing over the lack of an express grant for eating flesh? God did not express, among the first humans, what the permitted use of the brute animals was. Does it follow that they had no use at all? 3. But one may also guess why no mention of flesh is made in this grant. The first humans alone were living in Paradise. The variety of plants was surely great, and their sweetness was a delight, and their wholesomeness, and the ease of preparing them, so that flesh ought to have been foul by comparison. Here God, so to speak, acted toward the first humans as a physician giving advice: what, above all, in such an abundance of food flowing in, which pleases even the eyes, would serve their health. He did not explain what he would permit or forbid, but what would best serve them. But let me also offer this conjecture. The multitude of plants was vast, sown from the fertile earth as its mother. Brute animals, however, were hardly likely to have been created except in pairs of each kind. God therefore did not wish these, not yet multiplied at the beginning of the world, to be slaughtered for food, since there was plenty of food, both in quantity and in satisfying abundance. I see that Justin Martyr also agrees with this, in his Reply to Question 49 of the Orthodox. From this, however, let no one labour in vain to construct some religious prohibition.

units.la: XI. Pergit: Non conveniebat excellentia, in qua conditus homo: & statui ejus ante peccatum, ut animalia mactaret, quasi vitam suam nequiret sustentare, quin alteri eam eriperet, & illius se sanguine polluteret.
units.tr: XI. He goes on: the excellence in which man was created did not fit with his being, before the fall, a man who slaughters animals, as if he could not sustain his life unless he snatched it from another and polluted himself with its blood.

units.la: Haec ratio convenientior Pythagoreo homini, vel alii cuilibet Metempsychistae, vel Empedocli etiam, docenti oportere etiam erga animalia justitiam exercere, ne nempe non merita occidas, Plutarch. Orat. 2. Homo Christianus cognoscere & poterat & debuerat, regnum Dei non esse in quibus posterioribus excellentia statûs ante lapsum sita, Rom. XIV. 17. Atqui crudele, ut sustentes vitam, alteri eam eripere. Proh! Jupiter piacularis! An igitur crudele aliquod & minus humanitati conveniens post diluvium indulsit Deus homini? Sed pertinent haec ad humanam sapientiam.
units.tr: This argument suits better a Pythagorean man, or any other follower of metempsychosis, or even Empedocles, who taught that justice must be practised even toward animals, so that one does not kill those that do not deserve it (Plutarch, Oration 2). A Christian man could and ought to know that the kingdom of God does not consist in such things as the excellence of the state before the fall, Rom. 14:17. Yet it is cruel to take another's life in order to sustain one's own. Good heavens, Jupiter the expiator! Did God then grant man something cruel and less fitting to humanity after the flood? But these matters belong to human wisdom.

units.la: XII. Atqui argumentum praebet nobis infantium, quasi sese in illis explicantis naturae propensio ad fructus. Vix ullum perdici pomum non profert. Quid verò, vero, putas, contingeret, si cum paulatim infans ablactatur, maturis quibusdam & delicatis fructibus assuesceret? ib. Quid hoc ad statum innocentiae? Unde liquet, eandem futuram fuisse in eo statu conditionem infantium, quae est hodiernorum. 2. Infantium naturalis propensio ad fructus non est à naturali fastidio carnium, sed quia eorum est μετέχειν γαλακτος, & σεσηπότερον est τῶν τελείων. Alias magna vis consuetudinis in utramque partem, ut neque carnes fortassis appetant, qui plantis assueti, neque plantas, qui carnibus. Quae consuetudinis differentia in carnivoris & radicibus vescentibus animantibus est perspicua. Vide summum Philosophum Kenelmum Digbaeum de Natura corporum, cap. XXXVIII. pag. 326. 3. Largiamur cibos herbis esse τὸ ξέλπον; non inde sequetur τὸ ὄν, esum carnium prohibitum. Sed dedit hic Deus humanae prudentiae imperium.
units.tr: XII. Yet the infants provide us with an argument: in them the natural inclination of the nature to fruits shows itself. Hardly any infant fails to bring out the apple. What, indeed, do you think would happen if, as the infant is gradually weaned, it were accustomed to certain ripe and delicate fruits? Ibid. What has this to do with the state of innocence? From which it is clear that the condition of infants in that state would have been the same as that of infants today. 2. The infant's natural inclination to fruit does not come from a natural distaste for flesh, but because it is of the class that partakes of milk [metechein galaktos], and is more putrid than the mature. Otherwise there is great power of custom in both directions, so that perhaps those accustomed to plants do not crave flesh, nor those accustomed to flesh crave plants. This difference of custom is plain in carnivorous animals and in those that feed on roots. See the great philosopher Kenelm Digby, On the Nature of Bodies, ch. 38, p. 326. 3. Let us grant that herbs are the what is to be hoped for [to elpomenon]; it does not follow that the what is [to on], the eating of flesh, is forbidden. But here God gave the rule to human prudence.

units.la: XIII. Instat. Poetas, quibus moris fuerit, aliquas pristinae veritatis reliquias fabulis suis miscere, scripsisse, homines in aurea aetate, quae alia non fuerit ab ea, quam primi Parentes in Paradiso agebant, fructibus arborum vitiatas, quos terra absque cultura ferebat.
units.tr: XIII. He presses further: poets, who were accustomed to mix some remnants of the earlier truth into their fables, wrote that men in the golden age, which was no other than the age the first parents lived in Paradise, were nourished by the fruits of trees, which the earth bore without cultivation.

units.la: Testem interrogat Ovidium pag. 10. Poterat Curcellaeus Poetae, fabularum parenti, adjungere Dicaearchum in libris antiquitatum & descriptione Graeciae, ex quo Hieronymus contra Jovinianum tradidit, existimasse Gentiles, carnes sub Saturno, hoc est, in aureo Seculo, cum omnia humus funderet, neminem comedisse, sed universos vixisse frugibus & pomis, quae sponte terra gigneret. Sive Ovidio, sive Dicaearcho, sive quocunque alio nitatur, parum proficit. Quis enim sidem gentilibus habeat sanus, de statu innocentiae magnifica praedicantibus, quae vel nobis incognita, scripturarum beneficio usis? Res Sacras suis Traditionibus quam foede macularit Sathanas, innumera sunt documento, quae nihil attinet commemorare.
units.tr: He calls Ovid to witness, p. 10. Curcellaeus could have added to the poet, the parent of fables, Dicaearchus, in his books on antiquities and his description of Greece, from whom Jerome, against Jovinian, reports that the Gentiles thought that under Saturn, that is in the golden age, when the earth poured forth everything, no one ate flesh, but all lived on grains and fruits which the earth produced of its own accord. Whether one relies on Ovid, Dicaearchus, or anyone else, it achieves little. For what sane person would trust the Gentiles, who boast of magnificent things about the state of innocence, things that are unknown even to us who have the benefit of Scripture? How foully Satan has stained sacred matters with his own traditions is shown by countless examples, which it is not worth recalling here.

units.la: 2. Ovidio & Dicaearcho opponere licebit rigidissimum in hoc dogmate Pythagorae hyperaspistem Plutarchum, qui non obscure tradidit, primos homines carnibus vivitasse. Imo & defensionem primorum hominum affert ejusmodi: Tristissima, inquiunt, & terribilis apprime aetas nos excepit, cum in immensam atque difficillimam primi ortus incidissemus inopiam. Nondum suo loco Sol fixus haberat. Nondum certum conficiebat cursum. Nondum ortus ejus occasusque definitis distinguebatur limitibus. Neque suis statis conversionibus frugifera tempestatum anni intervalla discernebantur. Ad producendas nites fructus: ad artem culturae nullum suppeditabat instrumentum: nulla sapientia machina. Neque fames mor am patiebatur, neque aniversarium tempus sementis facta expectabat. Quid ergo mirum, si animalium carnibus usi sumus praeter naturam eo tempore, quo caenum edebatur, & cortex vorabatur ligni, & gramen invenire virens, ane radicem alicujus herba fortunatum putabatur: qui vero glandem gustassent atque comedissent, pra voluptate choros circa quercum aliquam, aut fagum duxerunt, vita datricem eam, matrem nutricemque appellantes. Vide, quae sequuntur orat. I. ꝛɩɛʃ σαρκοφαγίας. Quid quod apud eundem Empedoclea sententia, quod nostrae animae mortalibus corporibus sint illigatae, id ita interpretatur: quod panas ea tedium & ejus carnium pendant. Haec si vera, primos homines carnes comedisse, atque inde in mortalia corpora praecipites abiisse oportet. Apparet igitur, quam confusa, & invicem pugnantia Gentiles de his rebus scripserint.
units.tr: 2. Against Ovid and Dicaearchus it will be permissible to set Plutarch, the most rigid champion of Pythagoras' doctrine on this point, who did not obscurely teach that the first men lived on flesh. Indeed he also brings forward a defence of the first men of this kind: The most sorrowful and terrible age, they say, received us, when we fell into an immense and most difficult want at the first beginning. The sun had not yet held its fixed place. It did not yet complete a fixed course. Its rising and setting were not yet distinguished by definite limits. Nor were the fruitful intervals of the seasons of the year marked off by their regular turnings. For producing fruits there was no instrument for the art of cultivation: no skill, no machine. Nor did they suffer hunger, nor did they await the appointed time of sowing. What wonder, then, if we used the flesh of animals beyond nature, at that time when mud was eaten, and the bark of trees was devoured, and whoever found a green blade of grass or the root of some herb was thought fortunate; but those who had tasted and eaten an acorn danced in joy around some oak or beech, calling it the giver of life and the mother and nurse. See what follows in the oration Concerning Flesh-Eating [peri sarkophagias], Oration I. What of the fact that in the same author the Empedoclean opinion, that our souls are bound to mortal bodies, is interpreted thus: that they pay the penalty for that food and for flesh? If this is true, the first men must have eaten flesh, and from that fell headlong into mortal bodies. It is clear, then, how confused and mutually conflicting the Gentiles have written about these things.

units.la: XIV. Ad extremum objicit: Tantum abest, ut homo in illo statu carnibus vesceretur, ut ne quidem animantia, quae hodie rapto vivunt, eas tum attingerent. Deus enim in principio rerum nulli animantium terrestrium generi carnes in esum assignavit. pag. 11. Consentientia nobis scribit, quae nostrae causae minime nocent. Ipsi judicamus, simplicitate, moderatione, aliis etiam causis inductos primos homines, ut a carnibus abstinerent. Jus tantum & licentiam ipsis assertum imus. Caeterum non est magnopere mirandum, bruta animantia in eo statu raptu non victura. Nam fuit deterior eorum quam nostra conditio. Cur igitur illa carnibus viverent, abstinerent homines? Videmus hodieque majorem animalium, quam hominum frugalitatem. Neque enim appetunt delicias alias, neque pastu ultra saturitatem se facile ingurgitant. 2. Non tamen idonea ratio affertur abstinentiae interdictum Dei, Genes. L 29. 30. de quo loco supra satis actum. Cur vero quaedam animalia, tam ex quadrupedum, quam volucrum ordine carnes jam vorare videmus? Curcellaeus respondet: Praeter naturam illud esse, quam in Principio Deus illis indiderat. Ego cum nihil reperiam in carnium esu cum natura animantium pugnans, aliis causis, quam licentiae naturam violanti imputare malim. Quid si languidiore influxu coelestium corporum, segnius alimentum Terra produxit? quid si non ea vi, ut animantibus praecipue grandioribus nutriendis & saturandis herbae pares essent? Quid si ardentissimum odium, quo invicem correpta animantia quaedam, postquam semel vanitati objecta, causa fuit, ut laniandis invicem, vorandisque cupiditatem vindicta incitatam explerent? Alia plurima rima asferri possent, quae in Physicorum scholis exposita. Animantium natura, inquit, non usque adeo a statu integritatis degeneravit, quin si fames urgeat, herbis libenter vescantur. Id vero non tantum fame pressis, sed & aegrotantibus certum est accidere. Quadrupedia, quae silvestria sunt, eademque serrata dentibus, teste Philosopho, carnibus omnia vescuntur. Herbas tamen tangunt, cum morbo laborant. Canes herba ingesta evomunt, atque ita purgantur. Lupos etiam terram comedere, cum fament, testatur Aristoteles de Histor. Animal. lib. VIII. cap. V. quem, si libet, consule. In arca Noachi fieri potest, ut congruos cuique cibos ante Noachus parárit. Certè carnes pro carnivoris à Sapienti Noacho praeparatas, censuêre olim Origenes, homil. I h ad cap. VI. Genes. & Buteo de arca Noae. Sed & novimus esse fructus quosdam communes, quibus etiam carnivora pasci queant, ut ficus & castaneae. Ejusdem generis animalia verum est, non eodem se ubique cibo sustentare. Id vero totum est vel à casu, vel à consuetudine, quâ immutatum temperamentum, quae hic poene utramque paginam facit. Neque admirabilior ratio est, cur ursi in Alpibus herbis & pomis sylvestribus se oblectent, in Groenlandia carnibus saginentur; quàm cur olim carnibus se oblectárint & bubulorum caedibus Scythae, Sogdiani, Melanchlaeni, quos ex Herodoto Plutarchus nominavit loco ante citato; quin & Sarmatae, Islandi, Lituani: ab iis contrà maximam partem abstinuerint Aegyptii, Syri, Assyrii, Chaldaei, Scaligero in hoc argumento nominati, Exercit. CCVII. s. 2. Non desunt etiam exempla hominum, qui cùm priùs carnibus assuêssent, casu, mutato temperamento desueverunt, velut si in sylvis vel destinatione vel calamitate aliquando delitescendum esset. Quae etiam ratio abstinentiae Monachorum Aegyptiorum, de quibus Sozomenus.
units.tr: XIV. Finally he objects: So far is it from being the case that man in that state fed on flesh, that not even the animals which today live by prey ate it then. For God, in the beginning of things, assigned the flesh of no kind of land animal for food. p. 11. He writes things that agree with us, and which do little harm to our cause. We ourselves judge that the first humans were led to abstain from flesh by simplicity, moderation and other causes too. We only assert that they had the right and the liberty. Otherwise it is not greatly to be wondered at that brute animals in that state did not live by prey, for their condition was worse than ours. Why then should the animals live on flesh and men abstain? Even today we see that animals are more frugal than men. For they do not crave other delicacies, nor do they easily gorge themselves beyond satiety. 2. Yet no sound reason is offered for the prohibition of abstinence by God, Gen. 1:29-30, about which passage enough has been said above. But why do we now see some animals, both among the quadrupeds and among the birds, devouring flesh? Curcellaeus answers: That is contrary to nature, which God had implanted in them in the beginning. I, since I find nothing in the eating of flesh that conflicts with the nature of animals, would rather impute it to other causes than to a violation of their nature by licence. What if, through a feebler influx of the heavenly bodies, the earth produced food more sluggishly? What if not with such a force that herbs were sufficient to nourish and satisfy the animals, especially the larger ones? What if a most fierce hatred, by which certain animals, once they had been thrown into a state of vanity, seized one another, was the cause, so that their lust for mutual tearing and devouring was stirred by revenge and satisfied it? Many other causes could be brought forward, which are set out in the schools of the natural philosophers. The nature of animals, he says, has not so far degenerated from the state of integrity that, if hunger presses, they do not gladly feed on herbs. But this is certainly true not only of those pressed by hunger but also of the sick. Wild quadrupeds, which have serrated teeth, all feed on flesh, as the Philosopher testifies. Yet they touch herbs when they suffer from disease. Dogs vomit up herbs they have swallowed, and so are purged. Aristotle, in his History of Animals, Book 8, ch. 5, testifies that wolves also eat earth when they are hungry; consult him if you like. In Noah's ark it is possible that Noah, the wise man, prepared to each kind the food suited to it beforehand. Certainly Origen, in his First Homily on Gen. 6, and Buteo, On Noah's Ark, have long held that Noah, the wise man, prepared flesh for the carnivores. But we also know that there are certain fruits common to all, on which even carnivores can be fed, such as figs and chestnuts. It is true that animals of the same kind do not nourish themselves on the same food everywhere. But this is wholly due either to chance or to custom, by which the temperament is changed, which here almost fills one whole page. Nor is there a more wonderful reason why bears in the Alps delight in herbs and wild fruits, while in Greenland they are fattened on flesh, than why once the Scythians, Sogdians and Melanchlaeni, whom Plutarch named from Herodotus in the passage cited above, delighted in flesh and in the slaughter of oxen; and indeed the Sarmatians, the Icelanders and the Lithuanians; whereas, on the contrary, the Egyptians, Syrians, Assyrians and Chaldeans, named by Scaliger in this matter, Exercise 207, section 2, for the most part abstained from it. Nor are there lacking examples of men who, having previously been accustomed to flesh, through chance, when their temperament was changed, grew unaccustomed to it, as when at some time, by appointment or by calamity, they had to hide in the woods. This is also the reason for the abstinence of the Egyptian Monks, of whom Sozomen writes.

units.la: CAPUT III. In statu peccati, temporibus diluvium antegressis, carnium esum licitum fuisse, probatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. That in the state of sin, before the Flood, the eating of meat was lawful, is proved.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Proceditur ad statum peccati. Sententia Theodoreti, Tertulliani, Martyris, Merceri, Casauboni, Tostati, Carthusiani. Τεοφ̀ν
units.tr: The argument proceeds to the state of sin. The opinions of Theodoret, Tertullian, Martyr, Mercerus, Casaubon, Tostatus and the Carthusian.

units.la: τῶν νομιμων ἱερέων quid sit Athenaeo? Antediluvianis jus carnium & quaecunq; exercitium asseritur. 1. Probatur illud primò ex domi-nio repetito. 2. Curcellaei lubricitas. Ejusdem exceptiones. Hieronymi suffragium examinatur. 3. Secunda ratio a Sacri-ficiis Antediluvianorum. Adamus sacrificavit. Tenupha. Theru-ma. Ἀθυτα ἱερὰ ἰσθίειν. Μεθύειν unde Athenaeo? 4. Curcellaei exceptiones elisae. 5. Holocaustum ὁλοκάρπωμα. Scaligeri error. Ἐνδελεχισμὸς sive Sacrificium juge. Sal-masii sententia de duabus vesperis. Mincha. Piggul. 6. Habelis Sacrificium non fuisse holocaustum probatur. Pinguedines ovium. Mercerii, Grotii, Seldeni vota examinantur. Habelis Sacrificium non fuit sagmen. Locus Genes. XXXI. 54. 7. De ἐμπυεσμῷ Sacrificiorum. Locum habuisse non tantum in holo-caustis. Quis usus ovium Abelis? 8. Tertia ratio à vestibus peliceis Protoplastorum. Procopii, Gennadii, Theodori, Ori-genis error. Non unicum par animantium creatum. 9. Excep-tiones Curcellaei. 10. Quarta ratio à discrimine animalium mundorum & immundorum. De eo sententia Larchii, Theodo-reti, Bedae. 11. Exceptiones Curcellaei. 12. Quinta ratio de-fenditur. Adagium expositum: Amyclas silentium perdere. 13. Objectio ex Genes. IX. 4. Probatur ibi non de nova, sed de re-novata concessione agi. 14. Rationes concessionis carnium post-diluvianae examinantur. Curcellaus Tertulliano subscribit, car-nes indultas ob συλληρομαχίαν. Dogmatis impietas exaggera-tur. 15. Rationibus asseritur libertas esûs sanguinis ante dilu-vium. 16.
units.tr: What are "the lawful priests" [τῶν νομίμων ἱερέων] in Athenaeus? The right to eat meat, and its practice in general, is asserted for the antediluvians. 1. It is first proved from the dominion given again. 2. The slipperiness of Curcellaeus. His exceptions. Jerome's support is examined. 3. The second reason, from the sacrifices of the antediluvians. Adam offered sacrifice. Tenupha. Terumah. To eat unoffered sacred things [ἀθυτα ἱερὰ ἐσθίειν]. Where does Athenaeus get "to get drunk" [μεθύειν]? 4. The exceptions of Curcellaeus are overturned. 5. The holocaust [ὁλοκάρπωμα]. The error of Scaliger. The continual offering [ἐνδελεχισμὸς], or the perpetual sacrifice. The view of Salmasius on the two evenings. Minchah. Piggul. 6. It is proved that Abel's sacrifice was not a holocaust. The fat of the sheep. The views of Mercerus, Grotius and Selden are examined. Abel's sacrifice was not a peace offering. The passage Genesis 31:54. 7. On the burning [ἐμπυεσμῷ] of sacrifices. That it took place not only in holocausts. What use did Abel make of the sheep? 8. The third reason, from the skin garments of our first parents. The error of Procopius, Gennadius, Theodore and Origen. Not a single pair of each kind of animal was created. 9. The exceptions of Curcellaeus. 10. The fourth reason, from the distinction between clean and unclean animals. On this, the opinion of Larchus, Theodoret and Bede. 11. The exceptions of Curcellaeus. 12. The fifth reason is defended. The proverb explained: Amyclae lost by silence. 13. The objection from Genesis 9:4. It is shown there that the question concerns not a new grant but a renewed one. 14. The reasons for the grant of meat after the Flood are examined. Curcellaeus agrees with Tertullian that meat was granted because of the joint fight [συλληρομαχίαν]. The impiety of the doctrine is magnified. 15. By these reasons the freedom to eat blood before the Flood is asserted. 16.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Sic in Statu Innocentiae confido satis me obtinuisse licentiam car-nium vescendarum. Pergit Curcellaeus ad Statum Peccati, qui diluvium antecessit. Jam confiteor lubens, Patres nonnullos, quos longiori intervallo secuti Lyranus, Tostatus, Carthu-sianus, negare, concessas Antediluvianis carnes. Itaque amplifica-tam post diluvium concessionem statuunt, sive quòd indigentia ho-minum post diluvium facta major sit, Coelorum aspectu & influxu naturae humanae severiore facto, telluris salsis Oceani aquis inunda-ta. ta, multum triftiore & fteriliore facta, & mirum in modum valetu- dine hominis inde labefactata: sive quòd præviderit Deus, homines ad idololatriam fuisse proclives, & temere ac impie bruta animalia veneraturos: proinde concessum homini ex animantibus cibum, quo intelligeret, oppidò stultum & absurdum, iis rem divinam facere, qui in prædam ipsi divino indulta concesserint. Ita ferè Theodoretus. Tertullianum tamen jam Montanizantem parum est ut moremur, cui visum, concessas demum Postdiluvianis carnes, propter mortalium ὀνλητροχαρὸ Nàu ingravescentem. Quod est dictum & delictum hominis ad Manichæismum inclinantis. Doctissimus etiam Martyr loc. Comm. Class. III. cap. V. Patrum errori secundas fecit. Addo Mercerum, qui se stipat omnium Hebræorum suffragiis. Imò & Casaubonus in Athenæum lib. I. II. considerenter satis: Constat tam ex sacris, quàm ex aliis litteris, primis temporibus, ignota hominibus carnium manducatione, tantùm in honorem Numinis mactari solitas hostias. Piguit postea mortales olerum, & τῆς ζωῆς τροφῆς. Itaque cœpère carnibus vesci: sed parcè. Inde interpretatur illud Athenæi, visam antiquis Heroibus parùm convenientem τεραστῶν τῶν νεολεῶν ἐμψύχων, tenerarum animantium carnes. Nobis quidem non est hic animus aliquid asserere, quod temeritatem vel arrogantiam spiret. Itaque ne hoc quidem liquidò adfirmabimus, in universum carnes crebrum & quotidianum fuisse Antidiluvianis cibum. Rationibus tamen mihi videor non omnino invalidis instructus, quæ probatum dent, Antidiluvianis & jus & usum qualemcunque carnium concessum. Quas proinde prius producam, & à Curcellæi Exceptionibus defendam, quàm contraria argumenta sub incudem revocem.
units.tr: Thus, in the state of innocence, I trust I have sufficiently established the licence to eat meat. Curcellaeus goes on to the state of sin, which preceded the Flood. Now I gladly admit that some Fathers, and those who followed them at a longer interval, Lyra, Tostatus and the Carthusian, deny that meat was granted to the antediluvians. They therefore hold that the concession was enlarged after the Flood, either because the need of men became greater after the Flood, the aspect of the heavens and the influence on human nature having become harsher, the earth having been flooded with the salt waters of the ocean, made much sadder and more barren, and the health of men having been wonderfully weakened by this; or because God foresaw that men would be prone to idolatry and would rashly and impiously worship brute animals. Hence the food from animals was granted to man, so that he might understand it to be utterly foolish and absurd to perform sacred rites to those whose prey had been given by God himself. This is roughly the view of Theodoret. However, we need not dwell long on Tertullian, already leaning towards Montanism, who thought that meat was granted only after the Flood, because of the increasing wretchedness of mortals [ὀνλητροχαρὸ]. That is a saying, and a fault, of a man inclined to Manichaeism. The most learned Martyr too, in his Common Places, Class III, chapter V, gave second place to the error of the Fathers. I add Mercerus, who props himself on the agreement of all the Hebrews. Indeed Casaubon also, in his commentary on Athenaeus, Book I and II, says quite sensibly: It is established, both from the sacred writings and from other literature, that in the earliest times, when the eating of flesh was unknown to men, the victims were usually slaughtered only in honour of the deity. Afterwards men grew weary of vegetables and of the food of life [τῆς ζωῆς τροφῆς]. So they began to eat meat, but sparingly. From this he explains Athenaeus's statement that the ancient heroes thought the tender living creatures [τεραστῶν τῶν νεολεῶν ἐμψύχων], that is, the flesh of young animals, unsuitable. For my part, I have no wish to assert anything that breathes rashness or arrogance. So I will not even firmly affirm that the flesh of animals was a common and daily food of the antediluvians in general. Yet I seem to myself to be equipped with arguments that are not wholly weak, which will show that both the right and some kind of practice of eating meat were granted to the antediluvians. I will therefore set these out first, and defend them against the exceptions of Curcellaeus, before I call the opposing arguments back to the anvil.

units.la: II. Primò illud ἀνιξαλώτον, homini etiam lapso dominium in animantia illibatum constitisse. Manifestum facit locus Genes. IX. 2. 3. 4. Terror vester ac tremor sit super cuncta animalia. Omnia בידכם נתנו in manus vestras sunt data. Quibus verbis cum emphasi plenum dominium & eminens potestas homini restituitur. Nos autem, quousque illud dominium se extendat, abundè explicavimus capitis II. thesi IV. & V. Ut jam dubitari nequeat, quin jus dederit ad mactandum. Argumentis meis, quæ supra protuli, accedit ipsius Curcellæi vel consensus tacitus, vel lubricitas & inconstantia. Fatetur enim p. 29. in casu extremæ necessitatis licuisse, se carnibus animalium sustentare. Velut, inquit, si multiplicato genere hominum deficeret fructus aliqui in sterilem tilem rilem infulam, & cateris omnibus alimentis destitutam, sed quæ piscibus memoratur mari alueretur: quis dubitat, eos absque peccato piscium carnibus se potuisse EX-PLERE & vita mutorum istorum natabilium dispensatio sua consutere. Si jus non fuit datum mactandorum animantium, tuta ne casu quidem extremæ necessitatis licuit citra sonticam culpam. Quod ex præcepto Dei vel suâ naturâ malum est, quemadmodum ullo casu vel bonum vel indifferens exististi?
units.tr: II. First, that the dominion over animals, undiminished, remained with man even after the Fall, which is inviolable [ἀνιξαλώτον]. Genesis 9:2, 3, 4 makes this plain: Let your fear and dread be upon all the beasts. All things have been given into your hand [בידכם נתנו]. By these words the full dominion and eminent power are restored to man with emphasis. Now, how far that dominion extends we have explained at length in chapter II, theses IV and V. Hence it cannot be doubted that it gave the right to slaughter. To my arguments set out above is added the tacit consent, or rather the slipperiness and inconsistency, of Curcellaeus himself. For he admits on page 29 that in a case of extreme necessity it was lawful to sustain oneself on the flesh of animals. For example, he says, if, the human race having multiplied, some crop failed in a barren island, destitute of all other food, but which is said to be fed by fish in the sea: who doubts that they could then have fed themselves on the flesh of fish without sin, and that they could have stitched together the life of those swimming creatures in their own arrangement? If there was no right given to slaughter animals, then even in a case of extreme necessity it could not have been lawful without grievous guilt. What is evil by God's command or by its own nature, how could it ever be good or indifferent in any case?

units.la: III. Curcellæus ad argumentum excipit.
units.tr: III. Curcellæus takes exception to the argument.

units.la: 1. Dominium hominis tum fuisse plenum, tum quoad jus, tum quoad exercitium, quando Adam nondum adversus suum Creatorem peccaverat. Atqui illo tempore non mactabantur ad victum. Dedecuisset enim Paradisum laniena fœdare. pag. 26. 27. Resp. Plenum omnino fuit quoad jus. De exercitio non largior. Atqui, inquit, homo poterat animalia, si forte rebellassent, partim vi, partim astu voluntati sua subjicere, & ad parendum cogere. Multa hic peccata. Dominium restringit ad coercitionem. Probatum autem, non hanc tantum intelligi. Deinde supponit, animantia in statu integritatis rebellatura. Est autem rebellio vanitati animantium deputanda, cui post peccati ingressum demum sunt obnoxia facta. Denique dicit potuisse hominem animantia subigere. Quis neget, potuisse? Quæritur, an actu subegerit? Non de potentia vel jure, sed de actu & exercitio probationem suscepit. Sed cur dedecuisset Paradisum fœdari laniena permissa, utili, & in qua nihil inordinatum?
units.tr: 1. Man's dominion was then full, both as to right and as to exercise, when Adam had not yet sinned against his Creator. But at that time animals were not slaughtered for food. For it would have disgraced Paradise to defile it with slaughter. pp. 26, 27. Reply: The dominion was entirely full as to right. As to exercise I do not concede. But, he says, man could, if the animals happened to rebel, subject them to his will partly by force and partly by cunning, and compel them to obey. Many errors here. He restricts dominion to coercion, though it has been proved that this is not all that is meant. Next, he supposes that the animals would have rebelled in the state of integrity. But rebellion should be attributed to the vanity of the animals, to which they became liable only after the entrance of sin. Finally, he says that man could have subdued the animals. Who denies that he could? The question is whether he actually did so. I have undertaken to prove not the power or the right, but the act and the exercise. But why would Paradise have been disgraced by slaughter that was permitted, useful, and in which there was nothing disorderly?

units.la: 2. Multa alia ex animantibus commoda percipere hominem potuisse præter esum. pag. 27. Haud dubie. Neque enim simplex dominium, & ad pauca restrictum. Probares, Curcellæ, ad ista commoda non accumulatum jus mactandi. Vel enim ideo exclusum a dominio, quia Deus prohibuit carnibus vesci: vel quia carnes ad nutriendum ineptæ: vel quia crudele, cæde & vulneribus animantium se contaminare. Si prohibuit, ubi interdictum? Si crudelis mactatio, cur post diluvium a Sanctissimo Deo, qui crudelitatem & sævitiam odit, concessa? Inutiles ad nutrimentum carnes esse, imperitè & inconsultò dixeris.
units.tr: 2. Man could have derived many other benefits from animals besides eating them. p. 27. Undoubtedly. For dominion is not simply a matter of a few restricted uses. You would have to prove, Curcellæus, that the right to slaughter was not added to these benefits. Either man was excluded from the right to slaughter because God forbade him to eat flesh, or because flesh is unfit for nourishment, or because it is cruel to defile oneself with the slaughter and wounds of animals. If God forbade it, where is the prohibition? If slaughter is cruel, why was it granted after the Flood by the most holy God, who hates cruelty and savagery? To say that flesh is useless for nourishment is to speak ignorantly and rashly.

units.la: 3. Suffragium profert Hieronymi ex I. II. adversus Jovinianum, prolixè conceptum p. 27. 28. Resp. Hieronymus est in Curcellæi castris, quantum negotium præsens concernit. Proinde non omisimus jam supra in adversis partibus numerare. Fallitur autem magnopere cum Hieronymo Curcellæus. Nam Hieronymo utique non est propositum agere de temporibus antediluvianis, sed de suis. Ac negat dissere, suis temporibus licitum esse carnium usum. An igitur Dominus Jesus, perfectionis & puritatis exemplar prævaricatus est, cùm pisces edit? Cùm distribuit & locavit populo? An Apostolus, omnem Dei creaturam esse bonam, & nihil esse rejiciendum, quod cum gratiarum actione percipitur dictitans? Indigna sanè præsumptio. Tametsi ipsum argumentum Hieronymi leve est omnino & pulmoneum. Nam positione unius finis cæteros removet, quod vetant Dialecticorum regulæ. Dixit, ad medicinam creata animantia & plantas. An-ideo non ad esum? Et si ad medicinam, an mactare non licuit? Hoc tamen Pythagoricus noster fastidit, tanquam paradisi dedecus. Peccat Hieronymus, quod inductione animantium nos urget, quæ alimentis inepta, &, ut cum Tacito loquar, Hist. IV. vers. 62. 2. quæ profana fœdáque ducimus. Quanquam non omnibus eadem utilia pulchráque esse constat.
units.tr: 3. He offers the support of Jerome from the second book against Jovinian, quoted at length. pp. 27, 28. Reply: As far as the present matter is concerned, Jerome is in Curcellæus's camp. Therefore I have already noted above that he is on the opposing side. But Curcellæus is greatly mistaken about Jerome. For Jerome did not intend to treat of the antediluvian times, but of his own. He denies that the use of flesh was lawful in his own times. Did the Lord Jesus, then, the pattern of perfection and purity, sin when he ate fish? When he distributed and set it before the people? Or did the Apostle, who declares that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving? That presumption is truly unworthy. Yet Jerome's own argument is altogether slight and frothy. For by positing one end he removes the others, which the rules of the dialecticians forbid. He said that animals and plants were created for medicine. Therefore not for food? And if for medicine, was it not lawful to slaughter them? Yet our Pythagorean finds this loathsome, as a disgrace to Paradise. Jerome errs in urging us by the example of animals which are unfit for food and, to use Tacitus's words (Hist. IV, 62), which we regard as profane and foul. Although it is well known that the same things are not equally useful and pleasing to all.

units.la: IV. Secunda mihi ratio à Sacrificiis Antediluvianorum petita. Sacrificiis iratum numen Sancti Patres, non indulgente tantùm, sed instituente Deo, placârunt. De Habele notorium. Hariolamur etiam de Adamo. Nam vestigium mactatarum pecudum ad ἱλασμὸν pro peccatis apparet in tunicis pelliceis, quibus Adamum & uxorem ejus vestivit Deus Genes. III. 21. Unde enim tunicæ pelliceæ non mactatis pecudibus? Deinde hinc videtur nata lex Levit. VIII. 18. Sacerdos, qui offert holocausti victimam, habebit pellem ejus, ubi est vox Hebraea עור. Denique testis Apostolus: Vetus fœdus absque sanguinis effusione dedicatum non fuisse, & absque sanguinis effusione non fieri remissionem, Hebr. IX. vers. 18. 22. Vel igitur cum promissione illa de venturo semine mulieris nulla facta est Fœderis Dei cum homine spirituali dedicatio & instauratio, quâ peccatorum sperarét remissionem: vel non est facta sine sanguinis effusione, quæ est genuinus sacrificiorum character. Consentientes habeo Doctissimos Cloppenburgium & Schotanum. Illum in Schola Sacrific. pag. 12. 13. hunc in Heptaëm. p. 491. Accedit Judæus author Neve Schalon. L. IX. c. V. ראשון קרם שחשרה היה כלו קרבן ולא היה צריך לקרבן ואחר שחטא וארגיש בחסרון לו החטא רוצה לתקן הכעוות הקרובו קרבנו Adamus antequam peccaret, totus erat sacrificium, ideóque sacrificio non erat illi opus. Sed postquam peccavit, & sensit defectum, quem ei peccatum inule-rat; volens reparare quod perverterat, obtulit suum sacrificium. Atque hinc jam firmiter concludo, Antidiluvianos carnes comedisse. Nam perpetuus in Sacrificiis mos obtinuit, ut qui sacrificant, de altari viverent. Clarè Apostolus: Ignoratis, quòd oi tà ièoa ièyazóμενοι, ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ ἐσθίουσιν; οἱ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντες τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζονται, 1. Cor. IX. 13. Lex diserte sanxit: Omnis oblatio & sacrificium, & quicquid pro peccato ac delicto reddetur mihi, & edetis in sancta sanctorum, tuum eris & filiorum tuorum, Num. XVIII. 9. Ergo victimae fuerunt donum sacerdotum ac stipendium, qua parte non sunt combustae. Partes etiam victimae Sacerdoti eximias definit Deus, Exod. XXIX. 28. פֶּסֶל הַתְּרוּמָה pectusculum agitatum, & שׁוֹק הַתְּרוּמָה armum elevatum. Terupha vocatur oblatio, ob ritum elevandi. Nam Moses manus supponebat manibus novelli Sacerdotis, & elevabat eas sursum, ac deinde deprimebat deorsum; mox ab Oriente in Occidentem, ac demum à Meridie ad Septentrionem ducebat, si Jarchi & Hebraeis credere fas est. Terma verò oblatio existimatur, à sursum usque deorsum descendens & agitata. Comederunt igitur Sacerdotes carnes. Imò convivia ad id instituta. Videtur Gentilium Sacerdotibus idem in more positum fuisse, ut partem adolerent, partem comederent. Hinc hominem improbum Athenaeus vocat, qui ἀθύτους ἱερὰ ἐσθίει. Proverbium, quo notati, qui partem adolendam Deo non consecrarunt. Vide Casaubonum Animadverss. in Athen. I. 11. Quin & diserte idem Athenaeus ex Aristotele lib. X. p. 447. docet: μολύνειν dictum quasi μετὰ τὸ θύειν, quòd Ethnici peractis Sacrificiis solíti sunt in conviviis solennibus liberalius genio indulgere. Proinde etiam juris Hebraeorum lex centesima trigesima tertia est מִצְוַת אֲכִילַת שְׁאָר מִנְחוֹת Praeceptum de comedendis reliquiis munerum. Sed & naturalis ratio dictat, in usu hominum esse debere, quae Deo sacrificantur. Absque quo esset, non mereretur laudem Deo devovens illa, quae vel nullum vel mediocrem usum sibi praestant.
units.tr: IV. My second argument is drawn from the sacrifices of the antediluvians. The holy Fathers appeased the angry deity with sacrifices, which God not only permitted but instituted. This is well known of Abel. We may also conjecture about Adam. For the trace of slaughtered animals offered as expiation for sins appears in the leather tunics with which God clothed Adam and his wife (Gen. 3:21). For whence came the leather tunics, if not from slaughtered animals? Further, the law in Lev. 8:18 seems to have arisen from this: The priest who offers the victim of the burnt offering shall have its skin, where the Hebrew word is [עור] (ʿor). Finally, the Apostle is a witness: The old covenant was not dedicated without the shedding of blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission (Heb. 9:18, 22). Therefore either no dedication and renewal of God's covenant with spiritual man took place along with that promise of the future seed of the woman, by which hope of forgiveness of sins was given, or it did not take place without the shedding of blood, which is the genuine mark of sacrifices.
