I have in agreement the most learned Cloppenburg and Schotanus: the former in his Schola Sacrificiorum, pp. 12, 13; the latter in his Heptas, p. 491. To these is added the Jewish author of Neve Shalom, book 9, chapter 5: [ראשון קרם שחשרה היה כלו קרבן ולא היה צריך לקרבן ואחר שחטא וארגיש בחסרון לו החטא רוצה לתקן הכעוות הקרובו קרבנו] Adam, before he sinned, was wholly a sacrifice, and so had no need of a sacrifice. But after he sinned and felt the lack which sin had caused him, wishing to repair what he had perverted, he offered his sacrifice. And hence I now firmly conclude that the antediluvians ate flesh. For it became the constant custom in sacrifices that those who sacrificed should live from the altar. The Apostle states it clearly: "Do you not know that those who perform the sacred services eat of the temple, and those who wait upon the altar share with the altar?" (1 Cor. 9:13) [Οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι οἱ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζόμενοι ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐσθίουσιν; οἱ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντες τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζονται]. The law expressly ordained: "Every offering, sacrifice, and whatever is rendered to me for sin or trespass, shall be yours and your sons', and you shall eat it in the most holy place" (Num. 18:9). Therefore the victims were the gift and the stipend of the priests, in that part which was not burned. God also assigns to the priest the choice portions: the breast of the wave offering [חזה התנופה] (Exod. 29:28) and the thigh of the heave offering [שוק התרומה]. The offering is called tenupha because of the rite of waving it. For Moses placed his hands over the hands of the newly installed priest, lifted them upward, then lowered them downward, and then moved them from east to west, and finally from south to north, if we may trust Jarchi and the Hebrews. But the tenupha is thought to be an offering moved up and down and waved. The priests therefore ate the flesh. Indeed, feasts were instituted for this purpose. It appears that among the Gentiles the same custom was observed for their priests, that they burned one part and ate the rest. Hence Athenaeus calls a wicked man one who eats the sacred portions without burning (ἀθύτους); this is a proverb by which those were marked who did not consecrate a portion to be burned for God. See Casaubon's Animadversions on Athenaeus, I, 11. Indeed Athenaeus also expressly teaches from Aristotle, book 10, p. 447, that the word μολύνειν (to defile) is said as if from μετὰ τὸ θύειν (after sacrificing), because the Gentiles, when the sacrifices were finished, were accustomed to indulge their appetites more freely at solemn feasts. Accordingly, the 133rd commandment of Jewish law is the precept concerning eating the remainder of the offerings [מִצְוַת אֲכִילַת שְׁאָר מִנְחוֹת]. But natural reason too dictates that what is sacrificed to God should be put to human use. Otherwise, those who devote to God things that yield no use or only a mediocre use to themselves would not deserve praise.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sentit hoc argumento se premi Curcellaeus. Haud igitur desultorie cum eo congreditur. Respondet 1. Male consequentiam duci à Setulis diluvium consecutis ad ea, quae antecesserunt. Mores perpetuis mutationum vicissitudinibus esse obnoxios, & quae nunc atque hic observantur, olim & alibi fuisse incognita, & contrà, pag. 31. Atqui primò Apostolus cum dicit, eos, qui altari adsident, de altari participare, non quid hoc vel illo tempore factum sit, explicat, sed respicit ad rò ἐπιστρad illud, quod justum & æquum fuit. Sacerdotes jugulabant, excoriabant, secabant, coquebant. Quod operosum est. Æquum fuit igitur, ut pro mercede portionem sibi decerperent. Hinc Apostolus infert, non esse stipendiis præcones Evangelii defraudandos. Deinde laudi datum Abeli, quòd obtulerit non graciliores de grege, sed מחלביהן de adipibus eorum, Genes. IV. vers. 3. Hoc indicat, carnes comedi solitas. Secus non vertisset in gloriam Habelis, quòd graciliores sibi servavit, pinguiores Deo devovit. Ambrosius lib. II. de Caino & Abele cap. V: Abelem à Deo prælatum Caino, quòd pinguiora gregis offerret, sicut David docet, dicens: Sicut adipe & pinguedine repleatur anima mea. Et: Holocaustum tuum pinguescat. Hoc docens: Acceptabile esse sacrificium, quod pingue, quod nitidum, & quodam pabulo fidei ac devotionis, verbique cœlestis uberiore alimonia saginatum. Hinc Cajetanus Comm. ad Genes. IV. Pastorale, inquit, officium Abelis testatur, gregem ovium humanis usibus servisse, non solum præbendo lanas & agnos. Nisi fuissent agni hominibus ad esum, nulla fuisset laus Abelis ex eo, quòd primogenitos pingues elegisset ad Divinum Sacrificium. Perinde enim fuisset Abeli pingues atque macilentos sacrificare, si non propter esum carnium, sed propter solum pellium usum gregem pascebat. Quin & hoc Moses non obscure innuit, eodem ritu Habelem sacrificâsse, quo est sub lege sacrificatum. Sicut igitur sub lege pinguedo in altari Deo adolita, reliquiæ Sacerdotibus Sacræ, sic Habel Deo pinguedinem obtulit, sibi reliquias vindicavit. Imò cùm ante Mosaicam legem convivium ex Sacrificio celebravit Patriarcha Jacob Genes. XXXI. 54. non potuit ille ritus non manare ab antiquissima traditione. Denique accedit his omnibus ratio Præcepti Mosaici, quam Judæi perhibent apud Rabbi Levi Barzelonitam שבבר הוא לקרבן שיאכלוהו משרתי השם בעמם ולא שיתניו לפתותים לאכלם: Quia hoc est de dignitate Sacrificii, ut edant illud Ministri Dei Benedicti ipsi, non autem esuri inferiorum destinent.
units.tr: Curcellaeus feels that this argument presses him hard, so he does not dodge it but engages it directly. He replies, first, that it is a bad inference to argue from the sacrifices before the Flood to what came after them. Customs are subject to constant change: what is observed here and now was once unknown elsewhere, and the reverse also holds (p. 31). But first, when the Apostle says that those who wait at the altar share in the altar, he is not explaining what was done at this or that time. He looks instead to what was just and fair. The priests slaughtered, flayed, cut up and cooked the victims, which was laborious work. It was therefore fair that they should take a portion for their pay, and from this the Apostle infers that the heralds of the Gospel should not be cheated of their support. Next, Abel is praised because he offered not the leaner animals of the flock but מחלביהן of their fat (Gen. 4:3) [מחלביהן]. This indicates that flesh was customarily eaten. Otherwise it would not have redounded to Abel's glory that he kept the leaner animals for himself and devoted the fatter ones to God. Ambrose, book 2 of On Cain and Abel, chapter 5: Abel was preferred by God to Cain because he offered the fatter of the flock, as David teaches, saying: "Let my soul be filled as with fat and marrow." And: "Let your burnt offering be made fat." He teaches this: an acceptable sacrifice is one that is fat, sleek, and fattened on a certain pasture of faith and devotion, and on the richer nourishment of the heavenly Word. Hence Cajetan, in his commentary on Genesis 4: The pastoral occupation of Abel shows, he says, that the flock served human uses, not only by providing wool and lambs. Unless the lambs had been for men to eat, Abel would have earned no praise for choosing the fat firstlings for the divine sacrifice. For Abel would have sacrificed fat animals and lean ones alike, if he had pastured the flock not for the eating of meat but only for the use of its skins. Moses also hints, not obscurely, that Abel sacrificed in the same manner as sacrifice was later performed under the law. Just as under the law the fat was burnt on the altar for God and the remains were reserved for the priests, so Abel offered the fat to God and claimed the remains for himself. Indeed, when the patriarch Jacob celebrated a meal from a sacrifice before the Mosaic law (Gen. 31:54), that rite cannot but have come from the most ancient tradition. Finally, to all this is added the reason for the Mosaic precept, which the Jews give in Rabbi Levi Barcelonita: שבבר הוא לקרבן שיאכלוהו משרתי השם בעמם ולא שיתניו לפתותים לאכלם [it is part of the dignity of the sacrifice that the ministers of the blessed God eat it themselves, and not that they assign it to the hungry of the lower sort].

units.la: VI. 2. Sub lege, inquit; fuisse oblata plurima holocausta, quæ (ut nomen ipsum significat) tota consumebantur.
units.tr: VI. 2. Under the law, he says, many burnt offerings were offered, which (as the name itself signifies) were consumed whole.

units.la: Talia erant, quæ singulis diebus, mane & vespere, in Tabernaculo primùm, deinde in Templo Hierosolymitano fiebant, unde nec Sacerdotes, nec ulli alii quidquam delibabant. pag. 31. 32. Ita est. Hinc Holocaustum quasi ὁλον καυστόν, totum combustum. Frequenter etiam Græci converterunt ὁλοκαύτωμα, quòd totum in Dei fructum cederet: Καυστὰ dicunt, quæ ab ipsu muntur igne. Quod Latini non possunt exprimere, nisi voce adiendi. In Hebræo est עלה. ab ascensione in fumum. Alibi etiam [Hebrew: עולה אשה] Levit. I. 9. 13. Qua in re deceptus incomparabilis Scaliger, qui [Hebrew: אשה] conatus est reddere Sacrificium igniarium. Atqui non [Hebrew: אשר] simpliciter est igniarium Sacrificium, sed junctum cum [Hebrew: עולה]. Alias etiam in Sacrificio non holocausto significat eam partem, quam ignis vorat & consumit. Significantius etiam [Hebrew: כליל] vocat Moses Levit. VI. 23. cujus nullam partem Sacerdos decerpsit cap. V. 16. Tale omnino ὁλο-καύτωμα fuit [Hebrew: עולה תמיד] Graecis ἐνδελεχισμὸς, Sacrificium juge. Describitur Num. XXVIII. 3. 4. 5. 6. Duplex fuit juge Sacrificium. Unum, quod mane offerebatur ab ortu Solis. Alterum, quod [Hebrew: בין הערבים] inter duas vesperas. Salmasii Illustris sententia hodie fere inter eruditos recepta: [Hebrew: ערב] esse totum tempus pomeridianum, quod in duas partes antiquitus distribuebant. Unde dicebatur inter duas vesperas fieri, quod circa tertiam horam fiebat, ex nostra numeratione. Salmasio tamen cum alia, tum obstare illud videtur, quod sancitum Levit. VI. 2. ut holocausti adustio in altari fiat [Hebrew: כל הלילה עד הבקר] tota nocte usque ad mane. Est autem vero dissimile, holocaustum juge vespertinum a tempore pomeridiano ad matutinum usque igni altaris sufficientem fomitem ministrare potuisse. Confer Maimonidem in Summa Thalmud. Tract. de Precib. & Bened. Sacerdotum c. III. ss. 2. Sed haec ἐν παρόδῳ. Ceterum non sola holocausta penitus consumta, sed etiam Sacrificia, quorum sanguine aspergebat altare Templi interius Levit. VI. 30. Sacrificia etiam Sacerdotis v. 33. Denique Piggul, sive Sacrificium, de quo Sacerdos offerens tempore mactationis suscipit [Hebrew: פסול מחשבה] pravam cogitationem. De quibus vid R. Levi ad Praec. 142. 143. 145. & seq. Nam Sacerdotibus nefas fuit iis vesci.
units.tr: Such were the offerings made every day, morning and evening, first in the Tabernacle and then in the Temple at Jerusalem, from which neither the priests nor anyone else took anything (p. 31–32). That is so. Hence the holocaust is named as if holon kauston, wholly burnt [ὁλον καυστόν]. The Greeks often also rendered it holokauthoma [ὁλοκαύτωμα], because the whole went to God's portion; they call kausta those offerings that are burnt by fire itself. The Latins cannot express this except by a word of their own making. In Hebrew it is עלה, from ascending into smoke. Elsewhere it is also called [Hebrew: עולה אשה], Lev. 1:9, 13. In this matter the incomparable Scaliger was deceived, for he tried to render [Hebrew: אשה] as "a fiery sacrifice." But the term is not simply a fiery sacrifice; it is joined with [Hebrew: עולה]. Elsewhere too, in a sacrifice that is not a holocaust, it signifies the part which the fire devours and consumes. Moses calls it more expressively [Hebrew: כליל], wholly, Lev. 6:23, of which the priest took no part at all (ch. 5:16). The continual burnt offering, which the Greeks call enedelechismos, a perpetual sacrifice, was wholly of this kind: [Hebrew: עולה תמיד]. It is described in Num. 28:3, 4, 5, 6. There were two daily sacrifices. One was offered in the morning at sunrise; the other [Hebrew: בין הערבים], between the two evenings. The view of the illustrious Salmasius is now almost generally accepted among scholars: that [Hebrew: ערב] denotes the whole afternoon, which the ancients divided into two parts. Hence "between the two evenings" meant the time around the third hour by our reckoning. Yet Salmasius's view seems to be obstructed both by other things and by the fact that Lev. 6:2 ordains that the burning of the holocaust on the altar shall take place [Hebrew: כל הלילה עד הבקר], all night until morning. It is quite unlike that an evening holocaust could supply the altar fire with sufficient fuel from the afternoon until morning. Compare Maimonides in his Summary of the Talmud, tract on the Prayers and Blessings of the Priests, ch. 3, sect. 2. But this in passing. Moreover, not only holocausts, which were burnt up entirely, but also sacrifices whose blood was sprinkled on the inner altar of the Temple (Lev. 6:30), and the priest's own sacrifices (v. 33), were burnt entirely. Finally, there is the piggul, a sacrifice about which the priest offering it, at the time of slaughter, has [Hebrew: פסול מחשבה] an evil intention. On these see R. Levi on precepts 142, 143, 145 and following. For it was forbidden to the priests to eat of these.

units.la: VII. Quid ergo? Victas manus dabimus? Nempe, si probationem susceperit solidam, Adami & Habelis sacrificia holocausta fuisse. Hoc autem cur largiremur? Fuerunt praeter holocausta in lege alia etiam sacrificia. Puta ὁ[Greek] [Hebrew: שלמים] & ἱλαστικὰ, quae Moses vocat [Hebrew: כפרים] propitiatoria. De his Sacerdos sibi partem delibavit, & Sacro epulo consumsit. Moses vocat [Hebrew: מנחה] Apostolus θυσίας. Utraq; vox laxior. Tam [Hebrew: כפר] sive propitiatorium & pacificum, quam [Hebrew: עולה] sive holocaustum complectitur. Non fuisse holocaustum ex re ipsa patet. Obtulit enim de pinguedinibus gregis. Quod duplicem sensum recipere potest, vel, sacrificasse oves pinguiores: vel pinguepinguedinem ovium. Si prius, non constat Habelis laus, nisi graciliores in cibum proprium servavit. Si posterius, quod collata lege Levit. VI. 12. poene certum, necessum fuerit, adipem sacrificâsse, reliquias epulo θυσίᾳ consumpsisse. Sed & constat, quam significationem holocausto, quam propitiatorio sive ἱλαστήριον Hebraei tribuant. Illud summum & eminens Dei in omnia imperium, ac protestationem, quòd sacrificans se Deo totum devoveat, & in omnia obnoxium faciat, adumbrare. Hoc propitiationis & reconciliationis cum Deo negotium figurare. Illud suo Sacrificio videtur etiam Kainus intendisse. Propterea Mincham obtulit ex frugibus terrae, quas corrumpi penitus decuit. In quo igitur κατ᾽ ἐμὲ πάλιν Habelis praerogativa, si non in eo, quòd ἱλαστήριον cum Deo negotium curavit, quam supinè neglexit Kainus? Habet, fateor, Curcellaeus ὁμολογούμενος magnos viros, Mercerum, Grotium, Seldenum. In Mercero tamen constantiam desidero. Alibi enim, ubi contra esum carnium pugnat, argumento nostro, à Sacrificiis Antediluvianis petito, contranisus, pertendit fuisse holocausta, Comm. in Genes. IX. Quod evertit Comm. ad cap. IV. ubi negat igne coelesti Habelis Sacrificium appetitum, hac ratione: quòd ignis Sacrificia, quae comburebantur, utpote animalia, è Coelo devorâvit, non sacrificia cibaria, quae non urebantur, ut erant Habelis. Si cibarium fuit Habelis sacrificium, fuerint igitur carnes indultae ad esum. Grotio nihil hic utor. Neque fortasse ipse Curcellaeus. Contendit enim hoc argumento, Habelem Deo ne quidem animalem hostiam obtulisse, sed lanam & lac pinguissimum, ut obtineat, fuisse sacrificium Kaini & Habelis sagmen. Neque veretur Sanctorum Patriarcharum Sacrificia cum Gentilium holocaustis comparare. Qui specimen σπεκλάσεως S. Literarum requirit, istum locum inspiciat. Jam de Seldeno Doctissimo, quem suum Curcellaeus facit. Vellet holocausta sola ante legem in usu fuisse. Non enim celebratum epulum sacrum ex parte immolata. Quid ergo faciendum Sacrificio Jacobi, qui epulum sacrum post sacrificium celebravit, Genes. XXXI. 54. Nisi forte sacrificium Jacobi non religiosum fuit, sed civile, symbolum nempe externum icti foederis cum Labane, ut sic מנחה simpliciter sit mactare. Sed fac omnino, sacrificia Antediluvianorum holocausta fuisse. Non frangit vim argumenti. Nihil enim Deo sacrari potest, quin sit in usu hominum. In sacrificiis enim suam obligationem testabantur. Hinc devoverunt merito id, quo omnium maxime in hac vita sustentanda sunt quotidie usi.
units.tr: VII. What then? Shall we give up the struggle? Certainly, if the opponent has produced solid proof that the sacrifices of Adam and Abel were holocausts. But why should we concede this? Besides holocausts, there were other sacrifices under the law, such as the shelamim, peace-offerings [שלמים], and the atoning offerings, which Moses calls [Hebrew: כפרים], propitiatory. From these the priest took a portion for himself and consumed it in a sacred feast. Moses calls it [Hebrew: מנחה], and the Apostle thusiai, sacrifices. Both words are rather loose; [Hebrew: כפר], the propitiatory or peace offering, covers as much as [Hebrew: עולה], the holocaust. That it was not a holocaust is clear from the matter itself. For Abel offered "of the fat of the flock." This can bear a double sense: either that he sacrificed the fatter sheep, or that he sacrificed the fat of the sheep. If the former, Abel's praise does not stand, unless he kept the leaner ones for his own food. If the latter, which, when Lev. 6:12 is compared, is almost certain, then he must have burnt the fat and consumed the remains in a sacrificial feast. Consider also what meaning the Hebrews give to the holocaust and to the propitiatory or hilastērion. The former signifies God's supreme and eminent dominion over all things, and the declaration that the one sacrificing devotes himself wholly to God and makes himself subject to him in all things. The latter represents the business of propitiation and reconciliation with God. Cain seems to have intended the former by his offering; that is why he offered mincha from the fruits of the earth, which ought to have been wholly corrupted. In what, then, is Abel's preeminence, [κατ᾽ ἐμέ] in my view, if not in this, that he attended to the business of propitiation with God, which Cain carelessly neglected? I admit that Curcellaeus has on his side great men, whom he acknowledges: Mercerus, Grotius, Selden. Yet I miss consistency in Mercerus. For elsewhere, where he fights against the eating of meat, he meets our argument, drawn from the pre-Flood sacrifices, by contending that they were holocausts (Comm. on Gen. 9). He overturns this in his commentary on ch. 4, where he denies that Abel's sacrifice was consumed by heavenly fire, for this reason: because the fire from heaven devoured the sacrifices that were burnt, as animals, and not the food-offerings, which were not burnt, as Abel's were. If Abel's sacrifice was a food-offering, then the flesh was granted for eating. I do not use Grotius here, nor perhaps Curcellaeus himself. For he argues from this text that Abel did not offer an animal victim to God at all, but wool and the richest milk, and that the sacrifice of Cain and Abel was a sagmen. Nor does he hesitate to compare the sacrifices of the holy patriarchs with the holocausts of the Gentiles. Whoever seeks an example of [συγκαταβάσεως] condescension in Holy Scripture, let him look at that passage. Now as to the most learned Selden, whom Curcellaeus claims as his own: he would have it that only holocausts were in use before the law, for the sacred feast was not celebrated from the part that was slain. But what then shall we do with the sacrifice of Jacob, who celebrated a sacred feast after the sacrifice (Gen. 31:54)? Unless perhaps Jacob's sacrifice was not religious but civil, an outward symbol of the covenant struck with Laban, so that mincha simply means to slaughter. But grant entirely that the sacrifices of the pre-Flood people were holocausts. That does not break the force of the argument. For nothing can be dedicated to God that is not in human use. In sacrifices they testified their own obligation. Hence they rightly devoted that by which they most of all sustained themselves in this life, using it every day.

units.la: Hebr. מנחה minchah, oblatio.
units.tr: Hebrew minchah [מנחה], offering.

units.la: VIII. Si veteri, inquit, Traditioni credimus, Deus igne Coelitus demisso Abelis sacrificia, non Kaini contemisit. pag. 33. Plerique omnino, tum Hebraei, tum recentiores & veteres Theologi censent; Sacramentum approbatae victimae Habelis fuisse visibilem ἐμπυρισμὸν ab igne Coelitus descendente factum. Praivit Theodotio, qui ꞑ vertit ἐνεπύρισε. Secutus Hieronymus quaest. in Genesin: Unde poterat scire Cain, quod fratris ejus munera accepisset Deus, nisi illa traditio vera esset, quam Theodotio posuit? Cui secundas faciunt Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Cyrillus, Procopius, alii. Quin & sub lege, constituto jam in ara perpetuo igne Sacro, saepius extra ordinem ignis è Coelo lapsus victimas absumpsit. Sed, Curcellaee, an exceptis holocaustis inflammabile nihil fuit? An in Pacificis & hostiis pro peccato, quorum armus & pectusculum sacerdoti cessit, non fuit pinguedo combusta, ut fieret Deo odor bonae fragrantiae? An igitur sacrificium Habelis, & in eo adeps adolenda non potuit coelesti igni fomitem suppeditare? Nae falleris nimium! 4. Urget porro: Ex laudibus Habelis non evinci, carnium esum sub mundi initia fuisse receptum. Rationem quippe docere, nihil nisi optimum & praestantissimum Deo offerendum, ibid. Resp. Omnino nihil nisi optimum & praestantissimum Deo offerendum. Tametsi enim neque jucunditate vervecinorum viscerum, neque nidore sumptuosissimarum victimarum sibi delicias facit; attamen recitudo animi delectat, & pia ac illibata venerantium voluntas. Non potest autem optimum & praestantissimum esse, nisi maxima utilitate offerentem multet. Proinde, si ejusmodi Habelis Sacrificium fuit, ipsi ad esum utile esse debuit. Jam dicat, fuisse in usu maximo oves Habelis. Lac enim & lanam dedisse. Quae duo propterea oblata Deo Grotius dicit. Sed quid haec ad discrimen inter graciliores & pinguiores oves? Pinguedinem diserte Moses nominat. Quamobrem ad usum respicit, qui in cibo locum habuit. Deinde cibum Antediluvianorum Curcellaeus restringit ad alimentum ex herbis & oleribus virentibus. Ex quo sequitur, ne lacte quidem integrum fuisse vesci. Quod igitur tandem emolumentum praestiterunt Habeli pinguissimae oves, quibus cum se in Dei gratiam defraudaret, tanta Mosi ac Paulo in praedicatione fuit?
units.tr: VIII. If, he says, we believe the old tradition, God sent fire down from heaven and despised Abel's sacrifices, not Cain's. p. 33. Almost all of them, both the Hebrews and the more recent and older theologians, hold that the sign of Abel's accepted victim was a burning [ἐμπυρισμόν] caused by fire descending from heaven. Theodotion led the way, rendering the Hebrew word as "he ignited" [ἐνεπύρισε]. Jerome followed him in his Questions on Genesis: How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother's gifts, unless that tradition which Theodotion records were true? Chrysostom, Theophylact, Cyril, Procopius and others agree with him. Indeed, under the law, when a perpetual sacred fire had already been established on the altar, fire falling from heaven more than once consumed the victims outside the ordinary course. But, Curcellaeus, was nothing combustible used apart from the burnt offerings? Was not the fat burnt in the peace offerings and sin offerings, of which the shoulder and breast fell to the priest, so that it might become a fragrant odour pleasing to God? Could Abel's sacrifice, and the fat to be burnt in it, then not supply fuel for the heavenly fire? You are very much mistaken! 4. He presses further: From the praise of Abel it cannot be shown that the eating of flesh was accepted at the beginning of the world. For reason teaches that nothing but the best and most excellent should be offered to God, ibid. Reply: certainly nothing but the best and most excellent should be offered to God. For although God takes no delight in the taste of lambs' entrails or the savour of the most sumptuous victims, yet the uprightness of the soul pleases him, and the pious and unblemished will of those who worship him. But that cannot be the best and most excellent unless it is of the greatest use to the one offering it. Therefore, if Abel's sacrifice was of this kind, it ought to have been useful to him for food. Now let him say that Abel's sheep were of the greatest use, since they gave milk and wool. Grotius says these two were offered to God for that reason. But what has this to do with the difference between the leaner and the fatter sheep? Moses expressly names the fat. Therefore he has regard to the use which had a place in food. Moreover, Curcellaeus restricts the food of the people before the flood to nourishment from green herbs and vegetables. From this it follows that they did not even eat whole milk. What, then, finally, was the advantage to Abel of the fattest sheep, since he would have cheated himself of God's favour by them, if so much weight was laid on them by Moses and Paul in their preaching?

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Tertium argumentum succedit. Promimus inde, quod pellibus ferarum Deus Protoplastos nuditate sua percussos vestivit. Ac suo exemplo non obscure docuit, homines eodem modo de vestimentis mentis sibi providere posse & debeam. Sic autem Moses: Fecit Deus Adamo & mulieri tunicas pelliceas, & vestivit illos. Genes. III. 20. Mactari igitur animantia debuerunt. Quid ergo de carnibus fieri debuit? Comestae haud dubie fuerunt, non rejectae. Si rejectaneae, non igitur fuerunt ξλίσσα ξεναλὸν, 1. Tim. IV. 4. Procopium qui tuetur, nemo est, statuentem tunicas ex nihilo creatas. Neque Gennadius assensum impetrat: Non pelliceas fuisse vestes, sed arborum corticibus detractis consutas. Quem sequitur Theodorus Heracleotes. Origenes more suo ἀπαγορεύει. Intelligit ipsa corpora, quibus animae antea conditae sunt indutae. Utrique, Theodoro & Origeni haec ratio, cur a simplicitate verborum recedere ent: quod non potuerint esse pelles ex mactatis animantibus, cum Deus bina fecisset, & nullus adhuc partus editus esset. Quos merito hac nota perstringit Theodoretus: τὸ μὲν ἀξιέργον, τὸ δὲ ἀργυρινθῶδες. Ad rationem allatam respondet: ἐκ τοίνυν ξέργων τὰ γεγαμμένα, καὶ εἰδέναι, ὡς ἐδὲν ἄπρον τῷ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργῷ. Neque sane tanti est ratio Theodori. Nam unicum in qualibet specie par creatum esse, definitur ἄτερ χεαφῶν. Quid ergo si dicamus, ut sunt conservata septem paria mundorum, unum immundorum in arca, ad generis conservationem: ita ad primam propagationem totidem esse condita?
units.tr: The third argument follows. I infer from it that God clothed the first parents, struck by their nakedness, with the skins of wild beasts. By his own example he taught plainly that men could and should in the same way provide for the garments of the mind. Moses writes thus: God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them. Gen. 3:20. Therefore animals must have been slaughtered. What then ought to have been done with the flesh? Undoubtedly it was eaten, not thrown away. If it was thrown away, it was not nothing to be rejected [ἀπόβλητον], 1 Tim. 4:4. No one defends Procopius in his view that the tunics were created out of nothing. Nor does Gennadius win assent with his claim that the garments were not of skins but were sewn from bark stripped from trees. Theodore of Heraclea follows him. Origen, as is his custom, rejects the literal sense [ἀπαγορεύει]; he understands the bodies themselves, with which the souls were previously created, as the clothing. Theodore and Origen both have this reason for departing from the plain sense of the words: because they could not have been skins from slaughtered animals, since God had made only a pair of each, and no offspring had yet been born. Theodoret rightly marks them with this charge: the one is idle, the other fanciful [τὸ μὲν ἀξιέργον, τὸ δὲ ἀργυρινθῶδες]. He answers the reason given: therefore, from the works of the things made, know that nothing is impossible to the Creator of all [ἐκ τοίνυν ἔργων τὰ γεγαμμένα, καὶ εἰδέναι, ὡς οὐδὲν ἄπορον τῷ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργῷ]. Nor is Theodore's reason really worth much. For that a single pair of each kind was created is not defined anywhere without Scripture [ἄνευ γραφῶν]. What, then, if we say that, just as seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean were kept in the ark for preserving the kind, so the same number were created at the first propagation?

units.la: X. Excipit Curcellaeus
units.tr: X. Curcellaeus takes up the argument

units.la: 1. Exuvias potuisse adhiberi animantium, quae fato suo perierant. pag. 34. Resp. Asserit, non probat, potuisse. Eadem igitur facilitate rejicitur. Imo indignum & Deo & homine, vestitum conficere & inducere ex νεκρημάτων, morticinio animalis.
units.tr: 1. The skins of animals which had died of their own accord could have been used. p. 34. Reply: he asserts that they could have been used; he does not prove it. It is therefore rejected with equal ease. Indeed, it is unworthy of both God and man to make and put on a garment from a carcass [νεκρωμάτων], the corpse of an animal.

units.la: 2. Potuisse retineri exuvias animantium, quae Deo in Sacrificium fuerant oblata. ibid. Resp. Omnino contendimus, vestem Adami fuisse ex animali ad sacrificium mactato. Atque hoc ipso argumento supra Adami sacrificium ἱλαστικὸν comprobavimus. Sed & illud liquido jam constat, eadem animalia ad usum prostitisse, quae ad sacrificium.
units.tr: 2. The skins of animals which had been offered to God in sacrifice could have been kept. ibid. Reply: we strongly maintain that Adam's garment was made from an animal slaughtered for sacrifice. And by this very argument we have already proved Adam's sacrifice to be an atoning one [ἱλαστικόν]. But it is also now clearly established that the same animals were used for food as for sacrifice.

units.la: 3. Deum non improbasse, ut commoda ratione corium animantibus detraherent. Sed nullo indicio patefecisse, sibi placere, ut eorum carnibus vescerentur. ibid. Resp. Quomodo detraxerit, an ipse nullo ministrante, an ministerio vel Angelorum, vel Adami, definiant, quibus otium est infructuosas subtilitates consectari. Nos nihil dicere habemus. Non opus erat indicio, esum carnium Deo placere, cum sit in genere adiaphorum, quae affectus animi bona vel mala facit. Habebant aeque atque nos, homines illi primi legem Regiam, distantem justitiam, quam oportuit pro re nata exerceri. Deinde, si sumentium Moses ar-gumengumento est, non placuisse Deo esum carnium, eadem ratione concludi potest, non placuisse esum panis, cum nulla fiat mentio frumenti, vel potum lactis & vini, quae nullibi diserte verbis indulgentur.
units.tr: 3. God did not disapprove of their skins being removed from the animals in a convenient way. But he made no indication that he was pleased for them to be eaten. ibid. Reply: how he removed them, whether without any minister or through the ministry of angels or of Adam, let those decide who have leisure to pursue unfruitful subtleties. We have nothing to say about it. There was no need of any indication that the eating of flesh pleased God, since it belongs to the class of things indifferent, which the disposition of the soul makes good or bad. Those first men had, just as we do, the royal law and the distributive justice which had to be exercised as the occasion required. Moreover, if Moses's silence is taken as an argument that the eating of flesh did not please God, the same reasoning may conclude that the eating of bread did not please him, since no mention is made of grain, nor of the drinking of milk and wine, which are nowhere expressly granted in words.

units.la: 4. Si ita argumentari liceat, etiam excusabiles futuros Adamum & Evam, frustum vetitum comedentes. ib. Resp. Disparitatem etiam lippi vident. Adamus interdictum habuit, verbis conceptis exsertum. Illud torqueri nullo pretextu poterat. De non comedendis carnibus neque gry, neque my. Quod enim pro cibo determinavit oleta & herbas Deus, argumento non est, carnes ab usu removisse. Hoc jam supra discussimus.
units.tr: 4. If it is allowed to argue in this way, Adam and Eve would also be excusable for eating the forbidden fruit. ib. Reply: even the blear-eyed see the difference. Adam had a prohibition, stated in explicit words. That could not be twisted by any pretext. On not eating flesh there is neither gry nor my. For that God appointed herbs and vegetables as food is no proof that he removed flesh from use. We have already discussed this above.

units.la: XI. Quartum argumentum dictat descriptum a Mose ante diluvium inter animantia munda & immunda discrimen.
units.tr: XI. The fourth argument is drawn from the distinction, described by Moses before the flood, between clean and unclean animals.

units.la: De quo sic: De animantibus mundis sumes in arcam septena & septena. De immundis duo. Genes. VII. 2. 3. Hoc discrimen evidenter supponit carnium usum. Munda, quorum solita alimenta; immunda, quorum insolita. Varie quidem in exegesi hujus discriminis eruditi certant. Hebraeis placet, differentiam hic descriptam legis Mosaicae. Quasi Noachus legem anticipârit. Sic Jarchius: הטהורה לחיות ... לישראל למרו שלמד נח תורה. Consentiunt Theodoretus, Beda, Abulensis. Sic jam Noachus fuerit legi Mosaicae devinctus. Et munda ac immunda fuerint eadem, quae sub lege. Neutrum vero conveniens. Sed anticipaverit legem, Deo jubenter Ergo quemadmodum sub lege, quae munda fuerunt, ideo talia fuerunt, quia ad esum aeque atque ad sacrificia destinata: sic ob easdem causas munda quaedam fuerint tempore Noachi. Alii dicunt immunditiem fuisse ex instituto & opinione hominum, a sacrificiis segregantium animalia, sanguine, rapto, aut foedo genere escae victitantia. Quae sententia nihilo melior. Quasi humanae optionis sit in cultu Dei positivo, qualis sacrificiorum fuit, propria authoritate quidquam constitutum dare, quod non prior Deus mandarit diserte & praescripserit. Genebrardus Chronol. pag. 14. citat Prophetiam Enochi, extantem apud Aethiopes in Regno Reginae Sabae Abyssina Lingua, in qua tradebantur Dei mandata de Sacrificiis & Divino cultu, juxta quae Noë hostias obtulit de animantibus mundis & immundis. Sed suppositicium esse scriptum cum alii, tum nuper Cl. D. Hottingerus demonstravit. Quid ergo? Munda fuerunt, quae non fastidit natura. Immunda, quae foeda & profana, & quae, ut Tacitus loquitur, in usum namque necessitate veritis. Immundum autem reddit vel corporis forma, vel victus impurus & detestabilis, vel ad cibum ineptitudo, vel quod sanitati noxam adfert. Talia crocodili, serpentes, vultures, corvi, canes, & si quid aliud.
units.tr: Concerning which he says thus: Of clean animals you shall take into the ark seven and seven; of unclean animals, two. Gen. 7.2, 3. This distinction clearly presupposes the eating of flesh. Clean animals are those whose food is customary; unclean animals are those whose food is unusual. Learned men dispute variously over the explanation of this distinction. The Hebrews hold that the difference described here is that of the Mosaic law, as if Noah had anticipated the law. So Jarchi: [הטהורה לחיות ... לישראל ... למד נח תורה] "the clean beasts ... for Israel ... Noah taught the Torah." Theodoret, Bede and Abulensis agree. In that case Noah would already have been bound by the Mosaic law, and the clean and unclean animals would have been the same as under the law. Neither view is fitting. But suppose he did anticipate the law, at God's command. Then, just as under the law those animals were clean which were destined both for eating and for sacrifice, so for the same reasons some animals were clean in the time of Noah. Others say that uncleanness arose from the custom and opinion of men, who regarded as unclean those animals that feed on blood, carrion or foul food, and so kept them from sacrifice. This view is no better. As if it were a matter of human choice to lay down by its own authority anything in positive worship of God, such as sacrifice was, which God had not first commanded and expressly prescribed. Genebrardus, in his Chronology, p. 14, cites a prophecy of Enoch, extant among the Ethiopians in the Abyssinian language in the kingdom of the Queen of Sheba, in which the commands of God about sacrifices and divine worship were handed down, and according to which Noah offered victims of clean and unclean animals. But that this is a spurious writing has been shown, both by others and recently by the esteemed Mr Hottinger. What then? Clean animals were those which nature does not loathe. Unclean animals were those which are foul and profane, and which, as Tacitus puts it, are used only out of necessity. Uncleanness is imparted either by bodily form, or by impure and detestable food, or by unfitness for eating, or because it does harm to health. Such are crocodiles, serpents, vultures, ravens, dogs, and whatever else is like them.

units.la: XII. Evidentem rationem Curcellæus impetit. 1. Munda & immunda vocari propter Sacrificia, ut sanctissimo Deo nihil nisi mundum offer-retur: non propter esum. pag. 35. Resp. Instituto merè humano? Falsum. Divino? Non intercedo, quò minùs dicatur, instinctu Dei non sacrificata animalia nisi munda. Decuit enim immolari, quæ in usu hominum antecelluerunt. Quò pertinet, quòd jussus Noachus in Arcam septena & septena recipere. Quod sic eruditi exponunt, tanquam tria paria multiplicationi, septimum adjectum obligationi & Sacrificio inservīssent. An igitur non licita edi? Imò quia in naturali usu munda, ideo ad sacrificandum adhibita. Non contrà. Nec quæ sit inter sacrificia & animalium usum connexio, supra ex vero expositum est. Quin & ponderari velim, delectum ciborum figurâsse exclusas gentes à communione fœderis externi. Hinc delectu ciborum sublato, & concessâ facultate mactandi in Divina visione, Petrus conclusit: Nunc ex veritate cognosco, quòd non sit personarum respectus apud Deum, sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum, & operatur justitiam, Deo acceptus est, Actor. X. vers. 11. 12. &c. cum vers. 34. 35. Atqui ante diluvium rejectas esse gentes à communione Ecclesiæ, & externa ejus societate, non constat. Hoc judiciosè observatum etiam Pientissimo nostro Zwinglio. 2. Genes. IX. ubi Deus esum permittit, distinctionem istam ne verbo quidem attingi, & nullam prorsus animalium speciem, sed tantùm sanguinem excipi, ibid. Resp. Quis miretur? Distinctio enim inter munda & immunda non fuit ex Divino mandato propter pietatem & religionem inducta, sed homines ea immunda duxerunt, quorum naturaliter nausea capti fuerunt. Non igitur necessum Deo fuit distinguere vel excipere. Deinde quid opus erat temporalem exceptionem cum perpetua lege conjungere, si maximè constaret discrimen propter religionem inductum. Hoc erudite Calvinus monuit.
units.tr: XII. Curcellaeus assails this clear reasoning. 1. Clean and unclean are so called because of sacrifices, so that nothing but what is clean was offered to the most holy God, not because of eating. p. 35. Reply: By a merely human institution? That is false. By a divine one? I do not deny that it may be said that animals were sacrificed only if clean, by the instinct of God. For it was fitting that those animals which excelled in human use should be offered. To this belongs the command to Noah to take seven and seven into the ark. Learned men explain this as meaning that the three pairs served for multiplication, and the seventh, added, served for obligation and sacrifice. Are they therefore not lawful to eat? Indeed, they are clean because they are clean in natural use, and so they were employed for sacrifice. Not the reverse. Nor has the connection between sacrifices and the use of animals been left unexplained, as shown above from the truth itself. Indeed, I would have you consider that the distinction of foods foreshadowed the exclusion of the nations from communion in the external covenant. Therefore, when the distinction of foods was removed and permission was given to slaughter animals in the divine vision, Peter concluded: Now I perceive in truth that God shows no partiality, but in every nation the one who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him, Acts 10.11, 12, etc., with verses 34, 35. But it is not established that before the flood the nations were rejected from communion with the Church and from its external fellowship. This was also wisely observed by our most pious Zwingli. 2. Gen. 9: Where God grants the eating of animals, that distinction is not touched on even in word, and no species of animal at all is excepted, but only blood, ibid. Reply: Who would be surprised? For the distinction between clean and unclean was not introduced by a divine command for the sake of piety and religion, but men regarded as unclean those animals at which they were naturally revolted. There was therefore no need for God to make a distinction or an exception. Moreover, why would there have been any need to join a temporary exception to a perpetual law, if it were certain that the distinction had been introduced on account of religion? Calvin has learnedly pointed this out.

units.la: XIII. Quinta ratio inde nobis petita, quòd animalibus ad esum non mactatis, videatur, exundante immensâ multitudine, homines in diserimen vitæ adduci potuisse. Quis enim dubitet, quin populabunda vel agros invasissent, & fruges Terræ consumsissent, unde necessum fuisset tot hominibus cibum ex oleribus & herbis bis deficere; vel hominės ipsos perpetuis insidiis appetiissent. Unde nunquam à metu vacandi locus. Cùm ex Pythagoræorum de non edendis carnibus doctrina Amyclæ nefas duxissent, Serpentes occidere, tanta increvit multitudo, ut civitatem eam deleverint, teste Plinio. Unde vulgari adagio dicitur: Amyclas perdere serpentium. An idem non evenisset Antediluvianis? Excipit Curcellæus: Quoad domestica animalia, si hominum desit cura & labor, non valde multiplicari; & sibi relicta vel morbis peritura; vel feris in prædam fuisse tessera. Fugacia, authore experientia, non multiplicari etiam in locis illis, ubi nemo illa persequitur. pag. 36.37. Resp. Experientiam si rogaremus, fortasse alia omnia veritati daret. Videndi sunt rerum naturalium consulti, Plinius, Ælianus, Aldrovandus. Cumprimis Benedictio Divina obstat: Crescite & multiplicamini. Non negem accedente hominum cura facilius multiplicari. Argumento fuerit pecuaria apud diversas gentes. Absque tamen illa fuisset, multitudo animalium & exuberantia molestiam creasset. 2. Ergò feris carnes in prædam cessurae? Quidni igitur etiam hominibus? Non est, cur conditionem deteriorem fingamus hominis, quàm bestiarum. 3. Neque facile quisquam habere fidem potest dicenti; etiam in illis locis, ubi nemo feras persequitur, & cubilibus suis excutit, non adeò multiplicari. Quod enim in historia de Balearibus insulis commemorari solet, cuniculos ibi tantà copià aliquando grassatos, ut ad pellendam eorum vim Romanorum suppetiis opus esset, idem alibi sæpiuscule factitatum. Ac præcipuè Germania Gradivo tamdiu lacerata, & pœne in vastitiem data. Cujus cultui arte & industria postliminio quæsito quantum noceant turmatim irruentes feræ, & segetes vastantes, compertum satis est.
units.tr: XIII. The fifth reason, drawn from this, is that if animals were not slaughtered for food, it seems that men could have been brought into danger of life by an immense multitude overflowing. For who would doubt that they would have invaded the fields in swarms and consumed the fruits of the earth, so that it would have been necessary for so many men to be short of food from herbs and vegetables alone; or that they would have attacked the men themselves with constant ambushes? So there would never have been room free from fear. When the Amyclaeans, following the teaching of the Pythagoreans about not eating flesh, considered it a crime to kill serpents, such a multitude grew that they destroyed that city, as Pliny testifies. Hence the common proverb: "to destroy Amyclae by serpents." Would the same not have happened to the people before the flood? Curcellaeus objects: As for domestic animals, if the care and labour of men is lacking, they do not multiply greatly; left to themselves they either perish from disease or become prey to wild beasts. Fleeing animals, as experience shows, do not multiply even in those places where no one pursues them. pp. 36, 37. Reply: If we asked experience, perhaps it would give a different answer to everything. We should consult the students of natural things: Pliny, Aelian, Aldrovandi. Above all, the divine blessing stands in the way: Increase and multiply. I would not deny that they multiply more easily when human care is added. Herds among various nations are evidence of this. Yet without that care, the multitude of animals and their excess would have created a nuisance. 2. Therefore should flesh be left as prey to wild beasts? Why not then also to men? There is no reason for us to imagine a worse condition for man than for beasts. 3. Nor can anyone easily believe the claim that even in those places where no one pursues wild animals and drives them from their lairs, they do not multiply so greatly. For what is commonly recorded in history about the Balearic islands, that rabbits once swarmed there in such numbers that the Romans needed assistance to drive off their onslaught, has happened often enough elsewhere too. Especially in Germany, long torn by Gradivus and nearly laid waste. It is sufficiently well known how much wild beasts do harm when they rush in herds and devour crops, once cultivation was recovered by art and industry.

units.la: XIV. Atque sic constare arbitror, Antediluvianis jus competiisse carnium. Unum tamen est, quod ὀἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας magno in nos impetu intorquent, quódque suum etiam Achillem Curcellæus facit.
units.tr: XIV. And so, I think, it is established that the people before the flood had a right to flesh. There is one thing, however, which those on the opposite side [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] hurl against us with great force, and which Curcellaeus makes his own Achilles.

units.la: Videtur enim Deus post diluvium demum facultatem concessisse carnium, in verbis Genes. IX. 3. Omne quod movetur & vivit, erit vobis in cibium: quasi olera virentia tradidi vobis omnia. Verumtamen carnem cum sanguine non comedetis. Ergo diluvium retro nefas fuit. Hoc scutum obtendunt, quotquot adversum sustinent. Hebræos magna nube citat R. Manasse in Conciliat. quæst. IX. Aben-Esdras: הָיִר לֹא הָתִיר ... הַבָּשָׂר אַחַר הַמָּבוּל: Usque sic non concessit carnem usque post diluvium. Basilius: ἡ πρώτη νομοθεσία τῶν καρπῶν ἀπέλαυσιν σωφροσύνης, Prima legislatio fructuum fructuum usum concessit. Idem placuit Tertulliano, Origeni, & ut Mer-cerus loquitur, plerisque nostris in locum illum commentanti-bus." Pererius tamen, suffragiis adjutus Chrysostomi & Theo-doreti negat ex hoc loco confici, ante diluvium illicitum fuisse carnis esum. Censet ergo, non interdictum quidem esse: ab eo tamen viros religiosiores abstinuisse, puta posteros Sethi. Horum quidem Sanctitas & rectitudo celeberrima. Non persuadeor tamen, vel in universum abstinuisse, vel religiose inductos. Sic enim, Deo non mandante, ejus ob ἐφελοθρησκείαν offensam incurrissent. Addo, in Sacrificiis non potuisse sibi temperare. Paraeus, Calvinus inclinant, non de nova concessione agi Cap. IX. sed de renovata & repetita. Iam firmiter est nobis comprobandum. Primum igitur non erat consentaneum, ut homini post diluvium plus daretur potestatis in animalia ratione usus, quam vel initio mundi, vel a lapsu Adami. Sic enim per Ante-diluvianorum summam malitiam & exultantem petulantiam am-plitudinem potestatis extensiorem acquisivissent. 2. Si nova esset, non renovata legislatio, non potuisset Deus Sacrificiorum legem jam longe ante illa tempora sancire. Non potuit enim illa ratione ulla constare sine carnium concessione. 3. Eodem modo se habet concessio carnium, quo caeterae benedictionis & concessionis Divinae partes. Puta, quòd jubentur crescere & multiplicari: dominari super bestias terrae & volatilia Coeli: Comedere herbas & olera: abstinere à sanguinis effusione. Atqui hae posteriores leges non novae sed repetitae sunt. Nam etiam Adamo latas esse, quis dubitare potest? Talis igitur est etiam de carnibus νομοθεσία. 4. Si nova est carnium concessio, nova aeque fuerit oportet sanguinis comedendi prohibitio. Sic enim Moses: Omne reptile vobis erit in escam: sicut germen herbae vobis dedi omnia. Veruntamen carnem cum anima ejus, quae est sanguis, non comedetis. Atqui novum esse de sanguine non comedendo praeceptum, Curcellaeus constanter negat. Ergo nova etiam non fuit concessio carnium, sed repetita. Argumentum est ad hominem. 5. Minime probabile, veteres ante diluvium, quorum malitia ultra modum jam processerat, in illa rerum confusione abstinuisse animantium carnibus. Qui abstinerent à vorandis carnibus, qui ne quidem à fundendo sanguine hominis temperarunt: quorum profusa ingluvies intemperantia Christo notata? Si ederunt carnes, vel adversus legem, vel ex permissione. Si contra legem, crimen gravissimum fuerit, quia positivae legis transgressio. At [illegible, ~3 letters] de eo in recensione peccatorum, ob quæ aquæ mundo immissæ. Non igitur in usu carnium, sed in potestatis abusu deliquerint, quem Christus meritissimè traduxit. 6. Suffragium accumulo omnium gravissimi Interpretis Calvini: Ultra, inquit, progreditur Dominus, & animalia in cibum hominibus concedit, ut eorum carne pascantur. Quia autem nunc primum Moses hoc juris hominibus datum fuisse refert, colligunt omnes fere interpretes, homini ante diluvium fas non fuisse vesci carnibus, sed nativos tantum fructus terræ illis fuisse pro cibo. Sed argumentum non satis firmum est. Ego enim principium illud teneo: Deum hic non plus largiri hominibus, quàm dederat: sed tantum reddere, quod fuit ablatum, ut possessionem bonorum, unde fuerant depulsi, iterum ornant. Hactenus Calvinus. Quid igitur causæ, cur demum à diluvio Moses carnium mentionem fecerit? Nempe, quia Deus voluit legem sancire de sanguine & suffocato non comedendo. Hæc exceptio, quia opponi debuit generali concessioni, prius necesse habuit ipsam concessionem repetere, ut exceptio intelligi possit facilius. Eam viam Deus Legislator retinet, quam nuper ingressus cum Adamo erat. Gen. II. 16. Ex fructu omnis arboris hujus horti liberè comedes: Ex fructu verò arboris scientiæ boni & mali ne comedas. Exceptioni generalem concessionem substravit. Sic hoc loco. Carnem comedes sicut herbas, sed sanguinem non comedes. Quasi diceret: Quod sanguinis esu vobis interdico, non ideo coarcto potestatem vestram, non prohibeo, quò minùs carnibus vescamini. Vescimini liberè, æquè ac herbis. Sed sanguinem segregate, & cum carnibus ne comedite. Fatetur Curcellæus, responsum istud veri speciem habiturum, si constaret, licitum fuisse Adamo in statu integritatis carnem usurpare ad alimentum. Nos & responsum nostrum firmissimis rationibus adstrinximus, & probatum supra dedimus, in statu integritatis, & a lapsu Adami licitum fuisse. Nolumus igitur operam ludere.
units.tr: For God seems to have granted the permission to eat meat only after the flood, in the words of Genesis 9:3: Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green herbs I gave you all things. But you shall not eat flesh with its blood. Therefore it was wrong before the flood. Everyone who opposes us holds up this shield. Rabbi Menasseh cites a great cloud of Hebrews in Conciliator, question 9. Aben-Ezra says: He did not permit flesh until after the flood [לֹא הֻתַּר הַבָּשָׂר עַד אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל]. Basil says: "The first legislation concerning fruits granted the use of them" [ἡ πρώτη νομοθεσία τῶν καρπῶν ἀπέλαυσιν σωφροσύνης]. Tertullian, Origen, and, as Mercer puts it, most of our people commenting on that passage, held the same view. Pererius, however, relying on the support of Chrysostom and Theodoret, denies that this passage proves that eating flesh was forbidden before the flood. He thinks it was not forbidden, but that more devout men abstained from it, namely the descendants of Seth. Their holiness and uprightness are very famous, but I am not persuaded that they abstained altogether, or that they were moved to it by religious scruple. For without God's command they would have incurred his offence through self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκείαν]. I add that they could not restrain themselves in sacrifices. Paraeus and Calvin lean to the view that the passage does not speak of a new grant but of a renewed and repeated one. Now we must firmly establish the following. First, it was not consistent that man should receive after the flood more power over animals, by way of the use of reason, than he had at the beginning of the world or after Adam's fall. For through the utmost wickedness and exulting wantonness of the men before the flood they would have acquired a wider extent of power. Second, if the law were new and not renewed, God could not have sanctioned the law of sacrifices long before those times. For that law could not stand on any ground without a grant of flesh. Third, the grant of flesh stands in the same relation as the other parts of the divine blessing and grant: namely, that they are commanded to increase and multiply, to rule over the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven, to eat herbs and vegetables, and to abstain from shedding blood. Yet these later laws were not new but repeated. For who can doubt that they were also given to Adam? The legislation concerning flesh is therefore of the same kind. Fourth, if the grant of flesh is new, the prohibition of eating blood must also be new. For thus Moses says: Every creeping thing shall be food for you; as the green herb I gave you all things. But you shall not eat flesh with its life, which is its blood. But Curcellaeus steadfastly denies that the prohibition against eating blood is new. Therefore the grant of flesh was not new either, but repeated. This is an argument against the man. Fifth, it is very unlikely that the men of old before the flood, whose wickedness had already gone beyond measure, abstained from the flesh of animals amid that confusion of things. Would those who did not restrain themselves even from shedding human blood abstain from eating flesh, they whose unrestrained gluttony Christ noted? If they ate flesh, they did so either against the law or by permission. If against the law, it would have been a most grave crime, since it was a transgression of positive law. But [illegible] concerning this, in the list of sins for which the waters were brought upon the world, nothing is said. They therefore sinned not in the use of flesh but in the abuse of power, which Christ rightly condemned. Sixth, I add the testimony of the most weighty interpreter of all, Calvin: Further, the Lord goes on, and grants animals to men for food, so that they may be fed with their flesh. But since Moses now first reports that this right was given to men, almost all interpreters conclude that it was not lawful for man before the flood to eat flesh, and that only the natural fruits of the earth were his food. But the argument is not firm enough. For I hold to this principle: that God here bestows on men no more than he had given, but only restores what had been taken away, just as he again furnishes the possession of goods from which they had been driven. So far Calvin. What, then, is the reason why Moses mentioned the eating of flesh only after the flood? Surely because God wished to enact a law concerning not eating blood and what has been strangled. This exception had to be set against the general grant, so it was first necessary to repeat the grant itself, so that the exception could be understood more easily. God the Lawgiver keeps to the same method he had just used with Adam: Genesis 2:16, Of every tree of this garden you may freely eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat. He placed the general grant beneath the exception. So it is here: you shall eat flesh as you eat herbs, but you shall not eat the blood. As if he said: "What I forbid you to eat of blood, I do not on that account restrict your power or prohibit you from eating flesh. Eat freely, just as with herbs. But set the blood apart and do not eat it with the flesh." Curcellaeus admits that this answer would have the appearance of truth if it were established that Adam was permitted to use flesh for food in the state of integrity. We have supported both our answer and the position itself with very firm arguments, and above we have shown that it was lawful in the state of integrity and after Adam's fall. We do not wish, therefore, to waste our effort.

units.la: XV. Causam inquirit deinceps Curcellæus concessionis hujus Postdiluvianæ.
units.tr: XV. Curcellaeus next inquires into the cause of this post-Diluvian concession.

units.la: Theologos reddere quasdam hujus indulti rationes. Videlicet Terræ corruptionem per aquas maris salsas, quibus diluvii tempore operta fuerat, adeò ut non posset amplius tam probum atque antea hominibus alimentum suppeditare: item insignem humanarum virium diminutionem, quam arguit brevitas vitæ eorum, qui post diluvium nati sunt, si cum antediluvianis conferantur. Hæc judicat veritati consentanea. Ego neutrum calculo dignor. Quasi ante diluvium aquæ maris salsæ totum Terrarum rarum orbem non perfuderint. Et cataractis Coeli solutis aquae coelitus ruentes Terram, non falsae maris oppleverunt. Neque verius, quod vires humani corporis diluvio fractae sint. Decurtatę hominum vitae alia & altior causa. De caetero Postdiluviani neque corporis habitu, neque animi viribus infra homines anteriores fuerunt. Disputatio, quam subnectit de salubritate & praestantia herbarum prae carnibus, plane & est. Nam, quod in vestibulo nostrae tractationis monuimus, non est hic quaestio de medica à carnibus vel sanguine abstinentia, sed de religiosa, imperio Dei injuncta. Deinde ita agit, tanquam econsu carnes essent expungendae, quae veterum Pythagoreorum & Manichaeorum deliria fuerunt. Hinc adoptat & praedicat tantopere Tertulliani Montanizantis praeceps & periculosum dogma: eo fere modo Deum Noacho & Filiis ejus concessisse esum carnium, quo postea Israelitis propter duritiem cordis ipsorum, repudii libellum uxoribus dare permisit: nempe quia videbat vix aliter posse hominum gulam compesci, quàm liberam faciendo eis potestatem, cibos, quibus jam assueverunt, vel quos valde appetebant, usurpandi. Imò acri tibiâ decantat Philosophos & Sacerdotes Gentiles, Aegyptios, Persas, Indorum Gymnosophistas, ipsum Pythagoram, cujus duos libros laudat. Estne magis sive Manichaeorum, sive Encratitarum, sive Marcionitarum, sive Ebionitarum, sive Papistarum de carnibus doctrina, daemoniorum doctrina, quàm Curcellaei? Si de immoderato carnium usu loqueretur, non improbaremus? Nunc patet, in universum ipsi pravum existimari carnium esum. Quid enim aliud est, dicere: Carnes concessas ob πληροκαρδίαν hominum? Quae in V. T. ob duritiem cordis humani indulta sunt, ea ipse fuerunt lege restricta, adeóque mala. Sic polygamia, divortium, & si quid aliud. Haec enim cum lege divinitus data diserte pugnabant. Ideo Christus ad veterem normam conformavit. Quanto melius cum Apostolo dixisset: Omnis creatura Dei bona, & nihil rejectaneum, cum gratiarum actione susceptum. 1. Tim. IV. 4. Novi & persuasus sum in Domino Jesu, nihil pollutum à se ipso esse, nisi ei qui reputat aliquid pollutum esse. Rom. XIV. 14. Cur judicat fratrem, & conscientiam infirmi verberat, & perdit eum, pro quo Christus est mortuus? Et docet Regnum Dei esse βρῶσις καὶ πόσις, ut obliviscantur homines justitiae, pacis, gaudii in Spiritu Sancto, & τῶν βαρυλέρων ἐξ νόμος? Si ob πλυροκαρδίαν homini concessae carnes, cur Deus sibi in Sacrificiis illas devoveri curavit? Cur Christus, quem dicunt Spiritualem, Angelicam & excellentiorem illâ, quam Moses mandavit, vitam injunxisse, non correxit? Cur magis declaravit, nihil, quod ingreditur in os hominis, polluere posse? Imò ipsemet exemplar Sanctitatis & Justitiæ ab esu carnium cur non abhorruit? Nisi forte in eo peccavit Sanctissimus Salvator. Quem omnino βλασφημῶντες dicunt Legi Divinæ non obedire, & sic non obediendo peccare potuisse, in Resp. ad Excerpt. Specim. XVIII. Sed hâc jam provinciâ, in qua tam diu nos tanquam in diverticulo retinuit, decedamus.
units.tr: He says that theologians offer some reasons for this indulgence, namely: the corruption of the earth by the salt waters of the sea, with which it had been covered at the time of the flood, so that it could no longer supply food to men as good as before; likewise the marked diminution of human strength, which is shown by the brevity of life of those born after the flood, when compared with the people before the flood. He judges these views to agree with the truth. I think neither deserves a hearing. As if the waters of the sea had not flooded the whole round orbit of the lands before the flood! And when the floodgates of heaven were opened, the waters that poured down from heaven did not overflow the earth without salt. Nor is it truer that the strength of the human body was broken by the flood. The shortening of human life had another and deeper cause. Otherwise, those after the flood were in neither bodily make-up nor mental power inferior to the men before them. The discussion he appends about the wholesomeness and excellence of herbs over meats is quite and altogether beside the point. For, as we noted at the threshold of our treatment, the question here is not about abstinence from meat or blood for medical reasons, but about religious abstinence, enjoined by the command of God. Next he proceeds as if meat were to be struck off altogether, which was the delirium of the old Pythagoreans and Manichaeans. Hence he adopts and proclaims, with such emphasis, the headlong and dangerous dogma of Tertullian, the Montanist: God in much the same way granted to Noah and his sons the eating of flesh, as later he allowed the Israelites, because of the hardness of their hearts, to give their wives a bill of divorce; namely, because he saw that the gluttony of men could scarcely be restrained in any other way than by giving them freedom to take the foods to which they were already accustomed, or which they very much desired. Indeed, he sings loudly in praise of the Gentile philosophers and priests, the Egyptians, the Persians, the Gymnosophists of the Indians, and Pythagoras himself, whose two books he commends. Is the teaching about meat of the Manichaeans, the Encratites, the Marcionites, the Ebionites, or the Papists, a doctrine of demons, any more than Curcellaeus's? If he were speaking of the immoderate use of meat, would we not disapprove? It is now plain that he holds the eating of meat to be wrong in general. For what else is it to say that meats were permitted because of the over-fullness of heart [πληροκαρδίαν] of men? Those things which were granted in the Old Testament because of the hardness of the human heart were themselves restricted by the law, and so were evil: such as polygamy, divorce, and anything else of the kind, for these plainly contradicted the law given by God. Therefore Christ conformed them to the old norm. How much better it would have been to say with the Apostle: Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4:4), and I know, and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean of itself, except to him who considers something to be unclean (Rom. 14:14). Why does he judge his brother, wound the conscience of the weak, and destroy the one for whom Christ died? And why does he teach that the Kingdom of God is eating and drinking [βρῶσις καὶ πόσις], so that men forget justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, and the weightier matters of the law [τῶν βαρυτέρων τοῦ νόμου]? If meats were permitted to man because of over-fullness of heart, why did God take care to have them devoted to himself in the sacrifices? Why did Christ, whom they call spiritual, angelic, and more excellent than the life that Moses commanded, not correct it? Why did he rather declare that nothing which enters the mouth of a man can defile? Why did he himself, the pattern of holiness and righteousness, not shrink from eating meat? Unless perhaps the most holy Saviour sinned in this! They certainly, blaspheming, say that he did not obey the Divine Law, and that by not obeying he could have sinned, in the Reply to the Excerpt Specimen XVIII. But let us now leave this province, in which he has kept us so long, as if in a side-track.

units.la: XVI. Nunc paucis & stringendo rationes promemus, quòd usque ad diluvii tempora integer & liberimus constituerit sanguinis usus. Primò. Natura non dictat abstinentiam à sanguine. Nec quidem sequentibus temporibus legis naturalis hoc caput fuit, ut procedente nostra disputatione liquebit. Dictare igitur debuit Deus præcepto aliquo positivo. Quæcunque autem ex præcepto Dei positivo necessaria fuerunt, illa vel Scripturis mandata extant, vel alicubi leguntur à Sanctis Dei viris, quorum erat noscibilis religio, observata. Talis lex de non comedendo fructu vetitæ arboris, de Sacrificiis. Illa diserte scripto mandata. Hanc Sancti Dei viri, Adamus & Habel custodiverunt. Atqui lex de non comedendo sanguine neque scripta est, neque à quoquam observata legitur in primis Mosis capitibus. Ergo non fuit positiva.
units.tr: XVI. Now, briefly and concisely, let us set out the reasons why the free use of blood was permitted until the time of the flood. First, nature does not dictate abstinence from blood. Nor indeed in the following times was this a part of the natural law, as will become clear as our discussion proceeds. God must therefore have prescribed it by some positive precept. Now whatever was necessary by a positive precept of God either stands written in the Scriptures as commanded, or is read somewhere as observed by the holy men of God whose religion is known. Such was the law about not eating the fruit of the forbidden tree, and the law about sacrifices: the former expressly commanded in writing, the latter kept by the holy men of God, Adam and Abel. But the law about not eating blood is neither written nor read as observed by anyone in the first chapters of Moses. Therefore it was not positive.

units.la: 2. Talis fuit rebus adhuc integris homini data libertas, qualem Christus reparavit, & sub novo Testamento Christianis donavit. Atqui Christus nobis libertatem reparavit à jugo omnium ceremoniarum, & legum carnalium, qualis fuit post diluvium de non comedendo sanguine. Ergo eadem libertas homini integro competiit.
units.tr: 2. The freedom given to man while things were still whole was of the kind that Christ restored and bestowed on Christians under the New Testament. But Christ has restored to us freedom from the yoke of all ceremonies and carnal laws, such as was the law after the flood about not eating blood. Therefore the same freedom belonged to man in his integrity.

units.la: 3. Quod Christum & ejus in sanguine expiationem figurat, illius obligatio in statu innocentiæ locum non habuit. Non fuit enim Christus homini integro promissus. Sanguinis autem abstinentia Christi in sanguine expiationem figuravit. Sic enim Moses, כי הדם הוא בנפש יכפר, quoniam in sanguine est expiatio animæ, Lexit. XVII. 11. Non igitur in statu innocentiæ hæc obligatio inducta fuit.
units.tr: 3. What figures Christ and his atonement in the blood cannot have been binding in the state of innocence. For Christ was not promised to man in his integrity. But abstinence from blood figured Christ's atonement in the blood. For so Moses says: כי הדם הוא בנפש יכפר [for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life], Lev. 17:11. Therefore this obligation was not introduced in the state of innocence.

units.la: 4. Nulla lex obligat, antequam promulgata sit. Sicut nullum imperium vim habet non cognitum. Lex autem de abstinentia Sanguinis ante diluvium non fuit promulgata. Prima enim νομοθεσίας promulgatio extat Genes. IX. 4. Non igitur ante obligare coepit. Curcellæus, quia concessio carnium declarata videtur demum post diluvium, conficere voluit, antea illicitas fuisse carnes. Non igitur eodem jure concluderemus, quia post diluvium demum prohibitus sanguis, ante ea tempora usum liberum fuisse?
units.tr: 4. No law binds before it is promulgated, just as no authority has force if it is not known. But the law about abstinence from blood was not promulgated before the flood. For the first promulgation of the legislation stands in Genesis 9:4. Therefore it did not begin to bind before. Curcellaeus, because the permission to eat meat seems declared only after the flood, wished to conclude that meats were forbidden before. By the same right would we not conclude that, since blood was forbidden only after the flood, its free use had existed before those times?

units.la: CAPUT IV. A tempore Noachi usque ad Mosen sanguinis esum fuisse illicitum ex ceremoniali sanctione, probatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. That the eating of blood was forbidden by ceremonial sanction from the time of Noah until Moses, is proved.

units.la: A diluvio usque ad Mosen ceremonialiter illicitum fuisse esum sanguinis. 1. Locus Genes. IX. 4. Vulgatus notatur LXX. versio. Onkelosus. Vzielides, Iarchi, Aben-Ezra, Lutherus, Musculus, Mercerus explicant de membro animalis viventis. 2. 3. Ostenditur contra Curcellaeum, sententiam hanc neque novam esse, nec à Iudaeorum Magistris haustam. Iudaeorum deliria. Jonathae Vzielidis authoritas. Non odio Christianorum Iudaeos interpretari de membro animalis viventis. 4. Impugnatur tribus rationibus interpretatio de membro vivente. 5. Piscatoris rationes solvuntur. 6. Chrysostomi, Ludovici de Dieu explicatio de suffocato. Ostenditur, etiam suffocatum sub hoc praecepto contineri. Cur neget Curcellaeus? 7. Redditur genuina loci interpretatio. Anima pro vita. Versio Arabica. Persica Tavvusi. Iosephi suffragium. 8. Rationes praecepti vestiganatur. Ratio prima typica. Contra illam objectiones Curcellaei refelluntur. 9. Ratio Ethica praecepti. Chrysostomi calculus. Nephilim non gigantes fuisse. 10. Eugubinus perstringitur. Cruciare carnem pro sanguine non est occidere. 11. Rationem Physicam praecepti promunt Iudaei: Beemannus, Curcellaeus. Rejiciuntur. 12. Probatur, Praeceptum Noachicum ceremoniale fuisse. Quousque obliget omnes Noachidas? Terminus a quo rejectionis Gentilium. Locus Rom. III. vers. 2. explicatus. 13. Curcellaeus argumentum nostrum nec bene intellexit, nec dextre solvit. Locus Genes. XV. 15. 16. 14. Gentiles
units.tr: From the Flood until Moses, the eating of blood was ceremonially forbidden. 1. The passage Gen. 9:4. The Vulgate is noted, and the Septuagint version, Onkelos. Uziel, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Luther, Musculus and Mercerus explain it of a member of a living animal. 2, 3. It is shown against Curcellaeus that this opinion is neither new nor drawn from the Jewish masters. The follies of the Jews. The authority of Jonathan ben Uziel. The Jews do not interpret it of a member of a living animal out of hatred for Christians. 4. The interpretation of a member of a living animal is refuted by three arguments. 5. The arguments of Piscator are answered. 6. The explanation of Chrysostom and Ludovicus de Dieu, that it refers to what has been strangled. It is shown that even what has been strangled is contained under this precept. Why does Curcellaeus deny it? 7. The genuine interpretation of the passage is given. Soul for life. The Arabic version. The Persian of Tawusi. The support of Josephus. 8. The reasons for the precept are traced. The first reason is typical. Curcellaeus' objections against it are refuted. 9. The ethical reason for the precept. Chrysostom's reckoning. That the Nephilim were not giants. 10. Eugubinus is censured. To torment the flesh instead of the blood is not to kill. 11. The Jews offer the physical reason for the precept: Beemannus, Curcellaeus. It is rejected. 12. It is proved that the Noachic precept was ceremonial. How far does it oblige all the sons of Noah? The starting point of the rejection of the Gentiles. The passage Rom. 3:2 is explained. 13. Curcellaeus neither rightly understood our argument nor answered it properly. The passage Gen. 15:15, 16. 14. The Gentiles

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: HActenus oblique nobiscum egit Curcellæus. Nunc levato velo, apertius & directe impetum facit. Probare molitur: Omnem sanguinis esum, à Noachi sive potius diluvii tempore usque ad Mosen & Legem, per omnem Israëlitis latam, interdictum fuisse. Hoc verò ἀνεξαλωτον. Cæterum dubitatione non caret, utrum prohibitio sit à præcepto naturali, vel morali, an à ceremoniali? Circa hoc omnino vertitur quæstionis nostræ cardo. Prohibitionem nos agnoscimus. Negamus à morali præcepto manare. Hoc igitur nobis negotii dari intelligimus, ut primò genuinum loci Mosaici sensum, nonnihil involutum, expositum demus: deinde rationes interdicti vestigemus; ac demum hoc liquidò expediamus, prohibitionem à præcepto morali non scaturire, sed à ceremoniali. Quibus in aprico positis non erit ultra contentioni locus.
units.tr: Hitherto Curcellaeus has dealt with us obliquely. Now, with the veil lifted, he attacks more openly and directly. He labours to prove that every eating of blood, from the time of Noah, or rather of the Flood, down to Moses and the Law, was forbidden to all Israelites. This, indeed, is unassailable [ἀνεξάλωτον]. Yet it is not free from doubt whether the prohibition derives from a natural or moral precept, or from a ceremonial one. The hinge of our whole question turns on this point. We acknowledge the prohibition. We deny that it flows from a moral precept. Our task, then, is first to set out the genuine sense of the Mosaic passage, which is somewhat involved; second, to trace the reasons for the prohibition; and last, to settle clearly that the prohibition springs not from a moral precept but from a ceremonial one. Once these points are placed in the light, there will be no further room for dispute.

units.la: II. Deus igitur ubi homini illibatum dominium restituit, facit ipsi omnium rerum copiam, excepto sanguine. Verba Mosis: אך בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו Excepto quod carnem cum sanguine non comedetis. Genes. IX. 4. Sic vulgatus Interpres, qui utrum officio boni Interpretis ritè defunctus sit, merito dubites. Nam in medio relinquitur vox נפש. Peretius vulgatum tuetur. Frequens est, inquit, in S. Literis usus Figuræ, quam nominant Appositionem. Apponitur enim vox ad prioris vocis expositionem, ut hic illud, in sanguine suo, appositum est ad explicandum id, quod dictum fuerat in anima sua. Ita quidem est. Sed hoc Scriptori tantùm, non Interpreti licet, cujus est verbum verbo reddere. Septuaginta viralis habet: Κρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ φάγεσθε. Carnem in anima, sanguine non comedetis. Quæ versio magnopere sensum turbat. Quid enim est caro in sanguine animæ? Targum Onkelosi ita disponit, tanquam prohibiti essent Noachidæ carnem cum anima sua & sanguine comedere. Ita habet: ברם בשרא בנפשיה דמיה לא תיכולון, verumtamen carnem cum anima sua, sanguinéque ne comedetis.
units.tr: II. When God restored to man his undiminished dominion, he granted him the use of all things, except blood. The words of Moses are: "Only flesh with its life, which is its blood, you shall not eat" [אך בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו], "except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood." Genesis 9.4. So the Vulgate translator renders it, and one may rightly doubt whether he discharged the office of a good translator. For the word נפש is left undecided. Peretius defends the Vulgate. The figure which they call apposition, he says, is frequent in Holy Scripture: a word is placed in apposition to explain the preceding word, as here "in its blood" is added to explain what was said "in its life." That is so, but such licence belongs to the writer, not to the translator, whose task is to render word for word. The Seventy's version reads: "Flesh in the life of its blood you shall eat not" [Κρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ φάγεσθε]. This version greatly disturbs the sense. For what is flesh in the blood of the soul? The Targum of Onkelos arranges it as if the Noahides were forbidden to eat flesh together with its soul and blood. It reads: "barem bisra benafshiyeh demiyeh la tikhulun," that is, "but you shall not eat flesh with its soul and blood."

units.la: III. Uzielides paraphrastes respicit ad אבר מן החי. Sic igitur reddit: אך ברם בשרא דתליש מן חיותא חיא בזמן דבנפשיה ביה, או דתליש מן חיותא נביסתה וער דלא נפקא כולא נשמתא Verum carnem, quae lacerata est ex bestia vivente, quo tempore anima ejus in ipso est: aut quae lacerata est a bestia, dum mactatur, antequam exeat omnis anima ejus, ne comedatis. Uzielidem sequitur R. Sol. Jarchi, qui interpretatur אשר להם אבר מן החי in quibus est membrum de vivo. Nempe inquit: כל זמן שנפשו ברמו לא תאכלו בשר Omni tempore, quo est vita in sanguine ejus, non comedetis carnem. Eodem modo Aben-Ezras: כן טעמו אך בשר עם נפשו שהוא דמו לא תאכלו כטעם לא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר כי נפש כל בשר דמו בנפשו הוא האורת הנפש המתנועעת והמרגשת היא גוף: Sic sensus ejus est: Tantum carnem cum anima sua, quae est sanguis ejus, non edetis, juxta illud: Non edes animam cum carne, quia anima omnis caro sanguis ejus in anima ejus est: Haec anima motrix & sentiens est corpus. Subscribunt huic sententiae Musculus, Mercerus, ipse etiam Lutherus. Lutheri verba, in Genes. cap. IX. sunt: Prohibet Deus hoc in loco id corpus comedi, quod habet adhuc agitantem, viventem & movente animam; sicut milvus pullum gallinaceum, lepus oves vorat, non mactatas antea, sed vivas. Hanc crudelitatem interdicit hoc loco Dominus, & restringit illam mactandi licentiam, ne fiat belluino modo, ubi viva corpora, aut vivorum corporum partes vorantur: Sed ut conservetur legalis mactatio, qualis ad aram & in sacris fieri debebat esse: Ubi sine crudelitate mactabatur bestia, & bene abluta a sanguine tandem offerebatur Deo. Hanc puto simplicem & veram esse sententiam; quam etiam Judaeorum Magistri sequuntur, ne crudas carnes & adhuc palpitantia membra, Lestrygonum aut Cyclopum more, voremus. Musculi verba ad c. 1. sunt: Non prohibet, ne animalium sanguis fundatur. Alioquin quomodo ederentur? Sed crudelitatem ferinam prohibet, ne homo ad morem bestiarum cruentam animalium carnem voret. Quid necesse erat hac exceptione & prohibitione, si a cruenta feritate alienus est prorsus animus humanus? Reperiuntur gentes, quae carne humana vescuntur: quid mirum, si reperiantur, qui immani feritate magis bestias, quam homines referentes, carnem crudam, & calido adhuc cruore palpitantem vorent? Mercerus prolixius paulo. Non tamen sententiam ejus adscribere pigrabor. Hic, inquit, arctat generaliter tiam potestatem, quam dederat edendi animantes, & rationem ac legem prescribit, qua illis vesci debeant. Volo ita vos sanguinem animantium edendorum effundere, ut crudelitatem interim vitetis, ne eorum carnem simul cum sanguine comedatis. Variant hic Hebraei. Quidam putant hic vetari membrum ex vivo, ut dicunt, quod unum esse ajunt ex septem praeceptis tum traditis filiis Noë, ne scinderet ex animante vivente adhuc membrum ferarum more deterrerent ad edendum, id quod nimis belluinum sit & crudele, & cum ingluvie etiam conjunctum, expectare non posse, donec jugulatum sit animans, &c. Alii putant sic vetari דם מן הנפש sanguinem animantis adhuc viventis. Rambam putat, simplicitatem hujus contextus tantum ferre, ut אבר מן exponatur, non item de sanguine.
