Ego utrumque putarim hic includi, ne aut membrum ex animante adhuc vivo palpitans, aut etiam sanguis adhuc palpitans edatur. Nam esum alioquin sanguinis e jugulato animante, qui jam refrixerit, hic prohiberi non putarim, nisi ex consequenti. Id tandem in lege prohibetur, Levit. XVII. quia sanguis est anima animantis, ut eo loco ratio affertur. Ne scilicet ad sanguinis effusionem inde homines facile inciterentur ab effusione sanguinis animantium ad effusionem humani sanguinis, ut videmus lanios bestiarum fere crudeliores esse, & a sanguine humano haud valde abhorrere. Multa tamen ante legem, ea postea cauta, videmus fuisse observata. Et sane eadem ratio in his tribus obtinet. Corpus enim, non animam animantium voluit Deus concedi, quae est in sanguine posita. Hactenus Mercerus. Accedit huic etiam sententiae Salom. Gesnerus quaest. 7. in Genesin.
units.tr: III. The paraphrast Uzziel looks to the phrase אבר מן החי, a limb from the living. He therefore renders it: "But truly, the flesh that is torn from a living beast while its soul is in it, or that is torn from a beast while it is being slaughtered, before all its soul has gone out, you shall not eat" [Aramaic: dishtalish min chayta...]. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi follows Uzziel, and he explains the words "in which is a limb of the living" as "in which is a limb from the living." Namely, he says: "At every time when its life is in its blood, you shall not eat flesh" [כל זמן שנפשו ברמו לא תאכלו בשר]. In the same way Aben Ezra says: "Thus its sense is: only flesh with its soul, which is its blood, you shall not eat, according to that saying: You shall not eat the soul with the flesh, for the soul of all flesh is its blood in its soul. This moving and sensing soul is the body." Musculus, Mercer, and even Luther himself subscribe to this view. Luther's words on Genesis 9 are: God forbids in this place the eating of a body which still has a moving, living soul; just as the kite devours a chicken and the hare devours sheep, not slaughtered beforehand but alive. The Lord forbids this cruelty here, and restricts the licence of slaughter, so that it is not done in a beastly manner, where living bodies or parts of living bodies are devoured; but so that the lawful slaughter is preserved, such as ought to be done at the altar and in sacred rites, where the beast was slaughtered without cruelty, and, well washed from its blood, was at last offered to God. I think this is the simple and true sense, which also the Masters of the Jews follow, so that we do not devour raw flesh and limbs still quivering, after the manner of the Laestrygonians or the Cyclopes. Musculus's words on chapter 1 are: He does not forbid the blood of animals to be poured out; otherwise how could they be eaten? But he forbids savage cruelty, that man should not, after the manner of beasts, devour the bloody flesh of animals. Why was this exception and prohibition necessary, if the human mind were altogether free from bloody savagery? There are peoples who feed on human flesh. What wonder, then, if there are those who, with a barbarity more like beasts than men, devour raw flesh still quivering with warm blood? Mercer is somewhat fuller. I will not hesitate to set down his view. Here, he says, God generally restricts the power he had given to eat animals, and prescribes the manner and law by which they ought to be eaten. I want you to pour out the blood of the animals you eat in such a way that you avoid cruelty in the meantime, so that you do not eat their flesh together with the blood. The Hebrews differ here. Some think that the phrase "a limb from the living" is forbidden, which, they say, is one of the seven precepts given to the sons of Noah: that one should not tear a limb from a living animal, as the beasts do, since this is too beastly and cruel, and combined with gluttony, and one cannot wait until the animal has been killed. Others think that the blood of a living animal is thus forbidden [דם מן הנפש], the blood of an animal still alive. Rambam thinks that the simplicity of this context allows only that "a limb from" should be explained, not blood. I would suppose that both are included here, so that neither a limb torn from a still living animal, quivering, nor blood still quivering, is eaten. For I would not think that the eating of blood from a slaughtered animal which has already cooled is prohibited here, except by implication. That is forbidden in the Law at Leviticus 17, because the blood is the life of the animal, as the reason is given there: so that from the shedding of animal blood men might not easily be incited thereby to the shedding of human blood, as we see that butchers are almost more cruel than beasts and do not greatly shrink from human blood. Yet we see that many such things were guarded against before the Law, and afterwards. And certainly the same reasoning holds for these three things. For God wished only the body of animals to be granted, not their soul, which lies in the blood. Thus far Mercer. Salomon Gesner in his Question 7 on Genesis also agrees with this view.

units.la: IV. Huic posteriori interpretationi tristem se gerit Curcellaeus. Illam dicit esse adeo coactam, ut putet nemini unquam Christiano in mentem fuisse venturam, nisi aliqui recentiores Judaeorum Magistri praivissent, qui illa, quae ante pedes jacent inanimadversa praeterire soliti, acuminis laudem in paradoxis confingendis affectant, p. 42. Plus quam Siculas gerras & putidissima nugamenta Judaeorum posteriorum quis ignorat? Cui non dictus Hylas? Monstra sunt, in quae si incidisset Hercules, putasset sibi tertium decimum laborem venisse. Ut his de Androgyno, Lilitha, & frivola ratione pro mortuorum resurrectione figmentis jungi infinita alia possint, si exorbitare luberet. Sed hoc loco malem Curcellaeum judicium suum non praecipitasse. Nam nec cum caeteris Judaeorum febrilibus deliriis haec interpretatio comparari meretur, neque est χθὲς ἡ σήμερον Lucina obstetricante, nata. Quicquid etiam Grotius dicat: Christianorum odio Judaeos illam sententiam amplexos. Quamvis enim obrationes, quas confestim sum editurus, in illorum, qui ita interpretantur, sententiam discessionem facere nolim, existimo tamen non usque adeo coactam interpretationem. Imo si caetera recte haberent, expositio maxime literalis & simplicissima, quomodo Cajetanus & Piscator appellant, videri possit: Attamen carnem in anima sua, qua sanguis est, non comedetis; id est: dum adhuc praedita est anima sua & sanguine suo, dum adhuc vivit & palpitat. pitat. Quid hic magnopere coactum, vel equuleo subditum? Neque verum, Interpretibus illis Christianis, quos supra commemoravi, Luthero, Musculo, Mercero, Piscatori, Gesnero, & si quibus aliis, recentiores Judaeorum Magistellos praeviisse. De Jonathane quidem Uzielide nihil dicam, cujus Targum in Pentateuchum nequaquam à Judaeis quibusdam, ipso etiam Galatino & Postello pro antiquo veri Jonathanis celebratum, Drusii, Buxtorfii, Schikhardi & aliorum critico veru pridem confossum. Sed de Thalmudicis veteribus quid planius? Illi enim inter praecepta Noachidarum ultimo numerant loco אבר מן החי, quod plurimi negant intelligendum de sanguine occisi animalis separato, sed potius, ut verba aperte sonant, de membro viventis, quorum sententiam in praeliminaribus expositam dedimus. Et praeceptum illud ex ipsis Mosaicis verbis elici-unt. Confer Doctissimum Cuneum de Rep. Hebr. II. 19. & Seldenum, qui Veteres Talmudicos praeceptum Noachicum non aliter intellexisse probat. Nihil igitur causae fuit, cur hanc interpretationem recentiorem esse & musteam comminisceretur. Nisi forte, quia animus erat, Interpretes nostros tanquam transversos Judaicis fabulis abreptos pipulo differre. Sed & cur Grotius dixerit, Judaeos recentiores odio Christianorum hoc commentos, rationem non reperio. Quid enim est in illa interpretatione, quo dolere Christiani debeant magis, quam in quacunque alia? An quia hac ratione sica ex manibus Curcellaeo extorqueretur? Atqui meminerit, aequè Judaeos atrociter contra esum sanguinis depugnare. Neque tam stolidi sunt, ut odio Christianorum, quo etiam nocere nequeant, segetes ipsi suas vastare velint. Nemo gratis malus est. Quin Maimonides, cujus non est in universum sublesta fides, interdicti sic concepti aliam rationem affert: שכן היו עשים מלכי הגוים וגם לעבודת זרה היו עשים כן רוצה לאמר שהיו חתנים מן הבהמה אבר מדן ואוכלים אותו: Quoniam ita eo seculo facere solebant Gentilium Reges, etiam idololatriae causa ita faciebant. Scilicet animali abscindebant membrum aliquod, atque illud comedebant. Haec obiter, ne omnino indefensi interpretes nostri à Curcellaei asperiore Critica abirent, & ipse impune vindemiam faceret. Quid enim Novatoribus istis usitatius, quàm ut Theologorum nostrorum interpretationibus sequius & rigidius acceptis, invidiam conciliando, sibi delicias faciant?
units.tr: IV. Curcellaeus takes a gloomy view of this latter interpretation. He says it is so forced that no Christian would ever have thought of it, unless some more recent Masters of the Jews had gone before, who, habitually overlooking what lies plainly before their feet, aim at a reputation for cleverness by inventing paradoxes, p. 42. Who does not know the Sicilian squabbles and most putrid trifles of the later Jews? Who has not heard of Hylas? They are monsters, and if Hercules had fallen upon them, he would have thought a thirteenth labour had come to him. Infinite other such things could be added, about the Androgyne, Lilith, and the flimsy reasons for the resurrection of the dead, if one were willing to wander off. But in this place I would rather that Curcellaeus had not rushed to his judgement. For this interpretation does not deserve to be compared with the other feverish ravings of the Jews, nor is it born yesterday, with Lucina as midwife. Whatever Grotius may say: The Jews embraced that opinion out of hatred of Christians. For although I would not wish to dissent from the opinion of those who so interpret, which I shall soon publish with my arguments, I nevertheless think the interpretation is not so forced. Indeed, if the rest were sound, the most literal and simplest exposition, as Cajetan and Piscator call it, might seem right: Yet you shall not eat flesh in its soul, which is its blood; that is, while its soul and its blood are still in it, while it is still alive and quivering. What is so greatly forced here, or stretched on the rack? Nor is it true that those Christian interpreters I have mentioned above, Luther, Musculus, Mercer, Piscator, Gesner, and any others, went before the more recent little Masters of the Jews. As for Jonathan Uzziel, I will say nothing: his Targum on the Pentateuch, celebrated by certain Jews and even by Galatinus and Postel as the ancient work of the true Jonathan, was long ago thoroughly exposed by the critical work of Drusius, Buxtorf, Schickard and others. But what is plainer than the old Talmudic writers? For they number among the precepts of the Noahides, as the last in order, the phrase "a limb from the living" [אבר מן החי], which most deny should be understood of blood separated from a slaughtered animal, but rather, as the words plainly sound, of a limb of a living creature, whose sense we gave in the preliminaries. And they derive that precept from the very words of Moses. Compare the most learned Cuneus, On the Hebrew Commonwealth II.19, and Selden, who proves that the Ancient Talmudists understood the Noachic precept in no other way. There was therefore no reason why they should invent this interpretation as recent and new-fangled. Unless perhaps because they were eager to show that our interpreters, like men led astray by Jewish fables, differ from one another by a hair's breadth. But why Grotius said that the later Jews devised this out of hatred of Christians, I cannot find the reason. For what is there in that interpretation for which Christians ought to grieve more than in any other? Or is it because by this method the sickle would be wrested from Curcellaeus's hands? Yet let him remember that the Jews fight just as fiercely against the eating of blood. Nor are they so foolish as to wish to ruin their own crops out of hatred for Christians, which they could not even harm. No one is wicked for nothing. Indeed Maimonides, whose faith is not altogether contemptible, gives another reason for the prohibition so conceived: [שכן היו עושים מלכי הגוים וגם לעבודה זרה היו עושים כן... רוצה לומר שהיו חותכים מן הבהמה אבר מן ואוכלים אותו] For in that age the kings of the nations used to do so, and even for idolatry they did so. That is to say, they would cut off some limb from the animal and eat it. I have said these things in passing, so that our interpreters should not depart wholly undefended from the harsher criticism of Curcellaeus, and so that he should not reap his vintage with impunity. For what is more usual with those innovators than to take the interpretations of our theologians in the less favourable and harsher sense, and so to win ill will and make a delight of it for themselves?

units.la: V. Sed nunc rationes aperiamus, ob quas non videatur vere consentanea illorum interpretatio. Primò, quia non indiguerunt prohiberi, à quibus suopte impetu hominum indoles abhorruit. Quotusquisque enim inter homines adeò efferatus & tristis Polyphemus, qui carnes vivas deglutiat? Non minùs igitur hæc Caniballica Deus interdixit, quàm vel anthropophagiam, vel quidquam aliud, quod infra humanitatem subsidit, & ferinam crudelitatem olet. Maimonides quidem supra nobis adfirmavit, Gentilium quibusdam Regibus idololatriæ causâ feralem hunc ritum in usu fuisse. Iam ut de tempore Moses hoc concedatur, quemadmodum id nostro etiam tempore quidam restantur de Canibalibus, quos in sua navigatione prætervectus Columbus: unde patet vel Noachi tempore, quo lata hæc lex, vel ante Noachum ejusmodi ritum receptum fuisse? Quid ni vel Moses vel Christus, qui acriter in hominum illorum depravatos mores invecti, etiam hoc flagitium iis imputâssent? Sed fuerit hoc in more illis positum, cur magis crudelitatem illam legum repagulis compesceret, quàm flagitia alia his etiam graviora? Puta libidinem, raptum, idololatriam, Epicureismum, & si quid aliud? 2. Idem prohibet Deus Noacho, quod jubente eodem Israelitis Moses. Hic autem non interdixit esum membri viventis vel palpitantis, sed sanguinem animalis occisi. Patet; quic inter alia interdicti hanc rationem reddit, quòd sanguis sit destinatus altari ad expiationem. §. De non comedendo אבר מן הדם nulla est in toto Codice alia prohibitio. Cùm tamen vix unum præceptum sit ἀπαξ λεγόμενον, & non alibi repetitum sit. Neque quisquam memoratur, præcepti hujus limites transgressus sit. Quod magno indicio est, tale quid exerto præcepto nunquam sancitum esse. Tametsi vero directè noluit Deus infamem illam crudelitatem restringere, assentior tamen Cl. Riveto, illam indirectè etiam hac prohibitione comprehendi. Nam qui prohibet carnem cum sanguine manducare, ille certè prohibet carnes vivas manducare, quæ sine sanguine esse non possunt.
units.tr: V. But now let me set out the reasons why their interpretation does not seem truly consistent. First, those from whom the nature of men shrinks of its own accord did not need to be forbidden. Among men, how many are so savage and cruel a Polyphemus as to swallow raw flesh? God therefore forbade this cannibal practice no less than anthropophagy itself, or anything else that sinks below humanity and smells of brutal cruelty. Maimonides indeed asserted above that certain Gentile kings practised this savage rite for the sake of idolatry. Let us grant that this was so in Moses' time. Just as some people in our own time deny that there were cannibals, whom Columbus passed by on his voyage, it is clear that this practice was either received in the time of Noah, when this law was given, or before Noah. Why would Moses or Christ, who inveighed sharply against the depraved morals of those men, not have charged them with this crime too? But suppose this was customary among them. Why would God restrain that cruelty with the barriers of law rather than other crimes that were even more grave? Take lust, rape, idolatry, Epicureanism, or anything else. 2. God forbids Noah the same thing that Moses forbade the Israelites at God's command. But Moses did not forbid eating a limb of a living or quivering animal; he forbade the blood of a slaughtered animal. This is clear, since he gives the reason for the prohibition among other things: the blood is set apart for the altar, for atonement. The rule "On not eating a limb from the blood" [אבר מן הדם] has no other prohibition in the whole Code. Yet there is hardly one precept that is said only once [ἅπαξ λεγόμενον] and is not repeated elsewhere. Nor is anyone recorded as having transgressed the limits of this precept. This is strong evidence that such a thing was never sanctioned by an express precept. Although God did not directly intend to restrain that infamous cruelty, I agree with the distinguished Rivetus that it was also included indirectly in this prohibition. For he who forbids eating flesh with the blood certainly forbids eating living flesh, which cannot exist without blood.

units.la: VI. Piscator tamen, Theologus non è multis, rationibus hanc interpretationem suffulcit, quas carptim ad limam vocabimus. Ille enim morticina prohiberi putat versu 3. Ubi dicitur: Omne reptile, quod quidem vivum, esto vobis in cibum. Hæc prior exceptio. Altera sequitur. Tantummodo &c. Atqui hic jam esum membri viventis intelligit. Rationes ipsi tres.
units.tr: VI. However, Piscator, a theologian not of the common sort, supports this interpretation with arguments, which we shall examine one by one. For he thinks that carrion is forbidden in verse 3, where it is said: Every creeping thing that is alive shall be food for you. This is the first exception; the second follows: "Only" etc. And so he now understands the eating of a limb of a living creature. He has three arguments.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: 1. Quia sic sonent verba Dei; Ne comedite carnem in anima ejus, sanguine ejus. Qua verba, inquit, quàm simplicissimè ita sunt exponenda: Ne comedite carnem, dum est in anima sua, id est, in sanguine suo, hoc est, dum adhuc praedita est anima sua & sanguine suo, hoc est, dum adhuc vivit & palpitat seu tremit. Resp. Si caetera paria essent, non repugnaremus. Ipse verborum complexus ambiguus est. Reddi ergo debent convenienter materiae subiectae, quae hanc explicationem, uti vidimus, non patitur. 2. Lex de non comedendo sanguine est ceremonialis. At hic traduntur leges morales, pertinentes ad restaurationem mundi, ac proinde non ad solum Noachum, sed ad omnes ex eo nascituros? Resp. Ceremoniale est praeceptum. Sed pace rogata Magni Viri negaverim leges tantùm morales hic tradi. Voluit enim optimus Deus mundo regenerato figuram dare Messiae, cui servetur sanguis, ut in eo expiationem faciat. Nam quis dubitet, Deum hic potissimùm Ecclesiae suae, ut Messiam fide complecteretur, providere? Neque facilè quisquam probaverit, distinctam esse hanc legislationem de sanguine à legislatione Mosaica. Deinde hoc Symbolo Deus Noachidis declarare voluit, quàm rigida & inexorabilis sit altera illa moralis de non fundendo sanguine hominis prohibitio. 3. Quia lex proximè sequens de homicidio vitando, cum hac veluti ratio cohaeret, sumta ab effectu, quasi dicat Dominus: Nolo vos viva aut certè cruda & cruenta carne vesci, quia sic evaderetis crudeles & inhumani & proclives ad homicidia. At ego nolo, ut quisquam hominem occidat. Nolo igitur cruenta & viva carne vescamini. Resp. Hanc Ethicam rationem interdicti tam severi sanè multi stringunt tum Christiani, tum Hebraei. Quorum testimonia statim edituri sumus. Neque ego in universum hoc inficias iverim. Caeterum est haec inconsequens argumentatio, ut morale praeceptum sit, cujus ratio moralis est. Id quod cùm rationibus, tum exemplis inferius asseremus. Non solidae igitur sunt rationes. Neque solidius illud, quod exceptionem venatur in verbis illis: Omne reptile quod vivum. Quasi hac ratione excluderetur morticinum & discerptum. Non est exceptio, sed explicatior repetitio potestatis in omne gressile, (sic enim malunt vertere Interpretes τὸ רמש quàm reptile) quod est animal, à plantis contradistincte, quae non vivunt animalem vitam. Quinimò si hic exceptionem subintelligas, animalis mortui erit exceptio. Nam viventi opponitur mortuum, non morticinum. Quae ratio si obtinet, ne quidem morticinum animal, quippe quod non amplius vivit, ad esum exponi conveniet.
units.tr: 1. Because the words of God sound like this: Do not eat the flesh in its life, that is, its blood. These words, he says, are to be explained as simply as possible: Do not eat the flesh while it is in its soul, that is, in its blood, that is, while its soul and blood are still present, that is, while it still lives and throbs or quivers. Reply: If other things were equal, we would not object. The very combination of words is ambiguous. They must therefore be rendered in a way that suits the subject matter, which, as we have seen, does not admit this explanation. 2. The law on not eating blood is ceremonial. But here are given moral laws, pertaining to the restoration of the world, and therefore not only to Noah but to all who would be born from him? Reply: It is a ceremonial precept. But, with respect to that great man, I would deny that only moral laws are given here. For the most good God wished to give the regenerated world a figure of the Messiah, to whom the blood is reserved so that he might make atonement with it. For who would doubt that God here provided above all for his Church, so that it might embrace the Messiah by faith? Nor would anyone easily prove that this legislation concerning blood is distinct from the Mosaic legislation. Further, through this symbol God wished to declare to the sons of Noah how rigid and inexorable is that other moral prohibition against shedding human blood. 3. Because the law that immediately follows, on avoiding homicide, coheres with this as its reason, taken from its effect, as if the Lord said: I do not want you to eat living or at least raw and bloody flesh, because thus you would become cruel and inhuman and prone to homicides. But I do not want anyone to kill a man. Therefore I do not want you to eat bloody and living flesh. Reply: Many, both Christians and Hebrews, do indeed hold to this ethical reason for so strict a prohibition. We shall soon publish their testimonies. Nor would I in general deny this. Yet this argument is inconsequential, since a precept is not moral merely because it has a moral reason. We shall show this below by reasons and examples. So the arguments are not solid. Nor is that point solid which hunts for an exception in those words: Every creeping thing that is alive. As if by this reasoning carrion and torn flesh were excluded. It is not an exception, but a more explicit repetition of the grant over every moving thing (for the interpreters prefer to render the Hebrew [רמש] thus rather than "creeping thing"), which is an animal, as distinguished from plants, which do not live animal life. Indeed, if you supply an exception here, it will be an exception for a dead animal. For what is opposed to living is dead, not carrion. If this reasoning holds, it will not be fitting to offer even a dead animal, since it no longer lives, for food.

units.la: VII. Chrysostomus interpretatur de suffocato tantum. Ludovicus de Dieu de morticino. Nam ΘΝΗΣΚΩ saepe cadaver significare. Hoc ut in se verum, sic textum exhaurire non videtur. Latius enim patet, comedere carnem cum sanguine, quam comedere suffocatum & morticinum. Hinc in Apostolico canone distincta videmus sanguinem & suffocatum. Curcellaeus dicit, interpretationem illam cum verbis textus, si seorsim & per se considerentur, non male cohaerere. Non tamen omnino genuinam esse, quia alibi in lege eius morticinorum, quorum eadem est cum suffocatis ratio, concessus fuerit peregrinis inter Israelitas versantibus. Ergo morticina Noachi non fuisse prohibita, pag. 46. & 47. Quod merum est ξενοφύγετον, ut se facilius expediat ab instantia nostra inde depromta, quod peregrinis inter Israelitas versantibus licuerit sanguine vesci in morticino. Unde constat, non esse praeceptum hoc morale, quippe non obligans omnes. Ergo negat Noachidis prohibitum morticinum. Atqui quocunque modo explicet praeceptum Dei, non potest suffocatum excludi. In omni suffocato sanguis est. Qui igitur suffocatum edit, is sanguine simul vescitur. Ipse fatetur: Quo minus morticinis & suffocatis vesci non licuerit, nihil prohibuisse, nisi quod sanguis inde non accurate expressus & segregatus. Ergo propter sanguinem suffocatum fuit lege interdictum. Quemadmodum igitur dici potest, in generali prohibitione sanguinis suffocati interdictum implicitum non fuisse? Hic captus est, & rem solvet. Nam quod dicit; Gentiles post mortem animalis ex morticino sanguinem exemisse: unde quaeso fidem faciet assertioni? Quid est figmenta sua obtrudere, ἀβασανίστως accipienda & exosculanda, si hoc non est? Deinde verba Curcellaei sunt: Quod ad morticinorum & suffocatorum abstinentiam, quia pertinebat ad cultum ceremonialem solis Israelitis a Deo praescriptum, peregrini inter ipsos commorantes eam servare non tenebantur, pag. 48. Ergo morticinorum prohibitio pertinet ad cultum ceremonialem, qui solis Israelitis fuit praescriptus. Jam assumo, quod supra dixit, suffocata non aliam ob rationem prohibita fuisse, quam quia sanguis inde non accurate expressus fuit. Ergo propter sanguinem. Atque adeo etiam sanguinis interdictum ceremoniale fuit, & Israelitas solos obstrinxit. Quam sibi belle Disputator constat!
units.tr: VII. Chrysostom interprets it only of what is strangled. Ludovicus de Dieu interprets it of carrion, since the verb thnēskō [ΘΝΗΣΚΩ] often signifies a corpse. While this is true in itself, it does not seem to exhaust the text. For eating flesh with the blood extends more widely than eating what is strangled or carrion. Hence we see in the Apostolic canon that blood and what is strangled are distinguished. Curcellaeus says that this interpretation, if the words of the text are considered separately and on their own, does not coheres badly. Yet it is not wholly genuine, because elsewhere in his law carrion, which has the same character as things strangled, was allowed to sojourners living among the Israelites. Therefore carrion was not forbidden to Noah, pp. 46 and 47. This is a mere evasion [ξενοφύγετον], by which he may more easily free himself from our objection drawn from this point, namely that sojourners living among the Israelites were permitted to eat blood in carrion. From this it is established that this is not a moral precept, since it does not bind everyone. Therefore he denies that carrion was forbidden to the sons of Noah. But however he explains God's precept, what is strangled cannot be excluded. In everything strangled there is blood. Whoever eats what is strangled therefore eats blood at the same time. He himself admits: That carrion and what is strangled were not forbidden to be eaten arises from nothing except that the blood was not accurately drawn out and separated from them. Therefore the prohibition on what is strangled was made by law on account of the blood. How then can it be said that the prohibition of blood was not implicitly contained in the general prohibition of strangled flesh? He is caught here, and the matter will refute him. For as to his claim that the Gentiles drew blood out of carrion after the animal's death, who, I ask, will vouch for that assertion? What is it but thrusting forward his own fictions, to be accepted and kissed without testing [ἀβασανίστως], if this is not so? Then the words of Curcellaeus are these: As for abstinence from carrion and what is strangled, since it pertained to the ceremonial worship prescribed by God to the Israelites alone, sojourners living among them were not bound to observe it, p. 48. Therefore the prohibition of carrion pertains to the ceremonial worship, which was prescribed to the Israelites alone. Now I assume what he said above, that what is strangled was prohibited for no other reason than that the blood was not accurately drawn out of it. Therefore it was prohibited on account of the blood. And so the prohibition of blood too was ceremonial and bound the Israelites alone. How well the Disputant agrees with himself!

units.la: VIII. Quis ergo interdicti sensus? Non simplex, sed compositus positus ex interdicto ipso, & interdicti ratione, hoc ordine: Ve-rumtamen carnem cum vita sua, videlicet sanguine suo, non come-detis. Ut ita r anima sit pro vita. Id quod insolens non est in He-braico idiomate, quod nôrunt omnes, qui mediocriter periti & cal-lentes Linguæ Sanctæ. Atque hoc sensu occurrit etiam Exod. XXI. 23. Dabis animam pro anima, id est, vitam pro vita. Ita Jurisconsulti Cæsarei sæpissimè vocant supplicium anime emissionem. Qua autem ratione vita in sanguine collocetur, expli-cavit Aristoteles, neque Physici ignorant. 2. Ut sic implicetur ratio interdicti, quod simplex & nudum videri poterat. Verat igitur pri-mò comedere carnis sanguinem. Deinde rationem reddit: quia sanguis est locus vitæ. Hunc sensum complexus videtur Arabs, qui sic vertit: At vero carnem ne comedatis cum sanguine ejus, quia sanguis ejus anima est. Sic distin-guit interdictum à ratione. Persica Tavvusi ... Tantummodo carnem cum anima ejus, id est, sanguine ne comedatis. Merito igitur cum illis, quibus etiam Syrus & Samarita-nus assipulantur, nec non Interpretibus plurimis, Zwinglio, Paraeo, Ariae-Montano, Henrico Stephano, Tremellio, Riveto, de sanguine sive puro & segregato ac defæcato jam, sive visceribus concluso, hoc totum quicquid est, interpretamur. Quamobrem etiam Jose-phus Antiquit. Jud. I. 4. hac paraphrasi interdictum illustrat: Ἀλλὰ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων ... ἐσθίετε ... Ἔν τούτῳ γὰρ ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή. Aliorum animalium usum ad voluntatem ac libitum vestrum permit-to. Dominos enim vos feci omnium, tam terrestrium, quam natatilium, & eo-rumque per sublime ferrentur, absque sanguine. Nam in hoc inest anima. Hic igitur genuinus esto sensus, in quo haud ægri cum Curcellæo faci-mus.
units.tr: VIII. What, then, is the sense of the prohibition? It is not simple but compound, made up of the prohibition itself and the reason for it, in this order: "But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat." So that "soul" stands for "life." This usage is not unusual in the Hebrew idiom, as everyone knows who is reasonably skilled and practised in the Holy Tongue. In this sense it also occurs at Exod. 21:23, "You shall give life for life," that is, life for life. Thus the Imperial jurists very often call execution "the sending out of the soul." How life is located in blood Aristotle explained, and the natural philosophers are not ignorant of it. 2. So the reason for the prohibition is woven in, although the prohibition by itself might seem plain and bare. First it forbids eating the blood of the flesh. Then it gives the reason: "because blood is the seat of life." The Arab seems to have grasped this sense when he translates: "But do not eat the flesh with its blood, because its blood is its soul." In this way he distinguishes the prohibition from its reason. The Persian of Tavvusi: "Only do not eat the flesh with its soul, that is, its blood." Rightly, therefore, with those whom the Syrian and the Samaritan also support, and most of the interpreters, Zwingli, Pareus, Arias Montanus, Henri Estienne, Tremellius, Rivet, we interpret the whole of it, whatever it is, as blood either pure, separated and already purified, or enclosed in the viscera. Hence also Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, chapter 4, illustrates the prohibition with this paraphrase: "[But of the other animals ... you may eat ... For in this is the soul.]" I permit the use of the other animals to your will and pleasure. For I have made you lords of all, both of land and of water creatures, and of those that fly on high, but without blood. For in this there is a soul. Here, then, let this be the genuine sense, in which we gladly agree with Curcellaeus.

units.la: IX. Jam causas Divini hujus præcepti vestigemus.
units.tr: IX. Let us now trace the causes of this divine precept.

units.la: Nam Deo sapientissimo rationem interdicti constituisse, quis dubitet? Tametsi verò Sapientiæ Divinæ recessibus abstrusæ hærent, proclive tamen erit, quid probabile sit, edisserere. Judæi quidem rationes reddunt tum Ethicas tum Physicas. Ego Typicam adjicio. Ratio igitur prima, ob quam Noacho prohibitus sanguis, est typica: quia sanguis alteri destinabatur ad faciendam expiationem. Nempe ita convenie-bat bat sub cunabula regenerati mundi, ut expiatio Christi adumbraretur. Quae ratio sub lege in typicis sacrificiis pro expiatione criminum, ubi sanguis animalium immolatorum poni debuit super altari, vel ad basin fundi. Nam quia sanguis est quodammodo anima animalium, ideo convenienter immolari debuit pro expiatione animarum humanarum. Quia etiam animam sontem Deo fieri piacularem congruens fuit justitiae & veracitati Divinae. Deus misericors substituit vitam animalium. Qua ratione etiam substitutio Christi in locum peccatoris figurata. Rationem hanc typicam agnoscit & urget Chrysostomus. Quia, inquit, Sacrificia ex brutis perfectum erant, quasi docet illos dicens: Quia sanguis mihi segregatus est, Vobis caro: homil. 15. in Genes. IX. 4. Atque huc potissimum Deus respicit in textu, cum rationem interdicti illam perhibet, quod vita animalium sit in sanguine. Quasi diceret, sibi devoveri debere illud, in quo consistit vita animalium, ut hac ratione & obligationem hominis edoceret, & substitutionem Christi in locum peccatoris perspicua quadam imagine repraesentaret. Quid hac ratione certius & planius? Imo quid prius & antiquius esse potest? Et tamen Curcellaeus tussim ciet. Obducit 1. In lege quidem exceptionis hanc rationem dari: sed in prohibitione Noacho facta non attingi omnino, pag. 49. Resp. Idem interdictum est Noacho & Israelitis datum. Utrinque eadem typica ratio. Quod Israelitis injunctum, ratione expressa & perspicue exposita; idem Noacho praeceptum, ratione quidem non adeo aperta, sed nonnihil involuta, at quae Noachidis solertioribus indagari facile potuit, ad λογικὴν illam λατρείαν paulo attentioribus. 2. Ne verbulum quidem illic de Sacrificiis occurrere, unde suspicari quis possit, ad ea respici. Quis ergo credat principali dissimulato, aut silentio praeterito, legem de accessorio sufficiente latam? ibid. Resp. An stipitibus & saxis Deus locutus est, qui verbum ejus intelligere non possent? Deinde, non erat opus, ut de Sacrificiis mentionem faceret, quia illorum νομοθεσία jam diluvium praevertit. Abunde igitur fuit, exerto edicto sancire illud, quod nunquam antea sancitum, & quod ceu novus & explicatior typus ad Sacrificiorum legem accessit. Quid vero multis? Fatetur Curcellaeus, loci Levit. XVII. 11. 12. 14. & Genes. IX. 4. unum eundemque sensum & scopum esse, pag. 40. Jam scopus loci Levit. XVII. non est hic primarie, ut ostendat Deus, Dominium hominis non esse absolutum & illimitatum. Cui enim bono hoc docueretur, cum Israë. Israelitis palàm esse multis praecedentibus praeceptis, puta hoc ipso de sanguine & suffocato, de mundorum & immundorum discrimine, se non esse omnium rerum irrefragabiles Dominos. Sed xu-ceum ratio Deo est, quam exprimit Moses, quod expiationem facere debeat. Si igitur, quod diserte largitur Curcellaeus, utrinque unus & idem scopus est, cur negat rationem typicam in lege Noacho latam?
units.tr: For who would doubt that God, the most wise, established a reason for the prohibition? Although the reasons of divine Wisdom lie hidden in its secret recesses, it will nevertheless be easy to set out what is probable. The Jews, indeed, give reasons both ethical and physical. I add a typical one. The first reason, then, for which blood was forbidden to Noah is typical: because blood was destined for another purpose, namely to make atonement. For it was fitting that, under the cradle of the regenerated world, the atonement of Christ should be foreshadowed. This same reason operates under the law in the typical sacrifices for the expiation of sins, where the blood of the slaughtered animals had to be placed upon the altar or poured out at its base. For since blood is in a way the soul of animals, it was therefore fitting that it be offered for the expiation of human souls. It was also congruent with the justice and truthfulness of God that a guilty soul should be made an offering for sin. God, being merciful, substituted the life of animals. By this same reasoning the substitution of Christ in the place of the sinner is also prefigured. Chrysostom recognises and presses this typical reason: "Because," he says, "sacrifices from brute animals were perfect, he teaches them as if saying: because blood is set apart for me, flesh is for you" (Homily 15 on Genesis 9:4). And it is chiefly to this that God looks in the text, when he gives that reason, that the life of animals is in the blood. As if he were saying that what contains the life of animals should be devoted to him, so that by this means he might teach man his obligation, and set forth in a clear image the substitution of Christ in the place of the sinner. What could be more certain and plainer than this reason? Indeed, what can be earlier or more ancient? And yet Curcellaeus clears his throat. He objects, 1: "In the law of exception this reason is given, but in the prohibition made to Noah it is not touched on at all" (p. 49). Reply: the same prohibition was given to Noah and to the Israelites. On both occasions the typical reason is the same. What was enjoined on the Israelites, with the reason expressed and clearly set out, was commanded to Noah with the reason indeed not so plain, but somewhat wrapped up, yet one which the more shrewd of Noah's descendants could easily track down, and which those who paid closer attention could see as "rational worship" [λογικὴν λατρείαν]. 2: "Not even a little word occurs there about sacrifices, so that one could suspect they are in view. Who then would believe that a law about what is secondary was passed while the principal matter was concealed or passed over in silence?" (ibid.). Reply: Did God speak to stocks and stones, that they could not understand his word? Furthermore, there was no need for him to mention sacrifices, because their legislation [νομοθεσία] had already been forestalled by the flood. It was enough, therefore, that by an express edict he sanctioned that which had never been sanctioned before, and which came as a new and more explicit type added to the law of sacrifices. But why say more? Curcellaeus admits that the passages Lev. 17:11, 12, 14 and Gen. 9:4 have one and the same sense and aim (p. 40). Now the aim of the passage in Leviticus 17 is not primarily to show that man's dominion is not absolute and unlimited. For what good would it do to teach this to the Israelites, when it was already plain to them from many preceding precepts, such as this very one about blood and the strangled animal, and the distinction between clean and unclean, that they were not the irrefragable lords of all things? But the purpose God has is the one Moses expresses, that he should make atonement. If, therefore, as Curcellaeus expressly grants, both passages have one and the same aim, why does he deny that the typical reason was given in the law to Noah?

units.la: X. Sequitur ratio Ethica, sive Moralis. Illam Moses juxta priorem typicam, perspicuè connexit. Etenim sanguinem vestrum animarum vestrarum requiram de manu cunctorum animantium, sum etiam de manu hominis, & de manu fratris, vers. 5. ubi omnino illud Vau non copulativum esse existimo, quomodo Pagninus accepit: sed causale cum Vulgato & Stephano. Quasi diceret Deus: Vel ideo etiam jubeo, ut abstineatis à sanguine animalium, ut discatis à sanguine hominum effundendo abhorrere, quia vita hominis tanti apud me pretii est, ut ne bestiis quidem parcere velim, quae hominis sanguinem effuderint. Si igitur tam pretiosus in oculis meis est sanguis hominum, nolo ut bestiarum sanguinem comedatis, ne paulatim in feritatem degenerantes, humanum sitire incipiatis. Hanc rationem juxta priorem agnoscit Chrysostomus, quando l.c. subjungit: Τοῦτο δὲ ποιεῖ, ἀνωθεν ἀπαγορεύων αὐτοῖς τὴν ὁμοίαν, τὴν εἰς τὴν ἀνθρωπον. Hoc est: Hoc autem facit, divinitus prohibens hominum cædes, & ad eam ferocem impetum. Nempe erat nova quaedam mundi regeneratio diluvii cataclysmo omnibus praeter Noachidas haustis. Novam societatem novis legibus gubernari cordi est legislatori Deo. Et quidem eo tempore depravatissimis illis prioribus vicino maximè. Nam prohibitivas leges ex malis moribus nasci notorium est. Homines procaces nuper admodum humanis caedibus se miscuerant, partim jam antè grassati, partim ex inauspicato Sethitarum & Kainitarum conjugio prognati, qui feroces admodum & corporum lacertis terribiles, ad humanas caedes furiali face processerant. Ne deinceps, reparato humano genere, simili ferocia illis animus incalesceret, ut humanum sanguinem in vili habere desinerent, lege severa Deus cavet, & magno serio agit. Primum vetat vel brutorum sanguinem libare, ne eo vertente in indolem hominis, imbuerentur crudelitate, cui nuper excidio & clade sua mundus parentaverat. Et sanè Antediluvianos crudelitatis & homicidiorum scelere maximè ximè se alligâsse, constat ex infami illo genere Nephilim. Quos probabile est non tam Gigantes fuisse, sive, ut cum Augustino loquar, procerolos homines, quàm tyrannos, qui promiscuis caedibus omnia miscuerunt. Proinde assentior Josepho, qui γίγαντας vocat, καὶ παντὸς [illegible, ~6 letters] Antiq. Jud. I. 4. Quomodo Symmachus βιαίως, Aquila [illegible, ~6 letters] vertit. Quod & fortiùs inde constat, quòd Moses Tersam repletam dicit מלא quod plùs notat quàm [illegible, ~4 letters]. Deinde ut validius illos terreret, minatur, se vel à brutis, nedum ab hominibus humanum sanguinem requisituruin.
units.tr: X. There follows the ethical, or moral, reason. Moses clearly connects it with the typical reason just given. "For surely your blood of your souls I will require at the hand of every beast, and at the hand of man, and at the hand of his brother" (v. 5). Here I think the vav is by no means conjunctive, as Pagninus took it, but causal, with the Vulgate and Stephanus. As if God were saying: I also command this, that you abstain from the blood of animals, so that you may learn to shrink from shedding human blood, because human life is of such price in my eyes that I am not willing to spare even beasts that have shed human blood. If, therefore, human blood is so precious in my eyes, I do not want you to eat the blood of beasts, lest by degrees you degenerate into savagery and begin to thirst for human blood. Chrysostom recognises this reason alongside the former when, in the same place, he adds: "[But he does this, forbidding them from above the like, that is, the one to men.]" That is: he does this, divinely forbidding the slaughter of men and that fierce impulse. Clearly there was then a new regeneration of the world, all others except Noah's family having been swallowed up in the cataclysm of the flood. It is dear to God the lawgiver that a new society be governed by new laws. And indeed at that time, the most depraved of those earlier people were close at hand. For it is notorious that prohibitive laws are born of bad morals. Men of insolence had lately mixed themselves in human slaughter, some who had already been raging earlier, others born of the ill-omened marriage of the Sethites and the Cainites, who, very fierce and terrible for the muscles of their bodies, had proceeded to human slaughter with a frenzied torch. Lest afterwards, when the human race was restored, a similar ferocity should kindle their spirit, so that they might cease to hold human blood in cheap regard, God guards against it with a severe law, and acts with great earnestness. First he forbids even the drinking of the blood of brute beasts, lest, that blood turning into the human disposition, they be imbued with cruelty, the thing by which the world had lately paid the price in its own destruction and ruin. And indeed it is clear that the people before the flood were most bound up in the guilt of cruelty and homicide, from that infamous race of the Nephilim. It is probable that these were not so much giants, or, to speak with Augustine, rather tall men, as tyrants who mixed everything together with indiscriminate slaughter. Therefore I agree with Josephus, who calls them giants [γίγαντας], and [illegible] (Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, chapter 4). Symmachus renders it violently [βιαίως], and Aquila [illegible]. This is also more strongly confirmed by the fact that Moses says the earth was filled [מלא], which signifies more than [illegible]. Then, to terrify them the more forcefully, he threatens that he will require human blood not only from beasts but even from men.

units.la: XI. Eugubinus tamen Episcopus non iccirco se mihi approbat, qui cum videre, Deum tam rigidè homicidia coërcere, etiam sanguinis esum de effusione humani sanguinis, atque adeo de homicidio explicat. Quasi figurata esset locutio, & comedere carnem cum sanguine significaret hominem viventem, cujus vita sanguine potissimùm sustinetur, occidere, & fuso ejus sanguine vita privare. Ineptam alioquin esse connexionem sequentium verborum. Neque metaphoram illam in Sacris insolitatem esse. Hinc & Homerum phrasèos hujus imitatione bellum [illegible, ~4 letters] vocare, quòd eo multi absorbeantur & pereant. Praeterea sanguinis esum ad immunditiam nihil facere. Atqui illud [illegible, ~6 letters] inusitatum est, ut comedere carnem cum sanguine sit occidere. Fateor aliquando comedere carnem alicujus aequipollere huic, mortem alterius expetere. Cujus enim odio flagrant homines, & quos periisse cupiunt, illorum vel carnes appetit rabida, quam Poëta vocat, ο[?]ξis. Confer Psal. XXVII. 3. Sed comedere carnem cum sanguine pro caede & homicidio, insolitum est usurpari. Deinde ex rebus ipsis Eugubinus refellitur. Nam manifesta est exceptio sanguinis à carnibus v.3.&4. Carnem quidem animalium, sicut herbas dedi vobis: sed carnem cum sanguine, in quo est animalis vita, non comedetis. Exspirat itaque allegoriae ratio.
units.tr: XI. Still, Bishop Eugubinus does not win my approval for this reason: seeing that God restrains murder so strictly, he takes the prohibition on eating blood as referring to the shedding of human blood, and so to homicide. As if the expression were figurative, and "to eat flesh with its blood" meant to kill a living man, whose life is chiefly sustained by blood, and to deprive him of life by pouring out his blood. Otherwise, he says, the connection of the following words would be awkward. Nor is that metaphor unusual in the Sacred Writings. Hence Homer, imitating this manner of speaking, also calls war a thing that devours, because many are swallowed up and perish in it. Moreover, eating blood contributes nothing to uncleanness. But such a usage is unusual, that to eat flesh with blood should mean to kill. I grant that sometimes to eat a person's flesh amounts to the same thing as seeking another's death. For those whom men hate fiercely, and whom they wish to perish, the raging creature (as the poet calls it) seeks their flesh. Compare Psalm 27:3. But to use "eating flesh with blood" for slaughter and murder is an unusual usage. Further, Eugubinus is refuted by the facts themselves. For the exception of blood from flesh is plain in verses 3 and 4: "the flesh of animals, as I gave you the herbs; but flesh with its blood, in which is the life of the animal, you shall not eat." So the allegorical explanation falls away.

units.la: XII. Jam de Physica & Medica ratione. Contendunt Judaei sanguinem prohibitum inter alia etiam propter רע מזג malitiam temperamenti. Corporis autem temperamentum sequi animam & ejus mores. Nachmanides sic exprimit: [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: XII. Now to the physical and medical reason. The Jews contend that blood was forbidden, among other reasons, because of רע מזג, the evil of temperament. Moreover, the temperament of the body follows the soul and its morals. Nachmanides expresses it thus: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] Constat enim illud, quod comeditur migrare in corpus comedentis. Ac proinde, si homo edat sanguinem densiorem & crasstrasfusem in animae hominis oriuntur. Quemadmodum anima bestiae densa fuerit & trassa. Non etiam convenire [Hebrew: שפך דם האדם] ut devoret anima animam. Habere autem bestias animam, quae in sanguine sedem habeat. Physicam hanc rationem etiam Becmannus adoptat, & urget sine successu Curcellaeus pag. 183.184. De re ipsa non disputo. Esto insalubris & noxius animalium sanguis. Corruptus aliquando etiam & vitiatus, carne nondum corrupta. De qua re in Prolegomenis Medicorum plurica breviter attigimus. Sed hanc fuisse Deo rationem, nisi forsitan velis [Greek], nullo indicio cognoscimus. Imo proclivius dictu, non fuisse. Deus enim hoc loco non Medicum vel Physicum egit, sed religiosum praeceptum tulit, cui essent propter conscientiam dicto audientes. In naturalium ciborum [Greek], quae religionem non spectant, humanae prudentiae imperium dedit.
units.tr: [illegible] It is certain that what is eaten passes into the body of the eater. And therefore, if a man eats blood that is denser and thicker ... arise in the soul of the man, just as the soul of a beast would be dense and thick. Nor does it agree that [Hebrew: שפך דם האדם] (he who sheds man's blood) should devour soul with soul. Beasts, however, have a soul which has its seat in the blood. Becmannus also adopts this physical reason, and Curcellaeus presses it without success, at pages 183 and 184. I do not dispute the matter itself. Let the blood of animals be unwholesome and harmful; sometimes it is also corrupted and tainted even when the flesh is not yet spoiled. On this matter we have briefly touched upon a good deal in the Prolegomena of the physicians. But that this was God's reason, unless perhaps you wish to say [Greek], we know from no indication. Indeed it is easier to say that it was not. For God in this place was not acting as a physician or natural philosopher, but gave a religious precept, to which those who heard it were to be obedient because of conscience. In the matter of natural foods, which do not concern religion, he left the rule to human prudence.

units.la: XIII. Jam expedita & regia via est ad tertium: Utrum praeceptum illud morale, an ceremoniale fuerit? Nos ceremoniale fuisse, nulli dubitamus.
units.tr: XIII. Now the clear and royal road leads to the third question: whether that precept was moral or ceremonial. We do not doubt that it was ceremonial.

units.la: Fuit enim de re naturā suā indifferente, in cujus observantia, sequestrato positivo Dei mandato, nulla pars Sanctitatis constitit. Neque semper, neque omnes obligavit. Nam retro diluvium non fuit haec lex observata cum Sanctitatis & religiosi cultus opinione. Caruerunt enim mandato & promissione Dei, absque quibus est, [Greek] opus vitiosum reddit. Ac fuerunt aliquando tempora, quibus omnis illa obligatio expuncta, ac diserte declaratum: Omnem Dei creaturam bonam esse, nihilque rejectaneum: nihil polluere hominem posse, quod os hominis ingreditur: omnia munda jam esse. Imo cum antitypum jam praesto fuisset, & facta expiatio in Sanguine Christi, non potuit non typus exolescere. Et eo ipso tempore, quo quidam ad custodiam hujus praecepti obligati fuerunt, alii ab eadem soluti & liberi fuerunt. Intelligo autem ea tempora, quibus gentes rejectae ab externa visibili Ecclesia. Id quod factum existimo, non sub Abrahami tempora, sed quatuor demum Seculis post promissionem foederalem factam Abrahamo Genes. XV. 15. 16. Nempe quo tempore Gentilium mensura peccatorum impleta, matura fuit illorum rejectio, & nominatim posterorum Chami Cananaeorum devotio ad internecionem, per bella, quae geri coepta duce Josua contra Canaanaeos, & deinceps contra illos, tanquam semen Serpentis maledictum. ctum. Hucusque re diligenter perpensa, arbitramur Ecclesiam Dei non uni fuisse familiæ alligatam, sed ad illam jus habuisse omnes Noachidas. Tametsi vero plerique per apostasiam à veri Dei cultu deficerent, non minus tamen ad præcepta Noacho data servandæ obnoxii fuerunt. Sed rejectis illis à cognitione, cultu & omni spe Messiæ, adeóque jure Sacerdotii Ecclesiæ Judaicæ transcripto, ad præceptum illud de sacrificando, atque adeò etiam ad interdictum sanguinis, quippe quod Legislationi Sacrificiorum inserviit, tanquam ceremoniale, obligati non fuerunt. Cur enim typus & figura illis injungeretur, qui à Christi veri & realis Sacrificii futuri spe ac cognitione alieni & extorres fuerunt, idque certa destinatione & definitione consilii Divini, per quam abjecta Hagar & Ismaël, & τὸ ἀδελφὸν illud Judæis solis concessum, ut εἰς λόγια τῆς Θεοῦ illis crederentur, Rom. III. 2? Quo loco non hoc tantum indigeratur, quòd Judæi essent à Deo constituti Bibliothecarii Ecclesiæ. Nam cum Augustino hodieque illos haud gravatim agnoscimus Bibliothecarios & custodes Scripturæ V. T. non obstante illorum ab hoc accersitione rejectione. Sed hoc inprimis intellexit Apostolus, quòd habuerint Judæi verbi Dei ministerium per Prophetarum prædicationes, & ex verbo Dei institutum cultum, & ἀναμνήσεις τῆς λατρείας. Ad quas ἀναμνήσεις legem de sanguine pertinere, sole meridiano clarius, cùm adumbrarit potissimùm expiationem Christi, & inter leges illas carnales à Mose perspicuè numeretur. Quomodo igitur morale præceptum dici potest illud, quod primario & directè ad Christum habuit: quod neque semper neque omnes obligavit?
units.tr: For it was a thing indifferent by its own nature, in whose observance, apart from God's positive command, no part of holiness consisted. Nor did it bind always or everyone. For before the Flood this law was not observed with the belief that it was holy or part of religious worship. For they lacked God's command and promise, without which a work is made faulty, [Greek]. And there were times when all that obligation was struck out, and it was plainly declared: every creature of God is good, nothing is to be rejected; nothing that enters a man's mouth can defile him; all things are now clean. Indeed, since the antitype was already at hand, and atonement had been made in the blood of Christ, the type could not but fade away. And at the very time when some were bound to keep this precept, others were loosed and freed from it. I mean those times in which the nations were cast off from the outward visible Church. I think this happened not in the time of Abraham, but only four centuries after the covenant promise made to Abraham (Gen. 15:15-16). Namely, at the time when the measure of the sins of the Gentiles was filled, their rejection was ripe, and especially the devotion to destruction of the posterity of Ham's Canaanites, through the wars begun under Joshua against the Canaanites, and afterwards against them as the accursed seed of the Serpent. Having weighed all this carefully, we judge that the Church of God was not bound to one family alone, but that all the sons of Noah had a right to it. Although indeed most of them, through apostasy, fell away from the true worship of God, they were nonetheless still bound to observe the precepts given to Noah. But when they had been cast off from the knowledge, worship and every hope of the Messiah, and the right of priesthood had thus been transferred to the Jewish Church, they were not bound to that precept about sacrificing, and so also not to the prohibition of blood, which served the legislation of sacrifices, as a ceremonial thing. For why should a type and figure be enjoined upon those who were estranged and exiles from the hope and knowledge of Christ's true and real future sacrifice, and that by a certain destination and definite decree of the Divine counsel, by which Hagar and Ishmael were cast off, and that "advantage" [τὸ ἀδελφὸν] granted to the Jews alone, that "the oracles of God" [εἰς λόγια τῆς Θεοῦ] were entrusted to them (Rom. 3:2)? In that passage it is not only this that is implied, that the Jews were appointed by God as librarians of the Church. For with Augustine we still gladly acknowledge them as librarians and guardians of the Scripture of the Old Testament, despite their rejection by this calling. But the Apostle chiefly understood this: that the Jews had the ministry of the Word of God through the preaching of the Prophets, and the worship instituted from the Word of God, and the [ἀναμνήσεις τῆς λατρείας] reminders of the service. And that the law concerning blood belongs to these reminders is clearer than the noonday sun, since it chiefly foreshadowed the atonement of Christ, and is plainly counted by Moses among those carnal laws. How then can that be called a moral precept which primarily and directly had Christ in view, and which did not bind always or everyone?

units.la: XIV. Suboluit tale quid Curcellæo. Sed & sinistrè argumentum nostrum proponit, & se parùm feliciter expedit. Sinistrè proponit. Nam facit nos ita argumentantes: Prohibitione sanguinis, quam Deus Noacho fecit, non fuisse in perpetuum obligatos omnes ejus posteros: sed tantùm usque ad Abrahami tempus, cum quo Deus peculiari fœdere iniit, reliquas Gentes postea in viis suis ambulare permisit, nec eas unquam, quòd rescierentur sanguine, reprehendit, pag. 49. 50. Jam non difficeor, quosdam Theologos terminum à quo rejectionis Gentium ponere in Abrahamo. Omnia tamen diligenter reputando, malumus cum aliis, qui curatiùs hoc negotium egerunt, statuere, terminum à quo actualis rejectionis Gentium ab externa & visibili Ecclesia, à qua jam præputiati Gentiles non palabant tantùm, sed quasi flammantes frames Cherubim arcebantur, figendum esse in ducatu Josuæ, qui Cananæos sub jugum misit, posteritatem maledicti Chami. Tum enim Israëlitæ in formam Reipublicæ fuerunt redacti, cujus status Theocraticus fuit, ut bene appellat Josephus contra Apionem. Et hactenus pios Noachidas & Abrahamidas extra familiam Israëlitarum, Gentibus permixtos fuisse, exempla Jobi, Melchisedeci & Jethronis indubitabili sunt argumento. Quos, quia Deum sive in præputio sive in circumcisione pura mente coluerunt, & ϰομοθεσίαν Sacerdotii retinuerunt, simul cum Gentibus rejici ab Ecclesia & reprobari, bonitati Dei consentaneum non fuit. Imo vix aliter sentire licet, sive vaticinium Dei, sive impletionem ejus spectes. Vaticinium extat Genes. XV. 13. 16. ubi Deus negat ante quadringentos annos ab illa promissione Abrahamo facta servitutem Gentium cœpturam; nempe, inquit, v. 16. כי לא שלם עון האמרי עד הנה quia nondum impleta iniquitas Amorrhæi usque tunc Per Amorrhæum intelligit Cananæos omnes. Horum iniquitas nondum impleta tempore Abrahami. Nempe quia illorum cœtibus fideles permixti fuerunt, qui haud dubie servarunt illa ἀκαθάρτα τῆς λατρείας, quæ tum temporis lex sacrificiorum & interdictum sanguinis absolverunt, ideo Deus illis parcere voluit, usque ad tempus Josuæ, quo impleta mensura iniquitatis, tum ratione quantitatis, tum qualitatis. Huc pertinet, quod mandatum Israelitis est, ne abominarentur Idumæum, quia frater Israëlitarum, Deut. XXXIII. 3. 7. Sed ad summam non multum refert. Sive enim dicas, tempore Abrahami actu rejectas Gentes, sive tempore Josuæ, manet infracta vis argumenti, præceptum nempe Noacho datum non fuisse morale, quia vel Abrahami vel Josuæ tempore aliquos homines non obligavit, sed eos tantum, qui habuerunt Sacerdotii prærogativam, cujus beneficio Messias & ejus redemtio revelata fuit. Morale autem non est, quod aliquos tantum, non omnes in qualibet circumstantia obligat, quod omnes utique fateri debent.
units.tr: XIV. Something of this sort has dawned on Curcellaeus. But he both puts our argument awkwardly and extricates himself rather unhappily. He puts it awkwardly. For he makes us argue thus: That the prohibition of blood, which God gave to Noah, did not bind all his posterity forever, but only until the time of Abraham, with whom God made a special covenant; afterwards God allowed the remaining nations to walk in their own ways, and never rebuked them because they ate blood, pages 49 and 50. Now I do not deny that some theologians place the starting point of the rejection of the Gentiles in Abraham. Yet, weighing everything carefully, I prefer, with others who have handled this matter more carefully, to hold that the starting point of the actual rejection of the Gentiles from the outward and visible Church (from which the Gentiles, already uncircumcised, were not merely kept at a distance but barred as by the flaming sword of the Cherubim) is to be fixed in the leadership of Joshua, who put the Canaanites, the posterity of the accursed Ham, under the yoke. For then the Israelites were brought into the form of a commonwealth, whose state was theocratic, as Josephus rightly calls it in Against Apion. And that up to this point pious sons of Noah and of Abraham lived outside the family of Israel, mingled with the Gentiles, the examples of Job, Melchizedek and Jethro are sufficient proof. Since they worshipped God, whether in uncircumcision or in circumcision, with a pure mind, and retained the order of priesthood, it was not consistent with God's goodness that they should be cast out together with the Gentiles from the Church and reprobated. Indeed one can hardly think otherwise, whether you look at God's prophecy or at its fulfillment. The prophecy stands in Genesis 15:13-16, where God says that four hundred years after that promise made to Abraham the servitude of the Gentiles would begin; namely, as he says in verse 16, כי לא שלם עון האמרי עד הנה [ki lo shalem avon ha-Emori ad henah], "for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full." By the Amorite he means all the Canaanites. Their iniquity was not yet full in Abraham's time. Namely, because faithful men were mingled with their communities, who undoubtedly kept those impure things of worship which the law of sacrifices and the prohibition of blood then set aside, God wished to spare them until the time of Joshua, when the measure of iniquity was full, both in respect of quantity and of quality. To this belongs the command given to the Israelites that they should not abhor the Edomite, "because he is a brother of the Israelites" (Deut. 23:7 [in the Hebrew, 23:8]). But in sum it does not matter much. For whether you say that the Gentiles were actually rejected in the time of Abraham or in the time of Joshua, the force of the argument remains unbroken: the precept given to Noah was not moral, because it did not bind some men in the time of Abraham or of Joshua, but only those who had the privilege of priesthood, by whose benefit the Messiah and his redemption were revealed. But that is not moral which binds only some and not all in every circumstance, which everyone must in any case admit.

units.la: XV. Jam, quod secundo loco dixi, patebit, non satis se feliciter Carneadum hic expedire. Respondet igitur: Deum peculiare fœdus pangendo cum Abrahamo, cæteras gentes non liberâsse ab obligatione parendi mandatis, quæ ipse antea Noacho præscripserat. Permisisse quidem Deum post illud tempus in viis suis ambulare Gentes, id est, non visitâsse per Prophetas, neque officii sui admonuisse: sed non ita eis laxavisse frenum, ut impune possent possent facere quicquid luberet. Ergo illos, apud quos memoria interdicti Noa-cho facti adhuc supererat, ei parere debuisse; Caeteris autem, qui nullam ejus notitiam habuerunt, aut habere potuerunt, Deum misericordem non imputavisse ipsis in culpam, si contravenirent, quia ista res non fuerit ex eorum genere, quas unusquisque facile cognoscere poterat, adeo ut inexcusabiles sint, qui non obtemperant. Et propterea Deum populos a foedere suo alienos per Prophetas ob esum sanguinis non reprehendisse. pag. 10. Resp. 1. Confundit turpi exemplo mandata Dei, quorum naturalia alia & moralia, omnes & semper obligantia, sicut ignis & hic & apud Persas & semper unus; alia positiva Ceremonialia, quae ad Politiam Ecclesiae Dei pertinent. Ad illa Gentes etiam euntes in viis suis & extorres a foedere Dei, omnino obligatae fuerunt. Et hactenus non licuit iis impune facere quicquid lubebat. Sed non habentes legem, nempe scriptam, sibi ipsis lex fuerunt, & ἀνόμως etiam judicandae. Ad haec Ceremonialia positiva nullo modo fuerunt obligatae, quippe non Ecclesia, Lo Ruhamah, non πολίται, sed anathema profani, peccatores, in quibus Ecclesia fuit non pariens, denique canes, qui de mensa Domini panem non participarunt. Sed Judaeis solis λόγια ἐπιστάθηκαν, solis indicata verba Jacobi, & statuta ac judicia Israelis, Rom. III. 2. Psal. CXLVII. 17. Tale fuit illud de sanguine, ut evidenter a nobis probatum. 2. Quid? Sacrificiorum legem non etiam Noachus habuit? Nisi temere & privatae libidinis impetu sacrificavit. Ergo rejectae ab Ecclesia Gentes sacrificare nihilominus debuerunt? Falsissimum. Nam extraneus, qui accesserit, morietur, Num. III. 5. 6. Confer Num. XVII. XVIII. Et quemadmodum Israelitae, si quando temeraria apostasia Deo offensionem & fastidium crearunt, puniti sunt cessatione Sacrificiorum, quae fuit irae Divinae indicium; sic Gentiles certo ac immutabili Dei judicio & prava sua voluntate a Numine defi-cientes ad idololatricos cultus, jure merito a Sacrificiis prohibiti fuerunt. 3. Sed πεῶτον ψεῦδος in eo haud dubie est, quod Curcellaeus ex hypothesi prava Remonstrantica, quae Vocationem Universalem statuit omni aetate, cujus beneficio omnes jus habeant ad Ecclesiam & ejus privilegia, quibus solis neglectim habitis reus fiat homo mortem aeternam debendi; sentit, Gentiles omnes usque ad tempora Christi in Noacho vocatos, ad omnia Noachi mandata, sive Moralia sive Positiva obligatos fuisse. Hanc sententiam praefe-runt verba ejus Act XIV. 16. Permisit quidem Deus post illud tempus gentes in viis suis ambulare, id est, non visitavit per Prophetas, nec eos officii sui admonuit, &c. Quasi Deus in rejectione Gentium non speciali aliquo judicio sit usus, quo illos seclusit & ejecit ex Ecclesia: sed ipsi voluntarià tantùm apostasiâ se subducentes Ecclesiæ se aggregare dedignati fuerint. Ut permissio illa sit patientia tantùm, non etiam potentia, ut in alia causa contra Pelagium Augustinus loquitur. Quod omnino à vero remotum. Nam Gentiles justo Dei judicio ita sunt ab Ecclesia rejecti, ut citra spem reditus ante præfinitum tempus ipsis extra illam singulari Dei Decreto torpescendum fuerit. Hoc testatur illa Excommunicationis formula Matth. XVIII. 17. Sit tibi velut Ethnicus. Quò pertinet gravissima expostulatio Dei cum domo Israelis Ezech. XLIV. 6, 7, 8, 9. Indices rebellibus domui Israelis: Sic ait Dominus Jehovi: Satis vobis: Discedite ab abominationibus vestris. Qui introduxistis alienigenas, præputiatos carne, ut essent in Sanctuario meo, ut profanarent ipsam domum meam: qui obtulistis cibum meum, adipem & sanguinem, quum illi irritum fecerent fœdus meum: Neque observastis observationem rerum Sanctarum mearum, sed constituistis observatores observationis meæ in Sanctuario meo arbitratu vestro. Sic ait Dominus Jehovi: Nullus alienigena, præputiatus corde, & præputiatus carne, non veniet ad Sanctuarium meum: Nullus inquam alienigena, qui sit inter Filios Israelis. Hinc Christus illos vocat canes, Matth. XV. 26. Cum quo dicto conferendum illud: Foras canes, Apocal. XXII. 15. Accedit & hoc, quòd legem Circumcisionis, & reliqui cultûs Ceremonialis instituti in Populo Judaico, atque adeò etiam Sacrificiorum & interdicti sanguinis, quod ad illa relatum fuit, Apostolus vocat inimicitias illas, quibus per Christum demum sublatis Gentes Deo conciliatæ fuerunt, Eph. II. 15, 16. Quomodo Lex Dei inimicitiæ, quibus peremtis Deo conciliatæ Gentes, si inimicitiæ Dei cum gentibus vel ipso præputii charactere obsignatæ non fuerunt, quibus obstantibus ab Ecclesia, veluti murali sepimento interposito, ab ejus accessu arcebantur? Ut sit vanissimum illud de universali vocatione, communi fœdere, & necessitate servandi ea præcepta, quæ Ecclesiæ tradita in obsignationem Spei Messiæ venturi, figmentum. Hæc obiter attingi debuerunt, & opponi Curcellæo, qui, Ἐᾶν suam φυλάττειν, rejectionem Gentium definit solo hoc actu negativo Dei permittentis, ut eant in suis viis, non mittentis Prophetas, non admonentis officii. Aliud Scripturæ consultæ, & ex iis loca allegata, respondent. 4. Neque illud defæcatius, quòd dicit: Illis, qui praecepti Noachi memoriam non retinuerunt, non vertere in culpam ejus neglectum: quia haec res non sit ex earum genere, quae cognosci naturali lumine potuerunt. Atqui, si in persona Noachi hoc praeceptum datum est omnibus ejus posteris, rei fuerunt violati mandati, ac proinde haud dubie alicubi per Prophetas hoc facinus illis exprobratum: sive mandati illius memores fuerunt, sive oblivione capti. Si memores fuerunt, concedit. Si oblivione sepeliverunt, non ideo cessavit obligatio. Imo cum sua & majorum culpa memoriam illius mandati amiserint, oblivio rei necessariae in incrementum noxae vertit.
units.tr: XV. Now, what I said in the second place will show that Carneades does not extricate himself here very successfully. He replies: "God, by making a special covenant with Abraham, did not free the other nations from the obligation to obey the commands which he had earlier prescribed to Noah. God indeed permitted the Gentiles after that time to walk in their own ways, that is, he did not visit them through the Prophets or remind them of their duty; but he did not so loosen the reins that they could do with impunity whatever they pleased. So those among whom the memory of the prohibition given to Noah still survived ought to have obeyed him. But as for the others, who had no knowledge of it, or could not have had it, God, being merciful, did not impute it to them as a fault if they transgressed, because this matter was not of the kind that each person could easily recognise, so that those who do not obey are inexcusable. And for this reason God did not rebuke the peoples outside his covenant through the Prophets for eating blood." p. 10. Reply 1. He shamefully confuses God's commands. Some are natural and moral, binding everyone always, like fire, which is the same here and among the Persians and always one. Others are positive and ceremonial, pertaining to the polity of the Church of God. The Gentiles, even though they walked in their own ways and were exiles from God's covenant, were wholly bound by the former, and so far it was not permitted them to do with impunity whatever they pleased. But not having the law, namely the written law, they were a law to themselves, and are to be judged "lawlessly" [ἀνόμως]. They were in no way bound by those positive ceremonial commands, since they were not the Church, not "Lo Ruhamah," not fellow citizens [πολίται], but the accursed profane, sinners, in whom the Church did not bear fruit, and finally dogs, who did not partake of the bread from the Lord's table. But "the oracles were entrusted" [ἐπιστεύθησαν] to the Jews alone, the words of Jacob alone, and the statutes and judgments of Israel, Rom. 3:2; Ps. 147:17. Such was that about blood, as we have clearly proved. 2. What? Did Noah not have the law of sacrifices? Unless he sacrificed rashly and by the impulse of private lust. Therefore the Gentiles rejected by the Church ought nonetheless to have offered sacrifices? Most false. For the stranger who draws near shall die, Num. 3:5, 6. Compare Num. 17, 18. And just as the Israelites, when by rash apostasy they at any time caused offence and loathing to God, were punished by the cessation of sacrifices, which was a sign of divine wrath, so the Gentiles, falling away from the Deity by God's certain and unchangeable judgment and their own perverse will, were rightly forbidden sacrifices and drawn into idolatrous worship. 3. But the first falsehood is undoubtedly this: Curcellaeus, from the perverse Remonstrant hypothesis which posits a universal calling in every age, by whose benefit all have a right to the Church and its privileges, and by neglecting which a man becomes liable to eternal death, holds that all Gentiles up to the time of Christ were called in Noah and were bound to all of Noah's commands, both moral and positive. His words in Acts 14:16 favour this opinion: "God indeed permitted the Gentiles after that time to walk in their own ways, that is, he did not visit them through the Prophets nor remind them of their duty, etc." As if God, in rejecting the Gentiles, had used no special judgment by which he shut them out and cast them from the Church, but they, withdrawing by their own voluntary apostasy, had disdained to join themselves to the Church. So that permission would be only patience, not also power, as Augustine speaks in another cause against Pelagius. This is wholly remote from the truth. For the Gentiles were so rejected from the Church by the just judgment of God that, without hope of return before the appointed time, they were to lie benumbed outside it by a singular decree of God. This is attested by that formula of excommunication, Matt. 18:17: Let him be to you as a Gentile. To this pertains the most grave expostulation of God with the house of Israel, Ezek. 44:6–9: Judge the rebellious house of Israel. Thus says the Lord Jehovah: Enough for you! Depart from your abominations. You who have brought in foreigners, uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to profane my house, who have offered my food, the fat and the blood, while they made void my covenant. Nor have you kept the observance of my holy things, but have set up keepers of my observance in my sanctuary at your own pleasure. Thus says the Lord Jehovah: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall come into my sanctuary; no foreigner, I say, who is among the sons of Israel. Hence Christ calls them dogs, Matt. 15:26, and with that saying should be compared the words Outside are the dogs, Rev. 22:15. Add to this that the Apostle calls the law of circumcision and of the other ceremonial worship instituted among the Jewish people, and so also of the sacrifices and of the prohibition of blood, which was referred to them, the enmities by which the Gentiles, once these were removed through Christ, were reconciled to God, Eph. 2:15, 16. How could the law of God be those enmities, destroyed in order that the Gentiles might be reconciled to God, if God's enmity with the Gentiles had not been sealed even by the very mark of uncircumcision, by which, as by a wall interposed, they were kept from access to the Church? So that fancy about a universal calling, a common covenant, and a necessity of keeping those precepts which were handed down to the Church as a seal of the hope of the coming Messiah, is most empty. These points ought to have been touched on in passing and set against Curcellaeus, who, [ἐᾶν suam φυλάττειν] leaving them to keep their own way, limits the rejection of the Gentiles to this single negative act of God, that he permits them to go in their ways, does not send Prophets, does not remind them of their duty. The Scriptures, consulted, and the passages alleged from them, answer otherwise. 4. Nor is this more refined, where he says: "To those who did not retain the memory of Noah's precept, their neglect is not imputed as a fault, because this matter is not of the kind that could be known by the natural light." But if in the person of Noah this precept was given to all his posterity, they were guilty of violating a command, and therefore undoubtedly this crime was somewhere reproached to them through the Prophets, whether they were mindful of that command or were seized by forgetfulness. If they were mindful, he concedes the point. If they buried it in forgetfulness, the obligation did not therefore cease. Indeed, since through their own and their ancestors' fault they lost the memory of that command, forgetfulness of a necessary matter turned to the increase of their guilt.

units.la: §. Sed abrumpit filum Philonides historia Mosis, in qua clare testatum, Deum Gentilibus esum sanguinis in morticino permisisse. Cujus argumenti nervum inferius adstringemus. 6. Si naturali lumine Gentiles cognoscere non potuerunt, sanguinis esum illicitum esse, non igitur natura vitiosum est, illo vesci. Desinat ergo Curcellaeus traducere crudelitatem, feritatem ejus esus, & insanae paratragoediari.
units.tr: §. But he breaks the thread with the history of Moses, in which it is clearly attested that God permitted the Gentiles to eat blood in carrion. We shall tighten the sinew of this argument further below. 6. If the Gentiles could not know by the natural light that eating blood is unlawful, then eating it is not by nature wicked. Let Curcellaeus therefore cease to traduce the cruelty and savagery of that eating, and his insane theatrics.

units.la: CAPUT V: Curcellaei & Becmanni contrariae rationes solvuntur.
units.tr: Chapter V: The contrary arguments of Curcellaeus and Becmannus are answered.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Curcellai objectio. 1. 2. Non ideo omnes obligat lex, quia Noachlata. 3. Becmanni ratio: Praeceptum hoc morale esse, quia ratio ejus moralis, examinatur. 4. Morale definitur. Moralitatis indicia. 5. Inducuntur praecepta ceremonialia, quae moralem rationem adjunctam habent. Locus Ierem. VII. 22. à Maimonide explicatus. 6. Vestium externa mundities cur in Veteri Testamento praecepta? Cur circumdatio anguli capitis? Vestes ex lino & lana in Veteri Testamento illicitae cur fuerint? Cur mulier viri vestes non ausa gestare? כלאים. Azymi panes. 7. Causa discriminis ciborum ex Origene & Barnaba. 8. 9. Chrysostomi commentario in Genes. IX. 4. 5. 10.
units.tr: Curcellaeus's objection. 1, 2. The law does not bind everyone merely because it was given to Noah. 3. Becmannus's argument: this precept is moral because its reason is moral, examined. 4. Definition of the moral; signs of morality. 5. Ceremonial precepts are brought forward which have a moral reason attached. The passage Jer. 7:22 explained by Maimonides. 6. Why were outward cleanness of garments commanded in the Old Testament? Why the fringe on the corner of the head-covering? Why were garments of linen and wool forbidden in the Old Testament? Why did a woman not dare to wear a man's clothing? Mixtures [כלאים]. Unleavened bread. 7. The cause of the distinction between foods, from Origen and Barnabas. 8, 9. Chrysostom's commentary on Gen. 9:4, 5. 10.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: PRaeceptum Noacho datum, cujus hactenus vim & obligationem perpendimus, opinioni vulgari lethale vulnus infligere Curcellaeus dixit. Inanis jactantia. In aprico enim collocavimus, praeceptum illud ceremoniale, non morale fuisse. Nullam itaque obligationem in illos inducit, qui a ceremoniarum jugo per gratiam Christi liberati, atque adeo a molesta illa servitute sunt manumissi. Duo tamen obstare videntur, quorum prius Curcellaeus urget, posterius Doctissimus Becmannus.
units.tr: Curcellaeus said that the precept given to Noah deals a deadly blow to the common opinion. That is empty boasting. For we have made it plain that this precept was ceremonial, not moral. It therefore imposes no obligation on those who have been freed from the yoke of ceremonies by the grace of Christ and so released from that burdensome servitude. Two things, however, seem to stand in the way: the first is pressed by Curcellaeus, the second by the most learned Becmannus.

units.la: II.
