Curcellaei probatio talis: Ad universum genus humanum pertinere illud interdictum inde liquet, quod factum sit instauratori ejus Noacho, & filiis ipsius, ex quibus omnes reliqui homines ad hodiernum usque diem originem suam traxerunt. pag. 41. Resp. Universum genus humanum accipitur vel pro collectione omnium hominum in certa aliqua aetate, vel in omni omnium temporum aetate. Si priori modo accipitur, non intercedo. Non dubitandum enim, quin obligaverit totum hominum genus usque ad ea tempora, quibus a foedere externo & visibili societate Ecclesiae Gentiles exclusi fuerunt. Qui temporis tractus amplissimus fuit. Si posteriori, est mera λῆψις ἐν ἀρχῇ. Neque rationem magno emerim. Fuerit enim datum instauratori generis humani Noacho, & filiis ejus. An ideo omnibus hominibus in qualibet aetate mundi? Nempe ipsi datum fuit praeceptum, non ut homini, quomodo universi generis restaurator erat, sed ut fidei & principi membro Ecclesiae, cui expediebat in visibili symbolo manifestare sapientiam in mysterio occultatam, & unicum illud nomen, in quo ipsum salvari oportuit. Nam veritati liquido dedimus praeceptum hoc fuisse διαθήκης λατρείας, & pertinuisse ad legem de Sacrificiis. Ergo obligavit omnes Noacho satos, qui membra fuerunt hujus externae & visibilis Ecclesiae usque ad Christum. Si obfirmet animum adversarius, cogitet de Adamo. Is non restaurator fuit generis humani, sed πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν, 1. Cor. XV. 45. An propterea omnes leges ipsi & filiis latae ita universales fuerunt, ut homines universos ex ipso lege carnalis generationis descendentes in qualibet circumstantia obligárint? Quid ergo de lege Sacerdotii fiet, quam ipsi datam esse superius firmis rationibus evicimus? Nam illam neque semper, neque omnes omnino homines in qualibet circumstantia obstrinxisse, manifestius est, quam imber cum pluit.
units.tr: II. Curcellaeus's proof runs thus: That this prohibition pertains to the whole human race is clear from the fact that it was given to Noah, its restorer, and to his sons, from whom all other men have traced their origin down to the present day. p. 41. Reply: "the whole human race" is taken either as the collection of all men in a certain age, or as all men in the age of all times. If it is taken in the former sense, I do not object. For there is no doubt that it bound the whole human race up to the time when the Gentiles were excluded from the covenant and the outward, visible society of the Church. That span of time was very long. If it is taken in the latter sense, it is a mere [λῆψις ἐν ἀρχῇ] (begging the question). Nor do I think much of the argument. It was given to Noah, restorer of the human race, and to his sons. Does it follow that it was given to all men in every age of the world? The precept was given to him not as a man, in the sense that he was restorer of the whole race, but as a faithful and chief member of the Church, to whom it was fitting to make manifest in a visible symbol the wisdom hidden in the mystery, and that unique name in which he had to be saved. For we have clearly shown that this precept belonged to the [διαθήκης λατρείας] (covenant of worship) and pertained to the law of sacrifices. Therefore it bound all the descendants of Noah who were members of this external and visible Church until Christ. If the opponent stubbornly persists, let him consider Adam. He was not the restorer of the human race but a [πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν] (life-giving spirit), 1 Cor. 15:45. Were all laws given to him and to his sons so universal that they bound all men descended from him by the law of carnal generation, in every circumstance? What then becomes of the law of the priesthood, which we have above proved by firm arguments was given to him? For it is clearer than the rain when it falls that this law did not bind always, nor all men without exception, in every circumstance.

units.la: III. Pergit: Non ideo obligandi vim amisisse, quod sequentibus Seculis apud mortalium plerosque in desuetudinem abierit. Eodem enim jure dici possit, nos mandato inimicos diligendi, quod hodie a tam paucis observatur, non amplius teneri: Legibus quidem humanis contraria consuetudine derogari; sed aliter se rem habere in Divinis, qua tandiu nos devinxit, donec Deus aperto indicio, se nos ab eorum obedientia liberare ostenderit. pag.41. Agnoscimus contraria consuetudine legibus Divinis non derogari. Nam hominum infidelitas dominium Dei non enervat. Sed quae ipsi sequentia secula? Qui mortales? Si sequentia Secula usque ad Christi tempora, largior. Si Mortales, singulos homines usque ad Gentium servitutem, & ab hac Judaeos usque ad Christum, nec sic dissentio. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Quis tam futili ratione usus, ut hac occupatione opus fuerit?
units.tr: III. He goes on: Nor has it lost its binding force because in later centuries it fell into disuse among most mortals. For by the same right one could say that we are no longer bound by the command to love our enemies, which is observed today by so few. Indeed human laws are set aside by contrary custom; but it is otherwise in divine matters, which have bound us for so long, until God by a clear sign shows that he has freed us from obeying them. p. 41. We acknowledge that divine laws are not set aside by contrary custom, for human unbelief does not weaken the dominion of God. But what are the "later centuries"? And which mortals? If the later centuries up to the time of Christ, I grant it. If mortals, I do not dissent even so, provided single men are meant up to the servitude of the Gentiles, and from that the Jews up to Christ. But what has this to do with the matter? Who used so trivial an argument that this effort was needed?

units.la: IV. Posterior ratio, quae est Doctissimi Becmanni, speciosior longe est, & colore suo multis blanditur. Is Exercitat. XXVI. quam integram in hac quaestione consumsit, argumentum ex Genes. IX.4. primore loco urget, & munit hac instantia, quod praeceptum Noachi habeat adjunctam rationem moralem, qua pertinet ad praeceptum Decalogi Sextum: Non occides. Quia enim, inquit, homines ideo ab esu sanguinis abstinere debent, ut ne hominum sanguinem fundere gestiant, quare non referretur ad praeceptum Decalogi: Non occides? Quippe cum virtutibus & vitiis causae, occasiones & media omnis generis comprehendantur, pag.532. Axiomatis ratio-nis: Praeceptum esse morale, cujus ratio moralis. Cum hac objectione haud desultorie nobis confligendum est. Summis igitur velis utemur. Apparebit autem, si recte calculum posuerimus, plus coloris quam rei, verisimilitudinis quam necessitatis habere.
units.tr: IV. The latter argument, that of the most learned Becmannus, is by far the more plausible, and its colour flatters many. In his Exercitation 26, which he devoted entirely to this question, he presses first the argument from Gen. 9:4, and strengthens it with this instance: the precept given to Noah has a moral reason attached, which pertains to the sixth precept of the Decalogue, "You shall not kill." For, he says, if men ought to abstain from eating blood so that they do not desire to shed human blood, why should it not be referred to the precept of the Decalogue, "You shall not kill"? Since causes, occasions and means of every kind are included under virtues and vices. p. 532. The axiom of his argument is this: a precept is moral whose reason is moral. This objection must be met without idle play, so we shall use full sails. It will appear, however, if we have reckoned rightly, that it has more colour than substance, more plausibility than necessity.

units.la: V. Definiamus ergo primo morale, & quid ad moralitatem praecepti exigatur, dispiciamus. Morale dicit respectum ad eos actus creaturae rationalis, qui propter convenientiam vel disconvenientiam cum rationali natura, vel potius cum natura & praecepto Dei, quo finitur Sanctitas creata, moralem turpitudinem habent, vel honestatem moralem. A priori igitur morale demonstratur illud, cujus ostenditur convenientia cum tali Dei. Quia vero non omne praeceptum Dei necessarium explicite scriptum est, & praecessit tempestas, qua nihil omnino mandatum scripto, & praecepta aliquando Deus tulit, quae non omnino moralia; indiciis quibusdam cognosci debet, actum aliquem cum praecepto Dei omnes & semper per obligante, convenire vel disconvenire. Indicium ejusmodi duplex est. Primum, cum recta ratio, quam Philosophus ἐν Ἀλεξάνδρῳ saepissime appellat, ex principiis justi secum cognatis judicat, talem actum voluntati Dei, quae justa & sancta est, quam maximè convenire. Facultatem hujus judicii Deus concessit omnibus hominibus, ne humana societas, ignara virtutum & viriorum homini proprio-rum, in licentiam maximorum scelerum solveretur & despumaret, caedibus saeviret, furtis, adulteriis, fraudibus & facinoribus aliis se nefandum in modum obligaret, atque sic denique externa honesta-te, non jam hominum societas rationem utentium, sed belluarum existeret. Alterum indicium convenientiae vel disconvenientiae actus humani cum praecepto Dei, est clara consensio, si non omnium, at moratiorum gentium. Hoc innuit Philosophus, probaturus, summum bonum esse, quod omnes expetunt: Ο᾽ γὰρ πᾶσι δοκεῖ, inquit, τοῦτο εἶναι φαμέν. Ο᾽ δὲ ἀμφοῖν ἰσχύει τὴν πίστιν, ὃ πάντα πιστεύει ἔχει. Quod omnibus ita videtur, illud esse dicimus. Qui vero hanc persuasionem tollit, parum credibiliora afferet. Ethic. Nicomach. X. 2. Hinc & Heraclitus statuens λόγον ξυνὸν optimum esse veritatis πεπιστεύμενον, τὸ κοινὸν, inquit, φαινόμενα πάντα. Quae communiter ita videntur, fida sunt. Et Cicero Tuscul. Quaest. lib. 1. In re consensio omnium gentium jus naturae putanda est. Cui succinit Seneca Epist. CXVII. Argumentum veritatis est, aliquando omnibus videri. Et quemadmodum ἀληθὲς τῶν φύσει ὄντων ἄλλως ἐπιζητεῖται. Ethic. Nicom. II. 11. Sic impossibile, ut non omni tempore, & omnibus omnino hominibus, quod est ejusmodi, tanquam lege dictatum, faciendum videatur. Neque quicquam aliud ad moralitatem requiri videtur. Unde jam proclive judicatu, quam vim habeat Becmanni ratio: Morale est, inquit, quod moralem rationem habet. Nego. Quis ita morale praeceptum definivit? Sufficit ad morale praeceptum, ut ratio ex principiis congenitis justitiae & honestatis judicet, actum aliquem cum sancta & immutabili voluntate & natura Dei convenire: & ut in eo consentiant moratiores omnes. De caetero ratio moralis non est necessarium accidens moralis praecepti.
units.tr: V. Let us first define the moral and examine what is required for the morality of a precept. "Moral" denotes a relation to those acts of a rational creature which have moral baseness or moral honesty on account of agreement or disagreement with rational nature, or rather with the nature and precept of God, by which created holiness is defined. Therefore, a priori, that is shown to be moral of which agreement with such a will of God is shown. But because not every necessary precept of God is written out explicitly, and there was a period in which nothing at all was commanded in writing, and God at times issued precepts that were not wholly moral, it must be recognised by certain signs whether some act agrees or disagrees with a precept of God that binds always and for all. Such a sign is twofold. The first is when right reason, which the Philosopher very often calls [ἐν Ἀλεξάνδρῳ], judges from principles of justice that are innate to it that some act agrees most of all with the will of God, which is just and holy. God granted this faculty of judgment to all men, lest human society, ignorant of the virtues and vices proper to man, should dissolve into licence for the greatest crimes and foam over, rage with murders, thefts, adulteries, frauds and other wicked deeds, and bind itself in unspeakable ways; and so at last, with outward honesty gone, it would exist not as a society of men who use reason but as a society of beasts. The second sign of the agreement or disagreement of a human act with God's precept is clear consent, if not of all, at least of the more civilised nations. The Philosopher hints at this when he sets out to prove that the highest good is what all desire: "For what seems so to all," he says, "we say is so [Ο᾽ γὰρ πᾶσι δοκεῖ, τοῦτο εἶναι φαμέν]. But he who takes away this persuasion will bring forward things less credible [Ο᾽ δὲ ἀμφοῖν ἰσχύει τὴν πίστιν, ὃ πάντα πιστεύει ἔχει]." Ethic. Nicom. X. 2. Hence Heraclitus too, holding that the common reason [λόγον ξυνὸν] is the best guarantee of truth, says that the common [τὸ κοινὸν] is trustworthy: "All things that commonly appear so are trustworthy." And Cicero, Tusc. Quaest. book 1: "In a matter of the consensus of all nations, the law of nature is to be thought to lie." Seneca, Epist. 117, agrees: "A proof of truth is that it sometimes appears so to all." And just as the truth of things that are by nature is sought in another way [ἀληθὲς τῶν φύσει ὄντων ἄλλως ἐπιζητεῖται], Ethic. Nicom. II. 11, so it is impossible that what is of this kind should not at all times, and to all men absolutely, seem to be done, as if dictated by a law. Nor does anything else seem to be required for morality. Whence it is now easy to judge what force Becmannus's argument has: "The moral," he says, "is what has a moral reason." I deny it. Who has defined a moral precept in this way? It is enough for a moral precept that reason, from principles of justice and honesty implanted in us, judges that some act agrees with the holy and unchangeable will and nature of God, and that all the more civilised nations agree in this. Otherwise, a moral reason is not a necessary accident of a moral precept.

units.la: VI. Imo Ceremonialia praecepta saepe moralem rationem habere, patebit inductione multorum aliorum. Ac primo praecepti de sacrificando. Illud ceremoniale esse in confesso est. Qui tamen querelas Dei in Scripturis expendit, & nauseam sacrificiorum, quae saepiuscule captus fuit, facile intelliget, Deum legislatorem carnali illi praecepto rationem moralem adjunxisse. Nempe hanc, ut Deo potius quam falsis Numinibus hoc velut Sacramento se devoverent, miseriam suam praesentibus indiciis in mactatione animalium consirerentur, justitiae Dei sine idonea satisfactione ad Tartara usque flagraturae ritu hoc typico litarent; pro beneficiis tam spiritualibus quam corporalibus gratitudinis suae ac memoriae arrham apud Deum deponerent. Quas causas a Deo intentas esse liquet. Hinc, quoties Sacrificiorum cultum & [illegible, ~3 letters] homines illi ante praecepta Dei, & morales has rationes habere coeperunt, Deus vehementer indignationi vela dedit, & brutum illorum stuperum accusatione molestissima est executus. Maimonides sane non obscure hoc innuit More Nevoch. III. 32. ubi objectionem motam ex Jerem. VII.22. hac responsione expedit: Prima, inquit, intentio mea fuit, innuit Deus, ut apprehendatis me, neque alii serviatis, ut ego sim vobis in Deum. Vos mihi in populum. Hoc autem praeceptum meum de oblationibus datum est in hunc finem, ut exinde ad utilitatem vestram hoc disceretis. Et ea de causa transtuli illos cultus ad nomen meum, ut omnis idololatria deleatur, & unitas mea confirmetur. Vos vero venistis, & finem meum irritum fecistis, cultuque externo adhaesistis. Nam dubitastis de mea existentia, sicut dicitur: Negaverunt Dominum, & dixerunt: Non est ipse: & idolis servistis, Baali adolevistis, post Deos alienosivistis. Respexistis solum ad Templum Domini, & ad oblationes, quae non erant principalis intentio. Hactenus ille. Quis igitur non videt, praecepto Divino Ceremoniali de sacrificando, Dei destinatione adjunctam rationem moralem, & quidem multiplicem?
units.tr: VI. Indeed, ceremonial precepts often have a moral reason, as will be clear from the induction of many other examples. Take first the precept about sacrificing. That it is ceremonial is generally agreed. Yet whoever weighs God's complaints in the Scriptures, and the loathing for sacrifices that he so often expressed, will easily understand that God, as lawgiver, attached a moral reason to that carnal precept. This reason was that by this sacrament they should devote themselves to God rather than to false deities; that by present signs in the slaughter of animals they should acknowledge their misery; that by this typical rite they should propitiate the justice of God, which would otherwise burn in hell without fitting satisfaction; and that they should deposit with God a pledge of their gratitude and remembrance for benefits both spiritual and bodily. It is clear that these were the purposes God intended. Hence, whenever those men began to hold the cult of sacrifices and these moral reasons apart from God's precepts, God let loose his indignation and punished their brutish stupidity with the most grievous accusation. Maimonides plainly hints at this in More Nevochim III.32, where he resolves an objection raised from Jer. 7.22 with this answer: My first intention, God indicates, was that you should apprehend me and serve no other, that I should be your God and you my people. This precept of mine concerning offerings was given with this end in view, that from it you might learn what is for your good. For this reason I transferred those forms of worship to my name, so that all idolatry might be destroyed and my unity confirmed. But you came and frustrated my purpose, and clung to external worship. For you doubted my existence, as it is said: They denied the Lord and said: He is not; and you served idols, grew up to Baal, and went after strange gods. You looked only to the Temple of the Lord and to the offerings, which were not the principal intention. So far he. Who therefore does not see that to the ceremonial divine precept about sacrificing is joined, by God's design, a moral reason, and indeed a manifold one?

units.la: VII. Externam corporis munditiem Deus ab Israelitis in Vet. T. requisivit.
units.tr: VII. God required outward bodily cleanliness of the Israelites in the Old Testament.

units.la: Videlicet, ut in vestitu mundum custodirent, corpus lavarent, sudorem & sordes abstergerent, & si quid aliud. Praeceptum ceremoniale haud dubie fuit, quia ejus observantia per se Israelitas Deo non commendavit. Hinc Esajas LXVI.17. Qui sanctificant se & purgant in hortis, modo hic, modo isthic: qui carnem porcorum verant & murium, unā ruinā omnes involventur, dictum Jehova. Et tamen praecepti hujus Ceremonialis rationem moralem fuisse, palam est. Nempe ut hoc Symbolico praecepto docerentur, purificare opera & cor ab opinionibus pravis & moribus inhonestis. Jam constat, plurima praecepta esse, quae Deus solis Israelitis injunxit, ut idolatriam detestarentur. Sic enim prohibuit circumdationem anguli capitis, & anguli barbae Lev.XIX.27. Quae ratio? Quia ita tondere se & radere solebant Sacerdotes idololatrici, teste Maimonide More Nevoch. III.37. Non fuit integrum Israelitis gestare vestimentum ex lino & lana Lev.XIX.19. Sive quòd Deus hoc modo patefaceret, sibi in cultu sinceritatem placere: & ut lana ac linum miscéri non debuerunt, sic nec cultus miscéri oportere, quæ ratio a plerisque illius præcepti esse putatur: Sive quòd tum temporis Sacrificuli idololatrarum ita incedere solerent. Simul enim, inquit Maimonides, adhibebant tum plantas, hoc est, linum, & animalia, hoc est, lanam; ac præterea annulum, qui ex metallo aliquo erat, in digitis gestabant: sicut ista in libris ipsorum reperiuntur. Neque dispar ratio præcepti, Deut.XXII.5. ne mulier induat vestimenta viri. Invenies enim, inquit Maimonides, in libro [Hebrew] præcipi, ut vir gestet vestimentum muliebre coloratum, quando stat coram Stella Veneris. Similiter, ut mulier induat loricam & arma bellica, quando stat coram Stella Martis. Prohibuit lex [Hebrew] insitionem unius arboris in aliam. Ratio moralis est detestatio idololatriæ Zabæorum, si fides est Doctissimo Judæo. Hi enim confinxerunt, si arbori arbor insita-tur in tali vel tali Lunæ constitutione, si his vel illis suffumigetur, si hæc vel illa verba in ipso insitionis momento proferantur, ex insita illa arbore prodituram quidpiam, quod ad plurimas res conducat, & salutare sit. Oportere autem, ut cum una species in aliam inseritur, furculum inserendum manu teneat formosa puella, quam Vir præternaturali ratione corrumpat, ipsaque inter libidines plantulam arbori inserat. Atque hanc idololatriam, ut pudendam sic usitatissimam istis temporibus, Deum, ut detestarentur, præcepto illo contendisse. Azymis panis vesci imperabantur Israelitæ tempore Paschatis. Ratio moralis suberat, si Paulo interpretanti credimus. Sic enim ille: Expurgate vetus fermentum, ut sitis nova massa, sicut estis sine fermento. Nam Pascha nostrum pro nobis mactatum, Christus. Quare festum celebremus non in veteri fermento malitiæ & nequitiæ, sed in Azymis sinceritatis & veritatis, 1.Cor.V.7.8.
units.tr: That is, that they should keep themselves clean in their clothing, wash their bodies, wipe away sweat and dirt, and so on. This was undoubtedly a ceremonial precept, since its observance did not in itself commend the Israelites to God. Hence Isaiah 66.17: Those who sanctify and purify themselves in gardens, one after another, who eat the flesh of swine and mice, shall all be swept away together, says the LORD. Yet that this ceremonial precept also had a moral reason is plain: namely, that by this symbolic precept they might be taught to cleanse their works and hearts from wicked opinions and dishonest morals. It is established that there are many precepts which God imposed on the Israelites alone, so that they would detest idolatry. Thus he forbade the rounding of the corner of the head and the marring of the corner of the beard, Lev. 19.27. What is the reason? Because idolatrous priests used to cut and shave themselves in this way, as Maimonides testifies, More Nevochim III.37. It was not lawful for the Israelites to wear a garment of linen and wool, Lev. 19.19. Either God thereby showed that sincerity in worship pleases him, and just as wool and linen ought not to be mixed, so worship ought not to be mixed, which reason is thought by most to lie behind that precept; or else because at that time the priests of the idolaters used to go about in this way. For at the same time, says Maimonides, they used plants, that is, linen, and animals, that is, wool; and besides, they wore on their fingers a ring made of some metal; as these things are found in their books. The reason for the precept in Deut. 22.5 is no different: a woman shall not put on a man's garment. For you will find, says Maimonides, in the book [Hebrew] that it is commanded that a man wear a coloured woman's garment when he stands before the star Venus; and similarly, that a woman put on a breastplate and weapons of war when she stands before the star Mars. The law [Hebrew] forbade the grafting of one tree onto another. The moral reason is the detestation of the idolatry of the Sabeans, if we trust that most learned Jew. For they devised that if a tree is grafted onto a tree when the moon is in such and such a position, if it is fumigated with this or that, if these or those words are spoken at the very moment of grafting, something will come forth from that grafted tree which is useful for many things and is healthful. It was necessary, moreover, that when one species is grafted into another, a beautiful girl should hold the little shoot to be grafted in her hand, and that a man should defile her by supernatural means, and that in the midst of lusts she should insert the little plant into the tree. God commanded that precept so that they would detest this idolatry, which is as shameful as it was most common in those times. The Israelites were commanded to eat unleavened bread at the time of the Passover. The moral reason lay beneath it, if we believe Paul's interpretation. For he says: Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us. Therefore let us keep the feast not with the old leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, 1 Cor. 5.7-8.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Quid dicam de discrimine ciborum mundorum & immundorum? Cujus præceptum merè ceremoniale esse, Christiani omnes fatentur. Et tamen morales rationes non desunt, qui cumulent. Origenes lib.4.contra Celsum in hac re prolixus est. Cujus verba ex Græco translata adscribam: Mali quidam Dæmones, & ut sic loquar, tirannici aut gigantei, qui impie in verum Numen & cœlestes cœlestes Angelos se gessêre, ideóque è cœlestibus sunt, eirca corporum crassiora & inferiora in terris se agitant. Cumque habeant aliquam circa futura perspicaciam, ut qui à terrenis corporibus sint liberi, & in talibus negotiis multùm versati, hoc unicè studentes, humanum genus in abducant à vero Deo, insinuant se, in animantium fera ac rapacissimè, deinde & in calidiora, & ea, quoties volunt, quò volunt, movent, aut etiam talium animalium vim imaginosam incitant ad hos aut illos volatus motionésve, ut homines capti divinationibus, quæ per muta fiunt animalia, Deum cuncta continentem non querant, neque veram exerceant pietatem, sed cogitationibus suis decidunt in terram, in aves, in dracones, quin etiam in vulpes & lupos. Observatum enim est horum rerum peritis, prædictionis maximè notabiles per id genus animalia fieri, non valentibus, ut videtur, dæmonibus tantùm efficere in mansuetis animantium, quantum prava ista animantia possunt in aliis, quæ diximus, animantibus, ob id quod ista habent vitio simile, non vitium proprié, sed quasi vitium. Quamobrem, si quid aliud in Mose et miratus sum ipse, & dignum miratu existimo, hoc est, quòd cùm percepisset naturas animantium diversas, sive à Deo electas ea, quæ ad animantia, & ad dæmones animantium cuique affines pertinebant, sive propria ipse scientia perductus ad noscendos animantium gradus, omnia ea impura pronunciavit, quæ ab Ægyptiis aliisque gentibus vim divinandi habere credebantur, contrà verò omnia ea pura, quæ extra illum census essent. Hactenus Origenes. Quibus consentientia scribit Theodoretus l.7. adversus Græcos. Hinc Manetho: Νομοθετοῦντες ἡμῖν ἄλλα, μιᾶλιστα τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις ἐξιστομένοις ἐναλλάσσοντα. Cùm plurima instituisset alia, Ægyptiorum instituenti pugnantia. Non alias tamen hujus interdicti causas stringit Barnabas in Epistola, quam laudat Clemens Stromat. l.5. Verbam non pigrabor transcribere. Quod dixit Moses, inquit, non vescimini porco, neque aquila, neque oxyptero, neque corvo, neque pisce, qui squamis careat, in secreto intellectu (ἐν τῇ συνέσει) tria comprehendit dogmata. Quò tendat, diserte ipse in Deuteronomio ostendit: Et testabuntur populo meo justa mea. Non igitur præceptum proprié est, hoc vel illo non vesci: sed in spiritu dixit ista Moses. De porco hoc est, quod volumus: Nolite conglutinari cum hominibus illis, qui porcis sunt similes. Nam, dum luxu diffluunt, obliviscountur dominj sui: Ubi autem res contrà eunt, agnoscunt dominum. Nam & porcus ubi comedit, non novit dominum: Ubi esurit, clamat: & rursum, ubi quod edat. decepit, raxerit. Neque comedas, inquit, aquilam, neque oxypterum, neque milvum, neque corvum: Hoc dicit: Ne conglutinereris hominibus ejusmodi, qui labore ac sudore victum sibi nescient quaerere, sed aliena rapiunt injustè factis suis, insidiásque ponunt, specie sumta bona fide ambulantium. Sic & animantia illa odiosa, dum desidem, speculantur, quomodo alienis se pascant carnibus, noxia malo ingenio suo. Ne comedas etiam murenam, inquit, nec polypum, nec sepiam. Hoc dicit: Ne agglutinando te similem reddas hominibus talibus, qui perpetuò sunt impii & morti servantur: sicut piscium illi soli, qui damnantur in summo natant, nec in summo, ut capiantur, fluitant, sed in imo solo degunt. Sed nec dasypoden comedas, inquis. Cur verò? Id est: Ne fias puerorum corruptor aut similis talibus. Leges enim quoque anno ad ejectamenta alvi sit opulentior. Quae enim habet annos totidem & cavernas. Sed nec hyaenam, ait, vescere. Id est, nec adulter esto, aut similis adulteris. Unde hoc? Hoc enim animal quotannis mutat naturam, et nunc mas fit, nunc femina. Sed & mustelam merito odio habuit. Nimirum hoc monet: Noli similis esse illis, quos audimus ore infamia patrare: neque aggregare feminis in eum modum morigeran-tibus: nam animal illud ore concipit. De cibis ergo loquens Moses, tria dogmata in Spiritu locutus est. At illi pro cupiditate carnis sua simpliciter de cibis ea acceperê. At ursum illorum dogmatum cognitionem etiam David consecutus est. Dicit enim: Beatus Vir, qui non ambulavit in consilio impiorum, (nimirum quomodo pisces versantur in tenebris, in profundo abditis,) nec in via peccatorum non stetit; (nimirum ut illi, qui cum videant Deum timere, peccant porcorum instar) & in cathedra pestilentiae non sedit; (nimirum ut volucres, quae raptui imminent.) Habetes & ea, quae ad scientiam pertinent. Dixit Moses: Edite omne bisulcum ungulis & ruminans. Quid ait? Qui cibum sumit, agnoscit alterum suum, & in eo acquiescit. Bene dixit, ad praeceptum respiciens. Quid igitur dicit? Adhaerendum iis, qui Dominum timent; iis, qui in corde meditantur, quod accepêre in verbis, praeceptum: iis qui loquuntur justa Deique servant: iis, qui nôrunt meditationem esse justitiae opus: iis qui sermones Divinos ruminant. Quid verò bisulcum ungulis? Quia vir justus in hoc exo ambulat, & alterum eorum exspectat. Vide quàm pulchrè leges dederit Moses. Hactenus Barnabas. Eadem Philo habet lib. de agricultura, & libro, Pejorem insidiari meliori. Et ex Aristaeo Eusebius lib. VIII, c. 9. Quae adeo solicitè refero, tum ut consteret, stet, moralem rationem non necessario præceptum morale facere suum, quia hæc res per se utilem & liberalem cognitionem habeat.
units.tr: What shall I say about the distinction between clean and unclean foods? All Christians admit that its command is purely ceremonial. Yet there are still moral reasons offered by those who pile them up. Origen is lengthy on this point in Book 4 against Celsus. I will set down his words, translated from the Greek: Certain evil demons, tyrannical or giant-like, who behaved impiously toward the true Deity and the heavenly angels, and are therefore cast out of heaven, move about in the grosser and lower parts of bodies on earth. Since they have some foresight of future events, being free from earthly bodies and much occupied with such affairs, they study only this: to lead the human race away from the true God. They insinuate themselves into the fiercest and most rapacious animals, and then into warmer ones, and move them whenever and wherever they wish, or stir the imaginative power of such animals to this or that flight or movement. Thus men, captivated by divinations that are made through dumb animals, do not seek the God who contains all things, nor practise true piety, but by their thoughts they fall to earth, into birds, into serpents, and even into foxes and wolves. For those skilled in these matters have observed that the most notable predictions are made through this kind of animal, since the demons, it seems, are not able to do as much with tame animals as these wicked creatures can do in the other animals I have mentioned, because these animals have a vice like theirs, not a vice properly speaking, but something like a vice. Therefore, if I have myself admired anything in Moses, and think it worthy of admiration, it is this: that, having perceived the diverse natures of animals, whether chosen by God for this knowledge, or led by his own skill to know the ranks of animals, and the kinship of each animal to demons, he declared unclean all those creatures which the Egyptians and other nations believed had the power of divination, and on the other hand declared clean all those outside that class. Thus far Origen. Theodoret, in Book 7 against the Greeks, writes things agreeing with these. Hence Manetho: "Legislating for us other things, very much opposed to what the Egyptians prescribe" [Νομοθετοῦντες ἡμῖν ἄλλα, μιᾶλιστα τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις ἐξιστομένοις ἐναλλάσσοντα]: that is, when he had laid down many other institutions contrary to the institutions of the Egyptians. Yet Barnabas, in the Epistle which Clement cites in Stromateis Book 5, touches on other causes of this prohibition, and I will not hesitate to transcribe his words. He says: "What Moses said, 'You shall not eat the pig, nor the eagle, nor the hawk, nor the crow, nor any fish which lacks scales,' comprehends three doctrines in a spiritual understanding [ἐν τῇ συνέσει]." Where he is aiming, he himself shows plainly in Deuteronomy: "And they shall bear witness to my people of my righteous things." Therefore it is not properly a precept to abstain from this or that food, but Moses spoke these things in the Spirit. About the pig, this is what we mean: "Do not join yourselves to those men who are like pigs. For while they wallow in luxury, they forget their master; but when things go against them, they acknowledge the master. For the pig too, when it eats, does not know its master; when it is hungry it cries out, and again, when it has no food, it goes astray." Nor, he says, shall you eat the eagle, the hawk, the kite, or the crow. That is to say: do not join yourself to men of this kind, who do not know how to seek their living by labour and sweat, but unjustly seize what belongs to others by their deeds, and lay snares, taking on the appearance of men walking in good faith. So too those hateful animals, idle as they are, watch how they may feed on the flesh of others, harmful by their evil nature. Nor shall you eat the lamprey, he says, nor the octopus, nor the cuttlefish. That is to say: do not make yourself like such men, by joining with them, who are always impious and are kept for death; just as those fish alone that are condemned swim at the surface, and yet do not float on the surface to be caught, but dwell at the bottom of the sea. But you say, neither shall you eat the hare. Why? That is: do not become a corruptor of boys, or like such men. For the law also, by the year, would have the bowels more fruitful for excretion; for the hare has as many years as caverns. Nor, he says, shall you eat the hyena. That is: do not be an adulterer, nor like adulterers. Whence is this? Because this animal changes its nature every year, and now becomes male, now female. And he rightly hated the weasel as well. Assuredly this warns: do not be like those whom we hear commit infamy with the mouth, nor join with women who give themselves up in that way; for that animal conceives by the mouth. Therefore Moses, speaking about foods, spoke three doctrines in the Spirit. But they, for the desire of their flesh, took those things simply as about foods. But David also attained a knowledge of those doctrines. For he says: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly" (namely, as fish move in darkness, hidden in the depths), "nor stood in the way of sinners" (namely, as those who, though they seem to fear God, sin like pigs), "and has not sat in the seat of pestilence" (namely, like birds that hover ready to seize). You have also what pertains to knowledge. Moses said: "Eat every animal that is cloven-footed and chews the cud." What does he mean? He who takes food recognises his fellow and rests in him. He spoke well, looking to the precept. What then does he say? That one must cleave to those who fear the Lord; to those who meditate in the heart on what they have received in words, the precept; to those who speak what is just and keep God's ways; to those who know that meditation is a work of righteousness; to those who chew over the divine words. And what is meant by cloven-footed? Because the righteous man walks in this world and awaits the other. See how beautifully Moses gave the laws." Thus far Barnabas. Philo has the same in his book on agriculture, and in the book "The worse lies in wait for the better." And Eusebius, Book 8, chapter 9, has it from Aristeas. I report these things so carefully so that it may be established that a moral reason does not necessarily make a precept moral, since this matter in itself has a useful and liberal knowledge.

units.la: IX. Atque hactenus non veremur album calculum adjicere Sapientissimo Maimonidi, qui confidenter concludit, Omnia præcepta Dei ceremonialia, præter typicam rationem, (quam ego hic principaliter includi statuo, quamvis Maimonides dissimulet) facere ad animæ & rationem sive manifestam sive occultam continere. Ut jam ad oculum pateat infirmitas argumenti Clariss. Becmanni. Vel enim omnia ista præcepta, quorum jam contexuimus seriem, & quæ demonstravimus moralibus rationibus, quæ singulæ ad præceptum aliquod Decalogi vel formaliter vel virtualiter, referri possent, suffulta esse, sunt moralia, quod nemo sanus complecti audebit: vel illud non mox morale est, quod moralem rationem additam habet. Interim illud ad animum revocari velim, ejusmodi præcepta potissimum mystica esse, & ἐσαν habere ad futura. Mystica autem illa præcepta Deus pro πλυπικίλῳ σοφίᾳ sua, liberè vestivit etiam moralibus rationibus. Proinde præsente καιρῷ ἀποδώσεως præcepta illa obligationem amiserunt, cùm ratio moralis & interna hominis sanctitas, quam utcunque figurârunt, æternam obligationis vim retinere debeat.
units.tr: IX. Thus far we do not hesitate to add a white stone to the most wise Maimonides, who confidently concludes that all the ceremonial precepts of God, apart from the typical reason (which I here hold is principally included, although Maimonides conceals it), are made to contain a reason for the soul, whether manifest or hidden. So that the weakness of the argument of the most distinguished Becmann may now be plain to the eye. For either all those precepts, whose series we have already set out, and which we have shown to be supported by moral reasons, each of which could be referred formally or virtually to some precept of the Decalogue, are moral (which no sane man will dare to embrace), or else that is not at once moral which has a moral reason added to it. Meanwhile I would wish this to be called to mind: such precepts are above all mystical, and have a shadow [σκιάν] of things to come. Moreover, God, in his many-coloured wisdom [πλυπικίλῳ σοφίᾳ], freely clothed those mystical precepts also with moral reasons. Therefore, now that the time of recompense [καιρῷ ἀποδώσεως] is present, those precepts have lost their obligation, since the moral reason and the inward holiness of man, which they in some measure figured, ought to retain the eternal force of obligation.

units.la: X. Antea quàm de hac provincia decedo, aurei & mellitissimi oris, Chrysostomi locum libet coronidis loco adscribere. Ex quo liquebit, ipsum hoc mandatum pro cærimoniali habere. Nam diserè comparat cum lege data Adamo in statu innocentiæ de non comedendo fructu arboris vitæ. Verba sunt: ὅθεν αὐτὸν τὸν κανόνα ἐπάνω ἀποσωζόμενον, τὸν ἐπὶ ξύλου πλατυτάτου. Καθάπερ γὰρ ἐκεῖ μὴ τὸ πάντων ἐγχειρήσας τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ μόνον ἀπέχεσθαι ἐπέλευσεν. Οὕτω μὴ τὴν εὐλογίαν καὶ τὸ Φοβερὸν αὐτὸν καταστῆσαι τοῖς θηρίοις καὶ πάντα τὰ πετεινά, καὶ τὸ ὅρπαξ ὧν χεῖρας ποιῆσαι, φησι, πᾶν ἑρπετὸν ζῶν ὑμῖν ἔσται εἰς βρῶσιν, ὡς λάχανα χόρτου ὑμῖν δέδωκα τὰ πάντα. Ἐντεῦθεν ἀρχὴ κρεοφαγίας. Οὐχ ἵνα εἰς γαστρίμαργίαν αὐτὸς ἀλείψῃ, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἡμελλεν ἐξ αὐτῶν θυσίας ἀναφέρειν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καὶ εὐχαριστίας πείθειν τῷ δεσπότῃ, ἵνα μὴ δόξωσιν, ὡς ἀφθόρων ἐπέχεσθαι· διὰ τοῦτο τῆς βρώσεως τὴν ἐξουσίαν χαρίζεται, καὶ πάλιν τὴν ἀδείαν παρέχει, ὡς λάχανα χόρτου φησὶ, δέδωκα ὑμῖν πάντα. Εἶτα καθάπερ ἐπὶ ξύλου ἀδὰμ ἐπέλαβεν ἐπεπλάστῳ ἐκ τῶν πάντων ἀπολαύσαι, ἀπέχεσθαι· ὅτι ἐντεῦθεν μὴ τὸ πάντων ἀδὲς ἀφεξέψας τὴν ἐξισσιν, φησὶ.
units.tr: X. Before I leave this province, I wish to add, as a crown, a passage of Chrysostom, of golden and honey-sweet mouth. From it will be clear that he himself holds this command to be ceremonial. For he expressly compares it with the law given to Adam in the state of innocence, about not eating the fruit of the tree of life. The words are: "Hence [he kept] the rule itself, the one concerning the broadest tree [ὅθεν αὐτὸν τὸν κανόνα ἐπάνω ἀποσωζόμενον, τὸν ἐπὶ ξύλου πλατυτάτου]. For just as there, at the beginning, though he had given them everything, he commanded them to abstain only from the tree in Paradise, so here, having made the blessing and the dread of himself to the beasts and all the birds, and having made every creeping thing living for you to eat, he says, as I gave you all the herbs of the grass. Hence the beginning of eating flesh. Not that he might indulge gluttony, but because he was going to bring up sacrifices from them to men and to persuade them to give thanks to the Master, lest they should seem to be restrained as from incorruptible things. For this reason he grants the power of eating, and again gives the permission, as he says: I have given you all, as the herbs of the grass. Then, just as Adam was commanded to abstain from the tree, in order to enjoy all the things made from the whole, so here he says that he has removed the prohibition, so as not to forbid anything at all."

units.la: ἀπολαύσαι
units.tr: to enjoy [ἀπολαύσαι]

units.la: {Greek text, set in italic, as printed at the top of the page: "ἀλλὰ ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς ἐστὶ φάγεσθε. Τί δὲ βούλεται τὸ εἰρημένον; πῶς ἐν χρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς ἐστι πικτόν. Ὁ γὰρ ἄλογος ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ αἷμα τυγχάνει. Ἐπεὶ οὖν τὰς ἰδιότητας ἡμεῖς ἀποπλεῖς τὰς λόγῳ τῶν ἀλόγων, μονονουχὶ διδάσκει αὐτὰς, λέγων. Ὅτι τὸ μὲν αἷμα ἐμοὶ ἀφιέναι, τὸ δὲ χρέας ὑμῖν. Ταῦτα δὲ ποιεῖ, ἀναθὲν ἀπαναστέλλειν αὐτῶν τὴν ὁρμὴν, τὴν ὠμὴν τῆς ἀνθρωφονίαν."}
units.tr: "But in the blood of the soul you shall not eat [ἀλλὰ ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς οὐ φάγεσθε]." What does this saying mean? How can flesh be in the blood of the soul? For the blood is the soul of irrational creatures. Since we strip irrational creatures of the properties of reason, he (God) teaches them, as it were, by saying: "The blood I reserve for myself, but the flesh is for you." He does this, restraining their impulse and their raw cruelty against men, by a command. [Τί δὲ βούλεται τὸ εἰρημένον; πῶς ἐν χρέας ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς ἐστι πικτόν. Ὁ γὰρ ἄλογος ἡ ψυχὴ τὸ αἷμα τυγχάνει. Ἐπεὶ οὖν τὰς ἰδιότητας ἡμεῖς ἀποπλεῖς τὰς λόγῳ τῶν ἀλόγων, μονονουχὶ διδάσκει αὐτὰς, λέγων. Ὅτι τὸ μὲν αἷμα ἐμοὶ ἀφιέναι, τὸ δὲ χρέας ὑμῖν. Ταῦτα δὲ ποιεῖ, ἀναθὲν ἀπαναστέλλειν αὐτῶν τὴν ὁρμὴν, τὴν ὠμὴν τῆς ἀνθρωφονίαν.]

units.la: Hoc est. Ecce, quemadmodum Deus iterato custodiae eum canonem, quem in Protoplastis custodivit. Sicut enim ibi absolutis & conditis ab initio rebus omnibus, & copia facta vescendorum omnium, qua in Paradiso, arboris tamen unius fructu ne vescerentur, prohibuit: ita hic postquam homini beneficiis, etiam terribilem brutis effecit, ejusque imperio subdidit reptilia & volatilia, dicit: Omne repile vobis esto in cibum: sicut herbam vobis omnia dedi. Atque hinc arcesitur origo manducationis carnis. Non quidem Deus ventri illorum levocinari voluit: sed quia voluerunt victimas ex iis mactare homines, & Eucharistica sacrificia Deo libare, Domino suo; ne existiment abstinendum carnibus tanquam rebus sacratis, indulget potestatem edendarum carnium, & confidenter, ne verecundentur: sicut herbam, inquit, Vobis dedi omnia. Deinde, quemadmodum cum Adamo permisisset vesci omnibus rebus, excepto fructu arboris vetito: Sic etiam hic, postquam magna fiducia jussisset eos omnia comedere, inquit: Tantum carnem in sanguine animae ne comedatis. Quid igitur sibi vult quod dixit? Quid est caro in sanguine anima? Hoc est suffocatum. Nam brutorum anima sanguis est. Cum igitur Sacrificia ex animantibus Deo vellent offerre, tantummodo daret: Mihi sanguis separatus est; Vobis autem caro. Hoc autem facit divinitus prohibens cades. Haec ille. Nos perginus.
units.tr: This is it. See how God, once again, keeps the same rule that he kept with the first-formed man. For there, when all things had been finished and created from the beginning, and the use of all foods had been granted to be eaten in Paradise, he forbade only the fruit of one tree to be eaten. So here, after he had made even the beasts fearful of man and had placed under his rule the creeping and flying things, he says: "Every creeping thing shall be food for you, as the green herb I have given you all things." And from this the origin of eating flesh is derived. God did not wish, of course, to indulge their appetites; but because they wished to slaughter men as victims from among these animals and to offer Eucharistic sacrifices to God their Lord, he grants them the power to eat flesh, and does so freely, so that they need not be ashamed; "as the green herb," he says, "I have given you all things." Then, just as with Adam, when he had permitted him to eat of all things except the fruit of the forbidden tree, so here too, after he had commanded them with such great confidence to eat everything, he says: "Only you shall not eat flesh with the blood of the soul." What then does he mean by what he said? What is flesh in the blood of the soul? It is the meat of a strangled animal. For the soul of beasts is the blood. Therefore, when they wished to offer sacrifices from living animals to God, he granted only this: "The blood is separated for me; but the flesh is for you." He does this by divinely forbidding the slaughter. So he. We proceed.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: A Mose usque ad Christum esum sanguinis ceremoniali praecepto interdictum fuisse, probatur. Breviarium.
units.tr: That the eating of blood was forbidden by a ceremonial precept from Moses until Christ, is proved. Summary.

units.la: Progressio ad tertiam periodum sub Mose. 1. Loci Lev. III. 17. VII. 26. illustrati. Iudaeorum distinctio inter sanguinem animae & sanguinem membrorum proponitur & refellitur. 2. An sub interdicto
units.tr: Progress to the third period under Moses. 1. The passages Lev. III. 17. and VII. 26. are explained. The Jews' distinction between the blood of the soul and the blood of the limbs is set out and refuted. 2. Whether under the prohibition

units.la: rerdicto Mosis sanguis piscium confirmatur. Selden us & Curcel-laeus refutati. Respondetur illorum rationibus. Collectio piscium & locustarum. 3. Locus Levit. XVII. 10. 11. Anima sanguis. Sanguine carere. 4. Ratio praecepti Mosaici nonnisi typica. Parti-cula relativa כי & י. Arabs laudatur. 5. Maimonidis οχαρατς... prudenter accipiendus. 6. Praeceptum Mosaicum pure Cere-moniale fuisse probatur. Proselytus domicilii fuit אכל נבילות. 7. Positivum non idem quod Ceremoniale. Gradum consanguinitatis, polygamia, divortiorum prohibitio non est a jure positivo. Grotius perstringitur. Distinctio juris naturalis & positivi, ejusdemque usus contra Curcellaeum asseritur. 8. Praeceptum Noacho & Mosi datum distinctum non fuit. Praecepta de Sabbatho & sanguine disparata.
units.tr: The prohibition of Moses concerning the blood of fish is confirmed by Seldenus and Curcellaeus are refuted. Their arguments are answered. The gathering of fish and locusts. 3. The passage Levit. XVII. 10. 11. The blood is the soul. Being without blood. 4. The reason for the Mosaic precept is only typical. The relative particle [כי and י]. The Arab is praised. 5. Maimonides' ... is to be taken with caution. 6. The Mosaic precept is shown to have been purely ceremonial. A resident proselyte was forbidden to eat carrion [אכל נבילות]. 7. The positive is not the same as the ceremonial. The degrees of consanguinity, polygamy and the prohibition of divorce do not come from positive law. Grotius is taken to task. The distinction between natural and positive law, and its use, is asserted against Curcellaeus. 8. The precept given to Noah and the precept given to Moses were not distinct. The precepts about the Sabbath and about blood are separated.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: AD tertiam temporis periodum, quae a Mose usque ad Christum extenditur, gradum promovemus. In qua agnoscimus Judaeis Divino oraculo per Mosen cautum esse, ne sanguine vescerentur. Servabimus autem eundem etiam hic ordinem, quem supra. Primo interdictum in medium adferemus & luce majori tonabimus. Deinde causas interdicti carptim dicemus. Mox rationibus certis probatum dabimus, praeceptum non morale, sed Ceremoniale fuisse. Denique Curcellaei & Becmanni contrarias rationes ad libram veritatis appendemus. Ergo ad rem.
units.tr: We now advance to the third period of time, which extends from Moses to Christ. In it we acknowledge that the Jews were warned by the divine oracle, through Moses, not to eat blood. We shall keep the same order here as above. First we shall set out the prohibition and proclaim it in the clearest light. Then we shall briefly state the causes of the prohibition. Next, by sure arguments, we shall prove that the precept was not moral but ceremonial. Finally, we shall weigh the contrary arguments of Curcellaeus and Becmann in the balance of truth. So, to the matter.

units.la: II. Primus locus occurrit Levit. III. 17. & repetitur Lev. VII. 26. כל דם לא תאכלו כל מושבותיכם לאומה ולבהמה : כל נפש; אשר תאכל כל דם ונכרתה הנפש הוה מעמיה; Sanguinem non comedetis in ullis habitationibus vestris, nullius volucris vel bestiae. Quisquis homo comederit ullum sanguinem, utique excindetur ille homo e populis suis. Ubi simpliciter interdictum commemoratur, sine additamento rationum. Et sanguinem intelligit, sive fusum, sive visceribus adhuc contentum, sive eduliis mixtum. Judaei tamen distinguunt inter דם הנפש Sanguinem animae, & דם האברים Sanguinem membrorum. Illum prohiberi sub poena excidii: hunc sub poena מלקות flagellationis. Rationem distinctae poenae si desideras, illam promit R. Levi Barcelonita: דם הנפש הא בכרת שבמקום שבא בתורה הכרת ברם נאמר שם נפש.
units.tr: II. The first passage occurs at Lev. 3:17 and is repeated at Lev. 7:26: כל דם לא תאכלו כל מושבותיכם לאומה ולבהמה: כל נפש אשר תאכל כל דם ונכרתה הנפש ההוא מעמיה ("You shall eat no blood in any of your dwellings, whether of bird or of beast. Whatever person eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people"). Here the prohibition is recorded simply, without any added reasons. And it means blood whether poured out, or still contained in the viscera, or mixed with food. The Jews, however, distinguish between דם הנפש (the blood of the soul) and דם האברים (the blood of the members). The former is forbidden under penalty of excision (כרת), the latter under penalty of flagellation (מלקות). If you want the reason for the different penalty, R. Levi Barcelonita gives it: דם הנפש הא בכרת שבמקום שבא בתורה הכרת ברם נאמר שם נפש ("The blood of the soul is under excision, because wherever in the Law excision is mentioned, the word 'soul' is said there").

units.la: [Hebrew verse, two lines: נפש שת כי נפש הבשר בדם הוא ומה שפכו דם התבשל אלא דם האברים אין איסורו אלא כלאו שעליו נא כתים וכל דם לא תאכלו]
units.tr: [For the soul of the flesh is in the blood. And what is it that they spill? It is blood that is boiled. But the blood of the members is forbidden only by the general prohibition, on which it is written: "You shall not eat any blood."] [נפש שת כי נפש הבשר בדם הוא ומה שפכו דם התבשל אלא דם האברים אין איסורו אלא כלאו שעליו נא כתים וכל דם לא תאכלו]

units.la: Sanguis anima prohibetur sub poena excidii, quia si in lege mentio fit excidii propter sanguinem, anima vox additur: quia anima in eo est. Qui vero non anima sed membrorum sanguis est, nonnisi nuda negatione prohibetur: de hoc enim simpliciter dicitur: Nullum sanguinem comedetis.
units.tr: The blood of the soul is forbidden under penalty of excision, because when mention is made in the Law of excision on account of blood, the word "soul" is added: because the soul is in it. But the blood that is not of the soul but of the members is forbidden only by a bare negation, for of this it is simply said: You shall eat no blood.

units.la: Ergo hominem dicunt reum fieri excidii propter sanguinem, qui exit tempore mactationis, aut natium discissionis, aut capitis amputationis, quamdiu in illo rubedo conspicua fuerit. Eandem rationem esse sanguinis congregati in medio cordis, sanguinis in phlebotomia ebulliendo erumpentis. Flagellationem conciliare sanguinem, qui in mactatione, postquam sanguis naturalis effluxit, lente exprimitur: Sanguinem item membrorum, ut lienis, renum testiculorum, & qui se tempore mactationis ad cor aggregat. De qua re prolixe agitur Thalm. Mass. Kerith. cap. 5. Caeterum illam distinctionem praeter & contra legem Judaei invehunt, atque sic impie vincula legis Divinae laxant. Apertus est Moses in hoc loco, ubi sancit, ut excindatur anima potantis sanguinem. An tantum potantis sanguinem animae? Atqui non meminit דם Sanguinis anime. Sed in genere cujuslibet sanguinis. Secundum Rabbinorum mentem hoc loco Moses, qui in genere de quolibet sanguine loquitur; non poenam כרת sive excidii, sed poenam מלקות sive flagellationis intonare debuit. Contra autem factum videmus.
units.tr: Hence they say that a man becomes liable to excision on account of the blood that flows out at the time of slaughter, or of the cutting of the buttocks, or of the cutting off of the head, as long as red colour is visible in it. The same reasoning, they say, applies to blood gathered in the middle of the heart, and to blood that bursts out boiling in a bloodletting. They assign flagellation to the blood that is slowly squeezed out in slaughter after the natural blood has flowed away, and likewise to the blood of the members, such as that of the spleen, the kidneys, the testicles, and that which gathers towards the heart at the time of slaughter. This matter is discussed at length in the Talmud, tractate Kerithoth, chapter 5. But the Jews introduce this distinction beside and against the Law, and so impiously loosen the bonds of the Divine Law. Moses is plain in this passage, where he decrees that the soul of the one who drinks blood shall be cut off. Does he mean only the blood of the soul of the one who drinks? Yet he makes no mention of the blood of the soul. He speaks of blood in general, of any blood whatever. According to the mind of the rabbis, Moses in this passage, speaking generally of any blood, ought to have thundered not the penalty of excision (כרת), but the penalty of flagellation (מלקות). Yet we see the opposite done.

units.la: III. Ex Maimonide Curcellaeus probat, piscium sanguinem hoc interdicto non contineri. Et sane illorum non fit hic mentio, sed tantum עוף & בהמה Volucrium & bestiarum. Neque ritus mactationis piscium in lege traduntur. Et piscium collectio confertur cum mactatione ovium, & boum. Num. XI.22. Piscium igitur collectio sufficere videbatur. His rationibus videntur niti Seldenus & Curcellaeus. De locustis idem adfirmant. Obstare tamen videtur 1. quod Genes. IX.4. exceptio sanguinis fit, non tantum a carne bestiarum & volucrium, sed etiam piscium in aquis natantium, v.2.4. Eadem igitur ratione prohibita videtur piscium caro cum sanguine eorum, qua caro cum sanguine caeterorum animantium. 2. Quod discrimen munditiei & immunditiei etiam in piscibus notarum, Levit. XI.9.10. Hoc comedetis ex omnibus, quae sunt in aquis: Quod habet pinnas & squamas in aquis: tum per maria, tum in fluminibus illa comedetis. Quicquid quid vero non habet pinnas aut squamas, tum in fluminibus, ex omni reptili aquatico, denique ex omni animante, quae sunt in aquis, abominationi sunt vobis. 3. Locultas quas vocaverint Moses & Prophetae, non plane certum nobis est. Quis enim dissimulare potest tenebras & caliginem nostram circa nomina animalium Hebraeis usitata? 4. Cùm locustae, quocunque modo accipiantur, annumerari debeant animalibus commemoratis à Mose Genes. IX. 2. 3. à quibus excipit sanguinem vers. 4. clarum est, aequè illorum sanguinem illicitum, si modo sanguinem verum habent. Jam Curcellaei & Seldeni rationes quod attinet, non est ad eas responsu difficile. Non erat, cur hoc loco Moses piscium mentionem facerer. Nam agit de sanguine Sacrificiis destinato: & de notabili aliqua copia sanguinis. Pisces autem neque ad aram veniebant, neque pollent notabili aliqua copia sanguinis. Ritus quidem mactationis piscium nullibi exprimitur: Sed convenienti aliqua ratione sanguinem eximere potuerunt. Id quod sine mactatione fieri potuisse quis non intelligit? Neque piscium & locustarum אוסף collectio pro mactatione fuit. Certè loca allegata Num. XI. 22. Esaj. XXXIII. 4. id non evincunt. In priori congregatio piscium comparatur cum mactatione animalium. Sed in ipsa congregatio erat sufficiens ad esum praeparatio, ut non accederet religiosa cura ἀλαχείσεως inter mundos & immundos pisces, & illorum conveniens legi internecio? Alienum esse facile cognoscit, qui perpendit diligens examen Judaeorum secundum pinnas & squamas piscium. De quo vide R. Levi Barcel. ad praeceptum CL. Posterior locus Jesajae minus ad rem facit. Comparat Deus praedam hostium Christi cum אוסף הדסיל Collecta bruchorum. Jam hoc ipsum non caret dubitatione, utrum bruchi in lege mundi fuerint. Nam Rabbini octo species numerant טהור הגב locustarum, quae mundae sunt, inter quas nulla species est הדסיל bruchorum, quorum hic Jesajas meminit. Et locustas non omnes mundas fuisse colligitur ex lege Levit. XI. 22. Deinde אוסף הדסיל Collecta bruchorum dicitur non tam respectu esus & praeparationis ad illum, quam quia turmatim volare solent, atque ita etiam capi & occidi. Sic etiam facturum se grassanti hostium multitudini sub N. T. minatur Deus. Plinius testis, Lib. XI. 29. Propter fertilitatem hujus insecti aliquando in Syria homines militari imperio coactos prodiisse ad necandas locustas, & in Cyrenaica regione legem esse ter anno eas debellandi, primùm ova obterendo, deinde foetum, factum, posterme adulterio. Ex qua etiam noxia sterilitate factum, ut Principes Saxonici mandata typis excusa promulgarint, quibus subditos certo anni tempore ad collectas faciendas locustarum obstrinxerunt. Sed haec levia sunt. Dici tamen debuerunt, quia infirmis illis probationibus Judaeorum, detorsionibus locorum Scripturae, Curcellaeus aures hoc loco substrinxisse videtur.
units.tr: III. From Maimonides, Curcellaeus proves that the blood of fish is not included in this prohibition. And indeed no mention of them is made here, but only of birds and beasts (עוף ובהמה). Nor is a rite of slaughtering fish handed down in the Law. And the gathering of fish is compared with the slaughter of sheep and oxen (Num. 11:22). The gathering of fish therefore seemed sufficient. Selden and Curcellaeus seem to rest on these arguments. They affirm the same of locusts. Yet the following seems to stand in the way: 1. In Gen. 9:4 the exception of blood is made not only from the flesh of beasts and birds, but also from fish swimming in the waters (vv. 2, 4). By the same reasoning, therefore, the flesh of fish together with their blood seems forbidden, just as the flesh of other animals with their blood. 2. The distinction between clean and unclean is also noted among fish, Lev. 11:9–10: These you shall eat of all that are in the waters: whatever has fins and scales in the waters, both in the seas and in the rivers, these you shall eat. But whatever has no fins or scales, from every creeping thing of the waters, and from every living creature that is in the waters, shall be an abomination to you. 3. It is not entirely certain to us what locusts Moses and the Prophets meant. For who can deny that we are in darkness and fog about the names of animals used by the Hebrews? 4. Since locusts, however they are understood, must be counted among the animals mentioned by Moses in Gen. 9:2–3, from which he excludes blood in v. 4, it is clear that their blood is equally unlawful, if indeed they have true blood. As for the arguments of Curcellaeus and Selden, it is not difficult to answer them. There was no reason why Moses should mention fish in this place. For he is speaking of blood destined for sacrifices, and of a notable quantity of blood. Fish, however, were neither brought to the altar nor do they yield any notable quantity of blood. Indeed, the rite of slaughtering fish is nowhere expressed; but they could have drawn out the blood by some suitable method. Who does not understand that this could have been done without slaughter? Nor was the gathering (אוסף) of fish and locusts a slaughter. Certainly the passages cited (Num. 11:22; Isa. 33:4) do not prove it. In the first, the gathering of fish is compared with the slaughter of animals. But was the gathering itself sufficient preparation for eating, so that there would be no religious care to separate clean and unclean fish, and no suitable destruction of them under the Law? Anyone who weighs carefully the Jewish examination of fish by their fins and scales easily recognises that this is alien to the matter. The second passage of Isaiah bears less on the question. God compares the spoil of Christ's enemies with the gathering (אוסף הדסיל) of caterpillars. But even this is not free from doubt, whether caterpillars were clean under the Law. For the rabbis count eight kinds of locusts with a clean back (טהור הגב), among which there is no kind of caterpillar (הדסיל), which Isaiah mentions here. And that not all locusts were clean is gathered from the Law, Lev. 11:22. Then, the gathering of caterpillars (אוסף הדסיל) is spoken of not so much with respect to eating and preparation for it, as because they usually fly in swarms and so are also caught and killed in that way. So also God threatens to do to the swarming multitude of enemies under the New Testament. Pliny bears witness, Book 11, ch. 29: On account of the fertility of this insect, at one time in Syria men were forced by military command to go out to destroy locusts; and in the region of Cyrenaica there was a law to stamp them out three times a year, first by crushing the eggs, then the young, and afterwards the adults. Also from this harmful barrenness it came about that the Saxon princes issued mandates printed in type, by which they bound their subjects to gather locusts at a fixed time of the year. But these are trivial matters. Yet they had to be mentioned, because it seems that Curcellaeus, by means of these weak proofs and his twisting of passages of Scripture, has here dulled the ears of the Jews.

units.la: IV. Repetitur interdictum Levit. XVII.10, 11, 12, 13, 14.
units.tr: IV. The prohibition of Leviticus 17:10, 11, 12, 13, 14 is repeated.

units.la: Vir, qui comederit sanguinem, illi opponam iratam faciem meam, comedenti sanguinem, & excidam illum è medio populi mei. Nam quia anima cujusque carnis in sanguine est, idcirco destinavi vobis eum in altari, ad faciendam expiationem pro animabus vestris. Nam sanguis is est, qui pro anima expiationem fecerit. Ubi satis clara omnia. Explicatur etiam illud quod Genes. IX.4. בשר בנפשו דמו Nam hic perspicuè ponitur anima, id est, vita in sanguine. Audiamus explicantem Augustinum lib. II. contra adv. Legis & Proph. cap. 6. Sic, inquit, dictum est: Anima omnis carnis est sanguis, quomodo dictum est: Petra erat Christus, scilicet, non quia hoc erat, sed quia hoc significabatur. Non autem frustra lex voluit animam significare per sanguinem, rem scilicet invisibilem per visibilem: quia sanguis per venas omnes ab ipso corde diffusus, in nostro corpore plus caeteris humoribus principatur: ita ut ubicunque fuerit vulnus inflictum, non humor alius, sed ipse procedat: ita quoque anima, quia omnibus, quibus constamus invisibiliter praevalet. Hinc vetus adagium: Αἷμα καὶ ψυχὴ. Sanguis & anima, de re impensè nobis grata & adamata. Quomodo Antiphanes Comicus, Ἀργύ-ριον ἰσὺ αἷμα καὶ ψυχὴ βροτοῖς Argentum & anima & sanguis est mortalibus. Qua etiam ratione dicti sanguine carere timidi & nullius animi. Et Empedocles: Vim animi esse sanguinem circa praecordia. Eodem fere modo interdictum hoc conceptum est Deut. XII.16, 23. XV.23.
units.tr: "If any man eat blood, I will set my face against him that eateth blood, and will cut him off from among his people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul." All of this is quite clear. The statement in Genesis 9:4, בשר בנפשו דמו [basar benafsho damo], is explained in the same way, for there the soul, that is, the life, is plainly placed in the blood. Let us hear Augustine explaining it in Book II against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 6: "So it is said: 'The soul of every flesh is blood,' just as it is said: 'The rock was Christ,' that is, not because it was this, but because this was signified." The law wished the soul to be signified by the blood, an invisible thing by a visible one, and not without reason: because the blood, poured from the heart itself through all the veins, holds the first place in our body above the other humours, so that wherever a wound is inflicted it is not another humour but blood that flows out. So too the soul, because it prevails invisibly over all the parts of which we consist. Hence the old saying: "Αἷμα καὶ ψυχή" [haima kai psychē], blood and soul, a thing most pleasing and dear to us. So Antiphanes the comic poet: "Ἀργύριον ἰσὺ αἷμα καὶ ψυχὴ βροτοῖς" [argyrion esti haima kai psychē brotois], silver is blood and soul to mortals. For the same reason those who are timid and without spirit are said to lack blood. And Empedocles: the strength of the spirit is the blood about the heart. In much the same way this prohibition is framed in Deuteronomy 12:16, 23 and 15:23.

units.la: V. Jam de ratione praecepti Mosaïci. Contendo autem, non aliam à Mose exprimi, quàm typicam; nempe quia sanguis animalium loco vitae in aram venire debuit ad faciendam expiationem, ideo illicitus fuit ejus esus, videlicet ne Sacrificia profanarentur, & homines sibi vindicarent, quod Deus sibi eximium esse voluit ad significandam obligationem hominum, & figurandam substitutionem Christi. Ubi illud magnam vim habet, quòd Levit. XVII.11, occurrant rant particulæ relativæ כי & Vau, quia anima carnis est in sanguine, ideo dedi vobis illum in altari ad expiationem faciendam. Ut ita particula Vau illativa sit consequentis ex antecedenti: quia nempe anima stabulatur in sanguine & propitiatio animæ hic requiritur, ideo sanguis super altare eo officio defungatur. Quem usum habere aliquando in S.Scriptura illam particulam, notius est, quàm ut explicari debeat. Observavit hoc sapienter & accuratè Arabicus Interpres, qui ita habet: Quoniam anima carneorum omnium domicilium sanguis est, idcirco constitui illum vobis super altare, ut venia petatur per ipsum pro animabus vestris. Quæ versio perquam עשיתי est. Apostolus typicam hanc rationem expressit Hebr.IX.13.14. Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum & cinis juvenca aspergens inquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis puritatem: quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum se obtulit inculpatum Deo, purificabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, ut serviatis Deo viventi. Confer integrum illud caput nonum.
units.tr: V. Now on the reason for the Mosaic precept. I contend, however, that Moses expresses no reason other than a typical one: namely, that because the blood of animals had to come to the altar in place of life, to make atonement, its eating was therefore forbidden. The purpose was that sacrifices should not be profaned, and that men should not claim for themselves what God wished to be especially his, in order to signify the obligation of men and to foreshadow the substitution of Christ. Here it is of great weight that in Leviticus 17.11 the relative particles כי and ו occur: because the soul of the flesh is in the blood, therefore I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement. So the particle ו is inferential, marking a consequence from its antecedent: because the soul dwells in the blood, and the propitiation of the soul is required here, therefore the blood performs that office upon the altar. That the particle sometimes has this force in Holy Scripture is better known than needs explaining. The Arabic interpreter noticed this wisely and accurately, and his version reads: Since the blood is the dwelling-place of all flesh, I have therefore appointed it for you upon the altar, that pardon may be sought through it for your souls. This rendering is very close to the Hebrew [נתתיו]. The Apostle expressed this typical reason in Hebrews 9.13, 14: For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the unclean, sanctify to the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God. Compare that whole ninth chapter.

units.la: VI. Cæterum Maimonidis sententiam, quem contra Nachmanidem defendit Abarbanel, ut memorare hoc loco, ita in medio relinquere volumus.
units.tr: VI. Let us here mention, but leave undecided, the opinion of Maimonides, which Abarbanel defends against Nachmanides.

units.la: Scito, inquit, More Nevoch.III.46. quòd licet sanguis impurus & immundus admodum fuerit in oculis Zabiorum tamen ab illis comestus fuit, eò quòd existimarent, cibum hunc esse dæmonum: & quòd is, qui eum comedit, hac ratione communicationem aliquam cum dæmonibus acquirat, ita ut familiariter cum eo conversentur, & futura ei aperiant, prout vulgus ista dæmonibus attribuere solet. Fuerunt tamen quidam inter illos, quibus valde durum & difficile videbatur sanguinem comedere. Est enim res, à qua natura hominis abhorret. Hi mactantes bestiam aliquam, sanguinem ejus accipiebant, & in vase vel fossula colligebant: carnem verò mactatam circa illum sanguinem, in circulo sedentes comedebant, imaginantes sibi, in hoc opere, ipsis carnem comedentibus, Dæmones illum sanguinem comedere: & hunc ipsorum esse cibum, hócque medio amicitiam & fraternitatem & familiaritatem inter ipsos contrahi, quia omnes in una mensa edunt, & uno consessu accumbunt. Præterea opinabantur, Dæmones sibi in somno apparere, futura indicare, plurimúmque prodesse. Idcirco venit Lex Divina, qua perfectos reddit eos, qui norunt ipsam, ad auferendos istos inveteratos morbos, esum sanguinis prohibendo, & prohibitionem istam addita sanctione, plane ut in præcepto de idololatria, confirmando. De comedente enim sanguinem inquit Deus: Ponam faciem meam in comedentem sanguinem eodem modo, modo, quo deillo, qui filium suum Molocho immolat, Lev. XX.3. Ponam faciem meam in virum illum. Neque occurrit haec ratio loquendi in tertio aliquo praecepto, praeter ista duo, de idololatria & comestione sanguinis: quia illius comestio ad speciem aliquam idololatriae, Daemonum videlicet cultum, ansam & occasionem prabebat. Hactenus Maimonides. Cujus quidem rationes praeceptorum Ceremonialium, antiquitatis cerusa incrustatas, tanto a fide remotiores ducimus, quanto magis a Spirituali negotio τῆς ἐντυπάσεως τῶν μεθόντων discedunt; id quod subinde fieri constat. Ut cautos nos esse oporteat, ne illorum insidiis illaqueati a simplicitatis, & intentionis divinae tramite exorbitemus.
units.tr: Know, he says, in More Nevochim III.46: Although impure and very unclean blood was in the eyes of the Sabeans, nevertheless they ate it, because they thought it was the food of demons, and that whoever ate it thereby acquired some fellowship with demons, so that they would associate with him familiarly and reveal future things to him, as the common people are wont to attribute such things to demons. Yet there were some among them for whom eating blood seemed very hard and difficult, since it is a thing from which human nature shrinks. These, when they slaughtered some animal, took its blood and collected it in a vessel or small pit, and then, sitting in a circle, they ate the flesh slaughtered around that blood, imagining that in this act, while they ate the flesh, the demons ate that blood, and that this was their food, and that by this means friendship, brotherhood and familiarity were formed among them, because they all eat at one table and recline at one gathering. Moreover, they believed that demons appeared to them in sleep, foretold the future and were very helpful. Therefore the Divine Law came, which makes perfect those who know it, to remove these inveterate diseases, by forbidding the eating of blood and confirming that prohibition with an added sanction, just as in the precept about idolatry. For God says of the one who eats blood: I will set my face against the one who eats blood in the same way as against him who gives his son to Molech, Lev. XX.3: I will set my face against that man. Nor does this manner of speaking occur in any third precept besides these two, about idolatry and the eating of blood, because eating blood offered an occasion and opportunity for a certain kind of idolatry, namely the worship of demons. So far Maimonides. Yet we judge his reasons for the ceremonial precepts, encrusted with the wax of antiquity, to be the more remote from faith the more they depart from the spiritual business [τῆς ἐντυπάσεως τῶν μεθόντων], as is clearly sometimes the case. We ought therefore to be cautious, lest, ensnared by their traps, we wander from the path of simplicity and the divine intention.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Ex his, quae secundo loco diximus, prono alveo fluit, praeceptum Mosaicum pure Ceremoniale, non morale esse. Non habet enim aliam omnino rationem, quam typicam in cultu Israelitico. Ergo numerandum inter δικαιώματα λατρείας, per quae facta est ἀνάμνησις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν Hebr. IX.1. cum X.3, Id fortius etiam sic probatur. Si lex illa a Mose dictata non Ceremonialis, sed Moralis fuit, tum omnes homines in qualibet circumstantia obligavit. Nam quae Moralia sunt, & hactenus ad unum aliquod ex Decalogi praeceptis referuntur, illa omnibus hominibus lata esse, supra Curcellaeus confessus est. Atqui in illa periodo non omnes homines in qualibet circumstantia obligavit. Nam ab esu morticini, in quo sanguis fuit, solvit Legislator peregrinum in portis. Non comedes, inquit, morticinum, sed dabis illud peregrino in portis tuis, ut comedat illud, aut vendat peregrino, Deut. XIV.21. Quod tum Rabbini, tum Onkelosus intelligunt de גר תושב Proselytho domicilii, seu incircumciso, quem propterea vocat אוכל נבלה in Glossa Thalmud. ad Tit. Erakim c.7. quod nefas non esset illi morticina edere. Quin perspicue Seldenus illam sententiam, qua sanguinis esus Noachidis permissus, seu qua הותר הוא הדם מן sas esse decernitur eis edere sanguinem, etiam animalis viventis, plerumque fuisse apud Hebraeos receptissimam. Nec frangit vim probationis nostrae Curcellaeus, qui supra quasi anticipaturus reposuit, licuisse peregrino morticinum edere sanguine exempto & absterso. Si hoc verum, non video rationem, ob quam non aeque potuerint Israelitae morticinis probe abstersis & elotis vesci. Nam Legislator propter sanguinem in morticino permanentem illud prohibuit.
units.tr: From what we said in the second place, it follows easily that the Mosaic precept is purely ceremonial, not moral. It has no reason at all other than the typical one in Israelite worship. It must therefore be numbered among the ordinances of worship (δικαιώματα λατρείας) by which there is a remembrance of sins, Heb. 9:1 with 10:3. This is proved more strongly in this way. If that law, dictated by Moses, was not ceremonial but moral, then it bound all men in every circumstance. For those precepts that are moral, and so far as they are referred to one of the precepts of the Decalogue, were, as Curcellaeus has confessed above, given to all men. But in that passage it did not bind all men in every circumstance. For the Lawgiver releases the stranger within the gates from eating carrion, in which the blood remains. "You shall not eat carrion," he says, "but you shall give it to the stranger within your gates, that he may eat it, or sell it to a foreigner," Deut. 14:21. Both the rabbis and Onkelos understand this of the גר תושב [ger toshav], a proselyte of residence, that is, an uncircumcised man, whom for this reason the Gloss on the Talmud, tractate Eraqin ch. 7, calls אוכל נבלה [one who eats carrion], since it would not be unlawful for him to eat carcasses. Indeed Selden clearly shows that the opinion by which the eating of blood was permitted to the sons of Noah, that is, that they were allowed to eat blood, even of a living animal, was for the most part the most widely accepted among the Hebrews. Nor does Curcellaeus, who replied above as if anticipating us, that it was lawful for the stranger to eat carrion with the blood removed and drained, weaken the force of our proof. If this is true, I do not see why the Israelites could not equally have eaten carcasses properly drained and washed. For the Lawgiver forbade it because of the blood remaining in the carcass.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Hic in omnes partes se flectit Curcellaeus, ut quoquo modo ex labyrintho se explicet. Retexamus, quae subtiliter edisseruit. Noverat, quosdam distinguere inter praecepta Dei positiva & moralia. In illorum numero, non in horum esse praeceptum praesens. Rectam enim rationem non docere abstinentiam a sanguine, sed totum id pendere ex mera Dei prohibentis voluntate. Excipit 1. Male inter se confundi praeceptum Positivum & Ceremoniale, cum positivum latius pateat quam ceremoniale. Omne ceremoniale esse positivum, sed non vice versa. Hoc animadverti posse in gradibus consanguinitatis & affinitatis, qui conjugii impedimentum afferunt: item in polygamia & divortiis, aliisque ejusmodi rebus plurimis, quas Positivas esse constet, non ceremoniales. Ceremonias enim intelligi solos externos ritus ad cultum Dei pertinentes, quibus vel puritas Spiritualis, vel aliquid in Christo olim implendum adumbrabatur. p. 53. Resp. παλαιὰ π ν-μὴ, πελιά π λυγεί. Bene illud, Positivum non esse idem quod Ceremoniale. Illud est quodlibet jussum Dei, cujus ratio naturali ratione non cognoscitur. Hoc est species positivi, quod ἐαν habet vel ad significationem, vel ad ordinem Ecclesiasticum. Exempla utriusque obvia satis & expositi. Sed cur nobis hoc occinendum fuit? Non inde argumentamur, quia praeceptum hoc simpliciter positivum, sed quia positivum Ceremoniale primo modo, συμαντικὸν Christi. Sed illud nec micam sobrietatis habet, quod gradus consanguinitatis, qui jure divino matrimoniis impedimentum afferunt, & legem prohibitivam divortii & polygamiae a positivo Dei imperio derivat. De gradibus consanguinitatis, consentientes quidem habet Pontificios, quos operose inducunt Bell. l. de sacr. matr. tom. III. cap. XXVII. 14. 15. Gregorius de Valentia tom. 4. disp. 10. quaest. 5. punct. 3. Ut jam Syncretismus Curcellaei cum illis in propatulo sit. Atqui a naturali, non a positivo jure esse prohibitionem matrimoniorum in gradibus, argumento sunt multa. Ac praecipue illud, quod Gentes Cananaei praecepto illi obnoxii fuerunt, quos tamen non alterius legis quam naturalis copiam habuisse, certum & exploratum est. Idcirco ob praeceptorum illorum violationem Deo abominabiles fuerunt, Lev. XVIII. 24. 26. 27. Ne polluamini in omnibus illis, quibus contaminata sunt universa gentes, quas ego ejiciam ante conspectum vestrum, & quibus polluta est terra, cujus ego scelera visitabo. Quibus verbis non tantum graviora quatuor peccata, quorum mentio ibi facta, perstringi, ut Bellarminus vellet; sed etiam violatiolationem graduum prohibitorum, patet evidenter ex Lev. XX. 11. 12. 17. 19. Neque audiendus Grotius, qui in eodem Curcellaei luto haerens, ex Maimonide reperisse sibi duas causas harum rerum videtur: priorem naturalem quandam verecundiam, quae non sinat ortus auctores cum sua sobole, aut in se ipsis, aut etiam personas sanguine, aut nuptiali sanguinis commixtione proxime cohaerentes, mischeri: alteram vero, ne quarundam personarum convictus nimis quotidianus atque inobservatus, stupris & adulteriis occasionem daret, si amores tales possent nuptiis conglutinari.
