Et iccirco asserit: Communem illam existimationem a necessario naturae dictato originem non habuisse, sed a veteri traditione, de Jure Belli & Pacis II. v. 13. Si naturalis verecundia homines ab his gradibus abstinet, numquid igitur non naturali dictato restringuntur homines? Ipse Grotius supra l. 1. c. 11. monuit, legis moralis duplex indicium esse. Primum, si rationi conveniat, vel disconveniat aliquis actus. Alterum, si omnes moratiores aliquid in usu habeant. Si ob naturalem verecundiam gradus hi sunt prohibiti, annon quia contrarius actus disconvenit rationi? Et moratiores omnes gentes ab his gradibus abhorrent. Hinc Paulus de incesto homine, qui ducebat uxorem Patris: Talem incestum ne quidem inter gentiles nominari, 1. Cor. V. 1. Et si ex veteri traditione habuerunt positivum praeceptum, retro aliquot seculis promulgari debuit. Cujus promulgationis neque vola est, neque vestigium. Eadem ratio polygamiae & divortiorum. Nam naturalis sensus satis ea respicit: & abhorruerunt semper moratiores populi. Mallem igitur hic Curcellaeum se continuisse. Exempla multa alia in promtu erant. Sed sic intererat, dissensum suum & Spiritum antilogiae qualibet occasione testari. 2. Ubi agitur de obedientia, inquit, mandatis Dei exhibenda, necesse non est, scrupulose distinguere inter ea, quae juris sunt naturalis, & quae ad positivum pertinent. Illud enim aliquando est difficillimum, propter magnam, quae in quibusdam causis cernitur, inter utrumque jus differentiam. E. G. Utrum conjugium inter fratrem & sororem sit ex jure naturali illicitum, an vero tantum ex positivo. Nec tanti est momenti, ut aliqui putant, ista distinctia. Sufficit enim, ut de voluntate Dei bene simus edocti: de qua, ubi nobis constat, caeca, ut ita dicam, obedientia, absque haesitatione parendum est. pag. 54. Resp. Discrimen esse inter leges naturales & positivas voluntarias agnoscit Philosophus, lib. V. Ethicorum Nicom. cap. 1. & alibi saepius. Agnoscunt etiam Jurisconsulti apud Grotium de Jure Belli & Pacis l. 1. c. 1. ss. 13. 14. Sed & Moses perspicuè illud tradidit, qui toties distinguit inter מִשְׁפָּט jus constitutum naturæ, חֻקִּים ceremonias, & מִשְׁפָּטִים statuta forensia. De quo discrimine agit Maimonides More Nev. III. 26. Sed summum distinctionis illius usum, & parem necessitatem quis ignorare potest, paulò divini cultus & recti tenacior? Ejus neglectu factum saepius, ut Judæi praesentissimam & molestissimam Dei iram & indignationem provocarint. Quoties nempe supinè neglexerunt distinguere praecepta non bona, id est, non utilia & proficua ad justitiam, & bona. Ezech. XX. 25. 26, Misericordiam & sacrificia, Oseæ VI. 6. Matth. IX. 13; inter circumcisionem carnis & cordis, Deuteron. X. 16. inter res holocaustorum & praeceptum foederis, Jesaj. VII. 22. 23. Imo hac distinctione constat discrimen Judaismi & Christianismi. Illi enim ignorantes Dei justitiam & quaerentes suam justitiam propriam, intelligere illa δικαιώματα σαρκὸς, Deo substituere, Justitia Dei, non obedierunt, Rom. X. 3. An igitur non convenit hîc πνεῦμα λῶγον illam ἀληθειαν in consilio habere? Disparare praecepta foederis τῆς ἀληθείας à praeceptis accessoriis τῆς σκιᾶς? Quòd difficilis subinde est illa discretio, non ideirco discernenda non sunt, quae Deus discerni voluit, sed calculus spiritualis diligenter in eo ponendus. Et qui de voluntate Dei bene edoctus est, illi non potest obscurum esse, quid Deus maximè & validissimè fieri velit, quid debilitet nostram cum Deo communionem, quid cum eadem cohaerere possit. Hinc Apostolus conjungit τὴν χρηστὸν τῆς ἐλπίδος Θεοῦ, & τὴν ἀλλοφερόντων. Rom. II. 18.
units.tr: Here Curcellaeus turns himself in every direction, so that he may somehow extricate himself from the labyrinth. Let us unravel what he subtly argued. He knew that some distinguish between God's positive and moral precepts. The present precept, he says, belongs to the former class and not the latter. For right reason does not teach abstinence from blood, but all of this depends on the mere will of God forbidding it. He makes an exception: (1) "It is wrong to confuse a positive precept with a ceremonial one, since the positive extends more widely than the ceremonial. Every ceremonial precept is positive, but not vice versa. This can be noticed in the degrees of consanguinity and affinity, which present an impediment to marriage, and likewise in polygamy and divorces, and in many other things of this kind, which are clearly positive but not ceremonial. For by ceremonies we understand only the external rites pertaining to the worship of God, by which either spiritual purity or something to be fulfilled in Christ was foreshadowed." p. 53. Reply: παλαιὰ π ν-μὴ, πελιά π λυγεί [the old ... ]. He is right that positive is not the same as ceremonial. The former is any command of God whose reason is not known by natural reason. The latter is a species of the positive, which has to do either with a sign or with ecclesiastical order. Examples of both are obvious enough and have been set out. But why was this to be sung to us? We do not argue from this that the precept is simply positive, but that the ceremonial positive is of the first kind, a symbol of Christ. Yet his claim that the degrees of consanguinity, which by divine law hinder marriages, and the prohibition of divorce and polygamy, derive from the positive command of God, lacks all sobriety. Concerning the degrees of consanguinity, he indeed agrees with the Papists, whom Bellarmine, De sacramento matrimonii III, ch. 27, nn. 14-15, and Gregorio de Valencia, vol. 4, disp. 10, q. 5, punct. 3, laboriously lead in. Thus Curcellaeus's syncretism with them is plain to see. But there are many arguments that the prohibition of marriages within the degrees is from natural, not positive, law. Above all, the Canaanites were bound by that precept, and it is certain and well established that they had no other law than the natural one. Therefore they were abominable to God because of their violation of those precepts, Lev. 18:24-27: "Do not defile yourselves in any of these things, by which all the nations are defiled, which I will cast out before you, and by which the land is defiled, whose wickedness I will visit." By these words not only the four graver sins mentioned there are condemned, as Bellarmine would have it, but the violation of the forbidden degrees is also clearly shown from Lev. 20:11, 12, 17, 19. Nor should Grotius be heard, who, clinging to the same mire of Curcellaeus, seems to have found from Maimonides two causes of these things: the first a certain natural modesty, which does not allow authors of birth to mix with their own offspring, or with persons closely joined by blood or by the mixing of blood in marriage; the second, that the too daily and unguarded companionship of certain persons would give occasion for debauchery and adultery, if such loves could be cemented by marriage. And therefore he asserts: "That common opinion did not have its origin in a necessary dictate of nature, but in ancient tradition," On the Law of War and Peace II.v.13. If natural modesty restrains men from these degrees, are men therefore not restrained by a natural dictate? Grotius himself, in I.1.11, warned that there are two indications of the moral law: first, if an act agrees or disagrees with reason; second, if all more civilized peoples hold something in use. If these degrees are forbidden because of natural modesty, is it not because the contrary act disagrees with reason? And all the more civilized nations shrink from these degrees. Hence Paul, of the incestuous man who had his father's wife: "Such incest is not even named among the Gentiles," 1 Cor. 5:1. And if they had a positive precept from ancient tradition, it ought to have been promulgated some centuries back. Of such a promulgation there is neither trace nor vestige. The same reasoning applies to polygamy and divorces. For natural sense takes sufficient account of these, and more civilized peoples have always shrunk from them. I would therefore have preferred Curcellaeus to restrain himself here. Many other examples were at hand. But he wanted in this way to bear witness to his dissent and his spirit of contradiction on any occasion. (2) "Where it is a matter of obedience to be shown to the commands of God," he says, "it is not necessary to distinguish scrupulously between what belongs to natural law and what pertains to positive law. For the former is sometimes very difficult, because of the great difference that is seen in some cases between the two laws. For example, whether marriage between brother and sister is unlawful by natural law, or only by positive law." Nor is this distinction of such great importance, as some think. For it is enough that we are well taught about the will of God; where we know it, blind obedience, so to speak, is to be given without hesitation. p. 54. Reply: The Philosopher acknowledges a distinction between natural laws and positive voluntary laws, Nicomachean Ethics V.1 and elsewhere often. The jurists also acknowledge it, as Grotius cites, On the Law of War and Peace I.1.13-14. But Moses also taught it clearly, who so often distinguishes between מִשְׁפָּט [mishpat], law established by nature, חֻקִּים [chuqqim], ceremonies, and מִשְׁפָּטִים [mishpatim], forensic statutes. Maimonides treats of this distinction in More Nevochim III.26. But who can be ignorant of the supreme use of that distinction and its equal necessity, especially for those more strict about divine worship? By neglecting it, the Jews often provoked the most present and most grievous wrath and indignation of God. Whenever they carelessly failed to distinguish precepts that are not good, that is, not useful and profitable for righteousness, from those that are good: Ezek. 20:25-26; mercy and sacrifice, Hos. 6:6, Matt. 9:13; between circumcision of the flesh and of the heart, Deut. 10:16; between the things of burnt offerings and the precept of the covenant, Jer. 7:22-23. Indeed by this distinction the difference between Judaism and Christianity is established. For they, ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own righteousness, understood those ordinances of the flesh and substituted them for the righteousness of God; they did not obey it, Rom. 10:3. Should not a spiritual mind here take counsel with that truth? Should one not separate the precepts of the covenant of truth from the accessory precepts of the shadow? That this distinction is sometimes difficult does not mean that what God wanted to be distinguished should not be distinguished, but a spiritual reckoning must be diligently applied to it. And one who is well taught about the will of God cannot be unclear about what God wishes most strongly and most urgently to be done, what weakens our communion with God, and what can cohere with it. Hence the Apostle joins "the kindness of God's hope" and the "[things] of the others," Rom. 2:18.

units.la: IX. 3. Praeceptum Mosaicum, jam tempore Noachi latum morale tum fuisse, quia habuit additas duas rationes morales. Si igitur istud praeceptum non erat Ceremoniale, cum primò datum est, non evasisse tale, cum secundò repetitum fuit. pag. 55. Resp. Supra praeceptum Ceremoniale fuisse abundè comprobatum.
units.tr: IX. 3. The Mosaic precept was already a moral one when it was first given to Noah, because it had two moral reasons added. If therefore this precept was not ceremonial when it was first given, it did not become ceremonial when it was repeated a second time. p. 55. Reply: it has already been abundantly shown that the precept was ceremonial.

units.la: Simul ostensum, infirmam connexionem esse argumenti: Quod moralem habet rationem, illud morale est. Deinde unde nobis probat, Deum illa ratione, quia anima in sanguine, dominium suum magis stabilivisse, quàm significavisse vitam animalium sibi devovendam in sacrificiis & Sanctificationibus typicis? Hanc posteriorem interpretationem satis vindicavimus. 4. Accessisse huic praecepto aliquid ceremoniale, quale fuerit accurata & scrupulosa carnis ab omni sanguine expurgatio, quae Noacho non mandata. Exemplum esse in Saule 1.Sam.XIV.32.33. Quo pertineat multitudo regularum, quas posteriores Iudeorum magistri condiderunt. Secundo accessisse rationem novam, quia volebat Deus, ut sanguine victimarum expiatio fieret super altari pro ipsorum animabus. Sed aliam etiam rationem prohibitionis pure moralem ibi afferri, videlicet, quia anima in sanguine est, v.11. & 14. Ergo esse hoc praeceptum partim ceremoniale, partim morale, quemadmodum de Sabbatho & aliis quibusdam legalibus vulgo Theologi docent. pag. 56.57. Resp. Utriusque rei ceremonialis non est facta aliqua nova sub lege accessio, sed praecessit in limine mundi regenerati sanctio. In universum illis prohibetur esus omnis sanguinis. Igitur eo ipso mandata accurata sanguinis expurgatio a carne; eodem rigore praeceptum Noacho latum, quo sub Mose repetitum. Par ratio alterius. Non etiam Noacho ideo prohibuit, quia debuit in altari expiationem facere. Non est verisimile cum voluisse ejusmodi observantiam Noacho injungere, & tamen eum celare rationem illam ἐκπώσεως, quae apud Noachum & quemlibet fidelem utramque paginam facere potuisset. Bonitatis suae significationem Deus in eo edidit, quod iridem jussit esse Symbolum mundi non amplius diluvio inundandi. Et Ecclesiae, propter quam mundum conservat, invidisset Symbolum aliquod, quo admonita in spem erigerentur, praecedentium hominum peccata Messiae adventum non sufflaminatura? Imo in his ipsis verbis ceremonialis ratio implicata: quia vita in sanguine ejus. Quare supra evoluram dedimus. Proinde quod subjicit, moralem rationem etiam hic contineri v.11. & 14. ne hilum proficit. Et praeceptum hoc cum praecepto de Sabbatho nemo facile comparabit, qui inter utrumque discrimen vel leviter animadvertit. In Sabbatho morale fuit, quod Deo dicandus dies aliquis in septimana. Ceremoniale quod dies praecise septimus. In praesenti mandato quid simile? Morale, inquit, est, qua moralem rationem habet: Ceremoniale, qua ceremonialem. Ineptum. Praecepta enim non sunt determinanda ex addita ratione, sed ex fundamento praecipientis vel causae finalis. Sicut praeceptum de Sabbatho ex altera parte ideo morale, quia ratio naturalis praecepit: & altera parte ceremoniale, quia Deus libere mandavit hoc fine, ut ordini Ecclesiastico Israelitarum inserviat.
units.tr: At the same time it has been shown that the connection of the argument is weak: what has a moral reason is moral. Further, from where does he prove to us that God, by that reason, namely that the soul is in the blood, established his dominion more firmly than he signified that the lives of animals were to be devoted to him in sacrifices and typical sanctifications? I have sufficiently vindicated the latter interpretation. 4. He says something ceremonial was added to this precept, such as the careful and scrupulous cleansing of the flesh from all blood, which was not commanded to Noah. The example is in 1 Sam. 14:32-33. To this belongs the multitude of rules which the later teachers of the Jews drew up. Secondly, a new reason was added, because God willed that atonement be made by the blood of the victims upon the altar for their souls. But he says that another, purely moral reason for the prohibition is also given there, namely, because the soul is in the blood, vv. 11 and 14. Therefore this precept is partly ceremonial, partly moral, just as the theologians commonly teach concerning the Sabbath and certain other legal matters. pp. 56-57. Reply: no new ceremonial addition was made to either matter under the law; rather, the sanction had already come forth at the threshold of the regenerated world. In general, the eating of all blood is forbidden to them. Therefore by that very fact the careful cleansing of the flesh from blood was commanded, and the precept was given to Noah with the same strictness with which it was repeated under Moses. The same reasoning holds for the other reason. Nor did God forbid it to Noah on the ground that he was to make atonement on the altar. It is not likely that he wished to enjoin such an observance on Noah and yet hide from him that reason of expiation, which could have made both pages clear to Noah and to every believer. God displayed his goodness in this, that he commanded the rainbow to be a sign that the world would no longer be flooded by a deluge. And would he have denied the Church, for whose sake he preserves the world, some sign by which, once admonished, it might be raised to hope, and which would not hinder the sins of the earlier people from the coming of the Messiah? Indeed, in these very words a ceremonial reason is involved: because the life is in its blood. Wherefore we have given the explanation above. Therefore what he adds, that a moral reason is also contained here in vv. 11 and 14, avails nothing at all. And no one who has noticed even slightly the difference between the two will easily compare this precept with the precept about the Sabbath. In the Sabbath the moral element was that some day of the week was to be dedicated to God; the ceremonial was that it was precisely the seventh day. What is similar in the present command? It is moral, he says, because it has a moral reason; ceremonial, because it has a ceremonial reason. Absurd. For precepts are not to be determined from the reason added, but from the foundation of the one commanding or from the final cause. Thus the precept about the Sabbath is moral on one side, because natural reason dictates it, and ceremonial on the other, because God freely commanded it for this end, that it serve the ecclesiastical order of the Israelites.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Curcellæi & Becmanni objectiones solvuntur. Objectio prima ab addita promissione & comminatione præcepti. Pœna כרת sive excidii. Faciem ponere contra aliquem. Refellitur Maimonides. 1. Objectio secunda de peregrinis, qui prohibiti sanguinem edere. Proselythus justitiæ à Maimonide descriptus. Peregrini habitationis. Probatur, Moses Levit. XVII. intelligisse proselythos circumcisos. Frantzius & Grotius in ordinem redacti. 2. Probatur quinque rationibus, Sacrificia à proselytho habitationis offerri non potuisse. 3. Abusus distinctionis proselythi justitiæ & domicilii tangitur. גר non semper notat proselytum justitiæ. Locus Exod. XXII. 21. explicatus. Mercerus ad partes vocatus. גר תושב vocatus non nisi proselytus justitiæ. Proselytus שכירים. 4. Becmanni rationes solvuntur.5.
units.tr: The objections of Curcellaeus and Becmann are answered. The first objection is drawn from the promise and threat attached to the precept. The penalty of cutting off (כרת), or excision. To set one's face against someone. Maimonides is refuted. (1.) The second objection concerns the strangers who were forbidden to eat blood. The proselyte of righteousness as described by Maimonides. Strangers of residence. It is shown from Lev. 17 that Moses meant circumcised proselytes. Franzius and Grotius are brought into order. (2.) It is proved by five arguments that sacrifices could not be offered by a proselyte of residence. (3.) The misuse of the distinction between proselyte of righteousness and proselyte of residence is touched on. The word גר does not always denote a proselyte of righteousness. The passage Exod. 22:21 is explained. Mercerus is called to account. The one called גר תושב is none other than a proselyte of righteousness. The proselyte of hired servants. (4.) Becmann's arguments are answered.5.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: IAm audiamus pro morali mandato operosè concertantes. Curcellæus duo argumenta habet. Celeberrimus Becmannus quatuor. Sigillatim ad libellam veritatis applicabimus. Curcellæus primò: Præceptum hoc morale esse indicant, cùm singularis benedictio illud observantibus promissa: tum gravissima pœna transgressoribus ejus denuntiata, quarum similes præceptis ceremonialibus simul appositas non facilè invenies. De prima Deut. XII. 23. 24. 25. Hoc solùm cave ne comedas, &c. Ut bene sit tibi & Filiis tuis post te, cùm feceris quod placet in conspectu Domini. De secunda Lev. XVII. 10. Homo quilibet de domo Israel, & de advenis, qui peregrinantur inter vos, si comederit sanguinem, obsirmabo faciem meam contra animam illius, & disperdam illum de populo suo. Hic Maimonidem annotare, quoad phrasin illam: firmabo faciem meam contra animam illius, illam non occurrere in tertio aliquo præcepto, præter illa duo, de idololatria & comestione sanguinis. More Hannov. §.46. Prohibitionem autem idololatriae ad cultum Dei moralem pertinere, omnes fateri. pag.57.58. Eandem rationem urget Becmannus. Resp. 1. Omnia praecepta Dei, tam Ceremonialia quàm Morália, habent adjunctam promissionem benedictionis, si custodiantur, comminationem maledictionis, si iis contraveniatur. Generalis benedictio, vel maledictio subalternatim praeceptis Dei annexa, satis testatur serium Dei propositum. De foedere typico patet ex Deut.XXVI.17.18.19. Hodie tibi praecipit Deus, ut facias את החקים ואת המשפטים statuta Dei & judicia, (quorum illud de ritibus, hoc de civilibus praeceptis usitatè in Scripturis accipitur) & custodias ea, vel facias ea ex toto corde. Jussisti Deum, & ab ipso stipulatus es sponsionem, fore tibi in Deum; &c. Quae est excellentior benedictionis promissio, quàm esse in Deum populo servanti mandata? Quae promissio ipsi Abrahamo in foedere facta Genes.XVII.7. Ipsa moralia Dei praecepta non semper explicitam promissionem vel comminationem adjunctam habent. Sufficiebat legislatori in genere poenam violanti, & custodienti mercedem comitem adjungere. Qui facit ea homo, vivet in eis, Levit.XVIII.5. Maledictus, qui non servaverit verba legis hujus, Deut.XXVII. Neque specialiter hae conditiones praeceptis singulis applicantur. 2. Non desunt praecepta purè ceremonialia, quae Deus pari terrore munivit. Circumcisionem quanto Deus serio Abrahamidis injunxit? Masculus, cujus praeputii caro circumcisa non fuerit, delebitur anima illa de populo suo, quia pactum meum irritum fecit, Genes.XVII.14. Praeceptum de panibus fermentatis tempore Paschatis, donec circumageretur septem dierum orbis, non edendis, Deus gravissima oratione sanxit, Exod.XII.15. Qui fermentatos panes edit intra septem dierum spatium, ejus anima excindetur. Eadem gravitate Deus interdixit esum adipis, quâ esum sanguinis, Levit.VII.15. Quisquè comederit adipem ex iis jumentis, à quibus offert homo igne absumendum, utique excindetur homo ille, qui comederit à populis suis. Nulla gravior poena fuit, quàm כרת sive excidii. Per illam enim לא היה לעובר מיתה אבל אם מת בחטאו לו יהיה לו חלק לעולם הבא non quidem transgressori mors infligebatur, sed si peccato suo moriatur, non poterat particeps fieri futuri seculi, apud R. Mosen in tractatu de numero praeceptorum ad fund. 14. Quin idem docet Praef. in Mischnajoth שכל דבר שמיבין על זדונו כרת חייבין על שגגתו omnia, quae fiant proterve & superbè, mereri poenam excidii: si per errorem fiant, obligationem incurrere offerendi sacrificium pro peccato. Quo respexit spexit Apostolus Hebr. X. 26. 27. Hactenus igitur etiam præceptum de non comedenda adipe, & si quæ similia, moralibus deputanda fuerint. 4. In phrasi, faciem obscurare, vel povere contra aliquem, agnoscEt crisin Maimonidis. Sed soliditatem desidero. Significat iram Dei inflammatissimam, quâ succensus Deus ad excidium impiorum procedit. Scripturæ phrasi illa utuntur non tantùm in detestatione idololatriæ & ἀιματοφασίας, sed etiam in detestatione cuiuslibet prævaricationis insolentis. Hinc Deus Levit. XXVI. ubi severè prohibet idololatriam, profanationem Sabbathi & Sanctuarii, & contra mandat observantiam omnium mandatorum, rituum ac statutorum Dei, subjicit v. 14. 15. 16. Quòd si non auscultabitis mihi, neque facietis omnia mandata ista, si inquam, statuta mea spernatis, & judicia mea fastidiatis animâ vestrâ, ut non faciatis omnia mandata, & irritum faciatis foedus meum, oppönam vobis faciem iracundam, ut cadatis coram inimicis vestris. Et in genere David Psalm. XXXIV. 17. Facies Domini adversus facientes malum, ad exscindendum memoriam eorum è terrâ. Sed esto, comperat ista phrasis in simliam idololatriam & ἀιματοφασίαν, an ideo parem necessitatem vel turpitudinem moralem habent? An Deus non potest eâdem formulâ imprecationis incessere scelera, quæ vehementer tamen disparant? Ipse Curcellæus nobis supra largius est, Noachidas remotiores ἀιματοφασίας poenam non incurrisse, si ejus memoria ipsis integra non fuerit, quia naturali lumine hæc res cognosci non potuerit. De idololatria idem dici potest. Agnoscat igitur notorium discrimen.
units.tr: Let us now hear them, working hard against the moral character of the command. Curcellaeus has two arguments; the very famous Becmann has four. We will apply them one by one to the scales of truth. Curcellaeus first: They indicate that this precept is moral, since a particular blessing is promised to those who observe it, and the most grievous penalty is threatened against those who transgress it, and you will not easily find similar threats attached to ceremonial precepts. On the first, see Deut. 12:23–25: "Only take care that you do not eat," etc., "that it may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is pleasing in the sight of the Lord." On the second, Lev. 17:10: "Any man of the house of Israel, and of the strangers who sojourn among you, if he eats blood, I will set my face against that soul and will cut him off from among his people." Here I note, with regard to that phrase, "I will set my face against that soul," that it does not occur in any third precept apart from those two, concerning idolatry and the eating of blood (in the manner of the Hanover edition), §46. But that the prohibition of idolatry belongs to the moral worship of God, all admit," pp. 57–58. Becmann presses the same argument. I answer: (1.) All the precepts of God, both ceremonial and moral, have attached to them a promise of blessing if they are kept and a threat of curse if they are violated. The general blessing or curse, joined alternately to God's precepts, sufficiently witnesses to God's serious purpose. That this holds of the typical covenant is clear from Deut. 26:17–19: "Today the Lord commands you to do the statutes and the judgments (את החקים ואת המשפטים) of God" (of which the former is commonly understood of ritual precepts and the latter of civil precepts in the Scriptures), "and to keep them, or to do them, with all your heart. You have caused the Lord to be your God, and have stipulated with him a pledge that he will be your God," etc. What promise of blessing could be more excellent than to be a people of God who keep his commands? This is the very promise made to Abraham in the covenant, Gen. 17:7. The moral precepts of God themselves do not always have an explicit promise or threat attached. It was enough for the lawgiver, in general, to add a penalty for the one who violates and a reward for the one who keeps: "The man who does them shall live by them," Lev. 18:5; "Cursed is he who does not keep the words of this law," Deut. 27. Nor are these conditions applied specially to each individual precept. (2.) There are not lacking purely ceremonial precepts which God fortified with equal terror. How seriously did God enjoin circumcision on the seed of Abraham? "The uncircumcised male, whose flesh of the foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant," Gen. 17:14. The precept about leavened bread during the Passover, not to be eaten until the seven-day cycle was complete, God sanctioned with the most grievous words, Exod. 12:15: "Whoever eats leavened bread within the seven days, that soul shall be cut off." With equal gravity God forbade the eating of fat as he forbade the eating of blood, Lev. 7:25: "Whoever eats the fat of those animals from which man offers a fire offering to the Lord, that person shall be cut off from his people who eats it." No penalty was graver than כרת, or excision. For, as R. Moses says in his treatise on the number of precepts, on fundamental principle 14, "the transgressor was not subject to death, but if he died in his sin, he could not share in the future world." Indeed the same is taught in the preface to the Mishnah (Mischnajoth): "Everything done presumptuously and in pride deserves the penalty of excision; if done through error, one incurs the obligation of offering a sacrifice for sin." The Apostle looked to this in Heb. 10:26–27. So far, therefore, the precept about not eating fat, and any similar ones, must be counted among the moral precepts. (3.) In the phrase to darken the face, or to set the face against someone, I recognize the judgment of Maimonides. But I want solidity. It signifies the most inflamed wrath of God, by which God, kindled, proceeds to the destruction of the wicked. Scripture uses that phrase not only in detestation of idolatry and ἀιματοφασία (blood-speaking, i.e. the eating of blood) [ἀιματοφασίας], but also in detestation of any insolent transgression. Hence God, in Lev. 26, where he severely forbids idolatry and the profanation of the Sabbath and the sanctuary, and on the contrary commands the observance of all the commandments, rites and statutes of God, adds in vv. 14–16: "But if you do not listen to me, and do not do all these commandments, if, I say, you despise my statutes and loathe my judgments with your soul, so that you do not do all the commandments and break my covenant, I will set my angry face against you, so that you fall before your enemies." And in general David, Psalm 34:17: "The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth." But grant that this phrase occurs in the case of idolatry and ἀιματοφασία alike; do they therefore have an equal necessity or moral baseness? Can God not attack with the same formula of imprecation crimes which nevertheless differ greatly? Curcellaeus himself, further above, has granted us at greater length that the more remote Noachides did not incur the penalty for ἀιματοφασία, if the memory of it had not been preserved for them, because this matter could not have been known by the natural light. The same can be said of idolatry. Let him therefore acknowledge the notorious difference.

units.la: II. Altera ipsi ratio: Peregrinis inter Israelitas in terrâ Canaan versantibus, prohibitum fuisse, ne sanguine vescerentur, Levit. XVII. 10. Quicunque è familia Israelis aut è peregrina gente, quæ habitat inter eos, sanguine vescetur, &c. Mos enim ad solorum moralium præceptorum, aut quæ Noachi posteris data sunt, observationem obligatos fuisse: imo cæremonialia omnia iis custodire non licuisse. Hinc de Paschate Deus dicit: Omnis alienigena non comedet ex eo, Exod. XII. 4. 3. & in Thalmude tit. Sanhedrim: Paganum qui observaverit legem, esse mortis reum. Ergo intelliguntur hoc morale, non cæremoniale fuisse. p. 58. Resp. Distinguendum inter peregrinos seu Proselythos, qui origine Gentiles quocunque modo cum Israelitis coluerant. Alii ita peregrini fuerunt apud Israelitas, ut tamen Israelitarum religionem suscipe-rent, quam auspicabantur circumcisionis Sacramento, Baptismo Sacrificio. Ac propterea obligati fuerunt ad νόμον ἐντολῶν ὧν δόγμα-ta. Quomodo Apostolus dicit, Gal. V.3. Testificor omni homini circumci-denti se, quoniam debitor est legis universa facienda. Audiamus R. Mosen in tractatu Isure Biah: וכן לדורות כשירצה הגר ליכנס לברית ולהסתופף תחת כנפי השכינה ויקבל עליו עול תורה צדיק מילה וטפילה והוצאת קרבן ואם נקבה היא טבילה יקרבן כנאמר ככם גרו:
units.tr: II. His other argument: It was forbidden to the strangers living among the Israelites in the land of Canaan that they eat blood, Lev. 17:10: "Whoever of the house of Israel, or of the foreign people who dwell among them, eats blood," etc. For it is clear that they were bound only to the observance of the moral precepts, or those given to the sons of Noah; indeed, it was not lawful for them to keep any of the ceremonial precepts. Hence God says of the Passover, "No foreigner shall eat of it," Exod. 12:43, 45; and in the Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin: "A pagan who keeps the law is liable to death." Therefore it is understood that this was moral, not ceremonial. p. 58. I answer: one must distinguish between strangers, or proselytes, who by origin were Gentiles and who had in some way dwelt with the Israelites. Some were strangers among the Israelites in such a way that they nevertheless took up the religion of the Israelites, which they began by the sacrament of circumcision, baptism and sacrifice. And therefore they were bound to the νόμος ἐντολῶν ὧν δόγματα [the law of commandments consisting in decrees]. As the Apostle says, Gal. 5:3: "I testify to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law." Let us hear R. Moses in the treatise Isure Biah: "And so for generations: when a stranger wishes to enter into the covenant and to take shelter under the wings of the Shekhinah, and to accept upon himself the yoke of the Torah, he is a righteous proselyte: circumcision, and immersion, and the bringing of a sacrifice; and if it is a woman, immersion and the bringing of a sacrifice, as it is said, 'As you are, so the stranger shall be'" [וכן לדורות כשירצה הגר ליכנס לברית ולהסתופף תחת כנפי השכינה ויקבל עליו עול תורה צדיק מילה וטפילה והוצאת קרבן ואם נקבה היא טבילה יקרבן כנאמר ככם גרו].

units.la: Sic perpetuo cùm Ethnicus vult cooptari in foedus, & conquiescere sub alis Divinae Majestatis, submittendo se jugo legis, debet circumcidi, & baptizari, & offerre sacrificium. Quòd si sit foemina, debet baptizari & offerre Sacrificium juxta illud, Num. XV.15. Sicut vos, sic proselytus erit. Hi vocati גרי צדק peregrini justitiae, & גרי גרורים peregrini spontanei, qui sponte & salutis suae ac Gloriae Dei studio incitati religionem Judaeorum adoptarunt. Alii fuerunt peregrini habitationis גרי תושב quibus concessa inter Judaeos habitatio. Hi catenus fidem Judaicam profitebantur, quatenus idololatriae renuntiarunt, & se ad observantiam praeceptorum Noë obstrinxerunt. De caetero praeputiati manserunt. Vide Maimonidem in eod. tract. cap. 14. ubi dicit, ejusmodi Gentiles recipi כחשידי אומות עולם tanquam unum e piis Gentilibus mundi, & vocari inquilinum לפי שמותר לנו להשיבו בינינו בארץ ישראל quia, inquit, licet nobis dare illi locum habitationis inter nos in terra Israel. Jam anquiritur: Utros intellexerit Moses, proselythos per גרי בתוכם peregrinos in medio illorum? An peregrinos justitiae, an habitationis? Circumcisos, an incircumcisos? Si incircumcisos, sive proselythos habitationis Moses intellexit, causâ cecidimus. Contra autem pertendo: Mosen de proselythis circumcisis, non praeputiatis agere, 1. Quia proselythi praeputiati per legem non prohibiti sunt edere morticina, Deut. XIV.21. Unde per periphrasin proselythi illi incircumcisi Judaeis dicti אוכלי נבילות edentes morticina. Morticina autem non sunt sine sanguine, sed propter sanguinem non expurgatum Judaeis illicita fuerunt. 2. Suadet phrasis in eo loco adhibita גר ותושב peregrinus peregrinans; quae multiam de praeputiato occurrit. 3. De iisdem peregrinis sermo est Mosi versu decimo, ubi sanguinis esum lege refrænat, de quibus agit versu octavo & nono, ubi agit de holocausto ad portam tentorii conventus adducendo. Nam utrinque eodem modo & iisdem verbis legum de Sacrificio & esu sanguinis subjectum recipiens statuuntur Israe-lita litæ & peregrini in medio illorum. Atqui peregrini in medio Israelitarum, qui ritum sacrificandi docentur, non sunt peregrini praeputiati sed circumcisi. Hoc jam firmissimè probandum suscipio, ut eadem operâ demonstrem errorem noxium Wolphgangi Franzii & Hugonis Grotii. Quorum ille, paradoxo suo de universali vocatione velificatus, in Schola Sacrificiorum disp. IX. Thesi 26.32. contendit, peregrinos inter Israelitas peregrinantes & holocausta offerentes Levit. XVII.8.9. & Num.XV.14.15.16. fuisse Gentiles praeputiatos. Hic affini amore de salvatis etiam extraneis jugum legis Mosaicæ non subeuntibus, statuit: extraneis, qui alunde advenerant, & institutis Hebraicis non subjiciebantur, in templo Hierosolymitano victimas offerre licuisse. de jure Belli & Pacis II.16.
units.tr: Thus, always, when a Gentile wishes to be admitted into the covenant, and to rest under the wings of the Divine Majesty, submitting himself to the yoke of the law, he must be circumcised, and baptized, and offer a sacrifice. But if it is a woman, she must be baptized and offer a sacrifice, according to Num. 15:15: "As you are, so the proselyte shall be." Those called גרי צדק [proselytes of righteousness], peregrini justitiae (proselytes of righteousness), and גרי גרורים [proselytes of spontaneous choice], peregrini spontanei, who, moved by their own will and by zeal for their salvation and the glory of God, adopted the religion of the Jews. Others were strangers of residence, גרי תושב, to whom residence among the Jews was granted. These professed the Jewish faith only so far as they renounced idolatry and bound themselves to the observance of the precepts of Noah. In other respects they remained uncircumcised. See Maimonides in the same treatise, chapter 14, where he says that such Gentiles are received כחשידי אומות עולם [as one of the pious Gentiles of the world], and are called inhabitants, because, he says, it is lawful for us to give them a place of residence among us in the land of Israel. Now the question arises: which of these did Moses mean by the גר בתוכם, the stranger in the midst of them? Proselytes of righteousness, or of residence? Circumcised, or uncircumcised? If Moses meant uncircumcised proselytes, or proselytes of residence, I have lost the case. But I contend on the contrary that Moses is speaking of circumcised proselytes, not uncircumcised. (1.) Because uncircumcised proselytes were not forbidden by the law to eat carrion, Deut. 14:21. Hence by periphrasis those uncircumcised proselytes were called by the Jews אוכלי נבלות, eaters of carrion. But carrion is not without blood; it was forbidden to the Jews on account of the unpurged blood. (2.) The phrase used in that place, גר ותושב, stranger sojourning, suggests this; it occurs many times with reference to the uncircumcised. (3.) Moses is speaking of the same strangers in verse 10, where he restrains the eating of blood by law, and of whom he treats in verses 8 and 9, where he deals with bringing a burnt offering to the door of the tent of meeting. For in both places, in the same way and with the same words, the Israelites and the strangers in their midst are established as the subject of the laws concerning sacrifice and the eating of blood. But strangers in the midst of the Israelites, who are taught the rite of sacrificing, are not uncircumcised strangers but circumcised ones. I undertake to prove this most firmly now, so that at the same time I may demonstrate the harmful error of Wolfgang Franzius and Hugo Grotius. Franzius, sailing on his paradox of a universal calling, in his Schola Sacrificiorum, disp. 9, theses 26 and 32, contends that the strangers who sojourned among the Israelites and offered burnt offerings, Lev. 17:8–9 and Num. 15:14–16, were uncircumcised Gentiles. Here, from a related love of saved foreigners who did not submit to the yoke of the Mosaic law, he lays down: it was lawful for foreigners, who had come from elsewhere and were not subject to the Hebrew institutions, to offer victims in the temple at Jerusalem. On the Law of War and Peace, II.16.

units.la: III. Nimirum sanè illos ratio fugit. Nam 1. Gentiles decretorio Dei judicio ab Ecclesia rejectos & excommunicatos esse circa illud tempus, quo Israelitæ legitimâ Reipublicæ alicujus formâ conglutinati, jam supra perspicuè probavimus. Illa autem ἀνύγλωσσα, à fœdere & pactis Dei excludi & arceri, & simul Sacrificiorum cultu defungi posse, cùm tamen in illa potissimum lege Sacrificiorum, tanquam νόμῳ ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν, constituerit inimicitiam, quæ viguit tantisper, donec Christus eam in sua carne abolearet, Eph.II.14.15. Neque ulla potuit esse communio justitiæ & injustitiæ, lucis & tenebrarum, Christi & Belialis, fidelis & infidelis, vel consensio Templi Dei & Dæmoniorum, 2.Cor.VI.14.15.16. Quomodo igitur Gentiles præputiati, alieni à fœdere Dei, & ambulantes secundum seculum hujus mundi in præcipua parte cultus, qui habent typum futurorum bonorum, puta in altari cum Judæis convenire potuerunt? 2. Quia hic impetus Gentilium, Deo holocausta parantium à Judæis retundi debuit. Quod ubi ipsorum supinitate & negligentia desuper habitum, Deus illos gravissimè punivit. Huc pertinet illa Dei expostulatio, & severa interminatio de non introducendis in Sanctuarium iis, qui incircumcisi essent carne. Ezech.XLIV.9.10. &c. Sic ait Dominus, Nullus alienigena præputiatus corde, & præputiatus carne, veniet ad Sanctuarium meum: nullus, inquam, alienigena, qui sit inter filios Israelis, &c. 3. Maimonides, cujus suffragium hoc loco approbat Curcellaus, in tractatu de Regibus testatur, Gentilem præputiatum legi vacantem, reum esse mortis. Verba sunt גוי שעסק בתורה חייב מיתה לא יעסוק אלא בשבע במצות שלוש Gentilis, qui legi vacat, reus est mortis: ne vacet, nisi septem suis praeceptis tantum. Et pergit. Non tolerantur Gentiles novam legem introducere, sibique suo ingenio praecepta statuere. Verum Proselyti justitiae fieri debent, & ad omnia praecepta se adstringere, aut in lege sua debent manere nihil addendo aut detrahendo. 4. Moses Num. XV. 15. hunc peregrinantem inter Israelitas cum ipsis Israelitis comparat: Sicut vos, sic proselytus erit. Quae verba R. Mose in Tractatu Iure Biah sic explicat: Quemadmodum vos circumcisi estis, & baptizati, et offertis sacrificium, sic Proselytus ille, sive peregrinus in medio vestri debet circumcidi, baptizari & Sacrificium offerre. 5. Sacrificio Paschali non potuit vesci praeputiatus. Sic enim Deus: Quod si peregrinabitur apud te peregrinus, qui facere voluerit Pascha Jehova, circumciditur ei omnis mas, tunc demum accedito ad faciendum ipsum, & esto sicut ipse indigena terrae: at nullus praeputiatus vescitur illo. Ubi simul declaratam videmus formulam illam, Erunt sicut vos, de necessitate circumcisionis suscipiendae. Eadem autem hactenus fuit caeterorum sacrificiorum ratio, quae paschalis. Ex quibus rationibus ad liquidum perduco, Sacrificia a proselytho habitationis offerri non potuisse. Fuerit igitur peregrinus ille, cui prohiberur esus sanguinis peregrinus justitiae & circumcisus, aeque atque ille, cui sacrificiorum offerendorum facultas negatur Levit. XVII. 8. 9. 10.
units.tr: III. Surely they overlook this, to be sure. For, first, we have already shown clearly above that the Gentiles were rejected and excluded from the Church by God's decisive judgment at the time when the Israelites were bound together under some lawful form of commonwealth. That is an empty thing [ἀνύγλωσσα], to be shut out and barred from the covenant and promises of God, and at the same time to be allowed to take part in the worship of the sacrifices. Yet in that very law of sacrifices, as a law of commandments contained in ordinances [νόμῳ ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν], he set up an enmity which was to last only until Christ abolished it in his flesh (Eph. 2:14-15). Nor could there be any fellowship of righteousness and unrighteousness, of light and darkness, of Christ and Belial, of believer and unbeliever, or any agreement between the temple of God and idols (2 Cor. 6:14-16). How, then, could uncircumcised Gentiles, aliens from the covenant of God and walking according to the course of this world, meet with the Jews at the altar, in the chief part of the worship which had the type of the good things to come? Second, this zeal of the Gentiles in preparing burnt offerings to God ought to have been checked by the Jews. When they, through their own laziness and negligence, failed to do this, God punished them most severely. To this belongs that complaint of God and his stern threat against bringing into the sanctuary those who were uncircumcised in flesh (Ezek. 44:9-10, etc.): "Thus says the Lord: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall come into my sanctuary; no foreigner, I say, who is among the sons of Israel, etc." Third, Maimonides, whose authority Curcellaeus here approves, testifies in his treatise on kings that an uncircumcised Gentile who occupies himself with the Law deserves death. His words are: "A Gentile who occupies himself with the Law deserves death; he may occupy himself only with the seven precepts" [גוי שעסק בתורה חייב מיתה לא יעסוק אלא בשבע במצות שלוש]. And he goes on: "Gentiles are not permitted to introduce a new law or to set up precepts for themselves by their own ingenuity. But proselytes of righteousness must be made, and must bind themselves to all the precepts, or they must remain in their own law, adding nothing and taking nothing away." Fourth, Moses in Num. 15:15 compares this sojourner among the Israelites with the Israelites themselves: "As you are, so shall the proselyte be." Rabbi Moses explains these words in his tractate Yevamot thus: "Just as you have been circumcised and baptized and offer sacrifice, so that proselyte or stranger must be circumcised, baptized in your midst, and offer sacrifice." Fifth, an uncircumcised man could not eat of the Passover sacrifice. For God says: "If a stranger sojourn with you and want to keep the Passover of the LORD, every male of his shall be circumcised; then let him come near to keep it, and he shall be as a native of the land; but no uncircumcised person may eat of it." Here we see that formula, "they shall be as you," declared to demand the necessity of taking up circumcision. The rule for the other sacrifices was the same as for the Passover. From these arguments I clearly conclude that sacrifices could not be offered by a proselyte of residence. That stranger, then, who is forbidden to eat blood, must be a stranger of righteousness and circumcised, just as much as he to whom the right of offering sacrifices is denied (Lev. 17:8-10).

units.la: IV. Curcellaeo animus praesagiverat, nodum, quem supra adstringere laboravit, distinctione usitata inter proselythum circumcisum & incircumcisum incidi posse. Ergo reponit:
units.tr: IV. Curcellaeus had a presentiment that the knot which he labored to tie above could be untied by the common distinction between a circumcised and an uncircumcised proselyte. Therefore he replies:

units.la: Quamvis distinctionem istam non illibenter admittam, quae ad aliquorum Scripturae locorum intelligentiam utilis est, dico tamen nihil esse in prohibitione Levit. XVII. facta, quod nos cogat eam potius de peregrino justitia, quam de peregrino domicilii accipere, pag. 59. Resp. Bene, quod usum distinctionis agnoscit. Modo ne in aliud utatur, obsecutus domesticae suae hypothesi de salvatis etiam praeputiatis sub Oeconomia veteri Mosaica, quasi illi apud Israelitas domicilium metati חסידי אומות העולם revera pii Gentiles fuerint, & propter illam pietatem suam habuerint חלק בעולם הבא portionem in futuro seculo. Quomodo revera extra Christum, ad quem nulla fuit nisi in lege paedagogia, salvati fuissent. Nam illa septem Noachidarum praecepta, quorum capistro pios illos Gentiles alligarunt, complectebantur vel legis Dei Spiritualis catechesin, quam flagitabat paedagogia ad Christum, vel promissionem de Christo venturo. Quo errore Grotius, illius sectae familiaris, abreptus est, traducens Tryphonem & Judaeos, qui existimabant, etiam alienigenis, si salvi esse vellent, subeundum fuisse legis Hebraicae jugum. Cui merito negamus, illos nominari in Scripturis pios Gentiles praeputiatos, qui, ex quo desierunt esse catechumeni, in praeputio manserint. Sed haec συχνολόμενα ἐν παιδὸς. Caeterum proselytum justitiae in loco controverso intelligi, evidentibus argumentis jam modo firmavimus.2. Vocem גר non habere vim speciem discriminandi, saepe etiam de peregrino domicilii dici. 16. Resp. Mercero quidem arridet גר plerumque in specie sumi pro Gentili, qui factus adoptione Judaeus, & in eorum foedus receptus, neque etiam aliter sumi potest Deut. XXXV. 15. Ubi distinguitur à תושב. Nolim tamen hac ratione uti, qui sciam in Scripturis peregrinum in portis de proselytho habitationis usitate dici. Loca sunt Deut. XIV. 21. Exod. XX: 10. Deut. V. 14. Exod. XXII. 21. Ubi Deus גר לא תונה advenam non contristabis. Ubi bona pace Mercceri, (nam Judaeos recentiores non curo, qui haud dubie odio Christianorum impulsi explicant de proselytho justitiae) advenam interpretari consultius ducimus de peregrino habitationis, quem alibi Moses vocat advenam in portis. Graeca versio προσήλυτον παροικοῦντα, ut ita Israelitis commendetur hospitalitas, ratione hac addita, quia ipsi aliquando inter Aegyptios peregrini. Quae ratio non stringit, si de proselytho justitiae explicemus. Nam Israelitae in Aegypto ita peregrini fuerunt, ut tamen cum illis religionis societate non cohaeserint. 3. Neque majus robur esse in conjunctione duarum vocum גר תושב. Nullum enim discrimen indicari inter peregrinantes, vel peregrinationis eorum causas, nisi forte hoc, sic appellatos fuisse illos, qui intra Israelitas peregrinari consueverant: quod aliis de causis, quam ob religionem fieri poterat. pag. 60. Resp. Proselytus domicilii nunquam hoc nomine insignitur. Et I.XX. Interpretatio vertit προσήλυτον παροικοῦντα. Quasi dicas Sacris Judaeorum adhaerentem. Et sane peregrinus habitationis non potuit commode dici גר תושב peregrinus peregrinans. Nam hoc notat actum peregrinantis. Qui autem inter Israelitas habitabant, non peregrinabantur actu. At in proselythos justitiae optime competit. Illi enim non cogebantur in Judaea habitare. Qui enim per circumcisionem in Rempublicam Israelitarum
units.tr: Although I will not unwillingly admit that distinction, which is useful for understanding some passages of Scripture, I say nevertheless that there is nothing in the prohibition of Lev. 17 which compels us to take it of a stranger of righteousness rather than of a stranger of residence, p. 59. Reply: Good, that he acknowledges the use of the distinction. Only let him not use it for something else, humoring his own domestic hypothesis that those saved even under the Mosaic economy could be uncircumcised, as if those who settled among the Israelites were in truth pious Gentiles, and on account of that piety had a portion in the world to come [חלק בעולם הבא]. Yet in truth they would have been saved apart from Christ, to whom there was no access except through the pedagogy of the law. For those seven precepts of the sons of Noah, by which they bound those pious Gentiles as with a halter, comprised either the catechesis of the spiritual law of God, which the pedagogy toward Christ required, or the promise of the Christ who was to come. Grotius, a familiar of that sect, was carried away by this error, when he represented Tryphon and the Jews, who thought that even foreigners, if they wished to be saved, had to submit to the yoke of the Hebrew law. We rightly deny that those are called in the Scriptures pious uncircumcised Gentiles who, once they ceased to be catechumens, remained in uncircumcision. But these are the babblings of a child [συχνολόμενα ἐν παιδὸς]. Moreover, we have already confirmed by evident arguments that a proselyte of righteousness is to be understood in the disputed passage. 2. The word ger does not have the force of a distinguishing species, and is often said even of a stranger of residence. 16. Reply: Mercer indeed is pleased that ger is usually taken in the specific sense of a Gentile who, made a Jew by adoption, has been received into their covenant; nor can it be taken otherwise in Deut. 15:? where it is distinguished from [תושב]. Yet I would not wish to use this argument, since I know that in Scripture the stranger within the gates is commonly called a proselyte of residence. The passages are Deut. 14:21; Ex. 20:10; Deut. 5:14; Ex. 22:21, where God says [גר לא תונה] you shall not vex the stranger. Where, with due respect to Mercer (for I do not care about the more recent Jews, who undoubtedly moved by hatred of Christians explain it of a proselyte of righteousness), we judge it more prudent to interpret "stranger" as a stranger of residence, whom Moses elsewhere calls "the stranger within your gates." The Greek version has [προσήλυτον παροικοῦντα], so that hospitality is commended to Israel, with this reason added: because they themselves were once strangers among the Egyptians. This reason does not hold if we explain it of a proselyte of righteousness. For the Israelites in Egypt were strangers in such a way that they nevertheless were not joined with those people in fellowship of religion. 3. Nor is there greater force in the conjunction of the two words ger toshav. For no distinction is indicated between the sojourners or the causes of their sojourning, except perhaps that those were so called who were accustomed to sojourn among the Israelites; which could happen for other reasons than religion. p. 60. Reply: A proselyte of residence is never marked with this name. And the Septuagint translates [προσήλυτον παροικοῦντα], as if you were to say, one adhering to the sacred rites of the Jews. And indeed a stranger of residence could not properly be called ger toshav, a stranger sojourning, for this denotes the act of one who sojourns. But those who dwelt among the Israelites were not actually sojourning. Yet the term fits a proselyte of righteousness perfectly. For such were not required to dwell in Judea.

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] [?]tarum cooptati fuerunt, habitare potuerunt, etiam in longinquis regionibus, quin apud antipodas ipsos. Non minus quàm civitate Romana donari potuerunt, etiam qui extra Italiam habitabant. Et Judæi προσήλυτοι fuerunt etiam illi, qui ἐν τῇ Ἀσιαπορᾷ habitabant extra Judæam, inter Parthos, Medos, Elamitas, qui in Ponto, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphilia, Ægypto, Act. II.9. Ubi ex illis gentibus adfuisse dicuntur Judæi & Proselythi. Non ignoro, Gentiles ob aliam causam, quàm religionis, inter Judæos peregrinari potuisse, quod dicit Curcellæus. Tales fuerunt Proselythi שְׁמְרִים mercenarii, puta mechanici, quos Judæi ab utrisque prioribus distinguunt. Tales etiam peregrini, qui transibant, vel negotii expediendi causa eò veniebant, mox reditum ad suos parantes. Ejusmodi autem peregrinos hoc loco intelligi, nemo asseret, qui veritatem amat. Cur enim Deus his leges Israëlitarum figeret? Imò cur his magis, quàm cæteris omnibus? An desultoria illa in Terra Judææ peregrinatio ejusmodi legum repagulis se obnoxiam reddidit?
units.tr: [illegible] …tarum admitted into the commonwealth of the Israelites by circumcision could dwell even in distant regions, indeed even among the antipodes. They could be granted Roman citizenship no less than those who lived outside Italy. And those were proselytes of the Jews also who lived in the Diaspora outside Judea, among the Parthians, Medes, Elamites, who were in Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt (Acts 2:9), where it is said that Jews and proselytes from those nations were present. I am not unaware that Gentiles could sojourn among the Jews for some cause other than religion, as Curcellaeus says. Such were the proselytes [שְׁמְרִים], that is, hired workers, the artisans whom the Jews distinguish from the other two kinds. Such too were the travelers who passed through, or came there to transact business, soon preparing to return to their own people. But that anyone who loves the truth would assert such sojourners are meant in this passage, no one will say. For why would God impose the laws of the Israelites on them? Or why on them rather than on all others? Or did that wandering stay in the land of Judea make them liable to the bars of such laws?

units.la: V. Curcellæi rationibus expeditis, in promtu jam est, quo occurramus Becmanno.
units.tr: Having dispatched Curcellaeus's arguments, it is now at hand to meet Becmann.

units.la: Is quatuor argumentis statuminat præcepti hujus Mosaici moralitatem. 1. Quia dictione & repetitione satis emphatica conceptum sit. 2. Quia comminatio mortis violanti, et servanti promissio Benedictionis addita. 3. Quia lex illa in Nov. Test. musciam abrogata legitur. 4. Quia ratio addita sit moralis. Exerc. XXVI. Rationes parùm solidæ, neque sustinent veritatis radios. Ad primam. Quid vetat, quò minùs emphaticis ac gravibus verbis edicet Deus, quòd vehementer custodiri voluit μέχρι παρὰ δορᾷάσους? An præceptum aliquod ceremoniale non potuit maximo serio injungi? Circumcisionis præceptum, & administrationis Sacerdotii verbis non minùs efficacibus latum fuit. Ad secundam rationem respondimus thesi prima. Ad tertiam. Ubi abrogata est conceptis verbis lex de primogenitis Deo consecrandis, de purificationibus legalibus, de vestibus ex lino & lana non conficiendis, & innumeræ aliæ? Abundè dictum Apostolo: Lex erat pædagogus ad Christum. At postquam venit fides, non amplius sub pædagogo estis. Gal. III.24.25. Duo dicis novum, antiquavit prius; quod autem antiquatur est et senescit, prope est, ut evanescat. Heb. VIII.13. cum 8. Ne quis vos judicet in cibo & potu, &c. quæ sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi.
units.tr: He props up the morality of this Mosaic precept with four arguments: (1) because it is expressed with a sufficiently emphatic word and repetition; (2) because a threat of death is added for the violator and a promise of blessing for the one who keeps it; (3) because that law is read as abrogated in the New Testament only in part; (4) because a moral reason is added. Exercitation XXVI. The reasons are not very solid, and they do not withstand the rays of truth. To the first. What prevents God from enjoining with emphatic and weighty words what He wished to be guarded with the utmost care, μέχρι παρὰ δορᾷάσους? Or could no ceremonial precept be enjoined with the utmost seriousness? The precept of circumcision and the institution of the priesthood were given in words no less forceful. To the second reason we have replied under the first thesis. To the third. Where has the law concerning the consecration of firstborns to God, concerning legal purifications, concerning garments not to be made of linen and wool, and countless others, been abrogated in express words? The Apostle says enough: "The law was our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ. But after faith has come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster" (Gal. 3:24, 25). "In saying 'new,' he has made the first obsolete; and what is made obsolete and grows old is ready to vanish away" (Heb. 8:13), compared with verse 8: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, etc., which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ" (Col. 2:16, 17); compare Heb. 8:5; 10:1. To the fourth, we have already answered more than enough above. Let us therefore sound the retreat.

units.la: Colossii.16.17. cum Hebr. VIII.5.X.1. Ad quartam supra plus satis responsum. Receptui igitur canamus.
units.tr: Colossians 2:16, 17 compared with Heb. 8:5; 10:1. To the fourth, we have already answered more than enough above. Let us therefore sound the retreat.

units.la: CAPUT VIII. Probatur, in Novo Testamento sanguinis & suffocati esum esse liberum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. It is proved that in the New Testament the eating of blood and of what has been strangled is free.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Synopsis.

units.la: Transitur ad ultimam periodum sub Nov. Test. 1. Probatur abrogatam esse legem de sanguine. Argumentum primum ab antiquatione legum Ceremonialium, & libertate per Christum parta. 2. Argumentum Secundum ex Matth. XV. 11.17. Exceptio Curcellaei discutitur. An reus violatae legis, qui, tempore Christi mortem antecedente, ceremonialem aliquam legem omisisset? 3. Arg. 3. Rom. XIV. 14.17. Curcellaei exceptiones. Sacrificia in V. Test. quomodo Deus noluerit? Nazireatus. 4.5. Sicera Nazireatus finis. Nizirei haeretici. Exceptio de Scandalo infirmis dato aliena. Scandali divisio. Qui abstinent à sanguine, scandalo esse possunt. De scandalo Iudaeorum. De Scandalo Christianorum. 6. Christi baptismus. Iustitiam omnem implere. [Hebrew] Tertulliani locus. 7. Arg.4. ex 1.Cor.X.25. 8. Curcellaei exceptio. Disquiritur, quo tempore scripta prior ad Corinthios? Sententia Baronii, Calvisii, Usserii, Capelli. Alstedius fallitur. Idolothyтopum esus concessus. 9. Arg.5. ex Coloss.II.16.17.20.21. Epistola ad Colossenses quo tempore scripta? 10. Curcellaei Exceptiones ad Col.II. Esus humanarum carnium crudelis. Oviseum sanna. Querela Christianorum. Unde nata Gentilium calumnia? 11. Quaestio proposita. An in casu necessitatis liceat carnes hominum edere? Curcellaei criminatio contra Sancerranos. Scelus mulierum Samaritanarum & Hierosolymitana. Annibalis filius laudatur. Thuani narratio. Sancerravi Magistratus defensio. 12. Pythagoras an carnibus abstinuerit? multiris? 13. Arg.6. ex Tit.I.15. Responsio Curcellæi. Cretensium cum Iudæis communio. Taciti error. Cornelii à Lapide calumnia.14. Arg.7. ex 1.Tim.IV.1.2.3.4. Pelusiotæ circa locum illum crisis. Curcellæi & Becmanni exceptiones expenduntur.15.16. Arg.8. ex Act.X.10.11. Probatur, ibi etiam agi de esu animalium.16. Arg.9. ex Act.XV.10. Abstinentia à sanguine quomodo jugum dici possit? An ex hypothesi sententiæ Curcellæi in casu necessitatis sanguinem edere liceat? Curcellæus & Becmannus confundunt Medicam & Religiosam abstinentiam. Sextii Pythagoræ sententia de esu animalium. Curcellæi praya Philosophia.17.
units.tr: We pass to the last section under the New Testament. 1. It is proved that the law concerning blood has been abrogated. The first argument is drawn from the abolition of the ceremonial laws and the liberty won through Christ. 2. The second argument comes from Matthew 15:11, 17. The exception of Curcellaeus is examined. Could someone who, before Christ's death, omitted some ceremonial law be guilty of breaking the law? 3. The third argument, Romans 14:14, 17. Curcellaeus's exceptions. How God did not want sacrifices in the Old Testament. The Nazirite vow. 4–5. The end of the Nazirite's strong drink. The heretical Nazirites. The exception about giving offence to the weak is irrelevant. The division of offence. Those who abstain from blood can be a stumbling block. On the offence of the Jews. On the offence of Christians. 6. Christ's baptism. "To fulfil all righteousness." The passage of Tertullian. 7. The fourth argument, from 1 Corinthians 10:25. 8. The exception of Curcellaeus. The question is examined: when was the former Epistle to the Corinthians written? The opinions of Baronius, Calvisius, Usher and Cappel. Alsted is mistaken. The eating of meat offered to idols was permitted. 9. The fifth argument, from Colossians 2:16, 17, 20, 21. At what time was the Epistle to the Colossians written? 10. The exceptions of Curcellaeus to Colossians 2. The eating of human flesh is cruel. The mockery of the sheep's meat. The complaint of the Christians. Where did the Gentile slander come from? 11. A question is put: in a case of necessity, is it lawful to eat human flesh? The accusation of Curcellaeus against the people of Sancerre. The crime of the Samaritan and Jerusalem women. The son of Hannibal is praised. The narrative of de Thou. The defence of the magistrate of Sancerre. 12. Did Pythagoras abstain from flesh?

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: AD quartam periodum procedimus, in qua potissimum quæstionis cardo vertitur. Quæ enim huc usque à Curcellæo deproperata sunt, apparet huc in solidum collineare. Et sanè non tam curandum nobis, quid Deus à Noachidis vel Iudæis stricta lege requisiverit, quàm quid nos facere jubeat, ad quælibet majora imperata ipsi obnoxios. Hoc igitur ante omnia negotii nobis dabimus, ut libertatem Novi Testamenti circa hoc caput Scripturis apertis demonstratam in tuto collocemus.
units.tr: We come to the fourth section, in which the real hinge of the question turns. For what Curcellaeus has so hastily brought forward so far clearly aims at this point throughout. Indeed, we should not be so concerned about what God required of the sons of Noah or of the Jews under a strict law, as about what he commands us to do, we who are bound to obey any greater commands. Therefore, before all else, we will set ourselves this task: to place securely the freedom of the New Testament in this matter, a freedom demonstrated by plain Scripture.

units.la: II. Ergo post adventum Christi liber jam est eius sanguinis, quia lex præceptorum in dogmatis, cujus caput esse demonstravimus interdictum sanguinis, & quo constabat inimicitia, est antiquata Ephes.II.15. Et Chirographum, quod nobis in dogmatis erat contrarium, è medio sublatum, cruci affixum & expunctum ac cancellatum est, Col.II.14. Quare, inquit Apostolus, deinc neminem cognovimus secundum carnem (in carnali statu, quo vigebant Δικαιώματα σαρκὸς) Nam etsi Christum agnoverimus secundum carnem, (subjectum legi in infirmitate) at nunc non amplius agnoscimus. Quare si quis in Christo, nova creatura est, 2.Cor.V.16.17. Adeò ut, qui ultra hærent infirmis illis & egenis mundi fundamentis, dicantur tentare Deum, imponentes jugum cervici, quod nec patres ferre potuerunt, Act.XV.10. Proinde standum nobis esse in libertate, ne amplius jugo servitutis constringamur, Gal.V.1. Argumentum omni jam exceptione majus, postquam semel nobis probatum firmiter, præceptum illud Noacho & Israelitis latum merè cereceremoniale fuisse. Excipient tamen Apostolos in Synodo Hierosolymitana renovâsse legem. Cui exceptioni in sequentibus satisfaciemus.
units.tr: II. Therefore, since the coming of Christ, we are now free from the eating of blood, because the law of commandments contained in ordinances, the chief part of which we have shown to be the prohibition of blood, and by which enmity stood, has been abolished (Eph. 2:15). And the handwriting that was against us in its ordinances has been taken out of the way, nailed to the cross, blotted out and cancelled (Col. 2:14). Hence, says the Apostle, "from now on we know no one according to the flesh" (that is, in the carnal state, in which the ordinances of the flesh [δικαιώματα σαρκός] held sway). For although we once knew Christ according to the flesh (subject to the law in weakness), yet now we no longer know him in that way. So, "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature" (2 Cor. 5:16, 17). So much so that those who still cling to those weak and beggarly foundations of the world are said to tempt God, putting a yoke on the neck which neither the fathers were able to bear (Acts 15:10). Therefore we must stand in the liberty with which we have been set free, and not be bound again by the yoke of slavery (Gal. 5:1). This is an argument that is stronger than any objection, once it has been firmly proved to us that the precept given to Noah and to the Israelites was purely ceremonial. Yet they will object that the Apostles in the Synod of Jerusalem renewed the law. We will answer this objection in what follows.

units.la: III. Secundum argumentum, quia Christus ipse adversus Pharisaeos disputans, non obscurè libertatem circa cibum & potum in universum stabilit, Marth. XV. Pharisaei & Scribae Hierosolymitani haud dubiè à Collegio Pharisaeorum, quos Christi fama utebat, ablegati, ipsi movent quaestionem: Cur discipuli ejus, transgressi traditionem majorum, non lavant manus, quum edunt panem? v. 1.2. Christus primò retorquet criminationem, & graviori crimine eos arcessit. v.3.4. &c. Secundò demonstrat, observationem traditionum non esse cultum Dei, sed vanam ac detestabilem hypocrisin. v.7.8.9. Tertiò advocato populo discernit veram hominis pollutionem à ficta. v.11. Non quod intrat in os, polluit hominem, sed quod egreditur ex ore, polluit hominem. Quasi diceret, cibum ore sumtum, sive lotis sive illotis manibus, non reddere aliquem impurum, vel irae Divinae obnoxium. Ita enim se explicat Christus, cum in sententia ejus discipuli haererent. In qua, adnotante Grotio, supponit id, quod constabat inter Judaeos, cor sedem esse animi, ejus praesertim partis, quâ volumus, & ex quo culpa nascitur. Unde sequitur, si à cibo immunditia ad cor non pertingit, ne ad animum quidem pertingere. At cibus, dum adhuc permixtus suis faecibus est, non pertingit ad cor, sed in γαστέρα, in partem ventris depressiorem, in qua est ventriculus. Deinde purgatur cibus, & quicquid naturâ suâ immundum est, ac proinde hominii alendo non idoneum, illud per alvum ejicitur. Apparet ergo, nec ante nec post purgationem immundum in cibo polluere hominem. Hactenus Grotius. Caeterùm sententia Christi universalis est, quâ docetur ac insinuatur haud obscurè, sublato per Christum discrimine ciborum omnia jam munda esse, neque quidquam, quod ingreditur os, hominem polluere posse. Ergo etiam Sanguis, qui os ingreditur, nequaquam hominem polluere poterit. Respondet Curcellaeus: Verba Christi non esse accipienda universaliter, sed ad materiam subjectam restringenda. Non respicere Christum ad cibos, quos lex declarat esse mundos vel immundos, nec sibi propositum habuisse, docere, cibos, quos lex pro mundis duxit, non amplius pro immundis habendos. Sed hoc tantum, hominem non inquinari, etiamsi illotis manibus manducaret cibum. Proculdubio peccaturum fuisse, si quis occasione ex Christi responso sumta licentiam porcina vescendi sumsi arripuit. erripuisset, propter rebellionem adversus Dei mandatum. Nondum enim venisse tempus abrogandae legis. pag.168. 169. Resp. Sic solent cum Curcellaeo etiam Papistae excipere. Ac nominatim Jansenius. Non dubitamus verba Christi hoc loco ad subjectam materiam restringenda. Sed eo modo quo universalis propositio ad demonstrationem particularis quaestionis restringi debet, cujus tamen latitudo in subjecta materia non exhauritur. Nempe Christus a genere ad speciem sic procedit. Quicquid ingreditur in os, non polluit hominem. v.11. Atqui cibus, quem illotis manibus manducant discipuli, ingreditur in os. v.2. Ergo cibus, quem illotis manibus manducârunt discipuli, illos non polluit. Quis hic non intelligit, si propositio Major, adeoque sententia Christi, non accipiatur universaliter, effici argumentationem in prima figura ex puris particularibus, adeoque meram ἀδιαλεξίαν, Christo indignam? Quid? Ipse Curcellaeus sibi discors subjicit: Quanquam non negem, Christum ita generatim loquendo innuisse, tempus illud esse praeforibus, cum ubique gentium, abrogato ciborum discrimine, Deo serviendum esset in Spiritu & veritate. Sententia Christi respicit illud ipsum tempus, quo lata fuit, non illud, quod ante fores erat. Ergo jam tum universalis fuit. 3. Si quis invitatus hac sententia Christi, ex fide in Christum Messiam, qui munda & immunda, hoc est, circumcisos & praeputiatos, in sua carne conciliare debuit, cibos in lege immundos edisset, pro legis transgressore non fuisset habitus, neque reus rebellionis adversus mandatum Dei. Quamvis enim foedus antiquum suam ἰσχὺν habuerit usque ad tertium illum temporis articulum, quo Evangelium Christi exhibiti per Apostolorum praedicationem ἐξεδόθη, quatenus nempe ante illud tempus praedicatio Evangelii non est egressa extra populi Israelitici terram, & Christus ipse praxin publicam sacrificandi non tantum intactam reliquit, sed etiam confirmavit mandato, Matth. VIII. 4. tamen jam libertas tanta Ecclesiae affulsit, ut a peccato immunis esset, qui fide in Messiam praesentem ceremoniam aliquam legalem omisisset. Hinc lex & Prophetae usque ad Johannem, Matth. XI. 13. Et jam adfuit illud πλήρωμα χρόνου, Gal. IV. 1,2. Quo fortasse pertinet illa Christi aenigmatica locutio, Matth. IX. 14,15,16, &c. In quaestione etiam de loco cultus Divini, Christus mulieri Samaritanae respondet: Venit hora, & jam est, quando veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in Spiritu & veritate. Sed & pater tales quaerit ipsum adorantes, Joh. IV. 23. Ergo jam tum Christo nondum mortuo erat illa hora, & quærebat Deus ipse jam tum in Spiritu & veritate adorantes, non habito respectu ad locum, seu is Hierosolyma esset, seu mons Garizim, seu quilibet alius. Quæ causa est non ineptæ distinctionis Theologorum nostrorum inter statum vigoris, languoris, mortis & sepulturæ ceremoniarum legalium. Viguisse usque ad adventum Christi, & functas pædagogi munere: languescere cœpisse nato Christo, & ad ἀφανισμὸν properasse: mortuas, cum Christo: sepultas honestè ab Apostolis usque ad excidium urbis Sanctæ, cum qua Synagoga etiam humum & cineres quæsitavit.
units.tr: III. The second argument is this: Christ himself, disputing against the Pharisees, clearly establishes liberty in general with regard to food and drink (Matt. 15). The Pharisees and the scribes of Jerusalem, sent undoubtedly by the college of Pharisees whom Christ's fame troubled, raise the question themselves: Why do his disciples transgress the tradition of the elders, for they do not wash their hands when they eat bread? (vv. 1, 2). Christ first turns the accusation back, and summons them to a graver crime (vv. 3, 4, etc.). Secondly, he shows that the observance of traditions is not the worship of God, but vain and detestable hypocrisy (vv. 7, 8, 9). Thirdly, calling the people together, he distinguishes true defilement of a man from false (v. 11): It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a man. As if he were saying that food taken into the mouth, whether with washed or unwashed hands, does not make anyone unclean or liable to the wrath of God. For Christ explains himself in this way, since his disciples were stuck on the opinion they held. On this, as Grotius notes, he assumes what was agreed among the Jews: that the heart is the seat of the soul, especially of that part by which we will, and from which guilt arises. From this it follows that if impurity from food does not reach the heart, it does not reach the soul either. But food, while still mixed with its dregs, does not reach the heart, but the belly [γαστήρ], the lower part of the stomach, in which is the little stomach. Then the food is purified, and whatever is by its nature unclean, and therefore unsuitable for nourishing a man, is expelled through the bowels. It is plain, then, that unclean food, neither before nor after purification, defiles a man. So far Grotius. Moreover, Christ's saying is universal, by which it is taught and hinted quite plainly that, with the distinction between foods abolished through Christ, all things are now clean, and nothing that enters the mouth can defile a man. Therefore even blood, which enters the mouth, can by no means defile a man. Curcellaeus replies: The words of Christ are not to be taken universally, but restricted to the matter in hand. Christ was not looking at the foods which the law declares clean or unclean, nor did he intend to teach that foods which the law considered clean are no longer to be considered unclean. But only this: that a man is not defiled even if he eats with unwashed hands. Undoubtedly, if someone had seized the licence to eat pork from the occasion given by Christ's answer, he would have sinned, through rebellion against God's command, for the time for abrogating the law had not yet come. p. 168, 169. Reply: In this way, the Papists too are accustomed to make this exception with Curcellaeus, and especially Jansenius. We do not doubt that the words of Christ here are to be restricted to the matter in hand. But in the way that a universal proposition must be restricted to the demonstration of a particular question, a restriction whose breadth is not, however, exhausted by the matter in hand. Namely, Christ proceeds from the genus to the species thus: whatever enters the mouth does not defile a man (v. 11). But the food which the disciples eat with unwashed hands enters the mouth (v. 2). Therefore the food which the disciples ate with unwashed hands did not defile them. Who here does not see that, if the major premise, and so Christ's saying, is not taken universally, the argument becomes one in the first figure from purely particular premises, and so mere irrelevance [ἀδιαλεξία], unworthy of Christ? Why, Curcellaeus himself, at odds with himself, adds: Although I do not deny that Christ, speaking in general terms, hinted that the time was at the doors, when everywhere among the nations, with the distinction of foods abolished, God would be served in spirit and truth. The saying of Christ looks to that very time in which it was uttered, not to the time which was at the doors. Therefore it was already universal at that time. 3. If anyone, invited by this saying of Christ, through faith in Christ the Messiah, who was to reconcile the clean and unclean, that is, the circumcised and the uncircumcised, in his flesh, had eaten the foods unclean under the law, he would not have been held as a transgressor of the law, nor guilty of rebellion against God's command. For although the old covenant kept its force [ἰσχύς] up to that third point in time when the Gospel of Christ was given out [ἐξεδόθη] through the preaching of the Apostles, inasmuch as before that time the preaching of the Gospel had not gone out beyond the land of the Israelite people, and Christ himself not only left the public practice of sacrifice untouched but even confirmed it by command (Matt. 8:4), nevertheless such great liberty had already shone upon the Church that whoever in faith in the Messiah now present had omitted some legal ceremony was free from sin. The law and the prophets were until John (Matt. 11:13). And now the fullness of time [πλήρωμα χρόνου] had come (Gal. 4:1, 2). To this perhaps belongs that enigmatic saying of Christ (Matt. 9:14, 15, 16, etc.). In the question also about the place of divine worship, Christ answers the Samaritan woman: The hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such people to worship him (John 4:23). Therefore that hour was already at hand while Christ was not yet dead, and God himself was already seeking worshippers in spirit and truth, with no regard to place, whether it was Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, or any other. This is the reason for the not unskilful distinction of our theologians between the states of the legal ceremonies: their vigour, their decline, their death and their burial. They flourished until the coming of Christ, and then performed the office of the schoolmaster. They began to decline when Christ was born, and hastened to their disappearance [ἀφανισμός]. They died with Christ. They were honourably buried by the Apostles until the destruction of the holy city, with which the Synagogue too has grovelled in the dust and ashes.

units.la: IV. Tertium argumentum suppeditat Apostolus Rom. XIV. 14.17.
units.tr: IV. The third argument is supplied by the Apostle, Rom. 14:14, 17.

units.la: Novi & persuasus sum in Domino Iesu, nihil esse pollutum per se ipsum, nisi ei, qui existimat, quid pollutum esse. Non est regnum Dei esca & potus, sed justitia & gaudium & pax in Spiritu S. Judæi conversi ad Christum, quidam infirmiores adhuc, putabant abstinendum esse à cibis lege vetitis. Cæteri proveetiores jam ac præcipuè Gentiles contraniteban-tur, & Evangelicam libertatem opponebant. Hos conciliare conatur Paulus. Vetat, ne invicem se judicent. Imò hoc utrinque judicent, ne ponant scandalum fratri, v. 13. Et subjicit, se certò scire & persuasum esse, quòd per se nihil pollutum, sed tantùm λογιζομένῳ ei, qui reputat aliquid pollutum. Pollutionem intelligit non naturalem, sed religiosam. Hanc tamen scientiam moderatur lege charitatis, ne scandalo percellatur Frater. v. 15. Ac demum subjicit: Regnum Dei non esse escam ac potum, sed justitiam, & pacem, & gaudium in Spiritu S. Atque ita se planissimè explicat. Ea videlicet jam tempora esse, quibus nihil pensi habendum, quid edas vel bibas. Hoc enim jam in religione & regno Dei momentum nullum habere.
