Declarat igitur eadem ratione, esum sanguinis non amplius prohibitum, neque pollutum nisi τῷ λογιζομένῳ, neque in illo amplius regnum Dei verti. Si Præcepti illius legalis nexus nondum solutus fuit, sequitur, fuisse aliquid per se pollutum, & in esu ac potu adhuc regnum Dei volvi.
units.tr: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, except to the one who considers it unclean. The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and joy and peace in the Holy Spirit. Jewish converts to Christ, some of them still weak, thought they had to abstain from foods forbidden by the Law. Others, more advanced, and above all the Gentiles, opposed them and asserted Gospel liberty. Paul tries to reconcile these two sides. He forbids them to judge one another, or rather to judge this very thing, that they should not put a stumbling block before a brother (v. 13). He then adds that he knows for certain and is persuaded that nothing is unclean in itself, but only to the one who reckons something unclean [λογιζομένῳ]. By "uncleanness" he means not natural but religious uncleanness. Yet he restrains this knowledge by the law of charity, so that a brother is not struck down by offence (v. 15). Finally he adds that the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. In this way he explains himself most plainly: these are the times in which it does not matter what you eat or drink, since this now has no weight in religion or in the kingdom of God. He therefore declares by the same reasoning that the eating of blood is no longer forbidden, and is unclean only to the one who reckons it so [λογιζομένῳ], and that the kingdom of God is no longer overturned by it. If the bond of that legal precept had not yet been loosed, it would follow that something was unclean in itself, and that the kingdom of God was still at stake in eating and drinking.

units.la: V. Curcellæus multa excipiendo conatur pulverem oculis offundere. 1. Nihil per se pollutum, nisi quod Deus prohibuit. Tunc enim usurpare nos id non posse, quin polluamur. pag. 170. Simili responso fungitur Becmannus. Cibus, inquit, & potus per se bona sunt & munda, nec pollunt: quemquam sua natura. At interim quæEius Divinae legis, cui praestanda obedientia, merito à quibusdam esse olim Judaei, & Christiani hodie abstinent. Aliàs polluuntur, Exerc. XXVI. Resp. Non sunt fingendae prohibitiones & quoties ac relationes Divinarum legum nostro lubitu. Nam solus Deus habet jus νομοθέτης. Ille autem nusquam tulit legem universalem nullo tempore violabilem. Deinde Apostolus arbitri partes agit inter infirmiores & perfectiores Christianos. In illorum favorem sancit, fratres infirmos fide esse suscipiendos, non scandalizandos temerè, imò cibis legaliter immundis, ad aedificandos illos & fovendos, abstinendum esse. In horum gratiam, quòd recta sit eorum scientia & persuasio, nihil omnino pollutum esse, & bene illos judicare de cibo & potu, in quibus nulla pars regni Dei. Quo ergo modo infirmiores negabant munditiem legalem cibi & potus, perfectiores impugnabant, eo modo Paulus utrosque informat de usu cibi & potus. Judaei autem infirmiores negabant omnium ciborum & potus legaliter prohibitorum munditiem. Paulus approbat, neque quidquam excipit. Si quid fuisset exceptione dignum, & quod polluere posset, magnopere intererat illud monere. Sic enim infirmiores ex parte sublevari potuissent, caeteri accuratius instrui. Annon conveniebat aliquo saltem indicio significare exceptionem? Imò aliquatenus dici debuit regnum Dei consistere in esca & potu? 2. Illa verba: Non est regnum esca, potus, non ita universaliter esse accipienda, quasi nullam exceptionem admittant. Alioquin sequeretur, illum Dei regno nihil indignum committere, qui cibo & potu se ingurgitaret. Eodem jure concludi posse, non esse necessarium, ut Coena Dominica, quae in manducatione panis & potu vini consistit, in Ecclesia Christi celebretur: pag. 170. Resp. Mutuatus est exceptionem à Salmerone Jesuita & Bellarmino lib. II. de jejun. cap. 8. Qui si ad animam revocâsset, Apostolo sermonem esse de universali legitimo usu, non de damnato abusu cibi & potus: mundis omnia munda esse: pollutis & infidelibus nihil mundum esse, abstinuisset haud dubiè ram absurda & jejuna responsione. Et cum ipso Curcellaeus. Nempe universalis usus rei adiaphorae etiam universalem abusum habere potest. De Coena Dominica quod obducit, nihil ad rem. Apostolus perspicuè agit de eo cibo & potu, qui olim per legem immundus declaratus est. Hunc jam in universum negat polluere quemquam posse, nisi ἀναζόμενον. Sed panis & vinum in Sacra Domini Coena symbolicè à Christo constituta sunt in signa Sacramentalia, quæ in usu esse voluit usque ad tempus sui adventus ad judicium, 1. Cor. XI.24. Nullum autem tale præceptum de Sanguine, usque ad Christi judicis adventum obligatorium occurrit. 3. Paulum non loqui absolutè, sed per comparationem, veluti cùm Deus dicit: Misericordiam volo, & non Sacrificium. ib. Resp. Versus 14. habet manifestè absolutam negationem: Οὐδὲν χωρὶς ἀ' ἑαυτῆ. Deus verò cùm dicit, Misericordiam volo, non Sacrificium, Sacrificium interea revera voluit, non quidem tanquam conditionem icti fœderis operum, cùm populus ex Ægypto educeretur, sed tanquam κοσμικὴν λατρείαν, quæ in illo tempore esset pro umbra & elementaria institutione, ut legem non observantibus solamini essent. An hoc modo etiam voluit in cibo & potu verti regnum Dei? Ergo mansit sub Novo fœdere illa voluntas servandi Justificationes carnis. Si de sanguine asseris, etiam de cæteris debes. Nam generatim negat in cibo & potu consistere Regnum Dei. 4. Deum olim voluisse, ut Israelita, & qui inter illos votum Naziraatus fecerat, à quibusdam potuum & ciborum generibus abstinerent, non quòd in eo sanctitas proprie consisteret, sed quia eorum obedientiam in ejusmodi corporalibus exercitiis ipsi explorare placuit. ib. Resp. Naziræatus fuit institutum Veteris Testamenti. Ac quamdiu votum durabat, à tribus abstinebant, à tonsura capillorum, & vino, & omnibus, quæ ex vitibus proveniunt, & à contactu rei immundæ. Angelus de Baptista: Vinum & siceram non bibet. Luc. I.15. Idem de Samsone dictum. Sicera LXX. vertunt μέθυσμα. Lyra dicit: Esse omnem potum inebriativum. Jonathan pro esse vinum novum: יין vinum vetus. Drusio non displicet, ut sit potus factitius ex hordeo, qualis nostra cerevisia: vel ex pomis. De his sic Maimonides: Naziræatus finis est, ut per prohibitionem ab omnibus è vite profectis potibus, homo ad excellentiorem dignitatem perveniat, & rebus necessariis consentus esse discat. Nam qui sic à vino abstinet, vocatur sanctus, & collocatur in gradu Sacerdotis magni quoad sanctitatem, dum non audet se polluere Patre & Matre sua defunctis. More Nev. III.48. Non comperiuntur à certo ciborum genere sibi temperâsse, quod tamen Curcellæus scribit. Sed quid hoc ad rem? Naziræatus fuit à mandato Dei, Votum legale, & ἀναγκαῖον, ac viguit, quamdiu Ceremonialis legislatio, cum qua exspiravit. Obedientia omnino Deo placuit, non abstinentia. Si tamen in Novo Testa-
units.tr: V. Curcellaeus, by making many exceptions, tries to throw dust in the eyes. (1) Nothing is unclean in itself except what God has forbidden; for then we cannot use it without being defiled. p. 170. Becmannus gives a similar answer: Food and drink, he says, are good and clean in themselves, and do not defile anyone by their nature. Yet meanwhile those things which the Jews formerly, and Christians today, rightly abstain from, owing obedience to a divine law, are defiled (Exerc. XXVI). Reply: the prohibitions and the relations of divine laws must not be invented at our pleasure. For God alone has the right of lawgiver. He has never issued a universal law that could be violated at no time. Next, the Apostle acts as arbiter between the weaker and the more mature Christians. On behalf of the weaker he decrees that weak brothers are to be received in faith and not rashly offended, and that, to build them up and cherish them, one should abstain even from foods legally unclean. On behalf of the more mature he affirms that their knowledge and conviction are correct, that nothing at all is unclean, and that they judge rightly about food and drink in which there is no part of the kingdom of God. Therefore, just as the weaker denied the legal uncleanness of food and drink while the more mature attacked it, Paul instructs both sides about the use of food and drink in the same way. The weaker Jews, however, denied the legal prohibition of all foods and drinks. Paul approves this and makes no exception. If anything had been worth excepting, something that could defile, it would have mattered greatly to warn of it. For in that way the weaker might have been partly relieved and the others more accurately taught. Was it not fitting to signify the exception by at least some sign? Indeed, ought it not to have been said at least in some measure that the kingdom of God consists in food and drink? (2) The words "the kingdom is not food and drink" are not to be taken so universally as if they admitted no exception. Otherwise it would follow that someone who gorged himself on food and drink would commit nothing unworthy of the kingdom of God. By the same right one could conclude that it is not necessary for the Lord's Supper, which consists in eating bread and drinking wine, to be celebrated in the Church of Christ: p. 170. Reply: he has borrowed the exception from the Jesuit Salmeron and from Bellarmine (lib. II, de jejun., cap. 8). If he had recalled the mind of the Apostle, that the discussion concerns the universal lawful use of food and drink and not the condemned abuse of it, that to the clean all things are clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, he would undoubtedly have refrained from such an absurd and empty answer. And Curcellaeus agrees with him. Clearly the universal use of a thing indifferent can also have a universal abuse. What he objects about the Lord's Supper is beside the point. The Apostle is clearly speaking of that food and drink which were formerly declared unclean by the Law. He now denies that anything defiles anyone at all, except to the one who reckons it so [ἀναζόμενον]. But bread and wine in the holy Supper of the Lord were appointed by Christ symbolically as sacramental signs, which he willed to be in use until the time of his coming to judgment (1 Cor. 11:24). However, no such precept about blood, binding until the coming of Christ the judge, occurs. (3) Paul does not speak absolutely, but by comparison, as when God says: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. ib. Reply: verse 14 contains a plainly absolute negation: [Οὐδὲν χωρὶς ἀ' ἑαυτῆ]. But when God says, I desire mercy, not sacrifice, he did in fact desire sacrifice, not indeed as a condition of the covenant of works, when the people were led out of Egypt, but as [κοσμικὴν λατρείαν] worldly worship, which at that time was a shadow and an elementary institution, a comfort for those who did not keep the Law. Does it follow that he also willed the kingdom of God to be overturned in food and drink? So that wish to keep the statutes of the flesh remained under the New Covenant. If you assert this about blood, you must also assert it about the rest, for generally he denies that the kingdom of God consists in food and drink. (4) God once wished that the Israelites, and those who among them had made a vow of the Nazirite, should abstain from certain kinds of drinks and foods, not because holiness properly consisted in this, but because he was pleased to test their obedience in such bodily exercises. ib. Reply: the Nazirite vow was an institution of the Old Testament. As long as the vow lasted, they abstained from three things: from cutting the hair, from wine, and from everything that comes from the vine, and from contact with an unclean thing. The angel says of John the Baptist: He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink (Luke 1:15). The same is said of Samson. The Seventy render strong drink [μέθυσμα], an intoxicant. Lyra says it is every intoxicating drink. Jonathan, for "wine," has new wine, and for יין old wine. Drusius does not object that it means a drink made artificially from barley, like our beer, or from apples. Maimonides speaks of these things thus: The purpose of the Nazirite is that, by abstaining from all drinks that come from the vine, a man may attain a more excellent dignity and learn to be content with necessary things. For he who thus abstains from wine is called holy, and is placed in the rank of the high priest as to holiness, since he does not dare to defile himself even for his dead father and mother. (More Nevochim III.48). It is not found that they abstained from a certain kind of food, though Curcellaeus writes this. But what does this have to do with the matter? The Nazirite vow was from the command of God, a legal vow and [ἀναγκαῖον] necessary, and it was in force as long as the ceremonial legislation lasted, with which it expired. Obedience pleased God altogether, not abstinence. If, however, in the New Testament God had wished that to be observed, he would have had the power to command it. Now he has done nothing of the kind, but by a general rule has declared that no distinction of food or drink must now be regarded, that nothing defiles a man, and that to the clean all things are clean. Therefore obedience, which rests on the command and promise of God, cannot have any place in such a distinction of foods or drinks. The example of both abstinence and disobedience is found among the Nazaraeans, who once, as Epiphanius testifies, were more hostile to Paul and stubbornly defended the legal ceremonies, against whom many believe Paul wrote his Epistle to the Galatians.

units.la: Digitized by Google Testamento Deus illud custodiri voluisset, potestas fuisset ipsi praecipiendi. Nunc nihil tale fecit, sed generali canone definivit, nullum jam discrimen cibi vel potus attendi debere, nihil hominem polluere posse, omnia mundis munda esse. Non potest igitur in ejusmodi ciborum vel potus discrimine locum habere obedientia, quippe quae nititur mandato & promissione Dei. Exemplum & abstinentiae & inobedientiae in Nazaraeis est, qui Paulo olim, teste Epiphanio, infensiores, mordicus ceremonias legales propugnárunt, quibus proinde Paulum Epistolam ad Galatas opposuisse multi credunt.
units.tr: Testamento God would have had the power to command it if he had wished it kept. Now he has done nothing of the kind, but by a general canon has defined that no distinction of food or drink is now to be observed, that nothing can defile a man, and that all things are clean to the clean. Obedience, which rests upon God's command and promise, therefore cannot have any place in such a distinction of foods or drinks. The example of both abstinence and disobedience is found among the Nazaraeans, who once, as Epiphanius testifies, were more hostile to Paul and stubbornly defended the legal ceremonies; many believe that Paul therefore set his Epistle to the Galatians against them.

units.la: VI. Jam etiam in nos conatur argumentum retorquere, & nostro nos gladio confodere. Videamus ergo, quàm felix sit εὐεπτροπὴ ἐκ λόγῳ. Paulus, inquit, reprehendit eos, qui cum Fratrum infirmorum scandalo vescebantur cibis, per se quidem licitis, sed quos nonnulli illicitos credebant, quia lex illos prohibuerat: ideóque sic faciendo libertate sua ad aliorum perniciem abutebantur. Quod facit contra illos, qui sanguine vescuntur; Posito enim, istud esse indifferens, tamen quia multi sunt inter Christianos, qui inde tanquam mandati Apostolici vilipendio offenduntur, deberent potius; qui pietatis sunt studiosi, abstinere ab esca abstinere, ne contrarientur Apostoli mandato, quod immediatè antecedit. Si propter cibum Frater tuus contristatur, jam non secundum charitatem ambulas. Noli cibo tuo illum perdere, pro quo Christus mortuus est. Saltem qui ab esca sanguinis abstinent, ne minimi offendiculo esse possint, cùm ea non sit praeceptum, sed tantùm ad tempus prohibitum. Sed qui edunt, non habent causam levem metuendi, ne infirmos, qui credunt esse illicitum, libertate sua offendant. pag. 171. 172. Idem Becmannus urget. Qui etiam non Christianis tantùm infirmioribus à scandalo timet, sed & Judaeis, qui ingenti copia juxta Christianos in Germania, Gallia, Italia, Polonia, Bohemia habitant, & qui αἱματοφαγίᾳ nostra offensi magis à Christianis abhorrent. Exercit. XXVI. pag. 536. Respond. Mutant Curcellaeus & Becmannus instituta quaestionis elenchum. Disceptamus de jure sanguinis edendi, & de libertate per Christum parta. A jure libertatis distinctum est ejus exercitium. Nam jus ipsum in contrariam partem determinari nequit. Sed exercitium determinatur per fidem & charitatem. Per fidem, ne dubitante conscientia quicquam agatur, sed mens sufficienter de usu ciborum sit firmata. Per Charitatem, ne indifferentium usu offendantur infirmi. Ipse Apostolus hoc loco diligenter ligenter jus & exercitium libertatis distinguit. Primò jus libertatis asserit, cùm dicit: Novi & persuasum sum in Domino Iesu, quòd nihil per se ipsum sit pollutum, sed tantùm ei, qui existimat aliquid pollutum esse. v. 14. Et vers. 16. Ne blasphemetur vestrum τὸ ἀγαθόν. Et v.20. Omnia pura. Sic asserit Christianorum libertatem. Sed exercitium tamen limitat cancellis fidei & charitatis. Fidei v.23. Qui dubitat cùm edit, judicatus est, quia non facit ex fide. Quicquid autem ex fide non est, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. 23. Charitatis v.13.15.20.21. Ne alii alios judicemus. Hoc magis judicate, ne Fratri sitis offendiculo. Si ob escam Frater tuus contristatur, non ambulas secundum charitatem, &c. Nullius igitur momenti est exceptio, neque contra jus & libertatem edendi sanguinem militat, sed contra scandala in exercitio praepostero rei indifferentis. Deinde scandalum aliquando oritur ex illius vitio, cui scandalum objectum est, cùm qui offenditur, efficit, ut quod in se non est scandalum, sibi tale fiat: aliquando ex illius culpa, qui scandalum objecit. Illud vocatur acceptum, hoc datum. Datur autem tribus modis. Primò si quis hortando induxit in errorem, cùm esset vel magna praeditus auctoritate, vel magno ingenio, vel magnâ eloquentiâ. Secundò peccando in moribus & vita; nam exemplo suo minùs malos illexit in peccatum, improbos confirmavit. Tertiò, dum quis abutitur libertate sua per Christum. Quod faciunt, qui vel superbè sua libertate utuntur, vel insultant infirmis & minùs peritis, vel ea negligenter utuntur, ut sit lata culpa. Jam videamus, an scandali dati reatum contrahat, qui sanguinem edit. De Judaeis, qui Christianis permixti vivunt, praecisè nego. Non datur enim scandalum, sed accipitur ob propriam & sonticam culpam. Negant praefractè Messiam venisse, & sublato discrimine ciborum parietem intergerinum sustulisse. Ipse Christus Judaeis scandalum est, 1. Cor. I.23. Et si esu sanguinis non sunt offendendi Judaei, tum nec esu caeterorum ciborum, qui in lege immundi fuerunt. Nam ad illorum usum aequè tussiunt. Imò tum, cùm Judaei infirmi adhuc fuerunt, & quamvis Christi disciplinam secuti, hoc tamen caput nondum capere potuerunt. Paulus reprehendit Petrum, & συνυπόκρισιν Barnabae ac caeterorum Judaeorum, quos negat ὀρθοποδεῖν πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, quia se à Gentilibus metu Judaeorum propter communem convictum subduxerunt. Gal. II. 12, 13, 14. Quantò severiori censura digni sunt hodie illi, qui in Judæorum gentis, tenebroso velamine pectus circumtectæ, & Christianorum universam disciplinam perosæ, gratiam nos volunt cogere Ἰουδαΐζειν, Gal.II.14. De Christianis sic sentiendum. Qui non edit, quia opinatur præcepto morali contravenire sanguinis esum, is haud dubiè offendiculo est fratri, si non in abstinentia, saltem in causa abstinentiæ, nempe in persuasione hac, quòd contrarius actus sit moraliter vitiosus. Imò tacitè judicat fratrem in cibo & potu, contra quàm Paulus jubet Rom.XIV.3. Colossi.II.16. Et tanquam vivens in mundo & egenis ejus elementis, sic δογματίζεται. Μὴ ἅψῃ, μηδὲ γεύσῃ, μηδὲ θίγῃς, v.20.21. Atque sic reus est scandali dati primo modo, quatenus quodammodo hortando, vel authoritate, vel exemplo in errorem ac pravam persuasionem libertatis Christianæ contrariam illicit. Deinde peccat, quia non abstinet à sanguine hac fide, quòd omnia munda sint mundis. Quicquid autem ex fide non est, peccatum est, Rom.XIV.23. Qui edunt ex fide, neque judicant tamen non edentem, & maturo ac confirmato judicio id faciunt, ac sequuntur etiam in eo observationem ac sententiam totius Ecclesiæ, vel certè potissimæ in ea partis, & faciunt hoc tempore plenæ lucis, in qua nemo citra latæ culpæ reatum executire potest, quemadmodum illi accusari possunt scandali fratribus infirmis dati? Et aliam fuisse rationem infirmiorum fratrum tempore Apostoli, aliam tempore nostro, liquidò constat. Illi enim ex Judaismo ad Christi disciplinam se applicantes, præjudicio tamen hoc imbuti fuerunt de perpetuitate legis Ceremonialis, quæ μὴ λεγόμενος fuit. In iis igitur, quia manifesta fuit ἀπρωσία τῆς Ἀγαπῆς, prudentia Christianorum medicabilis, συγκατάβασιν locus fuit. Absque qua fuisset, haud dubiè anceps periculum imminebat, ne ad pristinum vomitum redirent. Hodie Evangelii doctrina ubique radiante, & ceremonialis legis usu & abrogatione omnibus æquè comperta, nullus est à tali periculo metus.
units.tr: VI. Now they also try to turn the argument against us and run us through with our own sword. Let us see how well-founded this argument [εὐεπτροπὴ ἐκ λόγῳ] is. Paul, they say, rebukes those who ate foods that were lawful in themselves, but which some believed to be unlawful because the law had forbidden them, and so by eating them they abused their liberty to the destruction of others. This, they say, applies against those who eat blood. For even granting that this is a matter of indifference, nevertheless, because there are many among Christians who take offence at it as a violation of an apostolic command, those who are zealous for piety ought rather to abstain from it, lest they go against the Apostle's command, which comes immediately before. If your brother is grieved because of food, you no longer walk in love. Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died. At least those who abstain from the flesh of blood, so that they may not be a stumbling block even to the least, since it is not a commandment but only a temporary prohibition. But those who eat have no slight reason to fear that they may offend weak brethren who believe it to be unlawful by their liberty. pp. 171, 172. Becmannus presses the same point. He fears offence not only for weaker Christians but also for the Jews, who live in great numbers alongside Christians in Germany, France, Italy, Poland and Bohemia, and who, offended by our blood-eating [αἱματοφαγία], shrink away from the Christians. Exercit. XXVI, p. 536. Reply: Curcellaeus and Becmannus change the terms of the question. We are disputing about the right to eat blood and about the liberty won through Christ. The exercise of this liberty is distinct from the right to it. For the right itself cannot be determined toward the opposite side, but the exercise is determined by faith and charity. By faith, so that nothing is done with a doubting conscience, but the mind is sufficiently assured about the use of foods. By charity, so that weak brethren are not offended by the use of things indifferent. The Apostle himself, in this place, carefully distinguishes the right of liberty from its exercise. First he asserts the right of liberty when he says: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but only to him who thinks something is unclean. v. 14. And v. 16: Let not your good [τὸ ἀγαθόν] be spoken evil of. And v. 20: All things are pure. So he asserts the liberty of Christians. But he nevertheless limits the exercise of it within the bounds of faith and charity. Faith, v. 23: He who doubts when he eats is condemned, because he does not act from faith. Whatever is not from faith is sin, Rom. XIV. 23. Charity, vv. 13, 15, 20, 21: Let us not judge one another. Rather judge this, that you put no stumbling block before your brother. If your brother is grieved because of food, you are not walking in love, etc. Therefore this exception has no weight, nor does it militate against the right and liberty of eating blood, but against offences arising from the wrongful exercise of a matter of indifference. Further, an offence sometimes arises from the fault of the one who is offended, when the one who takes offence makes something that is not in itself an offence into one for himself; and sometimes from the fault of the one who gives the offence. The former is called taken, the latter given. Offence is given in three ways. First, if someone by exhortation has led another into error, when he was endowed with great authority, great talent or great eloquence. Second, by sinning in morals and life; for by his example he has enticed the less wicked into sin and confirmed the wicked. Third, when someone abuses his liberty in Christ. This is done by those who either use their liberty arrogantly, or insult the weak and less skilled, or use it so carelessly that it becomes a grave fault. Now let us see whether he who eats blood incurs the guilt of giving offence. Concerning Jews who live mixed among Christians, I flatly deny it. For no offence is given; rather, they take offence through their own sinful fault. They stubbornly deny that the Messiah has come and that, with the distinction of foods removed, He has broken down the dividing wall. Christ himself is a stumbling block to the Jews, 1 Cor. I. 23. And if the Jews must not be offended by the eating of blood, then neither must they be offended by the eating of other foods which were unclean in the law, for those are equally used by them. Indeed, even when the Jews were weak, and although they followed the discipline of Christ, they were still not able to grasp this point. Paul rebuked Peter, and the hypocrisy [συνυπόκρισις] of Barnabas and the other Jews, whom he says did not walk uprightly [ὀρθοποδεῖν πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου] toward the truth of the Gospel, because out of fear of the Jews they withdrew from the Gentiles on account of shared fellowship. Gal. II. 12, 13, 14. How much more severely ought those to be censured today who, with the veil of the Jewish nation covering their hearts in darkness, and hating the whole discipline of Christians, want to compel us in grace to Judaize [Ἰουδαΐζειν], Gal. II. 14. Concerning Christians, one must think as follows. He who does not eat, because he thinks that eating blood violates a moral precept, is undoubtedly a stumbling block to his brother, if not in the abstinence itself, at least in the cause of abstinence, namely in this persuasion, that the contrary act is morally sinful. Indeed, he tacitly judges his brother in food and drink, contrary to what Paul commands, Rom. XIV. 3, Col. II. 16. And, as if living in the world and subject to its weak elements, he submits himself to decrees [δογματίζεται]: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, vv. 20, 21. And so he is guilty of giving offence in the first way, inasmuch as by exhortation, whether by authority or by example, he entices into error and into a perverse persuasion contrary to Christian liberty. Then he sins because he does not abstain from blood with this faith, that all things are clean to the clean. Whatever is not from faith is sin, Rom. XIV. 23. Those who eat from faith, and who do not judge the one who does not eat, act with mature and settled judgment, and in this they also follow the practice and opinion of the whole Church, or at least of its chief part; and they act in this time of full light, in which no one can commit such an act without incurring the guilt of grave fault. How then can they be accused of giving offence to weak brethren? It is clear that the situation of the weak brethren in the Apostle's time was one thing, and in our time another. For those who came from Judaism to the discipline of Christ were nevertheless imbued with the prejudice that the ceremonial law was perpetual, which was not to be mentioned [μὴ λεγόμενος]. Among them, therefore, since there was manifest lack of love [ἀπρωσία τῆς ἀγάπης], a remedy was to be applied by the prudence of Christians, and there was room for condescension [συγκατάβασις]. Without this there would undoubtedly have been a dangerous peril that they would return to their former vomit. Today, with the doctrine of the Gospel shining everywhere, and with the use and abrogation of the ceremonial law known equally to all, there is no fear of such danger.

units.la: Christi exemplum non nocet nobis, baptismum tanquam justitiæ opus suscipientis, quia decebat ipsum implere omnem justitiam, Matth.III.15. Ubi phrasis illa πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην, est Hebraicæ illi, judice Doctissimo Camerone, affinis מלא אחרי, quæ de Calebo usurpatur, Deut.I.36. Josi.XIV.14. quâ denotatur plenum Deo exhibitum obsequium. Quasi Christus Johanni diceret: Oportet me defungi non modò legali Oeconomia, sed & tua. & Tuâ. Doctrina enim Johannis neque merè legalis fuit, neque merè Evangelica. Ergo sub ipso novus quidam Ecclesiæ statüs, quia mutatio doctrinæ mutat statum Ecclesiæ, & doctrina indicat baptismum. Ergo Christus voluit Johannis Baptismo baptizari, quia voluit defungi omni Oeconomia. Itaque voluit subjici legi Ceremoniali, & Politicis Judæorum legibus, & baptismati Johannis, ita ut nihil fit, quod Christus non præstiterit, ut omnis generis peccatores consolationem haberent, eósque sui consortes faceret. Non indiguit igitur pro se baptismate Johannis Christus. Indiguit tamen in hac Oeconomia constitutus, in qua Deo aures ipsi perfodienti obedientiam stipulatus est. Hic ergo ostendat Curcellæus nobis τὸ πεῖνον, necessarium in se, perpetuum & nunquam mutabile præceptum Dei, quo solo τὸ πεῖνον nostrum finitur. Hic Rhodus, hic saltus! Tertullianus non magis nos ferit. Ejus verba de Poenit. c. 4.Nos pro nostris angustiis unum inculcamus, bonum atque optimum esse quod Deus præcepit. Audaciam existimo de bono Divini præcepti disputare: Neque enim quia noxium est, consulere debemus, sed quia Deus præcepit. Ad exhibitionem obsequii, prior est Majestas Divina potestatis, prior est auctoritas imperantis, quàm utilitas servientis. Hoc præclarè dictum Tertulliano in alia causa. Nobis autem opponi non debuit, qui non agnoscimus Universale præceptum, in qualibet differentia temporis obligatorium. Alias quanta improbitas foret, frenum mordere præceptorum Dei, & nostræ cupiditati illud laxare? Ne modò tantam amentiam nobis imputet!
units.tr: Christ's example does us no harm when he received baptism as a work of righteousness, because it became him to fulfil all righteousness, Matt. 3:15. Here the phrase πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην [to fulfil all righteousness] is, in the judgment of the most learned Cameron, akin to the Hebrew מלא אחרי [to fill after], which is used of Caleb (Deut. 1:36; Josh. 14:14) and denotes full obedience rendered to God. It is as if Christ were saying to John: I must complete not only the legal economy but also yours. For John's teaching was neither purely legal nor purely evangelical. Therefore under him a new state of the Church arose, since a change of teaching changes the state of the Church, and that teaching points to baptism. So Christ willed to be baptized with John's baptism, because he willed to complete every economy. Thus he willed to be subject to the ceremonial law, to the civil laws of the Jews, and to John's baptism, so that nothing is left that Christ did not perform, and so that sinners of every kind might have consolation and he might make them his companions. Christ therefore did not need John's baptism for himself. Yet he needed it as one placed in this economy, in which he pledged obedience to God who had pierced his ears. Let Curcellaeus show us here the τὸ πεῖνον [the necessary thing], the command of God that is necessary in itself, perpetual and never changing, by which alone our τὸ πεῖνον is ended. Here is Rhodes, here the leap! Tertullian does not strike us any harder. His words in On Repentance, ch. 4: We keep insisting, for our own straits, that what God has commanded is good and best. I think it presumptuous to dispute about the goodness of a divine command. We ought not to ask whether it is harmful, but because God has commanded it. In the rendering of obedience, the Divine Majesty of power comes first, the authority of the one commanding comes first, before the usefulness to the one serving. This was well said by Tertullian in another cause. But it ought not to be opposed to us, who do not acknowledge a universal command binding at every difference of time. Otherwise what wickedness it would be to bite the bridle of God's precepts and loosen it for our own desire! May he not impute such madness to us!

units.la: VIII. Quartum argumentum suppeditat idem Apostolus ad Corinthios scribens, 1.Cor.X.25. Quicquid in macello venditur, edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo ejus. Agit Apostolus de Idolothytis. Hactenus impugnavit Idolothyta quâ talia, formaliter dicta, Fugite idololatriam. v.14. Ne fiatis participes mensæ & calicis Daemoniorum, v.20. puta, comedendo cibos idolis oblatos eo modo, & iis circumstantiis, quibus censeamini eos quasi sacros, in honorem idoli comedere. Deinceps solvit quæstionem à Corinthiis motam: An Idolothytum comedi possit saltem materialiter, quà cibus & caro est? Respond. Apostolus: Omnia, quidem licere, sed non omnia edificare. v.23.24. Sic rursum distinguit jus ab exercitio, cui accidere potest, ut sit malum. Ac subjicit concessionem generalem: Omnia quæ in macello sunt sint, manducate, μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες, nihil discernentes, non haesitantes propter conscientiam. Vetat eos interrogare in macello, an carnes venum expositae idolis fuerint sacrificatae, necne? Solebant enim Gentiles carnes idolis oblatas, post sacrificium & epulum superfluas, mittere ad macellum vendendas, quarum lucrum ad Sacerdotes derivabatur. In macello autem censebantur ad communem & profanum usum redire. Ergo Apostolus declarat: Omnem jam cibum & potum indifferentem esse, & religionem ac conscientiam nullum amplius discrimen agnoscere, sicut factum in Veteri Testamento. Quae sententia cum generalis sit, necessario etiam sanguinem complecti debet. Nam in macello botulos & farcimina ex sanguine, usitatissimum Gentilium cibum, venum exposita esse, cui vel levis dubitatio incessere potest?
units.tr: VIII. The same Apostol supplies a fourth argument, writing to the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 10:25: Whatever is sold in the meat market, eat, asking no questions for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof. The Apostle is dealing with idol-offerings. Up to this point he has opposed idol-offerings as such, expressly: Flee from idolatry, v. 14; that you not become partners of the table and cup of demons, v. 20; that is, eating foods offered to idols in such a way and in such circumstances that you would be seen to eat them, as if they were sacred, in honour of the idol. Next he resolves the question raised by the Corinthians: whether an idol-offering may be eaten at least materially, as food and flesh? The Apostle answers: All things are lawful, but not all things edify, vv. 23–24. So again he distinguishes right from practice, which may happen to be evil. And he adds a general concession: Whatever is in the meat market, eat, μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες [asking nothing], making no distinction, not scrupling for conscience' sake. He forbids them to ask in the meat market whether the meats sold there had been sacrificed to idols or not. For the Gentiles used to send to the market for sale the meat left over from idol-offerings after the sacrifice and feast, and the profit from it went to the priests. In the market, however, such meat was regarded as returned to common and profane use. So the Apostle declares that now all food and drink is indifferent, and that religion and conscience recognise no further distinction, as was the case in the Old Testament. Since this statement is general, it must necessarily embrace blood too. For who could even slightly doubt that sausages and black puddings made of blood, the most common food of the Gentiles, were sold in the meat market?

units.la: IX. Curcellaeus magno nisu conatur argumentum dissipare.
units.tr: IX. Curcellaeus strives with great effort to dissipate the argument.

units.la: Summa exceptionis: Paulum hanc Epistolam scripsisse altero anno post concilium Hierosolymitanum: vel saltem exiguum admodum temporis spatium, inter utrumque, nempe Concilium & hujus Epistolae scriptionem, intercessisse. In hoc casu convenire, ut generalis haec sententia ex particulari decreto Synodico exponatur. Cum ergo Apostolus dicit: Omne quod in macello venit, manducate, &c. res ipsa indicat, ita esse accipiendum, nisi aliquod sit speciale interdictum, quo id prohibeatur. Tale autem fecisse paulo ante Apostolos, quorum decretis Paulus derogare nec volebat, nec poterat. Ab illo interdicto nos non habere ullam particularem relaxationem: ideoque non posse nos esse certos in conscientia, licitum esse sanguine vesci. pag. 174. 175. Resp. Circa tempus, quo Paulus praesentem Epistolam scripsit, in partes itur. In hoc consensus est, scriptam esse post Synodum Hierosolymitanam. Haec autem juxta Hieronymum & Baronium habita post Christum quinquagesimo quarto; juxta Calvisium, quadragesimo octavo; juxta Usserium Armachanum quinquagesimo primo. Epistola vero prior ad Corinthios juxta Baronium scripta est anno quinquagesimo septimo; juxta Calvisium quinquagesimo quinto, initio Veris; juxta Usserium quinquagesimo nono. Sive igitur Baronii computo stemus, anni tres, sive Calvisii, novem, sive Usserii, anni septem intercedunt. Qui postremus calculus rationibus temporum maxime convenire videtur. Scripsit enim suam Epistolam Ephesi, ubi se permansurum usque ad Pentecosten scribit, 1. Cor. XVI. 5. 6. 7. 8.
units.tr: The gist of his objection: Paul wrote this Epistle a year after the Council of Jerusalem, or at least there was a very short interval of time between the two, namely the Council and the writing of this Epistle. In this case, the general statement must be explained from the particular decree of the Synod. So when the Apostle says, "Whatever comes in the meat market, eat," etc., the matter itself indicates that it must be understood this way, unless there is some special prohibition by which it is forbidden. The Apostles had made such a decree shortly before, and Paul neither wished nor was able to derogate from their decrees. We have no particular relaxation from that prohibition, and therefore we cannot be certain in conscience that it is lawful to eat blood. p. 174, 175. Reply: On the time when Paul wrote the present Epistle, opinions differ. All agree that it was written after the Council of Jerusalem. That Council, according to Jerome and Baronius, was held in the fifty-fourth year after Christ; according to Calvisius, in the forty-eighth; according to Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, in the fifty-first. The earlier Epistle to the Corinthians, according to Baronius, was written in the fifty-seventh year; according to Calvisius, in the fifty-fifth, at the beginning of spring; according to Ussher, in the fifty-ninth. So whether we follow Baronius's computation, which gives three years, or Calvisius's, which gives nine, or Ussher's, which gives seven years intervene. This last reckoning seems most in agreement with the chronology of the times. For Paul wrote his Epistle at Ephesus, where he writes that he will remain until Pentecost (1 Cor. 16:5–8).

units.la: Transmisit Epheso epistolam per Stephanum, Fortunatum & Achaicum. Inter Synodum autem Hierosolymitanam, & ejus in Asiam Lydiacam adventum, in qua per urbes Epheso vicinas Evangelium prædicâsse videtur, interjungendi anni minimùm sex vel septem, ut apparer ex diligenti examine τῶν πλαγχθέντων ab Apostolo à cap. XV. Actorum usque ad caput decimum nonum, ubi Lucas mentionem agitat Paulini in Ephesum adventus, v. 1. Totidem annorum spatium agnoscit Illustris Armachanus & Capellus, qui tamen ab Usserio diversus in eo abit, quòd Synodum celebratam dicat anno quadragesimo quinto: Epistolam priorem ad Corinthios scriptam quinquagesimo primo, posteriorem sequente, ut & Epistolam ad Romanos. Fefellisse igitur calculus & Alstedium Chronologum & Curcellaeum videtur. Ex quo etiam omnis Curcellaei disputatio in spongiam incumbit. Si enim sex ad minimum anni inter Synodum & scriptionem hujus epistolæ intercedunt, annon censeri potest, generali hac concessione speciale interdictum de sanguine & suffocato, olim in Synodo ad tempus sancitum, abrogâsse? Cùm enim Apostolus ipse membrum Synodi fuerit, & optimè cognoverit illius interdicti sensum, planè consentaneum erat, hoc loco exceptionem, si non accuratè, at certè vel levi brachio attingere? Nam Corinthii Gentiles, antehac sanguinis esui assueti, tam universali & latâ sententiâ, nullo modo limitatâ, facilè potuissent in erroris hujus regionem induci, sanguinem jam licitum esse. Imò quod attentione dignissimum, Apostolus concessionem hanc opponit illis, qui casum movebant: utrum idolothyta saltem materialiter, quâ caro sunt, sine conscientia idoli, concedi possint? Jam notorium est, Apostolos in Synodo juxta esum sanguinis & suffocati prohibuisse ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων, v. 20. id est εἰδωλόθυτα, v. 29. & tamen generali concessione interdictum illud hoc loco Apostolus relaxat. Si concessio illa juxta sensum Synodi, generale ex speciali, exprimi debet, tum sequitur, ne quidem esum idolothyti Corinthiis integrum fuisse. Quomodo igitur satisfecit Apostolus quæstioni Corinthiorum? Et cui bono universalem illam sententiam subjunxit? Nam quòd Curcellaeus in explicatione loci Act. XV.20. innuit, Apostolos in Synodo idolothyta prohibuisse non materialiter, sed formaliter, quatenus in idoleo comedebantur cum aliqua idoli reverentia, id infra suo loco non convenire per omnia. veritati, demonstrabimus. X. Quin-
units.tr: He sent the Epistle from Ephesus through Stephanus, Fortunatus and Achaicus. Between the Council of Jerusalem and his coming into Lydian Asia, where he seems to have preached the Gospel in the cities near Ephesus, at least six or seven years must be interposed. This appears from a careful examination of the things Paul went through (τῶν πλαγχθέντων), from Acts ch. 15 to ch. 19, where Luke mentions Paul's arrival at Ephesus (v. 1). The Most Illustrious Archbishop of Armagh and Capellus also acknowledge a span of the same number of years, though they differ from Ussher in saying that the Council was held in the forty-fifth year, the earlier Epistle to the Corinthians was written in the fifty-first, and the later one, like the Epistle to the Romans, in the following year. So the calculation of Alstedius the chronologer and of Curcellaeus seems to have gone astray. From this, all of Curcellaeus's argument collapses like a sponge. For if at least six years lie between the Council and the writing of this Epistle, can it not be judged that this general concession has abrogated the special prohibition about blood and what is strangled, once enacted at the Synod for a time? For since the Apostle himself was a member of the Synod and knew very well the sense of that prohibition, was it not entirely consistent for him to touch this exception here, if not precisely, at least with a light hand? For the Corinthian Gentiles, who had been accustomed to eat blood before, could easily have been led by such a universal and broad statement, not limited in any way, into the error of thinking that blood was now lawful. Indeed, what is most worthy of attention: the Apostle sets this concession against those who raised the question whether idol-offerings, at least materially as flesh, could be granted without any conscience of the idol. It is now well known that the Apostles in the Synod forbade, along with the eating of blood and what is strangled, what is from idols (ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων, v. 20), that is, εἰδωλόθυτα [idol-offerings] (v. 29). Yet here the Apostle relaxes that prohibition by a general concession. If that concession must, according to the sense of the Synod, be expressed as the general from the special, then it follows that the eating of idol-offerings was not even allowed to the Corinthians in full. How then did the Apostle satisfy the Corinthians' question? And to what purpose did he add that universal statement? As for Curcellaeus's hint, in his explanation of Acts 15:20, that the Apostles in the Synod forbade idol-offerings not materially but formally, insofar as they were eaten at an idol's feast with some reverence for the idol, I will show in its proper place that this does not agree with the truth in every respect.

units.la: X. Quintum argumentum promimus ex Coloss. II. 16. 17. Ne quis vos judicet in cibo & potu, quæ umbra futurorum, Corpus autem Christi. Et v. 20. 21. Quid adhuc, tanquam viventes in seculo, decretis illis tenemini? Ne tetigeris, ne gustaris, ne contrectaris. Perstringit tum Gentilismum tum Judaïsmum, quorum ille decipere parabat per philosophiam & inanem fallaciam, hic secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi: uterque contra Christum, in quo inhabitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter, v. 8, 9. &c. Qui cum chirographum, quod nobis contrarium erat, expunxerit, dedit libertatem iis, qui cum Christo convivificati, ne quisquam eos in cibo vel potu judicet, neque constringat legalibus illis decretis, ne tangant, ne gustent, ne contrectent. Unde argumentum irrefragabile, necessimus pro libertate Christianorum in esu sanguinis. Qui enim in esu & potu non sunt obnoxii ullius, sive legis Divinæ, sive hominis judicio; neque tenentur legalibus illis decretis, illis liberum est, sanguinem tangere vel non tangere, gustare vel non gustare. Scripsit Paulus Epistolam ad Colossenses satis longo tempore post Hierosolymitanam Synodum. Misit enim Româ per Tychicum & Onesimum. Et in fine vinculorum suorum meminit cap. IV. 18. Atque adeo minimum tredecim anni inter Synodum & scriptionem hujus epistolæ intercedunt, ut pater attendenti. In eo certe intervallo temporaria lex Hierosolymis lata, Judæis conversis jam contra scandali metum obfirmatis, observari desita est: vel, si non desita, universali hac sententiâ Apostoli abrogata, nec extra scandalum obligare pergat.
units.tr: X. We bring forward a fifth argument from Colossians 2:16-17: Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. And verses 20-21: Wherefore, if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, (Touch not; taste not; handle not;) He attacks both Gentilism and Judaism: the former sought to deceive by philosophy and empty deceit, the latter by the tradition of men and the elements of the world. Both are set against Christ, in whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, verses 8-9, and so on. Since he has blotted out the handwriting that was against us, he has given freedom to those who have been made alive together with Christ, so that no one may judge them in meat or drink, nor bind them with those legal decrees: Touch not, taste not, handle not. Hence we have an irrefutable argument for the freedom of Christians in eating blood. For those who are not bound in eating and drinking, either by the judgment of God's law or of man, and who are not held by those legal decrees, are free to touch or not touch blood, to taste or not taste it. Paul wrote the Epistle to the Colossians a fairly long time after the Synod of Jerusalem; he sent it from Rome by Tychicus and Onesimus, and at the end he mentions his bonds (chapter 4:18). So at least thirteen years, as the attentive reader will see, lie between the Synod and the writing of this epistle. In that interval, certainly, the temporary law enacted at Jerusalem ceased to be observed, since the converted Jews had by then been strengthened against the fear of scandal; or, if it did not cease, it was abrogated by this universal sentence of the Apostle, and it cannot continue to bind outside the case of scandal.

units.la: XI. Respondet Curcellæus. 1. Hic nullam fieri mentionem sanguinis, nec prohiberi, ne quis judicet edentem. pag. 176. Resp. Quod de genere & de omni vel nullo prædicatur, illud prædicari etiam convenit de speciebus, ut docet ratio, & astipulantur Logicorum πειθες. 2. Nisi Apostoli verba limitentur, fore, ut multa absurda sequantur. Sic enim non debere judicari, si quis pravè se gerat circa cibum & potum. Respond. Est vanissima argutatio. Quamcunque libertatem circa cibum & potum, sive universalem sive particularem statuamus, semper hoc reponi poterit. Apostolus dicit, nos ad libertatem vocatos. Sed vetat tamen, ne libertatem arripiamus, ut datam carni occasionem, Gal. V. 13. Universalis rei indifferentis usus universalem abusum habere potest. Nam eæ res, quæ natura neque bonæ neque malæ sunt, in alterutram partem determinantur ab animi affectu & concupiscentia. Hinc Apostolus. Nihil per se immundum: sed λογιζομένω. Et scite Augustinus apud Posidon. in ejus vita, cap. 22. Non ego immunditiem obsonii, sed immunditiem cupiditatis timeo. 3. Etiam illum fore damnabilem, & dignum a quo omnes abhorrerent, qui vellet carne humana vesci, ut feri Cannibales faciunt. pag. 166. Respond. Hoc per se intelligitur, naturā suā turpe esse, & homine nedum Christiano indignum. Apostolus, explicans libertatem Christianorum, respicit ad cibum & potum, qui in V. T. Legaliter immundus censebatur. Hujus jam usum promiscuum concedit. In V. T. autem non censebatur caro humana legaliter immunda, sed naturaliter omnes ab anthropophagia abhorrebant. Hinc etiam Gentiles detestari piaculare m hunc esum. Martialis: Divi prandia nec refert Thyestæ. Et ut generis sui consortes Christianorum odio imbuerent Gentiles, juxta alia dira scelera Θυέστεα δεῖπνα iis imputārunt. Athenagoras. Τεῖα Οἰνφημίζουσιν ἡμῖν ἐγκλήματα, αἰτιότητα, Θυέστεα δεῖπνα, Οἰδυπόδειος μίξεις. Trium igitur flagitiorum infamis rumor de nobis spargitur: impietas, quæ Deos tollat, Epulā Thyestea & Oedipodii coitus. Quæ crimina Christianis objecta Athenagoras in postrema ejusdem orationis parte refellit. Quin & Justinus, qui vocat ἀνθρωποφαγίαν ἐπεχῶν βορᾶς, Tatianus, Tertullianus. Pii Martyres Galliæ, qui Viennam & Lugdunum Galliæ incolebant, in Epistola ad Fratres in Asia & Phrygia scripta inter alia queruntur: Quosdam Ethnicos, Christianorum servos captos, cum tormenta Christianorum reformidarent, militibus Sathanæ illos ad hoc incitantibus, Thyestæas Cœnas, & incestum Oedipodis contra se commentos esse, & alia, quæ nec eloqui, nec cogitare fas sit, apud Euseb. Hist. Eccles. V. 1. Quod minimè fecissent, nisi hoc flagitium ἀνθρωποβορείας omnium judicâssent atrocissimum. Videtur dira & insana criminatio illorum occasionem captâsse ex doctrina Christianorum, de augusto Cœnæ Dominicæ Sacramento, ad illos perperam ac malitiosè delata. Hinc Tertullianus: Dicimur sceleratissimi de Sacramento infanticidii & pabulo inde. In Dialogo Minutii Felicis Cæcilius paganus objicit Octavio Christiano: Infans farre contectus, ut decipiat incautos, apponitur.
units.tr: XI. Curcellaeus replies: (1) Here no mention is made of blood, nor is it forbidden that anyone should judge the one who eats it, p. 176. Answer: what is predicated of a genus, universally or not at all, is also rightly predicated of its species, as reason teaches, and the logicians' πειθες agrees. (2) Unless the words of the Apostle are limited, many absurdities will follow. For on this showing one ought not to be judged if he behaves badly with regard to food and drink. Answer: this is a most empty quibble. Whatever freedom we posit concerning food and drink, whether universal or particular, this same objection can always be raised. The Apostle says that we are called to liberty, yet he forbids us to use liberty as an occasion for the flesh, Galatians 5:13. The universal use of a thing indifferent can have a universal abuse. For things which by nature are neither good nor evil are determined to one side or the other by the affection and desire of the mind. Hence the Apostle: Nothing is unclean of itself, but to him that esteemeth anything to be unclean (λογιζομένω). And Augustine, cleverly, in Possidius's life of him, chapter 22: I fear not the uncleanness of the food, but the uncleanness of desire. (3) He also would be deserving of condemnation, and one from whom all would shrink in horror, who wished to feed on human flesh, as savage cannibals do, p. 166. Answer: this is self-evident, that by its nature it is foul and unworthy of any man, let alone a Christian. The Apostle, explaining the liberty of Christians, has regard to food and drink, which in the Old Testament was legally reckoned unclean. Curcellaeus now concedes the promiscuous use of these. But in the Old Testament human flesh was not reckoned legally unclean; rather, all men by nature shrank from anthropophagy. Hence the Gentiles also regarded this eating as an abomination. Martial: Nor does it matter that they are the feasts of Thyestes. And to fill the Gentiles with hatred for the Christians, who were of their own kind, they imputed to them, along with other dire crimes, Thyestean feasts (Θυέστεα δεῖπνα). Athenagoras: Three charges are brought against us, the Thyestean feast, the Oedipodean unions, and atheism, which removes the gods. Athenagoras refutes these accusations against the Christians in the last part of the same oration. So too Justin, who speaks of abstaining from man-eating food (ἀνθρωποφαγίαν ἐπεχῶν βορᾶς), Tatian, and Tertullian. The holy martyrs of Gaul, who lived at Vienne and Lyons, complain in their letter written to the brethren in Asia and Phrygia, among other things: That certain heathens, captured slaves of Christians, fearing the torments of the Christians, and with the soldiers of Satan urging them on, invented against them Thyestean banquets and the incest of Oedipus, and other things which it is not right to utter or even to think, quoted in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History V.1. They would not have done this unless they had judged this crime of man-eating to be the most atrocious of all. The dire and mad accusation seems to have taken its occasion from the doctrine of the Christians concerning the holy Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, which was wrongly and maliciously reported to them. Hence Tertullian: We are called most wicked because of the Sacrament of infanticide and the food that comes from it. In the Dialogue of Minucius Felix, the heathen Caecilius objects to the Christian Octavius: An infant covered with flour is set out, so as to deceive the unwary.

units.la: XII. Curcellæus aliud agendo quærit: An saltem in casu necessitatis & extremæ famis liceat latrantem stomachum ex diris huma-
units.tr: XII. Curcellaeus, while talking about something else, asks: may a person at least in a case of necessity and extreme famine appease the barking stomach with the dreadful feast of human flesh?

units.la: humanarum carnium epulis compescere? Non alio animo quaerit, quàm ut opportunitatem capiet Reformatos criminandi. Nam in obsidione Sancerrae in Gallia, anno post Christum natum millesimo quingentesimo septuagesimo, juxta Serrarium, Chytraeum, Thuanum & Calvisium, Parentes duo, vel Vetulae, vel dirissimae famis consilio, mortuae filiolae caput, jecur & ilia devorârunt. Quas horrendas dapes ex Magistratus Sancerrani Reformati decreto mortis supplicio expiârunt. Hoc supplicium criminatur tanquam Regie & crudeliter ab Anthropophagis illis expetitum. De re ipsa ut dicamus, haud dubie etiam in casu urgentis famis, desperatis rebus, praestat mortem magis prandere quàm humanas carnes. Est enim honesta mors turpi vita potior, & incolumitas ac decus eodem loco sita sunt. Tacit. Agric. XXXIII. II. Id quod pro vero etiam Curcellaeus asseruit. Nunquam enim Christiano turpe & horribile aliquid designare ad vitam lucri faciendam licet. Neque verum est, honestam esse quamlibet rationem expediundae salutis. Nobis enim unum hoc relictum; ut obsequio grassemur. De vita nostra faciet, quod è re nostra est, ille vitae & necis arbiter. Ipse mille artes habet, quibus pro salute nostra excubat, quando nobis res in anceps praecipitare videntur. In Samaritana obsidione videmus, cùm jam impiae mulieres ferales illas dapes appetiissent, Regem Joramum tristi hoc experimento motum, ut de deditione consilia animo volutaret. Quin & rebus in deliquii puncto haerentibus, exercitus Syriae panico terrore copiarum Israeliticarum perculsus, ab obsidione discessit, & tabernacula opum cibariorumque reliquit. Sic opimâ praedâ Israelitae potiti. Dei igitur bonitati in ejusmodi casu confidendum, qui non amat humani maleficii & fraudum suppetias. Contemplemur historiam calamitosissimam, quae in excidio Urbis Hierosolymitanae, furiosa fame invalescente, accidit, si fides est Josepho de Bello Judaico lib. VII. cap. 8. Ea jam fames incrementa habuit, ut calceamenta, coria scutis detracta, vetúsque foenum cibus esset. Matrem furiae agitaverant, ut filium raperet, quem lactantem habuit, & tragica ad ipsum oratione habitâ, eum occideret coctúmque medium comederet, adopertum verò reliquum servaret. Aderant contaminatissimi nidoris odore capti, qui cogerent ostendere, quod parabat. Ergo filii reliquias protulit. Illos horror cepit atque dementia, visúque ipso diriguerunt. Mox repleta eo scelere tota civitas. Ab omnibus autem, quos fames urgebat, properabatur ad mortem, & beati appellabantur, qui priùs, quàm id paterentur, interiissent. Citò etiam Romanis nuntiata calamitas. Eorum alii non credebant: alii miserabantur: multos vehementius ejus gentis odium capiebat. Cæsar autem Ethnicus adeò facinore hoc commotus, ut minaretur, scelus hujus nefarii victus sese patriæ ruinâ operturum, neque reliquum in orbe terræ, aut Sol inspiciat civitatem, in qua matres sic vescerentur. Prædixerant tantam calamitatem Paulus & Petrus, teste Lactantio lib. 4. cap. 21. Fore nimirum, ut corporibus suorum vescerentur, & consumerent se invicem &c. Eò quòd exultaverant super amantissimum & probatissimum Filium Dei. Prodigiosæ crudelitatis exemplum merito & cives, & Romanos, ac cum primis Imperatorem stupore perculit. Quanto rectius Annibalis filius in Italiam proficiscens consilium sibi datum, ut exercitum carnibus humanis edendis assuefaceret, ut hac ratione nunquam commeatu indigeret, detrectavit. Jam de Sancerrano Magistratu paucis Illustris Historicus Aug. Thuanus Hist. Lib. LV. postquam commemoravit famem prodigiosam, quam perpetiebantur Sancerrani, subjicit pag. 1055. Et ne quid ad extremæ necessitatis exemplum deesset, puella trienni ex fame mortua & jam elata, de consilio Vetula refossa, ipsis parentibus cibo fuit, qui tamen re comperta Magistratus sententia ad ignem damnati sunt: ut hæc obsidio Samaritana famis in Sacris libris memorata, Hierosolymitana à Flavio Josepho descripta, & Numantina historiis Romanis celebrata, quæ vix à multis creditur, fidem adstruat. Hîc decretorium stylum Curcellæus stringit, & tantùm non Draconis leges objicit, quàmvis qui in hac parte peccabat, durius censeam capite plectere, ut inter Reformatos factum in Sancerra obsidione. Atqui quis dubitet Magistratui graves constitisse decreti sui rationes, quas & Serrarius & Thuanus silentii supparo involverunt? Ipsum scelus ejusmodi, ut crudelitatem impietatemque in corpus humanum, in quo vivente imago Dei eluxerat, & quod jam quieti publico ritu destinabatur: denique horribile facinus, in filiam, quam editam in hanc lucem deglutiit, atque sic sua viscera in suis visceribus condidit, involvit. Accessit & hoc, quòd fame malesuada, & molesto interpellatore obsessos urgente, periculi metus incessebat, ne, si impunitate donarentur parentes, detestabili exemplo excitarentur rentur alii, ac tandem impetus in viventium corpora verteretur. Exemplo igitur unus fuit. Terror ad caeteros redire debuit.
units.tr: He does not ask this for any other purpose than to seize the chance of accusing the Reformed. For at the siege of Sancerre in France, in the year of our Lord 1570, according to Serrarius, Chytraeus, Thuanus and Calvisius, two parents, either old women or men driven by the counsel of dreadful hunger, ate the head, liver and entrails of their dead little daughter. For these horrible meals they paid the death penalty by decree of the Reformed magistrates of Sancerre. Curcellaeus accuses this punishment of being demanded by those cannibals as a royal and cruel thing. As to the matter itself, let us say that, undoubtedly even in a case of pressing famine, when all hope is lost, it is better to die than to eat human flesh. For an honourable death is preferable to a shameful life, and safety and honour lie in the same place (Tacitus, Agricola 33). Curcellaeus too has asserted this as true. For it is never lawful for a Christian to do anything foul and horrible in order to make a gain of life. Nor is it true that any means of saving one's life is honourable. For we have only this one thing left: to submit to God. He, the arbiter of our life and death, will do what is good for us. He has a thousand ways of watching over our safety when things seem to be plunging us into peril. In the siege of Samaria we see that, when the impious women had already desired those deadly meals, King Joram was moved by this sad experience to turn over in his mind terms of surrender. Moreover, when things were at a standstill, the army of Syria, struck with panic by the Israelite forces, withdrew from the siege and left its tents, wealth and provisions behind; thus the Israelites seized rich plunder. Therefore we must trust in the goodness of God in such a case, who does not love the help of human wickedness and fraud. Let us consider the most calamitous history that occurred at the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, when famine raged furiously, if we may trust Josephus, De Bello Judaico, book 7, chapter 8. The famine had grown so great that shoes and leather were stripped from shields and old hay was food. A mother was driven mad so that she snatched up the son she was nursing, and after making a tragic speech to him, she killed him, cooked half of him and ate him, and kept the rest covered. Men were present, drawn by the smell of that most defiled stench, who forced her to show what she was preparing. So she produced the remains of her son. Horror and madness seized them, and they were stunned at the very sight. Soon the whole city was filled with that crime. But from all whom famine pressed, there was a rush to death, and those were called blessed who died before they had to endure this. The calamity was soon reported to the Romans as well. Some of them did not believe it; others pitied; many felt a fiercer hatred for that nation. The pagan Caesar was so moved by this deed that he threatened that, having been overcome by the crime of this wicked act, he would cover the ruin of his country, and that the sun should not look upon any city on earth in which mothers fed in this way. Paul and Peter had foretold such a great calamity, as Lactantius witnesses (book 4, chapter 21): that they would indeed feed on the bodies of their own and consume one another, and so on, because they had exulted over the most beloved and most approved Son of God. The example of monstrous cruelty rightly struck with amazement both the citizens, the Romans and above all the Emperor. How much more wisely did Hannibal's son, when setting out for Italy, refuse the advice given him to accustom his army to eating human flesh, so that by this means it would never need supplies. Now, concerning the magistracy of Sancerre, let us say a few words. The illustrious historian Thuanus, Histories book 55, after recalling the prodigious famine that the people of Sancerre suffered, adds at page 1055: And so that nothing might be lacking as an example of extreme necessity, a girl of three years, who had died of hunger and was already buried, was dug up on the old woman's advice and became food for her own parents; but when the matter came to light, they were condemned to the fire by sentence of the magistrates. Thus this siege of Samaria, recorded in the Sacred Books of famine, the Jerusalem siege described by Flavius Josephus, and the Numantine siege celebrated in Roman histories, which is scarcely believed by many, lends its support to this account. Here Curcellaeus draws his decisive stylus and almost throws the laws of Draco at us, although I would judge that anyone who sinned in this matter should be punished by death, as was done among the Reformed at the siege of Sancerre. But who would doubt that the magistrate had serious reasons for his decree, which both Serrarius and Thuanus have wrapped in a cloak of silence? Such a crime, namely cruelty and impiety against a human body, in which the image of God had shone while it lived, and which was already destined for public burial rites; finally, a horrible deed against a daughter whom the mother had brought into this light and then swallowed, thus hiding her own entrails in her own entrails. There was also this, that since famine was harsh and the besieged were pressed by an troublesome intruder, there was a fear of danger: if the parents were granted impunity, others might be stirred up by the detestable example, and at last the assault would turn upon the bodies of the living. So the punishment fell on one person as an example. Terror was bound to return to the rest.

units.la: XIII. Nondum satis tenebrarum textui Apostolico offusum. Excipit igitur ad extremum: Ut antecedentia suadent: Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam &c. verisimile esse, Apostolum potius respexisse ad dogmata Pythagoreorum, qui esum carnium in universum damnabant, quàm ad solam legem Mosis, qua tantum aliqua animalium species prohibebantur, ita ut libertatem sanguine vescendi non indulgeat, cujus nullam plane mentionem fecit: non magis quàm carne humana, à qua semper paulò humaniores abhorruerunt. pag. 178.
units.tr: XIII. The Apostolic text is still not sufficiently obscured. So he finally brings forward this objection: As the preceding words suggest: "Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy," etc., it is likely that the Apostle had in mind rather the doctrines of the Pythagoreans, who condemned the eating of meat altogether, than the law of Moses alone, by which only certain species of animals were forbidden; so it does not grant liberty to eat blood, of which he made no mention at all, any more than to eat human flesh, which the more civilised have always abhorred. Page 178.

units.la: Respond. 1. Pythagoreos tangi non dubito. Tametsi de ipso Pythagora non omnino verè dicunt, carnibus ipsum abstinuisse. Agellii de ipso verba sunt lib. IV. c. 11. Opinio vetus falsa occupavit & convaluit, Pythagoram Philosophum non esitavisse ex animalibus. Idem abstinuisse fabulâ, quem Graeci κυάμων appellant. Sed Aristoxenus Musicus, nullo sapiens legumento Pythagoram dicit usum quàm fabis: porculis quoque minusculis & haedis tenerioribus victitasse, idem Aristoxenus refert. De hoc quicquid fiat, Philosophos ipsum secutos, ac Aegyptios, quorum disciplina imbutus est, σεμνοφαγίαν damnasse certum est. De quo vide Plutarchum, in peculiari de hac re libello.
units.tr: Reply 1. I do not doubt that the Pythagoreans are touched upon, although they do not say altogether truly that Pythagoras himself abstained from meat. The words of Aulus Gellius about him are (book 4, chapter 11): An old false opinion took hold and prevailed, that the philosopher Pythagoras abstained from animals. He is also said to have abstained from the bean, which the Greeks call kyamōn [κυάμων]. But Aristoxenus the musician says that Pythagoras used no food except beans, and that he lived on small pigs and tender kids; Aristoxenus reports this too. Whatever the truth of this, it is certain that the philosophers who followed him, and the Egyptians, by whose teaching he was steeped, condemned semnophagia [σεμνοφαγίαν], that is, a solemn abstinence from certain foods. On this see Plutarch in his special little book on this subject.

units.la: Hos igitur Apostolus haud dubiè pulsavit illis verbis: Ne quis vos decipiat per inanem Philosophiam, &c. Qua cautione nos dehortatus est ab omnium Philosophorum Gentilium erroribus, quorum pigmenta sunt: ratio Sapientiae, cultus voluntarius, summissio animi, ne parcatur corpori &c. 2. Judaeos tamen haud obscurè juxta Philosophos Gentiles pulsat, ad quos pertinent haec indicia. Decipere secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum: dogmata & decreta sua commendare de non tangendo, gustando, contrectando: judicare in cibo, potu, in parte diei festi, neomenia, aut Sabbatorum, quae sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi. 16. 17. Scripta enim est Epistola, ex communi sensu contra Simonem Magum, & pestilentis illius haeresis asseclas, qui teste Chrysostomo & Ambrosio, Angelos ceu mediatores nostros divino cultu mactarunt, & dogmati huic, monente Theophylacto, multas observationes Judaicas & Gentilitias addiderunt. Legem igitur Moisis respexit. Imò magis quàm Epicuraeos philosophos, uti apparet ex v. 16. 17. 3. Cùm igitur sub lege ceremoniali Mosis contineatur interdictum de sanguine, illud hac declaratione antiquavit. Legem naturalem de non vorandis humanis carnibus, quippe de qua nihil dixit Moses ad populum exserte, neque respexit, neque antiquare potuit. Atque sic manet adamantinis loris adstricta nostra demonstratio.
units.tr: It is therefore without doubt these that the Apostle struck with those words: "Let no one deceive you through empty philosophy," etc. By this caution he warned us against the errors of all the pagan philosophers, whose trinkets are: the appearance of wisdom, voluntary worship, humility of mind, and not sparing the body, etc. 2. Yet he touches the Jews, not obscurely, along with the pagan philosophers, to whom these marks belong: to deceive according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; to commend their dogmas and decrees about not touching, tasting, handling; to judge concerning food, drink, a part of a festival day, the new moon, or the Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's. (Col. 2:16, 17.) For the epistle was written, by common consent, against Simon Magus and the followers of that pestilent heresy, who, as Chrysostom and Ambrose witness, offered divine worship to angels as if they were our mediators, and, as Theophylact warns, added to this doctrine many Jewish and Gentile observances. He therefore had in view the law of Moses. Indeed, he had it in view more than the Epicurean philosophers, as appears from verses 16 and 17. 3. Since, then, the prohibition concerning blood is contained within the ceremonial law of Moses, the Apostle abrogated it by this declaration. But the natural law concerning not eating human flesh, about which Moses said nothing explicitly to the people, neither did he have it in view, nor could he abrogate it. And so our demonstration remains bound with adamantine thongs.

units.la: XIV. Sextum argumentum sequitur ex Tit.I. 15. Omnia sunt munda mundis: Pollutis autem & infidelibus nihil mundum, sed polluta est illorum mens & conscientia. Perstringit Apostolus Cretenses, quorum describit mores, v.12.13. Jubet nos redarguere, v.13. 14.16. ac curat in iis vitae & doctrinae morbum. Vitae morbum in verbis: Omnia munda sunt mundis &c. Morbus fuit Judaizantium, Judaicas fabulas & traditiones hominum complectentium, v.14. Quales fabulae potissimum erant, inquit Cornelius a Lapide ex Hieronymo & Chrysostomo, de servandis legis Ceremoniis, praesertim de servando ciborum delectu. Ergo hac sententia generali munditiem etiam sanguinis Apostolus declaravit. Curcellaeus respondet. 1. Non constare, illud de cibis particulariter intelligendum esse, qui non nominantur, pag.179. Respond. De cibis interpretantur Chrysostomus, Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Ambrosius, Vatablus, Erasmus, alii. Et patet ex rebus ipsis. Perstringit enim Judaizantes, qui dogmatizabant, in potu, cibo, festis, Sabbatho. Deinde ita interpretatur Apostolus, 1.Tim.IV.3.4. Neque mirum erat, Cretenses Judaica haec deliria adoptasse, quia magna fuit per maris viciniam communio Judaeorum cum Cretensibus, adeoque Judaei nobiles in Creta habitare soliti, teste Josepho, in sua vita, ubi hac de causa uxorem se ex Creta accepisse narrat. Quin & hinc natus videtur Cornelii Taciti error, qui Judaeos e Creta ascendisse asseverat, & Judaeos dictos quasi Idaeos ab Ida monte, qui est in Creta, Histor. V.2.1.2. Non erat cur cibos nominaret. Hoc enim ex se constabat, cum de munditie & immunditie ciborum Judaizantes disceptarint. 2. Haec adeo generalia esse, ut, nisi prudenter ex Apostoli mente limitentur, inde colligi queat, etiam furta, homicidia, adulteria Christianis esse licita, nihilque pro peccato habendum, nisi quod repugnante conscientia committitur. ib. Resp. Exceptiones malarum rerum in omni praecepto vel imperii vel indulgentiae praesupponuntur. Deus enim peccatum odit, neque est ἀκατάσχετος Spiritus. Utrum autem malus sit esus sanguinis, quaeritur & sub judice lis est. Impudentissimus Jesuita quidem Cornelius à Lapide non verecundatur Luthero impiam hanc consequentiam impingere: Si omnia munda mundis, ergo fornicatio quoque est munda mundis, puta fidelibus. Sicut enim, inquit, nihil justificat nisi fides, ita nihil coinquinat nisi infidelitas. Comm. ad h. l. Sed heus, Jesuita, frustra Herculi! Fumus est e ficubus. Fidelibus omnia munda esse recte Lutherus dixit, quatenus nihil immundum, quod sincera fide erga Christum geritur. An vero etiam scelera ex fide in Christum patrantur? Apage dementiam. Et tamen hi Sycophantae Evangelicam & salutarem de fide doctrinam jocularibus his convitiis quotidie mactant.
units.tr: XIV. The sixth argument follows from Titus 1:15: To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled. The Apostle rebukes the Cretans, whose manners he describes in vv. 12–13. He bids us rebuke them (vv. 13–14, 16) and addresses the disease of their life and their teaching. The disease of life is shown in the words To the pure all things are pure, etc. The disease was that of the Judaizers, who embraced Jewish fables and the traditions of men (v. 14). Cornelius a Lapide, following Jerome and Chrysostom, says that the fables chiefly concerned keeping the ceremonies of the law, especially keeping a distinction among foods. So by this general saying the Apostle also declared the cleanness of blood. Curcellaeus replies: 1. It is not certain that this must be understood particularly of foods, since none are named, p. 179. Reply: Chrysostom, Jerome, Theodoret, Ambrose, Vatablus, Erasmus and others explain it of foods, and the matter itself makes this plain. For the Apostle is rebuking the Judaizers, who taught about drink, food, feasts and the Sabbath. Moreover, the Apostle interprets it in the same way at 1 Tim. 4:3–4. Nor is it surprising that the Cretans adopted these Jewish follies, since there was great intercourse between the Jews and the Cretans across the nearby sea. Indeed, Josephus, in his Life, says that Jews of standing used to live in Crete, and for this reason he relates that he took a wife from Crete. Hence, it seems, comes the error of Cornelius Tacitus, who asserts that the Jews came from Crete and that they were called Jews as if Idaei, from Mount Ida, which is in Crete (Histories 5.2). There was no reason for him to name foods, since this was clear from the matter itself, when the Judaizers disputed about the cleanness and uncleanness of foods. 2. These statements are so general that, unless they are prudently limited according to the Apostle's mind, one could infer that even theft, murder and adultery are lawful for Christians, and that nothing is to be counted a sin except what is committed against the conscience. ib. Reply: Exceptions for bad things are always presupposed in every precept, whether of command or of permission. For God hates sin, and the Spirit is not [ἀκατάσχετος] unrestrainable. Whether the eating of blood is evil, however, is in dispute and is still under judgement. The most shameless Jesuit Cornelius a Lapide does not hesitate to fasten on Luther this impious consequence: If all things are pure to the pure, then fornication too is pure to the pure, that is, to the faithful. For just as, he says, nothing justifies except faith, so nothing defiles except unbelief. Commentary on this passage. But, you Jesuit, you labour in vain, like Hercules! It is smoke from figs. Luther rightly said that all things are pure to believers, insofar as nothing is unclean that is done in sincere faith towards Christ. But are crimes committed out of faith in Christ? Far from it, what madness! Yet these sycophants every day batter the evangelical and saving doctrine of faith with such jesting insults.

units.la: XV. Septimum argumentum stringimus ex gravissima Apostoli, 1. Tim. IV. 1.2.3.4.
units.tr: XV. We set out the seventh argument from the most serious passage of the Apostle, 1 Tim. 4:1–4.

units.la: Spiritus diserte dicit, quod posterioribus temporibus defluxuri sint quidam à fide, attendentes Spiritibus erroneis & doctrinis daemoniorum, prohibentium nubere, abstinere à cibis, quos Deus condidit ad percipiendum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus & iis, qui cognoverunt veritatem. Quia omnis Dei creatura bona est, & nihil rejiciendum, quod cum gratiarum actione recipitur. Ubi vili pendo Pelusiotae virgulam criticam, qui pro ἀπέχεσθαι judicavit legi debere ἀπέχεσθαι lib. IV. Epist. 122. Atqui & Latinis usitatum, ut alteri tantum e nominibus respondeat verbum, quale est; judicium & poenas exercere: cum judicium exerceatur, poenae sumantur. Apud Tacitum Germ. VII. 4. Mulieres cibos & hortamina pugnantibus gestare dicuntur: cum cibi gestentur, non hortamina. Ita hic ἀνωλυόντων respondet duntaxat τῷ γαμεῖν. Jam de re Apostolus daemoniorum doctrinam vocat, mandare abstinentiam à cibo. Et rationem reddit: quod omnis creatura Dei bona sit, & nihil rejiciendum, cum gratiarum actione susceptum. Ubi altius ascendit Apostolus ad creationis historiam, postquam Deus omnia, quae creavit, valde bona esse declaravit. Respondet Curcellaeus. 1. Nisi restrictio aliqua commoda hic fiat, sequi etiam Apostolos Daemoniorum doctrinam proposuisse, si non in perpetuum, saltem ad tempus, quo ipsorum constitutio vigere debuit. pag. 179. Resp. Inter Synodum & scriptam hanc Epistolam intercedebant anni praeterpropter quatuordecim. In eo intervallo notoria mutatio potuit accidere. Sed demus, illo tempore nondum legis illius frenum laxatum fuisse, an ideo Apostoli etiam stante generali illa sententia in Concilio daemoniorum doctrinam proposuerunt? Absit blasphemiae accusemus viros θεοφορουμένους. Tulerunt quidem legem de sanguine, sed non tam jus sanguinis sta-mitârunt, quàm exercitium illius cibi in præsenti casu scandali. Unde qui dicto audientes fuerunt, non tam censendi custodivisse præ-ceptum aliquod de cibo, quàm præceptum de charitate, cui repugnat scandalum datum. Idolothytorum esus, si religioso imperio mandatur, haud dubiè doctrina Dæmoniorum est. Apostolus enim diserte concessit 1.Cor.X. Et tamen Apostoli cum sanguine conjunxerunt. 2. Paulus videtur ad illos hæreticos respe-xisse, qui existimabant cibos aliquos naturâ esse malos, à quibus ve-scentes inquinarentur. Respond.
