Eodem frigido schemate in alia, simili tamen causa, elabi conantur Bellarminus & Baronius. Jam respexerit Paulus ad hæreticos tales, puta Marcionitas, Encra-titas, Manichæos. An igitur non respexit Tertullianum, & qui su-pra sustinuit affirmare, carnium concessionem propter ᾰ̓λη-ѳοκατ-ᾰ̓ ... hominum factam? Annon omnes eos, qui saltem hoc commune ha-bent, ut prohibeant cibos? Maximè cùm Apostolus ne verbo qui-dem attigerit causam prohibitionis, sed tantùm prohibitionem ex-presserit. Sæpe ejusdem facti diversæ sunt causæ. Damnat Scriptu-ra eos, qui solvunt Jesum. Solverunt autem aliter atque aliter Arius & Nestorius. An propterea non æquè uterque damnatus? Eadem hîc ratio. Cùm constat liberum permissum à Christo om-nium ciborum usum, conscientiæ quidem causâ, quicunque con-scientiæ causâ illam libertatem infringit, sive prohibeat cibum, quia naturâ malus, sive alio modo quolibet, Dæmoniorum doctrinam propugnat. Neque pingi potest illorum causa hoc colore: Cau-sam prohibitionis in textu allegari his verbis: Omne, quod Deus crea-vit, bonum est, neque quicquam rejectaneum, quasi diceret: Diabo-los illos Doctores prohibere cibos quosdam tanquam malos, cùm tamen omnes cibi sint boni, puri, nulli rejectanei. Non ideo ad eos solos re-stringi debet. Sic Christus Matth.XIX.14. discipulos Christo infan-tes subducturos compellat: Ne prohibete eos. Rationem addit: Eorum enim est Regnum cœlorum. Discipuli propter hanc causam non subduxerant. Et hanc causam allegat Christus. Ita hoc loco Spiri-tus S. damnat omnes, qui prohibent cibos religionis gratiâ, quia omnes cibi boni. Hanc tamen rationem non necessario negare de-buerunt, quotquot prohibuerunt. Ut, qui ἀματοφαγίαν conscien-tiæ gratiâ prohibent, ab hoc reatu eximi nullo pacto possunt.
units.tr: The Spirit speaks expressly that in later times some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to erroneous spirits and doctrines of demons, forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. Here I think little of the critical twig of Isidore of Pelusium, who judged that for [ἀπέχεσθαι] one should read [ἀπέχεσθαι] (Epist. Bk IV, letter 122). Yet it is also a Latin usage that a verb answers to only one of the nouns, as in to exercise judgment and punishments, where judgment is exercised but punishments are inflicted. In Tacitus, Germania ch. 7: the women are said to carry food and encouragement to the fighting men, where food is carried but not encouragement. So here [κωλυόντων] answers only to [γαμεῖν] (marrying). Now as to the matter itself, the Apostle calls the teaching of commanding abstinence from food a doctrine of demons. And he gives the reason: because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving. Here the Apostle rises higher, to the history of creation, after God had declared that all he had made was very good. Curcellaeus replies: (1) Unless some suitable restriction is made here, it follows that the Apostles too set forth a doctrine of demons, if not for ever, at least for the time in which their constitution was to hold. (p. 179). Answer: between the Synod and this written letter lay roughly fourteen years. In that interval a notable change could have occurred. But grant that at that time the bridle of that law had not yet been loosened: did the Apostles, even while that general sentence stood in the Council, set forth a doctrine of demons? Far be it that we should accuse of blasphemy men who were [θεοφορουμένους, God-borne]. They did indeed enact a law about blood, but they did not so much establish the right of blood as address the practice of that food in the present case of scandal. Hence those who obeyed their word are to be judged not so much to have kept some precept about food as a precept about love, which the giving of scandal opposes. The eating of food offered to idols, if it were commanded by religious authority, is undoubtedly a doctrine of demons; for the Apostle expressly allowed it in 1 Cor. 10. And yet the Apostles joined it with blood. (2) Paul seems to have had in view those heretics who thought some foods were evil by nature, so that those who ate them were defiled. Answer: Bellarmine and Baronius try to escape in the same cold fashion in another, though similar, case. Granted that Paul had in view heretics of that kind, such as the Marcionites, Encratites and Manichaeans. Did he then not have in view Tertullian, who above maintained that the permission to eat meat was given on account of the ... of men? Do not all those who at least share this one thing, that they forbid foods, belong to the same group? Especially since the Apostle did not touch even in a word on the cause of the prohibition, but only expressed the prohibition itself. Often the causes of the same act are various. Scripture condemns those who dissolve Jesus. But Arius and Nestorius dissolved him in different ways. Are they therefore not equally condemned? The reasoning here is the same. Since it is certain that Christ granted free use of all foods, for the sake of conscience indeed, whoever breaks that liberty for the sake of conscience, whether he forbids a food because it is evil by nature or in any other way whatever, champions the doctrine of demons. Nor can their cause be painted in this colour: The cause of the prohibition is alleged in the text in these words: Everything that God has created is good, and nothing is to be rejected; as if it said: those devilish teachers forbid certain foods as evil, whereas all foods are good, pure, and none to be rejected. Nor should it be restricted to them alone. So Christ, in Matt. 19:14, rebukes the disciples who were going to keep infants away from Christ: Do not forbid them. He adds the reason: For of such is the kingdom of heaven. The disciples had not kept them away for this reason. And Christ alleges this reason. So in this place the Holy Spirit condemns all who forbid foods for the sake of religion, because all foods are good. Yet all who have forbidden them were not bound to deny this reason necessarily. Thus those who forbid blood-eating [αἱματοφαγίαν] for the sake of conscience can by no means be freed from this guilt.

units.la: XVI. Bccmannus eadem ratione usus. Sed & alio responso defungitur. Regulam communem non includere in se exceptionem notabilem. Multas regulas legésque videri esse καθόλυ, sed juxta abilis nonnulla eximi exempla. Praeceptum hoc γεντικῶς sonare: Ne occidas. Et tamen Magistratum eo non obstringi. Per initium videri τῷ πνευτὸς monitum Paulinum: Mundis omnia munda. Et tamen excipi cibum potúmque, qui aggravat corpus, Luc.XXI.34. 1.Cor. VI.10. Sic regulam Synodicam Apostolorum excipere ἐιδικωτάτως morticinum & sanguinem. Exerc.XXVI. Respond. Verum,regulam communem non semper includere exceptionem notabilem. Sed nec exempla,quae adfert,sunt solida, nec applicatio ad praesens negotium. Non exempla. Regula est: Non occides. Nempe,privata libidine, ultionis exequendae causâ. Haec regula sensu legislatoris accepta non patitur exceptionem. Nemini occidere licet,impetu animi ad privatam vindictam procurrentis. Cùm Magistratus occidit, non exercet privatam vindictam. Sed Deus virgarum ac securis terrore armavit, ut esset ἐκδικος εἰς ὀργὴν τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι, Rom.XIII.1.4. Non est igitur exceptio à sensu regulae, sed à solis verbis regulae. Regula universalis est: Non occides, intellige, non jubente Deo, privata ultione inflammatus. Si exceptio est,debet contradicere regulae per formam enuntiati particularis affirmantis. Aliquem occidere licet privata authoritate, quae exceptio adversatur Scripturae. Eadem ratio alterius loci: Mundis omnia munda. Quando autem Christus dehortatur à saburra ciborum ac potu,haec non est exceptio à regula. Non fit enim oppositio manente subjecto. Qui cibis cor aggravârunt, non mundi sunt, sed immundi. Immundis autem, pollutis & infidelibus nihil mundum est, sed pollura est eorum mens & conscientia, Tit.I.15. Neque applicatio felicior est. Regula est: Omnis creatura Dei bona est, neque rejectanea, si cum gratiarum actione sumatur. Haec regula καθόλου est,neq; patitur instantiam. Nam τὸ ἀπέχεσθαι ἀιμάτων καὶ πνικτῶν non est instantia, sed pertinet ad aliud genus praecepti de charitate, opposita scandalis. Qui enim creatura Dei in se bona quidem vescitur cum scandalo fratris, non sumit cibum cum gratiarum actione: quia non ex fide, seu ad gloriam Dei, sine quibus est, omnis nostra actio mali labem traxit.
units.tr: XVI. Beccmann used the same argument, but he also meets the matter with another answer: The common rule does not contain in itself any notable exception. Many rules and laws seem to be universal, but some are rightly excepted by examples. This precept sounds generally: "You shall not kill." Yet the magistrate is not bound by it. At the beginning, Paul's warning seems to be spoken by the Spirit: "To the pure all things are pure." Yet food and drink which weigh down the body are excepted, Luke 21:34; 1 Cor. 6:10. So the Synodal rule of the Apostles excepts especially carrion and blood. Exercise 26. Reply: True, a common rule does not always contain a notable exception. But neither the examples he brings are sound, nor is their application to the present matter. Not the examples. The rule is: You shall not kill. Namely, out of private lust, for the sake of carrying out vengeance. Taken in the sense of the lawgiver, this rule admits no exception. It is not lawful for anyone to kill from a rush of feeling that runs to private vengeance. When the magistrate kills, he does not exercise private vengeance. But God armed the magistrate with the terror of the sword and rod, so that he might be [ἐκδικος εἰς ὀργὴν] "an avenger for wrath against him who does evil" (Rom. 13:1, 4). So the exception is not to the sense of the rule, but only to the bare words of the rule. The universal rule is: You shall not kill, that is, not at God's command, inflamed by private revenge. If there is an exception, it must contradict the rule in the form of a particular affirmative proposition: It is lawful to kill someone by private authority, and this exception is opposed to Scripture. The same reasoning applies to the other passage: To the pure all things are pure. When Christ warns against a load of food and drink, this is not an exception to the rule. For there is no opposition while the subject remains the same. Those who have weighed down their hearts with food are not pure but unclean. But to the unclean, the defiled and the unbelieving nothing is pure, but their mind and conscience are defiled (Titus 1:15). Nor is the application any more fortunate. The rule is: Every creature of God is good, and not to be rejected, if it is taken with thanksgiving. This rule is universal and admits no instance. For [τὸ ἀπέχεσθαι ἀιμάτων καὶ πνικτῶν] abstaining from blood and from things strangled is not an instance, but belongs to another kind of precept, concerning love, opposed to scandals. For whoever eats, in himself a creature of God that is good, but with scandal to his brother, does not take the food with thanksgiving, because he does not take it from faith, or for the glory of God, without which every action of ours is stained with evil.

units.la: XVI. Sunt qui in hoc negotio urgeant locum Act.X.10.11. &c. Ubi commemoratur visio coelestis, quam Petrus habuit, priusquam
units.tr: XVI. Some people in this matter press the passage Acts 10:10, 11, etc., where the heavenly vision that Peter had is recorded, before

units.la: quam ad Cornelium accederet. Et faciunt illud non sine ratione. In vase coelitus descendente erant omnia quadrupedia, reptilia terrae & volatilia coeli. Et facta vox ad Petrum: Surge Petre, occide & manduca. Quod Deus purificavit, tu ne commune ducito. Curcellaeus levi brachio se expediens, dicit, apparere, per animalia immunda significatos Gentiles incircumcisos, qualis erat Cornelius cum suis non bruta. Respond. Animalia immunda symbola fuerunt Gentilium: munda Judaeorum, juxta Hieronymum & Origenem. Probabilius tamen Justinus, sive quisquis author libri, quaest. 89. ad Orthod. in vase coelesti conclusa fuisse nonnisi animalia immunda. A mundis enim Petrus non abhorruisset, sed ea relictis immundis ad cibum sumsisset. Fuerunt autem immunda symbola Gentilium. Qui autem dat rem sub symbolo, is etiam symbolum dat, & ejus potestatem facit. Sicut qui annulum dat, quo fidem conjugalem obstringit, dat potestatem aeque in symbolum, annulum, atque in rem symbolo significatam. Non igitur nocet generali concessioni omnium animalium Petro declaratae, quod animalia in vase non fuerint vera & viva, sed quasi depicta & effigiata, ut vocat Cyrillus lib. 9. contra Julian. Sua enim natura Symbolum & res disparata esse debent. Huc accedit, quod sub lege immunditiies quorundam animalium declarata a Deo fuit Sacramentum constans rejectionis Gentium, quas animalibus immundis Deus sub lege comparavit. Cessante autem τυφῶσι, & maledictione Gentium adeoque illis in foedus Ecclesiae coeuntibus, conveniens etiam fuit discrimen ciborum, quo inimicitia a Christo abolita, e medio tolli. Reliqua Curcellaei ad hunc locum meram petitionem principii sapiunt.
units.tr: he came to Cornelius. And they do not do so without reason. In a vessel descending from heaven were all four-footed beasts, reptiles of the earth and birds of the air. And a voice came to Peter: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat. What God has cleansed, do not you call common." Curcellaeus, extricating himself with a light hand, says that it appears the unclean animals signified the uncircumcised Gentiles, such as Cornelius and his people were, and not brute beasts. Reply: the unclean animals were symbols of the Gentiles, and the clean ones of the Jews, according to Jerome and Origen. Yet Justin, or whoever is the author of the book, Question 89 in the Questions to the Orthodox, more probably holds that only unclean animals were enclosed in the heavenly vessel. For Peter would not have shrunk from clean animals, but would have left the unclean and taken the clean for food. The unclean animals, however, were symbols of the Gentiles. Now whoever gives a thing under a symbol also gives the symbol and conveys its power. Just as one who gives a ring, by which he binds conjugal faith, gives authority equally over the symbol, the ring, and over the thing signified by the symbol. It therefore does no harm to the general grant of all animals declared to Peter that the animals in the vessel were not real and living, but as it were painted and modelled, as Cyril calls them in book 9 against Julian. For by their nature a symbol and the thing must be distinct. Moreover, under the law the uncleanness of certain animals, declared by God, was a sacrament constituting the rejection of the Gentiles, whom God under the law compared to unclean animals. But with the dividing wall now gone, and the curse upon the Gentiles ended, and they now being joined into the covenant of the Church, the distinction of foods was also fitting, so that the enmity abolished by Christ might be removed from the midst. The rest of Curcellaeus's remarks on this passage smack of mere petitio principii.

units.la: XVII. Merito etiam inde primi solet contraria sententia, quod praeceptum illud de sanguine sit pars jugi illius, quo Patres nostri ante Christum illigati fuerunt.
units.tr: It is also with good reason that the opposing opinion usually arises from this: that the commandment about blood is part of that yoke by which our fathers before Christ were bound.

units.la: Et nos supra cum de libertate egimus, in cujus possessionem a Christo sumus inducti, hoc ursimus, ex Act. XV. 20. Curcellaeus omni rudente explicato rationem nostram infringit. 1. Mirari se, quod abstinentia tam levis jugum & onus vocetur. Quasi deceat Christianos adeo gula esse deditos, ut, nisi omnia, quae nanciscipossunt, absorbere liceat, conquerendi materiam habeant, pag. 183. Respond. Jugum grave vocavit Petrus omnia dogmata carnalia V. T. Tale dogma est etiam sanguinis interdictum. Jugum autem & onus est, vel respectu difficilis observantiae, vel quia pugnat cum Christiana libertate, quae ejusmodi decretis legalibus non obscure praeumbratur. Interdictum sanguinis est jugum, si non priori, at certe posteriori modo. Nam imponitur Christianis, ut inde judicandis. Intolerabile enim est servituti subjici liberum, ut putet se offendisse Deum, si sobrie usus fuerit donis Dei. Intolerabile jugum superstitio. Neque libertatem hic sollicite adeo defendimus, ut Sybariticas mensas muniamus, & doceamus obsonare pollucibiliter, ut ita cum Comico loquar. Fabulas Milesias relinquimus, quibus vacat, & qui amant. Nobis hoc institutum, ut cognosci possit, in qua simus libertate positi, & in quo consistat Regnum Dei, an in cibo & potu, an in justitia, sanctitate, misericordia? Et redarguuntur irreptitii, ψευδάδελφοι, qui intrant κατασκοπῆσαι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν, ad explorandam libertatem nostram, quam habemus in Christo. 2. Si quis diceret: praestare in gravi fame sanguine vesci, quam sinere se ab ea enecari, disputiendum esset, an prohibitio Apostolica eousque nos obligaret. Et putarem idem de sanguine posse judicari, atque David & Abimelech fecerunt olim de panibus Propositionis, nempe in tali casu mandatum Dei non obligare. ib. Respond. Hoc ex Curcellaei hypothesi, statuentis hic morale praeceptum, incidit in hanc quaestionem: An liceat mala facere, ut eveniant bona? Scripturae autem in universum negant. Incolumitatem vitae & decus pari libra esse, supra in simili quaestione vidimus. Esum sanguinis comparavit cum gravissimo scelere, idololatria Curcellaeus. Allegavit diras, quas Deus intonat in αἱματοφάγον. Ponam faciem meam contra illum. Esse in eorum genere esum sanguinis, quae sunt αἰσχρά, turpia & inhonesta. Et liceret homini Christiano ad vitandum malum triste, committere malum turpe? Ac malum tale, quod pari cum idololatria passu ambulat? Absit, hac disciplina Christianos imbui debere. Praeceptum de panibus propositionis non fuit de re in se bona, sed de re, quae ad externum cultum attinet, adeoque ceremoniale. Tale esse interdictum de non comedendo sanguine, Curcellaeus negat. Ergo dispar ratio. 3. Tantum abest, ut jugum sit haec abstinentia, ut contra Deus optime consuluerit nobis, cum vesci sanguine prohibuit, qui valetudini tum animae tum corporis noxius est; adeo, ut quicunque istud norunt, ab eo sponte abstinere debeant, etiamsi nulla lege vetentur. De valetudine animae id probatur, quia omnia animalia, quibus vescimur, stupida sunt, & gula, libidini, irae, aliisque id genus vitiis obnoxia. In sanguine autem uniuscuiusque peculiaris indoles est ingressa, ut Medicorum filii docent: Unde sequitur, ut qui eum cibum usurpant, mores istis animantibus similes paulatim & insensibiliter induant. Converti enim nequit in corporis nostri substantiam, quia ipsam sibi quodammodo assimilat. Nam hæc est omnis patientis natura, ut patiendo reagat in agens, quemadmodum accidit, cum manus mea calore alteram frigidam calefacere volo, ut ea frigore suo meam calorem imminuat. De corporis valetudine non minus evidens esse; Sanguinis esum nocere. Omnis enim sanguis pravum suppeditat alimentum, difficilis concoctu, ideoque obstructiones parit, quæ maximæ partis morborum sunt causæ. Quare qui conquerantur libertatem suam circumscribi per interdictum edendi sanguinem, idem facere videntur, ac si quis gravate ferret, se ab esu bufonum & colubrorum arceri. p. 183. 184. 185. 186. Resp. Hæc Philosophia etiam Becmanno blanditur. In quo tamen uterque à lineis excidit. Quærimus enim de religiosa abstinentia, quam negamus. Medicæ abstinentiæ judicatio hujus subsellii non est. Deus enim in Novo Testamento carnes hominibus nullo discrimine permisit. Et tamen alias noxias esse valetudini: alias temperamentum hominis ad mores indignos naturaliter inclinare, si mens divino munere habilis non est concupiscentiis suis frænandis, in promtu est omnibus. Bufones, Serpentes, Dracones, Vespertiliones, Noctuas, quis ignoret in eo genere esse? Propterea Deus in Vet. Test. immunda declaravit, ut significarent immunditiem Gentilium & peccatorum, quod supra ex Epistola Barnabæ nobis expositum. Et tamen non obstante hac eorum indole in Novo Testamento Apostoli omnia munda declarunt, & nihil jam pollutum esse propter conscientiam. Apud Senecam Sextius eandem ob causam ab animalibus abstinuisse dicitur: Sextius homini satis alimentorum citra sanguinem esse credebat, & crudelitatis consuetudinem fieri, ubi in voluptatem adducta esset laceratio. Adjiciebat: contrahendam materiam esse luxuria: colligebat bonae valetudini esse contraria alimenta varia, & nostris aliena corporibus. At Pythagoras omnium inter omnia cognationem esse dicebat & aliorum commercium in alias atque alias formas transeuntium. Ad quæ Sotioni respondet Seneca: Si vera sunt ista, abstinuisse animalibus innocentia est, si falsa, frugalitas est. Epist. 108. Scilicet hæc est illa Philosophia, quæ verborum habet speciem sapientia, per superstitionem fitionem ac humilitatem animi, & laesionem corporis, Colost. II. v. 23. A qua culpa μετεμψυχωσεως vix liberari potest Curcellaeus, cum dicit, eos, qui sanguinem animalium bibunt, istorum animalium mores similes paulatim & insensibiliter induere. Quasi μετεμψυχωσει aliqua Pythagorica animae brutorum, in sanguine hospitantes, in hominem transfunderentur. Quod ingreditur in os, Curcellae, non polluit hominem, quia in ventrem abit, & in secessum ejicitur, Matth. XV. 11. 17. Et, qui mundus est, ei haec omnia munda: Immundis autem & infidelibus omnia polluta, mens & conscientia. Tit. I. 15. Si qua feritate, gula, libidine, ira, stupore brura laborant, quemadmodum haec vita ac Spiritu spoliata, in sanguine jam separato, rudi, crasso & motus experte in animam nostram, mentem liberam, ac Deo cognatam, vim & pollentiam minimam habere censenda?
units.tr: We too, when above we treated of the liberty into whose possession we have been brought by Christ, pressed this from Acts 15:20. Curcellaeus, having unrolled every rope, attacks our argument. (1) He wonders that such a light abstinence should be called a yoke and a burden, as if it were fitting for Christians to be so given over to gluttony that, unless they may swallow everything they can get hold of, they have cause to complain (p. 183). Reply: Peter called the carnal dogmas of the Old Testament a grievous yoke. The prohibition on blood is such a dogma. A yoke and burden is so either with respect to the difficulty of observance, or because it conflicts with Christian liberty, which is not obscurely foreshadowed by such legal decrees. The prohibition on blood is a yoke, if not in the former way, then certainly in the latter, for it is imposed on Christians as something by which they are to be judged. For it is intolerable that a free person should be subjected to slavery, so as to think he has offended God if he has used the gifts of God soberly. Superstition is an intolerable yoke. Nor do we defend liberty here so anxiously as to fortify Sybaritic tables and teach people to feast luxuriously, to speak with the comic poet. We leave the Milesian tales to those who have leisure and who love them. Our aim is this: that it may be known in what liberty we have been placed, and in what the kingdom of God consists, whether in food and drink, or in righteousness, holiness and mercy. And the sneaking false brethren [ψευδάδελφοι, pseudadelphoi], who come in to spy out [κατασκοπῆσαι, kataskopēsai] our liberty which we have in Christ, are refuted. (2) If someone said that in severe famine it is better to eat blood than to allow oneself to be starved to death, it would have to be debated whether the apostolic prohibition binds us so far. And I would think that the same could be judged about blood as David and Abimelech once did about the bread of the Presence, namely that in such a case the command of God does not bind. Reply: this, on Curcellaeus's hypothesis, which holds that the precept here is moral, falls into the question: is it lawful to do evil that good may come? The Scriptures in general deny this. We have seen above, in a similar question, that the safety of life and honour are of equal weight. Curcellaeus compared the eating of blood with the most grievous crime, idolatry. He cited the curses which God thunders against the blood-eater [αἱματοφάγον, haimatophagon]: "I will set my face against him." He says that the eating of blood belongs to the class of things that are [αἰσχρά, aischra], shameful and dishonourable. And would it be lawful for a Christian to commit a shameful evil in order to avoid a grievous evil? And an evil that walks step for step with idolatry? Far be it; Christians ought not to be imbued with such a discipline. The precept about the bread of the Presence was not about a thing good in itself, but about a thing pertaining to external worship, and so ceremonial. Curcellaeus denies that the prohibition on not eating blood is of this kind. Therefore the reasoning is unlike. (3) This abstinence is so far from being a yoke that, on the contrary, God has most excellently provided for us when he forbade us to drink blood, which is harmful both to the health of the soul and of the body; so much so that whoever knows these things ought to abstain from it of his own accord, even if no law forbade it. Reply: as for the health of the soul, this is proved because all the animals we eat are stupid, and prone to gluttony, lust, anger, and other vices of that kind. But in the blood of each animal its own particular nature has entered, as the sons of physicians teach. Hence it follows that those who use that food gradually and imperceptibly take on the manners of those animals. For it cannot be turned into the substance of our body without first assimilating it to itself in some measure. For this is the nature of everything that is acted upon, that by being acted upon it reacts on the agent, just as happens when my hand, wanting to warm another cold hand, is itself cooled, so that by its coldness it diminishes my warmth. As for the health of the body, it is no less evident that the eating of blood is harmful. For all blood supplies a bad nourishment, hard to digest, and so produces obstructions, which are the causes of most diseases. Wherefore those who complain that their liberty is curtailed by the prohibition on eating blood seem to do the same as if someone were aggrieved at being kept from eating toads and snakes (pp. 183, 184, 185, 186). Reply: this philosophy flatters Becmann too, but both of them stray from the lines. For we are inquiring about religious abstinence, which we deny. The judgement of medical abstinence is not the business of this bench. For in the New Testament God has permitted meats to human beings without any distinction. And yet that some things are harmful to health, and others naturally incline the temperament of a person to unworthy manners when the mind, not being divinely enabled, is not able to curb its desires, is obvious to everyone. Who would not know that toads, serpents, dragons, bats and owls belong to that class? For this reason God in the Old Testament declared them unclean, to signify the uncleanness of the Gentiles and of sinners, as we have explained above from the Epistle of Barnabas. And yet, notwithstanding this nature of theirs, in the New Testament the Apostles have declared all things clean, and that nothing is now polluted on account of conscience. Among the writings of Seneca, Sextius is said to have abstained from animals for the same reason: "Sextius believed that there was enough food for people without blood, and that a habit of cruelty arises when the tearing of animals is turned into pleasure. He added that matter must not be gathered for luxury; he concluded that varied foods, and foods alien to our bodies, are contrary to good health. But Pythagoras said that there is a kinship among all things, and an exchange among beings passing into one form after another." To these things Seneca replies to Sotion: "If these things are true, abstaining from animals is innocence; if false, it is frugality." Letter 108. Plainly this is that philosophy which has the appearance of wisdom in words, through superstition, humility of mind, and bodily mistreatment (Colossians 2:23). From this fault of [μετεμψυχωσεως, metempsychoseōs] Curcellaeus can hardly be cleared, when he says that those who drink the blood of animals gradually and imperceptibly take on the manners of those animals. As if by some Pythagorean [metempsychosis] the souls of brute beasts, lodging in the blood, were transfused into a human being. What enters the mouth, Curcellaeus, does not defile a person, because it goes into the belly and is cast out into the drain (Matthew 15:11, 17). "To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; both their mind and their conscience are defiled" (Titus 1:15). If they are afflicted with some savageness, gluttony, lust, anger or stupidity of the beasts, is the blood, now separated from life and spirit, crude, thick and devoid of motion, to be judged to have the least power and potency against our soul, which is free and akin to God?

units.la: CAPUT IX. Objectio palmaria ex Act. XV. producitur, & ea occasione Parasceve Concilii Hierosolymitani explicatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. The chief objection from Acts 15 is brought forward, and on this occasion the preparatory matters of the Council of Jerusalem are explained.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Objectio Curcellaei palmaria ex Act. XV. 20. 28. 29. producitur. Haec occasione texitur Commentarius in Concilium Hierosolymitanum. Concilium institutum contra Cerinthum & Ebionem. Nazarei. Emissarii. Errores intestini Ecclesiae nocentissimi. Circumcisio compendium Iudaismi. Circumcisio definitur. Ejus minister Sacerdos. Mulieres habuisse Sacramentum analogum. Circumcisionis significatio. Papatus Iudaismum incrustat. Adiaphoristae pulsantur. Ecclesiae circumcisae duplex periodus distinguitur. Non exclusi faedere praeputiati usque ad Mosen. Idumaei, Aegyptii, Aethiopes, Colchi, circumcisi. Locus Ierem. IX. 29. Cathedra Mosis. Cathedram Petri falso jactant Pontificii. Circumcisio non habuit necessitatem medii. Curcellaus perstringitur, docens, incircumcisos ante Christum servari potuisse.
units.tr: Curcellaeus's chief objection from Acts 15:20, 28, 29 is brought forward. On this occasion a commentary on the Council of Jerusalem is woven. The Council was convened against Cerinthus and Ebion. The Nazarenes. Emissaries. The most harmful internal errors of the Church. Circumcision as a summary of Judaism. Circumcision defined. Its minister a priest. Women had an analogous sacrament. The meaning of circumcision. Papacy plasters over Judaism. The Adiaphorists are assailed. A twofold period of the circumcised Church is distinguished. The uncircumcised were not excluded from the covenant until Moses. Idumaeans, Egyptians, Ethiopians and Colchians were circumcised. The passage Ierem. IX. 29. The seat of Moses. The Papists falsely boast of the seat of Peter. Circumcision had no necessity as a means. Curcellaeus is attacked for teaching that the uncircumcised could be saved before Christ.

units.la: potuisse. Historia Izate Adiabenorum Regis examinatur. Tryphon & Manasse Ben-Israel immeritò allegati. Στάσις. Locus Gal.II.5. ὀφθ. Erasmus & Ambrosius consentiuntur. Paulus cur provocarit ad Concilium Apostolorum? Romani Pontifices non patiuntur in Concilio causam suam examinari. Carolus V. à Paulo III. iniquè habitus. Enanthiophanes expeditur. Clementis Constitutiones taxantur. Apollonii erronea traditio. Quæstio: An Apostoli inter se orbem terrarum diviserint? Qui Apostoli Concilio interfuerint? Locus Gal.II.9. Columna. δοκοῦντες. Presbyter. Presbyteri docentes ab Episcopis tempore Apostolico non distincti. πεσβυτέριον notat Collegium, non officium. Cur Hierosolymæ ad Concilium delectæ? Quæstio in Concilio venti-landa. ἀγῶνες. Ecclesia. Bellarminus notatur. Excipiendi ritus. Discutitur, an verba versus quinti sint Lucæ, an Pauli? Cornelii à Lapide rationes solvuntur. Αἵρεσις vox media. Cur adversati Paulo Pharisæi? An Pharisæi credentes in sectâ manserint? τηρεῖν νόμον.
units.tr: could be saved. The history of Izates, king of the Adiabenes, is examined. Tryphon and Manasseh ben Israel are wrongly cited. Stasis [στάσις]. The passage Gal. II. 5, ophth. [ὀφθ.]. Erasmus and Ambrose agree. Why did Paul appeal to the council of the Apostles? Roman Pontiffs do not allow their cause to be examined in a council. Charles V was unjustly treated by Paul III. Enanthiophanes is disposed of. The Constitutions of Clement are censured. The erroneous tradition of Apollonius. Question: did the Apostles divide the world among themselves? Which Apostles were present at the Council? The passage Gal. II. 9. Pillar. Seeming [δοκοῦντες]. Elder. Elders who taught were not distinguished from bishops in apostolic times. Presbyterion [πεσβυτέριον] denotes a college, not an office. Why was Jerusalem chosen for the Council? A question to be raised at the Council. Contests [ἀγῶνες]. The Church. Bellarmine is noted. Rites to be excepted. It is discussed whether the words of the fifth verse are Luke's or Paul's. The arguments of Cornelius a Lapide are answered. Heresy [αἵρεσις] is a middle word. Why did the Pharisees oppose Paul? Did the believing Pharisees remain in their sect? To keep the law [τηρεῖν νόμον].

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Sequitur objectio ex Act.XV.28.29. in qua jam Sacra commovet, & certam sibi palmam spondet Curcellæus. Sed & Græci, & quotquot in hoc negotio nobiscum remum ducere detrectant, hoc loco pugnant tanquam cum hasta, cum scuto. Et sanè non difficeor, controversiæ hujus decisionem inde repetendam. Synodi verba sunt: ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος, πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων. Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνικτῶν, καὶ πορνείας. Ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτούς, εὖ πράξετε. Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis, ne quid amplius imponeremus vobis oneris, quàm necessaria hæc, videlicet ut abstineatis ab idolothytis, & sanguine, & suffocato & fornicatione, à quibus si conservaveritis vosipsos, bene facietis. Age, benevole & philalethes lector, patere, quæso, princeps hoc Novi Testamenti Concilium, & ejus acta paulò curatiori nostra commentatione oculis tuis repræsentari, priusquam ad τὸ φωτεχον & ipsum controversiæ cardinem veniamus. Nam & utilem ac necessariam cognitionem ad ἀχμὴν quæstionis nostræ habebit, & dignum est illustre Concilium, quòd penitiori indagine, occasione ita se aptante, vestigetur. Describit nobis Concilium Lucas Act. XV. ab initio capitis ad versum usque tri-cesimum. Periochae tres sunt. Prima describit Lucas Ἀφορμὴ τοῦ Concilii, sive res ante Concilium gestas. Secunda Concilium ipsum, & orationem tum Petri tum Jacobi. Tertia Conciliarem sententiam literis mandatam. Parasceven complectuntur versus quinque primi, quorum haec series.
units.tr: Next comes the objection from Acts 15:28, 29, in which Curcellaeus already stirs up the sacred writings and promises himself certain victory. But the Greeks, and all who refuse to row with us in this business, fight here as if with spear and shield. And indeed I do not deny that the decision of this controversy is to be sought from this place. The words of the Synod are: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well" [ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος, πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων. Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνικτῶν, καὶ πορνείας. Ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτούς, εὖ πράξετε.]. Come, kind and truth-loving reader, allow me to place before your eyes this first Council of the New Testament, and its acts, with a somewhat more careful commentary of ours, before we come to the very hinge of the controversy. For this will give useful and necessary knowledge for the crux of our question, and it is fitting that so illustrious a Council should be examined with a deeper inquiry, since the occasion so offers. Luke describes the Council for us in Acts 15 from the beginning of the chapter to the thirtieth verse. There are three sections. The first, which Luke describes, is the occasion of the Council, or the events before the Council. The second is the Council itself, and the speeches both of Peter and of James. The third is the conciliar decision committed to writing. The first five verses contain the preliminaries, and their sequence is this:

units.la: 1. Καί τινες κατελθόντες ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐδίδασκον τοὺς ἀδελφούς. Ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ περιτμηθῆτε τῷ ἔθει Μωϋσέως, οὐ δύνασθε σωθῆναι.
units.tr: 1. And certain men which came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved. [Καί τινες κατελθόντες ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐδίδασκον τοὺς ἀδελφούς. Ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ περιτμηθῆτε τῷ ἔθει Μωϋσέως, οὐ δύνασθε σωθῆναι.]

units.la: 2. Γενομένης οὖν στάσεως καὶ συζητήσεως οὐκ ὀλίγης τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ τῷ Βαρναβᾷ πρὸς αὐτούς, ἔταξαν ἀναβαίνειν Παῦλον καὶ Βαρναβᾶν, καί τινας ἄλλους ἐξ αὐτῶν πρὸς τοὺς Ἀποστόλους καὶ πρεσβυτέρους εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, περὶ τῆς ζητήσεως τούτου.
units.tr: 2. When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain others of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question. [Γενομένης οὖν στάσεως καὶ συζητήσεως οὐκ ὀλίγης τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ τῷ Βαρναβᾷ πρὸς αὐτούς, ἔταξαν ἀναβαίνειν Παῦλον καὶ Βαρναβᾶν, καί τινας ἄλλους ἐξ αὐτῶν πρὸς τοὺς Ἀποστόλους καὶ πρεσβυτέρους εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, περὶ τῆς ζητήσεως τούτου.]

units.la: 3. Οἱ μὲν οὖν προπεμφθέντες ὑπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, διήρχοντο τὴν Φοινίκην καὶ Σαμάρειαν, ἐκδιηγούμενοι τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν. Καὶ ἐποίουν χαρὰν μεγάλην πᾶσι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.
units.tr: 3. And they, being brought on their way by the church, passed through Phenice and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles; and they caused great joy unto all the brethren. [Οἱ μὲν οὖν προπεμφθέντες ὑπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, διήρχοντο τὴν Φοινίκην καὶ Σαμάρειαν, ἐκδιηγούμενοι τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν. Καὶ ἐποίουν χαρὰν μεγάλην πᾶσι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.]

units.la: 4. Παραγενόμενοι δὲ εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἀπεδέχθησαν ὑπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, ἀνήγγειλάν τε ὅσα ὁ Θεὸς ἐποίησε μετ' αὐτῶν.
units.tr: 4. And when they were come to Jerusalem, they were received of the church, and of the apostles and elders, and they declared all things that God had done with them. [Παραγενόμενοι δὲ εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ἀπεδέχθησαν ὑπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, ἀνήγγειλάν τε ὅσα ὁ Θεὸς ἐποίησε μετ' αὐτῶν.]

units.la: 5. Ἐξανέστησαν δέ τινες τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς αἱρέσεως τῶν Φαρισαίων πεπιστευκότες, λέγοντες. Ὅτι δεῖ περιτέμνειν αὐτούς, παραγγέλλειν τε τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον Μωϋσέως.
units.tr: 5. But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses. [Ἐξανέστησαν δέ τινες τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς αἱρέσεως τῶν Φαρισαίων πεπιστευκότες, λέγοντες. Ὅτι δεῖ περιτέμνειν αὐτούς, παραγγέλλειν τε τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον Μωϋσέως.]

units.la: 1. Et quidam, qui descenderunt à Judea, docebant Fratres: Nisi circumcidamini secundum morem Mosis, non potestis salutem consequi.
units.tr: 1. And certain men who came down from Judaea taught the brethren: Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot obtain salvation.

units.la: 2. Cum ergo seditio & disceptatio esset Paulo non exigua & Barnabae adversus illos, statuerunt, ut ascenderent Paulus & Barnabas, & quidam alii ex illis, ad Apostolos & Presbyteros Hierosolymam, super hac quaestione.
units.tr: 2. Therefore, when there arose no small sedition and dispute between Paul and Barnabas and those men, they appointed that Paul and Barnabas, and certain others from among them, should go up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem about this question.

units.la: 3. Illi ergo deducti ab Ecclesia pertransibant Phoenicen & Samariam, narrantes conversionem Gentilium, & afferebant gaudium magnum omnibus Fratribus.
units.tr: 3. So they, sent on their way by the church, passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, relating the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brethren.

units.la: 4. Cùm autem venissent Hierosolymam, suscepti sunt ab Ecclesia, & ab Apostolis ac Presbyteris, annuntiaruntque quaecunque gesserant, Deo juvante eos.
units.tr: 4. When they came to Jerusalem, they were received by the church, and by the apostles and elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.

units.la: 5. Exorti sunt autem quidam é secta Pharisaeorum, dicentes, quòd oporteret circumcidere eos ac praecipere, ut servarent legem Mosis.
units.tr: 5. But certain of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying that it was necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.

units.la: Versus I. ET QUIDAM) Epiphanius haeres. 28. nominat Cerinthum. Hic, inquit, sub Apostolis quaestionem seditionis commovit, dicens, debere circumcidi homines. Cujus causa contra ipsum, & haeresin ejus, decreverunt de suis Actibus Apostoli sententiam, non debere jam homihominis Iudaismo, id est, circumcisioni, aliisque talibus superstitionibus vana parere carnalibus, qui de Gentibus veniebant in Christum Dominum nostrum Salvatorem. Eundem nominat Philastrius l. de haeret. 8. Aug. in Catal. haeres. Hieronymus Epist. 89. Epiphanius docet, eum etiam supra cap. X. Petro molestias concitasse, quod Cornelii domum esset ingressus, & infra, Paulo etiam persecutionem & turbas dedisse. Cerinthi Achates fuit Ebion, juratissimus etiam Pauli hostis. Quippe mentiebatur, Paulum gentilem, Proselythum tamen factum, ut Hierosolymis filiam Sacerdotis, quam deperibat, in nassam suam illiceret. Utrque & Cerinthus & Ebion vel antesignanos se, vel sectatores gesserunt Nazaraeorum, quos & Ceremonias legales mordicus propugnasse, & circumcisionem cum Baptismo retinuisse, & Paulo Apostolo supra modum infensos fuisse constat. Non placet aliis, ut Cerinthus & Ebion per quosdam intelligantur. Malunt igitur, Pharisaeos notari, quorum mentio agitata versu quinto. Quasi versus ille non Lucae esset, sed Pauli, pergentis narrare & exprimere illos, quos adversari sibi expertus est. Sic Eruditissimus Interpres Theodorus Beza sentire videtur, qui proinde v. 5. supplet: Sed, ajebant, quidam Pharisaei, &c. Qui tamen assensum hactenus non impetrat, ob rationes, quas infra promemus. Sive igitur Cerinthus & Ebion adversarii illi, quod probabile, fuerunt, sive alii, quos nullis coloribus novimus, parum agnoscere nostra interest.
units.tr: Verse 1. AND CERTAIN MEN) Epiphanius, in Heresy 28, names Cerinthus. He, he says, under the Apostles stirred up a seditious question, saying that men ought to be circumcised. Against him and his heresy the Apostles gave their judgment concerning their Acts: that men who came from the Gentiles to Christ our Lord and Saviour ought not now to submit to Judaism, that is, to circumcision and other such carnal superstitions, in vain. Philastrius names the same man in his book on heresies, chapter 8; Augustine in his Catalogue of Heresies; Jerome in Letter 89. Epiphanius teaches that he also caused trouble for Peter, above in chapter 10, because Peter had entered the house of Cornelius, and below that he gave Paul persecution and disturbances. Ebion was Cerinthus's companion, and also a most sworn enemy of Paul. Indeed he lied that Paul, though a Gentile made a proselyte, had done this in order to lure into his net at Jerusalem the priest's daughter with whom he was infatuated. Both Cerinthus and Ebion were either the standard-bearers or the followers of the Nazarenes, who, as is established, stubbornly defended the legal ceremonies, retained circumcision together with baptism, and were beyond measure hostile to the Apostle Paul. Others do not like the idea that Cerinthus and Ebion are meant by certain people. They prefer, therefore, that the Pharisees be noted, whose mention was raised in verse five, as if that verse were not Luke's but Paul's, going on to narrate and name those whom he had found to be his opponents. So the most learned interpreter Theodore Beza seems to think, who accordingly supplies in verse 5: "But, they said, certain Pharisees, etc." Yet he has not so far won assent, for reasons which we shall set out below. Whether, then, Cerinthus and Ebion were those adversaries, which is probable, or others whom we know by no marks, it matters little to us to recognise.

units.la: QUI DESCENDERUNT à JUDÆA) Antiochiam videlicet.
units.tr: WHO CAME DOWN FROM JUDEA: that is, to Antioch.

units.la: Paulus vocat falsos Fratres παρεισάκτους, qui subingressi sunt, Gal. II. 4. Subinductitios Tertullianus nominat lib. 5. contra Marcionitas. Beza scite emissarios, qui clanculum submissi. Quorum imaginem in hodiernis agyrthis liquido cernas, qui Missionariorum nomen sibi induerunt. Fuit ergo hic error in ipsa Ecclesia natus. Quales sunt omnium pestilentissimi & nocentissimi. Illi enim, qui ὑφ' ἑαυτῶν Ecclesiam Dei vexant, mitius feriunt, quia praevisi. Qui vero in visceribus haerent, personam mentiti fallacias machinantur, & incautos nec opinantes in errorum regionem inducunt. Ut non frustra Christus suos à fermento Pharisaeorum dehortatus fuerit Matth. XVI. 6.
units.tr: Paul calls them false brethren who crept in unawares, παρεισάκτους [pareisaktous], Gal. 2:4. Tertullian calls them secretly introduced men in book 5 against the Marcionites. Beza aptly calls them emissaries, sent in secretly. You can see their likeness clearly in the wandering rogues of today, who have taken the name of missionaries. So this error arose within the Church itself. These are the most pestilent and harmful of all. Those who harass God's Church openly strike more gently, because they are seen coming. But those who cling to its inner parts, pretending to be someone else, plot deceit and lead the unwary, who suspect nothing, into the region of error. So Christ rightly warned his people against the leaven of the Pharisees, Matt. 16:6.

units.la: NISI CIRCUMCIDAMINI) Haec summa doctrinae. Circumcisionem urgebant & legem Mosaicam. In circumcisione Spiri-
units.tr: UNLESS YOU ARE CIRCUMCISED

units.la: Spiritum olim duxit Judaismus. Hinc Paulus: Testor omni hominis circumciso, quòd debitor sit totius legis servandæ, Gal.V.3. Et hoc Sacramento apud Judæos Proselytos justitiæ initiatos & in fœdus adoptatos הַשָּׁמַיִם תּוֹרָה עַל עַיִן מִצְוֹת obligavit lex ad servanda omnia præcepta, ut loquitur R. David Kimchi in lib. Schoraschim Rad. גר. Fuit autem circumcisio Veteris Testamenti Sacramentum, quo Sacerdos ex mandato Dei circumcidebat cultro præputium, atque sic illos segregabat in populum Deo peculiarem. Pluscula tamen sunt, quæ evincant Sacerdotes fuisse ordinarios hujus Sacramenti Ministros. Hinc Mathias Sacerdos liberos eorum, qui ad Ethnicas superstitiones defecerant, circumcidit, 1.Machab.II.46. Verisimile, analogum Sacramentum etiam mulieres habuisse. Auctor Ni Zachon nominat Sacrificium partus. מצות מילת אונה שייכת בנשים ובמו כן יש להן מצות קרבן לידה שאינו שייך באנשים: Præceptum Circumcisionis non pertinet ad fœminas: ideóque traditum est illis Sacrificii partus præceptum: Sed לך לך ss.21. Cæterum, antiquo fœdere סנאו suam adhuc habente, habuit hic ritus ex divina institutione significationem & obsignationem gratiæ tum justificantis, quatenus erat σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης πίστεως, Rom.IV.11. tum sanctificantis, ut admonerentur circumcidere Jehovæ Deo cor suum, & cor seminis sui ad diligendum Jehovam Deum ex toto corde, ex tota anima & propter vitam, Deut.XXX.6. cum Rom.II.29. Quam significationem habuit cum hac modificatione, ut Ecclesiæ circumcisæ vindicaretur, non tantùm communis salus per fidem in Christum, verùm etiam τῆς παλαιᾶς διαθήκης θεοῦ θήκη seu fœderis principalis gratiæ hæc mantissa, ex Patribus circumcisis, non ex præputiatis gentibus Christum nasciturum. Unde jam manifestum, Pseudapostolos circumcisione tam rigidè exacta totum Christianismum impetiisse, paulatim eum sepulturos, si bene conatus vterteret. Horum indolis & ingenii non pœnitet hodie Papatum, qui usu sacrificii increnti & Ceremoniarum legalium, in quibus non est tamen exercitium veræ religionis saturam addunt sitienti, hoc est; Ecclesiam promissionis exhibitione satiatam, & quoad conscientiam consummatam, redigunt in ordinem Ecclesiæ sitientis, in servitutem elementorum mundi, Deut.XXIX.6. Quod enorme peccatum est, quia importat ignorationem sermonis justitiæ, Hebr.V.13. & discriminis Veteris ac Novi Testamenti & beneficiorum Christi. Notabilis locus Jerem. cap.
units.tr: This was the substance of their teaching. They urged circumcision and the law of Moses. Judaism long ago fell into the spirit of circumcision. Hence Paul: I testify again to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law, Gal. 5:3. And by this sacrament the law bound Jewish proselytes, initiated into righteousness and adopted into the covenant, to keep all the precepts, as R. David Kimchi says in the Book of Roots, root גר [ הַשָּׁמַיִם תּוֹרָה עַל עַיִן מִצְוֹת ]. Circumcision was the sacrament of the Old Testament, by which the priest, under God's command, cut the foreskin with a knife and so set them apart as a people peculiar to God. Yet there are several passages which show that priests were the ordinary ministers of this sacrament. Hence the priest Mattathias circumcised the sons of those who had defected to pagan superstitions, 1 Macc. 2:46. It is likely that women also had an analogous sacrament. The author of Ni Zachon calls it the sacrifice of childbirth: The precept of circumcision does not apply to women; therefore the precept of the sacrifice of childbirth was given to them; but [ לך לך ss.21 ]. Moreover, under the old covenant, which still had its Sinai [סנאו], this rite had by divine institution the meaning and seal of grace, both justifying, insofar as it was the seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. 4:11, and sanctifying, so that they might be reminded to circumcise the Lord their God in their hearts, and the hearts of their seed, to love the Lord their God with all their heart and all their soul, that they may live, Deut. 30:6, compare Rom. 2:29. It had this meaning with this qualification: that the circumcised Church was assured not only of common salvation through faith in Christ, but also, as an addition to the principal grace of God's old covenant, [θήκη], that Christ would be born from the circumcised Fathers, not from the uncircumcised nations. From this it is now plain that the false apostles, by pressing circumcision so rigidly, attacked the whole of Christianity, and would gradually bury it if they had succeeded. Papacy today does not regret the disposition and character of these men. By the increasing use of sacrifice and legal ceremonies, in which there is nevertheless no exercise of true religion, they add fullness to the thirsty, that is, they bring back the Church, already satisfied by the showing of the promise and made complete as to conscience, into the order of the thirsty Church, into bondage to the elements of the world, Deut. 29:6. This is a monstrous sin, because it implies ignorance of the word of righteousness, Heb. 5:13, and of the difference between the Old and New Testaments and the benefits of Christ. Notable is the passage in Jer. chapter

units.la: XI.15. Quid dilecto meo in domo mea? Quid videt Filius meus in Templo meo, quod ipsi placere possit? Facere illam sequisiam, maximos illos & plurimos? Etiam carnes Sacra transfibunt à Te. Sacrificia non amplius offerentur. Strenuè etiam imitantur Pseudapostolos illi hodie hypocritae, qui laborant in Religione ἀνύγκλωσιν συγκλάσεων, qui spinosum ponunt in prato, miscent sacra prophanis, obtentu Pacis Ecclesiasticae confundunt fas & nefas, Christum & Belialem, lucem & tenebras, mensam Christi & daemoniorum. Quid hoc aliud, quàm emancipare homines à servitute Dei, & mancipare Diabolo, ac atheismo tandem decumanam portam aperire?
units.tr: 11:15: What has my beloved to do in my house? What does my son see in my temple that could please him? Are these great and numerous sacrifices? Even the holy flesh shall pass from you. Sacrifices are no longer to be offered. Those hypocrites of today also eagerly imitate the false apostles, who labour in religion to mend what is broken [ἀνύγκλωσιν συγκλάσεων], who put thorns in the meadow, mix sacred things with profane, and, under the pretext of ecclesiastical peace, confound right and wrong, Christ and Belial, light and darkness, the table of Christ and of demons. What is this but to free men from the service of God, to hand them over to the devil, and at last to open the great gate to atheism?

units.la: SECUNDUM MOREM MOSIS) id est, disciplinam ac legislationem Mosis. Syrus appositè habet: מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה ritus legis. Ecclesiae circumcisae V. T. duas periodos fecit Christus, Joh. VII.22. Moses dedit vobis circumcisionem. Non quòd ex Mose sit, sed ex Patribus. Prior igitur periodus, qua viguit τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς μῆς, fuit ab Abrahamo usque ad Mosen, in qua fuere Ecclesiae Israeliticae incunabula. Ergo Abrahamus anno aetatis nonagesimo nono, & Ismael anno aetatis decimo tertio divino mandato circumcisi sunt, & omnes Viri domûs illius, tam vernaculi, quàm emtitii & alienigenae, Genes.XVII. Mandatum fuit Abrahamidis ad ampliorem χάριτον, seu confirmationem foederis gratiae, quod Sacramentis sacrificialibus jam antè in praeputio ipsi confirmatum fuit. Jam hoc etiam Sacramento Abrahami posteri intellexerunt, se cum Gentibus caeteris haud temerè permisceri debere, ut ita continua & ordinata serie noscì posset semen illud, in quo benedicendae venirent omnes Gentes, esse illud ipsum benedictum semen, quod Deus Abrahamo in foedere promisit. Censemus autem jure, per imperatam Abrahamidis circumcisionem reliquos Noachidas, qui in praeputio habuerunt jus sacerdotii, & ad idololatriam Gentilium non defecerunt, foedere in Christum confirmato non excidisse. Tametsi Idumaeus frater usque ad devotionem & apostasiam ad Gentilismum, quae paulò serius contigit, circumcisus fuit, & si quando ad Gentilismum defecit, potuit à Judaeis ad circumcisionem cogi, id quod historiis Graecorum & Hebraeorum traditum invenimus. Fuerunt quidem aliae etiam Gentes Orientales, quae Circumcisionis ritum suscepe-runt. Quarum quia obscura origo fuit, etiam accuratissimi scriptores in errorem impulsi sunt. Herodotus ait, solos omnium Mortalium, tasium, Ægyptios, Colchos, & Æthiopes id fecisse. Syros verò, qui in Palæstina sunt, ab Ægyptiis suscepisse. Sed est danda errori venia, quia initia rerum obscura sunt, nisi indubitato authore cognita. Minatur Deus apud Propheram Jeremiam cap.IX.29. Ecce dies veniunt, dicit Dominus, & visitabo omne circumcisum in praeputio. Unde quibusdam Hebraeis opinio incessit, circumcisas illas Gentes arte praeputium retraxisse. Sic author libri Aruch. Tales autem, inquit, erant Ægyptii, quia circumcisi quidem erant, quo tempore vivebant Josephi: at illo mortuo, adduxerunt sibi praeputium. Cujus sententia haud dubie falsa est: quamvis Johannes Drusius illi secundas faciat. Nam Ægyptios prisco more recutitos fuisse, suo adhuc tempore, docere nos possunt Herodotus, Strabo, Hieronymus, Ambrosius. Vide Doctissimum Cunaeum de Rep. Hebr.III.5. Ipse sensus Prophetae perspicuus & explicatus est. Nam distribuit περιτομὴν, circumcisos carne non animo, quales Judaei & Cacozeli, & ἀκροβυστίαν, praeputiatos Gentiles. Altera Periodus circumcisae Ecclesiae Vet. Test. fuit à Mose ad Christum. Quam periodum hoc loco tangunt Pseudapostoli. Atque sic Moisis, quem quo loco habuerint Judaei, non attinet dicere, authoritate & claritudine Antiochenorum fidelium oculos praestringunt. Sic Patrem suum Abrahamum & Familiarem illum Deo amicum Mosen in ore semper habuerunt, securi de voluntate Dei, quam spirituali συγγενεία non discreverunt. Quanto hodie etiam deteriores, qui non ad veram & divinam cathedram Mosis, sed ad inductam & fictitiam quandam cathedram Petri, in qua tamen collocant homines, qui non habent sermonem Dei in se permanentem, sed qui doctores sunt mendacii, & clavem cognitionis occultant, & à Christi fidelium q; Spiritu deficiunt, provocant, atque sic simplicioribus fucum faciunt? Nos nullam in N.T. novimus cathedram infallibilem nisi Dei & Christi, quippe in solius Dei regno sumus. Moisis certè cathedra sublata est, simul cum praesidentia שבט legisperitorum & Pharisaeorum, Genes.XLIX.10. Viderint ergo, ne cathedra, ad quam provocant, sit cathedra irrisorum, qui torquent scripturas, ne pareant illis. Psal.I.1. cathedra nequitiae, quae fingit aerumnam supra statutum, cui nihil addi vel demi potest, & cum Deo sociari non potest, Psal.LXXXIV.20.
units.tr: ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM OF MOSES: that is, the discipline and legislation of Moses. The Syriac aptly renders it [מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה], the ritual of the law. Christ divided the circumcised Church of the Old Testament into two periods, John 7:22: Moses gave you circumcision; not that it is from Moses, but from the Fathers. The first period, in which what was from the beginning [τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς] flourished, ran from Abraham to Moses, and in it lay the cradle of the Israelite Church. So Abraham, in his ninety-ninth year, and Ishmael, in his thirteenth year, were circumcised by divine command, along with all the men of that house, both native-born and bought and foreign, Gen. 17. This command was given to Abraham for the fuller grace [χάριτον], or confirmation, of the covenant of grace, which had already been confirmed to him in his foreskin by the sacrificial sacraments. From this sacrament too, Abraham's descendants understood that they must not carelessly mix with other nations, so that by a continuous and orderly succession that seed, in whom all nations would be blessed, might be recognised as that same blessed seed which God promised to Abraham in the covenant. We judge, moreover, rightly that the other Noachides, who in their foreskin had the right of priesthood and did not fall into Gentile idolatry, did not forfeit the covenant confirmed in Christ, although Abraham's command of circumcision was imposed on them. Although the Idumean brother was circumcised, to his devotion and apostasy into Gentilism, which happened rather later, and if at any time he defected to Gentilism, he could be compelled by the Jews to circumcision, as we find recorded in the histories of the Greeks and Hebrews. There were indeed other eastern nations too that adopted the rite of circumcision. Because their origin was obscure, even the most careful writers were led into error. Herodotus says that only the Colchians, the Egyptians, and the Ethiopians among all mortals did this, and that the Syrians of Palestine had received it from the Egyptians. But pardon must be granted to this error, because the beginnings of things are obscure unless known from an undoubted author. God threatens through the prophet Jeremiah, ch. 9:25: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will visit all who are circumcised in the foreskin. Hence some Hebrews came to hold the opinion that those circumcised nations had drawn back the foreskin by some art. So the author of the book Aruch: Such, he says, were the Egyptians, for they were circumcised while Joseph lived; but when he died, they drew the foreskin back over themselves. This opinion is undoubtedly false, although John Drusius gives it second place. For Herodotus, Strabo, Jerome and Ambrose can show us that the Egyptians were circumcised in the ancient manner even in their own time. See the most learned Cunaeus, On the Hebrew Commonwealth, 3.5. The very meaning of the prophet is clear and plain. For he distinguishes circumcision [περιτομὴν], those circumcised in flesh but not in heart, such as the Jews and the zealots, from uncircumcision [ἀκροβυστίαν], the uncircumcised Gentiles. The second period of the circumcised Old Testament Church ran from Moses to Christ. It is this period that the false apostles touch on here. And as to what the Jews thought of Moses, it is not necessary to say; by the authority and fame of the faithful Antiochenes they dazzle the eyes. Thus they always had Abraham their father and Moses, that friend of God, on their lips, secure about the will of God, which they did not distinguish by spiritual kinship [συγγενεία]. How much worse are those today, who appeal not to the true and divine seat of Moses, but to a contrived and fictitious seat of Peter, in which they nevertheless place men who do not have the word of God abiding in them, but are teachers of lies, who hide the key of knowledge, and who, having fallen from the Spirit of Christ's faithful people, deceive the simpler folk? We know of no infallible seat in the New Testament except that of God and Christ, for we are in the kingdom of God alone. Certainly the seat of Moses has been taken away, together with the rule of the sceptre [שבט] of the lawyers and Pharisees, Gen. 49:10. Let them see to it, then, lest the seat to which they appeal be the seat of the scornful, who twist the Scriptures so that men will not obey them, Ps. 1:1; the seat of wickedness, which devises trouble beyond what is ordained, to which nothing can be added or taken away, and which cannot be joined with God, Ps. 84:20.

units.la: NON POTESTIS SALVARI.) Non simpliciter circumcisionem urgent, sed ut necessariam ad salutem. Jam Christo nondum nato habuit necessitatem mandati. Nato autem & mortuo necessitas ex parabat. Videntur autem Pseudapostoli juxta necessitatem mandati etiam necessitatem medii docuisse. In quo quantopere falsi sint, apparet. In circumcisione enim, tanquam principali parte foedus spirituale cum Abrahamo non esse sancitum, discere poterat ex eo, quod circumcisionis mandatum ipsi datum in praeputio: quod neglectum in deserto per quadraginta annos: quod continuerit mysticam quandam & excellentiorem significationem, quam toties urgent Prophetae, ingeminantes, ut cor circumcidatur, non caro, Deut. X. 16. XXX. 6. Jerem. IV. 4. quod umbras destinati operis auferri conveniat, opere impleto. Jam duo accedunt, quibus omnium validissime, ne fideles ob neglectum infestarentur, reprimi poterant. Primum, quod in circumcisione fuerit significatio futuri temporis, cum illorum tempore minime conciliabilis, nempe illa: multiplicandum ex benedictione Divina semen Abrahami propter nasciturum ex illo semine Christum. Alterum, quod discriminare debuit Peculiarem Deo populum murali velut sepimento, à Gentibus, donec & illae in plenitudine temporum in tentoria Semi allicerentur, & imitarentur illam adeo memoratam Abrahami fiduciam, qua praesente inimicitias in hac lege validas exolescere decebat. Praeclare Irenaeus lib. IV. cap. 30. Quod autem circumcisionem non quasi consummatricem justitiae, sed in signo eam dedit Deus, ut cognoscibile perseveret genus Abrahae, ex ipsa Scriptura discimus. Dixit enim, inquit, Deus ad Abraham: Circumcidetur omne masculinum vestrum, & circumcidetis carnem praeputii vestri, & erit in signum Testamenti inter me & Vos. Haec omnia in Christo impleta videre poterant, mens ni laeva fuisset. Has rationes istis Zelotis etiam Curcellaeus objicere poterat. Sed aliam insistit viam. In qua nobis rursus cum eo certamen cerneendum. Adeo ubique scorias suas admiscet. Mirari se dicit, quod adeo duri fuerint Pseudapostoli in eo negotio, cum tamen omnium Judaeorum non eadem esset sententia, pag. 91. Ac deinde induit exemplum Izatae Adiabenorum Regis, qui in Religione Judaeorum à quodam Anania institutus existimabat, se non perfectum esse Judaeum posse, nisi circumcideretur. Idilli Ananiam dissuasisse hac oratione: Δυνάμεναν αὐτὸν, ἔφη, καὶ χωρὶς περιτομῆς τὸ θεῖον σέβειν, εἰς πάντως κέκρικε ζηλὼν καὶ πάντα τῶν Ιουδαίων. Τοῦτο ἐναι πυνάσπιτον δ' ἐξεπίμψασθαι. Licere ei, dixit, dicie, etiam absque circumcisione Deum colere, si Judaeorum instituta placeant. In hoc enim magis sitam religionem, quàm in circumcisione, Antiq Jud. XX.2. Allegat ὁμολογήσας Tryphonem apud Justinum Martyrem, & Menasse Ben Israel de resurrectione mortuorum. Quae haud dubie ad id sunt comparata, ut doceat, in Veteri Testamento Gentilibus viam ad salutem extra Mosen munitam fuisse. Quam sententiam fractis verecundiae repagulis aperto pectore defensum ivit in Scripto Gallico Amstelodami edito cap. 13. Cujus argumenta ibi allata Celeb. Theologus, Doctor Maresius ad partes vocavit Anti-Tirin. Tom. II. pag. 281. &c. Quem hoc ipso tempore in alio Curcellaei scripto expumicando eruditam & exactam, pro more, operam sumere accepimus. Sed foenum esse oporteat, qui levibus Curcellaei, quas hic attulit, vel ratiunculis, vel exemplis Pseudapostolos in ordinem redigere sustineret. Altioris indaginis res est. Probari conveniebat Scripturis, in Veteri Testamento post νομοθεσίαν Mosaicam Ecclesiae praeputiatae salutem promissam. Evidens est expostulatio Dei de potestate clavium neglecta contra incircumcisos carne Ezech. XLIV. 6.7.8.9. Et Apostolus legem circumcisionis unà cum reliquis cultus Ceremonialis mandatis divinis vocat inimicitias, quibus non ante mortem Christi peremptis Gentes Deo conciliatae fuerunt, Eph. I.15.16. Hanc etiam constantem Rabbinorum doctrinam, Praeputiatis olim Templi fores clausas, & Sacra prohibita fuisse, supra docuimus. Quibus Ananias illa praeposttera sua institutione leges dicere minimè debet. Quàm nefariis interpretamentis legem Dei paulò ante Christum Sacerdotes & Pharisaei depravarint & collusularint, nemini clam est, qui correctionem Christi Matth. V.XV. XXIII. ad animum revocat. Sed alia in promptu sunt, quibus ab hoc praesidio depellatur. Izates ille, quem Ezaten Tacitus A.XII.14.2. vocat, proinde hoc loco, cùm aliis in exemplaribus etiam Juliatas & Hyliatas reperias, ab Incomparabili & Desideratissimo nostro Frenshemio emaculatus; defuncto Parente Monobazo, Helenae Matris rogatu, & Magnatibus ac Satrapis Regni in vota missis, Adiabenorum Rex creatus est. Mater Helena Judaeorum disciplinae multò ante addicta. Ad eandem animum applicat, duce Anania, Izates. Et jam in eo fuit, ut circumcisionis Sacramento initiari se Judaismo peteret. Sed hic mater & Ananias tragulam injiciunt, quòd timerent, ne Adiabeni professum Judaeum vel non paterentur dominum, vel crebris insi-diis diis appeterent. Hinc illæ Præceptoris Ananiæ lachrymæ. Nam Izate circumcisionem urgente Ananias, ne & Regis fortunam & se periculis obiceret, omnia commentus, ut Rex conari & velle desisteret. Ergo fingit: Licere ei absque circumcisione Deum pie colere, si Judæorum institua placeant. In hoc enim magis situm religionem, quàm in circumcisione corporis: daturúmque Deum veniam, si necessitate coactus signaculum id omitteret, metu, ne qua exoriatur subditorum defectio. Hic Ananias Izaten traducere conatus est vel ad Proselythismum justitiæ, vel domicilii. Si prius, mentitus est, & desultoria levitate Regem delusit. Nam Dei præceptum de Proselytho justitiæ, qui verus Judæus: Esto sicut vos. Exod. XII. Num. XIV. Et incircumciso excidium intentatum. Quàm verò firma ratio à figmento mercatoris, qui Regiarum mulierum & Regis clementiam ambivit, quod hominum genus Polypo versatilius esse solet? Ne dicam, hoc parum dignum vero Judæo, id est, Confessore nominis Dei, dissuadere Regi circumcisionem tam graviter demandatam, hoc solo metu, ne purpuræ jacturam Rex faceret. Sed & loqui ipsum de casu necessitatis, quem tamen ipse fingit, palàm est. In vero autem necessitatis casu haud dubiè circumcisionis mandatum non obligavit, cùm in eo religio non vertatur. Si posterius, quid augas nobis vendit Curcellæus? An ergo Proselythi domicilii, qui fœdere Dei exclusi fuerunt, nec catechesin illam salutarem habuerunt de reconciliatione per Christum olim intercessura, sine circumcisione salvari potuerunt? Næ cæcus doctor cæcorum! Ertamen Ananias ad posteriorem hunc Proselythismum, omnia perpendenti, Regem voluisse traducere videtur. Jam &, cùm Tryphonem & Menassen Ben-Israel nobis obducit, in caducum parietem inclinat. Nam Tryphon in Disputatione cum Justino habita necessitatem circumcisionis multis adstruit: quem propterea in hac causa Grotius obelo notavit. Menasse Ben-Israel, cùm Gentes piè viventes participes facit futuri Seculi, non loquitur ex sacrorum sententia, sed Christianis caput demulcet, & ficum, quod ajunt, cupit. Nullus igitur est Curcellæus, & videt hic, quod nemo, qui sapit, videt.
units.tr: YOU CANNOT BE SAVED.) They do not press circumcision simply, but as necessary to salvation. Before Christ was born the command had a necessity of its own; after his birth and death the necessity lapsed. The false apostles seem to have taught that, along with the necessity of the command, there was also a necessity of the means. How far they were wrong in this is clear. From circumcision, as the principal part, one could learn that the spiritual covenant with Abraham was not ratified by it: the command was given to him while he was still uncircumcised; it was neglected in the wilderness for forty years; it carried a mystical and more excellent meaning, which the prophets press so often, repeating that the heart should be circumcised, not the flesh (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4); and the shadow of an intended work ought to be removed once the work was accomplished. Two further points could have most powerfully checked the faithful from being troubled by their neglect of it. First, circumcision signified a future time, which could hardly be reconciled with their own times, namely that through the divine blessing the seed of Abraham was to be multiplied on account of Christ, who would be born from that seed. Second, it was meant to separate the people peculiar to God from the Gentiles by a kind of wall, until in the fullness of time the Gentiles too would be drawn to the tent of the Seed and would imitate that much-mentioned faith of Abraham, by which, once it was present, the strong enmities of this law ought to have faded away. Irenaeus rightly says in book IV, chapter 30: "We learn from Scripture itself that God gave circumcision not as something that would complete righteousness, but as a sign, so that the race of Abraham might remain recognisable. For God said to Abraham: 'Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.'" All these things could have been seen fulfilled in Christ, had the mind not been perverse. Curcellaeus could have raised these reasons against those zealots too, but he takes another path. Here again we must contend with him, and see how everywhere he mixes in his own dross. He says he is surprised that the false apostles were so stubborn in that matter, since not all the Jews held the same view (p. 91). Then he brings forward the example of Izates, king of the Adiabeni, who, having been instructed in the religion of the Jews by a certain Ananias, believed that he could not become a complete Jew unless he were circumcised. Ananias, the story goes, dissuaded him with this speech: [Δυνάμενον αὐτὸν ἔφη καὶ χωρὶς περιτομῆς τὸ θεῖον σέβειν, εἴ γε πάντως κέκρικε ζηλῶν καὶ πάντα τὰ τῶν Ἰουδαίων.] "He said that it was permitted him to worship God even without circumcision, if he had decided to be zealous in all the Jewish customs. For religion lies more in this than in circumcision." (Antiq. Jud. 20.2.) He cites Tryphon, in Justin Martyr, who admitted it, and Menasseh Ben Israel on the resurrection of the dead. These are clearly brought forward to teach that in the Old Testament a way to salvation outside Moses was open to the Gentiles. Curcellaeus defended this opinion with an open heart, shameless, in a French writing published at Amsterdam, chapter 13. The learned theologian, Doctor Maresius, called his arguments there to account in Anti-Tirin, vol. II, p. 281 etc. We hear that at this very time Curcellaeus is undertaking, as is his habit, the learned and exact task of exposing another of his writings. But whoever would bring the false apostles into line with such light arguments and examples as Curcellaeus has offered here would have to be a hayseed. This is a matter of deeper investigation. It needed to be proved from Scripture that in the Old Testament, after the Mosaic legislation, salvation was promised to the uncircumcised Church. God's complaint about the neglect of the power of the keys against the uncircumcised in the flesh is plain: Ezek. 44:6–9. And the Apostle calls the law of circumcision, together with the other ceremonial commands of worship, enmities, which were not destroyed until the death of Christ, and by which the Gentiles were reconciled to God (Eph. 2:14–16). We have also shown above the constant teaching of the rabbis, that the gates of the Temple were closed to the uncircumcised and the holy things forbidden to them. By these things Ananias ought not to be permitted to set aside the laws with his perverse institution. How impiously the priests and Pharisees corrupted and twisted the law of God shortly before Christ is known to everyone who recalls Christ's correction (Matt. 5, 15; 23). But other things are at hand by which this defence is driven off. That Izates, whom Tacitus calls Ezaten (Ann. 12.14), is here emended by our incomparable and much-desired Freinsheim, since in other copies you also find Juliatas and Hyliatas. When his father Monobazus had died, Izates was made king of the Adiabeni at the request of his mother Helena and at the wish of the nobles and satraps of the kingdom. His mother Helena had long been devoted to the discipline of the Jews, and Izates, under the guidance of Ananias, turned his mind to the same. And he was already at the point of asking to be initiated into Judaism by the sacrament of circumcision. But at this his mother and Ananias threw a spanner in the works, because they feared that the Adiabeni would either not tolerate a Jewish ruler, or would attack him with frequent plots. Hence the tears of his teacher Ananias. For when Izates pressed for circumcision, Ananias, not wishing to expose both the king's fortune and himself to danger, devised everything so that the king would cease to attempt and to want it. So he invents this: "It is permitted him to worship God piously without circumcision, if the institutions of the Jews are pleasing." For religion lies more in this than in bodily circumcision; and God would pardon him if, compelled by necessity, he omitted that sign, from fear lest some revolt of his subjects should arise. Here Ananias has tried to lead Izates either to proselytism of righteousness or to proselytism of residence. If the former, he has lied and deceived the king with a flighty levity. For God's command concerning the proselyte of righteousness, who is a true Jew, is: "Let him be as you are" (Exod. 12; Num. 15), and for the uncircumcised there is threatened extermination. But how weak is the argument drawn from the fiction of a merchant who courted the kindness of royal women and of the king, a sort of people usually more changeable than a polyp! Not to mention that it is scarcely fitting for a true Jew, that is, a confessor of the name of God, to dissuade a king from circumcision, which was so gravely enjoined, out of this single fear, that the king might lose his purple. But that Ananias is speaking of a case of necessity, which he himself invents, is also plain. In a true case of necessity the command of circumcision certainly did not bind, since religion does not consist in it. If the latter, what do you sell us as profit, Curcellaeus? Could the proselytes of residence, who were excluded from the covenant of God and did not have that saving instruction about reconciliation through Christ which was to come in time, be saved without circumcision? Oh, blind teacher of the blind! Yet Ananias seems to have wished to lead the king toward this latter proselytism, if one weighs everything. And now, when he brings forward Tryphon and Menasseh Ben Israel against us, he leans on a crumbling wall. For Tryphon, in the disputation held with Justin, argues for the necessity of circumcision at length; Grotius therefore marked him with an obelus in this matter. Menasseh Ben Israel, when he makes the Gentiles who live piously partakers of the age to come, does not speak from the judgment of the sacred writings, but strokes the heads of the Christians and seeks, as they say, to get a fig. Curcellaeus, therefore, is nothing, and here he sees what no one who has sense would see.

units.la: Versus II. CUM ERGO SEDITIO ET DISCEPTATIO NON EXIGUA ESSET PAULO ET BARNABÆ CONTRA ILLOS)
units.tr: Verse 2. When therefore there was no small sedition and dispute between Paul and Barnabas and those men,

units.la: Lucas vocat. Si σὺν placet seditionem vertere, tum haud dubie ad Pseudapostolos referri debet, qui more demagogorum populum concitârunt, ut tumultuari & furere inciperet. Alienum enim ab ingenio Pauli & Barnabæ fuit, ut seditiosis clamoribus & orationibus populo ad commotionem publicam præirent. Veritati doctrinæ & restitudi-ni animi sui confisi popularem opem non concupiverunt. Vel certè esse debet catachresis & metalepsis, ut σὺν ponatur pro contentione, ex qua, si vehemens sit, seditio oriri solet. Syrus convertit: Conturbatio magna, & disceptatio. Sed & σὺν notare potest acrem dissensionem, secessionem & constans certamen. Ut intelligant in alia omnia dissensionem fecisse, & in adversis partibus disputando constanter permansisse. Quod convenit cum eo, quod dicitur Gal. II. ς. ὡς ἰδὲ ὡς ἀεὶ ἐχαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου μείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Quibus ne quidem ad momentum cessimus quoad subjectionem, ut veritas Evangelii permaneat apud vos. Ubi ὥρα rectius vertitur momentum, ut conveniat cum Chaldaico שעה quod usurpatur apud Danielem IV. ς. ubi significat ipsum temporis momentum, quo aliquid geritur. In eadem historia versatus Paulus σὺν suam sic exprimit, constantem nempe contradictionem & resistentiam. Ambrosius quidem in eo loco omittit particulam ὡς, quasi ad horam cesserint subjectione Paulus & Barnabas, adeoque σὺν illa fuerit interrupta. Id quod omnium Codicum Græcorum fidei repugnat. Erasmus tamen Ambrosio videtur favere, & Paulum in illa συζητήσει facere ad horam cedentem & succumbentem. Quomodo, inquit, non cessit, qui Timotheum coactus est circumcidere? Hausit hanc objectionem ex Divo Ambrosio, qui in Com. ad Gal. II. omnino, ut dixi, statuit: Paulum & Barnabam ad horam se subjecisse servituti, humiliantes se legi, ut circumcisio Timothea cessaret dolus et scandalum Judæorum. Paratos enim fuisse, sicut datur intelligi, commovere ipsi tumultum & seditionem. In hanc rem prolixus Ambrosius. Sed facile apparet, Erasmum cum Ambrosio errare. Nam circumstantia loci, temporis & personarum varia est. Timotheus matre Judæa, Patre Græco natus circumciditur, ne offendantur infirmiores Judæi. Ibi omnino cessit ruditati & infirmitati simplicium Judæorum. In hac autem actione, qua hæresiarchæ petulantes & præfracti Titum Græcis parentibus natum circumcidi voluerunt, cur idem faceret & vel ad momentum cederet. ret, non erat ratio. Cerinthus enim & Ebion, sive quibuscunque hic adversariis usus est Apostolus, non fuerunt infirmi Judæi, quorum esset scandalo metuendum, sed falsi fratres Gal. II. 4. quos proinde ψευδαδέλφους, κακὰς ἐργάτας, κατατομήν vocat Phil. III. 2. quos optat ἀποκόπτεσθαι Gal. V. 12.
