Et cederet talibus vel ad momentum, ac eo quidem tempore, quo hominum istorum molimini bus Christiana libertas periclitabatur? Absit animosum cætera Apostolum hic Thersiten faciamus!
units.tr: Luke calls it so. If σὺν is to be rendered "sedition," then it must undoubtedly be referred to the false apostles, who, after the manner of demagogues, stirred up the people so that they began to riot and rage. For it was foreign to the character of Paul and Barnabas to lead the people in seditious outcries and speeches toward public upheaval. Trusting in the truth of their teaching and the steadfastness of their own spirit, they did not seek popular help. Or else there must be a catachresis and metalepsis, so that σὺν stands for contention, from which sedition usually arises if it is vehement. The Syriac translates: great disturbance, and dispute. But σὺν can also denote a sharp dissension, a secession and a constant strife, so that they understand that they made dissension on all other points and persisted steadily in disputing with the opposing side. This agrees with what is said in Gal. 2: οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν εἴξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ εὐαγγελίου μείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς [to whom we did not yield in subjection even for a moment, that the truth of the gospel might remain with you]. Here ὥρα is more correctly rendered "moment," so that it agrees with the Chaldean [sha'ah], which is used in Daniel 4, where it means the very moment of time in which something is done. Paul, having been involved in this same history, expresses σὺν in the same way, namely as a constant contradiction and resistance. Ambrose, indeed, omits the particle ὡς in that passage, as if Paul and Barnabas had yielded in subjection for an hour only, and so σὺν had been interrupted. This is contrary to the faith of all the Greek manuscripts. Erasmus nevertheless seems to favour Ambrose, and makes Paul in that συζήτησις yield and give way for a time. "How," he says, "did he not yield, who was compelled to circumcise Timothy?" He drew this objection from Divus Ambrose, who in his commentary on Gal. 2 altogether holds, as I said, that Paul and Barnabas submitted themselves to servitude for an hour, humbling themselves under the law, so that the circumcision of Timothy might cease, lest the Jews be deceived and offended. For they were prepared, as it is intimated, to stir up tumult and sedition themselves. Ambrose is lengthy on this matter. But it readily appears that Erasmus errs with Ambrose. For the circumstances of place, time and persons are different. Timothy, born of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, is circumcised lest the weaker Jews be offended. There he certainly yielded to the simplicity and weakness of the plain Jews. But in this affair, in which the petulant and headstrong heresiarchs wanted Titus, born of Greek parents, to be circumcised, there was no reason why he should do the same, or yield even for a moment. For Cerinthus and Ebion, or whoever the adversaries were that the Apostle dealt with, were not weak Jews, whose scandal was to be feared, but false brethren (Gal. 2:4), whom he therefore calls ψευδαδέλφους, κακὰς ἐργάτας, κατατομήν (Phil. 3:2), and whom he wishes to be ἀποκόπτεσθαι (Gal. 5:12). Should he yield to such men even for a moment, and at that time, when Christian liberty was in danger from the schemes of these men? Far be it! Let us not make the Apostle here a bold Thersites in all other respects!

units.la: STATUERUNT) In Græco occurrit τάξαι. Ut de destinatione & ordinatione, adeóque φέρεσθαι illa vox in Scripturis usurpari solita sit, contra quàm in alio loco Socinistæ delirant. Statuerunt autem Antiocheni, nempe Ecclesia Antiochena, ut diximus ad V. 3. Erat hoc prudentiæ, providere rebus nutantibus, & anguem in herba opprimere, ne ad molestam seditionem res perveniret. Alia enim commoda supererant media, quæ prudenter hic arripiunt. UT ASCENDERENT PAULUS ET BARNABAS) Deligunt personas maximè idoneas. Hi enim errorem adversariorum deprehenderunt, & magno animo confutare cœperunt. Sed & in Apostolis documentum modestiæ & candoris ac mansuetudinis elucet. Apostolatu Dei fungebantur. Poterant igitur authoritate sua, spiritu Dei, quo induti ex alto fuerunt, freti τὸ ἀναλογίας expedire, & in alterutram partem aliquid decernere, ac decreto suo Ecclesiam adstringere. Attamen authoritatis suæ rationem non habent, & vadimonium obire ex Ecclesiæ τάξει properant. In quo prudentia etiam Pauli prædicari meretur. Nam hac sua obedientia consuluit infirmis. Multi sunt, quibus veritas displicet eo solo nomine, quòd certis quibusdam hominibus non placuit, qui in magna sunt authoritate, quibus proinde nihil non fidunt. Ergo tales authoritate mentiuntur. Cùm igitur alii fuerint ψευδαπόστολοι εἶναι, eos non detrectavit consulere, ne intercluderetur via Evangelio, & ut eadem opera pateret, se non docere aliud, quàm Apostoli, qui authoritate & æstimatione apud vulgus hominum eminebat. Sic alibi, etiamsi licuisset Paulo vivere de altari, noluit tamen, ne adversarii haberent quod objicerent, veritus nimirum, ne id officeret profectui Evangelii. Quorum si exemplo olim Romani Pontifices moveri potuissent, res Ecclesiæ æquabilius haud dubiè haberent. Cùm superiori seculo de religione non exigua effet σὸς ὁπ ηοσυζήτησις, statuerunt plures Ecclesiae Paulos & Barnabas suos mittere ad Concilium, in quo veri monstrator & almae ille Spiritus, ut loquitur Franciscus I. Galliarum Rex in sua ad Protestantes Epistola apud Sleidanum lib.8. ad A.C.1531. primas partes obtineat. Instigabantur Romani Pontifices, & immiti stimulo Caroli Imperatoris ac Ordinum Imperii incitabantur saepissime. Quibus obstinatissime reluctari sunt, causati, se Paulos esse, se Barnabas, se fidei ac morum arbitros infallibiles, & Christianismi Praetores. Et, ut Antichristi cutem palpes, Paulus III. Pontifex Carolum, apud ipsum pro Concilio celebrando instantem, comparavit cum Uzia, arcae ruinam minanti manum admovente; cum seditiosis Core, Dathan & Abirom adversus Mosen, & Aaronem, cornua obvertentibus; cum Uzia incensum in altari adolente, & multa ejusmodi adversus Imperatorem in ea Epistola insolenter jactavit, ceu videre est apud Joh. Wolphium Lect. Memorabil. Tom. II. pag. 539. Procul haec absunt a mitissimo Pauli & Barnabae ingenio, qui Ecclesiae petitioni se longe inferioris iubentes obsecundarunt, & cum ejus mandatis Hierosolymas ad Concilium iverunt. Sed, quoad Paulum attinet, est in hac re non levis dubitatio. Nam Gal.II.2. dicit: Se Hierosolymam ascendisse κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν, secundum revelationem. Hoc loco Lucas testatur, ipsum cum Barnaba ascendisse ex Ζήτησις Ecclesiae. Hae causae impulsivae profectionis repugnare videntur. Et sane haec Chrysostomo causa fuit, ut negaret eandem profectionem describi Gal.II.& Act.XV.ad Synodum nempe Hierosolymitanam. Caeterum nullo negotio sibi Paulus conciliatur. Nam decretum Ecclesiae & immediata revelatio non pugnant, sed subordinantur. Primum accepit a Deo revelationem. Postea Ecclesiam Antiochenam officii sui monuit. Vel certe, si praecessit Ecclesiae πὺξις, Divina revelatione ad exequendum Ecclesiae decretum instinctus fuit.
units.tr: THEY DETERMINED) In the Greek it is τάξαι. Thus the word is used of appointment and ordination, as is customary in the Scriptures, contrary to what the Socinians rave elsewhere. The Antiochenes, namely the Church of Antioch, determined this, as we said at v. 3. It was a matter of prudence to provide for wavering affairs and to crush the snake in the grass, lest the matter come to troublesome sedition. For other suitable means remained, which they prudently take up here. THAT PAUL AND BARNABAS SHOULD GO UP) They choose the most suitable persons. For these men detected the error of the adversaries and began to refute them with great courage. But in the Apostles also a proof of modesty, candour and gentleness shines forth. They were discharging the apostolate of God. They could therefore, relying on their authority, with the Spirit of God with which they had been clothed from on high, settle the matter by [analogy], and decide something one way or the other, and bind the Church by their decree. Yet they do not take account of their authority, and hasten to submit to the τάξις of the Church. In this the prudence of Paul also deserves to be praised. For by this obedience of his he consulted the weak. There are many to whom the truth is displeasing for the sole reason that it did not please certain men who have great authority, in whom therefore they trust in everything. Such men therefore lie with their authority. Since there were others who were ψευδαπόστολοι εἶναι, he did not disdain to consult them, lest the way be closed to the Gospel, and so that at the same time it might be made plain that he taught nothing other than the Apostles, who were eminent in authority and esteem among the common people. So elsewhere, although it would have been lawful for Paul to live from the altar, he nevertheless chose not to, lest the adversaries have something to object to, fearing no doubt that this would hinder the progress of the Gospel. If the Roman Pontiffs could have been moved by the example of these men long ago, the affairs of the Church would undoubtedly be on a more even footing. When in the last century there was no small dispute over religion, several Churches determined to send their own Pauls and Barnabases to a Council, in which, as Francis I, King of the Gauls, says in his letter to the Protestants reported by Sleidan (book 8, in the year 1531), veri monstrator & almae ille Spiritus should hold the first place. The Roman Pontiffs were urged on, and were very often spurred on by the harsh goading of Emperor Charles and the Orders of the Empire. They resisted most obstinately, alleging that they were Pauls and Barnabases, that they were the infallible arbiters of faith and morals, and the praetors of Christianity. And, to flatter the skin of Antichrist, Pope Paul III compared Charles, who was urging him to hold a Council, with Uzziah, who laid his hand on the ark as it was falling; with the seditious Korah, Dathan and Abiram, who turned their horns against Moses and Aaron; with Uzziah burning incense on the altar; and in that letter he insolently boasted of many such things against the Emperor, as may be seen in Johann Wolf, Lectiones memorabiles, vol. 2, p. 539. These things are far removed from the most gentle disposition of Paul and Barnabas, who, yielding to the petition of the Church, far below themselves, complied and went up to Jerusalem to the Council with its instructions. But as far as Paul is concerned, there is no slight doubt in this matter. For in Gal. 2:2 he says that he went up to Jerusalem κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν, according to a revelation. In this place Luke testifies that he went up with Barnabas by the ζήτησις of the Church. These impelling causes of the journey seem to conflict. And indeed this was the reason why Chrysostom denied that the same journey was described in Gal. 2 and Acts 15, namely to the Synod at Jerusalem. However, Paul is reconciled to himself without any difficulty. For a decree of the Church and an immediate revelation do not conflict, but are subordinated. He first received a revelation from God. Afterwards he reminded the Church of Antioch of its duty. Or at least, if the πύξις of the Church came first, he was moved by divine revelation to carry out the decree of the Church.

units.la: ET QUIDAM ALII EX ILLIS) Titum nonnulli intelligunt, & alios Paulo ac Barnabae concordes. Potius est, ut intelligamus aliquos ex grege Cerinthi & Judaizantium, quorum causam audiri aequae conveniebat. In quo candide & ingenue agunt Antiocheni, procul studiis amoris & odii veritatem simpliciter requirentes. AD APOSTOLOS) Qui Hierosolymis tum temporis domicilium meruti, ut sequitur. Quaeritur, qui illi? Nam non omnes Apostolos Hierosolymis tum fuisse, manifestum. De Jacobo, fratre Johannis certum, non amplius superstitem fuisse. Quippe ante septennium ab Herode Agrippa supplicio affectus est. Ut vel hoc uno argumento vel voΔείa, vel ἀλεαία Clementis Constitutionum etiam Baronio, Bellarmino, Cornelio à Lapide & aliis hic agnita, luce meridiana clarius deprehendi possit, qui lib. VI. Constitut. cap. XII. scribit, omnes duodecim Apostolos per orbem dispersos, instinctu Dei Hierosolymas venisse, & hanc quaestionem definivisse. Ut poenitere debebat erroris sui Turrianum, qui Clementem tanquam germanum adhuc propugnare sustinuit. Non nego, Apostolos aliquandiu post ascensionem Christi in coelum Hierosolymis mansisse omnes. Nam post caedem Protomartyris, persecutione magna effervescente, cui Saulus magno zelo ministraverat, Act. VIII. 1. manserunt Apostoli Hierosolymis, caeteris per universum orbem dispersis, quorum aliquot fuerunt millia Act. II. 41. IV. 4. Tametsi Hierosolymas nonnunquam ad tempus reliquerint, uti factum non longe post illam persecutionem à Petro & Johanne, qui, cum audissent Apostoli Samariam recepisse sermonem Dei, eo missi sunt: quibus precantibus & manus eis imponentibus receperunt illi Spiritum Sanctum. Quo tempore autem post illam ἀποστολη Hierosolymis discesserint ad praeconium Evangelii, altissimum est ubique silentium. Eusebius quidem lib. V. cap. 18. tradit ex Apollonio, quod Dominus praecepisset Apostolis, ne ante duodecimum annum Hierosolymis discederent. Quod minime cum historia congruit. Nam & infra quidam Hierosolymis manserunt, & ante alii Hierosolymis discesserunt. Hoc affine vero, post celebratam illam persecutionem non nimis diu ipsos Hierosolymis substitisse. Quod tamen ex Origene & Eucherio Lugdunensi, quibus annumerari potest Eusebius III. 1. Curcellaeus pag. 95. asserit, eἀποστολος ειςτ σφ τους ορεις Terrarum partes forte divisisse, in quas singuli Evangelium praedicatum irent: παραδοχεως recipiendum non ducimus. Eusebius quidem ex traditione commemorat, Thomam Parthiam sortitum, Andream Scythiam, Johannem Asiam, Petrum in Ponto, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, Asia & Roma praedicasse. Et lib. II. 16. Marcum ad Aegyptum missum, & Alexandriae Ecclesiae constituisse. Nicephorus II. 39. Philippum & Bartholomaeum in Syria ria & Asia Ecclesias constituisse tradit, & cap. 40. Thomam in Æthiopia, Parthia, Media, Taprobana Ecclesias plantasse. Quae partim incerta, partim falsa esse contendo. Nam constat iisdem in provinciis & locis plures Apostolos, tum uno & eodem tempore, tum diverso Evangelium plantasse, & Ecclesias constituisse. In Corintho docuerunt Paulus, Apollo, Cephas. Romae Paulus, &, si fides Eusebio, sub finem vitae Petrus. In Asia Johannes, Petrus, Paulus fuerunt: in Galatia Paulus & Petrus. Et erant Apostoli non tantum plantatores Ecclesiarum, sed etiam communes Inspectores & visitatores, quod multis & obviis exemplis doceri posset. Sed de illa orbis Terrarum divisione quicquid fiat, vix probari potest, eo tempore, quo iter Hierosolymam ex sanctione Ecclesiae Antiochenae Paulus inibat ad Apostolos, Hierosolymis alios commoratos, quam Jacobum, Cephan & Johannem, quorum nomina expressa sunt Gal. II. 9. Ubi singulare illud est, quod de triga illa Paulus dicit: οἱ δοκοῦντες στῦλοι εἶναι, qui putantur esse columnae. Duum generum columnae erant. Aliae sustentabant aedificium, aliae ornabant. Ejusmodi duae columnae ante Templum Solomonis constitutae. Columnas vocat utroque modo. Columnae autem erant Collegii Apostolici & Ecclesiae. Neque detrahit ipsis laudem hac dictione: qui putantur: tanquam rei veritate non fuisset. Chrysostomus dicit, ad rei veritatem Paulum assumere aliorum opinionem. Et id lubenter facere, quia putabantur esse columnae etiam adversariis. Est igitur honorificentissimum elogium, quo ipsos ex judicio etiam hostium, qui non nisi veritatis splendore subacti probos laudant, exornare, non suo tantum nomine voluit. Hoc ideo commemoro, ne verbis, ut crude jacent, acceptis, existimetur, lividius de illis Apostolis Paulum locutum.
units.tr: AND CERTAIN OTHERS OF THEM) Some understand this to mean Titus, and others to mean men who agreed with Paul and Barnabas. It is more likely that we should understand some from the party of Cerinthus and the Judaizers, whose case it was just as proper to hear. In this the Antiochenes act candidly and openly, seeking the truth plainly and far from the partisanship of love and hatred. TO THE APOSTLES) Who at that time had earned a dwelling-place for the time, as follows. The question is: who were they? For it is clear that not all the Apostles were then at Jerusalem. It is certain that James, the brother of John, was no longer alive, since he had been put to death by Herod Agrippa about seven years earlier. So that by this one argument alone, or by the falsehood [ψευδεία] or the truth [ἀλήθεια] of Clement's Constitutions, which Baronius, Bellarmine, Cornelius a Lapide and others also acknowledge here, it may be perceived more clearly than midday light. Clement says in book VI of the Constitutions, chapter XII, that all twelve Apostles, scattered throughout the world, came to Jerusalem by the impulse of God and settled this question. Turrianus, who ventured to defend Clement as still genuine, ought to repent of his error. I do not deny that all the Apostles remained at Jerusalem for some time after Christ's ascension into heaven. For after the death of the first martyr, when a great persecution broke out, in which Saul had zealously taken part (Acts 8:1), the Apostles remained at Jerusalem while the others were scattered throughout the whole world; some thousands of them were there (Acts 2:41; 4:4). Although they sometimes left Jerusalem for a time, as Peter and John did not long after that persecution, when they went to Samaria after hearing that the Samaritans had received the word of God; at their prayer and the laying on of their hands, those people received the Holy Spirit. But as to when after that mission they left Jerusalem to proclaim the Gospel, there is the deepest silence everywhere. Eusebius indeed, in book V, chapter 18, relates from Apollonius that the Lord had commanded the Apostles not to leave Jerusalem before the twelfth year. This by no means agrees with history, for some remained at Jerusalem later, and others left before. It is, however, quite probable that after that celebrated persecution they did not stay in Jerusalem very long. That they divided the parts of the earth by lot [εἰς τὰ ὅρια τῆς γῆς], into which each would go to preach the Gospel, as Curcellaeus asserts on page 95, relying on Origen and Eucherius of Lyons, to whom Eusebius (III. 1) may be added, I do not think should be received by tradition [παραδόσεως]. Eusebius indeed records from tradition that Thomas received Parthia by lot, Andrew Scythia, John Asia, and Peter preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, Asia and Rome. And in book II, chapter 16, that Mark was sent to Egypt and founded the church at Alexandria. Nicephorus (II. 39) relates that Philip and Bartholomew founded churches in Syria and Asia, and (chapter 40) that Thomas planted churches in Ethiopia, Parthia, Media and Taprobane. I contend that some of these are uncertain and some false. For it is established that in the same provinces and places several Apostles preached the Gospel and founded churches, sometimes at one and the same time, sometimes at different times. At Corinth Paul, Apollos and Cephas taught. At Rome Paul, and, if we trust Eusebius, Peter toward the end of his life. In Asia there were John, Peter and Paul; in Galatia Paul and Peter. And the Apostles were not only planters of churches but also common overseers and visitors, which could be shown by many obvious examples. But whatever may be made of that division of the world, it can hardly be proved that at the time when Paul set out for Jerusalem to the Apostles, by the authority of the Antiochene church, others were staying there besides James, Cephas and John, whose names are expressed in Galatians 2:9. Here that expression Paul uses of those three is distinctive: those who seem to be pillars [οἱ δοκοῦντες στῦλοι εἶναι]. There were two kinds of pillars: some supported a building, others adorned it. Two such pillars were set up before Solomon's Temple. He calls them pillars in both senses. They were pillars of the Apostolic college and of the Church. Nor does the phrase who seem detract from their praise, as though it were not the truth of the matter. Chrysostom says that Paul took up the opinion of others as if it were the truth, and was glad to do so, because they were thought to be pillars even by their adversaries. It is therefore the most honourable commendation, by which he wished to adorn them not merely in his own name but from the judgment even of enemies, who praise the upright only when they are forced by the sheer brilliance of the truth. I mention this so that no one should think, taking the words in their crude sense, that Paul spoke maliciously about those Apostles.

units.la: ET PRESBYTEROS) Generale nomen est, & complectitur eos omnes, qui sunt ex Ecclesiastico Senatu. Seniores Vulgata vertit. Syrus ܩܫܝܫܐ. Apud Erasmum Laurentius prolixè contendit: quoties dignitas significatur, Graeca voce fuisse utendum Presbyteri; quoties aetas, Senioris. Apostolus alibi distribuit Presbyteros in regentes & docentes. 1. Tim. V. 17. Qui bene praesunt, duplici honore digni habentur, maxime qui laborant in verbo et doctrina. Se aliquando etiam ipsi Apostoli presbyterorum nomine insigniverunt, ut 1. Pet. V. 1. Hoc tamen loco ab Apostolis distinguuntur.
units.tr: AND THE ELDERS) This is a general name, and it embraces all who belong to the ecclesiastical senate. The Vulgate translates it "seniores" (elders). The Syriac has qashisha. In his edition of Erasmus, Laurentius argues at length that the Greek word presbyteri should be used whenever office is meant, and seniores whenever age is meant. Elsewhere the Apostle divides the elders into ruling and teaching elders: 1 Tim. 5:17, Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in the word and doctrine. The Apostles themselves sometimes used the title of elder, as in 1 Pet. 5:1. In this place, however, they are distinguished from the Apostles.

units.la: Qui ergo illi Presbyteri ? Collegium ministrorum Ecclesiæ, puta Pastores, Rectores, Diaconi, omnes denique ad liturgiam aliquam publicam vocati, quod alibi Presbyterium sæpius nominatur. Ejusmodi Collegium haud dubiè Apostoli communi calculo instituerunt Hierosolymis, priusquam in diversa climata orbis Terrarum dispergerentur. Fecerant idem paulò ante cum ritu χειροτονίας Lystræ, Iconii, Antiochiæ Act. XIV. 23. Quem numerum in Concilio illi Presbyteri impleverint, exquisitius discutiendi locus erit V. 6. & 22. Nunc abundè sit observatum, illos qui in verbo laborabant ab Episcopis Apostolico tempore neque Divino, neque humano jure distinctos fuisse. Sic enim eosdem Apostolus vocat & Episcopos & Presbyteros, nullo discriminis indicio. Act. XX. 17.28. Tit. I. 3.6. 7.8. Ubi non tantùm Episcopi Presbyteri dicuntur, ne in τιμᾶτε hujus nominis tricetur aliquis, sed & Presbyteri Episcopi. Imò eadem functiones declarantur, iidem characteres, eadem requisita. Hinc etiam Presbyteri in enumeratione personarum Ecclesiasticarum omissi. Et sub Episcoporum nomine habiti, Phil. I. 1. ubi Episcopi immediatè à Presbyteris contradistincti. Episcopi titulo eò loci designari Presbyteros, agnoscit Chrysostomus. Accedit, quòd Presbyteris illis competebat jus χειροθεσίας 1. Tim. IV. 14. In quo loco supponimus, agi de Collegio Presbyterorum, non de dignitate Presbyterii, quæ non tam πρεσβυτέριον, quàm πρεσβῶν vocari solet. Vide Doctiff. Cameronem ad locum Matth. XVIII. 15. & Davidem Blondellum, qui consentientes citat Clementem Alexandrinum, Origenem, Eusebium, Epiphanium, Cyprianum; in Apolog. pro Hieronymo Sententia, sect. 3. pag. 89 90. Jam si Presbyteri habent potestatem jure Divino ordinandi, utique jure Divino non sunt Episcopis minores. Fieri enim nequit, ut dare quis possit, quod non contineatur in virtute causæ. Neque juvat excipere, Paulum authoritatem imposuisse manus, Presbyteros ordinâsse associative, ut loquuntur. Si socii fuerunt ordinationis Presbyteri, tum debuerunt etiam authoritatem conferre ordinationi. Etiam post Hierarchicum Episcopatum Episcopale munus, adeòque etiam authoritas Presbyteris concessa est, ut apparet ex Concilii Carthaginensis quarti canone secundo & tertio collatis. Sed & Hieronymus suo tempore non obscurè docuit, jure Divino pares esse Episcopos & Presbyteros. Notabilis ejus sententia Com. in Tit. I. Idem, inquit, est Presbyter, qui qui et Episcopus. Es, antequam Diaboli instinctu studia in religione suerent, et dicerentur in Populis: Ego sum Pauli, ego Apollo, ego autem Cephæ, communi Presbyterorum consilio Ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postquam verò unusquisque eos, quos baptizaret, suos putabat esse, nosn Christi, in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de Presbyteris electus super-poneretur cæteris, ad quem omnis Ecclesiæ cura pertineret, & Schismatum semina tollerentur. Imò hanc communem fuisse Ecclesiæ Veteris sententiam, quam sequioribus temporibus tenuerint Sedulius, Rabanus, Hincmarus, & alii, supra laudatus Blondellus demonstravit.
units.tr: Who then were those elders? The college of ministers of the Church, that is, the pastors, rulers, deacons, in short all who were called to some public service of the liturgy, which elsewhere is often called the presbytery. The Apostles undoubtedly established such a college by common vote at Jerusalem, before they were scattered into the different regions of the world. They had done the same a little earlier with the rite of ordination by the laying on of hands [χειροτονίας] at Lystra, Iconium and Antioch (Acts 14:23). What number those elders filled out at the Council will be a place for a more exact discussion at Acts 15:6 and 22. For now it is enough to have observed that those who laboured in the word were not distinguished as bishops from elders by divine or human right in the Apostolic age. For the Apostle calls the same men both bishops and elders, with no sign of difference (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:3, 6, 7, 8). Here not only are bishops called elders, lest anyone be offended at the honour [τιμῇ] of this name, but also elders are called bishops. Indeed the same functions are declared, the same characters, the same requirements. Hence the elders are also omitted in the enumeration of ecclesiastical persons, and were regarded under the name of bishops (Philippians 1:1), where bishops are distinguished directly from elders. Chrysostom acknowledges that elders are designated by the title of bishop in that place. Add to this that those elders had the right of laying on hands (1 Timothy 4:14). In this passage we suppose that the reference is to the college of elders, not to the dignity of the presbytery, which is not so much called [πρεσβυτέριον] as [πρεσβῶν]. See the most learned Cameron on Matthew 18:15, and David Blondel, who cites in agreement Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Epiphanius and Cyprian, in the Apology for Jerome's opinion, section 3, pages 89–90. Now if elders have the power of ordaining by divine right, then certainly by divine right they are not inferior to bishops. For it cannot be that someone should give what is not contained in the power of the cause. Nor does it help to except that Paul imposed hands by authority, while the elders ordained associatively, as they say. If the elders were partners in the ordination, then they must also have contributed authority to the ordination. Even after the hierarchical episcopate, the episcopal office, and therefore also authority, was granted to elders, as is clear from comparing canons two and three of the Fourth Council of Carthage. And Jerome in his own time taught plainly that bishops and elders are equal by divine right. His notable opinion in the commentary on Titus 1 reads: The presbyter is the same as the bishop. And before, at the instigation of the devil, there were factions in religion, and it was said among the people: I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, and I of Cephas, the Church was governed by the common counsel of the elders. But after each one began to think that those whom he had baptized were his own, and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one elected from among the elders should be placed over the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should belong, and the seeds of schisms should be removed. Indeed, Blondel, cited above, has shown that this was the common opinion of the ancient Church, which Sedulius, Rabanus, Hincmar and others held in later times.

units.la: HIEROSOLYMAM) Nempe è Zione prodit doctrina, & verbum Jehova Jeruschalaimis, Esaj. II. 3. Et commorabantur ibi ol Απόστολοι, Jacobus, Petrus, Johannes. Habebatur etiam honos urbi sanctæ & famosæ, pristino Ecclesiæ domicilio venerabili. Quin & Divina revelatione hic locus Concilio designatus. Imò fieri potest, ut persuaderent Pseudapostoli, Apostolos Hierosolymitanos cum Templo & ejus ceremoniis communicare. SUPER HAC QUAESTIONE) de necessitate Circumcisionis & rituum legalium, ac tota justificatione, quam per fidem & legem Mosis quæsiverunt. Negabat Paulus, Christo orbi representato, opus esse tali ad Christum pædagogo. Nihil jam prius & antiquius esse fide. Contra Pseudapostoli & Ceremonias ac legem & fidem requisiverunt, τὰ ἄμικτα uno fasce coarctantes. Versus III. ILLI ERGO DEDUCTI) συμπεμφθέντες deducti à viæ comitibus. Hoc enim est συμπέμπειν. Hinc συμπεμπτικὰ scripta, quæ amicis communicantur commendationis ergo. Sic licatum honori Pauli & Barnabæ. Omnibus enim comitatu hoc constare poterat, quàm chara & amica hæc capita. Aliàs videri poterant vel causam suam agere: vel ab Ecclesia Antiochena seorsim sentire. AB ECCLESIA) Ἐκκλησία proprie civium conventum significat, quod nemini obscurum esse potest. Respondet Hebraico קהל, quæ vox in V. T. nunquam significat coetum religionis gratiâ coeuntium, sed duntaxat coetum externum populi. Ut mirificè ratio fugiat Bellarminum, qui, cùm probare vellet Ecclesiæ visibilitatem, totus est in citandis Veteris Testamenti locis, quibus occurrit vox קהל. Quid enim ad rem, cùm Ἐκκλησία ibi non habeat ἀξίαν ad religionem? Sed in N. T. Ecclesia cœtum significat, & quidem cum relatione ad religionem, ac professione nominis Christiani. Et cum Ecclesia significet modo promiscuam multitudinem fidelium, nomen Dei sanctificantium, modo Collegium Presbyterorum sive Regentium, sive docentium, probabilius est, hoc loco posteriori significatu venire, ut sic delecti ex Presbyteris, qui & itineris comites essent, & Concilii membra [?], qui prudentia & dexteritate pollentes possent testari de Concilii successu.
units.tr: JERUSALEM) "For out of Zion shall go forth the doctrine, and the word of Jehovah from Jerusalem," Esaj. II. 3. The Apostles, James, Peter and John, were staying there. The holy and famous city also had honour, as the venerable former home of the Church. Indeed, this place was designated for the Council by divine revelation. It is even possible that the false apostles persuaded people that the Jerusalem apostles were in communion with the Temple and its ceremonies. ON THIS QUESTION) about the necessity of circumcision and the legal rites, and the whole justification that they sought through faith and the law of Moses. Paul denied that such a tutor was needed for Christ, who had now been presented to the world. Nothing is older or more important than faith. The false apostles, on the contrary, demanded both the ceremonies and the law and faith, binding together things that do not mix [τὰ ἄμικτα] in one bundle. Verse 3. THEREFORE THEY, BEING SENT ON THEIR WAY) [συμπεμφθέντες], escorted by companions on the road. For this is what συμπέμπειν means. Hence "συμπεμπτικά" letters, which are shared with friends for the sake of commendation. Thus the honour of Paul and Barnabas was given a fair hearing. For by their company it could be seen how dear and welcome these matters were. Otherwise they might seem either to be pleading their own cause or to hold views apart from the Church of Antioch. BY THE CHURCH) Ἐκκλησία properly means an assembly of citizens, which can be obscure to no one. It corresponds to the Hebrew קהל, a word which in the Old Testament never means a gathering of people who come together for the sake of religion, but only an outward assembly of the people. This is why Bellarmine's reasoning utterly fails him, since he, wishing to prove the visibility of the Church, is entirely taken up with citing Old Testament passages where the word קהל occurs. For what does that matter, when Ἐκκλησία there has no reference to religion? But in the New Testament Ἐκκλησία means an assembly, and indeed with reference to religion and the profession of the Christian name. And since "Church" sometimes signifies the mixed multitude of believers who sanctify the name of God, and sometimes the college of elders, whether governing or teaching, it is more probable that here it has the latter meaning, so that the men chosen from the elders, who were both companions of the journey and members of the Council, might be able, being powerful in prudence and skill, to bear witness to the outcome of the Council.

units.la: PERTRANSIBANT PHOENICEN ET SAMARIAM)
units.tr: THEY WERE PASSING THROUGH PHOENICIA AND SAMARIA)

units.la: Methodus itineris à Luca commemoratur, ut hac occasione inspergi possint, quae in itinere gesta. Necesse autem habuerunt Phoenicen & Samariam pertransire, quia hae inter Syriam & Judaeam interjacent.
units.tr: Luke records the method of the journey, so that on this occasion whatever was done on the way might be mentioned. They had to pass through Phoenicia and Samaria, because these lie between Syria and Judea.

units.la: NARRANTES CONVERSIONEM GENTILIUM)
units.tr: DECLARING THE CONVERSION OF THE GENTILES)

units.la: A se nempe & Barnaba recens conversorum. Res enim nova fuit, & dignissima commemoratu, Gentiles, quibus hactenus Christus crucifixus stultitia fuit, jam nomen Christi glorificare, & iis [illegible, ~3 letters] apertam. De quorum conversione agitur cap. IX. Pertinebat hoc ad [illegible, ~1 word], confirmationem eorum, qui Christum professi.
units.tr: Namely, by themselves and Barnabas, of those recently converted. For it was a new thing and most worthy of mention, that Gentiles, to whom until now the crucified Christ had been foolishness, were now glorifying the name of Christ, and to them [illegible, about three letters] was open. The conversion of these people is discussed in chapter IX. This pertained to [illegible, about one word], the confirmation of those who had professed Christ.

units.la: ET AFFERERBANT GAUDIUM)
units.tr: AND THEY BROUGHT GREAT JOY)

units.la: Haud secus, quam par erat, cum crescere animadverterent numerum ovium & communionem Sanctorum, & cives Regni Dei. Johannes III. epist. v. 3. Gavisus sum magnopere, cum venirent Fratres, & attestarentur Tua veritati, quemadmodum etiam Tu in veritate ambulas. Majus gaudium non habeo, quam cum audio, filios meos in veritate ambulare.
units.tr: Just as was fitting, since they saw the number of the sheep and the communion of the saints and the citizens of the Kingdom of God increasing. 3 John, verse 3: I rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and testified to Your truth, just as You walk in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in the truth.

units.la: Versus IV. CUM AUTEM VENISSENT HIEROSOLYMAM)
units.tr: Verse 4. WHEN THEY HAD COME TO JERUSALEM)

units.la: Sic inoffenso pede itinere defuncti Hierosolymae appellunt una cum comitibus.
units.tr: Thus, having completed the journey without stumbling, they arrived at Jerusalem together with their companions.

units.la: SUSCEPTI SUNT)
units.tr: THEY WERE RECEIVED)

units.la: Grati quidem acceptique tanti viri fuerunt etiam suo nomine, ut fores lubenter aperirent. Non tamen excipiuntur tanquam privati, sed tanquam Legati Ecclesiae Antiochenae.
units.tr: Indeed they were welcomed and accepted gladly, being such men, even for their own sake, so that the doors were willingly opened to them. Yet they were not received as private persons, but as envoys of the Church of Antioch.

units.la: AB ECCLESIA)
units.tr: BY THE CHURCH)

units.la: Coetu promiscuo fidelium: quales jam tum non exiguo numero Hierosolymis fuerunt.
units.tr: By the mixed assembly of believers, such as already at that time were in Jerusalem in no small number.

units.la: ET AB APOSTOLIS)
units.tr: AND BY THE APOSTLES)

units.la: Hoc magno argumento, Paulo cum Apostolis bene convenisse, cum ipso advenrante, aeque ac caeteri fideles, penulam, ut ajunt, scinderent. Qui fuerint illi Apostoli, li, ex iis, quae supra diximus, satis constat. Sic postea legimus, exemplo Ecclesiae, Apostolorum & Presbyterorum avidissime & honorificentissime exceptos Christianos, ejusdem religionis consortes, Romanus Episcopus, concordiae testificandae nomine, etiam Coenam Domini solebat adventantibus Episcopis in hospitium mittere.
units.tr: This is a strong argument that Paul agreed well with the Apostles, since when he arrived they, just like the other believers, tore their cloaks, as they say, in welcome. Who those Apostles were is quite clear from what we said above. Thus later we read that Christians, fellow members of the same religion, were received most eagerly and most honourably, following the example of the Church, the Apostles and the elders; and the Roman Bishop, as a sign of testifying to concord, used to send the Lord's Supper to the lodgings of visiting Bishops.

units.la: ANNUNTIANTIBUS) Haud dubie a conversione Gentilium, quam ipsi juvante Deo promoverant, auspicati, viam struxerunt ad praesens negotium, quod nomine Ecclesiae Antiochenae agitabant. Ut laeto nuntio de Gentilibus ὁμοψυχίαις benevolentiam fidelium caperent.
units.tr: ANNOUNCING) Undoubtedly, having begun with the conversion of the Gentiles, which they had promoted with God's help, they prepared the way for the present business, which they were conducting in the name of the Church of Antioch. So that by joyful news about the Gentiles they might win the goodwill of the believers [with one accord] [ὁμοψυχίαις].

units.la: VERSUS V. EXORTI SUNT AUTEM) Controvertitur, cujus sint haec verba, Lucae, an Pauli, filum orationis suae pertexentis? Hoc supra leviter tetigimus. Beza, judiciosissimus caeterum Interpres, facit verba Pauli, & interserit: Exorti sunt, ajunt. Puto, inquit, esse illa verba non Lucae: ideoque addidi verbum. Ajebant, ut ostenderem transitionem esse ab obliqua oratione ad rectam, cujus exemplum extat Luc. V. 14. VII. 4. 5. & infra XVI. 36. Sed & apud disertos Scriptores hujusmodi ellipsis in narrationibus eleganter usurpatur. Sic enim Caesar, Conjurationem nobilitas fecit, & civitati persuasit, ut de finibus suis cum omnibus copiis exirent: Perfacile esse, quum virtute omnibus praestarent, totius Galliae imperio potiri. Pro, Dixit enim perfacile esse. Sententiam Bezae defendit etiam Cornelius a Lapide, Daniel II. Jam supra innuimus, videri, verba haec potius Lucae Historiographi esse. Nam ex clara serie apparet, innuicum Paulus quaestionem Ecclesiae & Apostolis proponeret, interlocutos Pharisaeos, quorum importunitatem Lucas describere voluit. Deinde si versus quintus est Pauli, non Lucae, nihil impedit, quo minus ei etiam sextus, septimus & sequentes tribuantur, quippe qui cum quinto cohaerent. Neque video causam, si Pauli haec verba essent, cur non eosdem Pharisaeos Pauli adversarios Lucas versu primo expressisset. Exemplum, quod Beza adfert ex Caesare, non est simile. Nam ibi prior pericope verborum est Caesaris: adeoque sequentia verba facile intelliguntur ad Caesaris orationem pertinere. Hic prior pericope in versu quarto non Pauli est, sed Lucae. De caetero verum est, ejusmodi ellipses in Scripturis usitatas esse. Cornelius a Lapide tria objicit. 1. Syrum subaudire: Sed inquiunt. Resp. Interpolatio haec non est in Textu Syriaco, qui sic habet: bet: קמו דין אילין דהימו מן יולפנא דפרישא Surrexerunt autem homines, qui credentes erant de doctrina Pharisæorum. Subintelligere ipsum hæc verba: Sed inquiunt: quî poterat Cornelius divinare? Cùm non plùs habeat Syrus in versione, quàm quod apparet in textu Canonico? 2. Exposcit hoc vox eos: quæs? Utique Gentiles, quorum conversionem celebrabant Paulus & Barnabas. Sæpe enim Hebræi suppositum, vel nomen Substantivum intelligendum relinquunt ex historia circumstantia. Resp. Verisimile est, Apostolum, cùm annuntiavit Gentilium conversionem, in eadem oratione proposuisse statum quæstionis suæ, propter quem Concilium petiit: Utrùm mìdilicet Gentiles circumcidi debeant? Hócque posterius subticuisse Lucam. Hinc surrexisse ilico Pharisæos, & contradixisse: Omnino eos, subintellige Gentiles, circumcidi debere. Neque insolens in Scripturis, ut pronomen relativum exprimatur, subjecto ejus neque proximè neque remotè expresso. 3. Idem exposcere narrationem huius historiæ, quam facit S. Petrus apud S. Clementem lib. 6. Constit. & Apol. cap. 12. Resp. Quid sentire nobis de Clementis Constitutionibus liceat, ipse Cornelius suo nos exemplo paulò supra docuit, ubi nigrum theta eis præfixit.
units.tr: VERSE 5. BUT THERE AROSE) There is a dispute whose words these are, Luke's or Paul's, weaving the thread of his own speech? We touched on this briefly above. Beza, the most judicious interpreter otherwise, attributes the words to Paul and inserts: There arose, they say. I think, he says, that those words are not Luke's; therefore I added the word. They said, in order to show a transition from indirect to direct speech, of which an example exists at Luke 5:14, 7:4-5, and below 16:36. But even among eloquent writers this kind of ellipsis is elegantly used in narratives. Thus Caesar: the nobility formed a conspiracy and persuaded the state to leave its territories with all its forces, that since they excelled all in valour, it would be very easy to obtain command of all Gaul. Instead of: for they said it would be very easy. Cornelius a Lapide also defends Beza's view, Daniel II. Already above I hinted that these words seem rather to be Luke's, the historian's. For from the clear sequence it appears that, while Paul was putting the question of the Church and the Apostles, the Pharisees who interrupted were the ones whose importunity Luke wished to describe. Then, if the fifth verse is Paul's and not Luke's, nothing prevents the sixth, seventh and following verses from being attributed to him as well, since they cohere with the fifth. Nor do I see any reason, if these were Paul's words, why Luke in verse 1 would not have expressed that the same Pharisees were Paul's opponents. The example Beza brings from Caesar is not similar. For there the earlier part of the sentence is Caesar's own words, and so the following words are readily understood to belong to Caesar's speech. Here the earlier part, in verse 4, is not Paul's but Luke's. For the rest, it is true that such ellipses are common in Scripture. Cornelius a Lapide raises three objections. 1. He supplies the Syriac: But they say. Answer: this interpolation is not in the Syriac text, which reads thus: qumu din ilin dahimu min yulpana dperisha [Syriac transliterated]. Surrexerunt autem homines, qui credentes erant de doctrina Pharisaeorum. But they say: how could Cornelius divine these words? For the Syriac version has nothing more than what appears in the canonical text. 2. The word eos demands it: who? Surely the Gentiles, whose conversion Paul and Barnabas were celebrating. For the Hebrews often leave the subject, or the substantive noun, to be understood from the circumstances of the narrative. Answer: it is likely that the Apostle, when he announced the conversion of the Gentiles, in the same speech set out the state of his question, on account of which he asked for the Council: whether, namely, the Gentiles ought to be circumcised? And that latter point Luke passed over in silence. Hence the Pharisees rose at once and contradicted: that they, understood as the Gentiles, must indeed be circumcised. Nor is it unusual in Scripture for a relative pronoun to be expressed while its antecedent is expressed neither immediately nor remotely. 3. The narrative of this history demands the same, as St Peter gives it in St Clement, Constitutions book 6, and Apology chapter 12. Answer: what we may think of Clement's Constitutions, Cornelius himself taught us a little above, by his own example, where he prefixed a black theta to them.

units.la: E SECTA PHARISÆORUM) αἵρεσιν vocat Lucas: Quam vocem in meliorem partem sæpiuscule usurpari, nemo ignorat. Locus occurrit Act. XXIV. 14. Ubi αἵρεσις videtur explicare quod præcedit, ὁδὸς, vitæ ac doctrinæ genus & institutum, quæ vox propter Hebraismum obscura videri poterat. Et Pharisaismum vocat αἱρεσιώτατον αἵρεσιν Act. XXVI. 5. non quòd illum magnopere laudet, sed loquitur ex adversariorum hypothesi, ut rectè censet Beza. Fuerit igitur vox media, quales multæ lapsu temporum infamiam traxerunt à vulgo, loquendi domino. Syrus concinnè דעתא doctrinam convertit. De Pharisæorum secta non est hic dicendi locus. Videatur Scaliger in Elencho Trihæresii. Subornati Pharisæi autem surrexerunt, quia pristino & avito more se Zelotas pro lege Mosis gesserunt. Ergo etiam hîc causæ deesse nolunt, rati, ad honorem suum pertinere, ut primo coetu sententiam suam, ὡς κυρίων δόξαν proponant, quam omnes adorarent. In quo nonnihil fermenti veteris iis adhæsit. Adeò difficile est modestiâ ingenium, semel insolentiæ & elationi suetum, imbuere.
units.tr: FROM THE SECT OF THE PHARISEES) Luke calls it αἵρεσιν [sect]; that this word is quite often used in a better sense, no one is unaware. The passage occurs at Acts 24:14, where αἵρεσις seems to explain what precedes, ὁδός, the kind and institution of life and doctrine, a word which, because of its Hebraism, could seem obscure. And at Acts 26:5 he calls Pharisaism the strictest sect (αἱρεσιώτατον αἵρεσιν), not because he greatly praises it, but because he speaks from the hypothesis of his opponents, as Beza rightly judges. The word is therefore neutral, like many which by the passing of time have taken on a bad reputation from the common usage of speakers. The Syriac neatly translates it as deʻta [doctrine]. The sect of the Pharisees is not the place to speak at length about it; see Scaliger in the Elenchus Trihaeresii. The Pharisees who were suborned rose because they acted as zealots for the law of Moses in their ancient and inherited manner. So here too they are unwilling to lack a cause, thinking it belongs to their honour to propose their opinion at the first assembly, as the opinion of lords, which everyone should adore. In this there clung to them something of the old leaven. So difficult is it to imbue with modesty a disposition once accustomed to insolence and pride.

units.la: CREDENTES) Est Codex, qui habeat οὐκ ἐπιθυμεῖ. Levis varietas. An vero in secta Pharisaeorum mansere post doctrinam Christi receptam? Vix est, ut statuamus. Certe dogmatis Pharisaeorum doctrinae Christi mirifice repugnantibus nuntium remittere debuerunt. Qualia fuerunt de libero arbitrio, & ejus cum fato concursu, de quo vide Josephum lib. 11. Bell. Jud. cap. 12. Casaubonum Exercit. 1, Ss. 9. Scaligerum in Elencho Trihaeresii. Ubi & caetera eorum dogmata absurda delineantur.
units.tr: CREDENTES) There is a manuscript that has "οὐκ ἐπιθυμεῖ" (he does not desire). A slight variant. But did they remain in the sect of the Pharisees after the doctrine of Christ had been received? It is hard to conclude so. Surely they ought to have renounced the tenets of the Pharisees, which wonderfully clash with the teaching of Christ. Such were their views on free will and its concurrence with fate; on this see Josephus, Jewish War, book 2, chapter 8 (Bell. Jud. lib. 11, cap. 12 as printed), Casaubon, Exercitationes 1, section 9, and Scaliger in his Elenchus Trihaeresii, where their other absurd doctrines are also set out.

units.la: DICENTES, QUOD OPORTEAT EOS CIRCUMCIDERE)
units.tr: DICENTES, QUOD OPORTEAT EOS CIRCUMCIDERE)

units.la: Idem urgent, quod illi, qui Antiochiam turbarunt. Et fieri potest, ut ab illis ad prava ejusmodi consilia clanculum compellerentur.
units.tr: They press the same point as those who troubled Antioch, and it may be that they were secretly driven by them to such harmful counsels.

units.la: AC PRAECIPERE)
units.tr: AC PRAECIPERE)

units.la: Poterat utcunque eorum sententia tolerari, si libertatem faciendi vel omittendi indulsissent. Nam etiam Paulum circumcidisse Timotheum constat. Nunc necessitatem inviolabilem urgent. In qua re nihil votis illorum dari oportuit. Haud dubie speciosis praetextibus res acta. Magno serio hoc injunctum Abrahamo & Israelitis, quibus data circumcisio in foedus perpetuum. Christum Jesum passum se circumcidi: neque venisse, ut legem solveret, sed ut impleret. Accedebat Zelus praeposterus defendendi traditionem paternam. Sed non animadvertebant, hoc obesse gloriae Christi, qui pleno Sacrificio nos redemit, ut illius gratia nos servet sine circumcisionis observantia.
units.tr: Their opinion might have been tolerated in some measure, if they had granted the liberty of either doing or omitting circumcision. For it is agreed that Paul too circumcised Timothy. But now they urge it as an unbreakable necessity. In this matter nothing should have been granted to their wishes. The thing was doubtless done under specious pretexts. This was enjoined with great seriousness upon Abraham and the Israelites, to whom circumcision was given as an everlasting covenant. Christ Jesus himself submitted to circumcision; and he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Added to this was a misguided zeal for defending the traditions of the fathers. But they did not notice that this detracts from the glory of Christ, who redeemed us by a full sacrifice, so that by his grace he might save us without the observance of circumcision.
