units.la: Respondet Hebraico <bl>שמר</bl> quod in significatu exequendi & perficiendi accipitur. Consule Doctissimum Gataakerum Dissert. de Novi Instrumenti stilo cap. XVII.
units.tr: It corresponds to the Hebrew <bl>שמר</bl>, which is taken in the sense of carrying out and performing. Consult the most learned Gataker, Dissertation on the Style of the New Testament, chapter 17.

units.la: CAPUT X. Conventus Concilii, & Conciliaris Petri sententia illustratur.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. The gathering of the Council is set forth, and Peter's sentence is explained.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Conventus Apostolorum & Petri Oratio explicatur. Quo tempore Concilium sit celebratum? Ostenditur, eandem esse profectionem Pauli Hierosolymas Gal. II. & Act. XV. A quo termino numerandi anni quatuordecim, Gal. II. Paulus quo tempore conversus? Quis Concilium coegerit? Conciliorum usus Oecumenicum Papatum subruit. Episcopus & Grotius carpuntur, Conciliorum usum respuentes. Baronius exagitatur, scribens, Petrum persecutione coactum ire Romam Hierosolymas. Concilium Oecumenicum fuisse defenditur contra Ioverium. Apostolos nullum aliud Concilium celebrasse. Symbolum Apostolicum an in Concilio conscriptum? Canones Apostolorum adulterini. Presbyteros adfuisse cum suffragiis definitivis defenditur, & Bellarmini rationes solvuntur. Ἰδὲ ἐν. Cernere. Locus 2. Reg. XIV. 8. 11. elucidatus. Petrus cur primus surrexerit? Si praesedisset, non ideo Oecumenicus Papa esset. Non praesedisse ostenditur, & rationes Bellarmini excutiuntur. Ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων quid sit? Petrum non primum Gentibus praedicasse. Hebraismus in verbis: ἐξελέξατο ἐν ἡμῖν. Argumenta Petri, quibus probat Gentiles ad Ecclesiam pertinere. Καρδιογνώστης. Locus Hebr. IV. 13. explicatus. Πνεῦμα ἁγιοφήτας. Deus quomodo ἁγιωπλήστης? Fide purificare corda. Tentare Deum. Iugum ἀβάστακτον. Disputatur contra Bellarm. & Stapletonum, illud ad legem moralem pertinere. Μαθηταί. חלמידים, Gratia definitur. In statu integritatis etiam locus fuit gratia. Augustini locus in Enchir. explicatus. Pelagianismi progressus. Socinianorum & Pontificiorum cum Pelagianis Syncretismus. Thomae distinctio inter Gratiam gratis datam & gratos gratos facientem. Probatur, gratiam justificantem non esse qualitatem infusam. Fides quomodo justificet? Iesus à salvando. Socinus perstringitur, negans Christum satisfaciendo nos salvare. Patres V. T. eodem modo justificati, quo nos.
units.tr: The gathering of the Apostles and Peter's speech are explained. At what time was the Council held? It is shown that Paul's journey to Jerusalem in Gal. 2 and Acts 15 is one and the same. From what point are the fourteen years of Gal. 2 to be counted? At what time was Paul converted? Who convened the Council? The use of councils undermines the ecumenical papacy. Episcopius and Grotius, who reject the use of councils, are censured. Baronius is attacked for writing that Peter was driven by persecution to go from Jerusalem to Rome. That this was an ecumenical council is defended against Ioverius. The Apostles held no other council. Was the Apostles' Creed composed at the council? The Canons of the Apostles are spurious. That the elders were present with definitive votes is defended, and Bellarmine's arguments are answered. Ἰδὲ ἐν. To see. The passage in 2 Kings 14:8, 11 is clarified. Why did Peter rise first? If he had presided, he would not for that reason be the ecumenical Pope. It is shown that he did not preside, and Bellarmine's arguments are examined. What is ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων? Peter did not first preach to the Gentiles. The Hebraism in ἐξελέξατο ἐν ἡμῖν. Peter's arguments by which he proves that the Gentiles belong to the Church. Καρδιογνώστης. The passage in Heb. 4:13 is explained. Πνεῦμα ἁγιοφήτας. How is God ἁγιωπλήστης? To purify hearts by faith. To tempt God. The yoke ἀβάστακτον. It is argued against Bellarmine and Stapleton that this refers to the moral law. Μαθηταί. חלמידים. Grace is defined. Grace had a place even in the state of integrity. The passage of Augustine in the Enchiridion is explained. The progress of Pelagianism. The syncretism of the Socinians and Papists with the Pelagians. Thomas's distinction between grace freely given and grace making men pleasing. It is proved that justifying grace is not an infused quality. How does faith justify? Jesus from saving. Socinus is taken to task for denying that Christ saves us by satisfaction. The fathers of the Old Testament were justified in the same way as we are.

units.la: SIc vidimus, quæ celebrem & inclytam Apostolorum Synodum anteverterunt, ἐκκλησιαστικῶς ad illam. Sequitur ipsa Synodus, & Sententia Petri, Barnabæ, Pauli & Jacobi. Ἐκλήσεως Concilii coacti & sententia Petri versibus 6.7.8.9.10.11. comprehenduntur. Verba Lucæ: 6. Συνήχθησαν δὲ οἱ Απόστολοι καὶ οἱ Πρεσβύτεροι ἰδεῖν περὶ τοῦ λόγου τούτου. 7. Πολλῆς δὲ συζητήσεως γενομένης, ἀναστὰς Πέτρος εἶπε πρὸς αὐτούς. Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, ὑμεῖς ἐπίστασθε, ὅτι ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο διὰ τοῦ στόματός μου ἀκοῦσαι τὰ ἔθνη τὸν λόγον τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου καὶ πιστεῦσαι. 8. Καὶ ὁ καρδιογνώστης Θεὸς ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς, δοὺς αὐτοῖς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, καθὼς καὶ ἡμῖν. 9. Καὶ ἐδὲν διέκρινε μεταξὺ αὐτῶν, τῇ πίστει καθαρίσας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν. 10. Νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε τὸν Θεὸν, ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον τῶν μαθητῶν, ὃν οὔτε οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, οὔτε ἡμεῖς ἰσχύσαμεν βαστάσαι. 11. ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ πιστεύομεν σωθῆναι, καθ' ὃν τρόπον κἀκεῖνοι.
units.tr: Thus we have seen what preceded that famous and renowned Synod of the Apostles, ecclesiastically [ἐκκλησιαστικῶς], leading up to it. There follows the Synod itself and the sentence of Peter, Barnabas, Paul and James. The calling of the Council and Peter's sentence are contained in verses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11. The words of Luke: 6. "The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter [Συνήχθησαν δὲ οἱ Απόστολοι καὶ οἱ Πρεσβύτεροι ἰδεῖν περὶ τοῦ λόγου τούτου]. 7. And when there had been much debate, Peter rose and said to them: Men and brethren, you know that from early days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe [Πολλῆς δὲ συζητήσεως γενομένης, ἀναστὰς Πέτρος εἶπε πρὸς αὐτούς. Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοί, ὑμεῖς ἐπίστασθε, ὅτι ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο διὰ τοῦ στόματός μου ἀκοῦσαι τὰ ἔθνη τὸν λόγον τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου καὶ πιστεῦσαι]. 8. And God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit as he did to us [Καὶ ὁ καρδιογνώστης Θεὸς ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς, δοὺς αὐτοῖς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, καθὼς καὶ ἡμῖν]. 9. And he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith [Καὶ ἐδὲν διέκρινε μεταξὺ αὐτῶν, τῇ πίστει καθαρίσας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν]. 10. Now therefore, why do you tempt God, to put a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear [Νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε τὸν Θεὸν, ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον τῶν μαθητῶν, ὃν οὔτε οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, οὔτε ἡμεῖς ἰσχύσαμεν βαστάσαι]. 11. But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, in the same way as they [ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ πιστεύομεν σωθῆναι, καθ' ὃν τρόπον κἀκεῖνοι]."

units.la: 6. Convenerunt autem Apostoli & Presbyteri, ut disiicerent de hoc negotio.
units.tr: 6. And the apostles and elders came together to consider this matter.

units.la: 7. Quum autem magna disceptatio extitisset, surrexit Petrus, dicens eis: Vos scitis, quòd jam inde antiquitus Deus inter nos elegit, ut per os meum audirent Gentes verbum Evangelii, crederentque.
units.tr: 7. When there had been much debate, Peter rose and said to them: You know that from early days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe.

units.la: 8. Et qui novit corda Deus, testimonium prabuit illis, dans illis Spiritum sanctum, sicut & nobis.
units.tr: 8. And God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us.

units.la: 9. Nihilque discrevit inter nos et illos, cum fide justificaverit corda illorum.
units.tr: 9. And he made no distinction between us and them, since by faith he cleansed their hearts.

units.la: 10. Nunc ergo, quid tentatis Deum, ut imponatur jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neque nos portare potuimus?
units.tr: 10. Now therefore, why do you tempt God by laying a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?

units.la: 11. Sed per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus nos salvos futuros, quemadmodum et illi.
units.tr: 11. But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they.

units.la: VERSUS VI. CONVENERUNT AUTEM APOSTOLI) Nempe ad Concilium, in quo sententia oborta sopiretur. Distinctè autem videndum 1. quo tempore? De tempore hujus
units.tr: VERSE 6. THE APOSTLES CAME TOGETHER) Namely to the Council, in which the opinion that had arisen might be settled. We should consider distinctly, first, at what time? On the time of this

units.la: jus Concilii pauci consentiunt. Hieronymus, Beda, Baronius ad 54. annum post Christum natum referunt, qui fuit duodecimus Claudii. Calvisius refert ad annum quadragesimum octavum. Tanquam terminus a quo quatuordecim annorum, quorum fit mentio Gal. I.1. figendus esset in conversione Pauli, quam refert ad annum trigesimum quartum. Capellus subsistit intra quadragesimum quintum. Illustris Armachanus, & ante ipsum Johannes Funccius in Chronologia ad annum quinquagesimum primum referunt. Difficultas in duobus videtur consistere. Prius est: An profectio Hierosolymitana, cujus meminit Apostolus Paulus Gal. II.1.2.3. sit eadem cum profectione ad Concilium. Posterius: Si est eadem, a quo termino quatuordecim anni, quorum ibi mentio fit, sint computandi? Prius quod attinet, circumstantiae utriusque memoratae profectionis vix sinunt nos dubitare, quin fuerit una eademque. Ascendit enim cum Barnaba V.1. Praedicavit illis Gentium conversionem V.2. Actum de negotio circumcisionis V.3. Inducuntur Fratres V.4. Constantia Pauli praedicatur V.5. Hae circumstantiae exacte quadrant cum circumstantiis profectionis ad Concilium in praesenti capite traditis. Fuerit igitur eadem profectio. In quo suffragantur nobis plerique Patres, excepto Chrysostomo, cujus supra rationem discussimus. Obstare tamen adhuc videntur tria. Primum, quod Gal. II.2. dicitur iterum privatim cum Apostolis contulisse, cum tota Synodi actio fuerit publica. Alterum, quod Act. XV. dicitur ascendisse ad litem compenendam: Gal. II. vero ad conferendum cum Apostolis de sua doctrina. Tertium: Si Gal. II. ad Synodum respiceret, haud dubie ad illam contra aemulos provocaturum. Caeterum haec non sunt soluta difficilia. Respondeo igitur ad primum: Actionem quidem Synodalem publicam fuisse: attamen extra illam actionem Apostolum cum Petro, Jacobo & Johanne privatim collocutum plurima transegisse, quae ad emolumentum Ecclesiae & praedicationis Evangelii spectant. Neque aliter fieri potuit in illo temporis spatio, quod Conciliari negotio totum non potuit consumi. Ad secundum. Utrumque haud dubie Hierosolymis egit. Et privatim cum Apostolis contulit: & publice restitit emissariis. Ad tertium. Non appellavit ad Decretum Synodicum, quia ipse membrum Synodi fuit, ne aemuli vitio verterent. Deinde non obscure intendit digitum ad Synodum v.6. Ἐμοὶ γὰρ οἱ δοκοῦντες ... Quae verba Pauli hanc interpretationem recipere puto : nihil se ab Apostolorum primoribus didicisse, vel accepisse novi in doctrina, sed sententiam suam ab Apostolis approbatam. Hactenus ad liquidum perduximus, eandem esse professionem Gal. II. & Act. XV. Restat nunc videamus alterum, ex quo nostrae quaestionis momentum pendet: A quo termino quatuordecim anni, quorum mentio fit Gal. II. v. 1. sint inchoandi? Placet magnis Theologis, a tempore Passionis Christi, vel conversionis Pauli initium sumendum. Quibus assentiri non possumus. Nam dixerat prius Gal. I. 18. post tres annos conversionis suae se ex Arabia Hierosolymam reversum. Nunc dicit ἔπειτα, deinde, post illos videlicet tres annos. Ergo cum priori termino triennii connectit illos quatuordecim annos, quibus exactis Hierosolymas adscendit. Jam suppono, Paulum conversum anno Christi quadragesimo, contra quam Chronologi vulgo sentiunt, qui conversionem ejus ad annum proximum morti Christi rejiciunt. In universum hoc in confesso, Paulum conversum esse Stephano Martyrium passo. Martyrium autem Stephani septennio recentius est morte Christi, si fidem meretur Epitome Temporum, adnexa Chronico Eusebii Scaligeriano. Nicephorus lib. II. cap. 3. allegat Evodium, tradentem, Stephanum septimo a Christi morte anno lapidatum, & semestri sequente Paulum conversum. Evodio autem antiquissimo, quippe Petri in sede Antiochena successori fidem quis derogeт? Neque Tiberius Caesar, quem Christianis aequum Tertullianus Apol. cap. 5. facit, tam saeva persecutione Christianos impoti passus esset. Ut probabilius sit, Caligulam septimo post mortem Christi anno Imperii sui primordia hac persecutione polluisse. Accedit & illud, quod supra fidem sit, unius anni spatio geri potuisse, quae in octo primis Actorum Capitibus Lucas tradidit. Deinde tertio a conversione anno currente, qui fuit XLIII. Christi, postquam longo tempore Damasci Evangelium praedicasset, & Judaei illius interimendi consilium inivissent, adscendit Hierosolymas ad visendum Petrum. Ibi cum libere in nomine Domini Jesu loqueretur, & disceptaret cum Hellenistis, qui eum conabantur interimere, Act. IX. 29 Orans in Templo, Divino oraculo monitus est, ut cito Hierosolymis exeat, Act. XVII. 17. 21. Exivit igitur, deductus a Fratribus Caesariam, & emissus in Patriam suam Tharsum, Act. IX. 30. Ab hoc tempore exitus ex Hierosolymis fluxerunt anni XIV. ad Concilium usque. Ergo à Conversione ad Concilium usque anni elapsi sunt XXIV. Unde prono alveo & justo calculo fluit, convenisse Apostolos ad Concilium anno Christi quinquagesimo octavo. Jam de causa impellente Concilii. Loquor autem de eo, qui vocavit, & necessitatem conveniendi imposuit. De posterioribus quidem temporibus indubitato constat, nullum Concilium Oecumenicum convocatum nisi ab Imperatore. Cujus rei praeter historiam testis locuples est Socrates in Prooem. lib. 5. hist. Eccles. Συνεχῶς δὲ τῆς Βασιλέως τῆ ἰσχύι ἀπολαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ' ὡς Χειστιανίζειν ἠξίωντο, καὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας πεφυκότα ἤρτητο ἐξ αὐτῶν, καὶ οἱ μεγάλαι σύνοδοι τῆ αὐτῶν γενέσθαι καὶ γίγνονται. Imperatorum, inquit, mentionem propterea fecimus, quod ex illo tempore, quo Christiani esse caeperunt, Ecclesiae negotia ab iis pependerunt: atque adeo maxima Concilia de eorundem sententia & convocata fuerunt, & adhuc convocantur. Idem testatur Hieronymus apologia 2. adversus Ruffinum. Neque in V.T. Concilia ab aliis convocari fuerunt, quam à Regibus Israëlis. Neque ut à Prophetis, quod Bellarminus obiectat, sed ut à Regibus, quod clarum, in exemplo Regis Ezechiae. 2. Paral. XXIX. 5. 21. qui non Propheta, sed Rex fuit. An verò eadem ratio fuit Concilii hujus primi Apostolici? Si constaret, jam tum nutricios Ecclesiae fuisse, utraque manu largirer. Nunc nihil minus. Suprema in hoc mundo Ecclesiae potestas fuit Gentilis Imperator, & eo quidem tempore Claudius. Noluit autem Paulus καθίζεσθαι τὸς ἐξουθενημένους ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, 1. Cor. VI. 4. Ergo Ecclesiae ipsius consensu & arbitrio imperatum Concilium. Ut liberrimum emblema sit Pontificiorum, ac inter illos Horantii contendentis, solius Petri has partes fuisse. Quae res nevissimo apice constat. Contra αὐτοκρατορίαν illam & praerogativam Imperii, quam Petro Pontificii, non tam ejus charitate occaecati, quam studio Pontificis exornandi, tribuunt, nihil poene validius contendunt, quam praesens Concilium. Si Oecumenicus Papa à Christo constitutus fuit, cujus solius infallibili & decretorio judicio controversiae finirentur, quid opus fuit Concilio? Quidni ad ipsum appellarent solum, & Divinam ejus vocem, semotis caeteris arbitris, reverenter exciperent? Imo omnia sequentia Concilia irrefragabili argumento sunt, non unum & singularem hominem esse Oecumenicum judicem, sed penes multitudinem esse vim imperii, & definitionum supremam in hoc mundo potestatem esse AristocraHocraticam. Caeterum exemplo hujus Synodi in ordinem redigenda est temeraria Episcopii assertio, inter alia docentis; Omnes illos coetus esse illegitimos, periculosos & Tyrannicos, in quibus convenitur non tantum ad deliberandum, ventilandum, examinandum, & rationibus argumentisque persuadendum: sed etiam ad decidendam alterius in religione capitis sive veritatem sive necessitatem: in disput. de Synod. Thes. 3. §. 6. Quibus verbis consentientia habet Grotius Manuduct. in viam pacis pag. 16. 17. sive quisquis ejus libri author est, qui conventibus ejusmodi nimis tristis & iniquus est. Certe non ad ventilandum tantum dogma de necessitate circumcisionis convenerunt Apostoli, sed praecipue ad decidendum. Testantur id Synodi verba: Visum est nobis & Spiritui Sancto: V.22.28. Unde vocantur Dogmata ... Cap. XVI.4. Neque est, cur in eo latebras quaerant, Apostolos infallibiles fuisse, non sequentium temporum Doctores. Nam ad eosdem infallibiles Magistros Doctores in Conciliis per se fallibiles provocant. Deinde minimum hoc constat, magnae esse authoritatis ad consensum Concilia, & praesentissimum rebus dubiis solamen, cum Apostoli Ὁμοθυμαδόν, qui sufficienti pollebant authoritate per se singuli ad determinandam quaestionem controversam, maluerint vti Concilii uti.
units.tr: Council few agree. Jerome, Bede and Baronius place it in the fifty-fourth year after the birth of Christ, which was the twelfth of Claudius. Calvisius places it in the forty-eighth year. He thinks the starting point of the fourteen years mentioned in Gal. 1:1 must be fixed at Paul's conversion, which he places in the thirty-fourth year. Capellus keeps within the forty-fifth year. The illustrious Archbishop of Armagh, and before him Johannes Funccius in his Chronology, place it in the fifty-first year. The difficulty seems to consist in two questions. The first is: Is the journey to Jerusalem mentioned by the Apostle Paul in Gal. 2:1, 2, 3 the same as the journey to the Council? The second: If it is the same, from what starting point are the fourteen years mentioned there to be counted? As to the first, the circumstances of each of the two journeys hardly allow us to doubt that they were one and the same. For he went up with Barnabas (v. 1). He preached to them the conversion of the Gentiles (v. 2). The matter of circumcision was discussed (v. 3). Brethren are introduced (v. 4). Paul's constancy is praised (v. 5). These circumstances agree exactly with the circumstances of the journey to the Council related in this chapter. The journey was therefore the same. Most of the Fathers agree with us in this, except Chrysostom, whose reasoning we discussed above. Yet three things still seem to stand in the way. First, that Gal. 2:2 says he conferred again privately with the Apostles, whereas the whole action of the Synod was public. Second, that Acts 15 says he went up to settle a dispute, whereas Gal. 2 says he went to confer with the Apostles about his doctrine. Third: if Gal. 2 referred to the Synod, he would undoubtedly have appealed to it against his rivals. These difficulties, however, are not hard to resolve. To the first I answer: the action of the Synod was indeed public, but outside that action the Apostle conferred privately with Peter, James and John, and carried out many things that concern the benefit of the Church and the preaching of the Gospel. Nor could it have been otherwise in that span of time, which could not be entirely consumed by the business of the Council. To the second: he undoubtedly did both at Jerusalem: he conferred privately with the Apostles, and publicly resisted the emissaries. To the third: he did not appeal to the Synodal decree, because he himself was a member of the Synod, lest his rivals find fault with him. Moreover, he clearly points his finger at the Synod in v. 6: For those who seemed... I think these words of Paul admit this interpretation: that he had learned nothing new in doctrine from the leading Apostles, nor received anything, but that his opinion had been approved by the Apostles. So far we have brought it to clarity that Gal. 2 and Acts 15 refer to the same journey. It remains now to see the second matter, on which the weight of our question depends: From what point are the fourteen years mentioned in Gal. 2:1 to be begun? It pleases great theologians to take the beginning from the time of Christ's Passion or of Paul's conversion. We cannot assent to this. For he had said earlier, in Gal. 1:18, that after three years from his conversion he returned from Arabia to Jerusalem. Now he says then [ἔπειτα], afterwards [deinde], namely after those three years. Therefore he connects those fourteen years with the first point, the three years, after which he went up to Jerusalem. Now I assume that Paul was converted in the fortieth year of Christ, contrary to what the chronologers commonly hold, who put his conversion in the year nearest to the death of Christ. In general it is agreed that Paul was converted when Stephen suffered martyrdom. The martyrdom of Stephen is, if the Epitome of the Times appended to Scaliger's edition of Eusebius's Chronicle deserves trust, seven years later than the death of Christ. Nicephorus, book 2, chapter 3, cites Evodius, who relates that Stephen was stoned in the seventh year after Christ's death, and that Paul was converted half a year later. Who would call into question the authority of Evodius, the very ancient successor of Peter in the see of Antioch? Nor would Tiberius Caesar, whom Tertullian in his Apology chapter 5 makes favourable to the Christians, have allowed the Christians to suffer so savage a persecution. So it is more probable that Caligula polluted the beginnings of his reign with this persecution in the seventh year after Christ's death. To this is added that it is incredible that what Luke relates in the first eight chapters of Acts could have happened in the space of a single year. Then, in the third year after the conversion, which was the forty-third year of Christ, after he had preached the Gospel at Damascus for a long time, and the Jews had resolved to kill him, he went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter. There, while he spoke freely in the name of the Lord Jesus and disputed with the Hellenists, who tried to kill him (Acts 9:29), he was prayed in the Temple and, warned by a divine oracle, was told to leave Jerusalem quickly (Acts 22:17, 21). So he left, brought by the brethren to Caesarea, and was sent off to his homeland, Tarsus (Acts 9:30). From this time the years of his departure from Jerusalem run to the Council: fourteen years. Therefore from the conversion to the Council the years that elapsed are twenty-four. From this, on a smooth course and by a just calculation, it follows that the Apostles came together to the Council in the fifty-eighth year of Christ. Now about the cause that moved the Council. I speak of the one who called it and imposed the necessity of meeting. For the later times it is beyond doubt that no ecumenical council was ever convened except by an Emperor. Besides history, Socrates in the Prooemium of book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History is a rich witness: Συνεχῶς δὲ τῆς Βασιλέως τῆ ἰσχύι ἀπολαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ' ὡς Χειστιανίζειν ἠξίωντο, καὶ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας πεφυκότα ἤρτητο ἐξ αὐτῶν, καὶ οἱ μεγάλαι σύνοδοι τῆ αὐτῶν γενέσθαι καὶ γίγνονται. "We have mentioned the emperors," he says, "because from the time when Christians began to exist, the affairs of the Church depended upon them; and so the greatest councils were and are convened by their decision." Jerome also testifies to the same in his second Apology against Rufinus. Nor in the Old Testament were councils convened by anyone other than the Kings of Israel. Nor were they convened by the Prophets, as Bellarmine objects, but by the Kings, as is clear from the example of King Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 29:5, 21, who was not a prophet but a king. But was the reason for this first Apostolic council the same? If it were established that they were then already the nurses of the Church, I would give both hands for it. Now it is quite otherwise. The supreme power in this world over the Church was a Gentile Emperor, and at that time Claudius. But Paul did not wish those who are despised in the Church to sit in judgment (1 Cor. 6:4). Therefore the council was commanded with the consent and will of the Church itself. So much for that most liberal device of the Papists, and of Horantius among them, who contends that these parts belonged to Peter alone. This matter stands on the highest summit of certainty. Against that autocracy [αὐτοκρατορίαν] and prerogative which the Papists attribute to Peter, blinded not so much by his charity as by their zeal to adorn the Pontiff, scarcely anything is argued more forcefully than the present council. If the ecumenical Pope was appointed by Christ, by whose sole infallible and decisive judgment controversies were to be ended, what need was there for a council? Why would they not appeal to him alone, and reverently receive his divine voice, with all other judges set aside? Indeed all the following councils are an irrefutable argument that it is not one single man who is the ecumenical judge, but that the power of rule and the supreme authority of definitions in this world lie with the multitude, and that the power is aristocratic. Moreover, by the example of this Synod the rash assertion of Episcopius must be brought to order, who teaches among other things: All those assemblies are illegitimate, dangerous and tyrannical, in which men gather not only to deliberate, debate, examine and persuade by reasons and arguments, but also to decide the truth or necessity of a point of religion, in his Disputation on Synods, thesis 3, §6. Grotius, in his Manuduction to the Way of Peace, pp. 16–17, has words consistent with these, or whoever is the author of that book, who is far too gloomy and unfair toward such gatherings. Certainly the Apostles did not gather merely to debate the doctrine of the necessity of circumcision, but chiefly to decide it. The words of the Synod bear witness to this: It seemed good to us and to the Holy Spirit (vv. 22, 28). Hence they are called dogmata (Acts 16:4). Nor is there reason to seek a hiding place in this, by claiming that the Apostles were infallible, but not the teachers of later times. For to these same infallible teachers the teachers in councils, who are fallible in themselves, appeal. Furthermore, this at least is certain: councils have great authority for consensus and a very present solace in doubtful matters, since the Apostles, who each by himself possessed sufficient authority to determine the disputed question, preferred to use a council, being of one accord.

units.la: APOSTOLI) Petrus, Paulus, Jacobus, Johannes, quos supra jam enumeravimus. Jacobus, Josepho Judaeo & veteribus plerisque testibus, fuit Hierosolymitanus Episcopus.
units.tr: THE APOSTLES) Peter, Paul, James, and John, whom we have already listed above. James, according to Josephus the Jew and most early witnesses, was bishop of Jerusalem.

units.la: De quo nolim jam certare. Baronius contendit, Petrum persecutionis aestu Romā ad tempus Hierosolymam secessisse. Et sane intererat lucem fenerari oculis nostris, quos tanta hebetudo & caligo perculit, ut videre non possint, quemadmodum Divus ille Apostolus simul anno secundo Claudii fixa Romae sede Episcopali manserit ibi usque ad supremum supplicii diem, continuos viginti quinque annos; simul anno quinquagesimo octavo, qui quintus fuit Neronis, Hierosolymis a Paulo & Barnaba convenire potuerit. Quidni hederam suspenderemus tam provido Cardinali? Sed omne tulisset punctum & pro honore tanti viri fecisset, si assertionem suam in nostri gratiam solidis scripturarum vel antiquitatis documentis statuminatum ivisset. Absque quibus est, candido pectore dicam, non potest nobis vel invitis pluris esse, quam pomarius Hercules. Retinet nos, ne assensum prebeamus, quòd in ea tempora nulla incidat Romæ fidelium persecutio. Ac plura alia, quæ fusè sunt à nostratibus Theologis deducta. Consule doctissimum Vedelium de tempore utriusque Episcopatus: Molinæum de Novit. Papismi lib.II.8. nec non Clarissimum Oftonem, Professorem Tigurinum, singularem Amicum nostrum, quem honoris causâ nomino, in præclaro & nervoso hac de re scripto. Sed dubitatio hîc incidit non levis, quam auget Joverius initio constitutionum Ecclesiasticarum. Cùm enim tam pauci interfuerint Concilio huic Apostoli, neque plures fortâsse Presbyteri, quæstioni est: quo jure Concilia Oecumenica inter Hierosolymitanum primore loco numeretur? sed judicium, nisi fallor, ex exitu rerum hujus Concilii peti debet. Nam primò authoritas decretorum hujus Concilii erat Oecumenica: & longè major, quàm ullius deinceps habiti Concilii. Abiit enim in Canonem fidei, & partem Scripturæ Sanctæ. Deinde statutum est de rebus, quæ omnes undique Ecclesias spectarent. Denique non de Judaicis tantùm Ecclesiis, sed etiam de aliis omnibus actum, cùm distributæ provinciæ sunt inter Petrum & Paulum, ut huic quidem Gentium praedicatio, & patrocinium (ut loquitur Baronius ad annum 51. n. 16.) Petro autem, Jacobo & Johanni cura eorum demandaretur, qui ex circumcisione ad fidem pertinerent. Quæ omnia non cadunt in particularem aliquam synodum. Potest igitur optimo jure Apostolica hæc synodus Oecumenica vocari. Neque documentis indubitabilibus constat, excepta hac synodo ullum Concilium Oecumenicum ab Apostolis celebratum, quicquid garriant Scriptores Pontificii, quemlibet Apostolorum Conventum pro Apostolico Oecumenico Concilio obtrudentes. Multò minùs recipimus, quæ ex mera traditione Apostolica Concilia comminiscuntur. Quale illud est, quod fingunt Hierosolymis celebratum, priusquam in orbem dispergerentur Apostoli, in quo symbolum confecerint. Ruffinum quidem Aquilejensem, fateor, & ex eo Cassianum in Collationibus suis Hieronymum, Ambrosium, quos pro se citant Centuriatores, illud approbare. Verum multa indicio sunt, Apostolos non posse authores illius symboli censeri. Idem judicium ferri debet de Canonibus Apostolorum, quos in Concilio aliquo Apostolico fabrefactos vellent Turrianus l. 1. pro Canonibus Apostolorum, & Cariolanus in summa Conciliorum. Dissensum suorum circa ca illos Canones non dissimulavit Caranza in Summa Conciliorum statim à principio, & Franc. Sylvius in Additionibus. Et sanè sunt inter illos Canones, qui è diametro veris Apostolicis in scriptura obviis repugnant. Quales canon 17. qui secundas nuptias damnat: canon 27. qui tantùm Clericis, Lectoribus & Cantoribus nuptias permittit: Canon 68. ad jejunia in quadragesima Paschæ, & feriæ quartæ & Parasceves, conscientias alligat: can. 62. excommunicare præcipit Laicos suffocato vescentes; & si qui alii multi canones ἀπόκρυφοι, & scripturis contrarii, propter quos apocryphi declarati sunt ab ipso Gelasio dist. 15. can. Sancta Romana, quomodo etiam illos vocant Baronius ad A. C. 58. Bellarminus l. I. de Verbo Dei cap. 20. Minorem adhuc fidem merentur Concilia duo Apostolica, alterum coactum occasione assumptionis B. Virginis Mariæ, alterum Antiochiense, quod extat inter Concilia à Binio edita. Quæ jam à pridem nostratibus Theologis jugulata sunt.
units.tr: I would rather not dispute that point now. Baronius contends that Peter, because of the heat of the persecution, withdrew from Rome to Jerusalem for a time. Indeed, it would take a light to be borrowed for our eyes, which such great dullness and darkness have struck, if they cannot see how that divine Apostle could both have kept his episcopal seat at Rome from the second year of Claudius until the last day of his execution, a continuous twenty-five years, and at the same time, in the fifty-eighth year, which was the fifth of Nero, have been able to meet with Paul and Barnabas at Jerusalem. Why should we not hang up the ivy for so provident a cardinal? But he would have won the whole point and done honour to so great a man if he had gone on to establish his assertion, in our favour, on solid documents of Scripture or antiquity. Without these, I will say with an honest heart, it cannot be worth more to us, even against our will, than the apple-seller's Hercules. What holds us back from giving our assent is that no persecution of the faithful at Rome falls in those times. And there are many other reasons, which our own theologians have developed at length. Consult the most learned Vedelius on the date of both episcopates; Molinaeus, On the Novelties of Papism, book 2, chapter 8; and also the most distinguished Ofton, professor at Zurich, our special friend, whom I name out of respect, in his excellent and vigorous writing on this matter. But a not slight doubt arises here, which Joverius increases at the beginning of his Ecclesiastical Constitutions. For since so few Apostles, and perhaps not many elders, took part in this council, the question is: by what right is this council counted among the Ecumenical Councils, and first among them, as Jerusalem? But the judgement, unless I am mistaken, must be drawn from the outcome of this council's business. For first, the authority of the decrees of this council was ecumenical, and far greater than that of any council held afterwards. For they passed into the canon of faith and became part of Holy Scripture. Next, decisions were made about matters that concerned all the Churches everywhere. Finally, it was not only the Jewish Churches but all others that were dealt with, since the provinces were distributed between Peter and Paul, so that to Paul was assigned the preaching to the Gentiles and their patronage (as Baronius puts it, at the year 51, no. 16), while to Peter, James, and John was entrusted the care of those who came to the faith from circumcision. None of these features fits any particular synod. This apostolic synod can therefore rightly be called ecumenical. Nor does it appear from indubitable documents that any ecumenical council was held by the Apostles, apart from this synod, whatever the Papist writers chatter, foisting on us some gathering of the Apostles as an apostolic ecumenical council. Far less do we accept the councils they invent from pure apostolic tradition. Such is the one they feign was held at Jerusalem before the Apostles were scattered abroad, in which they composed the creed. I admit that Rufinus of Aquileia, and after him Cassian in his Conferences, and Jerome and Ambrose, whom the Centuriators cite on their side, approve it. But many indications show that the Apostles cannot be regarded as its authors. The same judgement must be passed on the Canons of the Apostles, which Turrianus, book 1, in defence of the Canons of the Apostles, and Cariolanus in his Summa of Councils, want to have been fashioned in some apostolic council. Caranza, in his Summa of Councils, did not conceal his disagreement with those canons from the very beginning, and so did Franciscus Sylvius in his Additions. And indeed among those canons are some which are flatly contrary to the true apostolic teachings found in Scripture. Such are canon 17, which condemns second marriages; canon 27, which permits marriage only to clerics, readers, and singers; canon 68, which binds consciences to fasting in Lent, on Easter, on Wednesday, and on Good Friday; canon 62, which orders the excommunication of laymen who eat what has been strangled; and several other canons that are apocryphal and contrary to Scripture, on account of which they were declared apocryphal by Gelasius himself, dist. 15, canon Sancta Romana; and this is how Baronius at the year 58 and Bellarmine, book 1, On the Word of God, chapter 20, also call them. Two apostolic councils deserve even less credit: one held on the occasion of the assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and the other the Antiochene council, which is found among the councils published by Binius. These have long since been demolished by our own theologians.

units.la: ET PRESBYTERI) Tum docentes, tum regentes. Ac illi quidem ab Episcopis non fuerunt eo tempore distincti, quod evidentibus rationibus supra evicimus. Hi, qui quoquo modo Ecclesiam rexerunt, & illi Apostolica ordinatione præfecti fuerunt. Bellarminus quidem lib.I. de Conciliis cap.XVI. distinguit in Concilio Hierosolymitano judices, Consultatores & Adprobatores. Apostolos fuisse judices: Presbyteros Consultatores: homines è plebe Adprobatores. Sic format Ideam Concilii, quale optat, & quale solum legitimum esse clamat Pontificia schola. Neque vero plane inops est pigmentorum. Nam, inquit, quod soli Apostoli & Presbyteri ad Concilium sint vocati, liquet ex versu sexto: Convenerunt Apostoli & Seniores videre de verbo hoc. Controversiam autem à solis Apostolis & Presbyteris ventilatam & discussam esse, inde manifestum est, quòd congregatis Apostolis & Senioribus, ut viderent de hac facta sit πολλὴ συζήτησις. Solos interim Apostolos controversiam definivisse, & decidisse, constat, partim quòd soli Apostoli, Petrus, Paulus, Barnabas & Jacobus inducuntur à Luca loquentes: partim quòd soli illi legantur sententiam tulisse, atque hac formula verborum sententiam definitivam protulisse: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis &c. Hic multa sunt quorum Bellarminum pœnitere debuit. Ac primùm illud, quòd Presbyteros dicit consultandi tantùm causa convenisse. Atqui de Presbyteris æquè ac de Apostolis dicitur: illos convenisse. venisse δῶν ἐςὶ τοῦ λόγε. Quæ Phrasis non notat tantùm consul- tantis, sed etiam definientis & judicantis actum. Deinde quæ in hac Synodo sunt judicata & definita, illa dicuntur κεκριμένα ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀπο- ςτόλων καὶ Πρεσβυτέρων. cap. XVI. 4. Quid planius? 2. Quòd Ecclesiæ, id est, fidelium, qui Concilio interfuerunt, partes non facit nisi ap- probantium. Quod fortiter refutat versus 22. Visum est Apostolis & Presbyteris σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. Et v. 23. dicuntur missæ literæ nomine Apostolorum, Presbyterorum & fratrum in Antiochiam, Syriam, Ciliciam. 3. Quòd judicium ἀμεταπτωτον rerum ad salutem pertinentium ordini certo transcribit, cùm Apostolus vendicet om- nibus, qui non sunt Ψυχικοὶ, qui sensuum & passionum suarum im- petu non avehuntur transversi, vel non ignorant sermonem justi- tiæ, sed πνευματικοὶ, 1. Cor. 15. 4. Quòd sic in Conciliis Judices in- ducit proprie dictos, & à quibus non valeat appellatio. Revera hominibus in rebus fidei non competit aliud judicium, quàm in- quisitionis, discretionis, consultationis, & hactenus etiam eccisio- nis, quatenus in foro externo unionis retinendæ gratiâ, Ecclesiæ subjiciuntur iis, quæ in commune per suos Deputatos delibera- runt & concluserunt. 5. Συζήτησις, quam Bellarminus objicit, fuit instituta non cum iis, qui consultativa tantùm suffragia habent, sed cum iis etiam, qui decisiva habent. Quis enim persuaderi potest, Apostolos Divino afflatos Spiritu necesse habuisse, ut in societatem suam Consiliarios tantùm admitteret, quorum mutuo attritu veri- tas emicaret? Lintrensis inter illos συζητητὰς ponit Paulum & Bar- nabam: quibus haud dubiè suffragia definitiva competierunt. 6. Ad- do, si verum est, quod Bellarminus dicit, malè consultum Ecclesiæ sequentium temporum: si nempe illis definiendi potestas conces- sa, qui absque consiliariorum ope ad decisionem inepti forent. 7. Si soli illi jus decisivum in hoc Concilio habuerunt, qui loquen- tes & animi sui sensa edisserentes à Luca inducuntur, quid dicemus de Johanne, cujus suffragium literis Lucæ non est mandatum. An igitur ab hac potestate Synodus virum Apostolicum exclusit? De- sinat ergo à silentio Lucæ causam pravam incrustare. 8. Neque in eo sanus est, quòd solos Apostolos dicit sententiam definitivam protulisse, hac formulâ: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis. Nihil feré clarius, quàm illo pronomine nobis juxta Apostolos intelligi Presbyteros & cæteros fideles. Nam subscripserunt non soli Apostoli, sed & Presbyteri, & reliqui Fratres, verf.23. Illis sic visum, quorum nomine haec Epistola scripta est, quis mediocriter dubitare potest? Illi autem non soli Apostoli fuerunt, ut patet attendenti. Manet igitur, etiam Presbyteros jus suffragii decisivi habuisse. Tametsi ex eo, quòd Presbyteri docentes jure Divino ab Episcopis non fuerint distincti, suapte sponte sequitur, Presbyteros illos suffragium definitivum habuisse. Nam Papistarum hypothesis est: In Conciliis de jure cum suffragio decisivo adesse omnes & solos Episcopos, & in his majores Praelatos Ecclesiae.
units.tr: AND THE ELDERS) Both those who taught and those who governed. Now those were not distinguished from bishops at that time, as we have proved by evident arguments above. These were those who in some way governed the Church, and they were set over it by apostolic ordination. Bellarmine, in book 1 On Councils, chapter 16, distinguishes in the Jerusalem council judges, consultors, and approvers. He says the Apostles were the judges, the elders the consultors, and men from the people the approvers. In this way he shapes an idea of the council as he would wish it to be, and as the Papist school alone cries out is lawful. Nor is he entirely short of colouring. For, he says, that only the Apostles and elders were called to the council is clear from verse 6: "The Apostles and elders came together to consider this matter." That the question was debated and discussed only by the Apostles and elders is plain from the fact that, when the Apostles and elders had gathered to consider this matter, there was much debate [πολλὴ συζήτησις]. Meanwhile, it is established that the Apostles alone settled and decided the controversy, partly because Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James alone are introduced by Luke as speaking, and partly because they alone are read to have given the sentence and pronounced the decisive judgement in this form of words: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us," etc. Here there are many points for which Bellarmine ought to be sorry. And first, that he says the elders came together only for the sake of consultation. But it is said of the elders, just as of the Apostles, that they came together [δῶν ἐςὶ τοῦ λόγε]. This phrase denotes not only the act of consulting but also of defining and judging. Next, what was judged and decided in this synod is said to have been decided [κεκριμένα ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων καὶ Πρεσβυτέρων] by the Apostles and elders (chapter 16, verse 4). What could be plainer? 2. The Church, that is, the faithful who took part in the council, he does not make a party to anything except approving. This he strongly refutes in verse 22: "It seemed good to the Apostles and elders with the whole Church [σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ]." And in verse 23 the letter is said to have been sent in the name of the Apostles, elders, and brethren to Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. 3. He transfers to a fixed order a judgement, unchangeable [ἀμεταπτωτον], on matters pertaining to salvation, although the Apostle claims for all who are not natural [Ψυχικοὶ], who are not carried away headlong by the force of their senses and passions, and who are not ignorant of the word of righteousness, but spiritual [πνευματικοὶ], 1 Cor. 15. 4. He thus introduces judges properly so called, from whom there is no appeal in such councils. In truth, in matters of faith no judgement belongs to men other than that of inquiry, discernment, consultation, and so far even of excommunication, insofar as, in the external forum, for the sake of keeping the unity of grace, the Church is subject to those things which have been deliberated and concluded in common by its deputies. 5. The συζήτησις which Bellarmine objects to was instituted not with those who have only consultative votes, but also with those who have decisive votes. For who can be persuaded that the Apostles, inspired by the Divine Spirit, needed to admit into their fellowship mere counsellors, by whose mutual friction the truth might shine forth? Lyranus places Paul and Barnabas among those debaters [συζητηταί], who undoubtedly held decisive votes. 6. I add that if what Bellarmine says were true, the Church of later times would have been badly provided for, namely if the power of defining had been granted to those who, without the help of counsellors, would be unfit for decision. 7. If only those had decisive right in this council who are introduced by Luke as speaking and expounding the sense of their mind, what shall we say of John, whose vote is not recorded in Luke's letter? Did the synod therefore exclude that apostolic man from this power? Let him therefore stop covering up a bad cause by Luke's silence. 8. Nor is he sound in this, that he says only the Apostles pronounced the decisive sentence, in this formula: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." Nothing is almost clearer than that by the pronoun us the elders and the other faithful are understood along with the Apostles. For not only the Apostles but also the elders and the rest of the brethren subscribed (verse 23). Who can reasonably doubt that it seemed so to those in whose name this letter was written? And those were not only the Apostles, as anyone attending will see. It remains, then, that the elders also had the right of decisive vote, even though from the fact that the teaching elders were not distinguished from bishops by divine right, it follows of its own accord that those elders had a decisive vote. For the hypothesis of the Papists is this: that in councils, by right, with decisive vote, all and only bishops are present, and among these the greater prelates of the Church.

units.la: UT DISPICERENT)
units.tr: THAT THEY MIGHT CONSIDER

units.la: ἰδεῖν. Saepe cernere idem est, quod serio contendere & depugnare. Quomodo Latinis usitata locutio: Certamen cernere. Neque minus Hebraeis. Unde רָאָה נִרְאָה videamus alter alterum, 1.Reg.XIV.8.11. Quae verbo Chaldaeus Paraphrastes convertit: Veni & statuto die congligamus. Hoc loco, ἰδεῖν idem est, quod, cum judicio rem prudenter examinare. Id quod fit, cum secundum scripturas & aeternam Dei voluntatem controversiae explicantur. Hoc ostendit, negotium illud non desultorie esse gestum, sed vehementi studio veritatis indagandae, quae in profundo jacet, & nisi acri ac linceo visu non penetratur.
units.tr: [ἰδεῖν] "To see" often means the same as to contend earnestly and fight it out. So the Latins use the phrase "to see a contest" (certamen cernere), and the Hebrews likewise: "let us see one another" [רָאָה נִרְאָה], 1 Kings 14:8, 11. The Chaldee paraphrast renders this in his version: "Come, and let us meet on an appointed day." Here ἰδεῖν means to examine a matter carefully and with judgement. This happens when controversies are explained according to the Scriptures and the eternal will of God. It shows that the business was not conducted carelessly, but with eager zeal to search out the truth, which lies deep and cannot be reached except by a keen, lynx-like sight.

units.la: DE HOC NEGOTIO)
units.tr: CONCERNING THIS MATTER

units.la: οὲ τοῦ λόγου τούτου. Ubi λόγος idem vocat, quod prius ζήτημα: controversiae caput. Discrimen tamen intercedere videtur. Nam ζήτημα quaestionem ipsam significat: λόγος cum quaestione rationes utrinque allatas.
units.tr: [περὶ τοῦ λόγου τούτου] Here λόγος is used for what he earlier called ζήτημα, the point of controversy. There seems, however, to be a difference between them. ζήτημα means the question itself, while λόγος means the arguments put forward on each side in the question.

units.la: Versus VII. CUM AUTEM MAGNA DISCEPTATIO EXTITISSET)
units.tr: Verse 7. WHEN THERE HAD BEEN MUCH DISPUTING

units.la: Συζήτησιν vocat Lucas. Innuit, utramque partem justam sententiam suam dicere, rationes adferre, contraria diluere: Concilium rationes solicite inquisivisse, quo tandem discussio quaestionis expediri posset. Haud dubie in illa συζητήσει ordo custoditus fuit, ne quid insolentius designaretur. Tametsi Pseudapostoli vix modum servare potuerunt, & mordicus sententiae suae institerunt, ut solet ejusmodi praeposteris Zelotis pertinacia esse pro muro.
units.tr: Luke calls it συζήτησις [συζήτησιν], a debate. He implies that each side stated its own opinion as just, brought forward its reasons, and refuted the opposing ones; the Council carefully investigated the arguments so that the discussion of the question might at last be settled. Without doubt the order of this συζήτησις was kept, so that nothing unbecoming was done. Yet the false apostles could scarcely keep to due measure, and they clung stubbornly to their opinion, as the obstinacy of such preposterous zealots usually does, which is like a wall.

units.la: quasi Princeps Apostolorum & Primus Ecclesiae, qui audita controversia in utramque partem disceptationis, hic eam primus quasi judex definit. Sic habet Cornelii à Lapide emblema. Nos Sanctissimi Apostoli & inter consortes suos facile principis laudibus minime equidem intercedimus. Sed Pontificiorum ficiorum καταγνῶσεως non possumus perferre, qui ex qualibet praerogativa Petri primatum concludunt; atque ex illo Monarchiam Romani Pontificis. Hoc enim agitur. Appellatione primatus doctrinae Hildebrandinae assertores dominationem infinitam intelligunt. Petri nomen ejusmodi disputationibus, ceu aliquod κωμικὸν δραματίον, ut ajunt, ad speciem jactatur. Petro enim nihil quicquam hic metitur, neque feritur. Romano Pontifici, non Petro haec opera omnis praestatur. Patres quidem, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus & alii observant, Petrum fuisse θερμὸν, fervido ingenio virum, & multorum quae fecit aut dixit, praecipuam causam assignant ipsius θερμότητος. Neque tamen θερμότης apud Graecos semper nomen vitii est. Sed saepius significat homines promptos ad agendum, animosos, & quorum manus saepe consilium antevertit. Unde Gregorius Nazianzenus orat. 26. θερμὰς sive ἀλκτύγες & μεγάλας φύσεις pro eodem ponit. Laudabilis omnino indoles, si recti notitia dirigatur. Ab hac θερμότηλ est, quod post illam συζήτησιν primus in hoc Concilio surgit, & gravissima oratione partibus acriter digladiantibus silentium imponit. In hac re ratione tantae πραγματείας quis non praerogativam aliquam Petro tribueret? Sed immane quantum haec differt a Suprematu, quem Petro & ejus Successoribus, quos fingunt, jure competere, Hildebrandistae pertendunt. Jam si Judicem statueremus & Praesidem hujus Concilii Petrum, controversiam definientem, non judicium tantum & suffragium suum interponentem, qualem faciunt hic Cornelius à Lapide, Bellarminus, Horantius, & alii Papistae, quantum proficient? Quis non intelligit immane discrimen inter Praesidem & Monarcham? Inter eum, qui suffragia aeque decisiva aliorum audit, colligit, ac tandem pronuntiat id, quod potissimum vota ferunt, & inter absolutum aliquem ac supremum judicem, qui potestate & jurisdictione pollet etiam in inferiores, & qui illis semotis solus arbitrari potest? Et, an sequenti tempore honos Praesidentiae Romano Episcopo nonnisi ex privilegio Oecumenici Papatus deferri potuit? Quidni haec causa praesidentiae esse potuit, quia erat Romanus Episcopus Patriarcharum primus? Sed neque inde Pontificia Schola Romano Episcopo jus praesidentiae in Conciliis sacrosanctum facere posset. Nam Beato Petro Romanum Pontificem in hoc munere successisse, nulli probant. Imo primis temporibus praesederunt non Romani Episcopi, sed quoscunque placeret ad hoc munus vocare Imperatori, quod D. Blondellus in suo de Primatu opere ad Sect.64. ss.3. prolixè & verè probat. Certè Concilium Nicenum Imperatore Constantino jubente moderatus est Hosius Cordubensis, quamvis illi Concilio interessent Silvestri Papæ nomine Victor & Vitus. Constantinopolitano præsedit Nectarius, suo quasi jure, cùm esset Constantinopolitanus Præsul: Ephesino Cyrillus Alexandrinus Patriarcha, non Cælestinus Romanus Pontifex, cujus legati iderant Arcadius & Projectus. Chalcedonense, cui coram Martianus interfuit, postquam Dioscurus, qui ab ipso Præses fuit designatus, in reatu constitutus fuit, nullos alios moderatores habuit, quàm Comites & Patricios à Martiano delegatos. Concilio quinto Constantinopoli celebrato ex decreto Justiniani, Præses adfuit Menas Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, cùm Concilio interesset Vigilius Papa. Quòd si hac Præsidentia, quam fingunt, Petri in Concilio Hierosolymitano jus acquisitum est idem Romano Episcopo, quid causæ est, cur illud avidè & strenuè non usurpârint, cùm usurpare soleant etiam à nemine concessa, sed vi rapta & occupata? Sed ut nervos & poplites succidamus Bellarmino, Horantio, Bailio, Gretsero & aliis, qui hic spes suas tenent, negamus constare, Concilio Hierosolymitano Petrum Præsidem datum fuisse. Hoc enim nullo argumento probari potest. Præsidis hæ partes sunt, ut in vota mittat judices, suffragia colligat, & secundum potiora suffragia quæstionem decidat. Qui Petrum in Apostolico Concilio hoc fecisse dicat, eum insign."
units.tr: "As the prince of the Apostles and the first of the Church, who, having heard the controversy argued on both sides, here first settles it as a judge." So reads the emblem of Cornelius à Lapide. We certainly do not begrudge the most holy Apostle the praise due to the chief among his fellows. But we cannot tolerate the Papists' fictitious καταγνῶσις [καταγνῶσεως], who conclude from any privilege of Peter's a primacy, and from that the monarchy of the Roman Pontiff. For this is what is really at stake. By the name of primacy the advocates of the Hildebrandine doctrine understand unlimited dominion. The name of Peter is thrown into such disputes, like some comic little play, as they say, merely for show. For nothing at all is measured against Peter here, nor is he struck. All this business is carried on for the Roman Pontiff, not for Peter. The Fathers, Chrysostom, Cyril and others, observe that Peter was θερμός [θερμόν], a man of fervent temperament, and they assign his ardour as the chief cause of many things he did or said. Yet among the Greeks θερμότης [θερμότης] is not always a word for a fault. It more often means men who are ready to act, spirited, whose hands often run ahead of their counsel. So Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 26, uses ἀλκτύγες [ἀλκτύγες] and μεγάλας φύσεις [μεγάλας φύσεις] (strong and great natures) to mean the same thing. It is altogether a praiseworthy disposition, if it is directed by knowledge of what is right. From this ardour it comes that, after that συζήτησις [συζήτησιν], he is the first to rise in this Council and with a most weighty speech imposes silence on the parties fighting fiercely. Considering the importance of such a matter, who would not grant Peter some kind of pre-eminence? But how enormously this differs from the Supremacy, which the Hildebrandists insist belongs by right to Peter and to his supposed successors! Now, if we were to make Peter the judge and president of this Council, settling the controversy, not merely interposing his judgement and vote as Cornelius à Lapide, Bellarmine, Horantius and the other Papists do, how much would they gain? Who does not see the vast difference between a president and a monarch? Between one who hears the votes of others, all equally decisive, gathers them, and at last declares what the greater number of votes favour, and an absolute and supreme judge, who has power and jurisdiction even over his inferiors, and who can decide alone with them set aside? And could the honour of presidency in a later age have been conferred on the Roman Bishop by any other privilege than that of an Ecumenical papacy? Why could this not be the reason for his presidency, namely that the Roman Bishop was the first of the Patriarchs? But even so the Papist school could not make the right of presidency in Councils a sacred right of the Roman Bishop. For no one can prove that the Roman Pontiff succeeded the Blessed Peter in this office. Indeed, in the earliest times it was not the Roman Bishops who presided, but whoever the Emperor was pleased to summon to this task, as D. Blondel in his work on the Primacy proves at length and truly, in Section 64, subsection 3. Certainly the Council of Nicaea was presided over by Hosius of Cordoba at the command of the Emperor Constantine, although Victor and Vitus were present in the name of Pope Silvester. The Council of Constantinople was presided over by Nectarius, as it were by his own right, since he was Bishop of Constantinople. At Ephesus, Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria, presided, not Celestine, the Roman Pontiff, whose legates were Arcadius and Projectus. At Chalcedon, where Martian was present in person, after Dioscorus, who had been appointed its president by him, was brought under accusation, it had no other moderators than the Counts and Patricians delegated by Martian. At the Fifth Council, celebrated at Constantinople by decree of Justinian, the president was Menas, Patriarch of Constantinople, although Pope Vigilius was present at the Council. But if this presidency of Peter, which they imagine, was in the Council of Jerusalem acquired for the Roman Bishop, why did they not eagerly and vigorously seize it, when they are accustomed to usurp even what no one has granted, but what is taken and occupied by force? But to cut the sinews and hamstrings of Bellarmine, Horantius, Bailly, Gretser and the others who place their hopes here, we deny that it is established that Peter was given as president of the Council of Jerusalem. For this cannot be proved by any argument. The duties of a president are these: to put the opinions of the judges to the vote, to collect the votes, and to decide the question according to the greater number of votes. Whoever says that Peter did this in the Apostolic Council must be

units.la: ter confidentem esse oportet. Primus equidem sententiam dixit, quod non est Præsidis. Non legitur cæteros Apostolos in vota misisse. Non collegit suffragia, nec conclusit sententiam. Non protulit per omnia talem sententiam, qualis in decreto apparet. Nam de idolothytis, sanguine, fornicatione nihil dixit. Imò hæc in Apostolum Jacobum longè melius competunt. Proinde Chrysostomus non obscurè innuit, Jacobo in hoc Concilio primas delatas esse. Verba ejus sunt Homil. 33. in acta: Ἐπίκοπος ἦν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις τῶ, διὰ τοῦτο λέγει, καὶ μὴ Πέτρου Παύλου φθέγγεται, καὶ ὑδεὶς ἀποσυμίζει, Ἰάκωβος ἀντέχεται, καὶ ἐν ἐπισκοπῇ. Ἐκεῖνος γὰρ ἦν τῶν ἀρχῶν ἐπισκεψεμένων. Erat hic Episcopus Ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ: istaque posterior loquitur. Post Petrum Paulus loquitur, neque quisquam eum comprimit. Jacobus pavitur, neque resilit. Huic enim Principaius commissum erat. Petrus quidem vehementius loquebatur. Iacobus vero clementius. Sic semper oportet eum, qui in magna est potestate, quae dura sunt aliis relinquere: ipsum vero mansuetius loqui. Bellarminus tamen serio pugnat, fuisse Petrum Concilii Praesidem. Rationes ipsi sunt quatuor 1. quia Hieronymus testetur in Epistola ad Augustinum, quae est undecima inter Epistolas Augustini. 2. Quia Petrus primus surrexit, & primus locutus est. 3. Quia quaestionem definiverit. 4. Quia teste Hieronymo, ejus sententiam omnes sint secuti, lib. 1. de Conciliis cap. XIX. Sed nec probabilitatem, nec necessitatem haec argumenta habent. Non primum. Nam Hieronymum Bellarminus mentitur. Verba ejus in Epistola ad Augustinum sunt: Non ignorasse Petrum principem hujus decreti, legem post Evangelium non esse servandam. Jam princeps sententiae vel decreti non est ille, qui praesidet coetui, in quo sententiae dicuntur: Sed qui primus eam sententiam dixit. Ita Cicero in Orat. pro Sextio: Princeps rogationis, Vir mihi amicissimus, Quintus Fabricius. Non secundum. Nam primo surrexisse & locutum esse Petrum, unde fidem Bellarminus facit? Atqui post ζήτησιν factam demum Petrus surrexit. In ipsa autem ζητήσεως illa glossa ordinaria agnoscit disceptasse Judices Concilii. Lintrensis, Paulum & Barnabam. Quomodo ζητεῖν potuerunt, non loquendo? Deinde non est praesidis, primo loqui decisivam sententiam, qualis apparet in oratione Petri. Primus quidem Praeses loquitur, thema consultationis proponendo, & sententias caeterorum judicum rogando: sed non decidendo, quod in vulgus notissimum est. Neque tertium solidius est. Definivit quidem quaestionem, quatenus ejus modo perspecto eam sententiam dixit, in quam decretum factum est. Talis autem definitio non Praesidis tantum est, sed Assessorum etiam, qui meliorem sententiam tuentur. Praesidis autem est ita definire, ut auditis suffragiis decretum pronuntiet. Nam, ut loquitur Hieronymus, sententiam dixit, in quam itum est, adeoque suam sententiam dixit, non decretum pronuntiavit. Deinde post Petri Orationem Jacobus de eadem re disserit, quod non fit post decretoriam vocem Praesidis. Denique Petrus in sua sententia non complexus est exceptionem idolothytorum, Sanguinis, scorrationis, quae tamen in decreto continentur. Ergo ejus sententia nullo modo censeri potest definitiva Praesidis. Quartum minus adhuc firmum est. Non necessarid Praeses est, cu-jus suis sententiam sequuntur alii. Id quod apparet in illis decretis, quae συνοδικῶς sunt conclusa, in quibus primi assessoris sententiam omnes sequuntur. Exemplo esse potest Nicæna Synodus, in qua Paphnutii de Cœlibatu Clericorum, sententiam omnes secuti sunt, etiam retractatis suffragiis jam latis. Neque tamen Paphnutius Præses fuit Concilii Niceni. Imò nunquam Præsidis sententiam sequuntur judices: sed in Judicum præpollentium sententiam Præses decretum format. An verò Gretsero Jesuitæ aures substringemus, dicenti: quicquid fiat de Conciliis & Consessibus Politicis, in Sacris aliter usum habere. Ibi qui primas tenet in sedendo, primas tenere in loquendo & definiendo, sicut & in subscribendo. Videlicet ex cerebro Jesuitico forma Conciliorum Sacrorum erat effingenda. In omnibus Conciliis Ecclesiasticis hic ordo custoditus fuit, ut primo loqueretur Præses, deinde vota stringerent Assessores, denique Præses definitivam sententiam formaret & ediceret. Neque ullum contrarium exemplum, vel ratio probabilis in medium afferri potest.
units.tr: remarkably bold indeed. To be sure, he gave his opinion first, which is not the president's role. We do not read that he put the opinions of the other Apostles to a vote. He did not collect the votes, nor conclude the matter. He did not state an opinion entirely like the one that appears in the decree. For he said nothing about things sacrificed to idols, blood, or fornication. Indeed these things belong far better to the Apostle James. Therefore Chrysostom clearly hints that the primacy in this Council was granted to James. His words, in Homily 33 on Acts, are: "He was the bishop of Jerusalem; therefore he speaks, and does not mention Peter or Paul, and no one contradicts him; James holds on, and in the episcopate. For he was one of those in authority" [Ἐπίκοπος ἦν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις τῶ, διὰ τοῦτο λέγει, καὶ μὴ Πέτρου Παύλου φθέγγεται, καὶ ὑδεὶς ἀποσυμίζει, Ἰάκωβος ἀντέχεται, καὶ ἐν ἐπισκοπῇ. Ἐκεῖνος γὰρ ἦν τῶν ἀρχῶν ἐπισκεψεμένων]. "This man was bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, and the latter speaks. After Peter, Paul speaks, and no one restrains him. James is quiet, and does not leap up. For the chief rule was committed to him. Peter indeed spoke more vehemently, but James more gently. So it is always fitting for the one who has great authority to leave harsh things to others, and to speak himself more mildly." Yet Bellarmine stubbornly maintains that Peter was president of the Council. His reasons are four: (1) "because Jerome testifies in his Letter to Augustine, which is the eleventh among Augustine's Letters"; (2) "because Peter rose first and spoke first"; (3) "because he settled the question"; (4) "because, according to Jerome, all followed his opinion," book 1 on Councils, chapter 19. But these arguments have neither probability nor necessity. Not the first. For Bellarmine misrepresents Jerome. Jerome's words in the Letter to Augustine are: "Peter, the prince of this decree, was not ignorant that the law should not be kept after the Gospel." Now the prince of an opinion or decree is not the one who presides over the assembly in which opinions are given, but the one who first gave that opinion. So Cicero, in the speech for Sextius: "The prince of the proposal, a man most dear to me, Quintus Fabricius." Not the second. For where does Bellarmine get his evidence that Peter rose and spoke first? But in fact Peter rose only after the debate had taken place. Yet in that very debate the ordinary gloss recognises that the judges of the Council disputed, Paul and Barnabas being parties. How could they have debated without speaking? Then it is not the president's role to speak first with a decisive opinion, such as appears in Peter's speech. The president does speak first, by proposing the subject of consultation and by asking the opinions of the other judges; but he does not decide, which is very well known to everyone. Nor is the third more solid. Peter did indeed settle the question, in so far as, having thus surveyed it, he stated the opinion upon which the decree was made. But such a settlement belongs not only to the president, but also to the assessors who defend the better opinion. The president's task is to settle in such a way that, once the votes have been heard, he pronounces the decree. For, as Jerome puts it, Peter "gave the opinion to which they went," and so he gave his own opinion; he did not pronounce a decree. Further, after Peter's speech James discourses on the same matter, which does not happen after the decisive voice of a president. Finally, Peter in his opinion did not include the exception for things sacrificed to idols, blood, and fornication, which nevertheless are contained in the decree. Therefore his opinion cannot in any way be regarded as the president's definitive judgement. The fourth is weaker still. The one whose opinion the others follow is not necessarily the president. This appears in those decrees which were concluded "synodically," in which all follow the opinion of the first assessor. An example can be the Synod of Nicaea, in which all followed the opinion of Paphnutius about the celibacy of clergy, even after votes already given had been retracted. Yet Paphnutius was not president of the Council of Nicaea. Indeed, judges never follow the opinion of the president; rather, the president frames the decree according to the opinion of the leading judges. But shall we stop the ears of the Jesuit Gretser, who says: "Whatever happens with political Councils and assemblies, in sacred matters the custom is different. There, whoever holds the first place in sitting holds the first place in speaking and in defining, as also in signing." Clearly the form of sacred Councils was to be fashioned from the Jesuit brain! In all ecclesiastical Councils this order was kept: first the president spoke, then the assessors gave their votes, and finally the president formed and announced the definitive judgement. Nor can any contrary example or probable argument be brought forward.

units.la: ET DIXIT EIS) Liberè suam sententiam protulit, in quam sequentes manibus pedibusque iverunt.
units.tr: AND HE SAID TO THEM) He freely set out his own opinion, and those who followed him went along with it heart and soul.

units.la: VIRI FRATRES) Amica compellatione & partes exulceratas ad silentium componit, & benevolentiam captat Assessorum.
units.tr: MEN, BRETHREN) With a friendly form of address he calms the exasperated parties to silence and wins the goodwill of the assessors.

units.la: VOS SCITIS) Ad scientiam provocat illorum, quibus res illæ Sacræ, ac præcipuè conditio ipsius, familiariter cognitæ & exploratæ fuerunt.
units.tr: YOU KNOW) He appeals to the knowledge of those with whom these sacred matters, and especially his own position, were familiarly known and tested.

units.la: QUOD JAM INDE ANTIQUITUS) ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἐκχαίων. Prosper. lib.2. de vocat. Gent. cap.18. interpretatur: ab æterno. Quasi ad æternam prædestinationem Dei respexisset Petrus. Quæ explicatio minus genuina videtur. Vulgatus & Erasmus habent: à diebus antiquis. Sic significamus ea, quæ ante longissimum tempus gesta sunt. Confer Deut.IV.32.XXXII 7. Hoc autem loco non videtur antiquissimum tempus notari, cùm designentur ea, quæ non multò post Stephani mortem acciderunt. Beza proinde vertit jam pridem. Arabs: A diebus primis. Æthiopicus: מאז à principio. Ut respiciat Petrus ad historiam Cornelii Centurionis, quæ non ita pridem contigit post illapsum in Apostolos Spiritum S. Capellus vertit: Antehac. Quomodo Jeremiah
units.tr: FROM ANCIENT DAYS) [ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἐκχαίων]. Prosper, in On the Calling of the Gentiles, Book 2, chapter 18, interprets it as "from eternity", as if Peter had looked back to God's eternal predestination. That explanation seems less genuine. The Vulgate and Erasmus have "from ancient days", and so we signify things done a very long time ago; compare Deut. 4:32 and 32:7. In this place, however, the most remote time does not seem to be meant, since the events designated happened not long after Stephen's death. Beza therefore translates "some time ago". The Arabic has "from the first days". The Ethiopic has "from the beginning" [mēʼaz]. Peter may be looking back to the story of the centurion Cornelius, which happened not long before, after the Holy Spirit fell upon the apostles. Capellus translates "formerly". As in Jeremiah

units.la: VIII. 28. מן היום קדמיא Syrus : à diebus antiquis. Optimè videtur Arabs mentem Petri explicatam dedisse : à diebus primis, nempe tum emissionis in orbem Terrarum Matth. XXVIII. 19. tum conversionis Gentilium, quae coepit in Cornelio Centurione, Actor. X. Hinc Jacobus v. 14. illud vertit πρῶτον. Habuit igitur Petrus in animo visionem, in qua jussus est occidere & mactare, id est, ad communionem gratiae Gentiles hactenus idololatricos invitare & convertere. Nempe adnotante Hesychio ἀρχαῖον, non tantùm πάλαιον significat, sed etiam πρῶτον. Cornelius à Lapide dicit : intelligi praeteritum tempus primo in actu exercito, tempus Conversionis Cornelii ; secundo in actu signato, Matth. XVI. 18. Ubi Petrus audivit à Christo : Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam. Bene est quod de conversione Gentilium, id est, de praedicatione verbi inter Gentiles Christi sive consilium sive promissionem explicat. Nam haec conversio communis fuit etiam caeteris Apostolis, qui aedificium illud Spirituale pari industria procurarunt. Cur igitur in Apostolis hoc ministerium notaret, in Petro dominationem? Bellarminus verò ex hoc loco decimam septimam praerogativam Petri exsculpit. Nempe primum omnium coepisse praedicare gentilibus, quemadmodum primus praedicavit Judaeis. Primùm demus hoc. Qua veri specie Pontificatum, pro quo omne hoc saxum volvitur, concluderet? An in praedicatione Evangelii est potestas? An in eo, quòd primus praedicavit? Purus putus ordo, nisi fallor, si alia non accesserint, potestatem non indicat, non Monarchiam Pontifici jactatam. Deinde, primum praedicâsse Gentibus Petrum, non est usque quaque certum. Samaritanis primus praedicavit Philippus. Eunuchum ex Æthiopia jam idem Philippus baptizaverat. Neque Petrus hoc loco dicit, se primum Gentibus praedicâsse. Nam de initio suae praedicationis loquitur, non comparat suae praedicationis initium cum caeterorum praedicatione. Jam si spectemus praedicationis amplitudinem, quis non majorem Paulo praerogativam concesserit? Etenim Petrus uni familiae praedicavit. Paulus primus omnium cum Barnaba delectus est à Spiritu S. ad publicum ministerium praedicandi Gentibus, Act. XIII. Aliud est, uni familiae convertendae destinari, aliud mitti ad gentes universas. Quomodo profectus est Paulus in Seleuciam, Cyprum, Salamina, Paphum, ubi Proconsulem convertit, Pamphiliam, Pisidiam, alió. Adeò ut ab Hierusalem rusalem & circumjacentibus regionibus, usque ad Illyricum imple-verit prædicandi Evangelii munus Rom.XV.19.
units.tr: 8:28. [min yomeh qadmayya] The Syriac has "from ancient days". The Arabic has, most aptly, given the sense of Peter's words as "from the first days": namely, both from the sending out into the whole world (Matt. 28:19) and from the conversion of the Gentiles, which began with Cornelius the centurion (Acts 10). Hence James (5:14) translates that by [prōton]. Peter therefore had in mind the vision in which he was told to kill and eat, that is, to invite and convert to the communion of grace the Gentiles, who had until then been idolaters. For Hesychius notes that [archaion] signifies not only [palaion] but also [prōton]. Cornelius à Lapide says: "the past time is to be understood in two ways: first, in an action already carried out, the time of Cornelius's conversion; second, in an action foretold, Matt. 16:18, where Peter heard from Christ: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." It is right that he explains this as the conversion of the Gentiles, that is, as Christ's plan or promise concerning the preaching of the word among the Gentiles. For this conversion was common also to the other apostles, who promoted that spiritual building with equal zeal. Why, then, would this ministry be noted in the apostles and a lordship in Peter? Bellarmine, however, carves out from this passage the seventeenth prerogative of Peter: namely, that "he first of all began to preach to the Gentiles, just as he first preached to the Jews." Let us grant this first. With what appearance of truth would he conclude the papacy, for which this whole stone is rolled? Is there power in preaching the Gospel? Is there power in having preached first? Unless I am mistaken, this is a bare order, which, if other things do not come in, indicates no power, and not the monarchy so boasted of for the Pontiff. Next, that Peter was the first to preach to the Gentiles is not certain in every respect. Philip was the first to preach to the Samaritans, and the same Philip had already baptized the Ethiopian eunuch. Nor does Peter say in this place that he was the first to preach to the Gentiles; for he speaks of the beginning of his own preaching and does not compare the beginning of his preaching with the preaching of others. Now if we consider the extent of preaching, who would not grant a greater prerogative to Paul? Peter preached to a single household; Paul was the first of all, together with Barnabas, chosen by the Holy Spirit for the public ministry of preaching to the Gentiles (Acts 13). It is one thing to be destined to convert a single household, another to be sent to all nations. How Paul set out to Seleucia, Cyprus, Salamis, Paphos, where he converted the proconsul, Pamphylia, Pisidia, and elsewhere, so that from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum he fulfilled the office of preaching the Gospel (Rom. 15:19).

units.la: DEUS INTER NOS ELEGIT) ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο. Paulo obscuriora sunt. Chrysostomus pro in nobis legit in vobis, explicatque, in Palæstina, vel, præsentibus vobis. Sed constans est lectio: ἐν ἡμῖν. A qua proinde non recedimus. Syrus מן פימי דילי גבא אלהא דנשמעון עממא Scitis, quòd ab antiquis diebus ex ore meo elegit Deus, ut audirent Gentes. Beza subintelligit me. Perinde ac si diceret Petrus: Quid tam longa disceptatione opus est? Non verebor de me ipso dicere, quod verum esse omnes nôstis me videlicet ex hoc nostro coetu & numero delectum esse à Deo, ex cujus ore gentes intelligerent & amplecterentur Evangelii doctrinam. Idem Doctissimus Beza aliorum etiam quorundam expositionem tangit, qui ἐν ἡμῖν volunt idem esse, quod ἡμᾶς. Nam sic construi apud Hebræos verbum בחר Hæc sententia planissima esse videtur. Quomodo in Vet.Testam. בחר יהוה בציון ἘΞΕΛΕΞΑΤΟ ὁ Κύριος ἐν Σιὼν, elegit Deus Zion. Et alibi בך בחר ἘΛΕΞΑΤΟ ἐν σοι, elegit te. Astipulatur huic expositioni ὁ πᾶν Heinsius in Exercitatione ad h.l. Electionis Dei meminit, tum ut ejus mentione fortius premat sententiam, tum ut ad Dei gratiam & beneplacitum referat effecta sui Ministerii, non ad proprias vires. Confer Galat.I.15.18. 1,Cor. XV.10. UT PER OS MEUM AUDIRENT GENTES VERBUM EVANGELII) Hoc primum est argumentum Petri, quo comprobat institutum thema, Gentilibus nempe Circumcisionem & reliqua mandata Ceremonialia non esse injungenda, inde petitum, quòd Deus cùm primò elegisset Apostolos mittendos in universum orbem, quod factum Matth.XXVIII.19. ac præcipuè & in specie se, diserta compellatione in cœlesti visione Act. X. non elegerit illos ad prædicandum Mosen, & ejus statuta Ceremonialia, sed ad prædicandum Gentibus verbum Evangelii. Hæc autem ita esse disparata, ut unà consistere & cohærere nullo modo possint. Nempe in præconio Evangelii manifesta fuit impletio oraculi Jerem.XXXI.31.32. Ecce, venient dies, inquit Dominus, & pangam cum domo Israël & cum domo Juda novum fœdus, quod pepigi cum Patribus illorum in die, quo illos robusta manu eduxi ex Ægypto, quod ipsi irritum reddiderunt. Sed hoc erit fœdus: Dabo illis Legem meam meam in medio illorum, & in corde illorum inscribam illam. & c. Cum desiverint illa statuta, à conspectu meo, inquit Dominus, etiam semen Israëlis desinet esse populus in conspectu meo. Hoc oraculum applicavit Paulus ad tempora Novi Testamenti Hebr. VIII. 9. 10. Unde versa ultimo ex novitate foederis concludit foederis antiqui ἀφανισμόν. Manifestum igitur est Petri argumentum, petitum à Christi mandato, & novitate foederis, inducente שבת Sabbathum, quietem à חקים statutis Ceremonialibus, adeóque etiam à Circumcisionis necessitate, & contra praedicationem gratiae in Evangelio. Huc pertinet testimonium Baptistae de Christo, opponentis Mosen & gratiam. Lex, inquit, per Mosen data est: Gratia autem & veritas per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum facta, Joh. I. 17.
units.tr: GOD CHOSE AMONG US) [en hēmin exelexato]. These words are rather obscure. Chrysostom reads "among you" instead of "among us", and explains it as "in Palestine", or "with you present". But the reading is constant: [en hēmin], and we therefore do not depart from it. The Syriac has "You know that from ancient days God chose from my mouth that the Gentiles should hear." Beza supplies "me". As if Peter were saying: why is so long a dispute needed? I will not hesitate to say of myself what you all know to be true: namely that I was chosen by God from this our company and number, so that from my mouth the Gentiles might hear and embrace the doctrine of the Gospel. The same most learned Beza also touches upon the exposition of certain others, who want [en hēmin] to mean the same as [hēmas]. For the Hebrews construe the verb [bachar] in this way. This opinion seems most plain. So in the Old Testament: [bachar YHWH bĕ-Tsiyyon], "the Lord chose Zion" [exelexato ho Kyrios en Siōn], and elsewhere [bach bachar], "chose you" [exelexato en soi]. Heinsius, in his Exercitation on this passage, agrees with this exposition, "the all" [ho pan]. He mentions the election of God both so that by mentioning it he may press the sentence more strongly, and so that he may refer the effects of his ministry to God's grace and good pleasure, not to his own powers. Compare Gal. 1:15, 18; 1 Cor. 15:10. THAT BY MY MOUTH THE GENTILES SHOULD HEAR THE WORD OF THE GOSPEL) This is Peter's first argument, by which he proves the proposition under discussion: that the Gentiles are not to be burdened with circumcision and the rest of the ceremonial commands. It is drawn from the fact that God, when he first chose the apostles to be sent into the whole world (which was done in Matt. 28:19), and especially and particularly himself, in a clear address in the heavenly vision (Acts 10), did not choose them to preach Moses and his ceremonial statutes, but to preach the word of the Gospel to the Gentiles. And these things are so far apart that they can in no way stand or cohere together.
