For in the proclamation of the Gospel the fulfilment of the oracle of Jer. 31:31-32 was made manifest: "Behold, the days come, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, which I made with their fathers on the day when I led them out of Egypt with a strong hand, which they broke. But this will be the covenant: I will put my law within them, and write it on their hearts, etc. When those statutes cease from before me, says the Lord, then the seed of Israel also will cease to be a people before me." Paul applied this oracle to the times of the New Testament (Heb. 8:9-10), and from the newness of the covenant at the end he concludes the [aphanismon] of the old covenant. The argument of Peter is therefore manifest: it is drawn from Christ's command and from the newness of the covenant, which brings in [shabbat], the rest from the [chuqqim], the ceremonial statutes, and so also from the necessity of circumcision, and is against the preaching of grace in the Gospel. To this belongs the testimony of the Baptist about Christ, setting Moses against grace: "The law," he says, "was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ our Lord" (John 1:17).

units.la: CREDENTQUE) Hoc secundum argumentum est, non minus solidum.
units.tr: AND THEY BELIEVE) This second argument is no less solid.

units.la: Nempe in Novo Testamento, in Domino Iesu Christo neque circumcisionem valere, neque praeputium, sed fidem, quae est per charitatem efficax, Gal. V. 6. quia unus est Deus, qui Circumcisionem justificabit ex fide, & praeputium per fidem, Rom. II. 30. Hinc Christus discipulos suos, quos in universum orbem misit, jubet praedicare, Salvatum iri quisquis credit & baptizatur: Marc. XVI. 16. Quid ergo, sic disputat Petrus, turbantur Gentiles credentes? Cur ipsis circumcisio mandaretur, cum fidem Christus solam iis commendari voluerit?
units.tr: Namely, in the New Testament, "in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love" (Gal. 5:6), because "there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith" (Rom. 2:30). Hence Christ commands his disciples, whom he sent into the whole world, to preach: "whoever believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16). What then, Peter argues, is the trouble with believing Gentiles? Why should circumcision be enjoined on them, when Christ wanted only faith to be commended to them?

units.la: Versus VIII. ET QUI NOVIT CORDA DEUS)
units.tr: Verse 8. AND GOD, WHO KNOWS THE HEARTS)

units.la: Solvit tacitam objectionem Judaizantium, quod Gentiles natura sua impuros & peccatores oporteat suscepta circumcisione & Mosaicis purificationibus se purgare, & mundos reddere. Ergo provocat ad Deum καρδιογνώστην, arcanum cordis & affectus intimi scrutatorem. Πάντων καρδιογνώστης idem Deum vocat Act. I. 24. Confer 1. Reg. VIII. 39. Prov. XV. 11. Scitè Bernhardus in Psal. XC. Conc. 15: Solus perfectè novit, quid sit in homine, videns in eo, & quod in se non videt. Sed ἐμφαλικώτατος habet Apostolus Hebr. IV. 12. Ζῶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ &c. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ. Πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ, ᾧ ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος. Ad quem locum Scholiastes: Πάντα γυμνὰ παρ' αὐτῷ. Καὶ οὐδενὶ συγκαλύμμα ἢ ἐσωπείῳ ἐαυτὸν ἐπικλέψας δύναται τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν. Τετραχηλισμένα δὲ, ἀπὸ μεταφορᾶς τῶν ἐσθιάτων ἐν τοῖς τραχήλοις ἡτημένων καὶ γεγυμνωμένων τῆς δοξῆς. Sed amplius quid insinuant verba Apostoli. Est enim in illa dictione aperta allegoria à ritu lanionum, sive victi- mariorum, à quibus animalia immolanda τεχνηλίζειν dicuntur: cùm non solum à collo suspensa excoriantur, sed per dorsi spinam etiam resupinata finduntur, ut tota foris & intus oculis pateant. Sic optimè Beza. Quo pertinet, quod Favorinus habet: τεχνηλίζειν, τὸ διχοτομεῖν, ἢγουν, τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐάχεως σχίζειν.
units.tr: He answers the unspoken objection of the Judaizers, that Gentiles, being unclean and sinners by nature, must purify themselves by accepting circumcision and Mosaic purifications, and so make themselves clean. Therefore he appeals to God as the knower of hearts [kardiognōstēn], the searcher of the secret and inward affections. Acts 1:24 calls God the same, "knower of all [pantōn kardiognōstēs]". Compare 1 Kings 8:39 and Prov. 15:11. Bernard well says in Psalm 90, sermon 15: "Only God knows perfectly what is in a man, seeing in him both what he himself does not see." But the Apostle uses a very vivid image in Heb. 4:12: "The word of God is living, etc., and there is no creature hidden before him. All things are naked and laid open to the eyes of him to whom we must give account [tetrachēlismena]." On this passage the scholiast says: "All things are naked before him, and no one can hide himself from his eyes by any covering or mask. Laid open [tetrachēlismena] is a metaphor from those who hang animals by the neck and strip them of their skin." But the words of the Apostle also suggest more. For the word contains an open allegory from the rite of the butchers, or sacrificers, from whom slaughtered animals are said to be "laid open" [technalizein]: they are not only flayed while hung by the neck, but are also split along the backbone while laid on their backs, so that the whole animal lies open to view outside and inside. So Beza rightly explains it. To this belongs what Favorinus says: "technalizein means to cut in two, that is, to split from the throat."

units.la: TESTIMONIUM PRÆBUIT ILLIS) Ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς.
units.tr: HE GAVE THEM HIS WITNESS) He bore witness to them [emartyrēsen autois].

units.la: Opponit testimonium Dei, quod nititur inspectione cordis, nempe regenerati, purificati. Hoc igitur tertium & momentosum Petri argumentum est. Qui intus & familiarissimè à Deo explorati testimonium acceperunt sinceritatis suæ, religionis, pietatis, fidei, ab illis cur plura exigitis? Num quid ultra necesse est illos urgere, quorum pietati & religioni non homo aliquis, qui variis ludibriis & oculiferiis decipi potest, sed Deus καρδιογνώστης attestatus est ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις αὐτῶν? Respicit ad exemplum Cornelii Centurionis, quem ad Christianismum convertit. Nam huic Deus in donis suis testimonium illustre perhibuit, & mundum eum, ac cum ipso omnes credentes declaravit hac oratione: Quod Deus purificavit, tu ne pollui. v. 15. & v. 28. Mihi Deus ostendit, non oportere communem vel pollutum dicere ullum hominem. Et cum jejunaret Cornelius, & in ædibus suis precaretur, ecce Vir ipsi adsistebat in veste splendida & dixit: Corneli, exaudita sunt preces Tuæ, & Eleemosynarum tuarum memoria coram Deo facta est. v. 30. 31. Hoc est testimonium καρδιογνώσεως. Nam preces, quo animo fundantur, nullus, qui cordis recessus & latebras ignorat, cognoscit, ideòque solus Deus hoc testari poterat. Si igitur Cornelium incircumcisum Deus testimonio suo omni exceptione majori mundum, fidelem, pium declaravit, non est æquum, ut illis circumcisio imperetur.
units.tr: He sets against this the witness of God, which rests on the inspection of the heart, namely of the regenerate and purified. This is therefore Peter's third and weighty argument. Why do you demand more from those whom God himself, who knows the heart and has searched them most intimately, has attested to have received testimony of their sincerity, religion, piety and faith? Is there any need to press further those whose piety and religion were not certified by some man, who can be deceived by various mockeries and shows, but by God, the knower of hearts, who bore witness to them "by their gifts" [epi tois dōrois autōn]? He is pointing to the example of Cornelius the centurion, whom he converted to Christianity. For God bore illustrious witness to him by his gifts, and declared him clean, and with him all believers, by this word: "What God has cleansed, do not you call common" (Acts 10:15), and "God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean" (Acts 10:28). And when Cornelius was fasting and praying in his house, behold, a man in shining clothing stood before him and said: "Cornelius, your prayers have been heard, and your alms have been remembered before God" (Acts 10:30-31). This is a testimony of knowledge of the heart. For no one who does not know the recesses and hiding places of the heart can know with what mind prayers are offered, and therefore God alone could bear this witness. If then God, by his own testimony, greater than any exception, declared Cornelius, though uncircumcised, to be clean, faithful and pious, it is not fair that circumcision should be imposed on them.

units.la: DANS ILLIS SPIRITUM SANCTUM) Etiam hæc pars testimonii Divini est, in quo consistit argumentum quartum. Explicat hunc locum Angelus Apoc. XIX. 10. ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστι τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς προφητείας, testimonium Jesu, est Spiritus Prophetiæ.
units.tr: GIVING THEM THE HOLY SPIRIT) This part too belongs to the divine testimony, and in it lies the fourth argument. The angel explains this place in Rev. 19:10: "the testimony of Jesus Christ is the Spirit of prophecy" [hē martyria tou Iēsou Christou estin to pneuma tēs prophēteias].

units.la: Est ergo Spiritus, quem Deus impertitus est fidelibus gentilibus, Spiritus Prophetiæ, quo Deus fidelibus Judæis testimonium perhibuit de Gentibus, quod & illi ad Christi communionem pertineant, & ad eam vocentur per Evangelii prædicationem, quandoquidem per illum Spiritum ipsis donatum Christum vocarunt runt Dominum Iesum. 1.Cor.XII.3. De communicatione huius Spiritus loquitur Lucas Act.X.44. quo potissimum Petrus respicit; Cum haec loqueretur Petrus, illapsus est Spiritus S. in omnes illos, qui sermonem illum audiverunt. Qua re valde attoniti Judaei, cum novitate rei vix se ipsos caperent.
units.tr: The Spirit, therefore, which God imparted to the faithful Gentiles, is the Spirit of prophecy, by which God bore witness to the faithful Jews concerning the Gentiles, that they too belong to the communion of Christ and are called to it through the preaching of the Gospel. For by that Spirit given to them they called Jesus Lord (1 Cor. 12:3). Luke speaks of the communication of this Spirit in Acts 10:44, to which Peter above all looks: "While Peter was speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word." At this the Jews were greatly astonished, and could scarcely take in the novelty of the thing.

units.la: SICUT ET NOBIS) Comparat effusionem visibilem Spiritus S. supra Gentiles cum illa, quae Apostolis accidit in tempore Pentecostes. Hinc Lucas de Gentilibus Spiritu S. perfusis: Audiverunt illos loquentes Linguis, & magnalia Dei edisserentes, Act.X.46. Quae proinde visibilis Spiritus S. participatio causa fuit, ut baptismum, id est, circumcisionem non manufactam illis Petrus conferret, quo loco circumcisionis, justificans & sanctificans Dei gratia ipsis obsignaretur.
units.tr: AS ALSO TO US) He compares the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Gentiles with that which happened to the Apostles at Pentecost. Hence Luke says of the Gentiles filled with the Holy Spirit: "They heard them speaking with tongues and declaring the magnificent works of God" (Acts 10:46). Therefore this visible participation in the Holy Spirit was the reason why Peter conferred on them baptism, that is, circumcision not made by hands, in which the grace of God, justifying and sanctifying, was sealed to them in place of circumcision.

units.la: Versus IX. NIHILQUE DISCREVIT INTER NOS ET ILLOS)
units.tr: Verse 9. AND MADE NO DISTINCTION BETWEEN US AND THEM)

units.la: Hoc quintum Petri argumentum, quo probat Gentilium communionem cum Sanctis Judaeis, propter quam non oporteat illis jugum imponere. Quia nempe Deus nihil discrevit inter Judaeos & Gentiles quo ad gratiam justificationis, sanctificationis & glorificationis. Quod alibi sic expressit: Ἐπ' ἀληθείας καταλαμβάνομαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐστι προσωπολήμψια ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλ' ἐν παντὶ ἔθνει φοβούμενος δεκτὸς αὐτῷ ἐστι. Act.X.34.35. Ante hac fuit Deus προσωπολήμπτης, & discrevit inter Judaeos & Gentes, quatenus in distribuendo suo spiritu & gratiae donis, quae nemini debendi reus fuit, respexit populum לאום לאו λαὸν περιούσιον eos nempe, qui in circumcisione Abrahami Parentis sui fidem sunt aemulati. Nunc illa προσωπολημψία & ἀφορεσις cessat, paries intergerinus, inimicitiae illae sublatae. Quemadmodum Judaeis Messias venit, sic Gentilibus. Quemadmodum illis annuntiari debuit Evangelium, sic his. Quemadmodum illi fide justificati, sic hi, quod sequitur.
units.tr: This is Peter's fifth argument, by which he proves that the Gentiles share fellowship with the holy Jews, and for that reason they should not be burdened with a yoke. God, namely, made no distinction between Jews and Gentiles as regards the grace of justification, sanctification and glorification. He expressed this elsewhere thus: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he who fears him is acceptable to him" [Ἐπ' ἀληθείας καταλαμβάνομαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐστι προσωπολήμψια ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλ' ἐν παντὶ ἔθνει φοβούμενος δεκτὸς αὐτῷ ἐστι] Acts 10:34-35. Formerly God was a respecter of persons (προσωπολήμπτης) and made a distinction between Jews and Gentiles, inasmuch as in distributing his Spirit and the gifts of grace, which no one could claim as a debt, he regarded the people [לאום לאו λαὸν περιούσιον], namely those who had imitated the faith of Abraham their father in circumcision. Now that respect of persons and that separation have ceased; the dividing wall is broken down and those enmities removed. As the Messiah came to the Jews, so he came to the Gentiles; as the Gospel had to be announced to them, so it had to be to these; as they were justified by faith, so are these, which is what follows.

units.la: FIDE PURIFICANS ILLORUM CORDA) In V.T. Judaeorum corda etiam fide purgabantur. Sed additae plurimae purificationes aliae externae. Jam his sublatis sola fides corda purgat. Tribuitur purificatio cordis etiam sanguini Christi. Diversimode tamen haec fidei & sanguini Christi competit. Fides purificat, ut est causa sanctificationem nostram dirigens, & eam DEO gratam acceptamque reddens, quomodo in Ethicis dicimus prudentiam virtutem regere. Deus autem corda per fidem purificat, risset, quia non tantùm habitum fidei infundit, sed ipsam etiam actum, quo Christum apprehendimus, & nos à peccatis lavamus. Sicut ludimagister puero, quem scribere docet, non calamum tantùm porrigit, sed etiam digitos ejus & ducit, & per ejus digitos literas pingit: sic Deus non donum tantùm fidei habitumq; infundit, sed etiam facit, ut actu credamus. Jam etiam sanguine Christi purificantur nobis corda, quatenus ejus merito & virtute acquisitus nobis est Spiritus sanctificans, qui fomitem peccati paulatim expurgat. Cùm igitur hac fide Gentilium corda sint purgata, concludit Petrus, illos Ecclesiæ membra esse sine obedientia illa legali, quam statuta Mosis ante adventum Christi rigido imperio exegerunt. Nam purgatio cordis per fidem est circumcisio cordis, quæ est in circumcisione Christi non facta manibus, Col. II. 11. Hanc autem præcipuè Deus curat, cùm illa manibus facta, cor non purificet, & terminum obligationis habeat.
units.tr: FAITH PURIFYING THEIR HEARTS) In the Old Testament the hearts of the Jews were also purified by faith, but many other external purifications were added. Now that these have been removed, faith alone purifies the heart. Purification of the heart is also ascribed to the blood of Christ. Yet these belong to faith and to the blood of Christ in different ways. Faith purifies as the cause that directs our sanctification and renders it pleasing and acceptable to God, just as in ethics we say that prudence governs virtue. God, however, purifies hearts through faith in a fuller sense, because he not only infuses the habit of faith but also the act itself, by which we lay hold of Christ and wash ourselves from sins. As a writing master, who teaches a boy to write, not only hands him the pen but also guides his fingers and through his fingers forms the letters, so God not only bestows the gift and habit of faith but also brings it about that we believe in act. Our hearts are also purified by the blood of Christ, inasmuch as by his merit and power the sanctifying Spirit has been obtained for us, who gradually cleanses away the fomes of sin. Since, therefore, the hearts of the Gentiles have been purified by this faith, Peter concludes that they are members of the Church without that legal obedience which the statutes of Moses enforced with a rigid rule before the coming of Christ. For the purification of the heart through faith is the circumcision of the heart, which is "the circumcision of Christ, not made with hands" (Col. 2:11). God especially cares for this, since circumcision made with hands does not purify the heart and has a limit to its obligation.

units.la: Versus X. NUNC ERGO QUID TENTATIS DEUM)
units.tr: Verse 10. NOW THEREFORE WHY DO YOU TEMPT GOD)

units.la: Tentat Deum, qui ejus mandata & promissiones in dubium vocat, vel qui voluntatem suam clarae voluntati Dei opponit. Experiri enim vult, an Deus verax sit, an constans, an serió mandârit, an contemptum sui vindicare in animo habeat? Hæc ergo gravis est πειρασμὸς, & magna ratio, quâ moti Judaizantes ab insano suo coepto desistant. Vult Petrus dicere: Deus noster per os Prophetarum suorum vaticinatus est in V. T. magnam Gentilium conversionem, & obedientiam gentium Christo fore. Christus nos jussit ire in universum orbem ad prædicandum Evangelium. Idem testatus nobis est suam voluntatem in imperata cœlitus conversione Cornelii, & post illam suum Spiritum Gentilibus præputiatis ministravit, & corda eorum fide purificavit. Hæc argumenta clarissima sunt, velle Deum, ut Gentiles in communionem nostram adoptemus, pro mundis eos habeamus, cum illis conversemur, & ceremoniali jugo illos non fatigemus. Cùm igitur his argumentis tam certis & manifestis occupati non credatis, sed firmiora documenta postuletis, nec promissionem Dei obsignetis, quòd verax sit, tentatis Deum, & vindictam ejus, nisi mentem mutetis, præsentem experimini.
units.tr: He tempts God who calls into doubt his commands and promises, or who sets his own will against the clear will of God. For such a person wants to test whether God is true, whether he is constant, whether he seriously commanded, whether he intends to avenge contempt of himself. This, then, is a grave temptation, and a strong reason by which the Judaizers, moved, may desist from their mad undertaking. Peter wants to say: our God, through the mouths of his prophets, foretold in the Old Testament a great conversion of the Gentiles and their obedience to Christ. Christ bade us go into the whole world to preach the Gospel. The same God has witnessed to us his will in the conversion of Cornelius, commanded from heaven, and afterwards ministered his Spirit to the uncircumcised Gentiles and purified their hearts by faith. These arguments are most clear: that God wills us to admit the Gentiles into our fellowship, to hold them clean, to live with them, and not to weary them with the ceremonial yoke. Since, therefore, you are occupied with such certain and manifest arguments yet do not believe them, but demand firmer proofs, and do not seal God's promise that he is true, you tempt God; and unless you change your minds, you will experience his vengeance upon you.

units.la: UT IMPONATUR JUGUM SUPER CERVICES DISCIPULORUM) Septima est Apostoli ratio. Quia Caco.
units.tr: THAT A YOKE MAY BE PUT UPON THE NECKS OF THE DISCIPLES) This is the Apostle's seventh reason, because the Cacozeli

units.la: Cacozel libertatem Christianam evertunt, & commutant cum intolerabili jugo. Jugi nomine intelligo tum Ceremonialem, tum moralem legem. Ceremonialis quo jure jugum dici poterit, nequit ambigi. Libertatem enim Judæorum mirifice constrinxit, & eos oneroso hoc & molestissimo cultu detinuit in servitute usque ad Christum. Moralis jugum est, quia per carnem infirmata vivificare non potest, adeoque effectum justificationis nunquam producere. Utramque legem Pseudapostoli urgebant, & addebant mantissæ loco fidem. Discipulos vocat Petrus recens conversos, discentes viam justitiæ & salutis, qui ad perfectionem nondum pertigerunt, sed tamen relicto τῆς ἀρχῆς τ̃ Χριστοῦ λόγον πρὸς τελειότητα φέρωμεθα. Hebr. VI. 1. Nuncupati autem sunt Christiani primitus μαθηταὶ dis- cipuli more Judæorum, qui eos omnes, qui singularem in modum religionis studio incumbebant, Doctore præeunte תלמידים Discipulos vocarunt.
units.tr: The Cacozeli overthrow Christian liberty and exchange it for an intolerable yoke. By "yoke" I understand both the ceremonial and the moral law. That the ceremonial law can rightly be called a yoke cannot be doubted. For it wonderfully constrained the liberty of the Jews and kept them in servitude until Christ by that burdensome and most troublesome worship. The moral law is a yoke because, weakened through the flesh, it cannot give life and therefore never produces the effect of justification. The false apostles urged both laws and added faith as a supplement. Peter calls the recently converted "disciples", learners of the way of righteousness and salvation, who have not yet reached perfection, but who nevertheless, "leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection" [τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ λόγον πρὸς τελειότητα φέρωμεθα] (Heb. 6:1). Christians were first called "disciples" [μαθηταί] after the manner of the Jews, who called "disciples" [תלמידים] all those who devoted themselves to religion in a particular way, with a teacher going before them.

units.la: QUOD NEQUE PATRES NOSTRI, NEQUE NOS PORTARE POTUIMUS) Importabile facit jugum, quia importabat servitutem maledictionis, & chirographi. De jugo chirographi verum quidem, grave illud fuisse & δυσβάστακτον, quomodo etiam Christus vocat Matth. XXIII. 4. Aug. serm. 9. de verbis Domini vocat sarcinam innumerabilium observationum, quae dura cervix Judæorum premenda erat, ne ad idola respiceret. Quam illud fuerit grave, si non alia argumento essent, sufficere illud posset, quòd tanta farrago fuerit Præceptorum in placitis, ut Judæi affirmativa numerent ducenta octodecim, negativa adæquent diebus anni, ceu videre est apud Maimonidem More Nevoch. III. 6. Attamen jugum illud à perfectioribus portabile fuit. Zacharias & Elisabeth dicuntur ambulasse in omnibus ἐντολαῖς & δικαιώμασι Κυρίου, justificationibus Domini, Luc. I. 6. Circumcisio onerosa & cum doloris acri sensu conjuncta. Attamen à Patribus portata. Sic reliquæ partes hujus chirographi. Quid ergo? Loquitur Petrus de lege morali primarió, & propter illam de Ceremoniali, propter obedientiæ rationem, quam habet Lex Ceremonialis non à se, sed à Lege morali, quæ jubet Deum amari ex toto corde, ac proinde ei obtemperare in omnibus. Nempe non de sola lege ceremoniali quæstio est, sed etiam de morali. Voluerunt enim per Mosen justificationem obtingere adversarii v. 5. & ejus legem eo usque observari debere, ut per eam observantiam serventur. Hoc onus importabile. Nempe lex per carnem infirmata vivificare non potest, Rom. VIII. 3. Opus igitur fuit valentioribus humeris, qui tantam molem suscriperent & sustinerent. Pontificii tamen, & illos secutus noster Curcellæus, nos verissimum illud dogma ex præsenti loco comprobantes non ferunt. Stapletonus in Antidotis Apostolicis ad hunc locum, disputat contra Calvinum & contendit, Petrum non agere de lege morali, sed tantùm de Ceremoniali. Atqui, Stapletone, Ceremonialis lex, & ejus jugum portari potuit, etiam ab ipsis hypocritis. Hoc fatetur Stapletonus, Cornelius à Lapide. Non porrigit tamen herbam uterque. Stapletonus, igitur respondet: importabile dictum, non quod omnino ferri non possit, sed quod difficulter. Iam hypocritæ potuisse implere, sed magno cum labore, fideles autem longè facilius, & expeditius, & jucundius, propter acceptum Spiritum adoptionis. Hæc nullo judicio dicuntur. Nam Petrus de Patribus loquitur, quos negat portare potuisse jugum, non de hypocritis solis. Omnes, qui portárunt legem, uno fasciculo comprehendit. Deinde magno intervallo disparata sunt hæc duo: difficulter portare, & non portare: δυσβάστακτον καὶ ἀβάστακτον. Hæc Petri phrasis certam & designatam rei experientiam indicat. Sed & oppositio manifesta est gratiæ Domini, per quam servatos Patres illos in sequenti versu Petrus dicit. Gratia autem significat peccatorum remissionem. Si per remissionem peccatorum servati Patres, tum non quia jugum legis portárunt. Si portássent sive facilè sive difficulter, tum non peccássent, & sine gratia fuissent salvati. Ergo non portárunt, sed portare tamen magnopere laborárunt. Bellarminus re manifestâ, non tamen vult committere, ut nobis victoria cedat. Constanter negat, intelligi per ζυγὸν ἀβάστακτον legem moralem. Rationes ipsi tres sunt. Prima, quia disputatur de lege Ceremoniali: an circumcidi conveniat converses ex Gentilibus? Secunda ex decreto Synodi: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis, nihil ultra vobis imponere oneris, quàm necessaria hæc, ut abstineatis vos ab immolatis Simulacrorum, sanguine, suffocato, & fornicatione. Hæc dici necessaria vel ex Ceremoniali, vel simpliciter universa. Non ex universa. Alioquin sequeretur, non esse necessarium non colere idola, non mœchari, non furari, & similia, quod absurdum. Ergo tantùm ex Ceremoniali. Tertia ex scopo Apostolorum, qui jugum à cervicibus Discipulorum depellere in animo habuerunt. Si legem legem moralem intellexerunt, sequi, Christianos ab obligatione legis moralis liberatos esse. Stapletonus addit quartam. Sic ipsum Christum tentâsse Deum, dicens: Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Haec argumenta magno animo à Bellarmino & Stapleton0 jactata, majori contemnimus, quia nihil soliditatis habent. Respondemus igitur distinctè. Ad primum. Fuit omnino occasio à circumcisione, & de ea disputatum in Synodo. Neque ideo tamen Petri verba de Ceremoniali Lege tantum agunt, quia non decretum continent, sed rationem decreti. Rationem autem saepe altius assurgere, quis ignorat? Hoc autem loco rationem decreti longius repeti necessum fuit, quia Ceremoniarum usus nunquam bene intelligi poterat nisi relatè ad Legem moralem. Ergo etiam Paulus in Epistola ad Galatas de Lege Ceremoniali disputare non potuit, quin ad universam legem assurgeret, & de ejus usu diceret. Hinc disputationem suam de justificatione per fidem orditur cap.II. vers.16. Scientes non justificari hominem ex operibus legis. Ubi de universa lege agit, & ex praemissis illis concludit cap.V.6. Circumcisionem nihil amplius valere. Eadem methodo hic Petrus utitur. Et est manifesta illatio talis: Legis onus est importabile. Circumcisio pertinet ad legis onus. Est ergo importabilis. Ad secundum. Necessaria fuerunt illa in decreto praecepta non ex Ceremonialis legis obligatione, sed lege morali, cum qua pugnant tum scortatio, tum scandalum, si casus praesto sit, quo mactabant infirmos illi, qui idolothyta, sanguinem & suffocatum comedunt. Neque adeo sequitur, non esse necessaria ex lege morali non colere idolum, non moechari. Nam Bellarminus ipse fassus est, πρόσκαιρον excipi, quia inter Gentiles pro adiaphora fuit habita. De qua re infra videbimus. Ad tertium. Fuerit scopus Apostolorum, ostendere, quod circumcisio non ultra obliger. Hoc enim revera agitur. Sed quaestionem suam concludunt ex medio hoc termino, nempe τῷ ἀδιαφόρῳ legis moralis, ad quam pertinet, Ceremonialibus mandatis obedire. Deinde dubitari nequit, quin etiam Lex moralis, secundum particularem aliquem sui finem, fuerit abrogata. In Veteri Testamento Lex moralis hactenus fuit jugum ἀδιάφορον, quatenus attulit timorem mortis, à quo ortus est Spiritus servitutis. Singularis enim fuit Oeconomia legis in ordine ad populum Israëliticum paedagogica, quia fuerunt sub lege, tanquam tutore rigido, severo, instante, flagellante. Libertatis jus habuerunt,
units.tr: WHICH NEITHER OUR FATHERS NOR WE WERE ABLE TO BEAR) He calls it an unbearable yoke because it bore the servitude of the curse and of the handwriting. It is true of the yoke of the handwriting that it was heavy and hard to bear [δυσβάστακτον], as Christ himself calls it, Matth. 23.4. Augustine, in sermon 9 on the words of the Lord, calls it a burden of countless observances, under which the stiff neck of the Jews had to be bowed, lest they look toward idols. How heavy it was, even if there were no other proof, could be shown by this alone: the mass of precepts about ceremonies was so great that the Jews count two hundred and eighteen affirmative precepts and the negative ones equal the days of the year, as may be seen in Maimonides, More Nevochim III.6. Yet that yoke could be borne by the more perfect. Zacharias and Elisabeth are said to have walked in all the commandments [ἐντολαῖς] and ordinances [δικαιώμασι] of the Lord, the justifications of the Lord, Luke 1.6. Circumcision was burdensome and joined with a keen sense of pain, yet it was borne by the Fathers. So it was with the other parts of this handwriting. What then? Peter speaks chiefly of the moral law, and because of it also of the ceremonial law, on account of the obedience which the ceremonial law owes not to itself but to the moral law, which commands that God be loved with the whole heart and therefore be obeyed in all things. Indeed the question concerns not only the ceremonial law but also the moral. For our opponents wished that justification be obtained through Moses, v. 5, and that his law be observed to such a degree that it be kept by that observance. This is an unbearable burden. For the law, weakened by the flesh, cannot give life, Rom. 8.3. There was therefore need of stronger shoulders, to take up and sustain so great a load. The Papists, however, and our Curcellaeus, who follows them, do not bear this, although we prove from this passage that most true doctrine. Stapleton, in his Antidotes to the Apostles, disputes against Calvin on this passage and contends that Peter is not dealing with the moral law but only with the ceremonial. Yet, Stapleton, the ceremonial law and its yoke could be borne, even by hypocrites themselves. Stapleton and Cornelius a Lapide confess this. Yet neither of them offers a handful of grass. Stapleton therefore replies: the saying is "unbearable" not because it could not be borne at all, but because it could be borne only with difficulty. Hypocrites could indeed fulfil it, but with great labour, whereas the faithful do so far more easily, expeditiously and joyfully, through the Spirit of adoption received. These things are said without any judgment. For Peter speaks of the Fathers, whom he says were not able to bear the yoke, not of hypocrites alone. He embraces all who bore the law in one bundle. Further, these two things are separated by a wide interval: to bear with difficulty, and not to bear at all: δυσβάστακτον καὶ ἀβάστακτον. This phrase of Peter indicates a certain and defined experience of the thing. But the opposition to the grace of the Lord is also plain, through which Peter says those Fathers were saved in the following verse. Grace, however, signifies the remission of sins. If the Fathers were saved through the remission of sins, then it was not because they bore the yoke of the law. If they had borne it, whether easily or with difficulty, they would not have sinned, and would have been saved without grace. Therefore they did not bear it, but they laboured greatly to bear it. Bellarmine, though the matter is clear, does not wish to yield, so that victory may not fall to us. He steadfastly denies that ζυγὸν ἀβάστακτον is to be understood of the moral law. He has three reasons. The first: because the dispute is about the ceremonial law: whether it is fitting for converts from the Gentiles to be circumcised? The second, from the decree of the Synod: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no burden beyond these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. These things are called necessary either from the ceremonial law or simply universally. Not universally. Otherwise it would follow that it was not necessary not to worship idols, not to commit adultery, not to steal, and the like, which is absurd. Therefore only from the ceremonial law. The third, from the aim of the Apostles, who intended to remove the yoke from the necks of the disciples: If they had understood the moral law, it would follow that Christians are freed from the obligation of the moral law. Stapleton adds a fourth: thus it would be to tempt Christ himself, who said: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." These arguments, boldly thrown out by Bellarmine and Stapleton, we despise all the more, because they have no solidity. We therefore reply distinctly. To the first. It was indeed the occasion of the dispute about circumcision, and it was discussed in the Synod. Yet Peter's words do not deal only with the ceremonial law for that reason, since they contain not the decree but the reason for the decree. Who does not know that a reason often rises higher? In this place the reason for the decree had to be traced back further, because the use of the ceremonies could never be well understood except in relation to the moral law. Therefore Paul, too, in his Epistle to the Galatians, could not dispute about the ceremonial law without rising to the whole law and speaking of its use. Hence he begins his disputation about justification through faith in chapter 2, verse 16: knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law. There he treats of the whole law, and from those premises he concludes in chapter 5.6: circumcision avails nothing any more. Peter uses the same method here. And the inference is plain: the burden of the law is unbearable; circumcision belongs to the burden of the law; therefore it is unbearable. To the second. Those precepts in the decree were necessary not from the obligation of the ceremonial law but from the moral law, with which both fornication and offence are at odds, if the case arose in which those who eat things sacrificed to idols, blood and what is strangled, would wound the weak. Nor does it follow that it is not necessary, from the moral law, not to worship an idol or not to commit adultery. For Bellarmine himself confessed that πρόσκαιρον is excepted, because among the Gentiles these things were held to be adiaphora. We shall see more about this matter below. To the third. Let the aim of the Apostles have been to show that circumcision no longer obliges. For this is in fact what is being done. But they conclude their question from this middle term, namely the τῷ ἀδιαφόρῳ of the moral law, to which it belongs to obey the ceremonial commandments. Further, it cannot be doubted that the moral law too, according to some particular end of its own, was abrogated. In the Old Testament the moral law was hitherto a ἀδιάφορον yoke, insofar as it brought the fear of death, from which the spirit of bondage arose. For the economy of the law was singular in its pedagogical ordering toward the Israelite people, since they were under the law as under a tutor who was rigid, severe, insistent and scourging. They had the right of liberty,

units.la: { } buerunt, sed non plenam fruitionem. Inde oculo intento in suum paedagogum metum mortis, & Spiritum servitutis conceperunt: altero oculo reflexo in suam adoptionem, fiduciam. In Novo Testamento jugum illud sublatum, quod consistebat in timore mortis & servitutis Spiritus. Ad quartum. Quomodo Christus Deum tentavit? An jugum illud legalis obedientiae justificandis imposuit? Cur ergo in hunc mundum venit, si alio modo peccatores salvari potuerunt? Intererat Sapientiae Divinae, hominem sibi & jugo suo relinquere, si reliquae vires fuerunt etiam in summa hominis contentione, quibus eluctari & ad ipsam quoquo modo emergere potuisset. Caeterum Christus in Novo Testamento ad legem homines amandavit, non quod doceret, eam ad salutem necessariam esse secundum impletionem, sed quia necessaria secundum poenitentiam.
units.tr: ...but not the full enjoyment of it. Hence, with one eye fixed on their pedagogue, they conceived the fear of death and the spirit of bondage; with the other eye turned back to their adoption, they conceived confidence. In the New Testament that yoke has been taken away, which consisted in the fear of death and the spirit of bondage. To the fourth. How did Christ tempt God? Did he impose that yoke of legal obedience for the purpose of justification? Why then did he come into this world, if sinners could have been saved in another way? It was a matter for the Divine Wisdom to leave man to himself and to his yoke, if there were remaining powers by which he could struggle, even with the utmost exertion of man, and somehow rise up to it. Moreover, Christ in the New Testament sent men back to the law, not because he taught that it is necessary to salvation as fulfilled, but because it is necessary as a means of repentance.

units.la: Versus XI. SED PER GRATIAM DOMINI JESU CHRISTI CREDIMUS NOS SALVOS FUTUROS)
units.tr: Verse 11. BUT WE BELIEVE THAT WE SHALL BE SAVED THROUGH THE GRACE OF THE LORD JESUS CHRIST)

units.la: Haec est conclusio Epexegesis. Veram salutis causam promit, gratiam Domini Jesu Christi, oppositè ad legem Mosis, tum sanctitatem perfectam exigentem, tum placita sua in dogmatis proferentem. Sed paulò diligentius singulos momentosae hujus sententiae apices excutiamus.
units.tr: This is the conclusion, an epexegesis. It states the true cause of salvation, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, set against the law of Moses, which both demands perfect holiness and proposes its own dogmas. But let us examine more carefully the individual points of this weighty statement.

units.la: PER GRATIAM) In genere gratia est, quicquid sine merito nostro accepimus. Accepimus autem esse, vivere, moveri, Act. XVII.28. Sic ipsa natura gratia est. Dedit enim Deus non merentibus, quippe non existentibus. Jussit ἐκ σκότους φῶς λάμψαι, 2.Cor. IV.6. Usitatum tamen Scripturis gratiam appellare, quod vim naturae nostrae superat, & à bonitate Dei superadditur. Censemus autem, hominem integrum non plane exsortem fuisse gratiae Divinae. Quamvis enim habuerit facultates, justitiam & cognitionem Dei, sine qua natura ejus recta, bona, spiritualis & κοινωνίαν τῶ πνεύματι nequidem cogitari poterat, contra quam hic periculosissime hallucinantur Pontificii; tamen suppositá liberali Dei cum homine conventione, in qua ipsi obedienti stipulatus est mercedem aeternae in coelo vitae, gratia Dei conspicua maximè fuit. Si in obedientia perseverâsset, naturalia quidem ipsi fuissent, extra foederalem conventionem, vita, & beatitudo & benedictiones Coelorum supernè, Abyssi subjacentis, uberum & vulvae, Genes. XLIX.25. & communio Spiritus ac ambulatio cum Deo. Haec, inquam, extra foedus ipsi naturalia fuissent. Accessit huic naturali conditioni hominis integri fœdus supernaturale Dei, quo homini Deus stipulatus est vitam æternam, Spiritualem, per translationem ex terrestri Paradiso post decursum obedientiæ curriculum in Cœlis degendam. Non est quidem hoc verbum promissionis Adamo supernaturaliter factum, directè in historia Sacra expressum: Omnino tamen implicitum habemus in Sacramento Arboris Vitæ in medio Paradisi, Genes. II.9. Et fœderalem conventionem intercessisse utcunque, constat ex Hos.VI.7. Et illi sicut Adam transgressi sunt fœdus. Hæc stipulatio, naturæ etiam integræ indebita, procul omni dubio gratia fuit. Hinc interpretor illud Augustini in aureolo ad Laurentium Enchiridio, cap.CVI. Etsi non peccâsset, sine gratia tamen nullum esse meritum, potuisset. Nempe tale meritum, cujus merces vita æterna extra Paradisum in Cœlo transfigenda. Homini peccatori etiam multiplex gratia affulget. Sed maximè illustris est illa, qua constat justificatio, & nostra cum Deo reconciliatio. Operæ pretium est contemplari ως ἀληθῶς βεβαίως, quibus artibus rectam de Gratia hac justificante persuasionem Sathanas ex animis hominum eximere laborârit. Nullam autem unquam pestilentius organon habuit Pelagio, per quem Virginis Ecclesiæ florem hactenus illibatum decerpere sustinuit. Omnis dimicatio suscepta pro Helenâ illâ, τῶ ἀνπξιόν, pro quo ipse, Manichæismi odium præferens, omni laterum contentione decertavit. Ergo initio negavit, ad dilectionem Dei esse opus gratiâ. Vi naturæ satis hoc fieri posse, & sine gratia legem Dei impleri, & tentationibus gravissimis resisti posse. Cùm Augustinus operosè comprobaret verum Dei amorem, cui retribuitur Spiritualis cum Deo communio, & ipsos actus charitatis, esse Spiritus S. donum, in quo habuit suffragium Concilii Carthaginensis tertii, Sardiniani & Arausicani, Pelagius pellem, non animum mutare coepit. Agnoscere enim coepit gratiam, & per eam gratiam intellexit possibilitatem naturæ à Deo conditæ, id est, rationalem voluntatem. Sed ostenderat, Augustinus, Scripturam de gratia tali loqui, quæ vires naturæ excederet. Ergo cum naturali gratia pariter currere jussit supernaturalem, sed solam externam, quam in legis doctrina collocabat. Graviter autem reprehensus & veritate subactus, addidit gratiam tertiam, qua ignoscuntur peccata, tanquam æquum meritum & funalem, quam necessanecessariam tamen omnibus esse negavit. Alios enim sine peccato innocuam vitam transigere: alios se ad poenitentiam renovare, & naturam suam instaurare. Contra quam assertionem Charthaginensis Synodus statuit Canone tertio: Gratiam Dei non solum peccata dimittere, sed etiam adjuvare, ne committantur. Depulsus igitur à sua sententia, quartam adjecit gratiam Christi, quam constituit in doctrina & exemplo Christi. Quemadmodum enim Adamus obfuit exemplo malo: Sic Christum profuisse exemplo bono. Contra quem strenuè pugnare perrexit antiquitas, & eò ipsum adigere, ut agnosceret quintam gratiam, virtutis Divinae auxilium intus per Spiritum Sanctum in homine operantis. In qua sententia post tot anfractus substitit, neque largiri unquam voluit, plus significare gratiam, nempe non solam intellectûs illuminationem, sed etiam voluntatis determinationem, & gratiam vel habitualem vel actualem voluntati additam. Hanc enim cum libero arbitrio ita pugnare, ut Manichaeismus evitari nequeat. Ergo hominem sui arbitrii viribus & propria voluntatis determinatione bonum spirituale, unionem cum Deo producere posse, ut jam justificationem naturae per gratiam quocunque modo adjutae foerum constanter fecerit.
units.tr: THROUGH GRACE) In general, grace is whatever we receive without merit on our part. We receive being, living, and moving, Acts 17:28. In this way nature itself is grace, for God gave to those who did not deserve it, indeed who did not yet exist. He commanded light to shine out of darkness, 2 Cor. 4:6. It is customary in Scripture, however, to call grace that which exceeds the power of our nature and is added to it by the goodness of God. We hold that man in his integrity was not wholly without the grace of God. For although he had faculties, righteousness and knowledge of God, without which his nature could not even be conceived as upright, good, spiritual, and [fellowship of the Spirit κοινωνίαν τῷ πνεύματι], a point on which the Papists err most dangerously, nevertheless, given the free covenant of God with man, in which he promised eternal life in heaven as the reward to Adam if he obeyed, the grace of God was supremely evident. If he had persevered in obedience, life, blessedness and the blessings of heaven above, of the deep that lies beneath, of breasts and womb, Gen. 49:25, and communion with the Spirit and walking with God would have been natural to him, apart from the covenant. I say these would have been natural to him apart from the covenant. To this natural condition of man in his integrity was added a supernatural covenant of God, in which God promised him spiritual eternal life, to be spent in heaven after the course of obedience, through translation from the earthly paradise. This promise was not indeed made to Adam supernaturally in words, expressly stated in sacred history; yet we have it implicitly in the sacrament of the tree of life in the midst of paradise, Gen. 2:9. That a covenant of some kind passed between them is clear from Hos. 6:7: But they like Adam have transgressed the covenant. This stipulation, not owed even to nature in its integrity, was beyond all doubt grace. Hence I interpret that saying of Augustine in his little golden book to Laurentius, the Enchiridion, chap. 106: Even if he had not sinned, there could have been no merit without grace. Namely, a merit whose reward is eternal life, to be passed in heaven outside paradise. Grace also shines on sinful man in many ways, but that grace is most conspicuous by which justification and our reconciliation with God are secured. It is worth considering with what arts Satan has laboured, [as truly and firmly ὡς ἀληθῶς βεβαίως], to snatch from men's minds the right conviction about this justifying grace. Yet he never had a more pestilential instrument than Pelagius, through whom he attempted to pluck the flower of the Virgin Church, unspoiled until then. Every contest undertaken for that Helen [worthy one τῷ ἀξίῳ] was fought by Pelagius, who, putting before him his hatred of Manichaeism, struggled with every effort of his strength. So at first he denied that love of God required the work of grace. He held that by the power of nature this could be done well enough, that the law of God could be fulfilled without grace, and that the most grievous temptations could be resisted. When Augustine laboriously proved that the true love of God, to which spiritual communion with God is granted, and the very acts of charity, are gifts of the Holy Spirit, a view supported by the Third Council of Carthage, the Council of Sardica and the Council of Orange, Pelagius began to change his skin, not his mind. For he began to acknowledge grace, and by grace he understood the capacity of nature created by God, that is, a rational will. But Augustine had shown that Scripture speaks of grace of a kind that exceeds the powers of nature. So Pelagius added a supernatural grace alongside the natural, but only an external one, which he placed in the teaching of the law. Yet, severely rebuked and forced by the truth, he added a third grace, by which sins are forgiven, as a just merit and [a foundation?] for it, which he nevertheless denied was necessary for all. For he said that some lead a sinless and innocent life, while others renew themselves to repentance and restore their nature. Against this assertion the Synod of Carthage laid down in its third canon: that the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps us that we may not commit them. Thus driven from his opinion, Pelagius added a fourth grace, that of Christ, which he located in the teaching and example of Christ. For just as Adam harmed by his bad example, so Christ benefited by his good example. Antiquity continued to fight vigorously against him and drove him to acknowledge a fifth grace, the help of divine power working within man through the Holy Spirit. In this opinion, after so many twists and turns, he stopped, and he never was willing to concede more, namely that grace signifies not only the illumination of the intellect but also the determination of the will, and grace either habitual or actual added to the will. For he thought that this could not be reconciled with free will without falling into Manichaeism. So he constantly maintained that man, by the powers of his own choice and the determination of his own will, can produce spiritual good and union with God, and thus that justification is a work of nature, aided by grace in some way.

units.la: Quamvis vero multum sudârit Grotius, ut evinceret, Pelagium quintam hanc gratiam non agnovisse, ne videantur in Pelagio opiniones hujus temporis esse damnatae; tamen ex historia hoc adeo liquet, ut nemo sanus dubitare possit. Vide Gerhardum Johannem Vossium, Polyhistora incomparabilem in Historia Pelagiana. Quam exiguo vel nullo intervallo causa Socinianorum & Pontificiorum disparata sit à Veteri Pelagiana, ignorare non potest, qui τὰ ἐκ τῆς ἀπάτης ipsorum penetravit. Socinus enim praefracte negat, Scripturas nomine gratiae quidquam aliud intelligere, quam Evangelii, id est, Mysteriorum, captum naturae superantium, revelationem. In qua re quàm perniciosè erret, intelligitur Scripturas vel à limine salutantibus. Illae non correctionem tantùm intellectus gratiae Divinae tribuunt, sed praecipuè voluntatis mutationem, & potentem tractum, & donum Spiritûs, per quem vocamus Dominum Jesum, & fidem, quae Christi justitiam apprehendit & applicat.
units.tr: Although Grotius laboured hard to prove that Pelagius did not acknowledge this fifth grace, so that the opinions of our own time might not seem condemned in Pelagius, yet from history this is so clear that no sane person can doubt it. See Gerhard Johannes Vossius, the incomparable polymath, in his Historia Pelagiana. How little or no interval separates the cause of the Socinians and the Papists from the old Pelagian cause cannot be unknown to anyone who has penetrated their [deceits τὰ ἐκ τῆς ἀπάτης]. For Socinus stubbornly denies that Scripture means by the name of grace anything other than the revelation of the Gospel, that is, of mysteries that surpass the grasp of nature. How greatly he errs in this is evident even to those who greet Scripture from the threshold. Scripture ascribes to the grace of God not merely a correction of the intellect, but chiefly a change of the will, a powerful drawing, and the gift of the Spirit, through whom we call upon the Lord Jesus, and faith, which lays hold of and applies the righteousness of Christ.

units.la: Et cùm mortuus sit in peccatis totus homo, revivisecens per gratiam Dei intellectus, quomodo ad vitam excitare potest voluntatem, quae malo est immortua? Corruptio carnis, ad subjiciendum dum se legi Divinæ, lex peccati, quæ est in membris, hominem sub mancipans, cor lapideum, incircumcisum, homo vetus, homo animalis, cor ἀσύνετον, arbor mala, satis superque arguunt voluntatis impotentiam, quæ justificationis jus nunquam attingere potis est. Pontificii nomine Gratiæ Dei infusas qualitates, justificationem producentes intelligunt. Thomas, qui in hac de Gratia doctrina cæteris senior est, distinguit inter gratiam gratis datam, & gratos facientem. Ad illam refert omnia dona Spiritualia, creatas seu infusas virtutes. Hanc dicit esse, quæ peccatores, suâ naturâ ingratos, Deo gratos acceptosque reddit. Ac sanè plausum nostrum Subtilissimus Doctor caperet, si hujus Gratiæ nomine intelligeret solum Dei favorem, quem ipse etiam acceptationem vocat. Nam revera quod nos gratos & acceptos facit Deo, est gratia Dei in Christo, & favor ac acceptatio Dei. Verùm, quia ad extremum hanc gratiam gratum facientem interpretatur qualitates quasdam in nobis à Deo per Spiritum suum creatas, ut est virtus Fidei, Spei, Charitatis, Regenerationis, & contendit iis nos justificari, immane quantum à veritatis janua abluit. Quærit: an hæc gratum faciens, sicut revera aliquid ponit in Deo acceptante, aliquid etiam ponat in acceptato? Quam quæstionem concludit intolerabilibus verbis: Hæc bona, vitam scilicet æternam, Deus non vult alteri indigno. Ergo Deus vult digno. Ergo cessat gratia, cui assurrexisse videbatur. Sed digno datur, inquit Thomas, qui dignus est dono supernaturali, infusa virtute. Minimè verò, inquam. Nam nulla creata virtus dignos nos tanto bono efficere poterit, nedum quæ est in nos collata. Inficitur enim contagione quicquid boni in nos à Deo instillatur. Præterea manifesti sunt Pontificii concordiæ cum Pelagio in doctrina de Gratia contractæ. Nam, singula diligenter reputando, non plus tribuunt Gratiæ, quàm illuminationem intellectus, & talem motum voluntatis, quem non sequatur necessariò & determinatè, ut revera non aliud sit, quàm invitatio, adhortatio, moralis suasio, & suavis motio ad actum supernaturaliter bonum. Quid hîc animadvertere possumus, quo à Pelagiana Pontificiorum causa discernatur? Quin communiter statuunt Scholastici hominem posse secundum legem communem usu naturalium, totam legem implendo, converti. Adeò ut Pius V. Gregorius XIII. Gregorium Ariminensem, statuentem, viribus naturæ non posse fieri ullum opus moraliter bonum, secundum omnes circumstantias, anathemate percussetit. Quicquid sit, nos constanti asseveratione tuemur, nomine illius Gratiae, qua in Scripturis dicimur justificari & servari, nihil creatum aut infusum in nos significari, sed solum Dei favorem ac benevolentiam, seu misericordiam in Christo Jesu, exclusis omnibus nostris sive naturalibus sive supernaturalibus operibus & dignitatibus. Idque quatenus est Gratia DOMINI JESU CHRISTI) Ergo gratia ab effectu justificationis & salutis excludit quicquid non est Jesus Christus, ideoque virtus & justitia infinita, qua sola noster ad thronum Dei accessus, & cum Deo communio parabilis fuit. Nam opponit hoc loco Petrus gratiam Jesu Christi jugo ἀβαστάκτῳ, quo, quia non portavimus, vivificatio dari non potuit. Ergo gratia justificans est gratia Jesu Christi, qui eadem opera Spiritum regenerationis nobis impetravit. Nempe, juxta verissimum Esajae vaticinium cap. XLIX. 4.6. impetravit Christus a Deo Patre, ut non in cassum laboraret, ad inane et vanum insumeret vim suam, sed ut haberet opere pretium apud Deum repositum: imo ut levius esset in oculis Dei, esse eum servum Dei ad erigendas tribus Israelis, daretúrque in lucem gentium, atque esset salus ejus ad finem terrae. Et Esaj. LIII. 10. 11. Dominus volentem enervare ipsum ad impotentiam redegit, hoc est, Diabolum, qui Christum oppugnabat, & calcem ejus admordebat, per ipsum destruxit; Ubi posuerit anima ejus satisfactionem, videbit semen, quod prolonget dies, & in cujus manu voluntas Domini proficiat. A labore, quem videbit anima ejus, satiabitur: in agnitione sui justus servus meus dabit justificationem multis, & peccata ipsorum ipse portabit. Id quod Apostolus breviter & ἐναργῶς tradidit Rom. V. 15. Gratia Dei, & donum in gratia unius hominis Jesu Christi in multos abundavit. Ob eam rem testatur Paulus: Nos Christo convivificatos esse, & conresuscitatos, & conlocatos in supercoelestibus in Christo Jesu, Ephes. II. 5. 6. Ergo vivificatione Christi mortui, & ejus resuscitatione & exaltatione in Caelum Deum Patrem Filio, ut jam perfecto & per passiones consummato principi salutis filiorum Dei, & sponsori pro iis adhuc in peccatis mortuis, obsignasse vivificationem & resuscitationem, & glorificationem nostri, qui jam nunc credimus, & omnium, qui crediturí sunt. Hoc significat gratia Dei, non ullum actum creaturae, propter quem acceptari mereatur. Diserte rursum Apostolus: Elegit nos, & praedestinavit ad adoptionem per Jesum Christum. ad laudem gloriæ & gratiæ ejus, in quâ nos ἐχαρίτωσεν ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, Ephes. I. 4. 5. 6. non in ulla dignitate nostra. Eadem vis hujus vocabuli, Gratia, quoties in negotio salutis nostræ nominatur? Paulus Rom. III. 24. Δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι. An gratiâ, id est, infuso habitu charitatis, contrarium habitum peccati expellentis? Constanter nego. Sed gratiâ, id est, gratuito Dei favore, exclusis sive naturalibus sive supernaturalibus nostris dignitatibus, per solam ἀπολύτρωσιν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Alias gratia non esset gratia, sed opus nostrum, quæ duo Apostolus negat cohærere posse. Neque nomine operum, quæ gratiæ opponit, ut piam intelligit Paulus externa tantum opera à lege mandata, sed omnes etiam internas virtutes, & fidem ipsam, quatenus opus est quoddam intellectûs & voluntatis; id quod manifestum est cuilibet, vel mediocriter in ea Epistola exercitato. Et Christus in hanc rem nimis apertus Luc. cap. XVII. vers. 10. Cum feceritis omnia, quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus, quia, quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Hîc omnem nostram, etiam perfectissimam obedientiam merito spoliat. Nominat omnia, quæ servi debent, & quæ imperio heri imponuntur. An tantum externa facta Deo debemus, & internis utiles Deo sumus, ut propter eorum dignitatem, favorem & acceptationem Dei mereamur? Absit insania. Hoc fortius pater ex Abrahami exemplo Rom. cap. IV. vers. 16. Justificatus est τῇ χάριτι. An gratiâ, id est, infuso supernaturali habitu? Atqui non ex operibus, ne haberet, quod coram Deo gloriaretur. Vers. 2. 4. 5. Hîc se expediat Pelagiana Schola. Justificatus non ex operibus. Quibus? Malis? At nemo unquam malis operibus justificationem tribuit. An adiaphoris? At neque de iis ulla unquam instituta disputatio. An externis, vel sine fide, & auxilio Dei factis? Atqui mala sunt opera externa, quæ non pullulant à recto affectu animi. Mala sunt, quæ sine fide fiunt. Mala, quæ sine auxilio speciali Dei. Cur disputaret Apostolus, malis operibus justificationem non deberi, quod nemo hominum animi compos asserere potuit? Restat, ut gratia Dei, quâ justificatus fuit Abraham, & omnes, qui credunt in eum, qui Jesum Dominum nostrum ex mortuis suscitavit, fuerit omni modo extra Abrahamum, & omnes fideles, in Deo, ejus favore, gratia, benevolentia, acceptatione in dilecto illo, Domino nostro Jesu Christo; quam propterea Jesajas vocat ישעיהו cap. XLII, vers. 1.
units.tr: Although the whole man is dead in sins, how can the intellect, made alive again by the grace of God, raise to life a will that is dead to good? The corruption of the flesh, which refuses to submit itself to the divine law, the law of sin that is in the members and enslaves man under it, the stony heart, the uncircumcised heart, the old man, the natural man, the heart [ἀσύνετον, senseless], the evil tree: these sufficiently and more than sufficiently prove the will's powerlessness, which can never reach the right of justification. The Papists understand by the name of the grace of God infused qualities that produce justification. Thomas, who is senior to all others in this doctrine of grace, distinguishes between grace freely given and grace making man acceptable. To the former he refers all spiritual gifts, created or infused virtues. The latter, he says, is what makes sinners, who by nature are unthankful, pleasing and acceptable to God. Indeed, that most subtle doctor would earn our applause if by the name of this grace he meant only the favour of God, which he himself also calls acceptance. For in truth what makes us pleasing and acceptable to God is the grace of God in Christ, and the favour and acceptance of God. But because at last he interprets this grace that makes us pleasing as certain qualities created in us by God through his Spirit, such as the virtues of faith, hope, charity and regeneration, and maintains that we are justified by them, he strays immeasurably far from the gate of truth. He asks whether this grace making us pleasing, just as it really posits something in God who accepts, also posits something in the one accepted. He concludes this question with intolerable words: God does not will these goods, namely eternal life, for another who is unworthy. Therefore God wills them for the worthy. Therefore grace ceases, to which it seemed to have risen. But it is given to the worthy, says Thomas, who is worthy of a supernatural gift, by an infused virtue. Not at all, I say. For no created virtue can make us worthy of so great a good, much less one that has been bestowed upon us. For whatever good is instilled into us by God is infected with contagion. Moreover, the agreement of the Papists with Pelagius in their doctrine of grace is clear. For if we weigh each point carefully, they attribute to grace no more than the illumination of the intellect and such a movement of the will as is not necessarily and definitely followed by the act, so that in truth it is nothing other than an invitation, exhortation, moral persuasion and gentle prompting to an act good in a supernatural way. What can we observe here by which the Pelagian cause of the Papists may be distinguished? Indeed the Scholastics commonly hold that man, by the common law of natural powers, can be converted by fulfilling the whole law. So much so that Pius V and Gregory XIII struck with anathema Gregory of Rimini, who held that by the powers of nature no morally good work can be done in all its circumstances. Whatever the case, we maintain with constant assertion that by the name of that grace by which we are said in the Scriptures to be justified and preserved, nothing created or infused in us is signified, but only the favour and benevolence of God, or his mercy in Christ Jesus, with all our works and dignities excluded, whether natural or supernatural. And this is so insofar as it is the grace of OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. Therefore grace, in respect of the effect of justification and salvation, excludes whatever is not Jesus Christ, and so excludes all virtue and righteousness of ours, by which alone our access to the throne of God and our communion with God were made possible. For here Peter sets the grace of Jesus Christ against the unbearable yoke [ἀβαστάκτῳ], which, since we have not borne it, could not give us life. Therefore justifying grace is the grace of Jesus Christ, who by the same work obtained for us the Spirit of regeneration. Indeed, according to the most true prophecy of Isaiah, chapter 49, verses 4 and 6, Christ obtained from God the Father that he should not labour in vain, nor spend his strength on emptiness and vanity, but that he should have his work laid up with God: indeed that it should be a lighter thing in the eyes of God that he be the servant of God to raise up the tribes of Israel, and be given as a light to the Gentiles, and that his salvation should reach to the end of the earth. And Isaiah 53, verses 10 and 11: The Lord reduced to impotence him who wished to weaken him, that is, the Devil, who attacked Christ and bit at his heel; through him he destroyed him. When his soul shall have set up satisfaction, he shall see a seed that prolongs its days, and in whose hand the will of the Lord shall prosper. He shall be satisfied from the labour which his soul shall see; by the knowledge of himself my righteous servant shall give justification to many, and he himself shall bear their sins. This the Apostle set forth briefly and clearly [ἐναργῶς] at Romans 5:15: The grace of God, and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abounded unto many. Therefore Paul testifies: that we are made alive together with Christ, raised up together, and seated together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, Ephesians 2:5, 6. Therefore, by the making alive of Christ when he was dead, and by his resurrection and exaltation into heaven, God the Father, with the Son now perfected and consummated through his sufferings as the author of salvation for the sons of God and as surety for those who are still dead in sins, has sealed the making alive, the raising up and the glorifying of us, who now believe, and of all who are going to believe. This is what the grace of God signifies, not any act of a creature on account of which he could deserve to be accepted. The Apostle again plainly: He chose us and predestined us to adoption through Jesus Christ, to the praise of the glory and grace of him, in which he made us accepted [ἐχαρίτωσεν ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ] in the beloved, Ephesians 1:4, 5, 6, not in any dignity of ours. Is the force of this word grace the same whenever it is named in the matter of our salvation? Paul, Romans 3:24: Being justified freely by his grace [Δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι]. Is it by grace, that is, by an infused habit of charity expelling the contrary habit of sin? I firmly deny it. But it is by grace, that is, by the free favour of God, with our natural and supernatural dignities excluded, through the sole redemption in Christ Jesus [ἀπολύτρωσιν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ]. Otherwise grace would not be grace but our work, and these two the Apostle denies can stand together. Nor does Paul, in the works which he sets against grace, understand merely the outward works commanded by the law, as the pious might, but also all inward virtues and faith itself, insofar as it is a certain work of the intellect and will; which is plain to anyone even moderately practised in that Epistle. And Christ is very clear on this point at Luke 17:10: When you have done all the things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants, because we have done what we ought to do. Here he rightly strips away all our obedience, even the most perfect. He names all the things that servants owe and that are imposed by the command of a master. Do we owe God only outward deeds, and are we useful to God only in our inward acts, so that on account of their worth we might deserve the favour and acceptance of God? Far be such madness. This is made plainer still from the example of Abraham, Romans 4:16: he was justified by grace [τῇ χάριτι]. Is it by grace, that is, by an infused supernatural habit? But not from works, lest he should have what to glory in before God, verses 2, 4, 5. Here the Pelagian school may show its skill: justified not from works. Which works? Evil ones? But no one has ever ascribed justification to evil works. Indifferent ones? But no dispute has ever been raised about these. Outward ones, or those done without faith and the help of God? But outward works are evil that do not spring from a right disposition of the mind. Those done without faith are evil. Those done without the special help of God are evil. Why would the Apostle dispute that justification is not owed to evil works, which no sane man could assert? It remains that the grace of God by which Abraham was justified, and all who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, must in every way be outside Abraham and all the faithful: in God, in his favour, grace, benevolence and acceptance in that beloved one, our Lord Jesus Christ; whom for this reason Isaiah calls [ישעיהו] in chapter 42, verse 1.

units.la: CREDIMUS) Fide adducitur gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Non alia sunt à parte nostra adductionis hujus & applicationis instrumenta. Est nempe fides radix salutis, cui tribuitur in S. Literis effectus unionis & communionis cum Christo, justificationis, sanctificationis, & vitæ æternæ. Hæc omnia fidei competunt, quatenus illa nos cum Christo συμφυτόὶ, complantat & συσσωμάτι-ζὶ, adcorporat, dum & promissionem ac donationem gratiæ Christi ratam & irrevocabilem facit per acceptationem, & consummat spirituale nostrum cum Christo matrimonium, & agglutinat ipsi affectus nostræ animæ, qui tanquam radius amoris repercussus vinculum illud indissolubile efficiunt. Hanc fidem efficit in nobis Spiritus Sanctus, qui fidelium corda, cùm vocantur, & adest hora salutis, ita Christo conciliat, quemadmodum naturaliter sumus affecti erga cibum, & infans erga lac maternum; ut sic bonis ejus satiari, & expleri cupiant, tandemque omissa omni σωτηλῆ, id est, animæ suæ suffugio ad aliud nomen vel præsidium in & sub Cœlo. Habac. cap.II.vers.4. Hebr.cap.X.vers.39. se & curas suas submissâ animi fiducia in Christum rejiciant. Hoc officium justificantis fidei solidè ignorant omnes justitiarii, qui legalis obedientiæ, & humanarum satisfactionum fragili vinculo illam συσσωμάτωσιν cum Christo quærunt.
units.tr: WE BELIEVE) Grace comes to us through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. On our side there are no other instruments for this bringing-in and application. Faith is the root of salvation, and Scripture ascribes to it the effects of union and communion with Christ, justification, sanctification, and eternal life. All of these belong to faith insofar as it plants us together with Christ [συμφυτόν] and joins us into one body [συσσωμάτιζει], incorporating us into him. It makes the promise and gift of Christ's grace firm and irrevocable through our acceptance, and it completes our spiritual marriage with Christ. It also joins the affections of our soul to him, and these, reflected back like a ray of love, make that bond indissoluble. The Holy Spirit works this faith in us. When the hearts of believers are called and the hour of salvation has come, he so reconciles them to Christ as we are naturally drawn to food, and an infant to its mother's milk, so that they long to be satisfied and filled with his goods. Then, setting aside all refuge [σωτηλῆ], that is, flight of the soul to any other name or protection under heaven, they cast themselves and their cares upon Christ with humble trust. Habac. cap. II, vers. 4. Hebr. cap. X, vers. 39. All the justiciaries who seek this union with Christ by the fragile bond of legal obedience and human satisfactions completely fail to understand this office of justifying faith.

units.la: NOS SALVATUM IRI) Σωθῆναι. Salus igitur est per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi.
units.tr: THAT WE SHALL BE SAVED) to be saved [Σωθῆναι]. Salvation, therefore, is through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Propter quam dulcissimum nomen Jesu Angelus ipsi induit, quia populum suum salvum faciet, Matth. cap. I. vers.21. Retinetur hoc nomen in Lingua Græca, Chaldaica, Syriaca, Arabica. Est autem hæc salus per Christum parta duplex, gratiæ nempe & gloriæ. Ad illam justificatio & sanctificatio; ad hanc glorificatio pertinet. Manifestæ sunt in hanc rem Scripturæ. Et tamen in nostra tempora reservati homines, qui hanc tam evidentem, támque clarè inculcatam veritatem de gratia Domini Jesu justificante, sanctificante & glorificante, sustinuerunt obnubilare, imò Orco sepelire. Socini gentem intelligo, quæ gratiam Jesu Christi σωτήριον negat se ad justificationem extendere, & ad Spiritum regenerantem, ac cor rude & præputiatum circumcidentem. Ergo Servatorem appellari, quia salutis æternæ viam revelavit, eandem tum vitæ suæ exemplo, tum martyrio, tum resurrectione mirificè confirmavit, & vitam æternam nobis ipsi fidem habentibus actu aliquando collaturus laturus sit. Negat ergo dare Christum nobis salutem, peccata nostra compensatione seu satisfactione delendo & expiando: de Iesu Christo Servatore lib. 1. cap. 1. Sic Schlichtingius: Christum Iesum venari, quia Dei nomine ad nos venit, foedus nobiscum pansit, ejusque promissiones ratas fore spopondit, & in se recepit, ad Hebr. VII. 22. An ergo Sponsor foederis Christus, salutis nostrae Princeps & Consummator, nihil aliud in nostri gratiam praestitit? Imo, an, qua Sacerdos, pro salutis nostrae impetratione, se Deo in Sacrificium non obtulit? Quae sunt partes, dictante Apostolo in Divina ad Hebraeos Epistola, veri Sacerdotis. Sed Sacerdotium Christi in eo consistere vult Socinus; quod ille, pro quo spopondit Christus, nempe Deus per ipsum Christum sua nobis promissa exhibeat. Christum enim, quatenus Sacerdos est, nihil magis in Caelis nunc agere, quam quod promissa Divina nobis praestet, hoc est, peccatorum poenas auferat, Divinis donis & muneribus nos cumulet, ut tandem nos Caelo asserat. Sic ergo Christus erit Sponsor pro Deo apud nos, & Sacerdos pro Deo apud homines: & cum ex hypothesi illorum sit merus homo, spondebit homo pro Deo, neque intercedet apud Deum, ut Sacerdos, sed regia potestate promissa Dei praestabit. Atqui Sacerdotis est victimam ponere pro eo, pro quo spopondit, & propter repraesentationem carnis in victimam petere haereditatem testamento scriptam, & eam justificare, ac sanctam & puram ad gloriam transmittere. Si gratia Domini Iesu, Sacerdotis nostri, non alia ratione salutem nobis impetrat, quam sub conditione obedientiae, & quidem ejus, quae Christum pro exemplari habeat, nunquam fidem facere poterit, nos assecuturos eandem gloriam, quin potius coget de salute nostra, si vere peccata nostra aestimemus, quae & admisimus, & per infirmitatem carnis admittemus, desperare. Sed mittamus detestabilem doctrinam, in qua non modica tum Samosateniani tum Pelagiani erroris veteris fibra appareret.
units.tr: For this reason the sweet name Jesus was given to him by the angel, because he will save his people, Matt. 1:21. This name is retained in the Greek, Chaldean, Syriac and Arabic languages. The salvation won through Christ is twofold, namely of grace and of glory. Justification and sanctification belong to the former, glorification to the latter. The Scriptures are plain on this matter. Yet in our times there have been men who have tried to obscure, indeed to bury in hell, this truth, so evident and so clearly taught, of the grace of the Lord Jesus which justifies, sanctifies and glorifies. I mean the Socinian sect, which denies that the grace of Jesus Christ [σωτήριον, saving] extends to justification, or to the Spirit who regenerates and circumcises the hard and uncircumcised heart. Therefore, they say, he is called Saviour because he revealed the way of eternal salvation, confirmed it wonderfully both by the example of his life, by his martyrdom and by his resurrection, and will at some time actually bestow eternal life on us who believe in him. He therefore denies that Christ gives us salvation by blotting out and atoning for our sins through compensation or satisfaction. (On Jesus Christ the Saviour, book 1, ch. 1.) Thus Schlichting: Christ Jesus comes to us because he came to us in God's name, opened a covenant with us, promised that its promises would stand, and took them upon himself, on Heb. 7:22. Is it then the case that Christ, the Surety of the covenant, the Prince and Perfecter of our salvation, performed nothing else for our benefit? Indeed, did he not, as Priest, offer himself to God as a sacrifice to obtain our salvation? These are the duties, as the Apostle says in the divine Epistle to the Hebrews, of a true priest. But Socinus wants the priesthood of Christ to consist in this: that he for whom Christ stood surety, namely God, should present his promises to us through Christ himself. For Christ, insofar as he is priest, does nothing more now in heaven than to grant us the divine promises, that is, to remove the punishments of sins, load us with divine gifts and benefits, and at last assert us to heaven. Thus Christ will be surety for God with us, and priest for God among men; and since on their hypothesis he is a mere man, he will stand surety for God as a man, and will not intercede with God as a priest, but will perform God's promises by royal power. Yet it is the office of a priest to lay down a victim for the one for whom he stood surety, and, on account of the representation of the flesh, to ask for the inheritance written in the testament, to justify it, and to send it holy and pure to glory. If the grace of the Lord Jesus, our Priest, obtains salvation for us in no other way than under the condition of obedience, and indeed of that obedience which takes Christ as its model, it can never give us certainty that we shall attain the same glory; rather, it will force us to despair of our salvation, if we truly weigh the sins we have committed and those we will commit through the weakness of the flesh. But let us dismiss this detestable doctrine, in which no small fibre of the old error of both Samosatenus and the Pelagians appears.

units.la: SICUT ET ILLI) Κάχνοι. Catechismus Rackovicnsis pag. 308. 309. Socinus lib. quod regni Poloniae, &c. cap. 5. pag. 62. Smalcius contra Francium disput. 4. de justificat. pag. 69. τὸ κάχνοι referunt ad τὸ ἔθνη, quorum meminit Petrus v. 7. 8. 9. Quia frequens fit, Relativum non ad proxime praecedens, sed paulo longinquius referri, & neutro sape relativum masculini generis jungatur, Iohan. cap. IX. vers. 22. Rom. cap. II. vers. 14. Sic eludere conantur perversi homines arguargumentum nostrum, quo probamus, Patres Veteris Testamenti Justificatos esse per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Et sanè hic locus haereticam illorum opinionem quoliber ariete fortius concundit. Nam de justificatione agitur, & idem τρόπος, idem modus justificandi declaratur tam Patres, quàm Petrum & fideles quoslibet Novi Testamenti, nempe per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi. Ergo nodum hunc simpliciter secant, non solvunt, de Gentibus sermonem esse, non de Patribus Veteris Testamenti. Atqui Socine, non Gentilium salus & justificatio est norma & causa exemplaris salutis fidelium, nec de salute Petri & fidelium in principali quaestione agitur, sed de salute Gentilium. Debuit ex mente Socini Petrus dicere: Lex non est imponenda cervici Gentilium vel discipulorum, quia etiam nos eodem modo salvabimur, quo illi. Quae hic argumenti necessitas? Imò quid facit haec oratio ad seipsum, qui potius pervertitur hoc ratiocinio, quàm tangitur? Deinde manifesta nimis est antithesis inter jugum & gratiam Jesu Christi. Jugum non portárunt Patres. Quo ergo modo justificati, quando non datur absque portatione & satisfactione relaxatio? Nempe gratia Jesu Christi, qui jugum maledictionis & chirographi suscepit, & illud in cruce portavit, portatum sustulit, atque sic nobis omnimodam libertatem acquisivit. Qui non videt particulam adversativam ἀλλὰ, negationi proximae respondere, nae ei nihil coloratum esse potest. Facessat igitur fraudulenta detorsio. Nempe revera quemadmodum in Adamo omnes moriuntur, sic in Christo omnes vivificantur, 1. Corinth. X. vers. 22. Neque est in quoquam salus extra Christum, Act. IV. vers. 12. quod ad Nov. Testam. non potest restringi, quia Apostolus eo loco urget necessitatem salutis per Christum consequendae. Deinde distertis verbis Christus dicitur redemisse τὰς ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεις illa quae erant sub primo foedere peccata, Hebr. IX. vers. 15. Quod nequit in eum sensum detorqueri, ut intelligantur peccata ejusdem generis, Christum nempe ejusmodi peccata sanguine suo redemisse, quae sacrificiis legalibus expiari non poterant. Pugnat hoc cum Apostoli scopo, qui est ostendere, sacrificium Christi necessarium esse. Nam si in Vet. Testam. peccata ullo sacrificio sunt expiata, nihil erat opus sacrificio in Novo Testamento. Sed Apostolus hoc voluit, peccata non fuisse expiata in Veteri Testamento. Itaque opus fuisse sacrificio in Novo Testamento. Alias Patres perisissent. Hinc verf. 22. dicit: Sine sanguinis effusione non esse remissionem. Posset hoc facilè refelli, si Patres sine sanguinis effusione redempti sunt. Intercessit quidem sanguis hircorum & taurorum. Sed negat Apostolus, illum potuisse purgare conscientiam, & indidem concludit, fuisse necessariam redemptionem per Christum. Imò vers. 23. dicit, necessum fuisse, ut Coelum purgetur praestantiori aliquo sacrificio. Coelum autem non ratione sui, sed ratione nostri sanctificatur. Nondum quidem Christus in Vet. Testam. homo factus est. Potuit tamen retroagi mortis Christi efficacia. Nam meritum Christi est causa moralis Justificationis, cujus haec ratio est, ut vim habere possit, cum nondum est actu, modo, ut loquuntur in Scholis, habeat esse cognitum. Cujus exempla sunt in vita quàm plurima. Nullum enim esse inter homines commercium posset, si vim promissa non haberent, nisi postquam sunt impleta.
units.tr: JUST AS THOSE TOO) [Κάχνοι]. Catechism of Racow, pp. 308, 309. Socinus, on the kingdom of Poland, ch. 5, p. 62. Smalcius against Francius, disputation 4 on justification, p. 69. They refer τὸ κάχνοι [and those] to τὸ ἔθνη [the Gentiles], which Peter mentions in vv. 7–9. Because it often happens that a relative refers not to the immediately preceding word but to something somewhat further back, and a neuter is often joined to a relative of masculine gender, John 9:22, Rom. 2:14. Thus perverse men try to evade our argument, by which we prove that the Fathers of the Old Testament were justified through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. And indeed this passage shatters their heretical opinion more forcefully than any battering ram. For it treats of justification, and the same manner, the same mode of justifying, is declared for the Fathers as for Peter and all the faithful of the New Testament, namely through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore they simply cut this knot rather than untie it, saying that the discourse is about the Gentiles, not about the Fathers of the Old Testament.
