units.tr: THAT THEY ABSTAIN FROM POLLUTIONS OF IDOLS, AND FORNICATION, AND WHAT IS STRANGLED, AND BLOOD) We shall weigh these matters somewhat more carefully at the end of the Council, on verse 29. Verse 21. FOR MOSES HAS, FROM ANCIENT TIMES, IN EVERY CITY, THOSE WHO PREACH HIM) The sentence has a reason from the occupation of the Gentiles, but the meaning itself is somewhat involved. Cornelius à Lapide interprets it as though James, by these words, were rebuking the Judaizers and bidding them mind their own affairs. For he makes him speak thus: There is no need for us Christians to be anxious about honouring Moses. Moses and the law are sufficiently honoured and celebrated by the Jews in their synagogues. Let the Jews, then, who are zealous for the honour of Moses, go to his synagogues and celebrate him there. For us Christians it is enough, in the Church, to have Christ, to whom Moses sent us (Deut. 18:18), and to celebrate His law. Cornelius ascribes the same opinion to Chrysostom. I do not know how truly. For Chrysostom wants James to give the reason why it was not necessary to write on this matter to the Jews who had embraced the faith of Christ, as it was to the Gentiles: namely,

units.la: pe quia illi sciebant, quid sui esset officii ex lege, quae in Synagoga secundum antiquam consuetudinem, singulis Sabbathis praelegebatur. Caeterum neutra interpretatio genuina videtur. Non prior. Nimis dura enim esset Jacobi sententia. Addo, hac ratione Christianos induci potuisse, ut Mosis lectionem sibi negligendam arbitrarentur. Nam Jacobus non tam de observatione rituum Judaicorum, quam de lectione Mosis loquitur. Nec posterior Chrysostomi. Nam ad quos potissimum scribendum esset, ne quidem in praecedentibus Jacobus meminerat. Cur igitur rationem redderet, cur Judaeis non esset de rebus his scribendum? Imo si hoc in animo habuisset Jacobus, rationem attulisset insufficientem, cur ad Judaeos non esset decretum Synodi perscribendum. Nam posito, ex lectione legis ipsis constitisse necessariam abstinentiam ab idolothytis, sanguine & suffocato, ex altera parte plane necessum erat scribi, quod caeterae partes ceremonialis legis nullam amplius obligandi vim habeant, adeoque illis operam dandam, ne Gentilibus illam molem non subeuntibus obstreperent, & illis obturbare pergerent. Grotius συνυποθεσιν esse dicit talem. Nempe quod ad Mosen attinet, non possent qui ex Judaeis sunt, queri, eum sperni ab alienigenis nostri gregis, quando in nostris non minus quam in Judaicis conventibus Moses, ita ut ab antiquo factum est, legitur, & quidem singulis Sabbathis. Sed obstat, quod de lectione in Concilio non fuerit actum, sed de obligatione ad observantiam Ceremoniarum. Neque enim quaestio de lectione legis agitata fuit. Curcellaeus pag. 103. refert hanc sententiam ad consilium Jacobi de scribendo ad Gentes. Nempe ideo scribendum ad Gentes, quia nisi id fieret, & declaretur, ipsos esse liberatos a rituum Legis observatione, putarent, se iis adhuc teneri, cum interessent Synagogis Judaeorum, in quibus lex Mosis, quae distincte praecipiuntur, singulis Sabbathis legi solet. Hanc interpretationem dicit sponte fluere. Flueret sane, si constaret, Mosen ab antiquis etiam inter Gentes habuisse, qui ipsum in Synagogis praedicent, quod nullo modo dici posse omnes vident. Certum est, scriptum fuisse decretum Synodi ad Gentes. Sed illis plane non quadrat illa ratio, ob quam sit scribendum, quia ab antiquis diebus Moses in Synagogis habet ipsum praedicantes etiam Gentiles. Non diffiteor sane ante captivitatem Babylonicam, & post eam, dispersis in Terrarum orbem Judaeis, etiam in Gentilium Civitatibus Synagogas fuisse, in quibus bus Moses praedicaretur. Quomodo Paulus Synagogam ingressus Antiochiae, Pisidiae, Act.XIII.14. Thessalonicae, Act.XVII.1. Beroae, Act.XVII.10. Athenis, Act.XVII.17. Ephesi, Act.XVIII.19. Sed Jacobum hoc intellexisse, cum antiquas aetates nominat, & Gentiles promiscuè has Synagogas intrandi, & Mosen praedicandi facultatem habuisse, planè vero est dissimile. Henricus Stephanus Jacobum facit ita loquentem: Moses antiquissimus Dei Propheta, vel, qui jam olim à prisciis temporibus legitur in Synagogis, omnes docet in suo Pentateucho, haec fugienda esse, in Annot. ad h.l. Sed, obsecro, an hic sensus non evertit totum Synodi decretum? An circumcisio, quam hic abrogarunt Apostoli, & tota illa νομοθεσία à Mose antiquissimo Dei Propheta, & antiquitus jam in Synagogis lecto, non fuit nomine Dei quàm severissimè mandata? Sed, inquias, Circumcisio fuit abrogata ab Apostolis, non lex de idolothytis & sanguine. Atqui rationibus Apostolorum hoc actum, ut universa lex Ceremonialis abrogaretur. Exceptio autem illorum facta, si à scortatione discesseris, non propter Mosis mandatum facta, sed propter metum scandali. Aretius in Commentario praeoccupationem esse dicit. Respondet enim, inquit, cur illa sola excipiat, reliquis omnibus damnatis Caeremoniis. Annon sic contemnitur Moses? Aboletur lex? Respondet: Non fiet. Ratio, quia Moses habet lectores suos omni Sabbatho apud Judaeos: quem ordinem non damno, legi illum volo, sed caeremonias non observari. Praeoccupationem aliquam agnosco. Non tamen, quam affert Aretius. Nam responsum non satis quadrat. Quippe simpliciter Jacobus dicit: Legi antiquitus Mosen. An deinceps legi debeat necne, minimo apice Apostolus non attingit. Theodorus Beza in Annotat. minoribus ad h.l. ita interpretatur: Fieri non posse, ut tam cito quasi uno impetu aboleantur Caeremoniae: quia jam à multis seculis assueti legis Doctrina, & Moses suos haberet praecones, ideo redimendam ad tempus breve concordiam esse, donec paulatim innotesceret clarius libertas per Christum parta. Ut sic praeoccupet Apostolus hanc objectionem: Cur caeteris mandatis Caeremonialibus abrogatis sanciant postliminio legem de Idolothytis, sanguine & suffocato? Respondet Apostolus: quia Moses ab omni tempore in suis Synagogis habet Zeloras. Ergo ut illos tantisper placemus, donec perspectam habeant libertatem Christianam, sancienda sunt mandata de sanguine & suffocato, cum illa antiquissima sint, quippe Noacho lata, ac proinde pro his sint vehementius pugnaturi : ac praeterea facilis sit horum abstinentia, neque adeo Judaismum involvant, sicut Circumcisio, & si quae talia. Haec interpretatio planissima est, & animo Apostoli plane consentanea, cum caeterae omnes, ut jam apertum fecimus, nodis & difficultatibus sint implexae.
units.tr: because they knew what their duty was from the law, which was read in the synagogue every Sabbath according to ancient custom. But neither interpretation seems genuine. Not the former: for James's sentence would be too harsh. I add that by this reasoning Christians could have been led to consider the reading of Moses as something they might neglect. For James speaks not so much of the observance of Jewish rites as of the reading of Moses. Nor is Chrysostom's view sound. For James had not even mentioned in the preceding words to whom it was chiefly to be written. Why then would he give a reason why it should not be written to the Jews? Indeed, if James had had this in mind, he would have offered an insufficient reason why the decree of the Council was not also to be written out for the Jews. For, granting that from the reading of the law the necessity of abstaining from idol-offerings, blood and what is strangled had been established for them, it was on the other hand quite necessary to write that the other parts of the ceremonial law no longer have any binding force; and therefore care had to be taken that the Gentiles, who did not undertake that burden, should not be disturbed by them, and that they should not go on troubling them. Grotius says the reason is a συνυποθεσιν [synypothesin], a supposition of this kind: Namely, as far as Moses is concerned, those who are of the Jews could not complain that he is despised by the aliens of our flock, since in our assemblies, no less than in the Jewish ones, Moses is read, as has been done from of old, and indeed every Sabbath. But it stands in the way that the reading was not discussed in the Council, but the obligation to observe the ceremonies. For the question of the reading of the law was not raised at all. Curcellaeus (p. 103) refers this opinion to James's counsel about writing to the Gentiles. Namely, it was to be written to the Gentiles because, unless this were done and declared, they would think that they were still bound to the observance of the rites of the Law when they attended the synagogues of the Jews, in which the law of Moses, which is distinctly prescribed, is usually read every Sabbath. He says this interpretation flows naturally. It would indeed flow naturally, if it were established that Moses had from ancient times been preached in the synagogues even among the Gentiles; but everyone sees that this can in no way be said. It is certain that the decree of the Council was written for the Gentiles. But that reason, for which it was to be written, does not at all fit them: because from ancient days Moses has been preached in the synagogues, even by Gentiles. I do not deny that before the Babylonian captivity, and after it, with the Jews dispersed through the whole world, there were synagogues even in the cities of the Gentiles, in which Moses was preached. So Paul entered the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:14), at Thessalonica (Acts 17:1), at Berea (Acts 17:10), at Athens (Acts 17:17), at Ephesus (Acts 18:19). But that James understood this, when he names ancient times, and that Gentiles had indiscriminately the freedom to enter these synagogues and to preach Moses, is clearly unlike the truth. Henricus Stephanus makes James speak thus: Moses, the most ancient prophet of God, or he who is read in the synagogues from of old, from the earliest times, teaches in his Pentateuch all men that these things are to be avoided, in his Annotations on this passage. But, I beg you, does not this sense overturn the whole decree of the Council? Was not circumcision, which the Apostles here set aside, and the whole of that legislation, from Moses the most ancient prophet of God, read of old in the synagogues, most strictly enjoined in the name of God? But you will say: circumcision was abrogated by the Apostles, not the law about idol-offerings and blood. Yet by the Apostles' reasoning this was done so that the whole ceremonial law might be abrogated. But the exception made for these things, if you exclude fornication, was made not on account of the command of Moses, but on account of fear of scandal. Aretius in his Commentary says it is an praeoccupatio [anticipation of an objection]. For he answers, he says, why he excepts those alone, all other ceremonies being condemned. Is not Moses thus despised? Is the law abolished? He answers: It will not be done. The reason is that Moses has his readers every Sabbath among the Jews. I do not condemn that order; I want it read, but the ceremonies not observed. I acknowledge some anticipation, but not that which Aretius brings forward. For the answer does not fit well enough. Simply, James says: Moses has been read from of old. Whether he ought to be read henceforth or not, the Apostle does not touch in the least degree. Theodore Beza, in his Smaller Annotations on this passage, interprets thus: It cannot be that the ceremonies should be abolished so quickly, as if by one onslaught; since men long accustomed to the teaching of the law, and Moses having his heralds, therefore a concord must be purchased for a short time, until the liberty won through Christ should gradually become more clearly known. So the Apostle anticipates this objection in this way: Why, with the other ceremonial commands abrogated, do they, by a return of right, ratify the law about idol-offerings, blood and what is strangled? The Apostle answers: because Moses from every age has had preachers in their synagogues. Therefore, that we may for the time being placate them, until they have a clear view of Christian liberty, the commands about blood and what is strangled are to be ratified, since these are most ancient, having been given to Noah, and therefore they will fight more vehemently for these; and moreover, abstinence from these is easy, nor do they involve Judaism to the same extent as circumcision and such like. This interpretation is most plain and quite consonant with the mind of the Apostle, since all the others, as we have already made clear, are entangled in knots and difficulties.

units.la: IN SYNAGOGIS UBI PER OMNE SABBATHUM LEGITUR) Patet hinc, lectionem legis die Sabbathi antiquissimam esse.
units.tr: In the synagogues, where the Law is read through every Sabbath) It is clear from this that the reading of the Law on the Sabbath day is very ancient.

units.la: Hebraei dicunt, a Mose introductam, & post captivitatem a Nehemia reductam illam consuetudinem. R. Maimonides in Jad Chazakath tract. de precibus & benedictione Sacerdotum cap. 13. [Hebrew text: המנהג הפשוט בכל ישראל ממשלימין את התורה בשנת אחת מתחלין בשנת שאחר הג הסוכות יקוּרין בסרך בראשית בשרייה אלא תולדות בשלישית ויאמר יה אל אברהם וקוראו והולכין על הסדר הזה עד שגומרין את התורה בח הסוכות ויאמר מי שמשלי את התורה בשלש שנים ואינו מנהג פשוט]
units.tr: The Hebrews say that this custom was introduced by Moses and restored after the captivity by Nehemiah. R. Maimonides, in Jad Chazakath, tract. on prayers and the priestly blessing, chapter 13: "The common practice throughout all Israel is that they finish the Torah within one year. They begin in the year after the Feast of Tabernacles, reading in order from 'In the beginning' (Bereshit), then 'These are the generations' (Toledot), then 'And the LORD said to Abraham' (Vayomer), and they proceed in this order until they finish the Torah on the eighth day of Tabernacles. Whoever completes the Torah in three years does not follow the common practice." [המנהג הפשוט בכל ישראל ממשלימין את התורה בשנת אחת מתחלין בשנת שאחר הג הסוכות יקוּרין בסרך בראשית בשרייה אלא תולדות בשלישית ויאמר יה אל אברהם וקוראו והולכין על הסדר הזה עד שגומרין את התורה בח הסוכות ויאמר מי שמשלי את התורה בשלש שנים ואינו מנהג פשוט]

units.la: Consuetudo est apud omnes Israelitas communis atque recepta, ut legem anno absolvant, incipientes a sequenti post festum tabernaculorum Sabbatho. Quo die legunt Sectionem primam Geneseos, In Principio creavit Deus &c. Secundo post Sabbatho legunt; Haec sunt generationes &c. Genes. VI.9. Tertio deinde: & dixit Deus ad Abraham. Hoc ordine deinceps procedunt in lectione legis, donec legem in festo tabernaculorum absolverint. Sunt qui legem tribus annis absolvunt. Sed non est haec consuetudo communis. Religiosissime hanc consuetudinem custodi-verunt. Cum Trajanus Imperator decrevisset, ne Judaei in Synagogis legem legerent, quod ante ipsum alii etiam Imperatores fecerant, maximae afflictionis loco hoc deputarunt. Proinde R. Jacuth numerat inter [Hebrew: שמדות] persecutiones, cum ait: [Hebrew: גזר שמד שלא] [Hebrew: קראו בתורה] Decrevit persecutionem, ne Judaei lectitarent legem.
units.tr: It is the custom among all Israelites, common and accepted, to complete the Law in a year, beginning with the Sabbath after the Feast of Tabernacles. On that day they read the first section of Genesis, "In the beginning God created," etc. On the second Sabbath after that they read, "These are the generations," etc., Genesis 6:9. Third, then, "And God said to Abraham." They proceed in this order in the reading of the Law until they finish the Law at the Feast of Tabernacles. Some complete the Law in three years, but this is not the common custom. They have kept this custom with the greatest devotion. When the Emperor Trajan decreed that the Jews should not read the Law in the synagogues, as some other emperors had done before him, they counted this among the greatest afflictions. Accordingly R. Jacuth, counting among the [שמדות] persecutions, says: [גזר שמד שלא קראו בתורה] He decreed a persecution, that the Jews should not read the Law.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: Chapter XII.

units.la: Epistola Synodica explicatur. Ecclesiam, id est, fideles promiscuos à cura rerum Ecclesiasticarum non esse arcendam. Sententia Ecclesiæ Gallicæ. Iudas Barsabas. Silas quis fuerit? Ejus elogium, Ἀναστελάζειν ψυχὴν. Exponere animam suam, qualis locutio? Psal. CXIX. 109. explicatur. Qua ratione Synodus Spiritus sententiam cognoverit? Valenburgii ad partes vocati. Disquiritur, cur Apostoli dicant: Visum est Spiritui Sancto ET NOBIS. Ἔπιταγαὶ distinctæ à συγγνώμαις. Rationibus septem probatur, Pontificios ex v.28. infallibilitatem Ecclesiæ in Scripturarum interpretatione præposterè concludere. Ex eodem versu Conciliorum infallibilitatem perperam confici, ostenditur quatuor argumentis. Libertas ab onere legis consideratur vel in jure vel in praxi. Quid de circumcisione Æthiopum statui debeat, dispicitur. Scaligeri & Franzii sententia rejicitur. Verba: ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων explicata. De iis sententia Salmasii, Stephani, Grotii, Cloppenburgii. Disputatur contra Bellarminum ex v.29. concludentem, Ecclesiam habere potestatem νομοθετικὴν. Exceptiones Bellarm. octo producuntur, & solvuntur. Idolothyta. Ἀλισγήματα. Βωμολόχα. Probatur, idolothytorum esum suâ naturâ non esse illicitum vel malum. Factum Antiochenorum & Constantinopolitanorum, quos Iulianus ad Idolothyta pellicere conatus. Augustini responsio ad casum à Publicola motum. Quid per sanguinem intellexerint Apostoli? Defenditur contra Curcellæum recepta in Codicibus vox πνικτῶν. Anquiritur, quid nomine πορνείας Apostoli intellexerint? Mantissa verborum: Quae sibi fieri non velint, alteri ne fecerint.
units.tr: The Synodal Letter is explained. The Church, that is, the faithful without distinction, is not to be shut out from the care of Church affairs. The view of the Gallican Church. Judas Barsabas. Who was Silas? His commendation, Ἀναστελάζειν ψυχήν [to expose one's soul]. What kind of expression is "to expose one's soul"? Psalm 119:109 is explained. By what reasoning did the Synod know the mind of the Spirit? The Valenburgii were called in as parties. It is asked why the Apostles say: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit AND TO US." The distinct meanings of ἐπιταγαί [commands] and συγγνῶμαι [concessions]. By seven reasons it is shown that the Papists wrongly conclude from verse 28 the infallibility of the Church in interpreting Scripture. From the same verse the infallibility of Councils is wrongly inferred, as is shown by four arguments. Freedom from the burden of the law is considered either in law or in practice. What should be decided about the circumcision of the Ethiopians is examined. The opinion of Scaliger and Franz is rejected. The words ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων [to abstain from things offered to idols] are explained. On these the views of Salmasius, Stephanus, Grotius and Cloppenburg are given. It is argued against Bellarmine, who from verse 29 concludes that the Church has a legislative power [νομοθετικὴν ἐξουσίαν]. Eight objections of Bellarmine are set out and answered. Idol-offerings. The ἀλισγήματα [pollutions]. The βωμολόχα [buffooneries]. It is proved that eating idol-offerings is not in its own nature unlawful or evil. The case of the Antiochenes and Constantinopolitans, whom Julian tried to entice to idol-offerings. Augustine's answer to the case raised by Publicola. What did the Apostles mean by "blood"? The reading πνικτῶν [things strangled], found in the manuscripts, is defended against Curcellaeus. It is asked what the Apostles meant by the word "fornication." A appendix of words: "What they do not wish done to themselves, they should not do to another."

units.la: Schikhardus refellitur, qui sentit, Apostolos praecepta Noachidarum imperasse.
units.tr: Schickhardt is refuted, who thinks the Apostles enjoined the precepts of the sons of Noah.

units.la: SIc Conciliares sententias Apostolorum illustravimus. Restat consilium de scribendo ad Antiochenos decreto Synodico, & Epistola ipsa, in qua decretum Synodicum conceptis verbis expressum. Pertexit Lucas versibus octo sequentibus.
units.tr: Thus we have explained the conciliar judgments of the Apostles. There remains the plan for writing to the Antiochenes the synodal decree, and the letter itself, in which the synodal decree is stated in express words. Luke goes on in the following eight verses.

units.la: 22. Τότε ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἐκλεξαμένους ἄνδρας ἐξ αὐτῶν πέμψαι εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν σὺν τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ Βαρνάβᾳ. Ἰούδαν, τὸν ἐπικαλούμενον Βαρσαβᾶν, καὶ Σίλαν, ἄνδρας ἡγουμένους ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.
units.tr: 22. Then it seemed good to the Apostles and the elders, with the whole Church, to choose men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brethren. [Τότε ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἐκλεξαμένους ἄνδρας ἐξ αὐτῶν πέμψαι εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν σὺν τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ Βαρνάβᾳ. Ἰούδαν, τὸν ἐπικαλούμενον Βαρσαβᾶν, καὶ Σίλαν, ἄνδρας ἡγουμένους ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.]

units.la: 23. Γράψαντες διὰ χειρὸς αὐτῶν τάδε. Οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι, καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί, τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Ἀντιόχειαν καὶ Συρίαν, καὶ Κιλικίαν, ἀδελφοῖς τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν χαίρειν.
units.tr: 23. Writing by their hand as follows: The Apostles and the elders and the brethren, to the brethren from among the Gentiles who are in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. [Γράψαντες διὰ χειρὸς αὐτῶν τάδε. Οἱ Ἀπόστολοι καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι, καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοί, τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Ἀντιόχειαν καὶ Συρίαν, καὶ Κιλικίαν, ἀδελφοῖς τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν χαίρειν.]

units.la: 24. Ἐπειδὴ ἠκούσαμεν, ὅτι τινὲς ἐξ ἡμῶν ἐξελθόντες ἐτάραξαν ὑμᾶς λόγοις, ἀνασκευάζοντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν, λέγοντες περιτέμνεσθαι, καὶ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον, οἷς οὐ διεστειλάμεθα.
units.tr: 24. Since we have heard that some who went out from among us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, telling you to be circumcised and to keep the law, to whom we gave no such instruction. [Ἐπειδὴ ἠκούσαμεν, ὅτι τινὲς ἐξ ἡμῶν ἐξελθόντες ἐτάραξαν ὑμᾶς λόγοις, ἀνασκευάζοντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν, λέγοντες περιτέμνεσθαι, καὶ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον, οἷς οὐ διεστειλάμεθα.]

units.la: 25. Ἔδωξεν ἡμῖν γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδὸν, ἐκλεξαμένους ἄνδρας πέμψαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς σὺν τοῖς ἀγαπητοῖς ἡμῶν Βαρνάβᾳ καὶ Παύλῳ.
units.tr: 25. It seemed good to us, being gathered together with one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul. [Ἔδωξεν ἡμῖν γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδὸν, ἐκλεξαμένους ἄνδρας πέμψαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς σὺν τοῖς ἀγαπητοῖς ἡμῶν Βαρνάβᾳ καὶ Παύλῳ.]

units.la: 26. Ἀνθρώποις παραδεδωκόσι τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
units.tr: 26. Men who have given up their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Ἀνθρώποις παραδεδωκόσι τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.]

units.la: 27. Ἀπεστείλαμεν οὖν Ἰούδαν καὶ Σίλαν, καὶ αὐτοὺς διὰ λόγου ἀπαγγέλλοντας τὰ αὐτά.
units.tr: 27. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will also tell you the same things by word of mouth. [Ἀπεστείλαμεν οὖν Ἰούδαν καὶ Σίλαν, καὶ αὐτοὺς διὰ λόγου ἀπαγγέλλοντας τὰ αὐτά.]

units.la: 22. Tunc visum est Apostolis, & Presbyteris, & toti Ecclesiae, delectos ex sese viros mittere Antiochiam, cum Paulo & Barnaba, Judae cognomento Barsabam & Silae, viros primarios inter Fratres.
units.tr: 22. Then it seemed good to the Apostles and the Presbyters, and to the whole Church, to send chosen men from among themselves to Antioch, with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, men of standing among the brethren.

units.la: 23. Mittentes per manus eorum haec scripta: Apostoli Presbyteri, & Fratres, his, qui sunt Antiochia, & in Syria & in Cilicia, Fratribus, qui sunt ex Gentibus, salutem.
units.tr: 23. Sending by their hands these writings: The Apostles, Presbyters and Brethren, to those at Antioch, and in Syria and Cilicia, the brethren who are of the Gentiles, greeting.

units.la: 24. Quoniam audivimus, quod quidam e nobis egressi, turbaverunt vos verbis, labefactantes animas vestras, jubentes vos circumcidi & servare legem, quibus non mandaveramus.
units.tr: 24. Since we have heard that certain persons from among us, going out, have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, bidding you be circumcised and keep the law, to whom we gave no command.

units.la: 25. Visum est nobis unanimiter congregatis delectos viros mittere ad vos, cum dilectis nostris Barnaba & Paulo.
units.tr: 25. It seemed good to us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul.

units.la: 26. Hominibus, qui exposuerunt animas suas pro nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi.
units.tr: 26. To men who have exposed their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: 27. Misimus igitur Judam & Silam, qui & ipsi verbis referant eadem.
units.tr: 27. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves also report the same things by word of mouth.

units.la: 28. Ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος, πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων.
units.tr: 28. For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things. [Ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος, πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων.]

units.la: 29. Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνικτῶν, καὶ πορνείας· ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς, εὖ πράξετε. Ἔρρωσθε.
units.tr: 29. That you abstain from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; keeping yourselves from which, you will do well. Farewell. [Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων, καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνικτῶν, καὶ πορνείας· ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς, εὖ πράξετε. Ἔρρωσθε.]

units.la: 28. Visum est enim Spiritui Sancto, & nobis, nequid amplius imponeremus vobis oneris, quàm haec necessaria.
units.tr: 28. For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, to impose on you no greater burden than these necessary things.

units.la: 29. Videlicet, ut abstineatis ab his, quae sunt immolata simulachris, & sanguine, & suffocato, & scortatione, à quibus si conservaveritis vosmet ipsos, bene facietis. Valete.
units.tr: 29. Namely, that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.

units.la: Versus XXII. TUNC VISUM EST APOSTOLIS ET PRESBYTERIS) Conclusò Synodi decreto, restabat, ut in notitiam pertingeret eorum, quorum in gratiam haec omnis suscepta deliberatio est. Ergo unanimi consensu deligunt, quos cum mandatis ad Antiochenos mitterent.
units.tr: Verse 22. THEN IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE APOSTLES AND THE PRESBYTERS. Once the decree of the Synod was concluded, it remained that it should come to the knowledge of those for whose sake this whole deliberation had been undertaken. So, by unanimous consent, they chose men whom they might send to the Antiochenes with their instructions.

units.la: ET TOTI ECCLESIÆ) Ergo suæ etiam partes Ecclesiæ fuerunt, non tantùm Episcoporum, Presbyterorum & Ecclesiæ Antistitum consensu & judicio decretum conditum, & ad Ecclesias missum. Unde patet Ecclesiam à rerum Ecclesiasticarum moderatione non esse removendam ad muta subsellia, in quibus sedentariam assentiendi & obediendi necessitatem tantùm perpetiatur. Quod factum à longo satis tempore in Hierarchico Papatu, qui in hunc finem Clericos à Laicis distinxit, & hac distinctione illorum detestabilem superbiam & dominationem; horum deplorandam in rebus divinis securitatem & neglectum strenuè fovet.
units.tr: AND TO THE WHOLE CHURCH. So the Church too had its part: the decree was framed and sent to the churches not only by the consent and judgment of the bishops, presbyters and leaders of the Church. Hence it is plain that the Church is not to be removed from the management of Church affairs and sent to silent benches, where it endures only the sedentary necessity of assenting and obeying. This has been done for a long time now in the hierarchical Papacy, which, to this end, distinguished clergy from laity, and by this distinction vigorously fosters the detestable pride and domination of the former and the deplorable complacency and neglect of the latter in divine matters.

units.la: Quanquam profectò contraria planè & e diametro opposita est Ecclesiarum Gallicanarum doctrina, quae, teste Edmundo Richerio, Syndico Collegii Theologici Parisiensis, libro de Ecclesiastica potestate, constanter asserunt, totam Jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam primariò & essentialiter Ecclesiæ convenire: Romano Pontifici & aliis Episcopis instrumentaliter, ministerialiter, & quoad executionem tantùm, sicut facultas videndi primariò & essentialiter convenit homini, instrumentaliter & quoad executionem oculo. Nos, ut eorum non ferimus ἀναρχίαν, qui Ecclesiæ Prophetas subjiciunt, & regimen Ecclesiæ democraticum inducunt, sic tyrannidem Pontificiam in deturbandis à negotiis Ecclesiasticis, quos vocant, Laicis non patimur, sed inter infamem utrumque scopulum navigamus. Liquidò enim constat, in summis Ecclesiæ negotiis, etiam plebi non unctæ dignationem habiram. Quæ major in Ecclesia Apostolica actio suscipi potuit, quàm determinatio quæstionis de justificatione, in qua est fidei acropolis? Et tamen, præsentibus ipsis Apostolis, quorum in summo fastigio authoritas fuit, etiam plebs ad consultandi munus advocata. Neque se expedit Jesuita Cornelius à Lapide, Ecclesiam decretum non condidisse, sed ab Apostolis conditum probâsse & sparsisse. Unde Epistolam nomine Apostolorum fuisse scriptam, & in ea ipsos locutos, non Ecclesiam. Equidem temere hoc & ab omni ratione imparatus asserit. Nam in inscriptione Epistolæ, in verbis: Ἀπόστολοι, καὶ πρεσβύτεροι, καὶ ἀδελφοὶ &c. Quid disertius esse potest? Qui illi Fratres ab Apostolis & à Presbyteris distincti? Utique Ecclesia, quæ ad missionem Apostolorum paulò suprà consenserat. Atqui illi Fratres in Epistola loquuntur æquè atque Apostoli & Presbyteri. Etiam illis ἔδοξε τοῖς ἔθνεσι, gentiles ab onere legis liberari debere.
units.tr: Yet the doctrine of the Gallican Churches is plainly contrary and diametrically opposed to this. According to Edmund Richer, syndic of the Parisian Theological College, in his book on ecclesiastical power, they constantly assert that the whole ecclesiastical jurisdiction belongs primarily and essentially to the Church, while it belongs to the Roman Pontiff and the other bishops only instrumentally, ministerially and as to execution, just as the power of seeing belongs primarily and essentially to a man, but to the eye only instrumentally and as to execution. We do not tolerate the anarchy of those who subject the prophets of the Church and introduce a democratic government of the Church, any more than we tolerate the Papal tyranny that thrusts from Church affairs those whom they call laity; rather we sail between the two infamous rocks. For it is clear that in the highest affairs of the Church even the common people, not anointed, have had a place of honour. What greater business could be undertaken in the Apostolic Church than the settling of the question of justification, in which lies the citadel of faith? And yet, with the Apostles themselves present, whose authority stood at the summit, the common people too were summoned to the office of deliberation. Nor does the Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide help himself by saying that the Church did not make the decree but that it was made by the Apostles and the Church only approved and spread it, so that the letter was written in the name of the Apostles, and it was they who spoke in it, not the Church. Indeed he asserts this rashly and without any reasoning to support it. For in the inscription of the letter, in the words Apostles, and presbyters, and brethren, etc., what could be more explicit? Who are those brethren, distinguished from the Apostles and from the presbyters? Surely it is the Church, which had consented a little above to the sending of the Apostles. Yet those brethren speak in the letter just as the Apostles and presbyters do. Also to them it seemed good [ἔδοξε τοῖς ἔθνεσι] that the Gentiles ought to be freed from the burden of the law.

units.la: DELECTOS EX SE VIROS MITTERE ANTIOCHIAM CUM PAULO & BARNABA)
units.tr: CHOOSING MEN FROM THEIR OWN NUMBER TO SEND TO ANTIOCH WITH PAUL AND BARNABAS

units.la: Paulus & Barnabas, cùm contra Zelotas steterint, & quæstionem controversam ventilandam ipsi proposuerint, non remittuntur soli, ne ipsis solida fides non habeatur. Ergo juxta illos deligunt viros, qui cum mandatis Concilii Paulum & Barnabam comitarentur, quò fideli sua narratione, saltem æmulis cavillandi facultatem excuterent.
units.tr: Since Paul and Barnabas had taken a stand against the Zealots and had themselves put the disputed question up for discussion, they were not sent alone, lest their sound faith be held in doubt. Accordingly, in agreement with them, the Council chose men who would accompany Paul and Barnabas with the Council's instructions, so that by a faithful account of the matter they might at least deprive their rivals of any opportunity to carp.

units.la: JUDAM COGNOMENTO BARSABAM)
units.tr: JUDAS SURNAMED BARSABBAS

units.la: Josephus Ant. I. 23. vocatur etiam Barsabas. Forte ejus Frater fuit hic Judas. Cæterum Barsabas idem est quod Filius Sabæ; sicut Barabbas idem quod Filius Abbæ, Bartimæus idem quod Filius Timæi; Barjona idem quod filius Jona. Utrum verò Saabas in nomine Barsabæ sit proprium, an appellativum, incertum est. Pagninus in Nomin. Hebr. facit appellativum, ut Barsabas dicatur Filius juramenti, sicut Bersebe puteus juramenti.
units.tr: Josephus (Ant. I. 23.) also calls him Barsabas. Perhaps this Judas was his brother. Barsabas means the same as "son of Saba", just as Barabbas means "son of Abba", Bartimaeus "son of Timaeus", and Barjona "son of Jona". Whether Saabas in the name Barsabas is a proper name or a common noun is uncertain. Pagninus, in his Hebrew Names, makes it a common noun, so that Barsabas means "son of the oath", as Beersheba means "well of the oath".

units.la: ET SILAM)
units.tr: AND SILAS

units.la: Silas Apostolum significat, inquit Hieronymus Epist. 143. Ubi eundem esse censet cum comite S. Pauli, Silvano, 2. Cor. I. 19. Nam & hunc Silam comitem fuisse Pauli apparet ex v. 40. & cap. XVI. 19. XVIII. 4. In Martyrologio Romano adscriptus est Catalogo Sanctorum die 13. Julii, ubi Silæ hæc elogia dantur: In Macedonia B. Sila, qui cùm esset de primis fratribus, & ab Apostolis ad Ecclesias Gentium unà cum Paulo & Barnaba destinatus, prædicationis officium gratia Dei plenum instanter consummavit, atque in passionibus suis Christum clarificans postmodum requievit.
units.tr: Jerome (Ep. 143) says that Silas signifies an apostle. He thinks it is the same man as Silvanus, the companion of St Paul (2 Cor. 1:19). It also appears that this Silas was Paul's companion, from verse 40 and chapters XVI. 19, XVIII. 4. In the Roman Martyrology he is entered in the Catalogue of Saints on 13 July, where the following praise is given to Silas: In Macedonia, Blessed Silas, who, being one of the first brethren and sent by the Apostles to the churches of the Gentiles together with Paul and Barnabas, zealously completed the office of preaching, full of the grace of God, and afterwards, bearing witness to Christ in his sufferings, rested.

units.la: VIROS PRIMARIOS INTER FRATRES) ἡγούμενοι, præeminentes & quasi duces cæterorum. Ita Pagninus. Syrus גברא רבריא Viros Principales inter Fratres.
units.tr: LEADING MEN AMONG THE BRETHREN: (hēgoumenoi [ἡγούμενοι]), the outstanding men and, as it were, leaders of the others. So Pagninus. The Syriac has gabra rabrayya, "principal men among the brethren."

units.la: Intererat sanè mittinon ex ultima linea Viros, qui dexteritate & authoritate sua animos exulceratos sedarent, & persuaderent, controversiam in Synodo legitimè decisam esse, ac decreto & dicto Synodi audientes facerent.
units.tr: It was certainly fitting to send men who, by their skill and authority, might calm inflamed minds, persuade them that the controversy had been lawfully settled in the Synod, and make them obey the decree and the judgment of the Synod.

units.la: Versus XXIII. MITTENTES PER MANUS EORUM HÆC SCRIPTA)
units.tr: Verse 23. SENDING THIS WRITING BY THEIR HAND

units.la: Per manus eorum, id est, ministerio eorum, usitato Hebraismo. Ipsos enim scripsisse minus probabile.
units.tr: "By their hand", that is, through their ministry, a customary Hebraism. For it is less probable that they themselves wrote it.

units.la: APOSTOLI, PRESBYTERI, & FRATRES) Vulgatus Interpres: Apostoli & Presbyteri, Fratres.
units.tr: THE APOSTLES, ELDERS, AND BRETHREN. The Vulgate translator reads: the Apostles and Elders, Brethren.

units.la: Quasi epitheton Fratrum ad Apostolos & Presbyteros referri deberet. Sed particulam copulantem constanter retinent Codices, & legit etiam Syrus Interpres. Ut ne quicquam latebrarum hic esse possit Jesuitis, qui Ecclesiam, ab Apostolis & Presbyteris contradistinctam, satagunt excludere à consortio epistolam Synodicam scribentium.
units.tr: It is as if the epithet "brethren" ought to be referred to the Apostles and Elders. But the manuscripts consistently retain the connecting particle, and the Syriac translator reads it too. So there may be no hiding place here for the Jesuits, who labour to exclude from the fellowship of those writing the synodal letter the Church, which is distinguished from the Apostles and Elders.

units.la: HIS QUI SUNT ANTIOCHIÆ, & IN SYRIA & CILICIA) Has enim Ecclesias Schisma corripuit. Quare his potissimum manus medicæ applicandæ. FRATRIBUS QUI SUNT EX GENTIBUS) Olim Proselythismus inter Judæos & Gentiles fraternitatem conglutinavit. Nunc fides Abrahami imitatione expressa fratres facit etiam præputiatos. Versus XXIV. QUONIAM AUDIVIMUS, QUOD QUIDAM E NOBIS EGRESSI TURBAVERUNT VOS VERBIS) Syrus: Terruerunt vel terrorem incusserunt. LABEFACTANTES ANIMAS VESTRAS:) Ἀνασκευάζοντες. Vulgatus: Evertentes, ἀνατρέποντες. Illud contrarium est τῷ οἰκοδομεῖν, ædificare: hoc τῷ στηρίζειν confirmare. Etiam Syrus & evertentes animas vestras. Tranquillitate fruentur Gentiles in consensu Evangelii. Hanc igitur nova doctrina Pseudapostoli exercitam habent, & supra modum labefactant. JUBENTES VOS CIRCUMCIDI & SERVARE LEGEM) Vide, quæ notavimus ad versum quintum. QUIBUS NON MANDAVERAMUS) ὡς ἐ διεσεταλάμεθα. Patet inde, Pseudapostolos Apostolorum Hierosolymitanorum
units.tr: TO THOSE WHO ARE IN ANTIOCH, AND IN SYRIA AND CILICIA. For it was these churches that the schism had troubled, so the healing hand was to be applied to them chiefly. TO THE BRETHREN WHO ARE OF THE GENTILES. Formerly proselytism bound Jews and Gentiles together in brotherhood. Now faith, expressed in the imitation of Abraham, makes brethren even of the uncircumcised. Verse 24. SINCE WE HAVE HEARD THAT SOME WHO WENT OUT FROM AMONG US HAVE TROUBLED YOU WITH WORDS. The Syriac: they terrified, or struck terror. UNSETTLING YOUR SOULS: (anaskeuazontes [ἀνασκευάζοντες]). The Vulgate: subverting (evertentes [ἀνατρέποντες]). The former is the opposite of (to oikodomein [τῷ οἰκοδομεῖν]), to build up; the latter of (to stērizein [τῷ στηρίζειν]), to confirm. The Syriac also has "and overturning your souls." The Gentiles enjoy tranquillity in agreement with the Gospel. Therefore the false apostles, practised in this new doctrine, have them, and unsettle them beyond measure. COMMANDING YOU TO BE CIRCUMCISED AND KEEP THE LAW. See what we have noted at verse 5. TO WHOM WE GAVE NO SUCH COMMAND. It is clear from this that the false apostles, pretending to the authority and mandate of the Apostles of Jerusalem,

units.la: norum authoritatem & mandatum ementitos, ut Paulo & Barnabæ grandiorem invidiam conciliarent. Apud Irenæum illa verba, ὡς ἐ διεσταλκαμεν subjiciuntur post ψυχὰς ὑμῶν.
units.tr: did so in order to win greater hatred for Paul and Barnabas. In Irenaeus the words hōs ouk diestalkamen [ὡς ἐ διεσταλκαμεν] follow psychas hymōn [ψυχὰς ὑμῶν].

units.la: Versus XXV. VISUM EST NOBIS UNANIMITER CONGREGATIS, DELECTOS VIROS AD VOS MITTERE)
units.tr: Verse 25. IT SEEMED GOOD TO US, BEING GATHERED TOGETHER WITH ONE ACCORD, TO SEND CHOSEN MEN TO YOU

units.la: πεμφθέντας ὁμοθυμαδὸν, id est, consentientibus, sive communi consensu animorum coactis & idem concludentibus.
units.tr: (pemphthentas homothymadon [πεμφθέντας ὁμοθυμαδὸν]), that is, agreeing, or brought together by common consent of minds and concluding the same thing.

units.la: CUM DILECTIS NOSTRIS PAULO ET BARNABA)
units.tr: WITH OUR BELOVED PAUL AND BARNABAS

units.la: Ornant illos elogio, & singularis affectus testimonio prosequuntur.
units.tr: They honour them with a commendation and attend them with a testimony of special affection.

units.la: Versus XXVI. HOMINIBUS QUI EXPOSUERUNT ANIMAS SUAS)
units.tr: Verse 26. MEN WHO HAVE EXPOSED THEIR LIVES

units.la: Suas animas, id est, se ipsos. Confer Psal. XVI. 10. Jerem. LI. 14. Marc. XIV. 34. Act. II. 27. 31. Apud Arabes & Hebræos nihil fere usitatius. Etiam Græcos Poëtas sic loquentes adducit Gattakerus contra Pfochenium cap. X. pag. 102. 103. quem ibi consule. Significant, Viros illos nequaquam meruisse, ut neglectim à nonnullis haberentur, cum pro Ecclesia seipsos, vitam suam, vel laborando & prædicando, vel adversa quaeque sustinendo, vel moriendo devoverint. Sic Psaltes Psal. CXVIII. 109. נַפְשִׁי בְכַפִּי תָמִיד Anima mea in manibus meis semper, hoc est, ut exponit Paraphrastes Chaldæus: Anima mea periclitatur, ac si in superficie manus mea esset, id est, obvia cuilibet expositia in prædam.
units.tr: Their lives, that is, themselves. Compare Psal. 16:10, Jer. 51:14, Mark 14:34, Acts 2:27, 31. Among the Arabs and Hebrews nothing is more common. Gattaker, against Pfochen (ch. X, pp. 102-103), whom consult there, also cites Greek poets speaking in this way. These words signify that those men by no means deserved to be regarded with neglect by some, since they had devoted themselves for the Church: their lives, whether by labouring and preaching, or by enduring every adversity, or by dying. So the Psalmist says (Psal. CXVIII. 109): "My soul is in my hands always" [נַפְשִׁי בְכַפִּי תָמִיד], that is, as the Chaldee paraphrast explains: My soul is in danger, as if it were on the surface of my hand, that is, exposed as prey to anyone who meets it.

units.la: PRO NOMINE DOMINI NOSTRI JESU CHRISTI) ad gloriam virtutis, meriti, veritatis Christi manifestandam, & in universum orbem transmittendam. Versus XXVII. MISIMUS IGITUR JUDAM ET SILAM, QUI ET IPSI VERBIS REFERANT EADEM)
units.tr: FOR THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST) to make manifest the glory, merit and truth of Christ, and to send it out into the whole world. Verse 27: WE HAVE THEREFORE SENT JUDAS AND SILAS, WHO THEMSELVES SHALL TELL YOU THE SAME THINGS BY WORD OF MOUTH)

units.la: Cum publica instructione missi, ut explicent sententiam Concilii.
units.tr: Sent with a public commission, to explain the mind of the Council.

units.la: Versus XXVIII. VISUM EST ENIM SPIRITUI SANCTO ET NOBIS)
units.tr: Verse 28: FOR IT HAS SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY SPIRIT AND TO US)

units.la: Duplex igitur ac subordinata authoritas munit Conciliare decretum, Spiritus S. & Ecclesiæ. Illa summa, eminentissima, independens. Hæc inferior & à summa dependens. Unde verò δόξαν, sententiam Spiritûs S. Apostoli cognoverunt? Triplex medium videntur habuisse cognoscendæ sententiæ Spiritus Sancti. Primum est Scriptura. Nam Jacobus Apostolus ex Scriptura Amosi demonstravit, ὅτι ἐκ τῶν δεξαμένων, & probabile est, plurimas rimas alias prophetias allegasse. Quare non vatant Spiritu sopo-ris Walenburgii Fratres, qui juxta alios gregales, Exam. III. de Catholi. Princip. locum hunc obducunt ad debilitandam Scripturarum authoritatem, & Ecclesiae statuminandam potestatem. Non enim, inquiunt, dixerunt: Visum est Spiritui S. & Scripturae, vel Spiritui Sancto huic & illi revelanti. Quam improba est oppositio Spiritus & Scripturarum; vocis & loquentis; Sententiae & ejus, qui sententiam protulit! Imo decretum suum referunt ad Spiritum Sanctum, per Scripturas Amosi testantem, onus ἀβάστακτον legis non esse Gentilibus imponendum. Alterum medium fuit Testimonium Dei, quo attestatus est Gentilibus per visibilem communicationem Spiritus Prophetiae, & purificationem cordis per fidem. Hoc infallibile testimonium, quo cognosci potuit Sancti Spiritus voluntas. Ultimum medium fuit haud dubie Spiritus prophetiae, qui illos in omnem veritatem direxit, promissus a Christo Joh. XIV. Quomodo intelligi debet locus Act. XIII. 2. 4. Ministrantibus illis Domino & jejunantibus, dixit illis Spiritus Sanctus: Segregate mihi Paulum & Barnabam. Et ipsi missi a Spiritu S. abierunt Seleuciam. Dixit Spiritus Sanctus, nempe per os eorum, quibus inspiratus fuit. Haec igitur Spiritus S. authoritas summa & ἀνυπεύθυνος fuit. Accessit authoritas ὑπεύθυνος Ecclesiae: Visum Spiritui Sancto & nobis. Mirifice hic paratragoediant Bellarminus, & socii. Nempe constare hinc, Spiritus Sancti sententiam tum demum Ecclesiae probari, cum accedit Ecclesiae authoritas. Alioquin, inquiunt, quorsum attinuisset dicere: Et nobis. Atque hic idem contingere, quod in Republica, ubi edicta Regum tum demum firma ac rata sunt, cum non modo Regi sic placuit, sed accessit etiam ad Regis voluntatem decretum & approbatio Senatus. Deinde quia Concilii illius decreta dicuntur Spiritus S. decreta, colligunt etiam reliqua Ecclesiae Pontificia Concilia dotem infallibilitatis habere. Sed praepostera est utraque Conclusio, & ex recta interpretatione Verborum Concilii facili negotio discutitur. Nempe sunt alia dogmata solius Spiritus Sancti: quae sunt ἀπλαγχνα. Alia sunt dogmata fratrum, non directe obligantia, sed in generali ad evitandum scandalum, quae sunt συγγνώμη. Sic distinguit Apostolus, 1. Cor. VII. 25. De Virginibus ἐπιταγὴ Κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω. Γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι ὡς ἠλεημένος ὑπὸ Κυρίου πιστὸς εἶναι. Sic hoc loco habemus ἐπιταγὴν & mandatum Spiritus Sancti. Nul-lum lum esse imponendum onus. Hoc decretum Spiritus S. est. Sed accedit etiam γνῶμη illorum, quibus datum est à Domino fidelibus esse, qui per Spiritum charitatis & prudentiæ dirigebant conscientiam etiam in liberis, & excubantes pro salute Fratrum videbant, quid necesse esset ex præceptis morum pro conditione temporum & hominum magis inculcare. Igitur ne illorum libertas vel ad licentiam, vel ad scandalum infirmorum cederet, erat ἐπάναγκες, ut monerentur Gentiles, non concedi illis cum libertate illa πνευματικὴν, nempe in polygamia & divortiis, idolothyta, morticina & sanguinem. Hanc potestatem habent hodiéque Fratres, ut per legem charitatis & Fidei restringant libertatem, qua ad licentiam homines abutuntur. Proinde δόξα Spiritus S. pertinet ad articulum fidei & mandatum conscientiam per se obligans: Sed δόξα Congregatorum, cum dicunt: Visum est nobis: pertinet ad potestatem Ecclesiæ, quæ non eò se extendit, ut novas leges condat, vel articulos fidei quatenus à se conclusos, sub obligatione conscientiæ proponat: sed ad ordinem Ecclesiæ conservandum, & promovenda ea, quæ ad observantiam utriusque tabulæ legis inserviunt. Nihil igitur hic interpretationi Ecclesiæ infallibili, vel Conciliorum prætoriæ potestati vel scriturvel metitur. Quod magis etiam hoc argumento liquet, quia illi, quibus juxta Spiritum Sanctum δόξε, non fuerunt tantum Apostoli, sed etiam Presbyteri & Fratres, nempe Ecclesia Hierosolymitana. Hi enim omnes decretum condiderunt. Omnes decreverunt missionem ad Antiochenos. Omnes scribunt: Apostoli, Presbyteri & Fratres. Quidni igitur, si justa est in Bellarmino argumentandi ratio, fas erit concludere, non solis Episcopis, sed etiam Presbyteris & Fratribus, id est, quibuslibet Ecclesiæ membris Sacrosanctam esse infallibiliter interpretandi verba Spiritus dotem, & authoritatem Conciliorum, quibus etiam Presbyteri & Fratres quilibet Ecclesiæ ut Judices intersunt, esse infallibilem, & irrefragabilem? Neutrum, nisi fallor, illorum sensum impetrabit. Desinant ergo ficulnea hæc folia legere. Sed presfius agamus. Vellent igitur primò, Spiritus S. sententiam non esse probabilem, nisi Ecclesiæ consensione & interpretatione nobis insinuatam. Jam I. operam ludunt, nisi Ecclesiæ suæ veritatem argumentis necessariis demonstrant. Quid enim juvat operosius disceptare, & definire, quæ sint Ecclesiæ privilegia, qua potestate polleat, nisi constat, Romanam nam Ecclesiam in ea commendatione esse, ut in ea privilegia ipsi potestas competat? II. Cum testantur Apostoli sibi visum, non tantum Spiritui Sancto, respiciunt ad τὸ ἱπάνωγκες, de quibus nullum speciale acceperant à Spiritu S. praeceptum. Quae tamen conveniebat restringi, quia multum hoc inserviebat ad Christianam charitatem, ut jam ostendimus. Quid hoc ad infallibilem Scripturarum interpretationem, cui fideles ἀβαυνίσως audientiam debeant? III. Prophetiam Amosi citat Jacobus: Petrus multiplicia & realia Dei testimonia. An igitur statui potest, prophetiam illam & Dei testimonia authore Spiritu Dei praedita ante Ecclesiae authenticam propositionem non fuisse Divina? An ante hoc Concilium non fuerunt credibilia? An Petrus dubitavit de illa quaestione; an Cornelius & qui cum eo fuerunt; an Paulus, an Fratres Antiocheni, antequam Hierosolymis descenderent ad ipsos? Sed fortasse habuerunt quidem pro vera sententia de libertate Ecclesiae Christiana, sed non pro articulo credenda. Imo Apostolus testatur Gal.II.4.5. se pro ista veritate decertavisse, ut veritas Evangelii apud eos maneret. Sed concedent & hoc. Dicent propter propositionem Apostolorum authenticam fuisse rem fidei. Atqui videmus Sanctum Petrum argumentis agere Act.XI.9.15.16. Etiam tum cum Fratres cum ipso egerunt, v.2. Ita argumentis egit hoc capite v.7.8.9.10.11. etiam Paulus & Barnabas, qui narrabant opera Dei. v.12. Neque Jacobus authoritatem Petri, sed verbum Dei ejus narrationi attestans allegat v.15. IV. In verbis visum est Spiritui S. significatur εὐδοκία & θέλημα Spiritus S. Atqui absurdum est, voluntatem & beneplacitum Spiritus S. suspendere ab authentica propositione Ecclesiae, ut non sit credendum, nisi Ecclesiae approbatio accedat. V. Sed posito δόξαν Apostolorum, Presbyterorum & fidelium se extendere etiam ad illud, quod Spiritui S. visum est, nempe ad πάσαν ipsam, ad articulum fidei, nihil tamen est, quo munire se Pontificii possint. Nam alia longe fuit ratio in Apostolica hac congregatione Apostolorum, alia Pontificis, quem faciunt non os tantum sed cor etiam Ecclesiae. Quae diversitas non in eo tantum consistit, quod illi, cum fuerint os Spiritus Sancti, per quod ipse locutus est, non potuerunt mentem Spiritus Sancti non recte & procul metu erroris proponere; hic autem Spiritum Dei non habet, nec sermonem Dei in se permanentem, neque aestimat, neque commendat, neque custodit testamentum stamentum Dei; etsi vel maximè hoc faceret, tamen, quia homo, cui non promissus paracletus ille ἀλλότριος, quo solo error & tenebræ discutiuntur, à recto deflectere, & in anceps desilire potest. Sed in eo cumprimis diversitas apparet, quòd Apostoli in Concilio congregati, singulari quadam necessitate compulsi dicere debuissent: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis; quæ necessitas cùm hodie Ecclesiam non urgeat, ad illam neque formula hæc pertinet, neque ex ea colligi potest, Spiritus Sancti mentem non esse credibilem, nisi per authenticam propositionem Ecclesiæ. Nempe, cùm Paulus prædicaret libertatem à lege, adversarii ejus fideles Ecclesiarum Gentilium induxerunt, aliter sedere sententiam Apostolis principibus, qui Hierosolymis docent. Illos enim & observare legem, & observandam mandare. Hoc in Epistola Synodica disertis verbis dicitur: Quoniam audivimus, quòd quidam egressi perturbárunt vos sermonibus, quibus hoc non præscripseramus. Cùm igitur Pseudapostoli, Petri, Jacobi, Johannis authoritatem mentientur, non rationibus tantùm Synodus eos refutare necessum habuit, sed etiam professione consensus Apostolorum, quibus contrariam sententiam affinxerant. Hæc igitur peculiaris ratio est, ob quam non scribendum simpliciter fuit: Visum est Spiritui Sancto, sed etiam: Visum est nobis. Quæ ratio cùm ubique locum habeat, apparet, quàm ἀνθρωποι hoc loco militent. VI. Est eadem ratio authoritatis Ecclesiæ, quæ est ratio authoritatis paternæ, cùm hortatur Filium. Hæc autem ratio paternæ authoritatis, ut etiam, dum præscribuntur illa, quæ suo pondere, nulla extrinsecus accedente alia authoritate se commendant, tamen authoritatis ejus mentio debeat fieri. Sic igitur, cùm Filium hortatur, ut Deum timeat, præceptum hoc est ejusmodi, ut suo pondere se commendet, absque Patris authentica propositione. Attamen, quia pater est, qui hortatur, hoc est, is, cui peculiariter hoc munus incumbit, decet eum authoritatis suæ meminisse. Si itaque sic agat Pater: Deus ⁂ Te, fili, exigit Numinis timorem, & ego Pater id ipsum abs Te exigo; éstne quisquam adeò insanus, ut Patrem hoc velle putet hac locutione, ut Filius arbitretur, non esse timendum Deum, nisi quia Pater hoc præscripsit? Eadem est in nostro hoc negorio causa. Nempe ea est Ecclesiæ authoritas, ut quamvis nihil habeat, quo cogere possit seu intellectum, seu exteriorem hominem, tamen propter muneris functionem, longe longè major, quàm cuiuslibet privati, vel etiam Doctoris in Scholà docentis, & rationibus aliquid demonstrantis. Propter hanc igitur authoritatem, quæ est à munere Divinitus instituto, licet Ecclesiæ formula uti: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis. In quo si contemnitur, duplo gravius peccatur, quia non modò res ipsa contemnitur, sed & ordo, quem Deus instituit. Jam ut de altero Consectario Bellarmini brevissimè dicam, urget necessitas. Quia igitur Conciliare decretum ad Spiritum Sanctum authorem refertur, colligit Conciliorum ἀναμαρτησίαν & infallibilitatem. ὡς οὐκ ἂν respondeo. I. Expositum jam satis superque à nobis, quo sensu hoc dixerint non soli Apostoli, sed juxta Apostolos etiam Presbyteri & Fratres. Quæ si rectè attendantur, compertum habebimus, pro Conciliorum infallibilitate tam non facere, quàm quod minimè.
units.tr: The decree of the Council is therefore supported by a twofold authority, one subordinate to the other: that of the Holy Spirit and that of the Church. The first is supreme, most eminent and independent; the second is lower and depends on the first. But how did the Apostles know the opinion [δόξαν] of the Holy Spirit? There seem to have been three means of knowing the mind of the Holy Spirit. The first is Scripture. For the Apostle James proved from the Scripture of Amos that these words agree with the prophets [ὅτι ἐκ τῶν δεξαμένων], and it is probable that he cited many other prophecies. Therefore the Walenburgian brethren, who in the view of others are their fellow-sectaries, are wrong to take this passage (Exam. III, on the Catholic principles) in order to weaken the authority of the Scriptures and to strengthen the power of the Church. For they say that the Apostles did not write: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to the Scripture," or "to the Holy Spirit revealing this or that." How wicked is the opposition they set up between the Spirit and the Scriptures, between the voice and the one who speaks, between the sentence and the one who pronounced it! Rather, they refer their decree to the Holy Spirit, who through the Scriptures of Amos testifies that the unbearable [ἀβάστακτον] yoke of the law is not to be laid on the Gentiles. The second means was the testimony of God, by which he bore witness to the Gentiles through the visible communication of the Spirit of prophecy and the purification of their hearts by faith. This is an infallible testimony by which the will of the Holy Spirit could be known. The last means was undoubtedly the Spirit of prophecy, who led them into all truth, as Christ promised (John 14). How the passage Acts 13:2, 4 should be understood: While they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said to them: Separate me Barnabas and Paul. And they, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia. The Holy Spirit said, that is, through the mouths of those in whom he was breathed. This authority of the Holy Spirit was therefore supreme and accountable to no one [ἀνυπεύθυνος]. To it was added the authority of the Church, answerable [ὑπεύθυνος]: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." Bellarmine and his companions make a marvellous fuss over this. They say that the opinion of the Holy Spirit is confirmed for the Church only when the authority of the Church is added: otherwise, they say, what would be the point of saying "and to us"? The same thing happens, they claim, in the state, where the edicts of kings are firm and valid only when the decree and approval of the Senate are added to the king's will. Then, because the decrees of that Council are called decrees of the Holy Spirit, they conclude that all the other Papist councils of the Church also possess the gift of infallibility. But both conclusions are absurd, and they are easily refuted by a correct interpretation of the words of the Council. For there are some doctrines that belong to the Holy Spirit alone; these are commands [ἐπιταγαί]. Others are the judgments of the brethren, which do not bind directly but are general, to avoid giving offence; these are counsels [συγγνώμη]. The Apostle distinguishes in this way at 1 Cor. 7:25: "Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord [ἐπιταγὴν Κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω]; but I give my judgment, as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy [Γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι ὡς ἠλεημένος ὑπὸ Κυρίου πιστὸς εἶναι]." So in this passage we have a command and mandate of the Holy Spirit: that no burden is to be laid on them. That is the decree of the Holy Spirit. But there is also the judgment [γνῶμη] of those to whom the Lord gave the grace to be faithful, who by the Spirit of love and prudence guided the conscience even in matters of liberty, and who, watching over the salvation of the brethren, saw what needed to be pressed more strongly from the precepts of morals according to the circumstances of the times and of men. Therefore, lest their liberty should give way either to licence or to the scandal of the weak, it was necessary [ἐπάναγκες] that the Gentiles be warned not to use that spiritual liberty in polygamy and divorce, in eating things sacrificed to idols, in carrion and in blood. The brethren still have this power today, to restrain by the law of love and of faith the liberty which men abuse for licence. Accordingly, the opinion of the Holy Spirit pertains to an article of faith and to a command binding the conscience in itself; but the opinion of the assembled men, when they say "It has seemed good to us," pertains to the power of the Church, which does not extend so far as to make new laws, or to propose articles of faith, as concluded by itself, under obligation of conscience; it extends only to preserving the order of the Church and to promoting those things which serve the observance of both tables of the law. Nothing here, therefore, gives support to the infallible interpretation of the Church or to the judicial power of Councils, whether in the Scriptures or elsewhere. This is made even clearer by the following argument: those to whom the decision belonged according to the Holy Spirit were not only the Apostles, but also the elders and brethren, namely the Church of Jerusalem. For all of them made the decree; all sent the mission to the Antiochenes; all write: the Apostles, elders and brethren. Why then, if Bellarmine's way of arguing is sound, should it not be right to conclude that not only the bishops but also the elders and brethren, that is, any members of the Church, possess the sacrosanct gift of interpreting the words of the Spirit infallibly, and that the authority of the Councils, in which even ordinary elders and brethren take part as judges, is infallible and irrefragable? Neither conclusion, unless I am mistaken, will win their assent. Let them therefore stop picking at these fig leaves. But let us press on. First, then, they would have us think that the opinion of the Holy Spirit is not credible unless it is made known to us by the consent and interpretation of the Church. Yet they labour in vain unless they demonstrate the truth of their Church by necessary arguments. For what good is it to dispute at length and to define what the privileges of the Church are and what power it possesses, unless it is established that the Roman Church is so recommended that these privileges and this power belong to it? II. When the Apostles testify that it seemed good to them as well as to the Holy Spirit, they look to the necessary things [τὸ ἐπάναγκες], about which they had received no special command from the Holy Spirit. Yet these were fitting to be restricted, because, as we have already shown, they served greatly the Christian love. What has this to do with the infallible interpretation of the Scriptures, to which the faithful owe an unhesitating hearing? III. James cites the prophecy of Amos; Peter cites many and real testimonies of God. Can it therefore be maintained that that prophecy and those testimonies of God, endowed with the Spirit of God as their author, were not divine before the authentic proposal of the Church? Were they not credible before this Council? Did Peter doubt that question, or Cornelius and those who were with him, or Paul, or the brethren at Antioch, before they came down to them at Jerusalem? But perhaps they held the view about the liberty of the Christian Church to be true, but not as an article to be believed. Indeed, the Apostle testifies (Gal. 2:4-5) that he contended for this truth so that the truth of the gospel might remain among them. But they will concede this too, and say that the thing was a matter of faith because of the authentic proposal of the Apostles. Yet we see St Peter reasoning from arguments (Acts 11:9-15), and also when the brethren contended with him (v. 2). Likewise Paul and Barnabas reasoned from arguments in this chapter (vv. 7-11), since they were relating the works of God (v. 12). Nor does James cite the authority of Peter to confirm his account, but the word of God (v. 15). IV. In the words it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit is signified the good pleasure and will of the Holy Spirit. But it is absurd to make the will and good pleasure of the Holy Spirit depend on the authentic proposal of the Church, so that it is not to be believed unless the approval of the Church is added. V. But even granting that the opinion of the Apostles, elders and faithful extended also to what seemed good to the Holy Spirit, namely to the whole matter itself, to the article of faith, the Papists still have no support here. For the situation of this apostolic assembly of Apostles was quite different from that of the Pope, whom they make not only the mouth but also the heart of the Church. This difference does not consist only in this: that the Apostles, being the mouth of the Holy Spirit through which he himself spoke, could not fail to set forth the mind of the Holy Spirit correctly and without fear of error; whereas the Pope does not have the Spirit of God, nor does he esteem, commend or keep the Word of God abiding in himself, nor does he guard the covenant of God. Even if he did all this most fully, he would still be a man, and not the Paraclete, the Other [ἀλλότριος], whose presence alone dispels error and darkness; and so he can turn aside from the right path and leap into doubtful matters. But the difference appears above all in this: the Apostles, gathered in Council, were compelled by a particular necessity to say: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Since this necessity does not press upon the Church today, this formula does not belong to it, nor can it be inferred from it that the mind of the Holy Spirit is not credible unless it is put forward by an authentic proposal of the Church. For when Paul preached liberty from the law, his adversaries, having drawn over the faithful of the Gentile churches, maintained that the opinion of the Apostle Peter and the others who taught at Jerusalem was different. For they insisted both that the law be kept and that it be imposed. This is stated in plain words in the synodal letter: Since we have heard that certain men who went out from us have troubled you with words, to whom we gave no such instruction. Since, then, these false apostles lied about the authority of Peter, James and John, the Synod was obliged to refute them not only by arguments but also by the public profession of agreement of the Apostles, to whom they had falsely attributed the opposite view. This, then, is the special reason why it was not enough simply to write: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit, but also: It has seemed good to us. Since this reason applies everywhere, it is evident how far from the truth the men of this place are fighting. VI. The authority of the Church rests on the same basis as the authority of a father when he exhorts his son. This basis of paternal authority is such that, even when those things are prescribed which commend themselves by their own weight, with no other authority added from outside, nevertheless mention of his authority ought to be made. So, when a father exhorts his son to fear God, this precept is of such a kind that it commends itself by its own weight, apart from any authentic proposal by the father. Still, because it is the father who exhorts, that is, the one on whom this office especially falls, it is fitting that he remember his authority. If a father should therefore speak thus: "God requires, my son, the fear of the Divine Majesty, and I, your father, require this of you as well," would anyone be so mad as to think that the father means by these words that the son should believe God is not to be feared unless the father has prescribed it? The same reasoning applies in our present matter. The authority of the Church is such that, although it has nothing by which it can compel either the understanding or the outward man, nevertheless, because of the function it performs, it is far greater than that of any private person, or even of a teacher in a school who demonstrates something by arguments. On account of this authority, which comes from an office divinely instituted, it is lawful for the Church to use the formula: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. If this is despised, the sin is doubly grave, because not only the thing itself is despised but also the order which God instituted. Now, to deal briefly with the second corollary of Bellarmine, the matter is urgent. Because the decree of the Council is referred to the Holy Spirit as its author, he infers the sinlessness and infallibility of Councils. My answer is: ὡς οὐκ ἂν [as would not]. I. It has already been explained at sufficient length, by us, in what sense not only the Apostles but also, following the Apostles, the elders and brethren said this. If these things are rightly considered, we shall find that they favour the infallibility of Councils as little as anything could, that is, not at all.

units.la: II. Non cohæret ulla ratione dogma, ut si Hierosolymitani Concilii decreta fuerunt Spiritus Sancti, talia sint etiam necessariò Concilia sequentium temporum. Nam ut ex eo, quod Apostolis etiam seorsim existentibus, prærogativa infallibilitatis in doctrina est indulta, nemo colligat; idem privilegium omnibus Pastoribus, etiam seorsim existentibus esse concessum: sic nemo ex eo, quod Apostolis simul existentibus concessum est, ut ne errarint, colliget, Pastoribus legitimis in unum congregatis concessum esse, ut ne errent.
units.tr: II. The doctrine does not hold together in any way: if the decrees of the Jerusalem council were from the Holy Spirit, it does not follow that councils of later times must be of the same kind. For just as no one infers, from the fact that the prerogative of infallibility in teaching was granted to the Apostles even when they were existing separately, that the same privilege was granted to all ministers even when they exist separately, so no one will infer, from the fact that it was granted to the Apostles while they existed together that they should not err, that it has been granted to lawful ministers gathered into one body that they should not err.

units.la: III. Si Concilia legitima sint, & pro indeclinabili norma habeant συγκατάθεσιν divinæ voluntatis, ibi exstantem, ubi liquido exstare constat, non intercedimus, quo minus dicantur infallibilia, semotis omnibus illis, quæ ad errorem ducunt. Sed legitima Concilia, ut notum est, dicuntur vel ea, in quibus celebrandis ritus externi observantur: vel ea, quibus nihil deest, non modò quoad formam extrinsecam, sed etiam quoad ea, quæ Deus intrinsecus requirit. Talia Concilia, sine fuco & fallacia congregata in nomine Christi, lubenter fatemur non posse errare in iis, quæ sunt alicujus momenti. Sed quænam illa Concilia sint, non inde constare dicimus, quòd vel in hoc vel illo coetu congregentur, qui pro peculio Dei se vendi tant; sed ex ipsis Concilii decretis, juxta illud: Probate Spiritus, an sint ex Deo? Nam ut congregatio aliqua instituatur, & simulet se habere Spiritum & Signacula veritatis, & Apostolicas virtutes, tam fieri potest facilè, quàm quælibet alia res sterili aliquo imitamento exprimi & simulari potest. Quamobrem judicamus, hominí aliquí prudentí prudenti, & animæ suæ consulenti, id operam dandum, ut cor ejus confirmetur gratiâ ex Scriptura per demonstrationem Spiritus Sancti ad conscientiam, & deinde, quod in Conciliis actum dictumve, recognoscere & examinare. IV. Quæ autem à longo tempore celebrata in Papali coetu Concilia, ita sanè agitata sunt, & Spiritu Papæ directa, ut potius conscriptis Patribus hac formulâ Conciliaria decreta obsignanda fuerint: Visum Spiritui Papæ & nobis. Sanè in famosa illa Tridenti habita Synodo, qui res Romanas familiariùs noverant, dixêre, omnia dogmata Romæ jam antè conscripta jussu Pontificis ad legatos suo tempore missa, ut præscriptum illud atque formulam in differendo Theologi sequantur. Nam ex iis complures, ac Episcopos quoque multos alere ibi Pontifices, & ridiculo proverbio dici solitum: Spiritum Sanctum subinde Româ Tridentum venire inclusum manticæ. Propterea nimirum, quòd crebrò Pontifex & celeribus equis, quod fieri voluit, per literas atque mandata suis ibi Legatis mandârit. Vide Sleidanum lib. XXII. Dúdithius Quinquecclesiensis Episcopus, Orator Cæsareus, declarat in Epistola ad Maximilianum Cæsarem, quid factum sit Tridenti. Verba sunt: Nihil habuit cum illorum conventu Spiritus S. commercii, omnia erant humana consilia, quæ immediea & sanè quam pudenda Pontificum dominatione consumebantur. Illinc responsa, tanquam Delphis aut Dodona expectabantur: illinc nimirum Spiritus ille Sanctus, quem suis Conciliis præesse jactant, tabellariis manticis inclusus mittebatur: quî, quod admodum ridiculum est, cùm aliquando, ut fit, aquâ pluviis exarescebant, non antè advolare poterat, quàm inundationes desedissent, ita fiebat, ut Spiritus non super aquas, ut in Genesi, sed secus aquas ferretur. O persensosame & singularem dementiam! Ratum nihil esse poterat, quod Episcopi, tanquam plebs, scisicerent, nisi Papa auctor foret.
units.tr: III. If councils are lawful, and have as their unswerving rule the agreement [συγκατάθεσιν] of the divine will, which is present there where it is clearly known to be present, we do not object to their being called infallible, all those things that lead to error being set aside. But lawful councils, as is well known, are those in which the external rites are observed in their holding, or those which lack nothing, not only as to the outward form but also as to those things which God requires inwardly. Such councils, gathered without pretence or deceit in the name of Christ, we gladly grant cannot err in matters of some importance. But we say that what councils these are does not become evident from the fact that they meet in this or that assembly, which claim to be sold to God's possession, but from the decrees of the councils themselves, according to that saying: Test the spirits, whether they are of God? For it is as easy for some assembly to be set up and to pretend to have the Spirit and the seals of truth and Apostolic virtues, as it is for any other thing to be expressed and counterfeited by some barren imitation. Wherefore we judge that any prudent man who cares for his soul must take care that his heart be confirmed by grace, from Scripture, through the demonstration of the Holy Spirit to the conscience, and only then recognise and examine what was done or said in the councils. IV. As for the councils which for a long time have been held in the Papal assembly, they have indeed been so managed and directed by the spirit of the Pope that the conciliar decrees were rather to be sealed with this formula, the Fathers having been written out: It has seemed good to the Spirit of the Pope and to us. Certainly in that notorious synod held at Trent, those who knew Roman affairs more intimately said that all the dogmas had already been drawn up at Rome beforehand, by the Pope's command, and sent to his legates at the proper time, so that the theologians might follow that prescribed formula and wording in their debates. For several of them, and many bishops too, were kept there by the popes, and there was a ridiculous proverb commonly used: that the Holy Spirit was from time to time brought from Rome to Trent, shut up in a mail-bag. This was, no doubt, because the Pope often sent by swift horses, through letters and commands to his legates there, whatever he wished to be done. See Sleidanus, book XXII. Dudithius, Bishop of Pécs and imperial envoy, sets out in a letter to the Emperor Maximilian what was done at Trent. His words are: The Holy Spirit had no dealings at all with that assembly; all were human counsels, which were consumed by the immediate and truly shameful domination of the Popes. From there answers were awaited as if from Delphi or Dodona; from there, no doubt, that so-called Holy Spirit, which they boast presides over their councils, was sent, shut up in mail-bags by couriers. And so it happened, which is quite ridiculous, that when at times, as happens, the waters had dried up from lack of rain, he could not fly there until the floods had subsided; so it came about that the Spirit was carried not over the waters, as in Genesis, but beside the waters. O mad and singular folly! Nothing could be valid which the bishops, like the common people, had decided, unless the Pope was its author.

units.la: NE QUID AMPLIUS IMPONEREMUS VOBIS ONERIS) Hoc decretum consentaneum est verbis tum Petri: non esse tentandum Deum, ut imponatur jugum super cervices discipulorum; tum Jacobi: non esse obturbandum iis, qui ex Gentibus convertuntur.
units.tr: THAT WE LAY NO MORE BURDEN ON YOU. This decree agrees with the words both of Peter, that God should not be tempted by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples, and of James, that those who are converted from the Gentiles should not be troubled.

units.la: Sic abrogant universam legis molem, quâ fuit gratiæ Jesu Christi contraria, ac præcipuè servitutem illam in dogmatis de circumcisione, Sacrificiis, Festis, neomeniis, &c. Cæterum libertas illa Christianorum, consiliari debet vel in conscientiæ jure, vel in praxi secundum conscientiam. Conscientiæ jus situm est in fidei {Greek}ἀντιφωνία, qua Christianus credit, sibi non esse ultra a Deo positam legem illam, quae olim erat veteri Ecclesiae posita, quia propter praesentem Christum cessat significatio temporis futuri, nec ritibus Legalibus ultra commodari potest absque Antichristiano mendacio, Christum non venisse, nec mortuum fuisse, sed venturum & morituram. Praxis autem ista libertatis accurate loquendo, non est fi-ta in illa ἀδιαφορία, qua quis pro re nata possit vivere vel Ἰουδαϊκῶς vel ἑλληνικῶς. Sed distinguendum tamen hoc loco inter praxin illam libertatis, cui intercessit servitutis aliquod temperamentum, a charitate Christiana. Horum, qui propter Zelotarum conscientiam aliquo se libertatis usu multabant, & inter praxin libertatis Christianae liberrimam & plenissimam. Haec suam temporis plenitudinem & ἀκμὴν habuit sub Templi & urbis Sanctae excidium, quando Judaei sunt facti Dei quod ad Evangelium inimici propter Ethnicos, Rom. cap.XI.vers.28. Qua plenissima praxi libertatis nihil quicquam observatur rituum hujusmodi, ac vitatur observatio tanquam res mortua & mortifera. Ex quo liquet, quid de Circumcisione Æthiopum, quam jam antiquitus receptam constanter retinent, sit sentiendum.
units.tr: Thus they abolish the whole mass of the law, which was contrary to the grace of Jesus Christ, and especially that bondage in matters of circumcision, sacrifices, feasts, new moons, and so on. Moreover, that liberty of Christians must be considered either in the right of conscience or in practice according to conscience. The right of conscience rests on the full assurance of faith [πληροφορία], by which the Christian believes that that law which was once laid upon the old Church by God is no longer laid upon him, because, on account of the present Christ, the signification of the time to come has ceased, and the legal rites can no longer be employed without Antichristian falsehood, namely the claim that Christ has not come, nor died, but will come and die. The practice of this liberty, however, strictly speaking, does not consist in that indifference [ἀδιαφορία], by which a man might live, as circumstances require, either as a Jew [Ἰουδαϊκῶς] or as a Greek [ἑλληνικῶς]. Yet here one must distinguish between that practice of liberty, to which some moderation of servitude was added, and Christian charity. Of these, the one who for the sake of the conscience of the Zealots used to restrain himself by some use of liberty, and the most free and full practice of Christian liberty. This practice reached its full time and peak [ἀκμὴν] at the destruction of the Temple and the holy city, when the Jews became enemies of God as regards the Gospel, on account of the Gentiles, Rom. chap. XI, vers. 28. In this most full practice of liberty nothing of such rites is observed, and their observance is avoided as a dead and deadly thing. From this it is clear what must be thought about the circumcision of the Ethiopians, which they have constantly retained since it was received in ancient times.

units.la: Josephus Scaliger de Emendat. Temp. lib. VII. pag. 111.640. Cum ex veteri consuetudine, inquit, circumciderentur Æthiopes, teste Herodoto & aliis Veteribus Scriptoribus, tamen accepto Christianismo, praeputia ex illa consuetudine ad hunc usque diem ponunt. Neque tamen ad illud coguntur ulla lege aut religione. Quare falso eos in hoc Ἰουδαΐζειν quidam hodierni scriptores tradiderunt. Addit alium ritum. Sed cum omnes Æthiopes, tam Christiani quam Muhamedani et Idololatra quoque, pueris omnibus a partu statim venas κροταφίτιδας cauterio inurere solent, quod eo facto a cerebri destillationibus sese tueantur, quidam inter illos superstitiosi hoc in religionem verterunt, & cum puer baptizatur, simul illi vena temporalis inurantur, & acceptum illud tempus ei rei faciendae diligere Deo sese credunt. Etiam Damianus a Goes, libro de moribus & fide Æthiopum, scribit; Moris esse Æthiopibus, ut cum baptismo conjungant circumcisionem masculorum & foemellarum, non quidem necessitate Sacramentali, sed politico tantum pretextu, ut hac nota discernantur tanquam filii credentis Abrahae a caeteris nationibus. Franzius in Schola Sacrific. Disp. IX. th. 70. negat damnandam illorum superstitionem, modo imperitis, & tales declarationes non intelligentibus nec attendentibus, nullum scandalum prabeatur apud vicinas [illegible, ~12 letters]us & exteras alias Ecclesias.
