Nos, pace rogata Incomparabilis Scaliger, damnandam illorum superstitionem in circumcisionis negotio, quicquid de caeteris illorum Ceremoniis, quas idem Scaliger & Osiorius lib. IX. rer. Em. tradunt, fiat, censemus, quia Ἀλλ' ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε Apostolus edicit: Ecce ego Paulus dico vobis: Si circumcidamini, Christus vobis nihil profuturum, Gal. V. 2. Ad τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν illam respondet Paulus: Eos, qui ex fide sunt, esse Filios Abrahae, Gal. III. 7. Et Genealogia illa secundum carnem ex Abrahamo, olim quidem fuit ἐθνος ... τῆς Ἰσραήλ, praerogativa aliqua populi Judaici. Sed postquam rami naturales defracti sunt, & aliae nationes praeter naturam insitae, nefas est Christianis in consanguinitate Abrahami secundum carnem gloriari. Hinc Apostolus: Nos posthac neminem novimus secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius novimus, 2. Cor. V. 16. Quae cognitio Christi & aliorum secundum carnem significat, non fidem incarnationis Christi, sed Fidei hoc κατὰ σάρκα, quo veteri Judaico more in carnali cognatione cum Messia, & Genealogia Patrum collocatur praeeminentia. Quod est contra canonem Jacobi, vetantis, ne habeamus fidem gloriae Domini nostri Jesu Christi ἐν προσωπολημψίαις. Jac. II. 1.
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger, On the Emendation of Times, book VII, p. 111.640: Although the Ethiopians were circumcised by ancient custom, as Herodotus and other ancient writers attest, nevertheless, having received Christianity, they have laid aside the foreskin in accordance with that custom down to the present day. Nor are they compelled to it by any law or religion. Wherefore some modern writers have wrongly reported that they Judaize in this. He adds another rite. But since all Ethiopians, Christians as well as Muhammadans and idolaters too, are accustomed to brand the temporal veins [κροταφίτιδας] of all boys with a cautery straight from birth, so that by this means they may protect themselves from discharges of the brain, some of them, being superstitious, have turned this into a religious matter, and when a boy is baptised, the temporal vein is branded at the same time, and they believe that the time received is suitable for doing this to please God. Damianus a Goes also writes, in his book on the customs and faith of the Ethiopians: It is the custom of the Ethiopians to join circumcision of males and females to baptism, not indeed from sacramental necessity, but only from a political pretext, so that by this mark they may be distinguished, as children of believing Abraham, from other nations. Franzius, in Schola Sacrifica, Disp. IX, th. 70, denies that their superstition is to be condemned, provided that no scandal is given to the imperfect, who do not understand or attend to such declarations, among neighbouring [illegible] and foreign other churches. We, with due respect to the incomparable Scaliger, judge that the superstition of those people in the matter of circumcision is to be condemned, whatever may be done about their other ceremonies, which the same Scaliger and Osorius, book IX of the Rerum Emanuelis, relate; because the Apostle lays down: Behold, I, Paul, say to you: If you are circumcised [Ἀλλ' ἐὰν περιτέμνησθε], Christ will profit you nothing, Gal. V. 2. To the promise [τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν] Paul replies: Those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham, Gal. III. 7. And that genealogy according to the flesh from Abraham was once indeed a nation... of Israel [ἐθνος ... τῆς Ἰσραήλ], some prerogative of the Jewish people. But after the natural branches were broken off, and other nations were grafted in contrary to nature, it is wrong for Christians to boast of kinship with Abraham according to the flesh. Hence the Apostle: From now on we know no one according to the flesh; yet even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him so, 2 Cor. V. 16. That knowledge of Christ and of others according to the flesh [κατὰ σάρκα] signifies not faith in the incarnation of Christ, but a faith of this kind, by which, in the old Jewish manner, pre-eminence is placed in carnal kinship with the Messiah and in the genealogy of the Fathers. This is against the canon of James, forbidding us to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory in respect of persons [ἐν προσωπολημψίαις], Jas. II. 1.

units.la: QUAM HAEC NECESSARIA) ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐπαναγκῶν τῶν.
units.tr: HOW THESE THINGS WERE NECESSARY) but of those things that are necessary [ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐπαναγκῶν τῶν]

units.la: Insolentia phrasews Virum caeterà ὀξυδερκέστατον, Claud. Salmasium perpulit, ut corruptum hunc locum scriberet, lib. de Fœnore Trapezitico pag. 440. Omnino, inquit, in Graecis legendum ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐπ' ἀνάγκης τῶν, non, ut vulgo est, ἐπάναγκες. Quod in hac constructione omnino Graecum non est, nec fieri potest. Ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἀνάγκης ἔχω, necesse habeo. Graeci dicunt, qui & ἐπάναγκες ἔχω possunt dicere: sed hic, ut Syntaxis hujus loci est, non convenit. Quae conjectura docta est, & locum haberet, nisi constans esset Codicum in contrarium lectio. Caeterum quod ad vocem ἐπάναγκες, Stephanus in Thesauro adnotat, esse nomen indeclinabile, non semper adverbialiter poni. Grotius docet, esse vocem pure Graecam, & apud Demosthenem & Plutarchum de iis rebus dici, quas lege fieri oportet, atque subaudiri ὄντων. Non dubito, quin Grotius ea respexerit loca, quae ex Demosthene & Plutarcho citavit Stephanus, & de iis omnino rebus dicta, quas lege fieri oportet. Sed & illud dubitationem habet, cur voce ἐπάναγκες Lucas usus sit ad ea, quae tamen admodum diversos necessitatis gradus habent. Nam abstinentiam à scortatione moraliter necessarium esse, certum est. Abstinentiam à cæteris vel præcepto positivo, non purè moralì, quod Curcellæus sustinet, vel propter scandalum, ut nobis videtur, necessariam esse non minùs in confesso est. Johannes Cloppenburgius in Schola Sacrificiorum pag. 181. nodum sic solvit: Vox Graeca ἐπάναγκες (quæ adverbium est, positum loco nominis, ut ἀναγκαῖον, ἀνάγκης & similia) non significat, si animadvertas, necessitatem absque consignificatione analogiæ ejusmodi, quâ, si cuncta dicas necessaria esse, subintelligitur tamen necessitatis imparitas, ut cuncta non sint ἀπλῶς necessaria. Prepositio enim ἐπὶ in compositione plurima vocabula ita modificat, ut non rerum significatarum τὸ ἁπλῶς exprimant semper, sed etiam solàm cum re significata vicinitatem aut affinitatem: qualia sunt ἐπιχαμῶ, nubilis, nuptiis vicina, ἐπιπαρθ. partui vicina, ἐπιθανὴς vel ἐπιθνᾴσκος morti vicinus, ἐπιτάξ opinabilis, ἐπιλευκὸς aliquantum densus, ἐπιξανθὸς leviter flavus, & similia. Quidni similiter ἐπάναγκες quasi aut propemodum necessarium: ut quamvis unum ex quatuor necessariis sit ἀπλῶς necessarium, à potiori numero tamen cuncta dicantur tantùm quasi necessaria. Digna sanè Doctissimi Viri crisis, quæ in numerum perveniat. Quam utut Curcellæus carpat, nihil tamen affert, quo possit vel leviter infringi. Nam si verum est, quod agnoscit, ἐπὶ passim in compositione hanc vim habere, quid obstet, quo minùs etiam huic loco ea significatio aptetur vel à potioribus, quæ sequuntur, vel ab omnibus, si πορνείαν non simpliciter fornicationem interpreteris? Bellarminus in rem suam vertit necessariam illam abstinentiam, ab Apostolis mandatam. Nempe de necessariis illis nihil præcepisse Christum, sed Apostolos novas has leges protulisse. Ergo Ecclesiam posse leges condere, quæ conscientiam obligent. Etiam Walenburgii Fratres Controv. VIII. Num. XI. hoc rextu pugnant, pertendentes: Posse Ecclesiam ex plenitudine potestatis & proprio motu leges præscribere, & ex re indifferenti necessariam facere. Dicam paucis, quo acquiescere possint, quibus mens læva non est. I. Agnoscimus Ecclesiam legum condendarum potestatem habere, quæ Divinæ sunt & conscientiam obligant, non ratione materiæ, sed ratione finis, quia inserviunt pietati, charitati, & rectæ observantiæ legum moralium. II. Negamus, in Ecclesia esse potestatem quandam αὐτοκρατορικὴν & νομοθετικὴν, ἀρχὴν & Βασιλείαν hominum, propter quam aliis liceat leges condere, dummodo, ut videri volunt, nihil præcipiant mandatis Dei contrarium: aliis necesse sit propter conscientiam, tiam, & sic in judicio Dei obedire. III. Hanc potestatem tantum abest ut stabiliat Apostolicum Concilium, ut evertat etiam quàm clarissimè, cùm dicit: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis, NULLUM amplius onus imponere. Si Spiritus S. & Apostolorum sententia est, ut nullum imponatur onus Christianis, sequitur, Praepositos Ecclesiae non habere potestatem obligandi conscientiam in ulla re non scripta. IV. Quod Apostolis facere licuit, illud sequentium temporum Ecclesia temerè, quippe non datum usurpat. Nam Apostoli non tantùm in iis, in quibus ἀπαξ aliquam κρίσιν habuerunt, sed γνώμην suam duntaxat liberè expectorârunt, dicere potuerunt: Δοκῶ γὰρ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα Θεοῦ ἔχειν, 1. Cor. VII. 40. Hoc Ecclesiae nunquam praedicare licet, nisi quando se cum regula Verbi Dei conformat. V. Apostoli non ex plenitudine potestatis & proprio motu conscientiam obligârunt, nec ex re adiaphora necessariam fecerunt. Hoc patet ex Paulo, ejusdem decreti infallibili interprete, cujus auctor fuerat, & qui sibi mentis suae probè conscius esse potuit. Is sic accepit dogma Concilii, non quòd mandata haec per se ex plenitudine potestatis sancita fuerint, sed quòd necesse fuerit conscientiam alienam non verberare, & charitatis causâ in hac parte Judaeis sic Mosis verba accipientibus se ἀσθενοῦντας praebere, ut videre est 1. Cor. X. 23. 24. 25. 27. 28. 29. 32. Quae est enim causa hujus necessariae ad tempus abstinentiae? Quia Moses ab antiquis diebus in Synagogis habet, qui eum praedicent v. 22. Ergo praeceperunt non in se illicita faciendo, sed à scandalo activo eos avocando. Quae res non caruit generali mandato in Scripturis expresso. Et sanè fatentur Pontificii in universum omnes, praeceptum Apostolicum non ad semper obligâsse, sed tantùm usque ad defectum casus scandali. Quare fateantur oportet, non per se & ratione materiae haec praecepta lata ab Apostolis conscientiam obligâsse, sed tantùm ratione finis, puta scandali evitandi. Bellarminus plurima affert, quibus argumento suo fidem concilier, & nervos responsioni nostrae succidat. Operae pretium est, malè ab ipso consuta retexere. Objicit. I. Alteri se, praeceptum Apostolicum obligâsse, ratione charitatis. Non tamen obstare, quò minus dicatur etiam per se obligâsse. Ut charitas est finis legum omnium Dei, tamen praecepta ipsa particularia de non occidendo, de non furando, non obligant ad diligendum Deum, sed ad abstinendum à re & bono alieno. Respond. Nihil simile habent exempla. [?]Præcepta de non furando & non occidendo, sunt moralia, & per se obligantia. Præcepta de sanguine & idolothytis nec moralia sunt, nec per se obligantia, sed ratione scandali. Deinde præposterè Legem de non furando accepit Bellarminus, cùm negat, eam ad charitatem obligare. An qui non concupiscit bona proximi, non amat ipsum? Imò Christus omnia præcepta ad dilectionem Dei & proximi reduxit. II. Intero Apostolorum decreto, nullam fieri scandali vitandi mentionem. Respond. Per se constabat. Et interpretatur ita Apostolus priori ad Corinthios, ut vidimus. Nempe Judæi ab his rebus abstinebant ex Lege; Gentiles non abstinebant. Apostoli contra Judæos abrogant Legis onus. Judæi non serunt vescentes. Ergo Apostoli Judæorum offensioni cavent. Quis ratione usus non cernit, ob scandalum vetari? III. Nunc non servari illa præcepta, non quia ratio scandali quomodocunque cessavit, sed quia cessavit universaliter, & proinde illa lex abrogata, præsertim in occidente. Respond. Quid, malum, ambages? Si lex conscientiis posita, cur non semper obligat? Quis potestate armatus tanta fuit, ut sustineret Apostolicam constitutionem, conscientiam per se obligantem, discingere? Cessavit omnino lex universaliter. Sed quæ ratio, si non defectus scandali? IV. Nondum pervenisse decretum ad Corinthios. Imò nullo tempore ipsos hoc præceptum habuisse. Respondisse igitur illi Paulum, quod respondendum erat, secundum jus naturæ. Respond. Atqui ad omnes Ecclesias Apostolicum decretum perferri debuit. Verum non multum refert, an pervenerit, necne? Potuerunt occasione præcepti Mosaici quærere, quis ejus sit sensus. Ergo Paulus iis respondit. Quod respondit, ad illos haud dubie pervenit. An scriberet aliquid pugnans cum decreto? Imò illud declarare debuit. Hoc facit, dum constanter inter potestatem distinguit, vescendi idolothytis, & inter praxin, propter scandalum determinabilem. Omnia mihi licent, inquit, sed non omnia expediunt. V. Apostoli vocant hanc legem onus. Ergo obligavit in conscientia. Respond. Imò profitentur, se nolle imponere onus. Ergo hæc abstinentia non fuit onus. Nempe non amplius per se conscientias obligârunt, nec quisquam ex iis judicari potuit, semota violatione præcepti de diligendo proximo. Sed fuerit onus. Non ideo ligavit per se conscientiam. Nam quævis observatio, etiam in se libera, habet aliquid oneris. VI. Vocantur necessaria. Non ergo liberè, sed necessariò observanda fuerunt. Respond. Non simplex hæc necessitas fuit, sed accidentalis & hypothetica, respectu aliorum, qui infirmiores fuerunt. Necessum fuit abstinere, si periculum scandali evitare vellent. VII. Chrysostomus hanc Epistolam vocat imperium. Respond. Chrysostomus homil. 33. in Acta dicit: Hanc Epistolam non habere Epicheremata aut Syllogismos, sed imperium. Esse imperium, quis negat? Imperium esse perpetuum, ac rationes materiæ obligans, probandum est. VIII. In Canonibus Apostolorum gravissimam poenam imponi prævaricatoribus: similiter in Concilio secundo Aurelianensi. Poenam autem tam atroces non posse imponi, nisi propter mortale peccatum. Respond. Canones Apostolorum apud peritos rerum authoritatem nullam habeant. 2. Nihil tamen diversum ab Apostolis Canonum horum authores statuunt. Vetant edere κρέα ἐν τῷ αἵματι, [?]θηριαλώτου, καὶ πνικτοῦ. Eadem ratio Aurelianensis Concilii. Utique eandem poenam merentur, qui Apostolicis mandatis contravenerunt, ubi obligavit, quam illi, qui Fratris conscientiam scandalo verberârunt.
units.tr: The unusual phrasing drove Claude Salmasius, otherwise a very sharp-sighted man, to declare this passage corrupt, in his book on Trapezitic usury, p. 440. Certainly, he says, in the Greek we must read ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐπ' ἀνάγκης τῶν [but of those things that are by necessity], not, as is commonly printed, ἐπάναγκες [necessary]. But in this construction the Greek is not idiomatic at all, and cannot be. Ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἀνάγκης ἔχω [I have it by necessity] means "I have need." The Greeks say this, and they could also say ἐπάναγκες ἔχω, but neither fits the syntax of this place. The conjecture is learned and would have weight, were it not that all the manuscripts read otherwise. Stephanus, in his Thesaurus, observes that ἐπάναγκες is an indeclinable noun, not always used adverbially. Grotius teaches that it is a purely Greek word, used in Demosthenes and Plutarch of things that must be done by law, with ὄντων [of things] understood. I do not doubt that Grotius had in mind the passages from Demosthenes and Plutarch which Stephanus cited, and which speak of things that must by all means be done by law. But there is also a difficulty in why Luke used ἐπάναγκες of things that have very different degrees of necessity. For that abstention from fornication is morally necessary is certain. That abstention from the other things is necessary, either by a positive precept (not purely moral, as Curcellaeus maintains) or, as it seems to us, because of offence, is no less generally agreed. Johannes Cloppenburgius, in his Schola Sacrificiorum, p. 181, unties the knot thus: The Greek word ἐπάναγκες (which is an adverb used in place of a noun, like ἀναγκαῖον, ἀνάγκης and similar words) does not signify, if you attend closely, necessity without the kind of analogical connotation by which, even if you say that all things are necessary, a difference of necessity is nevertheless understood, so that not all things are ἀπλῶς [absolutely] necessary. For the preposition ἐπὶ, in composition, modifies many words so that they do not always express the absolute sense of the things signified, but only a nearness or affinity to the thing signified: such are ἐπιχαμῶ [nearly on the ground], nubilis [nearly marriageable, close to marriage], ἐπιπαρθ. [close to childbirth], ἐπιθανὴς or ἐπιθνᾴσκος [near death], ἐπιτάξ [conjectural], ἐπιλευκὸς [somewhat dense], ἐπιξανθὸς [slightly yellow], and similar words. Why not likewise ἐπάναγκες as meaning "almost or nearly necessary," so that, although one of the four necessary things is absolutely necessary, yet all are called necessary only in a loose sense, from the greater number? This is certainly a worthy judgement of that most learned man, and one that deserves acceptance. Although Curcellaeus carps at it, he brings nothing by which it could be even slightly shaken. For if it is true, as he admits, that ἐπὶ in composition commonly has this force, what prevents this sense from fitting this passage, either from the weightier words that follow, or from all of them, unless you interpret πορνείαν [fornication] simply as fornication? Bellarmine turns that necessary abstention, enjoined by the Apostles, to his own purpose. Namely, that Christ had commanded nothing about these necessary things, but that the Apostles had put forward these new laws. Therefore the Church can make laws which bind the conscience. The brothers Walenburg also, in their Controversies VIII, n. XI, fight on this same ground, contending: The Church can prescribe laws from the fullness of power and by its own motion, and make necessary what is in itself indifferent. I shall say briefly, for those who have a sound mind, enough to rest content. I. We acknowledge that the Church has the power of enacting laws which are divine and bind the conscience, not by reason of their matter, but by reason of their end, because they serve piety, charity and the right observance of the moral laws. II. We deny that there is in the Church any sovereign and legislative power, a principality and kingship over men, by virtue of which it may be lawful for it to make laws for others, provided, as they wish it to appear, that they command nothing contrary to God's commands, and so that others must obey for conscience' sake, and thus in the judgement of God. III. The Apostolic Council is so far from establishing this power that it overthrows it as clearly as possible, when it says: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose NO further burden. If it is the mind of the Holy Spirit and of the Apostles that no burden be laid on Christians, it follows that the leaders of the Church do not have the power of binding the conscience in any matter not written down. IV. What it was lawful for the Apostles to do, the Church of later times rashly usurps, since it was not given to it. For the Apostles, not only in those matters in which they had once given a judgement, but also when they freely put forward their opinion, could say: For I think that I too have the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 7:40). The Church may never presume to say this, except when it conforms itself to the rule of the Word of God. V. The Apostles did not bind the conscience from the fullness of power and by their own motion, nor did they make necessary what was indifferent. This is clear from Paul, the infallible interpreter of the same decree, of which he was the author, and who could be well aware of his own mind. He understood the decree of the Council thus: not that these commands were sanctioned in themselves from the fullness of power, but that it was necessary not to wound another's conscience, and for the sake of charity, in this matter, to yield to the Jews who took Moses' words in this sense, and to become weak to them, as may be seen in 1 Cor. 10:23, 24, 25, 27, 28, 29, 32. For what is the cause of this abstinence, necessary for a time? Because Moses has, from ancient days, in the synagogues, those who preach him (v. 22). Therefore they commanded not that people do unlawful things themselves, but that they keep them from active offence. This matter did not lack a general command expressed in the Scriptures. Indeed the Papists themselves confess, in general, that the apostolic precept did not bind always, but only until the occasion of offence ceased. Wherefore they must confess that these precepts issued by the Apostles did not bind the conscience of themselves and by reason of their matter, but only by reason of their end, namely the avoidance of offence. Bellarmine brings forward many arguments by which he seeks to win credit for his position and to cut the sinews of our answer. It is worth our while to unpick what he has badly stitched together. He objects: I. The Apostolic precept bound others by reason of charity. Yet this does not prevent it from being said that it also bound in itself. Just as charity is the end of all the laws of God, yet the particular precepts themselves, against murder and against theft, do not bind us to love God, but to abstain from another's thing and goods. Answer: The examples have nothing similar. [The precepts against theft and murder are moral and bind in themselves. The precepts about blood and idol-meats are neither moral nor binding in themselves, but by reason of offence.] Moreover, Bellarmine takes the law against theft the wrong way round, when he denies that it binds to charity. Does not he who does not covet his neighbour's goods love him? Indeed Christ reduced all the precepts to love of God and of neighbour. II. In the whole decree of the Apostles there is no mention of avoiding offence. Answer: This was self-evident. And Paul interprets the Apostolic decree in this way in his first letter to the Corinthians, as we have seen. Namely, the Jews abstained from these things by the Law; the Gentiles did not abstain. The Apostles, on the other hand, abrogate the burden of the Law for the Jews. The Jews do not eat the meats. Therefore the Apostles guard against giving offence to the Jews. Who, using his reason, does not see that it is forbidden on account of offence? III. Those precepts are not now kept, not because the reason of offence has ceased in any way, but because it has ceased universally, and so that law has been abrogated, especially in the West. Answer: What, in heaven's name, the circumlocution? If the law was laid on consciences, why does it not always bind? Who, armed with such power, has been so bold as to undo an apostolic constitution which binds the conscience of itself? The law has indeed ceased universally. But what is the reason, if not the lack of occasion for offence? IV. The decree had not yet reached the Corinthians. Indeed, at no time had they had this precept. Therefore Paul answered them as he had to answer, according to the law of nature. Answer: Yet the Apostolic decree ought to have been carried to all the churches. But it matters little whether it reached them or not. They could have asked, on the occasion of the Mosaic precept, what its meaning was. Therefore Paul answered them. What he answered certainly reached them. Would he write something in conflict with the decree? Rather he ought to have declared it. This he does, while he constantly distinguishes between the power of eating idol-meats and the practice, which is to be determined by the avoidance of offence. All things are lawful for me, he says, but not all things are expedient. V. The Apostles call this law a burden. Therefore it bound the conscience. Answer: On the contrary, they profess that they did not wish to impose a burden. Therefore this abstinence was not a burden. Indeed they did not bind consciences of themselves any more, and no one could be judged by them, apart from the violation of the precept to love one's neighbour. But suppose it was a burden. It does not therefore bind the conscience of itself. For any observance, even one that is free in itself, has some burden. VI. They are called necessary. Therefore they had to be observed not freely, but of necessity. Answer: This necessity was not simple, but accidental and hypothetical, with respect to others who were weaker. It was necessary to abstain, if they wished to avoid the danger of offence. VII. Chrysostom calls this Epistle a command. Answer: Chrysostom, in his thirty-third homily on the Acts, says: This Epistle does not have epicheiremata or syllogisms, but a command. Who denies that it is a command? That it is a perpetual command, and that it binds by reason of its matter, has yet to be proved. VIII. In the Canons of the Apostles the gravest penalty is imposed on transgressors; and similarly in the Second Council of Orléans. But such atrocious penalties could not be imposed except for mortal sin. Answer: The Canons of the Apostles have no authority among those skilled in these matters. 2. Yet the authors of these Canons lay down nothing different from the Apostles. They forbid eating meat with the blood, [strangled and] the flesh of animals taken by beasts, and what is strangled [κρέα ἐν τῷ αἵματι, θηριαλώτου, καὶ πνικτοῦ]. The same reasoning applies to the Council of Orléans. Surely those who have transgressed the apostolic commands, where they bind, deserve the same penalty as those who have wounded a brother's conscience by giving offence.

units.la: Versus XXIX. VIDELICET UT ABSTINEATIS AB HIS QUÆ SUNT IMMOLATA SIMULACHRIS.
units.tr: Verse 29. Namely, that you abstain from those things which have been sacrificed to idols.

units.la: Primum ergo τὸ ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων est lex de non edendis idolothytis. Idolothyta sunt, quæ idolis vel simulachris immolata. Supra vocavit ἀλισγημάτα τῶν εἰδώλων. Irenæi Interpres habet: à vanitatibus idolorum. Heinsius refert ἀλισγημα ad pollutionem non quamvis, sed quæ est in cibis, qui idolis consecrantur. Sic sanè Daniel dicitur abstinuisse cibo, ὡς ἐ μὴ ἀλισγηθῇ ne pollueretur in mensa Regis. cap. 1. 18. Et Malach. 1. 6. 7. dicitur profanari mensas Domini propter [Hebrew] ἐπὶ τὰς ἡλισγημένους, panes pollutos. Hesychius: ἀλισγημάτων τῆς μεταλήψεως μιαρῶν βρωμάτων. Nempe Gentilium communis erat cum Judæis consuetudo, ex Sacrificio partem deligere ad convivium, quod in idoleo celebratum fuit. Sic Euander & Æneas fecerunt apud Virgil. Æneid. lib. VIII. Gyraldus de Diis Gentium in fine operis ex Herodoto refert, Gentiles, qui immolabant victimas, post sacrificium ex iis μερίδας domum apportâsse, ut eas domesticis distribuerent, & ad amicos transmitterent, atque sic etiam absentes Sacrificii participes efficerent. Sed & noti sunt satis Veteres βοσκολόχοι, qui fame & egestate pleni aras circuibant, & adulando victimarum partes emendicabant, aut scurrilibus dictoriis & jocis Sacerdotes vel adstantes stantes oblectabant. Unde Philosophus excessum urbanitatis, quae scurrilitas est, βωμολοχίας nomine insignivit Ethic. IV. Et Pol. lib. 6. ὁ δὲ κάλαξ καὶ βωμολόχος ἂν λέγοιτο. Caeterum idolothytorum esus lege Moysis interdictus Exod. XXXIV. 15. Ne ineas pactum cum hominibus illarum regionum, ne cum fornicati sunt cum Diis suis, & adoraverint simulachra eorum, vocet te aliquis, ut comedas מזבחות de idolothytis ejus. Specimen severae vindictae de transgressoribus expetitae luculentum habemus Num. XXV. v. 1, 2, 3. ubi Israelitae blandis illecebris & incantamentis foeminarum Moab idolothyta ederunt, & Beelphegor immolarunt; unde Moses criminis reos contra Solem suspendi jussit. Quam historiam prolixe & pulchre narrat Josephus Antiq. Jud. IV. 6. Iisdem artibus grassatus, sed irrito successu, Julianus Apostata Christianos Constantinopolitanos per idolothytorum esum ad idololatriam seducere paravit, ut narrat Nectarius Archiepiscopus Constantinopolitanus in Orat. quam habuit initio quadrages. Cuncta, inquit, cibaria, quae venum publice in foris exposita, Sacrificiis Diis immolatis infecit ac polluit, ut sic omnes illi cogerentur vesci cibis immolaticiis, nisi fame confici vellent; cum oraculo Theodori Martyris, quonam modo consulendum esset fidelibus fame periclitantibus, fuit Divinitus demonstratum: nempe, ut tunc locupanis cotto frumento omnes uterentur in cibum. Quod ditiores pauperibus liberaliter elargiti sunt per totam hebdomadam. Quando Julianus, desperans se quod vellet perficere posse, victus Christianorum constantia & constantia, rursus puros cibos absque ulla labe in foris apponi jussit. Caeterum merito contendimus, abstinentiam illam ab idolothytorum esu necessariam fuisse, non in se, sed propter causas necessarias, quas hic Apostolus procul dubio in consilio adhibuerunt. Quibus cessantibus Christianae libertati conveniens est, ab illorum esu vel temperare vel non temperare. Nemo felicius Synodi mentem ipso Paulo, qui decretum cum caeteris Apostolis ipse etiam condidit, nobis pandet. Hunc Corinthii rogarunt: Essétne fas, idolothytis vesci, necne? Hanc quaestionem enodatum ivit tribus integris capitibus, octavo, nono, decimo, prioris ad Corinthios. Atque ita omnino agit, ut jus edendi idolothyta asserat: Sed praxin temperandam docet multas ob causas. Patet ex textu multi non contemnendis rationibus. I. Docet non edenda esse idolothyta, quia οὐκ ἐν πᾶσι γνῶσις non est in omnibus scientia, nempe idolum nihil esse in mundo, & quòd nullus sit praeterquam unus Deus, cap. VIII.4.7. Ubi igitur est γνῶσις, scientia illa, esus idolothytorum est licitus, modò non obsit metus scandali, vel συνευδοκήσεως. II. Negat, cibum nos Deo commendare. ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα, inquit, ἐὰν φάγωμεν περισσεύομεν. Οὔτε ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα, cap. VIII.8. Concedit ergo esum idolothytorum, & inter adiaphora numerat. III. Verat, ne libertas Corinthiorum circa esum idolothytorum vergat in σκάνδαλον τοῖς ἀσθενέσιν in offensionem eorum, qui sunt infirmiores, versu 9. Vindicat ergo potestatem, sed praxin moderationi subjicit propter infirmiores. Quid clarius? IV. Quia evenire potest, ut in idoleo accumbente ille, qui scientiam habet, conscientia Fratris infirmi aedificetur εἰς τὸ εἰδωλόθυτα ἐσθίειν, versu 10.11. Proinde praepostera hac praxi, quae prudentia & charitate proximi non temperatur, peccari in Fratrem, & scandalo perceli infirmam ejus conscientiam. Manifestum est, non esum idolothyti per se pullari, sed scandalum, Christianae charitati contrarium. V. Toto capite nono suo exemplo comprobat libertatem Christianorum lege prudentiae esse moderandam & coërcendam. Se Apostolum, se liberum; Se potestate pollere ad edendum, bibendum, conjugem circumducendum, stipendium exposcendum. Sed, inquit, ἐλεύθερός εἰμι ἐν πᾶσιν, πάντων ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα, liber enim sum ab omnibus, me omnibus servivi ad dixi, cap. IX. 19.20.21. Hac sua prudentia ostendit Corinthiis, ita uti illos libertate idolothytorum vescendorum oportere, ut inserviant proximo, & infirmiorum fratrum conscientiam sublevent. Quis non videt, hanc rationem in applicatione non militaturam, si Corinthiis potestas non est data, & jus idolothytis vescendi? Curcellaeus brevi responsione ad argumenta haec discutienda defungitur: Apostolum ita loqui per concessionem, propter eos, qui de scientia sua gloriabantur, & actionem fidelibus indignam, nempe quòd in idoleo cum Gentibus accumberent, hac vano praetextu defendebant: Se scire idolum nihil esse, & ab eo, quod nihil est, inquinari non posse. Quibus ita obviam it: Volo ut vos se habeatis, quemadmodum dicitis: Attamen ab istis conviviis abstinere debetis in gratiam fratrum infirmiorum, quibus periculosissimum scandalum probetis. Quod ad me attinet, longè aliter sum animatus: mallem enim abstinere in aeternum, non solum ab istis victimis, sed ab omnium carnium esu, quàm aliquod offendiculum fratri meo probere. pag. 119. Respondetur. Non infringuntur hoc responso nostrae rationes. Probandum, Apostolum ἐνγχα- ἐνλιχῶς loquutum. Quid tam longo circuitu opus esset? Duo integra capita huic rei, octavum & nonum tribuit. Neque ullum vestigium est, voluisse indirecte & per concessionem cum Corinthiis agere. Imo versl. 8. Generalis & rotunda est assertio, Corinthiorum libertatem sufficiens: Cibus vos non commendat Deo, &c. Quis cibus? An communis & vulgaris? Imo de consecrato & devoto idolis est quaestio. Non moramur igitur nudam Curcellaei thesin.
units.tr: The law of abstaining from idol-sacrifices, "to apechesthai tōn eidōlothytōn" [τὸ ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων], is the first. Idol-offerings are those things sacrificed to idols or images. Above, the apostle called them "alisgēmata tōn eidōlōn" [ἀλισγήματα τῶν εἰδώλων], the "pollutions of idols". The translator of Irenaeus renders it "from the vanities of idols" (à vanitatibus idolorum). Heinsius refers "alisgēma" [ἀλίσγημα] not to any pollution, but to that which is in the foods consecrated to idols. So Daniel is said to have abstained from food "hōs ou mē alisgēthē" [ὡς ἐ μὴ ἀλισγηθῇ], lest he be defiled at the king's table (Dan. 1:8, 18 in some reckonings). And at Mal. 1:6–7 the Lord's tables are said to be profaned by "ἐπὶ τὰς ἡλισγημένους" [epi tas hēlisgēmenous], that is, polluted bread. Hesychius explains it as "alisgēmatōn tēs metalēpseōs miarōn brōmatōn" [ἀλισγημάτων τῆς μεταλήψεως μιαρῶν βρωμάτων], the foul foods of that partaking which is polluted. Certainly it was the common custom of the Gentiles and the Jews to set aside a portion of the sacrifice for a feast, which was celebrated in the idol's temple. So Evander and Aeneas did, as Virgil relates (Aen. 8). Giraldus, in the closing part of his work On the Gods of the Gentiles, reports from Herodotus that the Gentiles who offered victims, after the sacrifice, carried home "meridas" [μερίδας], portions of them, to distribute among their households and send to friends, so that even absent people might share in the sacrifice. The ancients are also well known as "boskolochoi" [βοσκολόχοι], men full of hunger and want who went round the altars and begged for shares of the victims by flattery, or amused the priests and bystanders with buffoonish jokes and witticisms. Hence the Philosopher named the excess of wit, which is buffoonery, "bōmolochia" [βωμολοχία] (Ethics 4), and in the Politics (bk. 6) he says that such a person would be called "ho de kalax kai bōmolochos" [ὁ δὲ κάλαξ καὶ βωμολόχος], a flatterer and altar-parasite. Moreover, the eating of idol-offerings was forbidden by the law of Moses, Exod. 34:15: "Make no covenant with the inhabitants of that land, lest, when they have gone a-whoring after their gods and sacrificed to their idols, someone invite you to eat of his sacrifices [mizbechot] from the idol offerings." We have a clear example of the severe punishment demanded against transgressors in Num. 25:1–3, where the Israelites, enticed by the flattering charms and spells of the women of Moab, ate idol-offerings and sacrificed to Baal-peor; Moses therefore ordered the guilty to be hanged in the sight of the sun. Josephus tells this story at length and beautifully (Antiq. Jud. 4.6). Julian the Apostate, using the same tricks but with no success, tried to lead the Christians of Constantinople into idolatry through the eating of idol-offerings, as Nectarius, Archbishop of Constantinople, relates in the oration he delivered at the beginning of Lent. "He polluted and defiled," he says, "all the foods that were publicly displayed for sale in the markets, by sprinkling them with sacrifices offered to the gods, so that all would be compelled to eat sacrificial food unless they wished to be worn down by hunger. When the faithful were in danger of starvation, it was revealed by divine oracle through the Martyr Theodore how they should act: namely, that they should all use boiled wheat as food. The wealthier distributed it generously to the poor throughout the whole week. Then Julian, despairing that he could accomplish what he wanted, and overcome by the constancy of the Christians, ordered pure foods, without any taint, to be set out again in the markets." Moreover, we rightly contend that that abstinence from the eating of idol-offerings was necessary not in itself, but on account of the necessary causes which the apostle undoubtedly took into account in the decision. When these causes cease, it befits Christian liberty either to refrain from such eating or not to refrain. No one will explain the mind of the Synod more happily than Paul himself, who also helped frame the decree with the other apostles. The Corinthians asked him: Is it lawful to eat idol-offerings or not? He resolved this question in three whole chapters, the eighth, ninth and tenth, of his first letter to the Corinthians. And he so argues that he upholds the right to eat idol-offerings, but teaches that the practice must be restrained for many reasons. The text makes clear that there are several reasons, not to be despised. I. He teaches that idol-offerings are not to be eaten, because "ouk en pasin gnōsis" [οὐκ ἐν πᾶσι γνῶσις], not all have knowledge, namely, that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God but one (1 Cor. 8:4, 7). Therefore, where there is gnōsis [γνῶσις], that knowledge, the eating of idol-offerings is lawful, provided the fear of giving offence or of syneudokēsis [συνευδόκησις], approving by consent, does not stand in the way. II. He denies that food commends us to God: "ean mē phagōmen, hysteroumetha; ean phagōmen, perisseuomen" [ἐὰν μὴ φάγωμεν, ὑστερούμεθα· ἐὰν φάγωμεν, περισσεύομεν], "if we do not eat, we are not the worse off; if we eat, we are not the better" (1 Cor. 8:8). Therefore he concedes the eating of idol-offerings and counts it among indifferent things. III. He forbids the liberty of the Corinthians regarding the eating of idol-offerings from becoming "skandalon tois asthenesin" [σκάνδαλον τοῖς ἀσθενέσιν], a stumbling-block to those who are weaker (v. 9). He therefore claims the power, but subjects the practice to moderation for the sake of the weaker. What could be clearer? IV. Because it can happen that, when the one who has knowledge reclines at a meal in an idol's temple, the conscience of the weak brother is built up "eis to eidōlothyta esthiein" [εἰς τὸ εἰδωλόθυτα ἐσθίειν], to eat idol-offerings (vv. 10–11). Therefore by this perverse practice, which is not tempered by prudence and love for the neighbour, one sins against the brother and the weak conscience is wounded by offence. It is plain that the eating of an idol-offering is not in itself wrong, but the offence is contrary to Christian love. V. Throughout the whole ninth chapter he proves by his own example that the liberty of Christians must be moderated and restrained by the rule of prudence. He is an apostle, he is free; he has power to eat, to drink, to lead about a wife, to demand support. But, he says, "eleutheros eimi en pasin, pantōn emauton edoulōsa" [ἐλεύθερος εἰμι ἐν πᾶσιν, πάντων ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα], "for though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all" (1 Cor. 9:19–21). By this his own prudence he shows the Corinthians that they ought to use the liberty of eating idol-offerings in such a way that they serve their neighbour and relieve the conscience of weaker brothers. Who does not see that this argument would have no force in application, if the Corinthians were not given the power, and the right to eat idol-offerings? Curcellaeus dismisses these arguments in a brief reply: the apostle speaks this way by concession, on account of those who boasted of their knowledge and defended an action unworthy of the faithful, namely that they reclined with the Gentiles at an idol's temple, with the empty pretext that they knew an idol to be nothing and could not be defiled by what is nothing. The apostle meets them thus: "I want you to be as you say; yet you ought to abstain from those feasts for the sake of weaker brothers, for whom you prove the danger of offence. As for me, I am far differently disposed: for I would rather abstain forever, not only from those sacrifices but from the eating of all flesh, than cause any stumbling-block to my brother." p. 119. We reply: our arguments are not overturned by this answer. It must be proved that the apostle spoke "enchalichōs" [ἐνλιχῶς]... (ἐνγχα- ἐνλιχῶς) by concession. Why would such a long detour be needed? He gives two whole chapters, the eighth and ninth, to this matter. And there is no trace that he wished to deal with the Corinthians indirectly and by concession. Indeed, in v. 8 the assertion is general and unqualified, sufficient for the liberty of the Corinthians: "Food does not commend us to God," and so on. What food? Ordinary and common food? No, the question is about food consecrated and devoted to idols. Therefore we do not linger over Curcellaeus's bare thesis.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Apostolus capite decimo ostendit, Corinthiis illicita esse idolothyta, quae eduntur ex infidelitate & cum professione idololatriae, vel ex infirmitate fidei, vel ex typho scientiae. Si eo modo & iis circumstantiis quis comedat, v.9. in idoleo, cum peragitur Sacrificium idololatricum, ut id vel faciat ad idolorum cultum, vel in fide unici Numinis nutet, vel certe censeri possit id facere ad idolorum cultum, & comedens profiteri idololatriam, perinde atque is, qui missae Pontificiae interest, censeri potest cultu Pontificiorum captus & delectatus hoc facere. Quamobrem, inquit, Filii charissimi, fugite a cultu idolorum, versl.14. Vult dicere: Ne vel Sacrificio idola colite, vel idolothyta, id est, Sacrificia eis immolata comedite, quasi Sacra & Sacrificia, uti ea comedunt Gentiles, peracto suo Sacrificio ad aras, vel in Templis idolorum. Sic enim participaretis eorum Sacrificiis, & censeremini iis consentire, ea tacite laudare, imo & offerre. Ac deinceps gravissimis rationibus probat, idolothytorum esum in hac circumstantia, utpote idololatricum, esse homine Christiano penitus indignum. Ex quo concludo, Apostolum idolothytorum esum non facere in se & sua natura malum, & illicitum, sed ex accidenti, in tali ἐξισάσει, qua quis illorum esu idolis litat, vel dubitat de vero Deo, vel idololatris συνωνυμία, vel infirmo Fratri scandalum affert. Quis autem dubitare poterit, quin res quaelibet, etiam maxime adiaphora in talibus circumstantiis illicita fiat? Secus autem est, si quis post convivium ejusmodi idololatricum vel solus domi, vel in idoleo, idololatra vel infirmis fratribus non inspectantibus, sive fame sive cupiditate stimulante idolothytis vescatur.
units.tr: The Apostle, in chapter ten, shows that idol-offerings are unlawful for the Corinthians when they are eaten from unbelief and with a profession of idolatry, or from weakness of faith, or from the pride of knowledge. If someone eats in such a way and in such circumstances, v.9, at an idol's feast, while an idolatrous sacrifice is being performed, so as either to do it for the worship of idols, or to waver in faith in the one God, or at least can be judged to do it for the worship of idols and, by eating, to profess idolatry, just as one who attends the Papist mass can be judged to do so, captivated by and delighting in the worship of the Papists. "Therefore, dearest sons, flee from the worship of idols," v.14. His meaning is: do not worship idols by sacrifice, nor eat idol-offerings, that is, sacrifices offered to them, as if they were holy things and sacrifices, as the Gentiles eat them after finishing their sacrifice at the altars or in the temples of idols. For thus you would share in their sacrifices and be judged to agree with them, to praise them tacitly, and indeed even to offer them. He then proves by very weighty reasons that eating idol-offerings in this circumstance, as idolatrous, is utterly unworthy of a Christian. From this I conclude that the Apostle does not make the eating of idol-offerings evil and unlawful in itself and by its nature, but only accidentally, in such a condition [ἐξισάσει] in which someone by eating them sacrifices to idols, or doubts the true God, or shares the name of idolaters [συνωνυμία], or gives offence to a weak brother. Who could doubt that anything whatever, even what is most indifferent, becomes unlawful in such circumstances? It is otherwise if someone, after such an idolatrous banquet, eats idol-offerings, whether at home alone or in an idol's temple, as an idolater, or with weak brothers not looking on, driven by hunger or by inordinate desire.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: In eadem quaestione Apostolus sic loquitur: Omnia mihi licent: sed non omnia aedificant. Si quis vos vocat infidelium, quicquid vobis apponitur, comedite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Si quis autem dicat: Hoc est idolothytum; ne comedite, propter conscientiam non suam, sed alterius, v.23.27.28.29. Planum est. Apostolum declarare Christianam libertatem in esu idolothytorum, sed propter conscientiam Fratris nolle illam exerceri, ubi ejus periculo exercitium constat.VIII. Neque aliam Apostolorum fuisse mentem, colligi potest ex Cyrillo,lib.7.contra Jul. Igitur negantes omnino idola existentia, neque Diis immolatum aliquid esse dicimus. Edimus autem pura conscientia, Deo gloriam dantes, qui nobis omnium edulium liberum, & non damnosum largitus est usum. Si autem quis infirmus adhuc est, nec validam mentem habet, existimatque esse aliquid etiam vere idolothytum, nondumque progressus est ad tam sinceram fidem; indulgemus sicut quidam Ludimagistri, parvulos instituentes, paulatimque provehentes ad parvam rei experientiam. De eadem re citatur cap.39. Theodori Abucate, & responsio Arethae, nec non Petri Antiocheni epistola ad Caerularium, a Leone Allatio de Consens. Orient. & Occid. Eccl. p. m. 1170. Ipsi Antiocheni, ad quorum Majores Synodicum decretum Apostolorum suo tempore missum fuit, hoc sensu decretum facto suo sunt interpretati. Cum enim, commemorante Theodoreto Hist. Eccles. III.14. & Nicephoro X.12. Julianus Apostata primum fontes, tum qui in urbe erant, tum qui Daphnae, sceleratis victimis contaminassET, quo singuli, qui aquam gustarent, tetra nequitiae labe inficerentur: deinde ea, quae in foro venum exponebantur, eadem sceleris macula inquinaret, Christiani quidem impense ea detestabantur, tamen, inquit Theodoretus μετελάμβανον ὁμως, Ἀποστολικῶ πειθόμενοι νόμῳ. Πᾶν γὰρ, Φησι, τὸ ἐν μακέλλῳ πωλούμενον ἐσθίετε, μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν, εἰσδέμενοι ve-scuntur, legi Apostoli obsecuti, ita jubenti: Quidquid in macello venditur, comedite, nihil dijudicantes propter conscientiam. Detrectârunt quidem idem facere Christiani Constantinopolitani, de quibus supra audivimus Nectarium. Sed fecerunt in odium Juliani, & idolorum summam detestationem, non quod libertas secus faciendi, & facultas deesset. Non potuit enim Apostata cibos communes illo contactu foedare, vel Daemonibus aut idolis sacros devovere: ita, ut qui illis vesceretur, censeri posset duci religione idoli, vel idolatriam profiteri. Esto enim, intenderit hoc Apostata. Unus tamen fuit, neque potuit vel rem ipsam, vel commune hominum judicium mutare, qui censebant rem hanc non idololatricam, sed adiaphoram esse. Augustinus Epistola centesima quinquagesima quarta ad Publicolam colam scribit: Siex acervp frugum partinem aliquam idololatria simu- lachris obtuleris, aut de vino nuper in torculari expresso, id non efficiet, quin possimus liberè eo uti, quod superest tam in torculari, quàm in area, quia de fontibus & puteis aquas haurire non veremur, unde illi acceperunt, ut idolis Sacra facerent. Multa in hanc rem disputat pius Pater Paulus etiam permultos dies Athenis fuit, & procul dubio fructi- bus & proventibus Atheniensis agri vescebatur, qui tamen Minerv æ consecratus erat. Imò cum & veteres consuesserent interdum li- tare fontibus & fluminibus, quòd eis Divinitatis nescio quid attri- buerent, & ob eam causam immolatas carnes aut exta nonnun- quam in ea projicerent, dubitatum est, an postea illis aquis Christia- nis uti liceret? Respondet Augustinus, utique licere. Nam scimus, inquit, esse complures, qui Sacra faciunt Soli, non tamen ob id ejus luce uti veremur, & adspectu radiorum ejus frui. Quin & inveniuntur infide- les, qui victimas immolant ventis, & nihilominus in nostris navigationi- bus utimur. Hactenus optime Augustinus, & plane ex vero. Sed quem alium casum ipsi commemoravit Publicola, illum ita solvit, ut paulò duriùs loqui videatur. Quidam, inquit Publicola, per deserta iter faciebat, idémque vehementissimè esuriebat, & fanum sive sacel- lum idolorum obvium habebat, ubi forte fortuna quasdam carnes appositas offendebat. Quærit ex Augustino: An ei, Christianam religionem professo, licuerit edere? Respondet Augustinus: Quia potest fieri, ut carnes illa non sint immolaticia, sed ibi casu à peregrinis relictæ, qui eò diverterint, vel ad prandendum, vel ad cænandum, ideo, cùm non constet fuisse immolaticia, is qui esurit, potest ea usurpare. Deinde, quasi sibi non satisfecerit, utitur hac distinctione: Is vel certò novit carnes esse immolaticias, vel certò non novit, vel dubitat. Si dubitat, aut certò non novit non esse immolaticia, liberè comedat. Verùm si certò constiterit, carnes esse immolaticias, ex Christiana pietate abstineat. Et supponit etiam manifestum mortis discrimen. Curcellæus hoc Augustini judicium magnopere prædicat pag.123. Verùm salva authoritate Magni Patris, non constare videtur ratio, cur Christianum esurientem oporteat morti potiùs se victimam dare, quàm ab ejusmodi victima idolis immolata temperare. Cùm enim sit Christianus, non edit idoli reverentiâ. Cùm sit solus in solitudine, non habet illic infirmos fratres, quos offendat. Neque communicat cum Dæmonibus, cùm ibi nullum sacrum agitetur. Multò minùs infidelibus exponit ponit libertatem suam condemnandam & blasphemandam, cùm ex hypothesi nulli in solitudine adsint. Quantò rectius Antiocheni Christiani, de quibus supra egimus, vitam redemerunt, his dapibus secuti Apostolicum mandatum: Edite, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. Est enim Domini Terra & plenitudo ejus.
units.tr: In the same question the Apostle speaks thus: All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify. If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake. But if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice, eat not, for conscience sake, not thine own, but the other's, vers. 23, 27, 28, 29. It is plain that the Apostle declares Christian liberty in eating food offered to idols, but is unwilling that this liberty be exercised for the sake of a brother's conscience, where it is clear that the exercise would put him in danger. VIII. That the Apostles held no other view may be gathered from Cyril, book 7 against Julian: Therefore, denying altogether that idols exist, we say that nothing is sacrificed to gods. We eat with a pure conscience, giving glory to God, who has granted us the free and harmless use of all food. But if anyone is still weak, and does not have a strong mind, and thinks that something is truly offered to idols, and has not yet advanced to so sincere a faith, we indulge him, as certain schoolmasters do when they teach little children and gradually lead them on to a small experience of the matter. The same matter is cited in chapter 39 of Theodore of Abucara, and the reply of Arethas, and also the letter of Peter of Antioch to Cerularius, in Leo Allatius, On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Church, p. 1170. The Antiochenes themselves, to whose elders the Synodal decree of the Apostles was sent in their own time, interpreted the decree in this sense by their own conduct. For when Julian the Apostate had polluted the springs, both those in the city and those at Daphne, with wicked sacrifices, so that each who tasted the water was infected with a foul stain of wickedness, and then had the things that were sold in the market defiled by the same stain of sin, the Christians indeed utterly detested these things; nevertheless, says Theodoret, they partook of them all the same, obeying the Apostolic law. "For," he says, "eat everything that is sold in the meat-market, asking no question for conscience' sake" [μετελάμβανον ὁμως, Ἀποστολικῶ πειθόμενοι νόμῳ. Πᾶν γὰρ, Φησι, τὸ ἐν μακέλλῳ πωλούμενον ἐσθίετε, μηδὲν ἀνακρίνοντες διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν], obeying the Apostle's law, which so commands: Whatever is sold in the shambles, eat, judging nothing for conscience' sake. The Christians of Constantinople, of whom we heard Nectarius speak above, indeed refused to do the same. But they did so out of hatred for Julian and great detestation of idols, not because the liberty to act otherwise was lacking or the opportunity was absent. For the Apostate could not defile common food by that contact, nor consecrate it to demons or idols, so that whoever ate it could be thought to be led by the religion of an idol or to profess idolatry. Grant, however, that the Apostate intended this. Still, he was only one man, and could change neither the thing itself nor the common judgment of men, who held that this matter was not idolatrous but indifferent. Augustine, in his hundred and fifty-fourth letter to Publicola, writes: If you have offered some part of a heap of grain to idol images, or if you have offered wine recently pressed in the winepress, this will not prevent us from freely using what remains, both in the winepress and on the threshing floor, since we do not hesitate to draw water from the springs and wells from which they took it to make sacrifices to idols. The pious Father discusses this matter at length. Paul also stayed many days at Athens, and undoubtedly ate the fruits and produce of the Athenian field, which nevertheless had been consecrated to Minerva. Indeed, since the ancients sometimes used to make libations to springs and rivers, because they attributed to them some kind of divinity, and for that reason sometimes threw into them the flesh or entrails of sacrificed animals, it was asked whether Christians might afterwards use those waters? Augustine answers that they certainly may. For, he says, we know that there are many who make sacrifices to the sun, yet we do not on that account hesitate to use its light and to enjoy the sight of its rays. Indeed there are even unbelievers who offer victims to the winds, and yet we use them in our voyages. Thus far Augustine speaks very well, and entirely from the truth. But the other case which Publicola himself mentioned, Augustine resolves in a way that seems to speak rather harshly. A certain man, says Publicola, was travelling through a desert, and was very hungry, and by chance came upon a temple or small shrine of idols, where he found some meat laid out. He asks Augustine: Was it lawful for him, since he professed the Christian religion, to eat it? Augustine answers: Because it may be that the meat was not sacrificed to idols, but was left there by chance by travellers who had stopped there either to lunch or to dine; therefore, since it is not established that it was sacrificed, the man who is hungry may make use of it. Then, as if he were not satisfied, he uses this distinction: Either he knows for certain that the meat has been sacrificed, or he knows for certain that it has not, or he doubts. If he doubts, or knows for certain that it has not been sacrificed, let him eat it freely. But if it is established for certain that the meat has been sacrificed, let him abstain out of Christian piety. And he also supposes a manifest danger of death. Curcellaeus greatly praises this judgment of Augustine, p. 123. But, saving the authority of the great Father, it does not seem clear why a hungry Christian should be obliged to give himself up as a victim to death rather than abstain from such a victim sacrificed to idols. For since he is a Christian, he does not eat out of reverence for the idol. Since he is alone in the wilderness, he has no weak brothers there whom he might offend. Nor does he have fellowship with demons, since no sacred rite is being performed there. Much less does he expose his liberty to condemnation and blasphemy before unbelievers, since by hypothesis no one is present in the wilderness. How much more rightly did the Christian Antiochenes, of whom we have spoken above, redeem their lives, following this Apostolic command with their meals: Eat, asking no question for conscience' sake. For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof.

units.la: ET SANGUINE) Tertullianus lib.de Pudicitia, & Cyprianus lib. ad Quirinum, censent, per sanguinem vetari homicidium. Imò Cyprianus legit, non simpliciter & sanguine, sed à sanguinis effusione. Tametsi Tertullianus videtur potiùs argumentatus à minori ad majus. Erubescat, inquit in Apologetico cap. 9. Vester error Christianis, qui ne animalium quidem sanguinem in epulis esculentis habemus, qui propterea etiam suffocatis & morticino abstinemus, ne quo sanguine contaminemur vel intra viscera sepulto. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechef. 4. Ut fideles recedant à more Barbarorum: Multi homines feri, & immanes more eorum viventes, sanguinem linguunt instar belluarum, &c. Tu verò Domini Dei servus, cum vesceris, vesce cum modestia, &c. Quasi vetaretur tantùm edere sanguinem more canum & lingere. Sic & Justinus in Quaest. cap. 145. Ut separarert, inquit, nos Deus à belluarum similitudine. Nempe Scythae & Tartari soliti olim in siti, equo, cui insidebant, venam aperire, & sanguinem ejus potare. Hinc Martialis in Amphitheatro: Venit & epoto Sarmata pastus equo. Plinius lib. XVIII. 10. Sarmatae, inquit, hac pulte alantur, et crudâ etiam farinâ equino lacte, vel sanguine è crurif venis admixto. Nos ultrò fatemur, sanguinis brutorum esum hoc loco intelligi. Videsis, quae praelibavimus cap. 1. Sect. V. VI. VII. VIII.
units.tr: AND BLOOD) Tertullian in his book on Modesty, and Cyprian in his book to Quirinus, hold that the word "blood" forbids murder. Indeed Cyprian reads it not simply as and blood, but as "from the shedding of blood." Yet Tertullian seems rather to argue from the less to the greater. In his Apology, chapter 9, he says: Let it shame you, that we Christians, who do not even have the blood of animals in our food, abstain from strangled meat and carrion, lest we be contaminated by any blood buried within the viscera. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 4, so that the faithful may turn from the custom of the barbarians: Many wild and savage men, living after their manner, lick up blood like beasts, etc. But you, servant of the Lord God, when you eat, eat with moderation, etc. As if the only thing forbidden were to devour blood and lick it like dogs. So too Justin, in the Quaestiones, chapter 145: That God might separate us, he says, from the likeness of beasts. Indeed the Scythians and Tartars were once accustomed, when thirsty, to open a vein of the horse they rode and drink its blood. Hence Martial in the amphitheatre: And the Sarmatian feeds even on a drunken horse. Pliny, book 18, chapter 10: The Sarmatians, he says, are fed on this porridge, and on raw meal mixed with mare's milk, or with blood drawn from the veins of the leg. We ourselves freely admit that the eating of the blood of brute animals is what is understood here. See what we have touched on in chapter 1, sections 5, 6, 7 and 8.

units.la: ET SUFFOCATO) Propter sanguinem in visceribus contentum Suffocatis etiam interdicunt. Curcellaeus, cùm praevidereт hanc vocem sibi nocere, simpliciter illam postulat tollere. Pugnat tum authoritate Irenaei, Tertulliani, Cypriani, Hieronymi, Ambrosii, Augustini, Paciani, Gaudentii; tum magni momenti, ut ipsi videtur, ratione pag. 131. 132. 133. Non placet, ut mutetur temerè. Habet illam Syrus, qui transtulit ܣܘܦܘܩܛܘ à Suffocato. Quin autem Syriaca Interpretatio omnibus illis Patribus à Curcellaeo allegatis, sit vetustior, nemo rerum peritus dubitare potest. Nam vel Apostolorum temporibus, vel paulò post ea tempora factam esse, constans est Orientalium traditio. Quin & Origines antiquitate paucis inferior, vocem retinet lib. 8. contra Celsum, ubi hanc rationem affert prohibitionis suffocatorum: quòd Gentiles censuerint, Suffocata esse Daemonum cibum. Sed & Tertullianus in Apologetico: Propterea suffocato etiam & morticinis abstinemus. Abstinuerunt igitur Christiani suffocatis. Quae ipsis abstinentiae ratio, nisi Apostolicum interdictum? Ut frustra pro se Tertullianum allegaverit Curcellaeus. Neque bona fide agit, cùm Augustinum pro se citat. Quamvis enim in ea periodo, quam producit Curcellaeus, non tangat, tamen paucis lineis interjectis loquitur de carnibus praefocatis. Hinc Concilium Constantinopolitanum sextum in Trullo habitum Canone 67. inter alia: Sacra Scriptura nobis praecipit, ut abstineamus à sanguine & suffocato & fornicatione. Confer etiam Canonem Apostolicum LXII. in quo cum sanguine suffocatum jungitur. Patres autem in contrarium adductos plerosque probabile est non expressisse suffocata, quòd censerent quodammodo sub sanguinis interdicto contineri. Potius igitur est, ut vocem πνικτὸν cum Stephano, Erasmo, Beza retineamus. Neque prohibet ratio, quam affert Curcellaeus, & quam magni momenti esse praedicat pag.135. Suffocatorum esum diserte fuisse Gentilibus lege Mosaica concessum, Deut.XIV.20.21. Non esse autem probabile, Apostolos, qui cetera omnia Israëlitis peculiaria legis Mosaicae onera tam studiose à Gentilibus conversis removebant, gravius ullum, quàm istud, quo omnes Noachi posteri tenebantur, imponere voluisse. Resp. Non tantum Gentilium ratio habenda fuit, sed etiam Judaeorum, quorum in gratiam sancitum, ut etiam Gentiles à suffocato abstinerent. Deinde falsò supponit omnes Noachidas usque ad Christum ad interdictum sanguinis fuisse obligatos. Demonstravimus supra, praeceptum illud Ceremoniale fuisse.
units.tr: AND STRANGLED) Because of the blood contained in the viscera, they forbid even what is strangled. Curcellaeus, seeing that this word harms his case, simply demands that it be removed. He fights against it with the authority of Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Pacian and Gaudentius, and with reasoning of great weight, as it seems to him, on pages 131, 132 and 133. It does not please me that it should be changed rashly. The Syriac version, which renders it with the Syriac word sōpōqṭō (from "strangled"), has it. That the Syriac translation is older than all those Fathers cited by Curcellaeus, no one who knows these matters can doubt. For it is a settled tradition of the Eastern churches that it was made either in the times of the Apostles or shortly after. Origen too, scarcely less ancient, retains the word in book 8 against Celsus, where he gives this reason for the prohibition of strangled meat: that the Gentiles thought strangled meat was food of the demons. But Tertullian too, in the Apology: For this reason we also abstain from strangled meat and carrion. Christians therefore abstained from strangled meat. What reason for this abstinence could they have had, except the Apostolic prohibition? So Curcellaeus has cited Tertullian in vain for his side. Nor does he act in good faith when he cites Augustine for himself. For although in the sentence which Curcellaeus quotes he does not touch the point, yet a few lines later he speaks of strangled flesh. Hence the Sixth Council of Constantinople, held in the Trullo, says in Canon 67, among other things: Holy Scripture commands us to abstain from blood and from what is strangled and from fornication. Compare also Apostolic Canon 62, in which what is strangled is joined with blood. As for the Fathers adduced on the other side, it is probable that most of them did not mention strangled meat because they thought it was somehow included under the prohibition of blood. It is better, therefore, to retain the word pniktón [πνικτὸν] with Stephanus, Erasmus and Beza. Nor does the reason which Curcellaeus gives, and which he declares to be of great weight, stand in the way: That the eating of strangled meat was expressly permitted to the Gentiles by the Mosaic law, Deut. 14:20-21. But it is not probable that the Apostles, who so diligently removed from the converted Gentiles all the other burdens of the Mosaic law peculiar to the Israelites, meant to impose on them any burden heavier than this one, by which all the posterity of Noah were bound. Answer: regard had to be paid not only to the Gentiles but also to the Jews, for whose sake it was enacted that even Gentiles should abstain from what is strangled. Further, he falsely supposes that all the sons of Noah were bound to the prohibition of blood until Christ. We have demonstrated above that that precept was ceremonial.

units.la: ET SCORTATIONE) Nihil abs re dicit Heinsius Doctissimus, Exercit. Sacr. pag.300. scribens: Nullum in his libris locum esse, in quo plus difficultatis invenerunt, plus reliquerunt Summi Viri.
units.tr: AND FORNICATION) The most learned Heinsius, in his Sacred Exercises, page 300, rightly says: There is no place in these books where the greatest men have found more difficulty, and left more unresolved.

units.la: Scrupulus in eo haeret, quemadmodum Apostoli cum interdicto temporaneo usus rerum adiaphorarum conjunxerint interdictum Scortationis, quam jus naturae & Romanae leges juxta Gentilibus prohibuerant. Communis responsio est, quam sequitur Erasmus in Paraphrasi & Piscator, quibus Curcellaeus noster se jungit, Scortationem adiaphoris accenseri, quia à Gentibus non habebatur pro flagitio, ut videre est 1.Cor.VI.15.16. Et notum est ex illo Terentiano: tiano: Non est flagitium, mihi crede, adolescentulos scortari, Adelph. Act. I. Sc. 2. Non satisfacit haec explicatio vel Bezae vel Heinsio. Et sane non videtur justum, Gentibus in universum omnibus impingere tam pravum judicium, eo quod inter Gentes essent, qui aut leve, aut ne peccatum quidem esse crederent. In jure Canonico c. Is qui Dist. 34. ex Canone XVII. Concilii Toletani concubinatus non obscure videtur permitti. Pariter in jure Civili manifeste sunt Constit. Impp. & responsa Juris consultorum veterum, pura in C. & Dig. tot. tit. de Concubin. quibus ad evitanda majora mala Constuprationum & adulterii, concubinatum tolerari sensere. Donec tandem Leo Imp. Constantinopolitanus Philosophus dictus concubinatum penitus sustulit, Novella 91. Et disputant Scholastici: Utrum formicatio simplex peccatum contra jus naturae sit? Negante id Durando in 4. Dist. 33. 4. 2. Quis ideo concludat, inter Christianos concubinatum pro re adiaphora haberi. Imo ne Pagani quidem desunt, qui damnarunt, quod prohibitum civili jure negatur. Sunt inter eos, qui amorem illegitimum aut nimium punire: Sophocles legitimum quoque, sed plerumque impotentem, nimiumque λυπηρὸν καὶ ὀργῆς πατρόθεν dixit. Musonius ne ἀκηρμοσύνην quidem λόγων, sive intemperantiam verborum admittendam censuit. Neque eam Gentilibus sententiam sedisse innuit Apostolus 1. Cor. VI. 15. 16. Sicut cum Rom. 1. 26. 27. foeminas ac mares proprio sexu foedissime inter se abusos dicit, nemo inde colliget, tanquam placitum commune aut omnibus approbatum, id esse accipiendum. Plautus in loco allato non ex sua sententia loquitur, sed ex persona ejus, quem describit. Quin & Comici interpres distinguit inter delictum & flagitium. Negari flagitium, non delictum. Ergo Beza interpretatur Spiritualem scortationem, quomodo passim idololatria dicitur. Non quidem crassam illam intelligit, quae est sine exceptione detestanda, sed quam illorum temporum & exortae contentionis circumstantiae requirebant. In hanc autem, inquit, sententiam me deduxit Paulus, hujus Epistolae Synodica optimus interpres, 1. Cor. VIII. & X. duas species constituens hujus inverdicti, unam τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων, extra Idolorum Templum & Sacrificia: alteram convivii in ipso Idolorum Templo, & ipsum Sacrificii appendicem. Hic igitur loci vult intelligi alteram speciem idolothytorum, puta accubitum in idolo, & caeteras hujusmodi. Sed manet pro-secto, feeto,imo magis etiam adstringitur nodus: Quamobrem Apostoli rebus tam indifferentibus sub eodem titulo junxerint mandatum rei suâ naturâ detestabilis vitandæ. Deinde non apparet ratio,cur necessitatis tantum causâ, non præcisè hîc damnetur πορνέια, si est idololatria. Nam gravissimum omnium peccatum esse quis dubitet? Jam quod ad Apostolum attinet, is decimo prioris ad Corinthios de idolothytis agit,quorum esum taxat in idoleo,conjunctum cum professione publica idololatriæ. Si idololatricum illum idolothytorum esum nomine πορνείας significâssent Apostoli in Synodo, magnopere intererat,ut ab Apostolo Corinthiis hoc explicaretur. Seldenus lib.VII.de jure Nat. & Gent.Hebr.cap.12.videtur intellexisse fornicationem non simpliciter,sed ejus speciem & gradum turpissimum adulterium & incestum,qui nomine πορνείας venit apud Apostolum 1.Cor.V.1. Quæ sententia planè vero non est consentanea. Docet Paulus illam πορνείαν ne inter Gentes quidem nominari. Ergo notorium crimen ab omnibus est habitum,atque sic naturæ instinctu vitatum. Cur igitur ejus interdictum novum stringerent? Imo cur conjungerent rebus suâ naturâ licitis? Heinsius oculatissimus, ingeniosam hîc & eruditam conjecturam protulit. Πορνείαν interpretatur, πορνικὴν θυσίαν. Sic enim Deus in lege præcepit Deut.cap. XXIII.18. Non offeres mercedem prostibuli, nec pretium canis in domo Domini. Ita Proverb.cap.VII.vers.14. dicit meretrix: ... Sacrificia pacifica mihi: Hodie reddam vota mea. Athanasius libro adversus Gentes,de fœminabus in Phœnicia Templis: Νομίζουσαι τῇ πορνείᾳ τὸν Θεὸν ἑαυτῶν ἱλάσκεσθαι. Meretricia oblatione placari sibi Deum putabant. Ubi voce πορνείας utitur pro θυσίᾳ πορνικῇ. Et sanè cum supra versu 20. non simpliciter πορνέια prohibeatur, sed ἀλίσγημα πορνείας, censeri potest, proxime ad mentem Spiritus Sancti accedere observationem. Nam ἀλίσγημα usitatè de cibis accipitur. Unum tamen obstare videtur. Si quæstum meretricium Apostoli prohibuissent, vel prohibuissent ut Sacrificio devotum,ut in lege Mosis factum est: vel ut cibum simpliciter. Posteriori modo nulla ratio fuit,ut prohiberetur: nec fortasse casus. Nec ipse Heinsius,nisi fallor,hoc pertendit. Nam de victima meretricia loquitur. Si priori modo, superflua propositio videtur; cùm jam omne idolothytum interdixerint. Qui ἀλίσγημα εἰδώλων prohibet,eâdem operâ meretricium quæstum idolis devotum tum prohibet. Quid ergo? Fornicationem prohibitam sanè credimus. Sed talem, quae judicio hominum pro scortatione non habebatur, sive à Judæis sive à Gentilibus, sed pro re naturâ suâ indifferente. Intelligo autem πορνείαν in Polygamia & divortiis. Quomodo Christus affirmat, eum, qui repudiat mulierem, ei μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ, & ducit aliam, μοιχᾶται, Matth. XIX. 9. Marc. X. 11. Luc. XVI. 18. Roma. VII. 3. 1. Cor. VII. 10. Fuisse autem hoc genus πορνείας inter Judæos & Gentiles tum usitatum, tum in vili habitum, abundè constat. De Judæis approbat Christus Matth. XIX. 9. Et agunt de divortiis Thalmudici integro tractatu פ Fuisse autem in hisce divortiis proprie dictam πορνείαν, certum est, quicquid videatur inter Scholasticos Thomas, Paludano, Durando, Abulensi, Cajetano, Bellarmino. Ex Politia Judaica temeraria divortiorum licentia ad Gentes etiam dimanavit. Solon Atheniensis lege sanxit, ut qui uxorem exturbàsset, dotem ille restitueret, alioquin interusurium sesquidrachmale ob moram solvere cogebatur. Alexander ab Alexandro lib. IV. genial. dier. cap. 8. Apud Athenienses libello repudii perrecte vel à viro vel ab uxore, an concedi deberet, Magistratus decernit. Diodorus Siculus lib. 12. Bibliothec. Charondæ lege datam mulieribus facultatem quacunque de causa de viris discedendi. De Romanis quidem prodidit Tertullianus Apolog. cap. 6. Per annos ferè sexcentos ab Urbe condita nullam domum repudium scripsisse. Id quidem sic accipiendum, quod ob reverentiam matrimonii concessâ per leges licentiâ non fuerint usi. Nam aliquid de divortiis cautum fuisse XII. Tabulis, ex Ciceronis Philippica secunda censet Hottomannus part. III. Com. ad XII. Tabulas. De Romulo Plutarchus memorat, quòd viro jus dederit, γυναῖκα ἐπιβάλλειν ἐπὶ φαρμακείᾳ τίκνων, ἢ κλεισῶν ἐπιβολῇ, καὶ μοιχᾶσθαι. Hinc Christiani imperatores exultantem illam divortiorum licentiam utcunque coercuerunt. De Polygamia etiam res testatissima est. Nam Judæos quidem quod attinet, Josephus Antiq. XVII. 1. Πάτριον ἐν ταύτῃ πλείονα ἡμῖν συνοικεῖν. Mos nobis Patrius, eodem tempore plures habere uxores. Pesictha ad Lev. XVIII. notissimum ait esse, eum qui dicat vetitum esse habere plures uxores, nescire quid sit de lege. Justinus Tryphoni in Dialogo exprobrat pag. 285. Magistri vestri ad hoc usque tempus quatuor & quinque uxores unumquemque vestrum habere permisérunt. Hinc Theodosius, Arcadius & Honorius Imperatores, quamvis multa in Judæis tolerarent, Polygamiam gamiam iis tamen permittere noluerunt l. 7. C. de Judaeis: Nemo Judaeorum morem suum in conjunctionibus retineat, nec juxta legem suam nuptias sortiatur, nec in diversa sub uno tempore conjugia conveniat. Tametsi in eo falluntur, quod legem nominant, cum perversae consuetudini illorum licentia non legi sit omnino deputanda. Ut nec Cuneo de Rep. Heb. II. 23. nec Grotio de Jure Belli & Pacis II. 5. necessum sit nos assentiri. Soli Pontifici apud Judaeos nefas fuit, uxores duas simul in matrimonio habere, ut traditur in Thalmud. in Massechta Joma cap. 1. Sed & plerasque gentes certum est, antiquitus ut divortiorum libertate, ita plurium foeminarum conjugio usas. Tacitus de moribus Germanorum cap. XVIII. 1. Prope soli Barbarorum Germani, singulis uxoribus contenti sunt, exceptis admodum paucis, qui non libidine, sed ob nobilitatem plurimis nuptiis ambiuntur. Vide Matthiam Berneggerum ad illum Taciti locum. Apud Graecos Cecrops primus, teste Athenaeo, μίαν ἐγὶ ἐζευξεν, unam foeminam uni marito attribuit. Quod tamen ne Athenis quidem diu observatum Socratis & aliorum exemplo constat. Disputat de ea re Euripides in Andromacha ex persona Hermionis, ubi concludit, propter tranquillitatem domesticam praestare, ut unica conjuge, qui sapiunt, oblectentur. Apud Aegyptios soli Sacerdotes unius foeminae conjugio utebantur, teste Herodiano lib. II. Quod si qui populi continentius egerunt, ut Romani, semper duabus uxoribus, divortio diu abstinuerunt. Firmiter igitur tenemus, hanc licentiam nomine πορνείας Apostolis prohibitam fuisse. Nam hoc solum tempore Christi & Apostolorum in controversiam est vocatum, an contra sanctitatem Christianorum militet isthaec licentia? Quamobrem etiam Christus a Pharisaeis tentatus de illa quaestione, cum acerrime inter se discipuli tum Hillelis, tum Schammai, tum Aquibae digladiarentur, definivit, in divortiis & polygamia esse πορνείαν veram. Constat igitur, quo titulo rebus indifferentibus Apostoli fornicationem conjunxerint.
units.tr: The difficulty here is how the Apostles, in joining a temporary prohibition of things indifferent to a prohibition of fornication, which the law of nature and the Roman laws had already forbidden to the Gentiles. The common answer, followed by Erasmus in his Paraphrase and by Piscator, and which our Curcellaeus adopts, is that fornication is counted among things indifferent, because the Gentiles did not regard it as a disgrace, as can be seen from 1 Cor. 6:15-16. And it is well known from that line of Terence: Non est flagitium, mihi crede, adolescentulos scortari, Adelph. Act. 1, Sc. 2. This explanation does not satisfy either Beza or Heinsius. Indeed it does not seem right to charge all the Gentils without exception with so wicked a judgment, merely because among the Gentiles there were some who thought it a light matter, or not even a sin. In the canon law, c. Is qui, Dist. 34, from the seventeenth canon of the Council of Toledo, concubinage seems plainly to be permitted. Likewise in the civil law there are clearly imperial constitutions and the opinions of the ancient jurists, scattered through the whole title of the Code and the Digest on concubines, by which they judged that concubinage was tolerated in order to avoid the greater evils of seduction and adultery. Until at last Leo the Emperor of Constantinople, called the Philosopher, entirely abolished concubinage, Novella 91. And the Scholastics dispute: whether simple fornication is a sin against the law of nature? Durandus, in 4 Dist. 33, 4, 2, denies it. Who then could conclude that among Christians concubinage is held to be a matter of indifference? Indeed, there are even pagans who condemned what the civil law does not forbid. Among them are those who punished illicit love, or excessive love: Sophocles said that even lawful love, when it is mostly unrestrained and excessive, is grievous and inherited from anger [λυπηρὸν καὶ ὀργῆς πατρόθεν]. Musonius did not even permit lack of restraint in words [ἀκηρμοσύνην λόγων], that is, intemperance of speech. Nor does the Apostle, in 1 Cor. 6:15-16, suggest that this opinion prevailed among the Gentiles. Just as, when in Rom. 1:26-27 he says that women and men most shamefully abused their own sex, no one would infer from this that it was a common opinion or one approved by all. Plautus, in the passage cited, does not speak in his own judgment but in the person of the man he describes. Indeed the commentators on comedy distinguish between a offence and a disgrace: it is denied to be a disgrace, not an offence. Therefore Beza interprets it as spiritual fornication, in the way that idolatry is everywhere called fornication. He does not indeed understand that gross kind, which is to be detested without exception, but the kind that the circumstances of those times and the dispute that had arisen required. But, he says, Paul, the best interpreter of this Epistle, led me to this opinion, when in 1 Cor. 8 and 10 he sets up two kinds of this prohibition: one of things sacrificed to idols [τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων], outside the temple of the idols and its sacrifices; the other of a feast in the very temple of the idols, and a kind of appendix to the sacrifice itself. Here, then, he wishes the second kind of idol-offerings to be understood, namely reclining at the idol, and others of this sort. But the knot certainly remains, and is even tightened the more: why would the Apostles have joined, under the same heading, things so indifferent with a command to avoid what is detestable by its very nature? Next, there appears no reason why fornication is condemned here only for the sake of necessity, and not absolutely, if it is idolatry. For who could doubt that it is the gravest of all sins? Now as far as the Apostle is concerned, in the tenth chapter of his First Epistle to the Corinthians he deals with things sacrificed to idols, whose eating he censures in the idol's temple, joined with a public profession of idolatry. If the Apostles in the Council had meant by the name of fornication that idolatrous eating of idol-offerings, it would have mattered greatly that the Apostle should explain this to the Corinthians. Selden, in book 7 of De Jure Naturali et Gentium Hebraeorum, chapter 12, seems to have understood fornication not simply, but a particular kind and the most shameful degree of it, adultery and incest, which in the Apostle's language comes under the name of fornication, 1 Cor. 5:1. This opinion is plainly not consistent with the truth. Paul teaches that such fornication is not even named among the Gentiles. Therefore it was a crime notorious and regarded as such by all, and so avoided by the impulse of nature. Why then would they have framed a new prohibition of it? Indeed, why would they have joined it to things that are lawful in their own nature? Heinsius, most keen-sighted, has put forward an ingenious and learned conjecture here. He interprets fornication as a sacrifice of harlotry [πορνικὴν θυσίαν]. For thus God commanded in the law, Deut. 23:18: You shall not bring the wages of a harlot, nor the price of a dog, into the house of the Lord. So too Prov. 7:14, where the harlot says: Peace offerings are with me; today I will pay my vows. Athanasius, in his book against the Gentiles, on the women in the temples of Phoenicia: thinking that their god was propitiated by fornication [Νομίζουσαι τῇ πορνείᾳ τὸν Θεὸν ἑαυτῶν ἱλάσκεσθαι].
