That is, they believed that God was appeased by a harlot's offering, where he uses the word fornication for a harlot's sacrifice. And indeed, since above, at verse 20, it is not simply fornication that is forbidden, but the pollution of fornication [ἀλίσγημα πορνείας], that observation may be thought to come close to the mind of the Holy Spirit, for pollution [ἀλίσγημα] is commonly used of foods. One thing, however, seems to stand in the way. If the Apostles had prohibited the earnings of harlotry, they would have prohibited them either as dedicated to a sacrifice, as was done in the law of Moses, or as food in general. In the latter sense there was no reason for it to be forbidden, nor perhaps any occasion. Nor, unless I am mistaken, does Heinsius himself maintain this, for he speaks of a harlot's victim. In the former sense the proposition seems superfluous, since they had already forbidden every idol-offering. He who forbids the pollution of idols [ἀλίσγημα εἰδώλων] by the same act forbids the earnings of harlotry devoted to idols. What then? We certainly believe that fornication is forbidden. But such fornication as by the judgment of men was not counted as fornication, whether by the Jews or by the Gentiles, but as a thing indifferent in its nature. I understand, however, fornication to mean polygamy and divorce. As Christ affirms, that whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication [μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ], and marries another, commits adultery [μοιχᾶται], Matt. 19:9; Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18; Rom. 7:3; 1 Cor. 7:10. That this kind of fornication was common and held in low esteem among the Jews and the Gentiles alike is abundantly clear. Christ approves it for the Jews, Matt. 19:9. And the Talmudists treat of divorces in a whole tractate, Gittin [גיטין]. That in these divorces there was properly so called fornication is certain, whatever Thomas, Paludanus, Durandus, Abulensis, Cajetan and Bellarmine may think among the Scholastics. From the Jewish polity the reckless license of divorce also spread to the Gentiles. Solon the Athenian by law decreed that whoever had driven out his wife should restore her dowry, otherwise he was compelled to pay, for the delay, interest of a drachma and a half. Alexander ab Alexandro, book 4 of Dies Geniales, chapter 8: Among the Athenians the magistrate decides by a written notice of divorce whether it ought to be granted, whether by the husband or by the wife. Diodorus Siculus, book 12 of the Library: by the law of Charondas women were given the power of leaving their husbands for whatever cause. Of the Romans Tertullian, Apology chapter 6, records: For nearly six hundred years from the founding of the City no household had written a bill of divorce. This must indeed be taken to mean that, out of reverence for marriage, they did not use the licence the laws allowed. For Hottoman, in part 3 of his commentary on the Twelve Tables, judges from Cicero's second Philippic that something about divorce was provided for in the Twelve Tables. Plutarch tells of Romulus, that he gave the husband the right to cast off his wife for the sake of drugs for children, or by locking her out, and to commit adultery [γυναῖκα ἐπιβάλλειν ἐπὶ φαρμακείᾳ τίκνων, ἢ κλεισῶν ἐπιβολῇ, καὶ μοιχᾶσθαι]. Hence the Christian emperors in some measure restrained that boundless licence of divorce. Concerning polygamy too the fact is very well attested. As for the Jews, Josephus, Antiquities 17.1: It is our ancestral custom to live with several wives at the same time [Πάτριον ἐν ταύτῃ πλείονα ἡμῖν συνοικεῖν]. The Pesikta on Lev. 18 says it is well known that whoever says it is forbidden to have several wives does not know what the law is. Justin, in his Dialogue with Trypho, reproaches them, p. 285: Your teachers until now have permitted each of you to have four or five wives. Hence the emperors Theodosius, Arcadius and Honorius, although they tolerated many things in the Jews, were unwilling to permit them polygamy, Code 1.7, On the Jews: Let no Jew retain his custom in marriages, nor contract marriage according to his own law, nor enter into several marriages at one time. Yet they are mistaken in calling it a law, since that licence of theirs, being a perverse custom, is not to be counted a law at all. So that we need not assent to Cuneus, On the Hebrew Commonwealth 2.23, nor to Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace 2.5. Only the High Priest among the Jews was forbidden to have two wives in marriage at one time, as is handed down in the Talmud, in the tractate Yoma, chapter 1. But it is certain also that most nations, from ancient times, practised polygamy of several women just as they practised freedom of divorce. Tacitus, on the customs of the Germans, chapter 18: The Germans are almost the only barbarians who are content with single wives, except for a very few who, not from lust but on account of their rank, are sought after by many marriages. See Matthias Berneggerus on that passage of Tacitus. Among the Greeks, Cecrops first, according to Athenaeus, yoked one woman [μίαν ἐγὶ ἐζευξεν], that is, assigned one wife to one husband. Yet it is known that even at Athens this was not observed for long, as the example of Socrates and others shows. Euripides disputes this matter in Andromache, in the person of Hermione, where he concludes that for the sake of domestic tranquillity it is better that those who are wise should be content with a single wife. Among the Egyptians only the priests used marriage with one woman, according to Herodian, book 2. And if some peoples have behaved with more restraint, as the Romans did, they long abstained from divorce and always had two wives. We therefore firmly hold that this licence was forbidden by the Apostles under the name of fornication. For this was the only point in dispute in the time of Christ and the Apostles, whether this licence was contrary to the holiness of Christians. Therefore too, when the Pharisees tempted Christ concerning that question, while the disciples of Hillel, of Shammai and of Akiba fought fiercely among themselves, he settled that in divorces and polygamy there is true fornication. It is clear, then, under what heading the Apostles joined fornication to things indifferent.

units.la: Caeterum sunt multi Codices, qui praeter memorata capita adduntconclusionem: Καὶ ὅσα ἐὰν μὴ θέλωσιν ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι, ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖν. Et quae sibi fieri non vultis, aliis ne feceritis. Jam olim ita legisse videntur Irenaeus, & Cyprianus. Sic etiam legunt versio Aethiopica, Complutensis, Regia Montani, Exemplar Cantabrigiense, & nonnulli MS. Confer Bezam in Notis, Ludovicum de Dieu, Seldenum, num, Junium. Non temerè mantissam hanc respui debere censeo, cùm & Irenæus vetustissimus Pater legerit, & Complutensis addiderit, quam constat expressam esse ad vetustissima & emaculatissima exemplaria. Quanquam nec Syrus interpres antiquissimus legit, nec alii Patres mentionem faciunt. Si genuinum est additamentum, hic proculdubio sensus fuerit animo Apostolorum consentaneus, ut Gentiles in capitibus his expressis subeunti animo cum Judæis condescendant, quippe quorum infirmitas & ἀβλεψία æqui consulenda, cùm requirat hoc Christiana charitas, & tota lex Mosis & Prophetarum, quam illâ sententiâ Christus velut in breviarium contraxit Matth. VII. 12. Luc. VI. 31. Adeóque per modum rationis fuerint addita, non mandati, quod pari passu cum necessariis illis incedat.
units.tr: Moreover, many manuscripts add to the above-mentioned chapters this conclusion: And whatever you do not wish to be done to yourselves, do not do to others [Καὶ ὅσα ἐὰν μὴ θέλωσιν ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι, ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖν]. Irenaeus and Cyprian seem to have read it this way long ago. The Ethiopic version, the Complutensian, the Royal (Montanus) edition, the Cambridge copy and several manuscripts also read it so. Compare Beza in his Notes, Ludovicus de Dieu, Selden, Junius. I think this appendix should not be rejected lightly, since Irenaeus, a very ancient Father, read it, and the Complutensian edition added it, which is known to have been drawn from the most ancient and most accurate copies. Yet the oldest Syriac translator does not read it, and the other Fathers do not mention it. If the addition is genuine, the sense is surely one consistent with the mind of the Apostles: that Gentiles, in the matters expressed in these chapters, should meet the Jews halfway in their feelings, since their weakness and lack of understanding must be taken into account. Christian charity requires this, and so does the whole law of Moses and the Prophets, which Christ condensed into that saying as into a summary (Matt. 7:12; Luke 6:31). Therefore it was added by way of reasoning, not as a command, since it keeps pace with those necessary points.

units.la: Judicant præterea Viri Docti, in expressis hoc loco capitibus renovata esse Præcepta Noachidarum, & loco Ceremonialium antiquatorum Gentilibus ad Christum conversis injuncta, ut hoc velut Sacramento Christo auctorarentur, sicut olim Proselythis habitationis hac lege concessa est Hebræorum civitas. Schikhardus in jure Regio Hebræorum, cap. V. pag. 129. Præcepta Noachidarum in primitiva etiam Ecclesia Christianorum, Gentibus conversis, loco Mosaicæ legis rigidissimæ, ex decreto Apostolorum & Synodi Hierosolymitanæ imposita fuerunt. Act. XV. 29. Mihi profecto non fit verosimile, Apostolis hoc institutum fuisse. Nam præcepta Noachidarum in hac serie Apostolorum tempore concepta fuisse, non est extra dubitationis aleam. Nullibi in Scripturis Sacris illorum facta est mentio. Sed neque Josephus, qui diligentissimè Hebræorum Antiquitates est ruspatus, vel summo digito attingit. Scribit quidem Auctor Sepher Ikkarim l. 3. cap. 7. שמרו רבותנו זל״כ בתחלת היצירה מיה נצטוה אדם על שבע מצות כמו שבארו זה במסכת סנהדרין פרק ארבע מיתות ;
units.tr: Learned men also judge that in the chapters expressed here the precepts of the sons of Noah were renewed, and were imposed on Gentiles converted to Christ in place of the abrogated ceremonial laws, so that they might be bound to Christ by this sacrament, just as the Jewish city was once granted to proselytes of residence under this law. Schickhard, in Jus Regium Hebraeorum, ch. 5, p. 129: The precepts of the Noachides were also imposed in the primitive Church of Christians, on converted Gentiles, in place of the most rigid Mosaic law, by the decree of the Apostles and the Synod of Jerusalem (Acts 15:29). To me it is certainly not likely that this was the Apostles' institution. For it is not beyond doubt that the precepts of the Noachides were conceived in the time of this apostolic series. Nowhere in Holy Scripture is any mention made of them. Nor does Josephus, who very diligently searched the antiquities of the Hebrews, touch on them even with a fingertip. The author of Sepher Ikkarim, book 3, ch. 7, indeed writes: [שמרו רבותנו ז״ל כ בתחלת היצירה מיה נצטוה אדם על שבע מצות כמו שבארו זה במסכת סנהדרין פרק ארבע מיתות] — Our teachers of blessed memory taught that at the beginning of creation Adam was at once commanded concerning seven precepts, as they explained in tractate Sanhedrin, chapter "Four kinds of death."

units.la: Doctores nostri f. m. tradunt initio creationis statim Adamum septem præcepta accepisse in Tract. Talmud Sanhedrin cap. 7. quod incipit: quatuor mortis species. Sed quàm certæ sint Doctorum Thalmudicorum traditiones, & quàm tuto illorum nitamur fide, nemini clàm est. Solent enim quælibet antiquitatis fuco incrustata credulis mentibus propinare. Deinde censent vulgò Hebræi, post septem Noachidarum præcepta accessisse statuta tria, de Sabbatho, judicio, & honore Parentum. Atque haec tria praeceptis Noachidarum non inclusa. An ergo anteriores ad praecepta de Sabbatho & honore Parentum custodienda obligati non fuerunt? Imo omnia diligenter reputando, vix unum ex his septem praeceptis Apostoli Gentilibus conversis mandarunt. Patebit li-quido ex inductione. Primum Noachidarum praeceptum, narrante Kozaeo & Maimonide fuit de idololatria, ne Deos alienos colerent. Reperio quidem, Apostolos tulisse praeceptum de idolothytis non comedendis, quatenus illorum esus cum professione idololatriae fuit conjunctus. Sed per se non fuisse idololatricum idolothytorum esum supra manifestum fecimus. Si praeceptum hoc Apostoli in animo habuissent, rectius & compendiosius dixissent Ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας. Imo necessum fuisset ita scribere. Nam extra idolothytorum esum variis modis cultus idololatricus exerceri potest. Secundum est de benedictione Numinis, ut solum Deum creatorem venerarentur. Tertium de Sanguinis effusione, ne homicidium patrarent. Non apparet, duo haec praecepta ab Apostolis hoc loco lata. Nam qui per sanguinem homicidium intelligunt, illos extra chorum saltare vidimus. Quartum de revelatione turpitudinum, ne vagis aut incestis libidinibus contaminarentur. Vellet quidem Seldenus, hoc interdictum in Synodo nomine πορνείας venire. Sed probabilior est, quam attulimus sententia, quia de ea scortatione, quam hoc praecepto prohibitam Judaei volunt, non fuit eo tempore quaesitum: Sed de divortiorum licentia. Hanc autem negant Judaei praecepto quarto restringi. Quintum de rapina, ne quid furarentur. Sextum de Judiciis, ut justitiam publice administrarent. Quae duo praecepta nullo apice hic tanguntur. Septimum de membro vivi. Videri posset, saltem postremum hoc mandatum nomine ἀιμα καὶ πνικτὸν subinnui ab Apostolis. Verum quidem in illorum Hebraeorum sententia, qui hoc praeceptum de esu sanguinis interpretantur. Sunt tamen permulti, qui non de Sanguinis esu Noachicum hoc praeceptum explicent, sed de esu membri viventis, quos assensu suo dignatur Seldenus. Et sane verba praecepti vix aliam patiuntur interpretationem. Nullum igitur ex his omnibus clare patrocinatur errori.
units.tr: Our teachers, of blessed memory, hand down that at the beginning of creation Adam at once received seven precepts, in the tractate Talmud Sanhedrin, chapter 7, which begins: "Four kinds of death." But how certain the traditions of the Talmudic teachers are, and how safely we may rest our faith on them, is known to no one in private. For they are accustomed to serve to credulous minds anything encrusted with the varnish of antiquity. Next, the Hebrews commonly hold that after the seven precepts of the Noachides three further statutes were added, concerning the Sabbath, judgment, and honour of parents. These three are not included among the precepts of the Noachides. Were those who came earlier then not bound to keep the precepts about the Sabbath and honour of parents? Indeed, on careful reckoning of everything, the Apostles scarcely enjoined on Gentile converts even one of these seven precepts. This will be clear from a survey. According to Kozaeo and Maimonides, the first precept of the Noachides was concerning idolatry, that they should not worship strange gods. I do find that the Apostles did issue a precept about not eating food sacrificed to idols, insofar as eating it was joined with a profession of idolatry. But we have shown above that eating idol-sacrifices was not in itself idolatrous. If the Apostles had had this precept in mind, they would have said more correctly and concisely From idolatry [Ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας]. Indeed they would have had to write it so, for apart from eating idol-sacrifices, idolatrous worship can be practised in various ways. The second is concerning the blessing of the Deity, that they should venerate God the Creator alone. The third is concerning the shedding of blood, that they should not commit murder. It does not appear that these two precepts were laid down by the Apostles in this passage. For those who understand blood to mean murder we have seen dancing outside the ring. The fourth is concerning the uncovering of nakedness, that they should not be defiled by wandering or incestuous lusts. Selden would wish this prohibition to be included in the Council under the name fornication [πορνείας]. But the view we have set forth is more probable, because the fornication which the Jews say this precept forbids was not the question at that time; the question was the licence of divorce. The Jews, however, deny that this is restrained by the fourth precept. The fifth is concerning robbery, that they should steal nothing. The sixth is concerning judgments, that they should administer justice publicly. These two precepts are not touched upon here by any hint. The seventh is concerning a living limb. It might seem that at least this last command is hinted at by the Apostles under the name blood and what is strangled [ἀιμα καὶ πνικτὸν]. This is true on the view of those Hebrews who interpret this precept as concerning the eating of blood. There are, however, very many who do not explain this Noachic precept of the eating of blood, but of eating a living limb, whom Selden deigns to approve. And indeed the words of the precept hardly allow any other interpretation. Therefore none of all these clearly supports the error.

units.la: A QUIBUS SI CONSERVAVERITIS VOS IPSOS) Si vobis temperaveritis ab iis, quae cum charitate Fratrum consistere non possunt.
units.tr: TO WHOM IF YOU SHALL KEEP YOURSELVES): If you refrain from those things which cannot agree with the charity of the brethren.

units.la: BENE FACIETIS) εὖ πράξετε. Syrus: ܘܒܪ ܬܫܪܝܢ ܢܫܬܘܒܘܢ ܡܢ ܗܠܝܢ ܫܦܝܪ ܬܪܝܢ: Cumque conservaveritis animas vestras, bene se habebunt. Irenaei Interpres addit: Ποιοῦμενοι ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ. Quae Tertullianus in libro de pudicitia ita reddit: A quibus observando recte agetis, vectante vos Spiritu Sancto. Clemens lib. VI. Constitut. cap. 12. scribit: Apostolos congregatos multa alia constituisse. Sic enim loquitur in eorum persona: His igitur literis missis remansimus nos plurimis diebus Hierosolymis, conquirentes unà, quae in communem utilitatem ad correctionem spectabant. Ac deinceps multa enumerat. Quae quia de librorum illorum sinceritate nimium dubitatur, pro certis complecti nolumus.
units.tr: YOU WILL DO WELL) εὖ πράξετε [eu praxete]. The Syriac reads: u-ḇar tišrin neštubun min halin shapir terin, which means: And when you have kept your souls, it will go well with you. The translator of Irenaeus adds: Doing it in the Holy Spirit [Ποιοῦμενοι ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, poioumenoi en pneumati hagiōi]. Tertullian, in his book on modesty, renders it thus: By observing these things you will act rightly, with the Holy Spirit carrying you along. Clement, in Constitutions book 6, chapter 12, writes that the Apostles, having assembled, drew up many other rules. For he speaks in their person: Therefore, after sending these letters, we remained many days in Jerusalem, seeking together what looked to the common good and to correction. He then goes on to list many more. Since the sincerity of those books is greatly doubted, we do not wish to accept these as certain.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. Solutio argumenti, ex decreto Synodi Apostolicae petiti. Breviarium.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. The solution of the argument taken from the decree of the Apostolic Synod. A summary.

units.la: Solvitur argumentum à decreto Concilii Apostolici petitum. Solutioni fidei conciliatur octo argumentis. Expediuntur instantiae decem Curcellei & Becmanni.
units.tr: The argument drawn from the decree of the Apostolic Council is resolved. The solution is confirmed by eight arguments. The ten objections of Curcellaeus and Becmann are dealt with.

units.la: I. Actis Synodi Hierosolymitanae paulò diligentius lustratis, difficultas, quam ex hoc loco nectunt adversarii, non multo negotio expedietur. Argumentum est: Visum est Spiritui Sancto & Apostolis ἐπάναγκες necessarium, ut conversi Gentiles abstineant à sanguine & suffocato. Ergo omnibus Christianis usque ad finem mundi est illicitum vesci sanguine & suffocato. Respond. Visum est Spiritui Sancto & nobis necessarium in qualibet conditione & circumstantia? Falsus hic sensus est. Praeclarè Augustana Confessio titulo de potestate Ecclesiastica, cùm de hac re agit: Est perpetua voluntas Evangelii consideranda in decreto. Nempe Scripturæ in voluntate Evangelii nobis patefacienda sunt uniformes. Prohibent hoc loco esum sanguinis & suffocati. Alibi declarant, nihil immundum esse: escam nos Deo non commendare: nihil hominem, quod os ingreditur, inquinare: conscientias nostras tali servitute non esse onerandas. Videndum igitur est & Spiritualiter dijudicandum, quæ sit Evangelii voluntas in decreto. Si prohibuerunt Apostoli esum sanguinis & suffocati in qualibet conditione & circumstantia fidelium, non igitur verum est, nihil immundum esse, non inquinare quod os ingreditur, conscientias nostras tali servitute non esse illigandas, & si quæ talia creberrime in tabulis Novi Testamenti occurrunt. Si quis igitur dixerit, prohibitum esse ab Apostolis sanguinis esum, non quod suâ naturâ in qualibet circumstantia sit illicitus, nec quod libertati per Christum partæ repugnet: sed, quòd in se quidem res sit indifferens, cæterum aliena quadam vi, cum per illum Christiana charitas violatur, reprobabilis; is profecto & voluntatem Evangelii comprehenderit, & Scripturas in speciem dissidentes sibi conciliaverit. Contendo autem, ideo Gentilibus conversis hanc fuisse necessariam abstinentiam à sanguine, non quòd res hæc faceret ad salutem animi, sed quòd charitas hortaretur, ut ad tempus mos geratur imbecillitati Fratrum quorundam Judæorum superstitiosorum, quibus nondum persuaderi poterat, omnia esse munda immundis: donec & illi proficerent ad perfectiora: ut sic discerent mutuis obsequiis fraternam charitatem alere. Quod si verum est, non potuit diutius illa lex obligare, quàm quoad duravit Fratrum infirmitas, ex libertate illorum, qui notitiâ salutari provectiores fuerunt, scandalum captantium. Hæc prudentiæ regula est, ut omnibus omnia fiamus, imbecillibus imbecilles, ut illos Christo lucremur: Judæis Judæi, ἀνόμοις ἄνομοι, non tamen ut ἄνομοι Θεῶ, sed ut ἔννομοι Χριστῶ. 1.Cor.IX.20.21.22. dum libertas nostra pravorum hominum fraudulentis speculationibus ne exponatur.Gal.II.4. nec periculum sit adeundum, ne lex cum Evangelio confundatur, & satura addatur sitienti. Ad Lesbiam hanc regulam sese ubique Apostoli, felicissimi juxta atque prudentissimi Spiritualis ædificii compaginatores, composuerunt. Nihil magis libertati Christianorum contrarium fuit, quàm Circumcisio. Quid verò Apostolus? Cùm Judæi illius abrogationem non caperent, Timotheum in illorum gratiam circumcidit, cum esset patre Græco oriundus, Act.XVI.3. Eandem hic viam Apostoli calcant. Antiochiæ atque alibi passim Judæorum multitudo fuit Messiam Jesum, mundi Sospitatorem fidei ulnis complectentium. Hos cum multa alia transversos averherent, & à Gentilium communione abriperent, tum hoc non leviter concussit, quòd viderent Gentiles idolothytis, suffocato & sanguine vesci, rati, hanc licentiam pertinere ad contemptum mandatorum Dei antiquissimorum, quibus renovari mundi primordia adstrinxit. Ergo ut scandalo ancipiti remedium promerent Apostoli, statuunt necessariam abstinentiam, & Gentiles levi libertatis usu multant. Hanc responsionem porro manifestis argumentis veritati dabimus.
units.tr: I. If the Acts of the Synod of Jerusalem are examined a little more carefully, the difficulty which the adversaries raise from this passage will be cleared up without much trouble. Their argument is this: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to the apostles, [ἐπάναγκες] necessary, that converted Gentiles should abstain from blood and from what is strangled. Therefore it is unlawful for all Christians, until the end of the world, to eat blood and what is strangled. Answer: Was it judged necessary to the Holy Spirit and to us in every condition and circumstance? That sense is false. The Augsburg Confession rightly says, in the title on ecclesiastical power, when it treats this matter: The perpetual will of the Gospel is to be considered in the decree. Clearly the Scriptures must be understood as consistent with one another in revealing the will of the Gospel. In this passage they forbid the eating of blood and of what is strangled. Elsewhere they declare that nothing is unclean; that food does not commend us to God; that nothing defiles a man which enters the mouth; and that our consciences are not to be burdened with such bondage. We must therefore consider, and judge spiritually, what the will of the Gospel is in the decree. If the apostles forbade the eating of blood and of what is strangled in every condition and circumstance of the faithful, then it is not true that nothing is unclean, that what enters the mouth does not defile, and that our consciences are not to be bound by such servitude, and so on, although statements of this kind occur very frequently in the tables of the New Testament. If anyone therefore says that the apostles forbade the eating of blood, not because it is unlawful in itself in every circumstance, nor because it conflicts with the liberty won through Christ, but because, although the thing is indifferent in itself, it becomes objectionable through some alien force, namely when Christian charity is violated by it, he will certainly have grasped the will of the Gospel and reconciled Scriptures that seem to disagree. I maintain, however, that the abstinence from blood was necessary for converted Gentiles, not because this thing contributed to the salvation of the soul, but because charity urged that, for a time, the weakness of certain superstitious Jewish brethren be indulged, since they could not yet be persuaded that all things are clean to the clean, until they themselves advanced to greater perfection; so that they might learn to nourish fraternal charity by mutual compliance. If this is true, that law could not bind longer than the weakness of the brethren lasted, while the liberty of those who were more advanced in saving knowledge was giving offence to those who were looking for it. This is the rule of prudence: that we become all things to all men, to the weak weak, that we may win them to Christ; to Jews a Jew, [ἀνόμοις ἄνομοι] to those without law as without law, [ἔννομοι Χριστῶ] yet not as without law toward God but as under the law of Christ. (1 Cor. 9:20–22), provided that our liberty is not exposed to the fraudulent speculations of wicked men (Gal. 2:4), and that there is no risk of confusing the law with the Gospel, or of adding a satire to one who is thirsty. The apostles, the most fortunate and most prudent builders of the spiritual edifice, everywhere shaped themselves to this rule. Nothing was more contrary to the liberty of Christians than circumcision. What then did the apostle do? When the Jews would not accept its abrogation, he circumcised Timothy for their sake, although he was the son of a Greek father (Acts 16:3). The apostles here tread the same path. At Antioch and elsewhere, a great multitude of Jews embraced Jesus the Messiah, the Saviour of the world, in faith. When many other things were turning them aside and tearing them away from communion with the Gentiles, this also shook them considerably: they saw the Gentiles eating food offered to idols, what is strangled, and blood, and they judged that this licence amounted to contempt for the most ancient commandments of God, by which he bound the beginnings of the world to be renewed. Therefore, to provide a remedy for this dangerous offence, the apostles decreed a necessary abstinence and imposed a light penalty on the Gentiles' use of their liberty. We shall now confirm this answer by clear arguments.

units.la: II. Primò. Scripturæ N.T. ejusmodi servitutem penitus abrogârunt, Matth.XV.11.17. Rom.XIV.14.15. 1.Cor.VIII.4.7.10. 1.Tim.IV.4. Tit.I.14.15. Quæ loca capite octavo penitus à nobis excussa & ab argutiis adversarii liberata sunt. Unicum addo. Si in iis locis, quæ testatum reddunt, nihil hominem inquinare posse, omnia munda esse immundis, omnia licere fidelibus, sed non omnia ædificare, nemini esse obturbandum his decretis: noli gustaveris, non tetigeris, &c. non declaratur illa etiam libertas ab interdicto sanguinis, Christo & Apostolo non fuisse committendum, ut exceptionem hanc non aliquando adderent, & vel levi indicio docerent, non esse concessionem generalem, & indefinitam, sed excipiendam esse hanc legem de idolothytis & sanguine. Quis enim credat, Apostolum tam obscura locutione ansam errandi dare voluisse, qui ubique prudentissimè fideles informavit, vile à pretioso, illicita à licitis disparavit? Rationem evidentem postulo, cur, cùm toties occasio ferret, exceptionis illius ab universali regula mentionem non injecerit? Synodi decretum de hac re paucis omnino verbis fuit conceptum, rationibus non multis, neque adeò claris munitum. Neque verò convenit decreta rationum additamento corroborare. Lex enim non disputat, sed jubet. Quò rectius fuerat alibi, ubi commodè fieri potuit, hanc rem fusiùs tractari, Synodi mentem illustrari, ac perspicuè demonstrari, præceptum hoc in qualibet circumstantia temporis & personarum obligare. Tantùm autem abest, ut hoc uspiam ab Apostolis factum sit, ut contra manifestè hunc sensum decretis his Paulus induat, quem nos in responsione nostra repræsentamus.
units.tr: II. First. The Scriptures of the New Testament have utterly abrogated such servitude (Matt. 15:11, 17; Rom. 14:14, 15; 1 Cor. 8:4, 7, 10; 1 Tim. 4:4; Titus 1:14, 15). These passages were fully examined in chapter eight and freed from the subtleties of the adversary. I add one thing. If in those passages, which testify that nothing defiles a man, that all things are clean to the unclean, that all things are lawful for believers but not all things edify, no one is to be troubled by these decrees, do not taste, do not touch, etc., then it is not declared that this liberty also extends to the prohibition of blood. Christ and the apostle would not have been obliged to refrain from adding an exception to it at some point, and to show by at least a slight indication that this is not a general and unlimited concession, but that this law concerning idol-offerings and blood must be excepted. For who could believe that the apostle, who everywhere formed the faithful most prudently and distinguished the worthless from the precious and the unlawful from the lawful, wanted to give occasion for error by so obscure a manner of speaking? I demand a clear reason why, when the occasion so often arose, he did not introduce a mention of this exception to the universal rule. The decree of the Synod on this matter was framed in very few words, supported by few reasons and not particularly clear ones. Nor is it fitting to strengthen decrees by adding reasons, for law does not argue but commands. It would have been better to treat this matter at greater length elsewhere, where it could conveniently be done, to clarify the mind of the Synod, and to demonstrate plainly that this precept binds in every circumstance of time and persons. Yet far from this having been done anywhere by the apostles, Paul, on the contrary, manifestly clothes these decrees with the very sense which we present in our answer.

units.la: II. Secundò
units.tr: II. Secondly

units.la: II. Secundò consideremus, quæ quæstio fuerit in Concilio agitata, & quemadmodum fuerit eadem ab Apostolis definita. Contenderunt Pseudapostoli Judæorum, Gentiles proselythos oportere circumcidi, & legem Mosis servare versu 1. & 6. Jam legis Mosaicæ caput non postremum fuit de sanguine & suffocato. Hoc igitur juxta cætera instanter etiam urserunt. Quod urserunt Pseudapostoli, hoc ipsis negarunt Apostoli. Hoc tum Paulus seorsim, tum Apostoli in conciliari sententia declarant. Paulus Gal. II. 5. Οἳς ἐδὲ ὡς ὑπεῖξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου διαμείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Quibus ne quidem ad horam subjectione, ut veritas Evangelii apud vos permaneat. Et Synodus versu 28. Non debere discipulis onus imponi. Si quid igitur decreverunt circa sanguinem & suffocatum, non eo modo Christianos obligat, quo Judæos in V. T. obligavit, nempe per se & suâ naturâ. Alias Paulus Pseudapostolis cessisset ad horam subjectione, nec Apostoli ab ipsorum cervicibus jugum illud ἀβάστακτον depulisset. Decreverunt ergo, ut obligatio ad illa præcepta duraret ad tempus, propter scandalum & legem Charitatis, in Fratrum infirmitate sublevanda.
units.tr: II. Secondly, let us consider what question was debated in the Council, and how the Apostles settled it. The false apostles of the Jews contended that the Gentile proselytes ought to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses (vers. 1 and 6). Now the chapter of the Mosaic law on blood and what is strangled was no minor part of that law. They pressed this point urgently along with the rest. What the false apostles pressed, the Apostles denied. Paul declared this on his own, and the Apostles declared it in their conciliar decision. Paul, Gal. 2:5: To whom we did not yield by subjection, not even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you. [οἷς οὐδὲ ὡς ὑπεῖξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ εὐαγγελίου διαμείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς]. And the Synod, in vers. 28, says that no burden should be laid on the disciples. If, then, they decreed something about blood and what is strangled, it does not bind Christians in the way it bound the Jews in the Old Testament, namely per se and by its own nature. Otherwise Paul would have yielded to the false apostles by subjection, even for an hour, and the Apostles would not have removed from their necks that yoke [ἀβάστακτον]. They therefore decreed that the obligation to those precepts should last for a time, on account of scandal and the law of charity, so that the weakness of the brethren might be relieved.

units.la: III. Tertiò. Apostolus Petrus suam conclusionem simpliciter ita format: Per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi (oppositam nempe jugo illi ἀβάστακτῳ v. 10.) credimus nos servari, sicut & illi. Simpliciter abrogat totam legem, & substituit gratiam Domini Jesu Christi. Jugum legis Curcellæus accipit de statuiis Ceremonialibus. Nos moralem conjungimus. Vel igitur Sanguinis & Suffocati abstinentia pertinet ad legem moralem, vel ad Ceremonialem. Si ad moralem, cur illam Apostoli vers. 20. & 29. excipiunt ab onere ἀβαστάκτῳ, quod de lege Ceremoniali sola Curcellæus interpretatur? Imò cur mandant tam pauca, & in quibus fatente Curcellæo, interna sanctitas non vertitur? Cur non etiam cætera præcepta moralia servanda exprimunt, si ipsis institutum fuit, præcepta moralia inculcare & infigere altius? Minimè profecto consentaneum fuit, hac exceptione præceptorum paucorum moralium uti, cùm jam satis constiterit, Apostolos non hoc agere, ut præcepta moralia, quoad sunt norma & exemplar necessariæ nostræ gratitudinis & sanctitatis & Spiritualis vitæ in regeneratis, abrogentur. Si ad Ceremonialem legem pertinent, quod nos verum esse contendimus, quæro, cur igitur eadem exceptione in sua conclusione Petrus non fue-rit rit usus, si exceptio illa complectitur præcepta perpetua, necessaria, & quæ sunt lata de rebus per se & naturâ suâ illicitis, & à lege Ceremoniali exceptis? Contra, Petrus totam legem, quæ portari non potuit, opponit gratiæ Domini Jesu Christi. Hîc magnopere expeto mihi conciliari conclusionem Petri, & conclusionem Synodi, si præcepta in decreto Synodi comprehensa habent necessariam, perpetuam & inviolabilem in quocunque casu obligationem.
units.tr: III. Thirdly. The Apostle Peter states his conclusion quite simply in this way: Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ (set, that is, against that yoke [ἀβάστακτῳ] of v. 10) we believe that we are saved, just as they are. He simply abrogates the whole law and puts in its place the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Curcellæus takes the yoke to mean the ceremonial statutes. We join the moral law to them. Either, then, abstinence from blood and from what is strangled belongs to the moral law, or to the ceremonial. If to the moral, why do the Apostles in vers. 20 and 29 exempt it from the burden [ἀβαστάκτῳ], which Curcellæus interprets as referring to the ceremonial law alone? Why do they command so few things, in which, as Curcellæus admits, inner holiness does not consist? Why do they not also name the other moral precepts that are to be kept, if their purpose was to impress and press home moral precepts more deeply? It was certainly not consistent for them to use this exception of a few moral precepts, since it has already been sufficiently established that the Apostles were not aiming to abrogate the moral precepts, insofar as they are the rule and pattern of our necessary gratitude, holiness and spiritual life in the regenerate. If they belong to the ceremonial law, as we maintain is true, I ask why Peter did not use the same exception in his conclusion, if that exception embraces perpetual and necessary precepts, and those laid down about things that are unlawful by their own nature and in themselves, and that are excepted from the ceremonial law. On the contrary, Peter sets the whole law, which could not be borne, against the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Here I greatly wish to have Peter's conclusion and the Synod's conclusion reconciled for me, if the precepts contained in the Synod's decree have a necessary, perpetual and inviolable obligation in every case.

units.la: IV. Quartò. Vox ipsa ἐπάναγκες, qua utuntur Apostoli v.28. necessitatis aliquam μείων innuit, qua conjunguntur ea, quæ necessitatem minimè parem habent, ceu videre est ex iis, quæ ad versum 28. sunt à nobis observata. Quintò. Ratio decreti Conciliaris expressa est versu 21. Moses enim ab antiquis ætatibus in singulis civitatibus habet, qui ipsum prædicent, in Synagogis, ubi per omne Sabbatum legitur. Vult dicere Jacobus: Ideo necessariam esse hanc abstinentiam ab idolothytis, suffocato & sanguine, quia Moses, id est, Pentateuchus ab antiquis ætatibus in Synagogis Civitatum legitur, adeóque familiarissimè innotescit omnibus antiquitas illius de sanguine mandati, ob quam existimatum haud dubiè omnibus Noachidis imperatum esse. Ne igitur hac abrogatione subitanea plùs nimium offendantur, & exculcerentur Judæorum animi, & à Christo abalienentur, vel saltem exemplo incitentur ad eedendum cum scrupulo conscientiæ, aliquo saltem indicio superstitiosoribus illis Judæis constare debere, non hoc agi, ut Mosis vilesceret auctoritas, pro qua Zelotæ isti tanquam pro aris & focis pugnârunt, Zelo minimè contemnendo, dum scientia & salutari discretione temperaretur & dirigeretur. Quem sensum in Commentario ad hunc locum clarissimè reddidimus. Quicquid ergo injunctum Gentilibus, hac mente injunctum est, ne nimia offensione animos Judæorum, defendendæ legis studio præpostero ac præcipuè præsentis præcepti antiquitate venerabilis occæcatos, à Christo & communione Gentilium abalienarent. Non existimamus quidem Jacobi atque Synodi adeò sententiam fuisse mediam inter sententiam Petri & Pauli ac Barrabæ, pro quibus Petrus stabat, ac inter Pharisæos Zelatores legis, quod nonnullis tribuit & confutat Curcellæus, pag. 145.146. Agnoscimus enim quoad substantiam non differre sententiam Petri & Jacobi; quamvis hîc præter κύριον ἔχον prudenter monuerit & consuluerit, qua ratione inter Gentiles & Judæos conversos
units.tr: IV. Fourthly. The very word ἐπάναγκες [necessary], which the Apostles use in v. 28, points to some lessening [μείωσιν] of necessity, by which things are joined that do not have an equal necessity, as can be seen from what we observed on v. 28. Fifthly. The reason for the Council's decree is stated in v. 21: For Moses from ancient times has in every city those who preach him, in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath. James means this: this abstinence from idol-meats, from what is strangled, and from blood is necessary because Moses, that is the Pentateuch, has been read in the synagogues of the cities from ancient times, and so the antiquity of that command about blood is most familiarly known to all, and on account of it it was undoubtedly thought to have been enjoined on all the sons of Noah. Therefore, lest by this sudden abrogation the minds of the Jews be too greatly offended, and be provoked and alienated from Christ, or at least, being moved by example, yield with a scruple of conscience, it ought to be made clear to those superstitious Jews, at least by some sign, that the purpose is not to make the authority of Moses cheap. For this authority those zealots fought as for their altars and hearths, and their zeal is by no means to be despised, provided it is tempered and directed by knowledge and salutary discernment. We have set out this meaning very clearly in our Commentary on this passage. Whatever, then, was enjoined on the Gentiles was enjoined with this intention: that they should not, by excessive offence, alienate from Christ and from fellowship with the Gentiles the minds of the Jews, who were blinded by a misguided zeal for defending the law and venerable chiefly for the antiquity of this present precept. We do not indeed think that the opinion of James and of the Synod was so much a middle course between the opinion of Peter and of Paul, and of Barabbas, whom Peter stood for, and that of the Pharisees, the zealots for the law, as Curcellæus attributes to some and refutes (p. 145, 146). For we acknowledge that, as to substance, the opinion of Peter and of James does not differ. Although James here, besides [κύριον ἔχον], wisely advised and provided in what way the converted Gentiles and Jews might be joined in friendship, and mutual intercourse and the duties of charity might be preserved.

units.la: versos versus amicitiæ connecti, & constare mutua conversatio & charitatis officia possint. Hoc tamen repeto, in Curcellæi sententia nullo pacto evitari posse, quin asseratur, sententiam Jacobi vel mediam fuisse inter sententiam Petri & adversariorum, vel plane Petro oppositam. Nam Petrus legem, quam Patres non potuerunt portare, in universum antiquat, & substituit gratiam. Nihil relinquit vel novis renovandis decretis, quibus sanciantur quædam per se & suâ natura ad honestatem ac sanctitatem necessaria. Jacobus autem, & eidem suffragata Synodus, ejusmodi præcepta sancit, quæ Curcellæus interpretatur ad sanctitatem esse necessaria. Vel igitur media fuerit sententia Jacobi, & Petro quodammodo opposita, quatenus ex mente Curcellæi negat jugum Patrum penitus sublatum esse, cum obligent adhuc ad sui observantiam illæ jugi partes de Sanguine & Suffocato: vel mandata illa Jacobi & Synodi non habuerunt perpetuam & necessariam obligationem, sed temporalem & transitoriam, propter scandalum & concordiam sanciendam Fratrum. Hunc mihi scrupulum qui expediet, is Phyllida solus habeto.
units.tr: I still repeat this: on Curcellæus's opinion there is no way of avoiding the claim that the opinion of James was either a middle course between the opinion of Peter and that of the adversaries, or plainly opposed to Peter. For Peter abolishes entirely the law which the Fathers could not bear, and puts grace in its place. He leaves nothing for new decrees to renew, by which certain things that are by their own nature necessary to honesty and holiness might be sanctioned. But James, and the Synod that agreed with him, sanction precepts of the kind that Curcellæus interprets as necessary to holiness. So either the opinion of James was a middle course and in some measure opposed to Peter, insofar as, in Curcellæus's view, it denies that the yoke of the Fathers was wholly removed, since those parts of the yoke concerning blood and what is strangled still bind to their observance; or those commands of James and of the Synod did not have a perpetual and necessary obligation, but a temporary and transitory one, on account of the scandal of the brethren and for the sake of securing their concord. Whoever will untie this knot for me may keep Phyllis for himself alone.

units.la: V. Curcellæus disputat, Jacobi sententiam non fuisse mediam inter sententiam Petri & adversariorum, pag. 146. In qua re nos ipsi adversamur minimè. Utrerque enim recte definivit, legem Ceremonialem esse abrogandam. Sed Jacobus simul in Concilio habuit rationem fraternæ concordiæ. In quo consentientem haud dubiè Petrum habuit, quamvis ipse non idem fecerit: quippe cui abunde fuit ea dicere, quæ ad propositam quæstionem propriè spectant. Interim rationes Curcellæi non omnino probamus. Tres affert. Prima. Quia ne ad tempus quidem breve concedebat istis Pharisæis. Inde potius ego assumo, præcepta hæc non fuisse, nisi propter concordiam ad tempus sancita. Si enim tulisset præcepta necessaria Ceremonialia semper obligantia, quod requirebant adversarii Zelatores, tum profecto iis cessisset ad breve tempus. II. Id quod Jacobus vult observari à Gentilibus, non fuisse in controversiam vocatum: ut nec vocari potuerit, nisi ut consequens quaddam eorum, quæ controvertebantur. Sed idcirco voluisse hoc præcipi Gentilibus, quia in illo graviter illos peccare animadvertebat, pag. 146, 147. Resp. Sic supponitur falsò, Gentiles in esu sanguinis peccâsse. Probavimus, illos ad legem illam in Vet. Test. obligatos non fuisse cap. VII. thes. 23. Ubi verò lex non est, ibi nec peccatum locum habet. 2. Si Gentiles non vocârunt in controversiam, at certè Judæi, qui cæco ardore Gentiles adstrin-gere laborârunt ad praeceptum antiquissimum, quod in Noacho to-ti generi humano latum interpretabantur. 2. Si ne Judæi quidem controversum hoc fecerunt, intererat tamen Apostolicæ prudentiæ, hanc potissimum viam ad conciliationem Judæorum & Gentilium deligere. Tertia. Zelotæ istos non disputâsse de rebus opinione sua in-differentibus, sed quàm maximè necessariis. Resp. Disputarunt de tota lege, cujus universas partes tanquam observatu necessarias mordi-cus defenderunt. Apostoli autem illam abrogatum eunt penitus, & adjungunt quædam officia, per se quidem indifferentia, sed opinione Judæorum necessaria, ad charitatem & concordiam obligantia.
units.tr: V. Curcellæus argues that the opinion of James was not a middle course between the opinion of Peter and that of the adversaries (p. 146). In this matter we by no means oppose him. For each of them rightly defined that the ceremonial law is to be abrogated. But James at the same time, in the Council, took account of fraternal concord. In this he undoubtedly had Peter in agreement, although Peter himself did not do the same, since it was enough for him to say those things which properly concern the question proposed. Meanwhile we do not wholly approve Curcellæus's arguments. He brings three. The first: because he did not even grant those Pharisees a short period. From this I rather conclude that these precepts were not laid down except for a time, for the sake of concord. For if James had laid down necessary ceremonial precepts binding always, as the zealous adversaries demanded, he would surely have yielded to them for a short time. II. What James wants observed by the Gentiles was not called into controversy, nor could it have been, except as a certain consequence of the things that were disputed. But he wanted this commanded to the Gentiles because he noticed that they were sinning gravely in it (p. 146, 147). Answer: this is falsely assumed, that the Gentiles had sinned in eating blood. We have shown that they were not bound to that law of the Old Testament (ch. VII, thes. 23), and where there is no law, there sin has no place. 2. If the Gentiles did not bring this into controversy, certainly the Jews did, who with blind zeal laboured to bind the Gentiles to that most ancient precept, which they interpreted as having been given to the whole human race in Noah. 3. If not even the Jews made this a point of contention, it was still a matter for Apostolic prudence to choose this route above all others for reconciling Jews and Gentiles. The third: those zealots did not dispute about matters indifferent in their opinion, but about things as necessary as possible. Answer: they disputed about the whole law, all of whose parts they stubbornly defended as necessary to observe. The Apostles, however, abrogated it entirely, and added certain duties which, indeed, are indifferent in themselves, but are necessary in the opinion of the Jews, and bind to charity and concord.

units.la: VI. Sextò. Apostoli cum sanguine conjungunt τὸ πνικτὸν, suf-focatum. Et nos in Commentario contra Curcellæum, qui vocem il-lam ἀλισθηλον καὶ ἀποσολιμαῖον facere voluit, probavimus, illam ge-nuinam omnino esse, ac proinde ἀναμφιλέκτως recipiendam. Quin tamen edere morticinum vel suffocatum suâ naturâ licitum & in-differens sit, dubitari nequit. Et confitetur hoc aliquoties ipse Cur-cellæus. Ratio etiam evidens est, quia in Veteri Testamento Deus promisit gentilibus ejus esum. Non potest autem Deus ulli homi-ni permittere quidquam suâ naturâ turpe & illicitum. Habemus igi-tur, illa ἐπάναγκες non ἀπλῶς talia fuisse, sed κατὰ τι, & eo modo, quem in responsione nostra explicavimus. Septimò. Conjungunt etiam necessariam abstinentiam ab esu Idolothytorum. Nos autem in Commentario ad versum 29. occupavimus probare octo argu-mentis contra Curcellæum, Idolothytorum esum esse prohibitum, non quòd suâ naturâ sit turpis & illicitus, sed quòd iis temporibus non potuerit non cum maximo scandalo & periculo seductionis conjungi. Interprete sumus usi omni exceptione majore Apostolo Paulo, qui hanc rem accurate tractat capitibus octavo, nono, & de-cimo priori ad Corinthios. Non est nobis animus, quæ ibi fuse dicta sunt, hoc loco repetere. Quæ idolothytorum, eadem sangui-nis est ratio. Utrumque conjungitur. Utrumque caput fuit legis Ceremonialis in Veteri Testamento. Quæ ibi necessitatis ratio fuit, eadem hic obtinet. Sed videamus, quid respondeat ad hoc argu-mentum Curcellæus. Duo potissimum excipit. Primum. Non esse verisimile, Paulum legem illam, statim atque promulgata fuit, iuxta revoluisse, faciendo liberum, quod ibi ut necessarium fuerat prescriptum:
units.tr: VI. Sixthly. The apostles join to blood τὸ πνικτὸν [things strangled]. In my Commentary against Curcellaeus, who wanted to replace that word with ἀλισθηλον καὶ ἀποσολιμαῖον, I showed that it is wholly genuine and therefore to be received without dispute [ἀναμφιλέκτως]. Yet there can be no doubt that eating carrion or strangled meat is in its own nature lawful and indifferent. Curcellaeus himself admits this in several places. The reason is also plain: in the Old Testament God promised the Gentiles the use of it. But God cannot permit anyone anything that is shameful and unlawful in its own nature. We therefore conclude that those necessary things [ἐπάναγκες] were not unlawful absolutely, but in a certain respect, and in the way I explained in our reply. Seventhly. They also join the necessary abstinence from the meat of idol sacrifices. In my Commentary on verse 29 I undertook to prove, by eight arguments against Curcellaeus, that the eating of idol sacrifices was forbidden not because it was in its own nature base and unlawful, but because at that time it could not but be joined with the greatest scandal and danger of seduction. In this matter we have followed, beyond any exception, the Apostle Paul, who treats it carefully in the eighth, ninth and tenth chapters of his first letter to the Corinthians. I have no intention of repeating here what was said there at length. The reasoning about idol sacrifices is the same as that about blood: the two are joined together. Each was a part of the ceremonial law in the Old Testament. Whatever reason of necessity applied there applies here too. But let us see how Curcellaeus replies to this argument. He takes exception chiefly to two points. The first: it is not likely that Paul, as soon as that law was published, overturned it, making free what had been prescribed there as necessary.

units.la: cinco eâm non magnum tempus elapsum sit inter Synodum & scriptionem epi-stolarum ad Romanos & Corinthios, pag. 151.152. Resp. 1. Quantum temporis inter Synodum & Scriptionem illarum epistolarum inter-cesserit, expositum est à nobis capite octayo. Post breve temporis interstitium notoria mutatio accidere potuit, ut in eo nihil prasidii collocandum fuerit. 2. Extra calcem hic sermo decurrit. Non hoc dicimus, Paulum in suis Epistolis decretum Synodicum abrogâsse. Absit. Sed interpretatus illud est, & germano & genuino sensu in-duit. Nempe hanc fuisse decreti mentem: Liberos esse Christianos quoslibet à statutis illis Ceremonialibus & carnalibus. Cæterum, quia rebus sic comparatis libertatis illius praxis eo tempore, quo libertatem istam non omnes intellexerunt, præjudiciis nimium fasci-nati ingenti periculo constitit, præstare ut abstineant, imo propter charitatis legem necessariò illos abstinere debere. Tantum igitur abest, ut decretum Synodicum abrogaverit, ut magis etiam adstrin-xerit, facta mentione infirmorum Fratrum, quorum conscientiæ præpostero libertatis usu illaqueatæ supra modum offendantur. Sed extra eum casum plenam libertatem Christianis concessam esse declarat. Secundum. Nullum occurrere locum in epistolis Pauli aut alibi in Scripturis, in quâ expressè permittatur sanguine vesci. Quod ta-men necessum fuerit, ut aliquid valeret ad tam apertam & claram prohibitionem relaxandam, &c. pag. 153.154. Resp. Si Spiritui S. & Apostolis visum fuisset illa mandata absolutè & in qualibet circum-stantia ad tempus observanda imponere, tum, fateor, necessum suis-set alicubi aperte illorum vincula relaxari. Nunc minimè opus fuit, nec fieri potuit, cùm scriptoribus Sacris non constiterit ille tempo-ris articulus, quo cessatura fratrum infirmitas. Profitetur Paulus: Si cibus offendit fratrem meum, non comedam carnem in æternum, ne fratrem meum scandalizem, 1.Cor.VIII.13. Eadem omnium fide-lium ratio fuit, quibus in S. Scriptura prudentia & charitas insatiabi-liter commendatur. Quæ naturâ suâ turpia vel honesta sunt, illa verbo Dei sunt determinata. Sed in moderatione libertatis & re-rum indifferentium usu Deus prudentiæ imperium dedit. Parium par ratio est. Cùm igitur idolothytorum usus extra casum scandali ab Apostolo sit concessus, eadem ratione sanguinis usus extra ca-sum scandali ab ipso permissus fuerit. Neque quidquam defuit aliud, quàm occasio, qua se aptante, sicut in quæstione de idolothytis fa-stum étum est, formalibus terminis æquè libertatem Christianorum expressisset. 3. Sæpius jam animadversum, quæstionem nostram non tam de praxi libertatis, quàm de ejus jure institutam esse. Potuit autem jus constare, si vel maximè in æternum praxis vel exercitium juris illicitum & inhonestum esset, propter accidens alicujus notabilis casus. Quomodo Apostolus docet, se habere jus carnium edendarum, sed in æternum se à carnibus temperaturum, si fratrem ille esus scandalizet. Objectio igitur Curcellæi in spongiam incumbit. Negamus enim, unquam abrogari debuisse Apostolicam legem in sensu Synodi acceptam, positis ponendis, casu nempe & circumstantiis illis, quarum respectu illa Apostoli sanxerunt. Non est igitur, cur tabulas, & documenta à nobis postulet, in quibus exarata hæc abrogatio totidem verbis legitari potuit.
units.tr: Curcellaeus, pp. 151–152, says that not much time had elapsed between the Synod and the writing of the epistles to the Romans and the Corinthians. Reply, (1): how much time passed between the Synod and the writing of those epistles I have set out in chapter eight. After a short interval a notable change could have occurred, so that nothing was to be placed there as a safeguard. (2): This argument runs outside the point. We do not say that Paul abrogated the Synod's decree in his epistles. Far from it. Rather, he interpreted it and gave it its true and genuine sense. Namely, the intention of the decree was this: Christians are free from those ceremonial and carnal statutes. But since things were so arranged, the practice of that liberty at a time when not all had understood it, and were too much bound by prejudices, carried great danger; therefore it was better that they abstain, and indeed that they must necessarily abstain, on account of the law of charity. So far was the Synod's decree from being abrogated that it was even made more binding, by mention of weak brothers whose consciences, troubled by an inappropriate use of liberty, are excessively offended. Apart from that case, however, it declares that full liberty is granted to Christians. The second objection: There is no place in Paul's epistles, or elsewhere in Scripture, where the eating of blood is expressly permitted. Yet this would have been necessary, in order to relax so plain and clear a prohibition, etc. pp. 153–154. Reply: If it had seemed good to the Holy Spirit and the apostles to impose those commands to be observed absolutely and in every circumstance for a time, then, I admit, it would have been necessary for their bonds to be openly relaxed somewhere. But now there was no need, nor could it be done, since the time at which the weakness of the brothers would cease was not known to the sacred writers. Paul declares: If food offends my brother, I will never eat meat again, lest I offend my brother (1 Cor. 8:13). The reason was the same for all the faithful, to whom prudence and charity are commended without ceasing in Holy Scripture. Things that are in their nature shameful or honourable are determined by the Word of God; but in the moderation of liberty and the use of indifferent things God gave the rule to prudence. Equal cases are treated equally. Since the use of idol sacrifices, outside the case of scandal, was permitted by the Apostle, by the same reasoning the use of blood, outside the case of scandal, was permitted by him. Nothing was lacking except an occasion which, when it arose, as happened in the question of idol sacrifices, would have expressed the liberty of Christians equally in formal terms. (3): It has been noted often already that our question concerns not so much the practice of liberty as its right. But a right could stand even if the practice or exercise of the right were, for ever, unlawful and dishonourable on account of some notable accident. So the Apostle teaches that he has the right to eat meat, but that he would abstain from meat for ever if that eating should scandalize a brother. Curcellaeus's objection therefore comes to nothing. For we deny that the apostolic law, understood in the sense of the Synod, ever ought to have been abrogated, when the conditions and circumstances for which the apostles enacted those things are assumed. There is therefore no reason for him to demand charters and documents in which this abrogation could have been set down in so many words.

units.la: VII. Octavo denique non alienum ab instituto fuerit, ut ad rectæ rationis libellam exigantur verba illa Synodi. Visum est Spiritui Sancto ET NOBIS, nec non sequentia: à quibus si vos conservaveritis, BENE FACIETIS. Hæc enim ejusmodi sunt, ut consilium potius præferant, cui in hac vel illa circumstantia necessario obsequendum sit, quàm necessarium aliquod & Catholicum præceptum. Non absimilis est locutio Pauli, 1. Cor. cap. VII. vers. 7. Hoc dico κατὰ συγγνώμην, non κατ' ἐπιταγήν. Volo omnes homines esse sicut ego sum, vers. 40. Beatior est vidua si sic manserit, κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην. Ex quibus verbis nemo, nisi fallor, conficiet, illam Apostoli sententiam de cœlibatu, qui bonus & necessarius pene erat, propter ἐπιστασιν ἀνάγκην, esse præceptum universale & perpetuum. Nam satis declaravit in hoc articulo libertatem Christianorum. Sic hoc loco Lucas distinguit ἐπιταγὴν & συγγνώμην: illam in verbis: Visum est Spiritui Sancto: hanc in sequentibus: Et nobis, ἔπιγνωσιν, pertinet ad articulum fidei, de justificatione per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi, & abrogatione legis. Συγγνώμη vero Apostolorum præsenti conditioni Ecclesiæ consulentium, ad mandata illa ἀπέχεσθαι de Sanguine, idolothytis, Suffocato. Sic etiam verba quæ sequuntur: Si ab his vos conservaveritis, BENE FACIETIS. Hæc sunt verba magis consulentium prudenter, quàm præceptum aliquod perpetuum, nullo casu violabile, dictantium. Nam præcepta absolutè necessaria propter internam quandam Sanctitatem, rigidius imperari solent. VIII. His
units.tr: VII. Lastly, it would not be out of place for the words of the Synod to be weighed by the standard of right reason: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit AND TO US, and the following: If you keep yourselves from these things, YOU WILL DO WELL. For these words are of such a kind that they present advice, which must be followed in this or that circumstance, rather than some necessary and universal precept. Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7:7 is not dissimilar: I say this by concession [κατὰ συγγνώμην], not by command [κατ' ἐπιταγήν]. I wish all men to be as I am (v. 40). She is happier if she remains so, according to my opinion [κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην]. From these words no one, unless I am mistaken, will conclude that the Apostle's judgment about celibacy, which was good and almost necessary because of the present necessity [ἐπίστασιν ἀνάγκην], is a universal and perpetual precept. For he sufficiently declared the liberty of Christians on this point. So here Luke distinguishes command [ἐπιταγήν] from concession [συγγνώμην]: the former in the words It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, the latter in what follows, and to us, [ἐπίγνωσιν], which pertains to the article of faith concerning justification through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the abrogation of the law. The concession [συγγνώμη] of the apostles, however, consults the present condition of the Church, regarding those commands to abstain [ἀπέχεσθαι] from blood, idol sacrifices and what is strangled. So also the words that follow: If you keep yourselves from these things, YOU WILL DO WELL. These are words of people giving prudent counsel rather than dictating some perpetual precept, admitting of no violation in any case. For precepts that are absolutely necessary on account of some inner holiness are usually imposed more rigidly.

units.la: VIII. His argumentis, confido, apud modestos, & quorum animo veri & recti cupido penitius sedet, communi Theologorum nostrorum responso ad objectionem ex Apostolica Synodo petitam, fidem abunde nos facturos. Caeterum quae adversarii ex Synodo illa presfius contra nos urgent, facile quidem solvi ex iis possunt, quae in Commentario a nobis sunt adnotata. Ne tamen vel hic vadimonium deserere videamur, carptim & stringendo diluemus, quae a Curcellaeo & Becmanno instantiae hic nobis obducuntur. Objiciunt igitur.
units.tr: VIII. With these arguments, I trust, we shall amply satisfy modest readers, and those whose minds are more deeply possessed by a desire for what is true and right, that the common answer of our theologians to the objection drawn from the apostolic Synod is well founded. Yet the points which our opponents press harder against us from that Synod can easily be resolved from what I have noted in the Commentary. Nevertheless, so as not to seem to be deserting the cause even here, I shall briefly and concisely answer the objections which Curcellaeus and Becmann throw up against us here. They object, then:

units.la: I. Omnia mandata Dei tanquam perpetuae durationis amplexi debemus, nisi Deus nobis contrarium alibi declaraverit. Quod natura ejus docet, qui nulli mutationi est obnoxius. Ego Dominus, & non mutor, Malach. III. 6. Curcell. pag. 140. Repf. Mandatum de Sanguine & Suffocato consideratur vel ratione materiae, vel ratione finis. Ratione materiae fuit necessarium, & constanter duravit usque ad tempus correctionis, quod fuit tempus Messiae. Eo autem tempore Deus declaravit, abrogari debere, cum adesset corpus Christus, quem illae v. 5. umbrae respexerunt. Pertinuit enim Sanguis ad expiationem in Sacrificiis. In Novo autem Testamento totus ille Sacrificiorum cultus abolitus, & substitutum Sacerdotium Christi, qui semel immolatus est ad multa peccata auferenda, Hebr. IX. 28. Ad de omnia argumenta, quae capite octavo deduximus, ex quibus meridiano jubare clarius est, Deum noluisse, ut obligatio ad hoc Praeceptum sit perpetuae durationis. Ratione finis, quatenus inservit Christianae charitati, cui oppositum est infirmi fratris conscientiam verberare, non est abrogata, sed durat ejus obligatio, quamdiu casus tales emergunt. Extra verò casum scandali non durat, neque unquam est abrogata, vel abrogabitur etiam, quia in hoc sensu sancita non fuit.
units.tr: I. We ought to embrace all the commands of God as of perpetual duration, unless God has declared otherwise elsewhere. His nature teaches this, for he is subject to no change. "I am the Lord, and I do not change" (Mal. 3:6). Curcellaeus, p. 140. Reply: The command concerning blood and what is strangled is to be considered either in respect of its matter or in respect of its end. In respect of its matter it was necessary, and it lasted constantly until the time of correction, which was the time of the Messiah. At that time, however, God declared that it must be abrogated, since the body of Christ was present, to which those shadows (v. 5) looked. For blood pertained to expiation in the sacrifices. But in the New Testament that whole cult of sacrifices has been abolished, and the priesthood of Christ has been substituted, who was offered once to bear the sins of many (Heb. 9:28). To all the arguments which I drew out in chapter eight, from which it is clearer than midday sunlight that God did not wish the obligation to this precept to be of perpetual duration, I add this. In respect of its end, insofar as it serves Christian charity, to which it is opposed to wound the conscience of a weak brother, it has not been abrogated, but its obligation lasts as long as such cases arise. Outside the case of scandal, however, it does not last, nor has it ever been abrogated, nor will it be, because it was not sanctioned in this sense.

units.la: IX. II. Nullum habemus exemplum decreti alicujus solenniter facti, ut ad breve tantum tempus durare deberet. Curcel. ibid. Respondeo. Cum umbra luctatur. Negamus ad breve tempus durare debuisse decretum, in Synodi sensu acceptum. Si vel hodie locum haberent circumstantiae, quae tempore Apostolorum, validissime nos constringeret, ut juri nostro renuntiaremus. III. Vellem scire ex iis, qui dicunt, interdictum ad tempus tantum obligasse, quantum fuerit illud tempus, seu quandiu Christianos eo obligatos fuisse existimerent. Ff mente. Quod nemo definire aggreditur, quin se in magnas angustias conjiciat. Curcel. pag. 142. Respondeo. 1. Vellem scire, quamdiu lex de Suffocato & idolothytis obligaverit, quàm certum & explora-tum est perpetuae durationis non fuisse. 2. Tempus, quo desinit obli-gatio, noverit ille, qui compertum habet, qua tempestate evanue-rit periculum scandali, ortum ex infirmitate Fratrum, qui libertatem Filiorum Dei in Novo Testamento nondum aestimare didicerunt. Ad historicorum subsellia pertinet isthaec judicatio. IV. Si obligavit hac lex quamdiu fuerunt, infirmi, tum obligat adhuc hodie. Nam multi sunt nunc Christiani, qui istius mandati transgressione offendun-tur, non tantum omnes Graeci, qui ideo Occidentales vocant, αἱματοφάγους, sed etiam multi pii & religiosi homines in Germania, Gallia, & Anglia. Ne quid dicam de Judaeis in medio nostri habitantibus. Curcel. pag. 143. Respondeo. 1. Esto, obliget hodie ratione scandali. Non nocet hoc juri libertatis, sed exercitio. Res in se maximè indifferentes, in electione tamen malè fiunt, quando cum offendiculo proximi ea est conjuncta. Semper ad aedificationem, quando quippiam instituitur, est respiciendum. Non sumus nati nobis ipsis tantum, sed Christo, Ecclesiae atque proximis. 2. Alia ratio fuit Apostolicorum temporum, alia nostrorum. Illa inciderunt in incunabula Christianismi, ad quem Judaei cum recens converterentur, veterem suam religionem in externi cultus Ministerio cum nova commutare debuerunt. Hìc non potuit evitari, quin varie afficerentur, animo aliquandiu fluctuarent, & anticipites consilii haererent. Quamobrem fas & pium fuit, tamdiu illorum infirmitatem sublevare quoad majorem notitiam proveherentur. Nostrorum temporum quae similis ratio esse potest? Quando in Judaismo Christiani non sunt educti, non praejudiciis ejusmodi à longa consuetudine capti, sed de voluntate Dei plenissimè in Evangelio edocti. 3. Si qui sunt inter Christianos verè infirmi, qui nondum libertatem Evangelii animo complectuntur, qui nostra abstinentia aedificari possunt, quis dubitat, quin iis haec charitas praestari debeat, ne temerè eorum conscientia cibo nostro laedatur. 4. Quoad Graecos, illi non infirmis, sed fortibus sunt annumerandi. Insultant enim graviter Occidentalibus, eos in hac causa judicant, & atrocibus censuris perstringunt: libertatem eam, quam habemus in Christo, insidiis appetunt, & abstinentiam à sanguine tanquam necessarium fidei articulum à nobis postulant: stulant: quod videre est in eorum conciliis & canonibus. In eorum igitur gratiam abstinere esset libertatem prodere, beneficia Christi contemnere, hominum nos servituti addicere, συνυποζεύγνυ-σθαι ἀλλ᾽ ἐὰν μὴ ἐφ᾽ ὅμοιο-ν τὰς ἀληθείας τῆς Εὐαγγελίας, Galat. II. v. 14. Multa sunt natura sua indifferentia, quae in necessariis mutarunt Graeci. Qui tamen illos imitari vellet gratia scandali vitandi, is in Syrtes proclivi gradu incideret, Charybdin nequicquam fugiens. Sufficere debet, quod illos a nobis dissentientes non damnamus, Judaismum non objicimus, sed errorem in iis toleramus. 5. De Judaeis diximus cap. VIII. sect. 6. quo remittimus lectorem. Huic enim praesenti objectioni satis ibi occurrimus. Miror hac ratione non etiam porcinam Christianis interdici, & caeteros cibos, quos pro immundis Judaei habent, ne scilicet nostra libertate boni illi & infirmi Fratres, plus aequo offensi, inanceps desiliant.
units.tr: IX. II. We have no example of any decree solemnly enacted that was meant to last only a short time. Curcellaeus, ibid. I answer: he is fighting a shadow. We deny that the decree, taken in the sense of the Council, was meant to last only a short time. If the circumstances that existed in the Apostles' time were present today, they would bind us just as strongly to give up our right. III. I should like to know from those who say that the prohibition obliged only for a time, how long that time was, or how long they believe Christians were bound by it. Which no one undertakes to define without putting himself in great difficulty. Curcellaeus, p. 142. I answer: (1) I should like to know how long the law about what is strangled and what is offered to idols obliged, since it is clear and established that it was not meant to last forever. (2) The point at which the obligation ends will be known to the one who has found out when the danger of scandal, arising from the weakness of the brethren who had not yet learned to value the freedom of the sons of God in the New Testament, passed away. That judgment belongs to the benches of the historians. IV. If this law obliged as long as there were weak people, then it still obliges today. For there are now many Christians who are offended by the breaking of this command: not only all the Greeks, whom for this reason the Westerners call blood-eaters, but also many pious and devout people in Germany, France and England. Not to mention the Jews living among us. Curcellaeus, p. 143. I answer: (1) Grant that it still binds today on account of scandal. That does not harm the right of liberty, but only its exercise. Things that are in themselves wholly indifferent become wrong in the choosing when they are joined with a stumbling block to a neighbour. We must always look to edification when we undertake anything. We are not born for ourselves alone, but for Christ, the Church and our neighbours. (2) The reason in the time of the Apostles was different from ours. Those people lived at the cradle of Christianity. Jews who were newly converted had to exchange their old religion, with its ministry of external worship, for the new one. Here it could not be avoided that they were variously affected, wavered in mind for a while and hung in doubt about what to do. Therefore it was right and proper to relieve their weakness for as long as it took for them to advance to greater knowledge. What similar reason can there be in our time? Christians are not brought up in Judaism, nor held captive by such prejudices from long custom, but are fully taught the will of God in the Gospel. (3) If there are any among Christians who are truly weak, who have not yet embraced the freedom of the Gospel in their minds, and who can be built up by our abstinence, who doubts that this charity should be shown to them, so that their conscience is not rashly wounded by our food? (4) As for the Greeks, they should not be counted among the weak but among the strong. For they bitterly insult the Westerners, judge them in this matter and attack them with savage censures. They seek by snares to take away the liberty we have in Christ, and they demand abstinence from blood from us as a necessary article of faith. This can be seen in their councils and canons. To abstain for their sake would therefore be to betray liberty, to despise the benefits of Christ, and to make ourselves slaves to men: to be yoked together with them, but unless [they walk] in accordance with the truth of the Gospel [συνυποζεύγνυσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἐὰν μὴ ἐφ᾽ ὅμοιον τὰς ἀληθείας τῆς Εὐαγγελίου], Galatians 2:14. Many things that are indifferent by nature the Greeks have turned into necessities. Yet anyone who wished to imitate them for the sake of avoiding scandal would fall into the Syrtes by a steep slope, while trying in vain to flee Charybdis. It should be enough that we do not condemn those who differ from us, that we do not charge them with Judaism, but tolerate their error. (5) We have spoken about the Jews in chapter VIII, section 6, to which we refer the reader. For there we have sufficiently met this present objection. I am surprised that by the same argument pork is not also forbidden to Christians, and the other foods which the Jews regard as unclean, lest those good and weak brethren, too much offended by our liberty, leap headlong into doubt.

units.la: XV. Decretum hoc authoritate ipsius Spiritus Sancti conciperetur, v. 28.
units.tr: XV. This decree was framed by the authority of the Holy Spirit himself, v. 28.

units.la: Bermannus pag. 584. Apparet, quanta authoritatis debeat istud decretum esse, quod non proprie ab ipsis hominibus, sed ab ipso Spiritu Sancto, quo regebantur Apostoli, dictatum sit. Nam si magni facimus singulos Novi Testamenti libros, quia persuasi sumus scriptores illorum a Spiritu Sancto fuisse inspiratos: quanto magis hoc epistolion, quod tot magni viri, Spiritu Sancto pleni, dictaverunt? proinde non est ullo pacto vero simile, in eo solum agi de rebus indifferentibus, & quae ad exiguum tempus, vitandi scandali causa, observari debuerunt. Curcell. pag. 109. Resp. Spiritus Sancti praecepta non omnia sunt perpetua & de rebus natura sua necessariis. Quis enim statuta Ceremonialia Veteris Testamenti neget authore Spiritu Sancto edita esse? Et tamen neque perpetua fuerunt, neque de rebus per se necessariis, sed de rebus natura sua maxime differentibus. 2. In Commentario diximus ἐπιστολή sive articulum fidei de abrogatione legis, referri debere ad authorem Spiritum Sanctum; συγχώρησις de necessaria abstinentia idolothytorum, sanguinis, &c. ad Apostolos, quibus datum est fidelibus esse in domo Dei. Atque hanc esse rationem distinctionis: Visum Spiritui Sancto & nobis. Quanquam non est negandum, Apostolos impulsu Spiritus Sancti haec praecepta tulisse: Hoc tantum contendimus, non habuisse illos speciale mandatum Christi, vel Dei, sed φερομένης πνεύματι ἁγίῳ in rebus his disposuisse. Quomodo Paulus salutaria quaedam monita & consilia Corinthiis dedepromsit, de quibus tamen non habuit speciale mandatum Christi, poterat nihilominus dicere: Ἀοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα Θεοῦ ἔχειν. 2.Cor.VII.25.40. Sic propheta Nathan dicit Davidi: Vade, & quicquid est in corde tuo, fac, quoniam Dominus est tecum, 2.Sam.VII.3. Eodem modo Apostoli potuerunt sapienter ea mandare, quae ad salutem Ecclesiae spectant, quamvis speciali mandato Christi ad id non incitarentur. 3. Patimur decreto huic Synodico magnam authoritatem constare in eo sensu, qui fuit ab authoribus Apostolis intentus. Hoc tantum negamus, mentem Apostolorum, ut obligent haec mandata in quacunque circumstantia, etiam extra offendiculi casum. Nihil igitur ad rem faciunt, quae hic Curcellaeus obvertit, sed pro amphora urceus, ut ajunt. VI. Ea, quae decernunt hic Apostoli, vocant necessaria. v.28. Becman.l.c. Non potuerunt validius obligare in perpetuum fideles ad sibi abstinendum, quam necessaria vocando. Curcell. pag.112.113. Resp. Res non uno modo necessarias esse, non ignorant viri. Aliae natura sua necessariae. Aliae ex hypothesi efficientis, finis, eventus, adjuncti &c. Et tamen ex nuda voce non verentur tam imbelle argumentum cudere. Non dicam, non simpliciter haec praecepta ἀναγκαῖα vocari, sed τὰ ἐπάναγκες, quae vox notat μεῖωσιν, quemadmodum in Commentario dictum. Sic necessarium olim fuit abstinere a fructu arboris scientiae boni & mali. An iccirco praeceptum illud perpetuum fuit? VII. Distinguunt Apostoli idco inter legem Ceremoniales, quas vocant onus, & inter morales, quas Gentibus conversis praescribunt, verf.28. Becman.l.c. Resp. Miror, haec mandata praeceptis moralibus adjungi, cum praecepta moralia ratione suae materiae semper nobis virtualem aliquam sanctitatis Divinae partem repraesentent, haec autem sancita sint tantum Ἐν βρώ-μασι καὶ πόμασι, Hebr.IX.10. Saltem legem de Suffocato comedendo, quam Becmannus, secus quam Curcellaeus fecit, agnoscit geminam, nulla probabili ratione moralem facere potest, cum ab ejus obligatione in Veteri Testamento Gentiles relaxati fuerint. 2.Vocant quidem Apostoli legem ceremonialem onus, quatenus & dura fuit & difficilis observatu, & propter ejus neglectum ubique & semper judicari potuerunt. Atque hactenus illius oneris pars fuit abstinere a sanguine & Suffocato. Apostoli autem postliminio sanxerunt illam abstinentiam, non quatenus fuit pars oneris, quomodo Deus in V.T. mandavit, sed quatenus in casu scandali charitati ChriChristianae ministravit. VIII. Esum Sanguinis & Suffocati æquiparant scortationi. Becman. l. c. Scortationem prohibitam esse non solum propter offendiculum, sed etiam, quia in se mala est, omnes Christiani ultro largiuntur. Quidni ergo idem dicamus de sanguine, cujus abstinentia tanquam pariter necessaria ab Apostolis in eodem commate nobis commendatur? Junxisse enim res adeo diverse naturæ, ut istas esse velint absque ulla limitatione? Curcell. pag. 12. Respondeo, 1. Conjungi ea, quæ disparem plane habent obligationis ac necessitatis rationem, neque alienum profecto nec novum est. Deut. VI. 1. Hæc sunt præcepta & statuta & judicia, quæ præcepit Dominus Deus Vester. Per מִשְׁפָּטִים intelliguntur præcepta moralia, per חֻקִּים Ceremonialia, per מִשְׁפָּטִים forensia, in quo consentiunt Interpretes. Quis eandem necessitatem & in obligatione durationem in his omnibus statuere ausit? Exod. XX. 9. Memento diei Sabbathi: non facies opus, &c. Conjunguntur duo, quorum prius Ceremoniale, posterius morale. In Veteri Testamento nihil pœne frequentius, quam conjunctio præceptorum moralium & Ceremonialium. Hebr. VI. 1. 2. Nec rursus fundamentum jaciamus pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis, & fidei in Deum, baptismatum doctrina, ac manuum impositionis, & resurrectionis mortuorum & judicii æterni. Singula hæc parem necessitatem non habere in propatulo est. Ergo conjunguntur, quæ imparem necessitatem habent, ab Apostolis, quia hoc exigebat occasio & circumstantiarum ratio. 2. In Commentario excusimus, quomodo conjungatur cum rebus natura sua indifferentibus fornicatio. Nempe quatenus fornicatio in Polygamia & divortiis, tum a Judæis, tum a Gentilibus non est in vitiis numerata, sed libera & indifferens utrinque habita. Hinc Apostoli necesse habuerunt illam prohibere, & turpitudinem ejus ostendere vel hac ratione, quod licentia illa divortiorum sit vera μοιχεία, verbo Dei & sensu omnium Gentium damnata. 3.
