Non multo deterius vitium est scandalum, temere & maligne fratribus infirmis objectum. Hinc Christus tam grave supplicium homini illi intendit, per quem scandalum venit, Matth. XVIII. 7. Cum igitur præceptum illud de sanguine in eo demum casu offendiculi obliget, atque adeo propter scandalum vitandum, patet, non sine ratione conjuncta esse præcepta, quorum violatio est cum pari gravitate reatus, neque turpitudine multum disparata. IX. Hoc decretum Epistola Synodica comprehendunt, & per viros primarios Judæ dam & Silam solemniter miserunt. Becman.1.c. Resp. Quis decreti Apostolici authoritatem, cui sanum sinciput est, vellicare ausit? Non agitur hoc, ut decretum a quopiam in dubium revocetur, & ejus gravitas, sed ut implicatum decreti sensus evolvatur, & genuina Apostolorum mens deprehendatur. X. Idem decretum subinde legitur repetitum, Act.XV.32, XVI.4. XXI.25. Becman.1.c. Resp. Decretum Apostolicum non frustra est conditum. Quid miremur ergo, quod subinde repetitum & inculcatum Gentilibus fuit? Sed qui hoc scopum ferit? Fatemur, magnam vim fuisse decreti omnibus promulgandi. Iccirco in canonem divinum etiam a Spiritu Sancto receptum. De hac re minime controvertitur, sed de genuino decreti sensu.
units.tr: Bermannus, p. 584. It is clear how great the authority of this decree must be, since it was dictated not properly by the men themselves but by the Holy Spirit himself, by whom the Apostles were ruled. For if we hold each single book of the New Testament in high regard, because we are persuaded that its writers were inspired by the Holy Spirit, how much more should we regard this letter, which so many great men, full of the Holy Spirit, dictated? Therefore it is in no way likely that it deals only with indifferent matters, and with things that were to be observed for a short time for the sake of avoiding scandal. Curcellaeus, p. 109. Answer: not all the precepts of the Holy Spirit are perpetual or concern things that are necessary by their own nature. For who would deny that the ceremonial statutes of the Old Testament were issued under the authorship of the Holy Spirit? And yet they were neither perpetual nor concerned with things necessary in themselves, but with things that by nature differ greatly. (2) In the commentary we said that the letter, or article of faith, concerning the abrogation of the law should be referred to the Holy Spirit as author; the concession [συγχώρησις] concerning the necessary abstinence from things offered to idols, from blood, and so on, should be referred to the Apostles, to whom it was given to be in the house of God for the faithful. And this is the basis of the distinction: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Although it must not be denied that the Apostles issued these precepts under the impulse of the Holy Spirit, we only contend that they did not have a special command from Christ or God, but ordered these things moved by the Holy Spirit [φερομένης πνεύματι ἁγίῳ]. Just as Paul gave the Corinthians certain wholesome admonitions and counsels, for which he nevertheless had no special command from Christ, yet he could still say: I think that I also have the Spirit of God [δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ πνεῦμα θεοῦ ἔχειν], 1 Corinthians 7:40. So the prophet Nathan said to David: Go, do all that is in thy heart, for the LORD is with thee, 2 Samuel 7:3. In the same way the Apostles could wisely enjoin those things that concern the salvation of the Church, even though they were not moved to do so by a special command of Christ. (3) We allow that great authority belongs to this synodal decree in the sense that was intended by the Apostles who wrote it. We only deny that the mind of the Apostles was that these commands should bind in every circumstance, even outside the case of stumbling. Therefore what Curcellaeus here objects has nothing to do with the matter, and is, as they say, a jug offered for an amphora. VI. What the Apostles decree here they call necessary. Verse 28. Becanus, loc. cit. They could not have bound the faithful more strongly, to abstain from these things for ever, than by calling them necessary. Curcellaeus, pp. 112–113. Answer: learned men are not unaware that things are necessary in more than one way. Some are necessary by their own nature, others from the hypothesis of the agent, the end, the outcome, the attendant circumstances, and so on. And yet they do not hesitate to build such a feeble argument on the bare word. I will not say that these precepts are called simply necessary [ἀναγκαῖα], but things needful [τὰ ἐπάναγκες], a word that marks a qualification [μείωσιν], as was said in the commentary. So it was once necessary to abstain from the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Does it follow that that precept was perpetual? VII. For this reason the Apostles distinguish between the ceremonial laws, which they call a burden, and the moral laws, which they prescribe to the converted Gentiles, verse 28. Becanus, loc. cit. Answer: I am surprised that these commands are joined to the moral precepts, since moral precepts, by reason of their subject matter, always present to us some virtual part of divine holiness, whereas these were enacted only in meats and drinks [ἐν βρώμασι καὶ πόμασι], Hebrews 9:10. At least the law about eating what is strangled, which Becanus, unlike Curcellaeus, acknowledges as twofold, cannot be made moral by any probable reasoning, since the Gentiles were released from its obligation in the Old Testament. (2) The Apostles do indeed call the ceremonial law a burden, insofar as it was both hard and difficult to observe, and because it could be judged in every place and at all times by neglect of it. And so far, abstaining from blood and from what is strangled was part of that burden. But the Apostles restored that abstinence by a new enactment, not insofar as it was part of the burden, as God commanded in the Old Testament, but insofar as in a case of scandal it served the Christian charity. VIII. They equate the eating of blood and of what is strangled with fornication. Becanus, loc. cit. That fornication is forbidden not only because of the stumbling block, but also because it is evil in itself, all Christians willingly grant. Why then should we not say the same of blood, whose abstinence is commended to us in the same verse as equally necessary by the Apostles? Or did they join things of such different natures in order that they should be taken without any limitation? Curcellaeus, p. 12. Answer: (1) It is neither foreign nor new that things which have a plainly different reason of obligation and necessity should be joined together. Deuteronomy 6:1: These are the commandments and the statutes and the judgments, which the LORD your God commanded. By the word for judgments [מִשְׁפָּטִים] are understood the moral precepts, by the word for statutes [חֻקִּים] the ceremonial, and by the word for judgments [מִשְׁפָּטִים] the forensic, in which the interpreters agree. Who would dare to assert the same necessity and duration of obligation for all these? Exodus 20:8–9: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy... thou shalt not do any work, etc. Two things are joined, of which the first is ceremonial and the second moral. In the Old Testament there is almost nothing more frequent than the joining of moral and ceremonial precepts. Hebrews 6:1–2: Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. It is plain that these single items do not have equal necessity. Therefore things that have unequal necessity are joined together by the Apostles, because the occasion and the nature of the circumstances required it. (2) In the commentary we explained how fornication is joined with things that are indifferent by nature. Namely, insofar as fornication in polygamy and divorces was not counted among the vices, either by the Jews or by the Gentiles, but was held to be free and indifferent on both sides. Hence the Apostles had to forbid it and show its shamefulness, even on this ground, that that licence of divorce is true adultery, condemned by the Word of God and by the sense of all nations. (3) Scandal, rashly and maliciously thrown in the way of weak brethren, is no much less grave a vice. Hence Christ threatened such a grievous punishment against the man through whom scandal comes, Matthew 18:7. Since, then, that precept concerning blood binds only in that case of stumbling, and therefore for the sake of avoiding scandal, it is clear that the precepts were joined not without reason, the violation of which carries an equal weight of guilt and is not greatly different in baseness. IX. This decree the Synodal Letter contains, and it was solemnly sent by the leading men Judas and Silas. Becanus, loc. cit. Answer: who would dare to pluck at the authority of the Apostolic decree, to which every sound mind is devoted? This is not done to call the decree into question by anyone, or to question its weight, but so that the entangled sense of the decree may be unfolded and the genuine mind of the Apostles may be grasped. X. The same decree is read again and again repeated, Acts 15:32, 16:4, 21:25. Becanus, loc. cit. Answer: the Apostolic decree was not framed in vain. Why then should we wonder that it was repeated and impressed again and again on the Gentiles? But who aims at this point? We admit that the decree had great force for being published to all. For this reason it was also received by the Holy Spirit into the divine canon. On this matter there is no dispute at all, but about the genuine sense of the decree.

units.la: CAPUT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Argumentum à consentiente Antiquitate ventilatur, & peroratur.
units.tr: The argument from the consenting antiquity is discussed and brought to a conclusion.

units.la: Breviarium.
units.tr: Summary.

units.la: Argumentum ab Antiquitate pericum examinatur. Distinguitur antiquitas. Ostenditur dispar ratio primorum temporum & hodiernorum. Iudaeorum frequentior olim conversio, quàm hodiè. 1. Augustini locus producitur & defenditur ab objectionibus Curcellaei. Baptismus in aspersione vindicatur. Evanthus, Hieronymus, Nicolaus I. consentientes introducuntur. 2.3. Suffragia Tertulliani, Minutii Felicis, Biblidis foeminae, Clementis Alexandrini, Authoris quaestionum & responsionum, Origenis, Canonum Apostolicorum, Concilii Gangrensis, Aurelianensis secundi, Constantinopolitani Sexti, Cyrilli Hierosolymitani, Chrysostomi, Leonis Sophi examinantur. 4-8. Graecorum quorundam liberè sanguinem edentium praxis ex Petro Antiocheno & Balsamone ostenditur, & peroratur. 8.
units.tr: The argument from antiquity is examined. Antiquity is distinguished. The different situations of the earliest times and of the present are shown. Jews were converted more often in the past than now. 1. A passage of Augustine is produced and defended against the objections of Curcellaeus. Baptism by sprinkling is vindicated. Evanthius, Jerome and Pope Nicholas I are introduced as agreeing. 2, 3. The testimonies of Tertullian, Minucius Felix, the woman Biblis, Clement of Alexandria, the author of the Questions and Answers, Origen, the Apostolic Canons, the Council of Gangra, the Second Council of Orléans, the Sixth Council of Constantinople, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom and Leo the Wise are examined. 4-8. The practice of certain Greeks who freely eat blood is shown from Peter of Antioch and Balsamon, and the matter is concluded. 8.

units.la: I. Tandem
units.tr: I. At last

units.la: I. TArdem veniendum ad argumentum petitum à sensu antiquitatis. Curcellæus pro se jactat universæ Ecclesiæ Christianæ consensum, quæ Apostolicam istam constitutionem semper habuerit pro æternæ durationis præcepto, quod ante ultimum adventum Christi abrogari non debeat. Et addit. Siquo in dogmate gloriari licet, de traditionis universitate & constantia, istud est, vel inter prima, sanguine non licere vesci, pag. 155 Respondeo. 1. Scitum quidem est Tertulliani effatum contra Praxeam: Id verum quodcunque prius: id adulterinum quodcunque posterius. Antiquitas enim prima rerum origo est, & natura, quam res unaquæque sortitur. Hæc autem talis, qualis esse debuit, nempe vera, & consistit in revelatione infallibili Dei, Prophetarum, Christi & Apostolorum. In hanc antiquitatem omnis refundi debet certitudo. Hinc Ignatius in epist. 6. quæ ad Philadelph. memorat, sibi à quibusdam objectum: Ἐὰν μὴ ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις εὕρω τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον, οὐ πιστεύω. Nisi in antiquis Evangelium invenero, non credam. Quibus ita respondet: Ἐμοὶ ἀρχεῖα ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς, ὁ ἀπαράβατος σταυρὸς αὐτοῦ θάνατος καὶ ἀνάστασις. Mihi pro archivis est Jesus Christus, cui non parere manifestum est exitium. Justinus Apolog. 1. 1.46. τὸ ἐθη τῆς ἀληθείας ὑμῶν, τῶν ἀνοήτων, consuetudinem ante veritatem habere illos, qui sunt imperiti & amentes. Nempe antiquior omnibus Deus, Christus, Veritas. Cum igitur voluntatem Evangelii ex antiquissimis scripturis, nempe verbo Dei explicatam & evolutam dederimus, non est cur curæ cordique habeamus, quæ dixerint vel fecerint illi, qui nos vel remoto vel exiguo intervallo præiverunt. Ubi enim doctrina certa ab incerta est discernenda, malè provocatur ad τὸ πατρικὸν δόγμα, ad antiquitatem eorum, qui inde sapere debuerunt, unde & nos. 2. Nisi firmiter approbatur in eo sensu esum sanguinis ab antiquitate damnatum esse, in quo nos illum licitum esse contendimus, plus omnino erit in opinione, quam in calculo. Quid enim? An pia antiquitas, Concilia, Patres, quorum venerabilis est nobis authoritas, non potuerunt ideo esum sanguinis damnare, quod viderent, non expedire, non ædificare, charitati nocere, offensionem generare? An ideo damnare tantum potuit, quia res per se mala & illicita, & olim in Veteri Testamento prohibita, & Christianæ libertati contraria? Quidnam facere potuerit studio Ecclesiæ amplificandæ, & sanciendæ concordiæ tum Gentilium tum Judæorum, qui circa ea tempora ampliori accessione Ecclesiam Christianam beârunt, quàm hodierno tempore, quo vix unus & alter ex Judæis ad nos convertitur, justo Dei judicio, quo magis magisque ob infidelitatem tum Parentum, tum suam ipsorum illis crescit & effertur pertinax superstitionis ingenium, ac vix in nostram pietatem, quantumcunque simulent, sincerè mutabile. Notum ex historiis, Seculo adhuc quinto ex Judæis nonnullos ad Christum conversos. Cùm enim Alexandriâ plurimi Judæi expellerentur à Cyrillo, Adamantius Medicus Constantinopolin ad Atticum profectus est, & Christianam religionem est professus, teste Socrate Hist. Eccles. VII. 13. Cúmque Pseudo-Moses Cretensis, incarnatus dæmon, nefandis fraudibus grassatus, Judæos, spe reductionis in terram Canaan lactatos, miserabili clade affecisset, πολλοὶ τῶν ἐν Κρήτῃ Ἰουδαίων ἐχειραντο, multi Judaeorum Creta Christiani facti sunt, commemorante eodem Socrate VII. 37. De Attico Judaeo vide Zonaram l. 3. pag. 34. De Judaeo Duditho, qui Alexandriae sub Anastasio conversus, historiam recitat Elmacinus. Hodie ejusmodi proselythi sinceri sunt phoenicë rariores.
units.tr: I. At last we must come to the argument taken from the sense of antiquity. Curcellaeus boasts of the agreement of the whole Christian Church, which has always held this Apostolic constitution to be a precept of everlasting duration, one that is not to be abrogated before the last coming of Christ. And he adds: If in any doctrine we may boast of the universality and constancy of tradition, it is this: that among the first, it is not lawful to eat blood, p. 155. I reply. 1. The saying of Tertullian against Praxeas is well known: Whatever is earlier is true; whatever is later is spurious. For antiquity is the first origin of things and the nature which each thing receives. This antiquity, however, is such as it ought to be, namely true, and it rests on the infallible revelation of God, of the Prophets, of Christ and of the Apostles. All certainty must be traced back to this antiquity. Hence Ignatius, in his letter to the Philadelphians (ch. 6), reports that someone objected to him: Unless I find the Gospel in the ancient records, I do not believe. To which he replies: Jesus Christ is my archive, his inviolable cross, death and resurrection. For me the archives are Jesus Christ, to disobey whom is manifestly destruction. [Ἐμοὶ ἀρχεῖα ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς]. Justin, Apology 1, ch. 46: Those who are foolish and senseless put custom before truth [τὸ ἔθη τῆς ἀληθείας ὑμῶν, τῶν ἀνοήτων]. Clearly God, Christ and Truth are older than all things. Since therefore we have set forth the will of the Gospel from the most ancient Scriptures, namely the Word of God explained and unfolded, there is no reason for us to care much about what those said or did who went before us, whether at a long or a short interval. For where certain doctrine must be distinguished from uncertain, it is wrongly appealed to as the paternal doctrine [τὸ πατρικὸν δόγμα], that is, to the antiquity of those who ought to have been wise from the same source from which we are. 2. Unless it is firmly established that the antiquity condemned the eating of blood in the sense in which we contend it is lawful, there will be far more opinion than reckoning in the matter. For what? Could not the godly antiquity, the Councils and the Fathers, whose authority we revere, condemn the eating of blood simply because they saw that it was not expedient, not edifying, harmful to charity, and productive of offence? Or could they have condemned it only because the thing is evil in itself and unlawful, and was once forbidden in the Old Testament, and contrary to Christian liberty? What could they have done, out of zeal to enlarge the Church and to secure the harmony of both Gentiles and Jews, who in those times enriched the Christian Church with a much larger accession than in the present age, when scarcely one or two Jews are converted to us? This is by the just judgment of God, by which, because of the unbelief both of their parents and of themselves, the stubborn character of their superstition grows and is exalted more and more, and can scarcely be changed sincerely to our piety, however much they pretend. It is known from histories that even in the fifth century some Jews were converted to Christ. For when very many Jews were expelled from Alexandria by Cyril, the physician Adamantius went to Constantinople to Atticus and professed the Christian religion, as Socrates testifies (Hist. Eccl. 7.13). And when the pseudo-Moses of Crete, a demon incarnate, employing unspeakable frauds, afflicted the Jews, who had been lured by the hope of return to the land of Canaan, with a wretched disaster, many of the Jews in Crete were made Christians [πολλοὶ τῶν ἐν Κρήτῃ Ἰουδαίων ἐχειραντο], as the same Socrates recounts (7.37). On the Jew Atticus see Zonaras, book 3, p. 34. Elmacinus recounts the story of the Jew Duditho, who was converted at Alexandria under Anastasius. Today such sincere proselytes are rarer than the phoenix.

units.la: II. Quando autem traditionis universalitatem & constantiam tam impotenter jactat Curcellaeus, opponimus ei Augustinum, Hieronymum, Evanthum, Nicolaum I. Papam, qui praecepta illa Apostolica eo sensu, quo etiam nos, sunt interpretati. Hi, nisi fallor, jactantiam illam & superbum triumphum Curcellaei satis retundunt. Augustinus maximè in eam rem clarissimus & apertissimus est, cujus authoritas, si nominum splendor quaeritur, quantivis esse debet. Ejus verba sunt, lib. 32. contra Faustum Manichaeum, cap. 13. In actibus Apostolorum hac lege praeceptum ab Apostolis, ut abstinerent tantum Gentes à fornicatione, & ab immolatis & à sanguine, id est, nequaquam ederent carnem, cujus sanguis non esset effusus. Quod alii non sic intelligunt: sed à sanguine praeceptum esse abstinendum, ne quis homicidio se contaminet. Hoc nunc discutere longum est & non necessarium: quia etsi hoc tunc Apostoli praeceperunt, ut ab animalium sanguine abstinerent Christiani, ne praefocatis carnibus vescerentur, elegisse mihi videntur pro tempore rem facilem, & nequaquam observantibus onerosam, in qua cum Israelitis etiam Gentes, propter angularem illum lapidem duos parietes in se condentem, aliquid communiter observarent, simul & admonerent, in ipsa arca Noë, quando Deus hoc hoc jussit. Ecclesiam omnium Gentium fuisse prefigurasse: cujus facti Prophetia, jam gentibus ad fidem accedentibus, incipiebat impleri. Transacto vero illo tempore, quo illi duo parietes, unus ex circumcisione, alter ex praeputio venientes, quamvis in angulari lapide concordarent, tamen suis quibusdam proprietatibus distinctius eminebant, & ubi Ecclesia Gentium talis effecta est, ut in ea nullus Israelita carnalis appareat, quis Christianus hoc observat, ut turdos, vel minutiores aviculas non attingat, nisi quarum sanguis est effusus? Aut leporem non edat, si manu a cervice percussus, nullo cruento vulnere occisus est? Et qui forte pauci adhuc ista tangere formidant, a caeteris irridentur. Ita omnium animos in hac re tenuit illa sententia veritatis: Non quod intrat in os vestrum, vos coinquinat, sed quod exit: nullam cibi naturam, quam admittit Societas humana, sed quae iniquitas committit peccata condemnans. Non video, quî clarius, nervosius & concinnius magnus ille Pater sententiam nostram exprimere & repraesentare, & vim argumenti adversariorum infringere potuerit. Videamus distincte. Dicit igitur. I. Apostolos elegisse rem pro tempore facilem. Non igitur rem perpetuo duraturam, & in qualibet circumstantia obligaturam. II. Causam reddit, cur pro tempore elegerint rem facilem & minus onerosam: ut propter Israelitas etiam Gentes propter angularem illum lapidem, duos parietes in se condentem, aliquid communiter observarent. Sic causam illorum praeceptorum facit concordiam Judaeorum ac Gentilium, ut in unum corpus facilius conglutinarentur. Scite utitur similitudine ejusmodi compaginationis. Sicut enim in parietibus videmus fieri, ut superinducendus novus priori constructo firmius inhaereat, prominentes relinqui lapides, qui velut nexus quidam recens erectum sibi firmiter conjungant: sic Apostoli in Spirituali hoc aedificio, ut partem novam, venientem ex praeputio, connecterent cum Judaeis, passi sunt hos veluti lapides copulantes prominere, donec aedificio ad umbilicum perducto & confirmato, quod prominebat, tanquam contextui illi probrosum & deforme tolleretur. Confer quae non inepte in hanc rem disseruit Baronius Annal. Tom. I. ad A. C LI. III. Dicit, nemi-nem Christianum talia observare, ubi Ecclesia Gentium talis est effecta, ut in ea nullus Israelita carnalis appareat. Et si qui earum rerum religione ducuntur, eos a caeteris irrideri. Habemus igitur non doctrinam tantum Augustini nobis per omnia consentaneam, sed etiam praxin illorum temporum. Quin Augustinus verissime hoc enuntiaverit, nemo ambigere potest, qui cogitat in plena luce ipsum scripsisse. Si qui igitur sequentibus temporibus superstitione incitante abstinuerunt, cum idonea non esset abstinentiae causa, illorum non est aequum rationem magnam haberi. IV. Confirmat Augustinus sententiam suam dicto Christi: Non quod intrat in os vestrum, vos coinquinat, sed quod exit. Et rationem addit, quod nullam sibi naturam hominis respicere debeant, sed peccata, quae iniquitas humana commisit. Sic nobis per omnia adstipulatur.
units.tr: II. When Curcellaeus so intemperately boasts of the universality and constancy of tradition, we oppose to him Augustine, Jerome, Evanthius and Pope Nicholas I, who interpreted those Apostolic precepts in the same sense in which we do. These, unless I am mistaken, sufficiently repel that boast and proud triumph of Curcellaeus. Augustine is most clear and open on this matter, and if the splendour of names is sought, his authority must count for as much as any. His words, in book 32 against Faustus the Manichaean, ch. 13, are: In the Acts of the Apostles the Apostles prescribed by this law that the Gentiles should abstain only from fornication, from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, that is, that they should by no means eat flesh whose blood had not been poured out. Others do not understand it so, but hold that abstaining from blood was prescribed so that no one should defile himself by murder. To discuss this now is long and not necessary; for even if the Apostles then prescribed that Christians abstain from the blood of animals, so as not to eat meat that had been strangled, they seem to me to have chosen, for the time, a thing easy and by no means burdensome to those who observed it, in which the Gentiles, along with the Israelites, because of that corner stone which joins the two walls in itself, should observe something in common, and at the same time to admonish them, as God commanded in the very ark of Noah, that the Church of all nations was foreshadowed; the prophecy of this fact began to be fulfilled when the Gentiles were already coming to the faith. But when that time had passed, in which those two walls, one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision, although they agreed in the corner stone, nevertheless stood out more distinctly with certain peculiarities of their own, and when the Church of the Gentiles had become such that no carnal Israelite appears in it, what Christian observes this, that he does not touch thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been poured out? Or that he does not eat a hare if it has been struck on the neck by hand and killed without any bloody wound? And those who perhaps still fear to touch such things, are mocked by the rest. Thus that saying of truth held the minds of all in this matter: It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out; no nature of food which human society admits, but the iniquity which commits sins condemns. I do not see how that great Father could have expressed and presented our view more clearly, more vigorously and more neatly, or could have broken the force of the adversaries' argument. Let us look at it point by point. He says, therefore: I. The Apostles chose a thing easy for the time. Therefore not a thing to last forever and to bind in every circumstance. II. He gives the reason why they chose for the time a thing easy and less burdensome: so that, because of the Israelites, the Gentiles too should observe something in common, because of that corner stone which joins the two walls in itself. So he makes the reason for those precepts the concord of Jews and Gentiles, so that they might be more easily cemented into one body. He uses such a likeness of joining aptly. For as we see in walls, a new stone laid over the older structure adheres more firmly when stones are left projecting, which like a kind of bond firmly join the newly raised part to it; so the Apostles, in this spiritual building, in order to connect the new part coming from uncircumcision with the Jews, allowed these projecting stones, as it were binding them together, to stand out, until, when the building had been brought up to its height and made firm, what projected was removed as shameful and unsightly to that structure. Compare what Baronius, not unskilfully, set out on this matter (Annals, vol. 1, at the year 51). He says that no Christian observes such things now, since the Church of the Gentiles has become such that no carnal Israelite appears in it; and if some are held back by scruples about such things, they are mocked by the rest. We have therefore not only Augustine's teaching, which agrees with ours in every respect, but also the practice of those times. Indeed, no one who considers that he wrote in full light can doubt that Augustine said this most truly. If therefore some in later times, moved by superstition, abstained when there was no suitable cause for abstinence, it is not fair that their reasoning should be given great weight. IV. Augustine confirms his opinion by Christ's saying: It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out. And he adds the reason, that they ought to regard no natural quality of man, but the sins which human iniquity has committed. So in every respect he supports us.

units.la: III. Invidet nobis consensum tanti Patris Curcellaeus. Ergo omnem intentionis suae aciem colligit, ut hac nos voluptate privet. Distinguit inter id, quod Augustinus ex sua mente dicit, et id quod tanquam Historicus de praxi Ecclesiae sui temporis refert. Quod ipse existimavit, interdictum sanguinis obligasse ad tempus tantum, non debere majoris ponderis esse, quam tot aliorum contrarium consensum. Et si liberum fuisse sibi credidit, viam a Majoribus tritam deserere, multo minus se teneri ipsum exorbitantem sequi. Quod vero memorat, paucos isto tempore abstinuisse a Suffocato, id sibi non adversari, quia existimet, istam abstinentiam a Suffocato non fuisse ab Apostolis praescriptam. Non dicere autem Augustinum, ullum Christianum merum sanguinem edisse aut potasse, pag. 166.167. Bene est, quod libertatem sibi arrogat simpliciter ab Augustino dissentiendi. Sic nos jure hactenus aequat, ut simpliciter ausimus improbare illos, quos pro se non sine insolente pompa producit. Sed & vel hac una ratione motus desinat traditionis universalitatem jactare. Dixit quidem Augustinus, Christianos sui temporis non amplius temperare a Suffocato. Nec nominat in praxi Christianorum sanguinem. Sed res ipsa eodem redit. Si enim Suffocatum ederunt, tum etiam sanguinem. Nimis enim dilutum est, quod dicit, sanguinem fuisse expressum. Unde fidem fecit dicto? Hoc maxime animadversione dignum, quod dicit Augustinus: Si hoc Apostoli praeceperunt, ut ab animalium sanguine abstinerent Christiani, ne praefocatis carnibus vescerentur, elegisse mihi videntur rem pro tempore facilem. Hic manifestum est, ipsum pro ἀναγκαῖον habere, abstinere a sanguine, & praefocatis vesci carnibus. Nam prius explicat per posterius. Scilicet in ea fuit sententia, Apostolos, cum scripserunt, necessum esse, ut abstineant a Sanguine & & Suffocato, non duo capita sed unum prohibuisse. In quam sententiam etiam alios ivisse, certum est. Sed & hoc perpendimus, voluisse Augustinum, quod sententia tuetur, idem etiam observatione suae aetatis hominum defendere. Tuetur autem sententia, Apostolos sanguinem prohibuisse pro tempore. Ergo idem etiam tuetur praxi hominum suae aetatis. Alias quam ἀπέχεσθαι πνικτῶν subjecisset Christianorum praxin? Quid ergo? Loquitur de Suffocatis tantum, de turdis aviculis, lepore, quia creber hic & quotidianus cibus fuit, qualis non fuit purus sanguis. Deinde excipit: Non testari illud Augustinum de omnibus ubique gentibus Christianis, quod facere absque evidenti mendacio non potuisset, sed tantum de suis Africanis, & forte de non adeo multis. Natum esse illud familiare schema, ut ad omnes aliquis provocet, statim atque sibi de numero aliquo consciens est. ibid. Resp. Nimis aperta sunt Augustini verba: Ubi Ecclesia Gentium talis effecta est, ut nullus jam in ea carnalis Israelita appareat, quis jam hoc Christianus observat? Et statim illos Christianos opponit paucis, qui propter abstinentiam illam superstitiosam ceteris deridiculo sunt. Novit haud dubie prudentissimus Pater, quid extra Africam gereretur. Nec tam contemptim locutus esset de Christianis extra Africam degentibus. Denique obvertit: Quod irriderentur illi pauci, non arguisse illorum errorem, sed profanitatem ceterorum. Sic irrideri hodie, qui baptismum fieri cuperent non per aspersionem, sed, ut in Veteri Ecclesia fiebat, per totius corporis in aquam immersionem. ibid. Resp. Sic profanus fuerit ipse Augustinus, qui non obscure risu dignos fuisse innuit. Profanus non est, qui voluntatem Dei, Spiritualem λόγον secutus, recte interpretatur. Quod de Baptismo adspergit, condonamus ingenio novarum rerum appetentissimo. Novimus quidem, antiquitus crebrius usitatam immersionem, quam aspersionem baptismo. Non semper tamen immersionem obtinuisse, non inepte probat Aquinas, quia aliquando ob multitudinem fieri non potuit, ut Act. II. & IV. Perfusionis etiam exemplum habemus in Historia de Martyrio B. Laurentii. Confer de hac re Vossium de Baptismo, pag. 37. 38. & Danaeum ad Enchrid. August. p. m. 145. Ritus ille usurpari desitus est, ut quibusdam Historicis videtur, tempore Constantini Copronymi, cum aquam baptismatis excremento alimoniae conspurcaret. Thomas etiam affert causam, honestatem, propter quam decentius sit hodie adultos adspergere, quàm nudatos toto corpore immergere.
units.tr: III. Curcellaeus begrudges us the agreement of so great a Father, and so he gathers all the force of his argument to deprive us of this pleasure. He distinguishes between what Augustine says from his own judgment and what he reports as a historian about the practice of the Church in his own time. Curcellaeus himself thought that the prohibition on blood bound only for a time, and that it ought not to carry more weight than the contrary consensus of so many others. And if he believed that he was free to abandon the path trodden by our forebears, he is still less bound to follow a man who departs from it. As for Augustine's report that few abstained from what was strangled in his time, Curcellaeus says this does not oppose him, because in his view that abstinence from strangled meat was not prescribed by the Apostles. He adds that Augustine does not say that any Christian ate or drank pure blood (pp. 166–167). It is well that he claims for himself the liberty simply to dissent from Augustine, so that he matches us in the right to reject those whom he brings forward on his own side, not without an insolent display. But even for this reason alone he should stop boasting of the universality of the tradition. Augustine did indeed say that the Christians of his time no longer refrained from what was strangled, and he does not name blood in the practice of Christians. But the matter comes to the same thing. If they ate what was strangled, they also ate blood. It is far too thin to say that the blood had been drained out. On what basis does he make good his claim? What is most worthy of notice is what Augustine says: "If the Apostles commanded that Christians abstain from the blood of animals, so that they might not eat meat that had been strangled, they seem to me to have chosen a thing easy for the time." Here it is plain that he regarded abstaining from blood and eating strangled meat as one and the same necessary thing [ἀναγκαῖον], for he explains the first by the second. He clearly held the view that the Apostles, when they wrote that it was necessary to abstain from blood and from what was strangled, forbade not two items but one. It is certain that others also took this view. But we also perceive that Augustine wished to defend by the observance of his own age what the view he upholds maintains. And that view maintains that the Apostles forbade blood for a time. Therefore it also maintains the practice of the men of Augustine's age. Otherwise, why would he have added "to abstain from things strangled" as a description of the practice of Christians? Well then? He speaks only of strangled things, of thrushes, of hare, because these were a frequent and daily food, whereas pure blood was not. Then he adds: "Augustine does not bear witness about all Christians everywhere that he could not have said without plain falsehood, but only about his Africans, and perhaps not about very many. That familiar figure of speech has arisen, by which someone appeals to everyone as soon as he is conscious of some number on his side." (ibid.) Answer: Augustine's words are far too clear: "Where the Church of the Gentiles has become such that no carnal Israelite any longer appears in it, who among Christians now observes this?" And at once he sets against them the few Christians who, because of that superstitious abstinence, are a laughing-stock to the rest. The most prudent Father undoubtedly knew what was done beyond Africa, and he would not have spoken so contemptuously of Christians living outside Africa. Finally he objects: "That those few were laughed at does not prove their error but the profanity of the rest. In the same way, today those who would wish baptism to be administered not by sprinkling but, as was done in the Old Church, by immersion of the whole body in water are mocked." (ibid.) Answer: Then Augustine himself would be profane, since he obscurely implies that these men deserved ridicule. He is not profane who, following the will of God and the spiritual reasoning [λόγον], interprets rightly. As for what he says about baptism by sprinkling, we pardon it as the work of a mind very eager for novelties. We know indeed that in antiquity immersion was used more often than sprinkling in baptism. Yet that it did not always prevail, Aquinas rightly proves, since at times it could not be done because of the multitude, as in Acts 2 and 4. We also have an example of pouring in the account of the martyrdom of St Laurence. On this matter compare Vossius, On Baptism, pp. 37–38, and Daneus on the Enchiridion of Augustine, p. 145. That rite, as some historians think, ceased to be used in the time of Constantine Copronymus, when the baptismal water was polluted by the excrement of the child's nourishment. Thomas also gives a reason: decency, on account of which it is now more becoming to sprinkle adults than to immerse them stripped of their whole body.

units.la: IV. Post tempora Augustini non statim obsolevit inter Christianos sanguinis & Suffocati esus. Testem interrogamus Evanthum, authorem satis quidem antiquum, Gregorio tamen, cujus librum Pastoralem adducit, posteriorem. Is suo tempore scripsit epistolam contra eos, qui sanguinem animalium immundum esse judicabant. Eam enim opinionem fovisse scribit quosdam in partibus Cæsar-Augustanis. Adeo non fuit ista communis hominum sive sententia sive praxis. Cùm objiceretur locus Act. XV. eum sic solvit, id pro tempore constitutum propter infirmitatem Christianorum ex Judæis. In quam sententiam allegat tum Augustinum contra Faustum Manichæum, tum Hieronymum. Objiciebantur etiam Canones Conciliorum. Respondit Euanthus: Nec ego me ista fateor ignorare, sed in antiquis canonibus ista reperiuntur, quando adhuc Ecclesia ex circumcisione & Præputio ad fidem congregabatur: quando adhuc non solido cibo sed lacte nutriebatur. Tale quid ad Corinthios Apostolus dixisse noverint, & in Actibus Apostolorum facta invenient. Nunc verò Ecclesia Dei solido cibo, fide roborata consistit, ut viriliter contra impetus haereticorum pugnet, non in infantium mollitie enervata succumbat. Edita est illa Epistola à Canisio ex Manuscriptis Monasterii Sanctogallensis, Lect. Antiq. Tom. V. part. 2. Augustini responsione supra allata & defensa defungitur etiam Nicolaus I. in responso ad Consulta Bulgarorum, capite nonagesimo. Sed hæc delibasse, sufficiat. Curcellæus plures ex Antiquitate in theatrum producit. Sic numerat suas, ut pauper, pecudes, non ponderat. Non gravabimur tamen singulorum verba paulò quæsitiùs inspicere, & periculum facere, quantùm adversariis prosint.
units.tr: IV. After the time of Augustine, the eating of blood and of what was strangled did not at once fall out of use among Christians. Let us question as a witness Evanthius, an author indeed rather ancient, yet later than Gregory, whose book, the Pastoral, he cites. In his own time he wrote a letter against those who judged the blood of animals to be unclean. For he writes that certain people in the regions of Caesarea-Augusta cherished this opinion. So far was this view, whether as doctrine or as practice, from being common among men. When the passage of Acts 15 was objected, he resolved it thus: that it was "decreed for the time, on account of the weakness of the Christians from among the Jews." To this opinion he appeals both to Augustine against Faustus the Manichaean and to Jerome. The canons of councils were also objected. Evanthius replied: "I do not confess that I am ignorant of these things, but they are found in the ancient canons, when the Church was still gathered to the faith from circumcision and uncircumcision, when it was still nourished not by solid food but by milk. They may know that the Apostle said something of this kind to the Corinthians, and they will find things done in the Acts of the Apostles. But now the Church of God stands strengthened by solid food and by faith, so that it may fight manfully against the assaults of heretics, and not succumb enervated by the softness of infants." That letter was published by Canisius from the manuscripts of the monastery of St Gall, Lectiones Antiquae, vol. 5, part 2. Nicholas I also dispatches the matter, in his answer to the Bulgarians' questions, chapter 90, using the answer of Augustine cited and defended above. But it is enough to have touched on these things. Curcellaeus brings many witnesses from antiquity onto his stage. He counts them out as a poor man counts his cattle, without weighing them. We shall not, however, be burdened by examining the words of individual witnesses a little more carefully, and by testing how far they help our adversaries.

units.la: V. Primus est Tertullianus in Apolog. cap. IX. Gentiles refutaturus, qui infanticidia Christianis & Thyestæas coenas objiciebat: Erubescat error vester Christianis, qui nec animalium quidem sanguinem in esculentis epulis habemus, qui propterea quoque morticinis & Suffocatis abstinemus, ne quo modo sanguine contaminemur, vel intra viscera sepulto. Denique inter testamenta Christianorum borulos etiam errore distentos admovetis: certissimi scilicet, illicitum esse penes illos, per quod eos exorbitare vultis. Porro quale est, ut quos sanguinem pa-ceris sanguinis horrere confidit, humane inhiare credatis? Nisi forte suaviorem eum experti. Hic docet Tertullianus, veteres abstinuisse à sanguine & Suffocatis. Tria repono. Primò, à temporibus Tertulliani ad nostra tempora non licere argumentari. Plures illo tempore fuerunt causæ, ob quas Christiani abstinere tenebantur, quæ hodie non habent locum. Secundò, Tertullianum non de solo sanguine loqui, sed etiam de suffocatis. Suffocatis autem per legem Apostolicam vesci licere, concedit Curcellæus. In hac re igitur diversus abit à Tertulliano. Quod si fas & integrum fuit Curcellæo, eadem nos libertate in interdicto sanguinis frui permittat. Respondet: Christianos abstinuisse à morticinis & suffocatis ex scrupulo, ne quid in iis sanguis superesset, non ex interdicti Apostolici authoritate. Qui igitur fit, quòd eundem scrupulum non habuerit in consilio ipse etiam Curcellæus, ne suffocata comederet, cùm periculum sanguinis edendi difficulter evitari posit. Sed fateamur, quod res est. Tertullianus utrumque legit in codice αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ. Ergo ex authoritate Apostolica, non ex scrupulo sibi temperavit. Tertiò, cùm alias ob causas, tum ob hanc sibi etiam temperâsse videntur, ne Gentiles, qui genuinum Apostolici interdicti sensum non perceperunt, ansam arriperent Christianos blasphemandi, quòd ne Mosis & Apostolorum quidem præceptis obsequentes se gererent. Tanta apud illos fuit Apostolici culminis reverentia, ut etiam speciem vitarent inobedientiæ erga illos. Secundus Curcellæo testis est Minutius Felix in Octavio. Nobis homicidium nec videre fas est, nec audire, ut nec edulium pecudum in cibis sanguinem noverimus. Tertius Biblis fœmina, quæ commemorante Eusebio Histor. Eccl. lib. V. cap. 1. in tormentis de Christianis, quibus Gentiles βοεῖς τῶν παιδίων objecerant, anquisita, masculè tandem post multas Sathanæ tentationes respondit, πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιοῦτοι, οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζῴων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἔξον. Quomodo infantes comederent illi, quibus ne irrationalium quidem pecudum sanguine vesci licet? Minutii Felicis eadem ratio est, quæ Tertulliani. Quod Biblidem fœminam attinet, non assentior quidem Suarezio, qui de solo suffocato illam loqui asserit, de lege positiva lib. 9. cap. 20. Imò in genere sanguinem pecudum nominat. Non dubitamus, quin ea ætate multas ob causas Christiani abstinuerint. Interim, quin ullo casu licear vesci, non expresserunt. Probant ejusmodi di exempla factum, non negant jus contrarium. Quartus est Clemens Alexandrinus Pædagog. lib. III. cap. 3. ubi, cùm retulisset, Scythas sanguinem equorum & Arabes Camelorum potare solitos, subjungit: Pereant ergo immanes bellua, quibus est cibus sanguis. Neque enim hominibus fas est, tangere sanguinem, quibus corpus nihil est aliud quàm caro sanguine exculta. Loquitur de barbaro & Scythico more promiscuè sanguinem ligurientium, unde crudeles & feroces sunt facti. Si ultra extendit, liberè dissentimus.
units.tr: V. The first is Tertullian in the Apology, chapter 9, when he refutes the Gentiles who objected to the Christians infanticide and Thyestean feasts: "Let your error be ashamed before the Christians, who do not even have the blood of animals in our food, who for that very reason also abstain from carrion and what is strangled, lest in any way we be defiled by blood, even if it lies buried within the viscera. Finally, among the wills of Christians you bring forward even mushrooms swollen with error, quite certainly because you want that to be unlawful among them through which you wish them to go astray." Moreover, how is it that you believe those whom you feed with blood shrink from blood, and gape for human flesh? Unless perhaps they have tasted it and found it sweeter. Here Tertullian teaches that the ancients abstained from blood and from things strangled. I make three replies. First, from Tertullian's time to ours it is not permissible to argue by inference. There were, at that time, many causes for which Christians were bound to abstain, which today have no place. Second, Tertullian is not speaking of blood alone but also of things strangled. Curcellaeus concedes that by the Apostolic law it is lawful to eat things strangled. In this matter, therefore, he departs from Tertullian. If it was right and proper for Curcellaeus to do so, let him permit us the same liberty in regard to the prohibition of blood. He replies: "Christians abstained from carrion and strangled things out of scruple, lest any blood remain in them, not by the authority of the Apostolic prohibition." Why then is it that Curcellaeus himself did not have the same scruple in his counsel, not to eat strangled things, since the danger of eating blood can hardly be avoided? But let us confess what the matter is. Tertullian read both in his copy: "of blood and of what is strangled" [αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ]. Therefore he abstained from them by Apostolic authority, not out of scruple. Third, it seems that they abstained for this reason as well as others, lest the Gentiles, who had not grasped the genuine sense of the Apostolic prohibition, should seize an occasion to blaspheme the Christians, because they did not even conform to the precepts of Moses and the Apostles. Among them there was such reverence for the Apostolic authority that they even avoided the appearance of disobedience towards them. Second, Minucius Felix in the Octavius is a witness for Curcellaeus: "For us it is not right even to see or hear of murder, so that we may not know of the flesh of animals as food with blood in it." Third is Biblis, a woman who, as Eusebius recalls in Ecclesiastical History 5.1, when the Christians were under torture and the Gentiles had charged them with eating infants, was questioned, and at last, manfully, after many temptations of Satan, answered: "How could such people eat infants, to whom it is not even permitted to eat the blood of irrational animals?" [πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιοῦτοι, οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζῴων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἔξον]. The reasoning of Minucius Felix is the same as Tertullian's. As for the woman Biblis, I do not agree with Suarez, who asserts that she spoke only of what was strangled, on positive law, book 9, chapter 20. Indeed she names blood of animals in general. We do not doubt that in that age Christians abstained for many reasons. Meanwhile they did not express that there was any case in which it was lawful to eat blood. Such examples prove the fact but do not deny the opposite right. Fourth is Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, chapter 3, where, after recounting that the Scythians were accustomed to drink the blood of horses and the Arabs the blood of camels, he adds: "Let those savage beasts perish, for whom blood is food. For it is not right for men to touch blood, for whom the body is nothing other than flesh refined by blood." He is speaking of the barbarous and Scythian custom of indiscriminately lapping up blood, from which they became cruel and fierce. If he extends it further, we freely dissent.

units.la: VI. Quintus est auctor quæstionum & Responsionum ad Orthodoxos. quæst. 145. Cùm ex iisdem constet sanguis, ex quibus caro, quare Deus carnium animalium esum permittit, carnis autem in sanguine esum interdicit? Excepto, inquit, quòd carnem in sanguine non comederis. Respondet. Ut ea quoque in re Deus nos àferarum immanitate secerneret, quæ in laniatu carnium, sanguinem quoque eorum lambunt, quorum vorant carnes. Hic primò incertus est & dubius illarum responsionum author. Tribuunt nonnulli librum Justino Martyri. Quorum opinio à Criticis Sacris jampridem est jugulata. Etenim facit mentionem Manichæorum: vocabula habet seriùs nota ... Multa scribit vero Justino contraria. Citat Irenæum, quem Justino constat fuisse posteriorem. Sed quisquis fuerit ille Author, non multùm ex eo emolumenti capere poterit Curcellæus. Agit enim manifestè de prohibitione sanguinis, facta tempore Noachi, & rationem reddit, cur Deus sanguinem prohibeat, carne indulta. Sextus est Origenes libro VIII. contra Celsum. Suffocata sunt animalia mortua, non expresso ex illis sanguine, quæ utique Dæmonum esse ajunt cibum, cujus illi ardore pascantur. Hæc idcirco vetantur in cibum assumi, ne nos Dæmonum cibis nutriamur, & nobiscum maligni Spiritus coalantur, si pariter cum illis vescamur Suffocatis. Miror, voluisse etiam Origenem sibi consentaneum Curcellæum producere. Atqui ille non de sanguine agit, sed de suffocatis, quæ negat Curcellæus in texta tangi, adeoque licita esse concedit. Deinde quàm frivola ratio est, quam reddit, interdicti Suffocatorum Origenes? Septimum testimonium arcessit ex Canone Apostolorum LXIII. Si quis Episcopus vel Presbyter vel Diaconus, vel omnino ex Sacerdotali catalogo, comederit carnes in sanguine anima ipsarum, vel quid à feris captum, vel morticinum, deponatur. Hoc enim lex prohibuit. Si autem sit Laicus, segrego... gregetur. De Canonibus Apostolicis sæpius diximus. Nullam merentur fidem, nec Apostolis authoribus gaudent. Deinde inde sibi præsidium quæritat, unde perniciem metuere debet. Prohibent Canones non sanguinem magis quàm Suffocata. Neque hic tergiversari debet, Suffocata prohiberi, ex quibus sanguis nondum est expressus. Nam in genere vocant Πνικτὰ καὶ Ἀπνιστα. Eodem modo prohibuerunt Suffocata, quo sanguinem. Suffocata autem per se non est nefas comedere, imò licitum est illud edulium Curcellæo confitente. Ergo neque sanguis per se illicitus. Octavum testimonium profert ex Concilio Gangrensi: Nonum ex Concilio Secundo Aurelianensi: Decimum ex Constantinopolitano in Trullo. Concilii Gangrensis canon 11. sic habet: Si quis carnem edentem absque sanguine & idolis immolato & Suffocato, cum pietate & fide condemnat, ut spem non habentem propter hujusmodi perceptionem, anathema sit. Sic, fateor, edicit canon, ex quo Franciscus Silvius recte colligit, apparere, diu observatum fuisse in quibusdam locis. Nam universalem fuisse praxin ex hoc canone non potest confici. Non fuit enim Universale Concilium, sed provinciale, proinde, quæ fuerit observatio Christianorum extra Græciam, non docet. Probari etiam debet, ideo damnâsse, quia per se illicitus & pravus fuit. Exercitium enim juri contrarium aliquando præcipi posse, minimè inficias imus. Concilii II. Aurelianensis canon ita habet: Catholici, qui ad idolorum cultum revertuntur, vel qui cibis idolorum cultibus immolatis gustu illicita præsumtione utuntur. Similiter & hi, qui bestiarum morsibus extincto, vel quolibet morbo aut casu Suffocato vescuntur ab Ecclesiæ coetibus arceantur. Non animadvertit Curcellæus, ne quidem sanguinis mentionem in canone fieri, sed Suffocati tantùm. Et cùm Concilium Nationale fuerit, pauci Patres non potuerunt Christianorum omnium libertati Divinitus indultæ compedes injicere, nisi necessitas id postularet. Non dicam, quàm obscura fuerit hæc Synodus Aurelianensis, quàm altum de ea in antiquitate silentium, quàm denique quædam ejus decreta Apostolicam simplicitatem & sinceritatem parùm redoleant. Concilii Constantinopolitani Sexti in Trullo habiti Canon 67. sic sonat. Sacra Scriptura nobis præcipit, ut abstineamus à Sanguine et Suffocato & fornicatione. Merito igitur damnamus eos, qui cujuscunque animalis sanguinem arte aliqua condiunt, & sic comedunt. Qui hoc fecerit, Clericus deponatur, Laicus excommunicetur. communicetur. Damnatio est injusta, quippe quae nititur sinistra interpretatione Apostolici Decreti.
units.tr: VI. The fifth witness is the author of the Questions and Answers to the Orthodox, question 145: Since flesh and blood consist of the same things, why does God permit the eating of animal flesh but forbid eating flesh with the blood? Except, he says, that you shall not eat flesh with the blood. He answers: So that God might separate us, even in this matter, from the savagery of wild beasts, which, when they tear apart flesh, also lick up the blood of the creatures whose flesh they devour. Here, first of all, the author of these answers is uncertain and doubtful. Some attribute the book to Justin Martyr, but this opinion was long ago cut down by the sacred critics. For the work mentions the Manichaeans and uses terms ... that became known only later. Moreover, it writes many things contrary to Justin. It cites Irenaeus, who is known to have been later than Justin. But whoever that author was, Curcellaeus will not be able to gain much advantage from him. For he clearly treats of the prohibition of blood, made in the time of Noah, and gives the reason why God forbade blood after flesh had been granted. Sixth is Origen, in book 8 against Celsus: Animals that have died strangled, without the blood having been drained from them, are said to be the food of demons, by whose craving they are nourished. These are forbidden to be taken as food so that we may not be fed with the food of demons, and so that the evil spirits may not associate with us if we eat strangled things along with them. I am surprised that Curcellaeus wanted to produce Origen as one agreeing with himself. Yet Origen does not treat of blood but of strangled animals, which Curcellaeus denies are touched in the text, and so he concedes they are lawful. Next, how flimsy is the reason Origen gives for the prohibition of strangled things! The seventh witness he summons from the Canon of the Apostles, LXIII: If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or indeed anyone from the priestly list, eats flesh with the blood, its soul, or what has been caught by wild beasts, or carrion, let him be deposed. For the law has forbidden this. But if he is a layman, let him be separated. We have often spoken of the Apostolic Canons. They deserve no trust and do not rejoice in Apostolic authors. Next, he seeks a defence from the very thing he ought to fear as a ruin. The Canons prohibit not blood more than strangled things. Nor should he here evade by saying that strangled things are forbidden, from which the blood has not yet been drained. For in general they call them Πνικτὰ καὶ Ἀπνιστα [strangled and unstrangled]. In the same way they forbade strangled things as they forbade blood. But strangled things in themselves are not wrong to eat; indeed, that food is lawful, as Curcellaeus himself confesses. Therefore blood too is not unlawful in itself. The eighth witness he brings from the Council of Gangra, and the ninth from the Second Council of Orléans; the tenth from the Council in Trullo at Constantinople. Canon 11 of the Council of Gangra reads thus: If anyone condemns, with piety and faith, one who eats flesh without blood, meat offered to idols, or what has been strangled, as one not having hope because of such eating, let him be anathema. So, I admit, the canon decrees, and from it Franciscus Silvius rightly concludes that it is apparent this was long observed in certain places. For a universal practice cannot be inferred from this canon. For it was not an Ecumenical Council but a provincial one, and therefore it does not teach what the observance of Christians outside Greece was. It must also be proved that they condemned it because it was in itself unlawful and wicked. For we by no means deny that an exercise contrary to law may sometimes be commanded. The canon of the Second Council of Orléans reads thus: Catholics who return to the worship of idols, or who presumptuously use with taste foods offered in idol worship, and likewise those who eat what has been killed by the bites of beasts, or by any sickness or accident, or strangled, are to be kept away from the assemblies of the Church. Curcellaeus does not notice that the canon makes no mention even of blood, but only of the strangled. And since it was a national council, a few fathers could not have put shackles on the freedom given by God to all Christians, unless necessity demanded it. I will not say how obscure this Synod of Orléans was, how deep is the silence about it in antiquity, and finally how some of its decrees little savour of Apostolic simplicity and sincerity. Canon 67 of the Council of Constantinople, the Sixth, held in Trullo, sounds thus: Holy Scripture commands us to abstain from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. Therefore we rightly condemn those who season the blood of any animal with some art and so eat it. Whoever does this, if a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be excommunicated. The condemnation is unjust, since it rests on a perverse interpretation of the Apostolic Decree.

units.la: VII. Undecimus est Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, Catech. IV.
units.tr: VII. The eleventh is Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis IV.

units.la: Scribunt Apostoli & Seniores omnibus Gentibus communem Catholicam Epistolam, ut inprimis idolothytis abstineant, deinde & sanguine atque Suffocato. Nam hominum multi feri & immanes, moréque canino viventes, sanguinem lambunt agrestium & ferocium belluarum instar suffocata devorant, abunde. Tu autem servus Christi cum sis, comedens, reverentia modestiaque adhibita comede. Posteriora Cyrilli verba sunt ambigua, & sic accipi possunt, ut servus Christi in edendo sanguine & Suffocato moderatus sit, nec instar belluarum crudeliter sanguinem lambat. Si in universum crudelitati deputet sanguinis esum, candidè improbamus. Duodecimus est Chrysostomus in Act. Apostol. Homil. XXXVIII. ubi, postquam praeceptum Apostolicum enarrasset, subjicit: Caeterum ostendit, non esse sermonem ad gratificandum compositum, nec ad parendum illis, quasi infirmis, sed contrarium. Magnum enim & Doctorum pudor fuisset, superfluumque fuisset onus. Videlicet brevem epistolam, nihil habentem abundans, neque epicheremata, neque Syllogismos, sed imperium, erat enim legislatio Spiritus. Frigida certè erudití caetera Patris ratiocinatio. Non est superfluum onus, quod propter infirmioris conscientiam imponitur. Et decretum cum fuerit, quamvis temporale, sapienter conditum, non debuit epicheremata vel Syllogismos habere, sed imperium pro ratione fuit. Caeterum sat Syllogismorum & epicherematum nectit Paulus capite octavo prioris ad Corinthios, & in Epistola ad Romanos capite decimo quarto, ubi prolixè argumenta explicat, ob quae aliquando ab usu rerum indifferentium temperare conveniat. Decimus tertius & ultimus est Leo Imperator, cujus Constitutio L VIII. in interdicto hoc consumitur. Superfluum esset huc Novellam transcribere. Poenam gravissimam constituit in violatorem, ut, si quis sanguinem in cibum convertere deprehensus fuerit, sciat, se bonorum publicationi subjiciendum, & ubi acerbum in modum flagris caesus, ac cure tenus foedè tonsus erit, perpetuo Patria exilio multandum esse. Sufficiat annotasse, illas Constitutiones ne quidem Leonis Sophi superstitis adhuc tempore vigorem habuisse. Audiamus Jurisconsultum eminentissimum Jacobum Cujacium lib. XVII. Observat. cap. 31, Novellarum constitutionum, inquit, Leonis Sophi tantum abest. est, ut aliqua apud nos sit authoritas, ut nec ejus ætate unquam obtinuerint. Nam quod nostris hodie, idem etiam sæpe Imperii Romani principibus evenisset, ut quæ constituerunt, judicia populi non reciperentur.
units.tr: The Apostles and Elders write to all the Gentiles a common Catholic Epistle, that they abstain first of all from idol-offerings, then also from blood and from what is strangled. For many men are savage and brutal, living like dogs; they lick blood like wild and fierce beasts, and devour strangled meat in abundance. But you, since you are a servant of Christ, when you eat, eat with reverence and moderation. The latter words of Cyril are ambiguous, and may be taken to mean that the servant of Christ, in eating blood and what is strangled, is restrained and does not lap up blood cruelly like the beasts. If he means that the eating of blood is cruel in general, we readily approve. The twelfth is Chrysostom on Acts, Homily XXXVIII, where, after explaining the apostolic precept, he adds: Moreover, he shows that the speech was not composed to please, nor to yield to them as to the weak, but the contrary. For it would have been a disgrace to the teachers, and a superfluous burden, if a short letter, lacking nothing and not overflowing, had contained neither epicheiremata nor syllogisms, but command; for it was the legislation of the Spirit. The rest of this learned Father's reasoning is certainly feeble. A burden is not superfluous when it is imposed on account of a weaker conscience. And a decree, even if temporary, if it was wisely framed, need not have contained epicheiremata or syllogisms, but command was its reason. Moreover, Paul does weave in enough syllogisms and epicheiremata in the eighth chapter of his first Epistle to the Corinthians and in the fourteenth chapter of his Epistle to the Romans, where at length he explains the arguments on account of which it is sometimes fitting to refrain from the use of indifferent things. The thirteenth and last is the Emperor Leo, whose Constitution LVIII deals with this prohibition. It would be superfluous to transcribe the Novel here. It lays the most severe penalty on the transgressor: if anyone is caught turning blood into food, he is to know that he is liable to confiscation of his goods, and, having been cruelly beaten with whips and foully shorn to the scalp, he is to be punished with perpetual exile from his homeland. It is enough to note that these Constitutions did not even have force in the time of Leo the Wise, who was still living. Let us hear the most eminent jurist Jacques Cujas, Observations, Book XVII, chapter 31: Of the Novels of Leo the Wise, he says, there is so little authority among us that they did not hold sway even in his own age. For what happens to our rulers today has often happened also to the princes of the Roman Empire: the judgments of the people did not accept what they decreed.

units.la: VIII. Ex quibus apparet, nihil causæ esse, cur universalem traditionem οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας crepent, cùm vix unus & alter ipsis clara consensione patrocinetur. De modernis Criticis, Grotio, Salmasio, Blondello, Vossio non magnopere laboramus. Si virorum præstantium, ac Theologorum cumprimis, qui talia curatius & pensiculatius agunt, quasi per saturam exquirenda suffragia essent, vel millesimo cum fœnore pensaremus paucorum, qui in alia omnia eunt, jacturam. Nolumus autem nos quærere, quid homines sentiant, sed quid sentire nos velit Dominus. Orientis & Meridiei pleraque Ecclesias novimus quidem hac superstitione imbutas, quam in hoc nos scripto corrigimus. Sed cùm in hoc, tum in aliis etiam capitibus orthodoxas in Occidente Ecclesias Orientalibus sentire saniùs, persuasissimi sumus, sic tamen ut propter ejusmodi ἀσθενήματα Ecclesiæ veræ axioma minimè illis invideamus. De cætero compertum habemus, Græcos non in universum omnes à sanguine abstinere. Petrus Antiochenus, Græcus homo, in epistola, quam Cerularío opposuit, inter alia multa de hac re sic loquitur. Εὐρίσκεις ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἔξω πόλεως τὸ ὄνον αἷμα ἐσθίοντας, καὶ μαγειρεῖ τὸ ἐν ταῖς ἀφθαλμίαις τῶν κατηλῶν ἀπολλύμενα καλέντερα μετὰ ὄνων ἀλογὴ χοιρείνῳ αἵματι. Invenies in ipsa Constantinopoli, & extra eam mulieres, qui sanguinem suillum comedunt, & testimonium dant, quæ in caponarum foribus proponuntur, laxiora intestina, sanguinis sui plena. Et Balsamon in Can. LXIII. Apostolorum τὰ δὲ ἐν ὀρνέων θηρευτῶν ἢ κυνῶν, ἢ παρδάλεων θηρεύομενα, καὶ πνιγόμενα πῶς ἀπὸ λιμῶν ἐσθίοντας, ἀγνοῦ. Σημείωσαι ἓν τὸν κανόνα ἀπὸ τῆς Λατίνας ἀλλαφόρως τὰ πνικτὰ ἐσθίοντας. Quæ autem à venatoriis avibus vel canibus capiuntur & suffocantur, quomodo ab aliquibus comedantur, nescio. Nota ergo Canonem propter Latinos, qui suffocata indiscriminatim comedunt. Ergo quidam ex Græcis vescuntur. Neque Latini aliter pulsandi, quàm quia edunt ἀλλαφόρως indiscriminatim. Idem Balsamon in Canonem LXVII. Trullanum. Οἱ δὲ Λατῖνοι ἀλλαφόρως ἐσθίουσι πνικτά. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ Ἀ-δριανοπολῖται, ὡς ἀκούω, τοῖς αἵμασι τῶν ζώων χρῶνται μὴ ἐδωδίμων πνῶν. Latini vero indiscriminatim Suffocata comedunt; sed etiam Adrianopolitani, ut audio, animalium sanguine cum esculentis quibusdam utuntur.
units.tr: VIII. From these things it appears that there is no reason why those on the other side [οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας] should make a clamour about universal tradition, since scarcely one or two of them defend it with any clear agreement. We do not labour much over the modern critics, Grotius, Salmasius, Blondel, Vossius. If we had to weigh the votes of distinguished men, and especially of theologians who treat such matters more carefully and exactly, as though testimonies were to be gathered by a kind of medley, we would set off the loss of the few who go in every other direction against a thousandfold interest. We, however, do not wish to ask what men think, but what the Lord wills us to think. We know that most churches of the East and South are indeed steeped in this superstition, which in this writing we correct. But we are thoroughly persuaded that the Orthodox churches of the West, both in this and in other chapters, think more soundly than the Eastern churches; yet, on account of such weaknesses, we do not begrudge the Eastern churches the status of the true Church. Moreover, we have learned for certain that the Greeks do not all in general abstain from blood. Peter of Antioch, a Greek, in the letter he opposed to Cerularius, speaks thus among many other things on this matter: You will find, in the city itself and outside the city, people who eat the blood of asses, and women who eat swine's blood, and the looser intestines, full of their blood, which are set out at the doors of the poulterers, bear witness to it. [Εὐρίσκεις ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἔξω πόλεως τὸ ὄνον αἷμα ἐσθίοντας, καὶ μαγειρεῖ τὸ ἐν ταῖς ἀφθαλμίαις τῶν κατηλῶν ἀπολλύμενα καλέντερα μετὰ ὄνων ἀλογὴ χοιρείνῳ αἵματι.] And Balsamon, on Canon LXIII of the Apostles: As for what is taken by hunters of birds or of dogs, or of leopards, and strangled, how some eat it, I do not know. Note that the canon is aimed at the Latins, who eat strangled things without distinction. [τὰ δὲ ἐν ὀρνέων θηρευτῶν ἢ κυνῶν, ἢ παρδάλεων θηρεύομενα, καὶ πνιγόμενα πῶς ἀπὸ λιμῶν ἐσθίοντας, ἀγνοῦ. Σημείωσαι ἓν τὸν κανόνα ἀπὸ τῆς Λατίνας ἀλλαφόρως τὰ πνικτὰ ἐσθίοντας.] Therefore some of the Greeks do eat such things. Nor are the Latins struck for any other reason than that they eat indiscriminately [ἀλλαφόρως]. The same Balsamon, on the sixty-seventh Canon of the Trullan council: The Latins eat strangled things indiscriminately; but also the Adrianopolitans, as I hear, use the blood of animals which are not fit for food with certain edible things. [Οἱ δὲ Λατῖνοι ἀλλαφόρως ἐσθίουσι πνικτά. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ Ἀ-δριανοπολῖται, ὡς ἀκούω, τοῖς αἵμασι τῶν ζώων χρῶνται μὴ ἐδωδίμων πνῶν.]

units.la: nimirum. Hoc in Adrianopolitanis non valde perstringit, sed duntaxat dicit, nescire se causam, ob quam hoc faciunt. Eadem igitur cum Latinis æquitate agant, non tanquam canonum violatores, impios castigent, condemnent. Hoc unum insatiabiliter cogitent, Christiano homini OMNIA LICERE, NON OMNIA ÆDIFICARE. In quo Apostolico axiomate, felici omine, desinam.
units.tr: Indeed. He does not greatly censure the Adrianopolitans on this point, but only says that he does not know the cause for which they do it. Therefore let them deal with them with the same fairness as with the Latins, and not punish and condemn them as impious violators of the canons. Let them keep this one thing constantly in mind: ALL THINGS ARE LAWFUL FOR A CHRISTIAN, BUT NOT ALL THINGS EDIFY. With this apostolic axiom, under a happy omen, I shall end.

units.la: Sanguis. De ejus esu quaestio est difficilis.2. 3. humani esus crudelis.3. non quaeri de abstinentia medica vel physica.5.6. sed de religiosa.6.7. status controversiae fingitur.7.8. Sententiarum divortia.8.9.10. &c. In statu integritatis & retro diluvium licitum fuisse esum ejus probatur.13.14.42. à tempore Noæ ad Mosen usque sanguinis prohibitionem merè ceremonialem fuisse probatur.44–60. & objectionibus occurritur.60–69. rationes prohibiti post diluvium sanguinis.51. &c. à Mose usque ad Christum esum sanguinis ceremoniali praecepto interdictum fuisse fusè probatur.70–80. & objectionibus satis fit.80–88. distinctio inter sanguinem animæ & membrorum elicitur.70. In N.T. esum sanguinis liberum esse, probatur 8. argumentis.88–113. Objectioni ex Act. 15:20.29. motæ fusè occurritur.113–230. inprimis,216. &c. de Ecclesiæ veteris circa quaestionem hanc sensu fusè disseritur.231–f.
units.tr: Blood. Its eating is a difficult question, 2, 3. Human eating of it is cruel, 3. The question is not about medical or physical abstinence, 5, 6, but about religious abstinence, 6, 7. The state of the controversy is set out, 7, 8. The divergent opinions, 8–10, etc. In the state of integrity and before the Flood, eating it is proved to have been lawful, 13, 14, 42. From the time of Noah to Moses, the prohibition of blood is proved to have been purely ceremonial, 44–60, and objections are met, 60–69. Reasons for the prohibition of blood after the Flood, 51, etc. From Moses to Christ, eating blood is shown at length to have been forbidden by a ceremonial precept, 70–80, and objections are answered sufficiently, 80–88. A distinction between the blood of the soul and the blood of the limbs is drawn, 70. In the New Testament, eating blood is proved to be free by eight arguments, 88–113. The objection raised from Acts 15:20, 29 is answered at length, 113–230, especially 216, etc. The sense of the early Church on this question is discussed at length, 231 ff.
